Exam A1: Elementary Structural Analysis

A1 Practice Paper 1

Problem 1 [A1-001] Reactions and free-body diagrams of determinate beams and frames

A steel footbridge girder over a ravine in Muskoka is modelled as a beam ABC. It has a pin support at A and a roller support at B, 8.0 m from A, and the girder overhangs 3.0 m beyond B to a free end C. The girder carries a uniformly distributed deck load of 12 kN/m on span AB only, a 25 kN point load acting downward 2.5 m from A, and a 40 kN downward point load at the free end C. A bracket bolted to the girder 6.0 m from A applies a pure clockwise couple of 30 kN·m. A wind-borne drift load applies a horizontal force of 18 kN at C, acting toward A. Treat the supports as frictionless and take the pin at A as the only horizontal restraint.

  1. (a) Describe the free-body diagram, then find the vertical reaction at B. [6]
  2. (b) Find the vertical reaction at A. [5]
  3. (c) Find the horizontal reaction at A, as a positive number if it acts toward C. [3]
  4. (d) Find the magnitude of the resultant reaction at A. [6]
(a)

Free body: the whole girder isolated, with Ax and Ay at A, By at B, the 12 kN/m load resultant of 96 kN acting 4.0 m from A, the 25 kN load at 2.5 m, the 40 kN load at 11.0 m, the 18 kN horizontal at C and the 30 kN·m clockwise couple (a couple has the same moment about any point). Take moments about A, counter-clockwise positive: By(8) - 96(4) - 25(2.5) - 40(11) - 30 = 0. The clockwise couple contributes -30. By = (384 + 62.5 + 440 + 30)/8 = 114.6 kN upward. The 18 kN horizontal acts along the girder axis, so it has no moment about A.

Answer: 114.6 kN

(b)

Vertical equilibrium of the free body: ΣFy = 0 gives Ay + By = 96 + 25 + 40 = 161 kN. Substituting By = 114.6 kN gives Ay = 161 - 114.6 = 46.4 kN upward. As a check, take moments about B: taking clockwise moments positive, 8Ay - 96(4) - 25(5.5) + 30 + 40(3) = 0 gives Ay = (384 + 137.5 - 30 - 120)/8 = 46.4 kN, which agrees. Both reactions are positive, so the girder does not lift off either support under this load case.

Answer: 46.4 kN

(c)

The roller at B offers no horizontal restraint, so the pin at A must resist the whole horizontal load. ΣFx = 0: the 18 kN force at C acts toward A, so Ax must act in the opposite direction, toward C, with Ax = 18.0 kN. Because the line of action lies along the girder axis, the force produces no additional moment about A or B and does not change the vertical reactions found in parts (a) and (b). The pin therefore carries horizontal load that the roller cannot share.

Answer: 18.0 kN

(d)

The resultant at A combines the vertical and horizontal components at the pin. R = √(Ax² + Ay²) = √(18.0² + 46.4²) = 49.8 kN. Its angle from the horizontal is atan(Ay/Ax) = 68.8°. The pin and its bearing plate must be checked for this resultant and not for the vertical component alone, which would be used only to size the anchor bolts. The result is dominated by the vertical component. The sign of the resultant is not needed for sizing the bearing, only its magnitude and direction.

Answer: 49.8 kN

Problem 2 [A1-002] Shear and bending moment diagrams for beams with point and distributed loads

A simply supported timber floor beam in a heritage mill conversion in Kitchener spans 10.0 m between a pin at A and a roller at B. It carries a triangularly distributed load that is zero at A and rises linearly to 15 kN/m at B, together with a single 30 kN point load acting downward 3.0 m from A. Ignore the self-weight of the beam. The engineer needs the shear and bending moment diagrams to check a proposed steel flitch plate reinforcement. The beam is fully braced against lateral buckling, and the flitch plate will be sized for the moment found, so the engineer wants both the location and the value of the extreme bending moment.

  1. (a) Find the reaction at A. [4]
  2. (b) Find the distance from A at which the shear force is zero. [5]
  3. (c) Find the maximum bending moment in the beam. [6]
  4. (d) Find the bending moment at midspan and state, with the numbers, whether the maximum moment occurs there. [5]
(a)

The triangular load has total W = ½(10)(15) = 75 kN, acting at 2L/3 = 6.667 m from A (the centroid of a triangle lies one third of the base from the large end). Moments about B: RA(10) - 75(10 - 6.667) - 30(7.0) = 0, so RA = (250.0 + 210.0)/10 = 46.00 kN. Then RB = 75 + 30 - RA = 59.00 kN. Check by moments about A: RB(10) = 75(6.667) + 30(3) = 590, giving RB = 59.0 kN, which agrees.

Answer: 46.00 kN

(b)

For x greater than 3 m the shear is V(x) = RA - 30 - 0.75x². The load intensity at x is 1.5x kN/m, so the load to the left of the section is the triangle area ½(x)(1.5x) = 0.75x². Setting V = 0 gives 0.75x² = 46.00 - 30, so x = 4.619 m from A. Shear starts positive at A, drops by 30 kN at the point load (to 9.25 kN, still positive) and then decreases smoothly through zero at this section, which is therefore where the bending moment is a maximum.

Answer: 4.619 m

(c)

Taking moments of the forces to the left of x = 4.619 m: M = RA x - 30(x - 3) - (0.75x²)(x/3), since the centroid of the triangular load to the left is x/3 from the section. M = 46.00(4.619) - 30(4.619 - 3) - 0.25(4.619)³ = 139.3 kN·m. This is the maximum because dM/dx = V changes sign from positive to negative here. This value governs the flexural stress check on the flitch plate. The peak value should be reported to the nearest tenth of a kilonewton-metre, and it is also the value used in the flexural stress calculation.

Answer: 139.3 kN·m

(d)

At midspan x = 5 m: M = RA(5) - 30(2) - 0.25(5)³ = 230.0 - 60 - 31.25 = 138.8 kN·m. The maximum of 139.3 kN·m is slightly larger and occurs 0.381 m from midspan, so the maximum does not occur exactly at midspan. The difference is only 0.4 percent, so a midspan check is close here, but it is unconservative and should not be used without confirming where V = 0. Checking more than one section is good practice whenever a distributed load is not uniform.

Answer: 138.8 kN·m

Problem 3 [A1-003] Member forces in determinate trusses by joints and sections

A roof truss over a rail maintenance shed near Sudbury has a bottom chord ABCD with joints at x = 0, 4, 8 and 12 m (y = 0) and top chord joints E, F, G at x = 2, 6 and 10 m, all at a height of 3.0 m above the bottom chord. The members are AB, BC, CD, EF, FG, AE, EB, BF, FC, CG and GD. The truss has a pin support at A and a roller support at D. Loads: 50 kN downward at B, 30 kN downward at C, 20 kN downward at F, and a wind force of 15 kN acting horizontally to the right at E. All joints are frictionless pins and member self-weight is ignored. Use positive for tension.

  1. (a) Find the vertical reaction at D. [3]
  2. (b) Using a vertical cut between joints F and C, find the force in member FG. [6]
  3. (c) Using the same cut, find the force in member FC. [5]
  4. (d) Using the same cut, find the force in member BC. [6]
(a)

Take the whole truss as the free body. ΣFx = 0: Ax + 15 = 0, so Ax = -15 kN (15 kN acting to the left at A). Moments about A, counter-clockwise positive: Dy(12) - 50(4) - 30(8) - 20(6) - 15(3) = 0. The wind force acts to the right at a height of 3 m above the supports, so its moment about A is clockwise, the same sense as the downward loads, and it increases Dy. Dy = (200 + 240 + 120 + 45)/12 = 50.42 kN upward. Then Ay = 100 - Dy = 49.58 kN, which a check of moments about D confirms.

Answer: 50.42 kN

(b)

Cut vertically between F and C (x = 7 m). The cut passes through FG, FC and BC only. Take the free body to the left. Moments about C (x = 8, y = 0) eliminate FC and BC. Counter-clockwise moments of the external forces about C: Ay(-8) + 50(4) + 20(2) - 15(3) = -201.67 kN·m (the 15 kN load at E, 3 m above C, is clockwise about C). A tensile force T in FG pulls the left body to the right at height 3 m and has a clockwise moment of 3T. Equilibrium: -201.67 - 3T = 0 so FG = -67.2 kN, negative, so FG is in compression.

Answer: -67.2 kN

(c)

Still using the left free body, sum vertical forces. The vertical component of FC is its force times 3/√13 = 0.832, since FC rises 3 m over a horizontal run of 2 m. With FC taken as tensile it pulls the left body toward C, that is downward and to the right. ΣFy: Ay - 50 - 20 - FC(0.832) = 0, so FC = (49.58 - 70)/0.832 = -24.5 kN. The negative sign means compression, consistent with a diagonal carrying shear downward toward the roller end.

Answer: -24.5 kN

(d)

Take moments about F (x = 6, y = 3), which eliminates FG and FC. For a tensile BC at height 3 m below F, the clockwise-to-counter-clockwise sign gives +3T counter-clockwise. The other terms: Ay(-6) = -6Ay, the horizontal reaction Ax of 15 kN to the left at A gives -45, the 50 kN load at B gives +100 (lever arm 2 m), and the loads at E and F give zero. So 3T - 6(49.58) - 45 + 100 = 0 and BC = (6Ay - 55)/3 = 80.8 kN tension. The same result comes from the full joint-by-joint matrix solution, which confirms the section method.

Answer: 80.8 kN

Problem 4 [A1-004] Three-hinged arches and cables

A parabolic three-hinged arch forms the main span of a pedestrian bridge in Ottawa. The supports A and B are at the same level and 24.0 m apart. The crown hinge C is at the midspan, 6.0 m above the supports, and the arch axis follows y = 4hx(L - x)/L², where x is measured from A. The deck delivers a uniformly distributed load of 20 kN/m to the left half of the span only (A to C), and a 60 kN downward point load acts on the right half, 18.0 m from A, from a maintenance vehicle parked at that location. Both supports are pinned hinges that can carry horizontal thrust, and self-weight is ignored.

  1. (a) Find the vertical reaction at B. [4]
  2. (b) Find the horizontal thrust at the supports. [6]
  3. (c) Find the bending moment in the arch rib at the section 6.0 m from A. [5]
  4. (d) Find the axial force in the rib at that section. [5]
(a)

There are four reaction components (Ay, By, and a horizontal reaction at each support), found from the three equations of equilibrium plus the zero-moment condition at the crown hinge. Moments about A for the whole arch: By(24) = 20(12)(6) + 60(18) = 1440 + 1080 = 2520, so By = 105.0 kN upward. The horizontal reactions at A and B are equal and opposite because there is no horizontal load. Then Ay = 20(12) + 60 - By = 195.0 kN. A check with moments about B gives Ay(24) = 20(12)(18) + 60(6) = 4680, so Ay = 195.0 kN, which confirms the result.

Answer: 105.0 kN

(b)

The bending moment at the crown hinge is zero. Taking the free body AC (left of the crown) and moments about C (x = 12 m, height 6 m): Ay(12) - 20(12)(6) - H(6) = 0. H = (195.0(12) - 1440)/6 = 150.0 kN. Using the right portion as a check: By(12) - 60(6) - H(6) = 0 gives H = (105.0(12) - 360)/6 = 150.0 kN. Both halves agree, so the thrust is 150.0 kN at each support, acting inward toward the span.

Answer: 150.0 kN

(c)

At x = 6 m the rib height is y = 4(6)(6)(18)/24² = 4.50 m. Take the left free body and moments about the section: M = Ay x - w x²/2 - H y = 195.0(6) - 20(36)/2 - 150.0(4.50) = 135.0 kN·m. The positive sign is sagging. For comparison the moment in a simply supported beam would be 1170 - 360 = 810 kN·m, so the thrust reduces the section moment by a large amount, which is the main economy of an arch over a beam.

Answer: 135.0 kN·m

(d)

The rib slope at the section is dy/dx = 4h(L - 2x)/L² = 0.500, so θ = 26.57°. The vertical shear on a beam of the same span at the section is V = Ay - 20(6) = 75.0 kN. Resolving the thrust and the shear along the tangent to the rib gives the axial force N = H cos θ + V sin θ = 150.0(0.8944) + 75.0(0.4472) = 167.7 kN, compressive. The radial shear in the rib at this section is H sin θ - V cos θ = 0.0 kN.

Answer: 167.7 kN

Problem 5 [A1-005] Axial force, shear and moment diagrams of determinate frames

A single-bay steel frame supports a conveyor gallery at a mine head frame in Timmins. Column AB is 5.0 m high with a pin support at A. Beam BC is 8.0 m long, horizontal, and joined rigidly to the column tops at B and at C. Column CD is 5.0 m high with a roller support at D that provides vertical restraint only. A horizontal wind-induced force of 18 kN acts to the right on column AB, 2.5 m above A. A uniformly distributed load of 20 kN/m acts downward over the full length of beam BC. Self-weight is ignored. Use sagging as positive in the beam.

  1. (a) Find the vertical reaction at D. [5]
  2. (b) Find the bending moment in the beam at joint B. [5]
  3. (c) Find the distance from B along the beam at which the beam shear is zero. [4]
  4. (d) Find the maximum sagging bending moment in beam BC. [6]
(a)

Free body of the whole frame. The roller at D gives only a vertical reaction Dy and the pin at A gives Ax and Ay. Moments about A (counter-clockwise positive): Dy(8) - 20(8)(4) - 18(2.5) = 0, since the UDL resultant of 160 kN acts at 4.0 m and the wind load is clockwise about A at a lever arm of 2.5 m. Dy = (640 + 45)/8 = 85.62 kN upward. Then ΣFy gives Ay = 160 - Dy = 74.38 kN, and ΣFx gives Ax = 18 kN acting to the left. The sum of the moments about D, with these values, is zero.

Answer: 85.62 kN

(b)

Cut the column just below joint B and take the free body AB. The forces on it are Ay at the base (vertical, passes through B's vertical line so zero moment), Ax = 18 kN to the left at the base, and the 18 kN wind force to the right at 2.5 m above A. The moment at B is the sum of the moments of these about B: the reaction Ax contributes 18(5) = 90 kN·m and the wind load contributes -18(2.5) = -45 kN·m with opposite sense, so the joint moment is 45.0 kN·m. The rigid joint transmits this same moment into the beam, with tension on the outer face of the column and sagging in the beam end.

Answer: 45.0 kN·m

(c)

Consider a section in the beam at distance x from B and the part of the frame to its left. The vertical shear transferred from the column is Ay = 74.38 kN (upward) and the UDL to the left of the section is 20x. Shear V(x) = 74.38 - 20x. Setting V = 0: x = 3.719 m from B. This is less than the 8 m beam length, so the shear changes sign inside the span and the moment is a maximum there. The column axial force at B is the vertical reaction Ay, and the beam axial force is zero, because the 18 kN wind force is balanced by Ax on the same free body.

Answer: 3.719 m

(d)

Beam moment at distance x from B: M(x) = 45.0 + 74.38x - 10x². At x = 3.719 m, M = 45.0 + 74.38(3.719) - 10(3.719)² = 183.3 kN·m sagging. At the far end C (x = 8 m) the moment is 0.0 kN·m, as required because the roller at D cannot provide a moment and column CD carries no horizontal load. That boundary check confirms the equilibrium and the sign convention used. The maximum sagging moment is the value used for the beam flexure check, and the joint moment found in part (b) is the hogging check for the connection.

Answer: 183.3 kN·m

A1 Practice Paper 2

Problem 1 [A1-006] Influence lines for reactions of beams

A two-lane highway overpass in Hamilton has a continuous deck idealised as a beam ABC with a pin at A, a roller at B, 10.0 m from A, and an overhang BC extending 4.0 m beyond B to a free end. Traffic loading on the structure consists of a single concentrated axle load of 90 kN that can be placed anywhere, together with a uniformly distributed lane load of 18 kN/m that can be applied over any length, in any position. The permanent load, including self-weight, is 6 kN/m over the whole length from A to C. The designer must size the hold-down bolts at A.

  1. (a) State the influence line ordinate for the reaction at B when a unit load is at C. [3]
  2. (b) Find the maximum downward reaction at B due to the traffic loading. [5]
  3. (c) Find the maximum upward reaction at A due to the traffic loading. [5]
  4. (d) Find the net reaction at A for the worst uplift combination of permanent load plus traffic load, and state whether hold-down is needed. [7]
(a)

Influence line for By: place a unit load at distance x from A and take moments about A: By(10) = 1(x), so By = x/10. This is a straight line from 0 at A, to 1.0 at B (x = 10 m), continuing to 1.40 at the free end C (x = 14 m). The ordinate exceeds 1.0 on the overhang because the beam acts as a lever pivoting about the pin at A, so a load on the overhang is magnified at B.

Answer: 1.40

(b)

The influence line for By is positive everywhere, so the maximum reaction loads the whole length with the lane load and puts the 90 kN axle at C where the ordinate is largest. Area under the line = ½(14)(1.4) = 9.8 m, so the distributed part is 18(9.8) = 176.4 kN, and the axle adds 90(1.4) = 126.0 kN. Maximum By = 302.4 kN. Loading the overhang as well is correct here because every ordinate is positive. The permanent load is not included in this part, which asks only for the traffic effect. Place the axle at the largest ordinate, which is at the free end.

Answer: 302.4 kN

(c)

The influence line for Ay is 1 - x/10, which equals 1.0 at A, zero at B and -0.4 at C. For maximum upward reaction at A, load only the positive portion from A to B, area = ½(10)(1.0) = 5.0 m, giving 18(5.0) = 90 kN from the lane load, and put the 90 kN axle at A with ordinate 1.0, adding 90 kN. Maximum Ay = 180.0 kN upward. The overhang is left unloaded because loading it would subtract from this reaction.

Answer: 180.0 kN

(d)

For the worst uplift at A, load only the overhang BC where the ordinate is negative. Area of the negative part = ½(4)(0.4) = 0.8 m, so the lane load gives -18(0.8) = -14.4 kN and the axle at C gives 90(-0.4) = -36.0 kN, a total live reaction of -50.4 kN. The permanent load acts over the whole beam: net area under the line is 5.0 - 0.8 = 4.2 m, so the permanent reaction is 6(4.2) = 25.2 kN upward. Net Ay = 25.2 - 50.4 = -25.2 kN. Because it is negative the support is pulled upward, so the hold-down bolts at A must resist 25.2 kN.

Answer: -25.2 kN

Problem 2 [A1-007] Influence lines for shear and moment in beams

A 16.0 m simply supported prestressed concrete girder at a rail grade separation in London, Ontario is checked at a section S located 6.0 m from the left support A. The live load is a single 120 kN concentrated load that can be placed anywhere on the girder, together with a uniformly distributed live load of 25 kN/m of any length and position. Sign convention: shear is positive when the left part of the girder tends to move upward relative to the right part, and moment is positive when it causes sagging. Treat the girder as a single span with no continuity, and carry all results to the nearest tenth of a kilonewton or kilonewton-metre.

  1. (a) Give the influence line ordinates for shear at S immediately to the right of S, and immediately to the left of S. [3]
  2. (b) Find the maximum positive shear at S. [6]
  3. (c) Find the maximum negative shear at S. [5]
  4. (d) Find the maximum bending moment at S. [6]
(a)

Place a unit load at x from A. If the load is to the right of S, the shear at S equals the left reaction, RA = (16 - x)/16, so just right of S the ordinate is (16 - 6)/16 = 0.625, decreasing linearly to zero at B. If the load is to the left of S, the shear at S equals RA - 1 = -x/16, so just left of S the ordinate is -6/16 = -0.375, falling from zero at A to -0.375 at S. The two branches are parallel and differ by 1.0 at S, the unit jump expected at the section. Part (a) answer: +0.625 just right of S and -0.375 just left of S.

Answer: +0.625 just right of S and -0.375 just left of S

(b)

Maximum positive shear: load only the region where the ordinates are positive, that is the portion SB. The area of the positive triangle is ½(10)(0.625) = 3.125 m, so the UDL gives 25(3.125) = 78.1 kN. The concentrated load goes at the peak ordinate just right of S: 120(0.625) = 75.0 kN. Maximum positive V = 153.1 kN. The load on SB is 25 kN/m over 10 m, and the load on AS is left unloaded since it would reduce the result.

Answer: 153.1 kN

(c)

Maximum negative shear: load only the negative region AS. Area = ½(6)(0.375) = 1.125 m, so the UDL contributes 25(1.125) = 28.125 kN of negative shear, and the point load placed just left of S adds 120(0.375) = 45.0 kN. Maximum negative V = -73.1 kN, about 48 percent of the positive extreme, because section S lies nearer the left support. The two extremes are not used together: they are alternative load arrangements. The maximum negative shear is smaller than the maximum positive shear because the section is closer to the left support.

Answer: -73.1 kN

(d)

The influence line for moment at S is a triangle with peak ab/L = 6(10)/16 = 3.750 m under S, zero at both supports. Its area is ½(L)(peak) = ½(16)(3.750) = 30.0 m². Load the full span with the UDL: 25(30.0) = 750.0 kN·m. Place the 120 kN load at S: 120(3.750) = 450.0 kN·m. Maximum M at S = 1200.0 kN·m. This is the section moment, not the absolute maximum, which occurs at midspan. Both the concentrated and distributed loads are applied in the same position as they affect the same influence line, so their effects add.

Answer: 1200.0 kN·m

Problem 3 [A1-008] Influence lines for truss member forces

A highway bridge in northern Ontario has two identical Pratt trusses, each of six panels of 4.0 m (span 24.0 m) and a constant height of 5.0 m. The bottom chord joints are L0 to L6, the top chord joints are U1 to U5 above L1 to L5, and L0 and L6 carry the pin and roller supports. Members are the bottom chord L0L1 to L5L6, top chord U1U2 to U4U5, end posts L0U1 and U5L6, verticals U1L1 to U5L5, and diagonals U1L2, U2L3, U4L3 and U5L4. Traffic load reaches each truss through stringers and floor beams at the bottom chord panel points only. The design live load per truss is a 30 kN/m lane load of any length, and one 80 kN axle load. Tension is positive.

  1. (a) Find the influence line ordinate for bottom chord member L2L3 with a unit load at L2. [3]
  2. (b) Find the maximum tension in L2L3 from the lane load and axle. [6]
  3. (c) Find the maximum tension in diagonal U2L3. [6]
  4. (d) Find the maximum compression in diagonal U2L3, as a positive number. [5]
(a)

The influence line is found by placing a unit load at each bottom chord panel point in turn and solving the truss; the check below uses a section. Cut through panel L2L3: the cut passes through U2U3, U2L3 and L2L3. The top chord and diagonal meet at U2 (x = 8 m, y = 5 m), so taking moments about U2 isolates L2L3. For a unit load at L2 (x = 8 m) the left reaction is 16/24 = 0.667, and with the unit load directly below U2 it has no moment about U2. Then F(5) = 0.667(8), so F = 1.067, positive, hence tension. The influence line ordinates at L1 to L5 are 0.533, 1.067, 0.800, 0.533, 0.267, linear between panel points.

Answer: 1.067

(b)

All ordinates of the influence line for L2L3 are positive, so the maximum tension loads every panel point: the area under the line is the sum of the trapezoids, which is 12.800 m. The lane load gives 30(12.800) = 384.0 kN. The 80 kN axle goes at the peak ordinate, 1.067 at L2, giving 80(1.067) = 85.3 kN. Maximum tension = 384.0 + 85.3 = 469.3 kN. The load is transmitted to the panel points through the floor system, so the line is straight between panel points.

Answer: 469.3 kN

(c)

The influence line for U2L3 has ordinates -0.213, -0.427, 0.640, 0.427, 0.213 at L1 to L5, changing sign inside panel L2L3 at x = 9.60 m, found by linear interpolation between the L2 and L3 ordinates. Maximum tension loads only the positive part: area = 4.610 m. The lane load gives 30(4.610) = 138.3 kN and the axle at L3, where the ordinate peaks at 0.640, gives 80(0.640) = 51.2 kN. Maximum tension = 189.5 kN. Only the part of the span to the right of 9.60 m is loaded, while the left of it is unloaded.

Answer: 189.5 kN

(d)

Maximum compression in U2L3 loads only the negative part of the influence line, from the left support to x = 9.60 m. Area of the negative part = 2.049 m, so the lane load gives 30(2.049) = 61.5 kN. The axle goes at L2 where the ordinate is -0.427, so 80(0.427) = 34.1 kN. Maximum compression = 95.6 kN. Since the diagonal reverses sign under moving load, it must be designed for both tension and compression, for example by a diagonal that can resist both.

Answer: 95.6 kN

Problem 4 [A1-009] Maximum shear and moment envelope under a moving wheel train

A 15.0 m simply supported steel bridge girder at an industrial crossing in Sarnia is traversed by a four-axle crane carriage. Axle loads and spacings, from the front axle backward in the direction of travel, are 80 kN, then 120 kN at 2.5 m behind the front axle, then 120 kN at 1.5 m behind that, and then 60 kN at 3.0 m behind that. The carriage can travel in either direction, and all four axles stay on the girder for the critical positions. Ignore self-weight and impact. Distances are measured from the 80 kN axle.

  1. (a) Find the total load and the distance of its line of action from the 80 kN axle. [3]
  2. (b) Find the maximum reaction at either support. [5]
  3. (c) Find the absolute maximum bending moment in the girder. [8]
  4. (d) Find the distance of the section of absolute maximum moment from the nearer support. [4]
(a)

Total load R = 80 + 120 + 120 + 60 = 380 kN. Taking moments of the axle loads about the front axle: R x̄ = 80(0) + 120(2.5) + 120(4.0) + 60(7.0) = 300 + 480 + 420 = 1200 kN·m, so x̄ = 1200/380 = 3.158 m behind the 80 kN axle. The resultant lies between the 120 kN axles, 0.658 m behind the first 120 kN axle and 0.842 m ahead of the second. This is the position used in the Barré theorem for the absolute maximum moment.

Answer: 3.158 m

(b)

The reaction at a support is largest when the heavy axles are as close to it as possible while all load stays on the girder. Place the 80 kN axle at support B, so the other axles are 2.5, 4.0 and 7.0 m back, at 12.5, 11.0 and 8.0 m from A. Then R_B = Σ P x/L = (80(15) + 120(12.5) + 120(11.0) + 60(8.0))/15 = 300.0 kN. Reversing the carriage, with the 60 kN axle at the support, gives a smaller value (283 kN), and removing any axle from the span reduces the sum. A scan of both directions in 0.0025 m steps confirms the maximum reaction 300.0 kN, which is also the maximum shear in the girder.

Answer: 300.0 kN

(c)

The absolute maximum moment occurs under one wheel when that wheel and the resultant of all loads sit equidistant from midspan (Barré). The wheel nearest the resultant is the first 120 kN axle, 0.658 m from the resultant, so place it 0.329 m from midspan on the side away from the resultant. With the 80 kN axle leading to the right, this axle is 7.829 m from A and the resultant is 7.171 m from A. Then R_A = 380(7.829)/15 = 198.3 kN and M = 198.3(7.829) - 120(1.5) - 60(4.5) = 1102.7 kN·m. A scan of every wheel at every position in both directions of travel gives the same maximum, 1102.7 kN·m, under axle number 2.

Answer: 1102.7 kN·m

(d)

At the critical position the section under the controlling axle is 7.829 m from A, so it lies 15 - 7.829 = 7.171 m from the nearer support B, and 0.329 m from midspan. This matches the Barré rule, which puts the wheel half the distance between itself and the resultant on one side of midspan: that offset is 0.329 m. The section of absolute maximum moment is therefore not at midspan but very close to it, and the girder must be checked there as well as at midspan.

Answer: 7.171 m

Problem 5 [A1-010] Beam deflection by double integration

A simply supported aluminum sign-gantry beam of span 6.0 m at a Highway 401 interchange has a constant flexural rigidity EI = 25 000 kN·m². The beam carries a snow-and-ice load that varies linearly from zero at the left support A to 40 kN/m at the right support B. Take x from A, with deflection positive downward, and neglect shear deformation and self-weight. The designer needs the elastic curve from the double integration method to check a serviceability limit of span/360. The load is acting downward on the full span, the supports are a pin at A and a roller at B, and the beam has no axial force. Work in kilonewtons and metres, and report the deflection in millimetres.

  1. (a) Find the support reaction at A. [3]
  2. (b) Find the slope at A. [5]
  3. (c) Find the distance from A to the section of maximum deflection. [5]
  4. (d) Find the maximum deflection and state whether the span/360 limit is met. [7]
(a)

The load intensity is w = 40x/6 kN/m. The total load is ½(6)(40) = 120 kN, acting at 2L/3 = 4.0 m from A. Moments about B: RA(6) = 120(2.0) gives RA = 40.0 kN. Check: RB = 120 - 40 = 80 kN, and moments about A give 80(6) = 120(4.0), which agrees. The reaction at A is the smaller because the load is concentrated toward B. The reaction at B is the remaining 80 kN, which can be used as a check on the moment equation later.

Answer: 40.0 kN

(b)

Bending moment at x from A: M(x) = RA x - (load to the left)(x/3) = 40x - (load to the left)(x/3), where the left load is ½(x)(40x/6) = 3.333x² acting x/3 from the section, so M = 40x - 1.111x³. With y positive downward the differential equation is EI y'' = -M. First integration: EI y' = -20x² + 0.2778x⁴ + C1. Second: EI y = -6.667x³ + 0.05556x⁵ + C1 x + C2. Conditions y(0) = 0 give C2 = 0, and y(6) = 0 gives C1 = 168.00 kN·m². Slope at A: y'(0) = C1/EI = 168.00/25 000 = 0.00672 rad, downward.

Answer: 0.00672 rad

(c)

The maximum deflection is where the slope is zero: -20x² + 0.2778x⁴ + 168.00 = 0. This is a quadratic in x², and the root inside the span gives x = 3.116 m from A. That is 0.519 of the span, beyond midspan (3.0 m), because the larger load near B pushes the largest deflection toward B. The known result for this loading is 0.5193L, which the number matches. The deflection is a maximum where the slope is zero, which occurs near but not at midspan.

Answer: 3.116 m

(d)

Deflection at x = 3.116 m: y = (-6.667x³ + 0.05556x⁵ + 168.00x)/EI. The numerator is 338.11 kN·m³. Dividing by EI = 25 000 kN·m² gives 0.01352 m = 13.5 mm downward. The span/360 limit is 6000/360 = 16.7 mm. Since 13.5 mm is less than 16.7 mm, the limit is met, with a margin of 19 percent, so the serviceability check passes for this load. Use the same elastic curve equation for the check and keep all lengths in metres until the final conversion.

Answer: 13.5 mm

A1 Practice Paper 3

Problem 1 [A1-011] Beam deflection by the moment-area method

A simply supported steel runway beam in a machine shop in Hamilton spans 6.0 m between a pin support at A and a roller support at B. A hoist trolley stops with its wheel group producing a single downward point load of 40 kN acting 2.0 m from A. The beam has E = 200 GPa and a constant second moment of area I = 3.0 × 10⁻⁴ m⁴, so EI = 60 000 kN·m². Self-weight is negligible and no horizontal load acts. The plant engineer wants the elastic curve found with the moment-area theorems, using the bending moment diagram divided by EI and measuring tangent deviations from the tangent drawn at support A. Standard deflection tables may be used only as a check, not as the method.

  1. (a) Find the vertical reaction at A and the maximum bending moment. [3]
  2. (b) Find the slope of the elastic curve at A, in milliradians. [5]
  3. (c) Find the vertical deflection under the load, in millimetres. [6]
  4. (d) Find the vertical deflection at midspan, in millimetres. [6]
(a)

Take moments about B for the whole beam. The supports carry vertical reaction only because there is no horizontal load. Ay × 6.0 = 40 × (6.0 - 2.0), so Ay = 40 × 4.0 / 6.0 = 26.67 kN upward. Vertical equilibrium gives By = 40 - 26.67 = 13.33 kN. The bending moment grows linearly from A to the load, so the maximum occurs under the load and equals Ay × 2.0 = 26.67 × 2.0 = 53.33 kN·m, sagging. This value fixes the M/EI diagram used in every later part: a triangle rising from zero at A to 53.33/EI under the load and falling back to zero at B.

Answer: 26.67 kN; Mmax = 53.33 kN·m

(b)

The first moment-area theorem gives slope change from the area of the M/EI diagram, and the second gives the tangent deviation of B from the tangent at A as the moment of that area about B. The whole triangle has area ½ × 6.0 × 53.33 = 160.0 kN·m² (divided by EI). Its apex is 2.0 m from A, so the centroid lies (0 + 2.0 + 6.0)/3 = 2.667 m from A, which is 3.333 m from B. Then tBA = 160.0 × 3.333 / EI = 533.3 / EI. B does not deflect, so the tangent at A has slope θA = tBA / L = 533.3 / (6.0 × 60 000) = 1.481 × 10⁻³ rad, or 1.481 mrad, clockwise (the beam dips downward moving away from A).

Answer: 1.481 mrad

(c)

Call the point under the load C, 2.0 m from A. The tangent drawn at A lies above the beam at C by θA × 2.0 = 1.481 × 10⁻³ × 2.0 = 2.963 × 10⁻³ m. The beam lies below that tangent by the tangent deviation tCA, the moment about C of the M/EI area between A and C. That area is a triangle ½ × 2.0 × 53.33 = 53.33 kN·m² with its centroid 2.0/3 = 0.667 m from C, so tCA = 53.33 × 0.667 / 60 000 = 0.593 × 10⁻³ m. The deflection is 2.963 - 0.593 = 2.370 mm downward. Check: Pa²b²/(3EIL) = 40 × 4 × 16 / (3 × 60 000 × 6.0) = 2.370 mm, so the two methods agree.

Answer: 2.370 mm

(d)

Midspan is point D, 3.0 m from A, where M = 26.67 × 3.0 - 40 × 1.0 = 40.0 kN·m. The tangent at A is above the beam at D by θA × 3.0 = 4.444 mm. The tangent deviation tDA is the moment about D of the M/EI area from A to D, split into three pieces. The triangle from A to the load has area 53.33 and its centroid is 1.667 m from D, giving 88.89. The rectangle of height 40.0 and width 1.0 m has centroid 0.5 m from D, giving 20.0. The small triangle of height 13.33 and width 1.0 m has area 6.667 and centroid 0.667 m from D, giving 4.444. The total is 113.33 / 60 000 = 1.889 mm, so ΔD = 4.444 - 1.889 = 2.556 mm. This exceeds the deflection under the load because the load is off centre and the maximum deflection falls nearer midspan.

Answer: 2.556 mm

Problem 2 [A1-012] Beam deflection by the conjugate beam method

A steel girder in an ore-handling yard at Thunder Bay is supported by a pin at A and a roller at B, 6.0 m from A, and it overhangs 2.0 m beyond B to a free end C. A hanging conveyor idler applies a downward load of 30 kN at C. Self-weight is neglected and EI = 45 000 kN·m² is constant along the full length of 8.0 m. The deflections must be found with the conjugate beam method: draw the real bending moment diagram, load a conjugate beam with M/EI, choose conjugate supports so that conjugate shear equals real slope and conjugate moment equals real deflection, and then use statics. Take sagging moments as positive and report the sense of each rotation.

  1. (a) Find the reaction at B on the real girder. [3]
  2. (b) Find the slope at A using the conjugate beam, in milliradians. [5]
  3. (c) Find the slope at B, in milliradians. [5]
  4. (d) Find the vertical deflection at the free end C, in millimetres. [7]
(a)

Take moments about A for the real girder. The 30 kN load acts 8.0 m from A and the roller reaction By acts 6.0 m from A, so By × 6.0 = 30 × 8.0 and By = 40.0 kN upward. Vertical equilibrium gives Ay = 30 - 40 = -10 kN, so the pin at A pulls downward with 10 kN and the girder tends to lift off it. The bending moment at B is -30 × 2.0 = -60 kN·m, hogging, and between A and B it varies linearly as M = -10x. The moment is zero at A and at C. This hogging diagram, divided by EI, is the load on the conjugate beam.

Answer: 40.0 kN

(b)

Choose the conjugate supports. A real end pin becomes a conjugate end roller, a real interior support becomes an internal hinge, and a real free end becomes a conjugate fixed support. So the conjugate beam is a roller at A, a hinge at B and a fixed end at C. The load on AB is a triangle of M/EI, zero at A and 60/EI at B; because the moment is hogging it acts upward and has area ½ × 6.0 × 60 = 180/EI, centroid 4.0 m from A. A hinge carries no moment, so for segment AB take moments about B: V_A × 6.0 = 180 × 2.0 and V_A = 60/EI, acting downward. Then θA = 60/45 000 = 1.333 × 10⁻³ rad, 1.333 mrad, anticlockwise (the span hogs upward).

Answer: 1.333 mrad anticlockwise

(c)

The shear in the conjugate beam at B equals the real slope there, and a hinge transmits shear. Just left of B the conjugate shear is the 180/EI upward load minus the 60/EI downward reaction at A, so 120/EI upward net. Therefore θB = 120/45 000 = 2.667 × 10⁻³ rad, or 2.667 mrad, clockwise, because the overhang tips down. Check with the first moment-area theorem: θB - θA = area of M/EI between A and B = -180/EI, so θB = +1.333 - 4.000 = -2.667 mrad, with anticlockwise positive. The result matches and confirms that the roller at B is rotating downward toward the loaded end.

Answer: 2.667 mrad clockwise

(d)

The real deflection at C equals the bending moment at the conjugate fixed support C. Collect the conjugate loads to the left of C. Segment BC carries a triangle of M/EI with peak 60/EI at B and zero at C; its area is ½ × 2.0 × 60 = 60/EI acting upward, with centroid 1.333 m from C. The shear arriving from the hinge is 120/EI upward and acts 2.0 m from C. The moment at C is 120 × 2.0 + 60 × 1.333 = 240 + 80 = 320/EI. So ΔC = 320/45 000 = 7.11 × 10⁻³ m, or 7.11 mm downward. Check: θB × 2.0 + PL³/(3EI) for the overhang = 5.333 + 1.778 = 7.111 mm, in agreement.

Answer: 7.11 mm downward

Problem 3 [A1-013] Truss deflection by virtual work (unit load)

A small roof truss over a mechanical penthouse in a Sudbury arena is pinned at A and carried on a roller at C. Joints A, B and C lie on a horizontal bottom chord with AB = BC = 4.0 m. Joint D is the apex, 3.0 m directly above B, and the rafters AD and DC run from D to the supports. A vertical hanger BD joins B to D. An air-handling unit hangs from joint B and applies a downward load of 60 kN. Chord members AB and BC have area 2000 mm², the rafters have area 3000 mm², and the hanger has area 1500 mm². All members have E = 200 GPa and all joints are frictionless pins. Use the unit-load method of virtual work, with tension positive.

  1. (a) Find the axial force in rafter AD. [4]
  2. (b) Find the axial force in chord AB. [3]
  3. (c) Find the vertical deflection of joint B, in millimetres. [8]
  4. (d) Find the horizontal movement of the roller at C, in millimetres. [5]
(a)

The load sits at joint B on the line of symmetry, so each support takes half: Ay = Cy = 30 kN. The rafter AD rises at slope 3 over 4 horizontally and has length 5.0 m, so its vertical component is 3/5 of its force. At joint A the 30 kN upward reaction must be balanced vertically by the rafter alone, because chord AB is horizontal. The rafter pushes down on the joint, so it is in compression, and 0.6 × F = 30 gives F = 50.0 kN. Hence the force in AD is -50.0 kN, compression. The member DC carries the same force by symmetry. Joint D then checks: two rafters push up 30 kN each, and the hanger pulls down 60 kN, so the apex is in balance.

Answer: -50.0 kN

(b)

At joint A the rafter in compression pushes the joint outward toward the left along its axis, with horizontal component 0.8 × 50.0 = 40.0 kN. The pin at A has no horizontal load, since no horizontal force acts on the truss, so chord AB must pull the joint to the right with 40.0 kN. A member that pulls on a joint is in tension, so AB = +40.0 kN. Symmetry gives BC = +40.0 kN as well. The hanger BD carries the hung load directly: joint B has the two collinear chords and one vertical member, so the vertical balance 60 - F_BD = 0 gives BD = +60.0 kN tension. These real forces F are used in the virtual work sum.

Answer: +40.0 kN (tension)

(c)

Apply a virtual unit load downward at B. By symmetry the reactions are 0.5 each. The unit-load forces are f_AD = f_DC = -0.5/0.6 = -0.8333, f_AB = f_BC = +0.6667 and f_BD = +1.0. Then ΔB = Σ F f L/(AE), with AE = 400 000 kN for the chords, 600 000 kN for the rafters and 300 000 kN for the hanger. Each chord gives 40 × 0.6667 × 4.0 / 400 000 = 0.2667 mm, so the two give 0.5333 mm. Each rafter gives (-50)(-0.8333)(5.0) / 600 000 = 0.3472 mm, so the two give 0.6944 mm. The hanger gives 60 × 1.0 × 3.0 / 300 000 = 0.6000 mm. Sum: ΔB = 1.828 mm downward, positive because the real and virtual work agree in sign.

Answer: 1.83 mm downward

(d)

Apply a virtual horizontal unit load at C directed away from A. The pin at A supplies the horizontal balance, and no vertical reaction arises. Joint C then has the horizontal chord BC and the inclined rafter DC; because there is no vertical force, the rafter force is zero, and BC carries f = +1.0. At joint B the chord AB continues the same force, f_AB = +1.0, and the hanger and rafters have f = 0. So only the two chords contribute: ΔC = (40 × 1.0 × 4.0 / 400 000) × 2 = 0.400 × 2 = 0.800 mm. The result is positive, so C moves 0.800 mm away from A, which is simply the total elongation of the bottom chord, the sum of FL/AE for AB and BC.

Answer: 0.800 mm away from A

Problem 4 [A1-014] Beam and frame deflection by virtual work

A steel bracket frame carries the head pulley of a conveyor in a plant in Windsor. The frame is L-shaped: a vertical column 4.0 m high is fixed at its base, and a horizontal arm projects 3.0 m from the top of the column as a cantilever. A single downward load of 20 kN acts at the free end of the arm. The arm has flexural rigidity EI = 16 000 kN·m² and the column has EI = 24 000 kN·m². Axial and shear deformations are ignored and self-weight is neglected. Use the principle of virtual work with real and virtual bending moment diagrams, taking the integral over the arm and the column separately, to find the movement of the free end.

  1. (a) Find the vertical deflection of the free end, in millimetres. [6]
  2. (b) Find the horizontal deflection of the free end, in millimetres. [5]
  3. (c) Find the rotation of the free end, in milliradians. [5]
  4. (d) State the percentage of the vertical deflection that comes from bending of the column. [4]
(a)

Measure x from the free end along the arm. The real bending moment in the arm is M = 20x, which grows from zero at the tip to 60 kN·m at the column, and in the column it is constant at 20 × 3.0 = 60 kN·m. A virtual unit downward load at the tip gives m = x in the arm and m = 3.0 in the column. Then Δv = ∫M m dx / EI. Arm: 20 ∫0 to 3 of x² dx = 20 × 9 = 180, divided by 16 000 gives 11.25 mm. Column: 60 × 3.0 × 4.0 = 720, divided by 24 000 gives 30.00 mm. The total is 41.25 mm downward. Both terms are positive because the real and virtual moments have the same sense everywhere.

Answer: 41.25 mm

(b)

Apply a virtual horizontal unit load at the tip, acting to the right. It acts along the axis of the arm, so it produces no virtual moment in the arm, m = 0 there. In the column, at distance s below the arm level, the lever arm is s, so m = s. The real moment is still 60 kN·m in the column. Then Δh = (1/EI_column) ∫0 to 4 of 60 s ds = 60 × (4.0²/2) / 24 000 = 60 × 8.0 / 24 000 = 480 / 24 000 = 0.0200 m, or 20.0 mm. The sign is positive, which means the free end moves to the right, away from the column, in the sense of the virtual load, because the arm load turns the frame clockwise.

Answer: 20.0 mm to the right

(c)

Apply a virtual unit couple at the tip. A couple has the same moment everywhere, so m = 1 in the arm and in the column. The rotation is θ = Σ ∫ M m dx / EI. Arm: 20 ∫0 to 3 of x dx = 20 × 4.5 = 90, divided by 16 000 gives 5.625 × 10⁻³ rad. Column: 60 × 1 × 4.0 = 240, divided by 24 000 gives 10.000 × 10⁻³ rad. The sum is 15.625 × 10⁻³ rad, which is 15.63 mrad clockwise, in the same sense as the load moment about the column. The column contributes more than the arm even though it is stiffer, because its moment is large over its whole 4.0 m.

Answer: 15.63 mrad clockwise

(d)

The column's share of the vertical deflection is its virtual work term divided by the total: 30.00 / 41.25 = 0.7273, or 72.7 percent. The arm contributes the remaining 27.3 percent, 11.25 mm. The column dominates because the whole 60 kN·m moment acts on it for 4.0 m and because the rotation of the column top is multiplied by the 3.0 m lever arm of the arm. Design meaning: stiffening the column would be more effective than stiffening the arm. For example, raising the column EI by 50 percent to 36 000 kN·m² would cut the column term from 30.0 to 20.0 mm, a larger saving than any realistic change to the arm.

Answer: 72.7 %

Problem 5 [A1-015] Deflection by strain energy and Castigliano's theorem

A reinforced-concrete canopy beam projecting from the entrance of a school in Kingston is idealized as a cantilever 3.0 m long, fixed at the wall. It carries a uniformly distributed load of 8 kN/m over its full length from snow and self-weight, and a point load of 12 kN from a lighting post located 2.0 m from the wall, which is 1.0 m from the free tip. The flexural rigidity is EI = 12 000 kN·m² along the whole beam, and shear and axial energy are neglected. Use Castigliano's second theorem with a fictitious load or couple at the tip, writing the moment as a function of x measured from the free end.

  1. (a) Find the bending moment at the fixed support. [3]
  2. (b) Find the vertical deflection of the tip, in millimetres. [7]
  3. (c) Find the rotation of the tip, in milliradians. [5]
  4. (d) Find the total bending strain energy stored in the beam, in joules. [5]
(a)

Take the free-body of the whole cantilever. The distributed load has resultant 8 × 3.0 = 24 kN acting at the midpoint, 1.5 m from the wall, giving 24 × 1.5 = 36.0 kN·m. The post load of 12 kN acts 2.0 m from the wall, giving 12 × 2.0 = 24.0 kN·m. The moment at the support is the sum, 36.0 + 24.0 = 60.0 kN·m, hogging, with tension on the top face. The vertical reaction is 24 + 12 = 36 kN. This also matches M at x = 3.0 m in the expression used below, which is w x²/2 + P (x - 1) = 36 + 24 = 60 kN·m.

Answer: 60.0 kN·m

(b)

Add a fictitious downward load Q at the tip. With x from the free end, M = Qx + 4x² for 0 ≤ x ≤ 1.0 and M = Qx + 4x² + 12(x - 1) for 1.0 ≤ x ≤ 3.0, so ∂M/∂Q = x. Castigliano gives δ = (1/EI) ∫ M (∂M/∂Q) dx with Q set to zero. The UDL part is ∫0 to 3 of 4x² × x dx = 4 × 81/4 = 81. The post part is 12 ∫1 to 3 of (x - 1) x dx = 12 × [(27 - 1)/3 - (9 - 1)/2] = 12 × 4.667 = 56.0. Total 137, so δ = 137 / 12 000 = 0.01142 m = 11.42 mm downward. Both integrals are positive because the loads and the fictitious Q act in the same direction.

Answer: 11.42 mm

(c)

Add a fictitious couple C at the tip, so M = C + 4x² + 12(x - 1) over the loaded portion and ∂M/∂C = 1 (the sense is chosen so that it adds to the moment from the loads). The rotation is θ = (1/EI) ∫ M (∂M/∂C) dx with C = 0. The UDL part is ∫0 to 3 of 4x² dx = 4 × 9 = 36. The post part is 12 ∫1 to 3 of (x - 1) dx = 12 × 2.0 = 24. The sum is 60, and θ = 60 / 12 000 = 5.0 × 10⁻³ rad = 5.00 mrad, the tip turning downward. Because ∂M/∂C is the constant 1, the rotation equals the area of the M/EI diagram, which is the first moment-area theorem and confirms the result.

Answer: 5.00 mrad

(d)

The bending strain energy is U = ∫ M² dx / (2EI) with M = 4x² for 0 to 1 m and 4x² + 12(x - 1) beyond. Over the full length, expanding M² on the loaded portion gives three terms. The square of the UDL moment, 16 x⁴ integrated from 0 to 3, is 777.6. The cross term, 96 x²(x - 1) integrated from 1 to 3, is 1088.0. The square of the post term, 144 (x - 1)² integrated from 1 to 3, is 384.0. The total is 2249.6, and U = 2249.6 / (2 × 12 000) = 0.09373 kN·m = 93.7 J. The cross term shows that the energy of the combined loading is more than the sum of the energies of each load applied alone, so superposition does not apply to strain energy.

Answer: 93.7 J

A1 Practice Paper 4

Problem 1 [A1-016] Force method for one-degree indeterminate beams

A steel lintel beam over a loading-dock opening in a warehouse in Brampton is built into a masonry pier at A, which may be treated as a perfectly fixed support, and rests on a roller bearing on a steel column at B, 7.0 m from A. A single downward load of 70 kN from a hoist rail acts 3.0 m from A. The flexural rigidity is EI = 60 000 kN·m² and is constant. Use the force (flexibility) method with the vertical reaction at B as the redundant, using a cantilever as the released structure. Self-weight is ignored. A site survey later finds that the column at B has settled 8.0 mm, and the designer must see how the settlement changes the force in the column.

  1. (a) Find the reaction at B. [6]
  2. (b) Find the fixed-end moment at A. [4]
  3. (c) Find the sagging bending moment under the load. [4]
  4. (d) Find the reaction at B after the 8.0 mm settlement of the column. [6]
(a)

Release the redundant by removing the support at B, leaving a cantilever fixed at A. The 70 kN load at a = 3.0 m produces a tip deflection at B of Δ_P = P a² (3L - a) / (6EI) = 70 × 9.0 × (21 - 3) / (6EI) = 1890 / EI, downward. A unit upward force at B gives the flexibility coefficient f_BB = L³ / (3EI) = 343 / (3EI) = 114.33 / EI. Compatibility requires zero net deflection at B: Δ_P - R_B f_BB = 0, so R_B = 1890 / 114.33 = 16.53 kN upward. The value is small compared with the 70 kN load because the load sits near the stiff fixed end, where the beam resists deflection on its own.

Answer: 16.53 kN

(b)

With R_B known, use statics on the whole beam. Taking moments about A, the fixed-end moment resists the net of the load moment and the reaction moment: M_A = P a - R_B L = 70 × 3.0 - 16.53 × 7.0 = 210.0 - 115.71 = 94.29 kN·m. The sign is hogging, with tension on the top face at the pier. Vertical equilibrium gives R_A = 70 - 16.53 = 53.47 kN upward. As a check, a propped cantilever carrying a mid-region point load should have a fixed-end moment smaller than the 210 kN·m of an unpropped cantilever, and 94.29 is indeed much smaller, which shows the prop is carrying useful load.

Answer: 94.29 kN·m

(c)

Under the load, at 3.0 m from A, the section moment can be found from the right side: M = R_B × (7.0 - 3.0) = 16.53 × 4.0 = 66.12 kN·m, sagging. The check from the left side is R_A × 3.0 - M_A = 53.47 × 3.0 - 94.29 = 160.41 - 94.29 = 66.12 kN·m, which agrees. The bending moment diagram therefore has a hogging peak of 94.29 kN·m at the pier and a sagging peak of 66.12 kN·m under the load, and the hogging peak governs the design of the section. The moment changes sign between A and the load, at a point where the sloping line crosses zero.

Answer: 66.12 kN·m

(d)

When the support settles by δ = 8.0 mm = 0.0080 m, the compatibility condition becomes Δ_P - R_B f_BB = δ, because the cantilever tip must now end up 8.0 mm lower than the level of the original support. Convert to numbers: Δ_P = 1890 / 60 000 = 0.03150 m and f_BB = 114.33 / 60 000 = 0.0019056 m/kN. Then R_B = (0.03150 - 0.00800) / 0.0019056 = 12.33 kN. The column force falls by 4.20 kN, and the fixed-end moment at A rises to 210.0 - 12.33 × 7.0 = 123.7 kN·m. Settlement relieves the sagging support and loads the rigid pier more, which is why settlement matters in indeterminate structures.

Answer: 12.33 kN

Problem 2 [A1-017] Force method for indeterminate trusses

A rectangular bracing panel on a steel loading platform in Oshawa is 4.0 m wide and 3.0 m high. Its joints are A at the bottom left, B at the bottom right, C at the top right and D at the top left. The perimeter members AB, BC, CD and DA each have area 2400 mm², and two diagonals AC and BD cross without being connected to each other, each with area 1600 mm². E = 200 GPa throughout. Joint A is a pin and joint B is a roller on a horizontal surface. A wind load of 40 kN acts horizontally to the right at D and a 30 kN load acts downward at C. The truss is one degree indeterminate. Take diagonal BD as the redundant, with tension positive, and use the force method.

  1. (a) With BD removed, find the force in diagonal AC. [4]
  2. (b) Find the force in the redundant diagonal BD. [6]
  3. (c) Find the final force in member AB. [5]
  4. (d) Find the final force in diagonal AC. [5]
(a)

Remove diagonal BD to leave a determinate truss. Moments about A for the whole truss: By × 4.0 = 30 × 4.0 + 40 × 3.0, so By = 60.0 kN upward, Ax = 40 kN to the left and Ay = -30 kN, a downward pull. Joint D has only DA (vertical) and CD (horizontal) once BD is gone, so DA = 0 and CD = -40 kN, compression. Joint B has only AB (horizontal) and BC (vertical): AB = 0 and BC = -60 kN, compression. At joint C, horizontal balance gives 40 - 0.8 F_AC = 0 and F_AC = +50.0 kN, tension. The vertical balance 60 - 30 - 0.6 × 50 = 0 confirms it.

Answer: +50.0 kN

(b)

Apply a unit tension pair in BD to the released truss. The resulting forces f1 are AB = -0.8, BC = -0.6, CD = -0.8, DA = -0.6, AC = +1.0 and BD = +1.0. The compatibility equation says the relative movement of the cut ends of BD is zero, so X = -Σ F0 f1 L/A ÷ Σ f1² L/A, with E cancelling. The numerator terms (in kN per m²) are AC: 50 × 1.0 × 5.0 / 0.0016 = 156 250; BC: (-60)(-0.6)(3.0) / 0.0024 = 45 000; CD: (-40)(-0.8)(4.0) / 0.0024 = 53 333; sum 254 583. The denominator is 2 × (0.64 × 4.0 + 0.36 × 3.0) / 0.0024 + 2 × 5.0 / 0.0016 = 9283. So X = -254 583 / 9283 = -27.42 kN, which is compression.

Answer: -27.42 kN

(c)

The final force in each member is F = F0 + X f1. For AB the released-structure force F0 is zero because joint B has no horizontal load, and f1 = -0.8. Thus F_AB = 0 + (-27.42)(-0.8) = +21.94 kN, tension. The negative redundant force and the negative unit force multiply to a positive result, so the bottom chord is put into tension by the compressed diagonal. Check at joint B: the roller carries only vertical force, so the horizontal components must balance, and the 21.94 kN tension in AB pulls the joint left while the compressive BD pushes it to the right with 0.8 × 27.42 = 21.94 kN, a perfect balance.

Answer: +21.94 kN

(d)

Superpose again for diagonal AC: F_AC = F0 + X f1 = 50.0 + (-27.42)(1.0) = 22.58 kN, tension. The statically determinate analysis overestimated this member by more than a factor of two, because the second diagonal shares the shear in the panel. The other final forces are BC = -60 + (-27.42)(-0.6) = -43.55 kN, CD = -40 + 21.94 = -18.06 kN, DA = +16.45 kN and BD = -27.42 kN. Joint C is a check: the compressed top chord CD pushes the joint right with 18.06 kN while AC pulls it left with 0.8 × 22.58 = 18.06 kN, so the horizontal forces balance. Both diagonals work, which is consistent with a cross-braced panel that resists wind from either direction.

Answer: +22.58 kN

Problem 3 [A1-018] Slope-deflection method for continuous beams

A two-span steel girder carries a service road over a creek near London, Ontario. Span AB is 6.0 m and carries a uniformly distributed load of 20 kN/m. Span BC is 5.0 m and carries a single 50 kN point load at midspan. The girder is fixed into the abutment at A, rests on a roller at the pier B and on a simple roller support at the far end C. The flexural rigidity is constant at EI = 48 000 kN·m². Use the slope-deflection method with counterclockwise moments and rotations positive. Support B does not settle. Eliminate the rotation at the simply supported end C by using the modified equation for a member with a pin at the far end.

  1. (a) Find the rotation of joint B, in milliradians. [5]
  2. (b) Find the end moment M_AB at the fixed support. [4]
  3. (c) Find the end moment M_BA on span AB at the pier. [5]
  4. (d) Find the vertical reaction at C. [6]
(a)

Fixed-end moments, counterclockwise positive: for span AB, wL²/12 = 20 × 36 / 12 = 60, so FEM_AB = +60 and FEM_BA = -60; for span BC, PL/8 = 50 × 5.0 / 8 = 31.25, so FEM_BC = +31.25 and FEM_CB = -31.25. Since A is fixed, θA = 0. Because C has zero end moment, M_BC = (3EI/L)θB + FEM_BC - ½ FEM_CB = 0.6 EI θB + 31.25 + 15.625 = 0.6 EI θB + 46.875. Also M_BA = (2EI/6)(2θB) - 60 = 0.6667 EI θB - 60. Joint B requires M_BA + M_BC = 0, so 1.2667 EI θB = 13.125 and EI θB = 10.36 kN·m². Then θB = 10.36 / 48 000 = 0.2159 × 10⁻³ rad, which is anticlockwise.

Answer: 0.2159 mrad

(b)

The slope-deflection equation at the fixed end is M_AB = (2EI/L)(2θA + θB) + FEM_AB, with θA = 0 and L = 6.0 m: M_AB = (2EI/6) θB + 60 = 0.3333 × 10.36 + 60 = 3.454 + 60 = 63.45 kN·m. The positive sign means the moment acts anticlockwise on the left end of the member, which is a hogging moment at the abutment, tension in the top flange. It is only slightly larger than the fixed-end moment of 60 kN·m, because joint B rotates only a little and so the span behaves almost as a fully fixed-fixed beam at the abutment end.

Answer: 63.45 kN·m

(c)

At the pier end of span AB the equation is M_BA = (2EI/6)(2θB + θA) + FEM_BA = 0.6667 × 10.36 - 60 = 6.908 - 60 = -53.09 kN·m. The negative sign means a clockwise moment on the right end of the member, which is again hogging at the support. Equilibrium of joint B is checked by M_BC = 0.6 × 10.36 + 46.875 = 53.09 kN·m, which is equal and opposite to M_BA, so the sum is zero as required. The hogging moment at B is 53.09 kN·m and governs the top flange design at the pier.

Answer: -53.09 kN·m

(d)

Take span BC as a free body and use moments about B, anticlockwise positive. The end moment at B is +53.09 and there is no moment at C. The roller reaction at C acts upward 5.0 m from B and gives +5.0 R_C. The 50 kN load acts downward 2.5 m from B and gives -125. So 5.0 R_C - 125 + 53.09 = 0 and R_C = (125 - 53.09) / 5.0 = 14.38 kN upward. For comparison a simply supported span would have 25 kN at each end, so the fixity at B moves load from C to the pier: the reaction at B on this span is 50 - 14.38 = 35.62 kN.

Answer: 14.38 kN

Problem 4 [A1-019] Slope-deflection method with support settlement

A two-span steel girder carries a pedestrian link in a hospital in Ottawa. Span AB is 6.0 m and carries a uniformly distributed load of 15 kN/m. Span BC is 4.0 m and carries no load. Joint A is a pin that cannot carry moment, joint B is an interior roller on a pier, and joint C is fixed into a concrete core wall. The flexural rigidity is constant, EI = 36 000 kN·m². The pier at B settles 6.0 mm below its original level. Use the slope-deflection method with counterclockwise moments, rotations and chord rotations positive, and with the end moment at A equal to zero.

  1. (a) Find the rotation of joint B, in milliradians. [6]
  2. (b) Find the end moment M_BA on span AB. [4]
  3. (c) Find the end moment M_CB at the fixed support C. [4]
  4. (d) Find the vertical reaction at A. [6]
(a)

The settlement of B rotates chord AB clockwise, ψ_AB = -0.006 / 6.0 = -0.00100 rad, and rotates chord BC anticlockwise, ψ_BC = +0.006 / 4.0 = +0.00150 rad. With θC = 0, the stiffness factors are 2EI/6 = 12 000 and 2EI/4 = 18 000 kN·m. FEM_AB = +45 and FEM_BA = -45. M_AB = 12 000 (2θA + θB + 0.003) + 45 = 0 gives 24 000 θA + 12 000 θB = -81. Joint B needs M_BA + M_BC = 0, giving 12 000 θA + 60 000 θB = 90. Eliminating θA gives 54 000 θB = 130.5, so θB = 2.417 × 10⁻³ rad anticlockwise. Then θA = -4.583 × 10⁻³ rad.

Answer: 2.417 mrad

(b)

Substitute into the equation for the pier end of span AB: M_BA = 12 000 (2θB + θA - 3ψ_AB) - 45 = 12 000 (0.004833 - 0.004583 + 0.003) - 45 = 12 000 × 0.003250 - 45 = 39.0 - 45 = -6.0 kN·m. The hogging moment at B is only 6.0 kN·m, far smaller than the 45 kN·m fixed-end value, because the sinking pier has relieved the support. The check is M_BC = 18 000 (2θB - 3ψ_BC) = 18 000 (0.004833 - 0.004500) = +6.0 kN·m, which cancels M_BA exactly and satisfies joint equilibrium.

Answer: -6.00 kN·m

(c)

At the fixed wall C the equation is M_CB = (2EI/4)(2θC + θB - 3ψ_BC) with θC = 0 and no fixed-end moment because span BC is unloaded: M_CB = 18 000 (0.002417 - 0.004500) = 18 000 × (-0.002083) = -37.5 kN·m. This is much larger than any moment due to the load alone, since BC carries no load, so it comes entirely from the settlement. The moment is the clockwise-on-member sense at C, producing tension in the top flange at the wall. It is a warning that differential settlement can govern the design of the stiff fixed end.

Answer: -37.5 kN·m

(d)

Take span AB as a free body, moments about B, anticlockwise positive. The pinned end has M_AB = 0 and M_BA = -6.0 kN·m acts at B. The reaction R_A acts upward 6.0 m to the left of B, which gives a clockwise moment of -6.0 R_A. The distributed load of 15 × 6.0 = 90 kN acts downward 3.0 m left of B and gives +270. Then -6.0 R_A + 270 + 0 - 6.0 = 0 and R_A = 264 / 6.0 = 44.0 kN upward. A simply supported span would give 45 kN, so the settlement changes the end reaction only slightly, while it changes the moments substantially.

Answer: 44.0 kN

Problem 5 [A1-020] Moment distribution for continuous beams

A three-span continuous steel beam supports a warehouse mezzanine floor in Barrie. Joints A and D are simple supports at the ends, and B and C are interior roller supports. Span AB is 5.0 m and carries a uniform load of 12 kN/m. Span BC is 6.0 m and carries a 60 kN point load 2.0 m from B. Span CD is 4.0 m and carries a uniform load of 20 kN/m. The flexural rigidity EI is constant. Solve by moment distribution, treating the pinned far ends A and D with the modified stiffness 3EI/L and the modified fixed-end moment so that no carry-over is needed to them. Use anticlockwise end moments positive.

  1. (a) Find the distribution factor at B for span BC. [4]
  2. (b) Find the final hogging moment at B, in kN·m. [6]
  3. (c) Find the final hogging moment at C, in kN·m. [5]
  4. (d) Find the vertical reaction at D. [5]
(a)

Relative stiffnesses with EI = 1: the stiffness of BA with a pinned far end is 3/4 × (1/5.0) = 0.1500, and that of BC with a fixed-type far end is 1/6.0 = 0.1667. At joint B the distribution factors are DF_BA = 0.1500 / 0.3167 = 0.4737 and DF_BC = 0.1667 / 0.3167 = 0.5263. At joint C, DF_CB = 0.1667 / (0.1667 + 3/4 × 1/4.0) = 0.1667 / 0.3542 = 0.4706 and DF_CD = 0.5294. Factors at each joint sum to 1.0. The stiffer span BC attracts the larger share of the unbalanced moment at B, as expected.

Answer: 0.5263

(b)

Fixed-end moments: AB, ±12 × 25 / 12 = ±25; BC, Pab²/L² = 60 × 2.0 × 16 / 36 = +53.33 at B and -26.67 at C; CD, ±20 × 16 / 12 = ±26.67. Pinned ends are released first: the modified FEM at B on BA is -25 - ½ × 25 = -37.5 and the modified FEM at C on CD is +26.67 + ½ × 26.67 = +40.0. First balance at B: the unbalance is -37.5 + 53.33 = +15.83, so BA gets -7.50 and BC gets -8.33, and the carry-over to C is -4.17. Then balance at C and repeat. After five cycles the moments settle. M_BC = +43.91 kN·m, M_BA = -43.91 kN·m. The hogging moment at B is 43.91 kN·m.

Answer: 43.91 kN·m

(c)

Continue the table at joint C. After the carry-over of -4.17 from B, the unbalance at C is -26.67 + 40.0 - 4.17 = +9.17, so CB gets -4.31, CD gets -4.85, and the carry-over to B is -2.16. The second cycle at B corrects by about +1.0 and +1.1 with a carry of +0.57, and so on; the changes shrink rapidly with each cycle. The totals converge to M_CB = -34.83 kN·m and M_CD = +34.83 kN·m, so the joint is in equilibrium. The hogging moment at the second support is therefore 34.83 kN·m, smaller than at B because the neighbouring span CD is short and its pinned end offers a softer restraint.

Answer: 34.83 kN·m

(d)

Consider span CD alone, simply supported at D, with the end moment M_CD = +34.83 kN·m applied at C and a distributed load of 20 × 4.0 = 80 kN acting 2.0 m from C. Take moments about C, anticlockwise positive: the reaction R_D acts upward 4.0 m from C and gives +4.0 R_D, the load gives -80 × 2.0 = -160, and the end moment gives +34.83. So 4.0 R_D = 160 - 34.83 and R_D = 31.29 kN upward. A simply supported span would give 40 kN, so the hogging moment at C reduces the reaction at D by 34.83 / 4.0 = 8.71 kN.

Answer: 31.29 kN

A1 Practice Paper 5

Problem 1 [A1-021] Moment distribution for frames without sidesway

A single-storey steel service frame at a water treatment plant in Kitchener consists of a column AB, 4.0 m high, rigidly fixed to its footing at A, and a horizontal beam BC, 6.0 m long, rigidly connected to the column at B. The far end C rests on a roller bearing that gives no moment restraint. Both members have the same flexural rigidity EI and are inextensible. A pipe rack applies a uniformly distributed downward load of 20 kN/m over the full length of BC. A rigid horizontal tie anchors joint B to the adjacent concrete wall, so B cannot translate sideways and the frame cannot sway. Analyse the frame by moment distribution, taking clockwise end moments on a member as positive and using the modified stiffness for BC because its far end is a roller.

  1. (a) Find the magnitude of the modified fixed-end moment at B on member BC, after the roller end C has been released and its carry-over included. [4]
  2. (b) Find the distribution factor for member BA at joint B. [3]
  3. (c) Find the magnitude of the final moment at the B end of the column, M_BA. [5]
  4. (d) Find the magnitude of the final fixed-base moment M_AB at the footing. [3]
  5. (e) Find the vertical reaction at the roller C. [5]
(a)

For a beam fixed at B and released at C, the usual fixed-end moments for a full-span uniform load are wL²/12 = 20(6²)/12 = 60 kN·m, with M_BC = -60 and M_CB = +60. Because C is a roller, its moment must end at zero, so +60 is cancelled by applying -60 at C. Half of that, -30, carries over to B, giving the modified value M_BC = -60 - 30 = -90 kN·m. This equals wL²/8 = 20(36)/8 = 90 kN·m, the fixed-end moment of a propped cantilever. The anticlockwise sign at B means the beam end tries to rotate against the joint. Using this value avoids a second balancing cycle at C.

Answer: 90 kN·m

(b)

At joint B the members meeting are BA and BC. Member BA is fixed at A, so its stiffness is 4EI/L = 4EI/4.0 = 1.0 EI. Member BC is released at C, so the modified stiffness is 3EI/L = 3EI/6.0 = 0.5 EI. The sum is 1.5 EI. The distribution factor for BA is DF_BA = 1.0/1.5 = 0.667 and for BC it is DF_BC = 0.5/1.5 = 0.333, which add to one as they must. The column takes the larger share of the unbalanced moment because it is the stiffer member and the far end is fully fixed, while the pinned beam end is more flexible. EI cancels because both members share the same value.

Answer: 0.667

(c)

Joint B carries an unbalanced moment equal to the sum of the fixed-end moments on its members: 0 on BA (no load on the column) plus -90 on BC, which is -90 kN·m. The joint is balanced by applying +90 kN·m, shared by the distribution factors. Balancing moment in BA = 0.667(90) = +60 kN·m, and in BC = 0.333(90) = +30 kN·m. The final column moment is M_BA = 0 + 60 = 60 kN·m, clockwise on the column end. As a check, M_BC = -90 + 30 = -60 kN·m, so M_BA + M_BC = 0 and joint B is in equilibrium. Because BC used the modified stiffness, no further distribution is needed.

Answer: 60 kN·m

(d)

The column is fixed at A, so the balancing moment applied at B in member BA carries over to A with a carry-over factor of one half. The carry-over moment is 0.5(60) = 30 kN·m. Member BA carries no load, so its fixed-end moment at A is zero and the final moment at the footing is M_AB = 0 + 30 = 30 kN·m, clockwise on the column end A, with the sign meaning the column is bent with its tension face on the same side as at B. The base therefore needs an anchorage detail capable of resisting 30 kN·m. Note that the base moment is exactly half the top moment because there is no load between A and B.

Answer: 30 kN·m

(e)

Isolate beam BC and take moments about B. The end moment of the beam at B is M_BC = -60 kN·m, anticlockwise on the beam, and C is a roller with M_CB = 0. The uniform load has a resultant of 20(6) = 120 kN acting 3.0 m from B, which gives a clockwise moment of 360 kN·m about B. Clockwise positive: -60 + 120(3.0) - R_C(6.0) = 0, so R_C = (360 - 60)/6.0 = 50 kN upward. Check by vertical equilibrium: the load is 120 kN, so the vertical force at B on the beam is 70 kN. That equals the axial compression carried down the column AB, which the footing must resist along with the 30 kN·m moment.

Answer: 50 kN

Problem 2 [A1-022] Stiffness, carry-over and fixed-end moments including modified stiffness

A two-member continuous girder in a parking structure in Hamilton consists of member AB, 5.0 m long, fixed against rotation at A, and member BC, 4.0 m long, with a simple bearing at C that gives no moment restraint. The members meet at an unyielding joint B that is free to rotate. Member AB has flexural rigidity EI = 40 000 kN·m². Member BC has a section 1.5 times as stiff, so its rigidity is 1.5EI. Only member AB is loaded: a single concentrated downward load of 80 kN acts 2.0 m from A. The supports do not settle. Clockwise end moments and rotations are positive. Use fixed-end moments, member stiffnesses with the modified value for BC, and joint equilibrium at B.

  1. (a) Find the fixed-end moment at the A end of member AB. [4]
  2. (b) Find the fixed-end moment at the B end of member AB. [3]
  3. (c) Find the modified rotational stiffness of member BC at B, in kN·m per radian. [4]
  4. (d) Find the rotation of joint B, as a magnitude in milliradians. [5]
  5. (e) Find the final moment at A, M_AB. [4]
(a)

With both ends fixed, a point load P at distance a from A and b from B gives a fixed-end moment at A of Pab²/L². Here P = 80 kN, a = 2.0 m, b = 3.0 m and L = 5.0 m. The magnitude is 80(2.0)(3.0²)/5.0² = 80(2.0)(9)/25 = 57.6 kN·m. For a downward load the clamped left end must resist the sagging tendency by pushing the end of the member anticlockwise, so with clockwise taken as positive FEM_AB = -57.6 kN·m. The magnitude, 57.6 kN·m, is the larger of the two end moments because the load is nearer A. These moments are what the supports would apply if joint B were temporarily locked against rotation.

Answer: 57.6 kN·m

(b)

The same loading gives the fixed-end moment at B as Pa²b/L². FEM_BA = 80(2.0²)(3.0)/5.0² = 80(4)(3)/25 = 38.4 kN·m. For a downward load the clamp at the right end pushes the member end clockwise, so in the clockwise-positive convention FEM_BA = +38.4 kN·m. The magnitude is smaller than at A because the load lies nearer A. Check by equilibrium of the fixed-fixed beam: the sum of end moments is 57.6 + 38.4 = 96.0 kN·m, and the simple-beam moment under the load is 80(2)(3)/5 = 96 kN·m, which equals the sum of the end moments' magnitudes, so the pair is consistent. Locking joint B gives a restraining moment of 38.4 kN·m, which is to be released when the joint is freed.

Answer: 38.4 kN·m

(c)

Member BC is pinned at C, so the stiffness at B is the modified value 3EI/L, using the member's rigidity of 1.5EI. K_BC = 3(1.5)(40 000)/4.0 = 3(60 000)/4.0 = 45 000 kN·m/rad. This is the moment needed to produce a unit rotation at B when C is free to rotate. Had C been fixed, the stiffness would be 4EI/L = 60 000 kN·m/rad, so releasing C reduces the stiffness to three quarters of that value, and member BC then carries no moment to C (carry-over factor zero). For comparison, member AB has K_BA = 4(40 000)/5.0 = 32 000 kN·m/rad, so the joint stiffness at B totals 77 000 kN·m/rad.

Answer: 45 000 kN·m/rad

(d)

Joint B is a free joint with no applied moment, so the member end moments at B must sum to zero. M_BA = FEM_BA + (4EI/L)θ_B and M_BC = (3EI_BC/L)θ_B, with θ_B in radians and clockwise positive. FEM_BA is +38.4 kN·m. Then +38.4 + (32 000 + 45 000)θ_B = 0, so θ_B = -38.4/77 000 = -4.987 × 10⁻⁴ rad. In milliradians the magnitude is 0.499 mrad. The sign is negative, so joint B turns anticlockwise once it is unlocked, which makes sense because the clamped-end moment of 38.4 kN·m that held it was clockwise and is released. A rotation of this size is small, about 2.5 mm of chord movement over a 5 m member, so the small-angle slope-deflection relations are valid.

Answer: 0.499 mrad

(e)

Member AB is fixed at A, so θ_A = 0 and the slope-deflection equation gives M_AB = FEM_AB + (2EI/L)θ_B, with clockwise positive. The coefficient 2EI/L = 2(40 000)/5.0 = 16 000 kN·m/rad. With FEM_AB = -57.6 kN·m and θ_B = -4.987 × 10⁻⁴ rad, the carry-over term is 16 000(-4.987 × 10⁻⁴) = -7.98 kN·m, which has the same sense as the fixed-end moment, so M_AB = -57.6 - 7.98 = -65.6 kN·m, a magnitude of 65.6 kN·m anticlockwise on the member (hogging at A). Compare with the carry-over rule: releasing the 38.4 kN·m locked at B and sharing it by stiffness gives 15.96 kN·m to AB at B, and half of that, 7.98, is added at A. The answer is larger than 57.6 and below 76.8 kN·m, the value for a fully pinned B.

Answer: 65.6 kN·m

Problem 3 [A1-023] Least work and energy methods for indeterminate structures

A conveyor support girder at a quarry near Bancroft spans 8.0 m horizontally. It is rigidly fixed at the left support A and rests on a roller bearing at B, at the same elevation as A. The girder has a constant flexural rigidity EI = 50 000 kN·m² and negligible axial deformation. It carries a uniformly distributed load of 12 kN/m over its full length and a concentrated load of 40 kN acting downward 3.0 m from A. Treat the vertical reaction R_B at the roller as the redundant, and solve using Castigliano's second theorem (the principle of least work), ignoring shear deformation. Determine the reactions that result and the effect of the support condition on the load path.

  1. (a) With the roller removed, find the downward deflection of the free end B of the resulting cantilever, in mm. [4]
  2. (b) Find the deflection of end B per unit upward force applied there, in mm/kN. [3]
  3. (c) Using the condition ∂U/∂R_B = 0, find the roller reaction R_B. [5]
  4. (d) Find the vertical reaction at A. [3]
  5. (e) Find the magnitude of the fixed-end moment at A. [5]
(a)

Remove the roller so the girder is a cantilever of length L = 8.0 m. For the energy approach, with x measured from B, the bending moment from the loads is M = -wx²/2 for the uniform part, and an extra -P(x - 5.0) for x > 5.0 m, the point load being 3.0 m from A. Applying a unit load at B gives m = -x. The deflection is δ = ∫Mm dx/EI. The distributed part gives wL⁴/(8EI) = 12(4096)/8 = 6144/EI. The point-load part gives Pa²(3L - a)/(6EI) = 40(9)(21)/6 = 1260/EI. Total = 7404/EI = 7404/50 000 = 0.14808 m = 148.1 mm downward.

Answer: 148.1 mm

(b)

A unit upward force at the end of a cantilever is the flexibility coefficient f_BB. Apply a virtual unit load: m = x measured from B, and the strain-energy derivative gives f_BB = ∫m² dx/EI = ∫₀⁸ x² dx/EI = L³/(3EI). Substituting L = 8.0 m, f_BB = 512/(3 × 50 000) = 3.4133 × 10⁻³ m/kN = 3.413 mm/kN. This is the second derivative of the strain energy with respect to R_B, which is always positive; it confirms the stationary value is a minimum (least work). The result is the reciprocal of the stiffness of the cantilever tip, 293 kN/m, so a 10 mm tip movement needs about 2.9 kN.

Answer: 3.413 mm/kN

(c)

The total strain energy is a function of the redundant R_B. Since the roller does not settle, the vertical deflection at B is zero, which is the same as ∂U/∂R_B = 0 by Castigliano's second theorem. Write the deflection at B as the free-end deflection from the loads minus that produced by R_B: δ_B = 7404/EI - R_B(L³/3EI) = 0. Then R_B = 7404/(512/3) = 7404/170.667 = 43.38 kN upward. The units balance: kN·m³ over m³ gives kN. The roller therefore carries about 31 percent of the total vertical load of 136 kN, close to the three-eighths share of a uniform load alone, because the point load sits nearer the fixed end.

Answer: 43.4 kN

(d)

Apply vertical equilibrium to the whole girder. The total downward load is the distributed load 12(8.0) = 96 kN plus the concentrated load of 40 kN, a total of 136 kN. The upward reactions are R_A and R_B, so R_A = 136 - 43.38 = 92.62 kN upward. Check by moments about B, with counterclockwise positive: R_A(8) - M_A - 96(4) - 40(5) = 0, which uses the fixed moment found in the next part. The fixed end carries 68 percent of the total load, which is why the fixed support, and not the roller, governs the design of the anchorage. The sign of the reaction is positive, so there is no uplift at A.

Answer: 92.6 kN

(e)

Take moments about A for the whole girder. The load moments about A are the uniform load, 96 kN at 4.0 m, giving 384 kN·m, plus the point load 40 kN at 3.0 m, giving 120 kN·m, for a total of 504 kN·m. The roller reaction produces an opposing moment R_B(8) = 43.38(8) = 347.07 kN·m. The fixed-end moment is M_A = 504 - 347.07 = 156.93 kN·m, which is hogging (tension in the top fibre at A). Compare with a simple cantilever carrying the same loads, where the root moment would be 504 kN·m. The roller reduces the root moment by about 69 percent, which shows how much the redundant support shares the demand.

Answer: 156.9 kN·m

Problem 4 [A1-024] Indeterminate structure with settlement or temperature change, comparing methods

A prismatic steel girder carrying a service walkway over a drainage canal in Brampton is continuous over three supports in a line: a pin at A, a roller at B and a roller at C. The two spans AB and BC are each 6.0 m long, and the girder has constant EI = 30 000 kN·m². A uniformly distributed load of 10 kN/m acts downward over both spans. The designer wants to know how much the central support reaction changes if a soil survey predicts that support B could settle downward by 15 mm over the life of the structure while A and C stay level. Use the flexibility method with R_B as the redundant and check with the three-moment equation. Take sagging moments as positive.

  1. (a) Find the central reaction R_B before any settlement occurs. [3]
  2. (b) Find R_B after support B settles 15 mm, using the flexibility method. [5]
  3. (c) Using the three-moment equation, find the magnitude of the hogging moment at B after the settlement. [5]
  4. (d) Find the reaction at A after the settlement. [3]
  5. (e) Find the settlement of B, in mm, at which the central reaction becomes zero. [4]
(a)

Remove the roller at B so that the girder becomes a simple span of 12 m between A and C. The deflection at midspan under a uniform load is 5wL⁴/(384EI) with L = 12 m, so δ_B0 = 5(10)(12⁴)/(384 × 30 000) = 5(10)(20 736)/(11 520 000) = 0.09 m. A unit upward force at midspan gives f_BB = L³/(48EI) = 1728/(48 × 30 000) = 0.0012 m/kN. Compatibility without settlement requires R_B f_BB = δ_B0, so R_B = 0.09/0.0012 = 75 kN. This equals 5wL/8 for the full 12 m length, the classical result for two equal spans, and represents 62.5 percent of the 120 kN total load.

Answer: 75 kN

(b)

With a settlement Δ = 15 mm = 0.015 m downward, the girder is no longer required to have zero deflection at B; the final deflection at B must equal the support movement. Compatibility: δ_B0 - R_B f_BB = Δ, where both terms are downward, measured on the released structure. R_B = (0.09 - 0.015)/0.0012 = 0.075/0.0012 = 62.5 kN. The settlement unloads the central support by 12.5 kN, which is 17 percent. The settlement flexibility is easy to understand: the girder simply sags into the gap and sheds load to the end supports, but it cannot drop the whole way because it must still bend continuously over the roller. Both δ values are positive when the girder deflects downward.

Answer: 62.5 kN

(c)

For a continuous beam with supports A, B, C, the three-moment equation with M_A = M_C = 0 and equal spans L = 6.0 m is 2M_B(L + L) = -(wL³/4 + wL³/4) + 6EI(Δ_B/L + Δ_B/L). The load term is -2(10)(216)/4 = -1080. The settlement term is 6(30 000)(0.015/6.0 + 0.015/6.0) = 180 000(0.005) = 900. So 4L M_B = 24M_B = -1080 + 900 = -180 and M_B = -7.5 kN·m, a hogging moment of 7.5 kN·m. Without settlement, M_B would be -1080/24 = -45 kN·m. Check: moment at B from the reactions, R_A(6) - 10(6)(3) = 28.75(6) - 180 = -7.5 kN·m. The flexibility result in part (b) agrees.

Answer: 7.5 kN·m

(d)

By symmetry R_A = R_C. Vertical equilibrium for the girder gives R_A + R_B + R_C = w × 12 = 120 kN. With R_B = 62.5 kN, R_A = R_C = (120 - 62.5)/2 = 28.75 kN upward.
