Compare with the unsettled case, where R_A = (120 - 75)/2 = 22.5 kN. So the end supports pick up 6.25 kN more each. As a check, take moments about B for span AB alone: 28.75(6.0) - 10(6)(3.0) = 172.5 - 180 = -7.5 kN·m, which equals M_B from the three-moment equation. The end reactions remain positive, so the pin at A and roller at C do not uplift and no tie-down is needed there.

Answer: 28.75 kN

(e)

The central reaction goes to zero when the girder sags freely, as a simple 12 m span, without touching B. That happens when the support settlement just equals the free deflection at midspan: Δ = δ_B0. From part (a), δ_B0 = 0.09 m = 90 mm. Using the compatibility relation R_B = (δ_B0 - Δ)/f_BB, setting R_B = 0 gives Δ = 0.09 m. Any settlement larger than 90 mm would leave B out of contact, and the structure would behave as a simple span of 12 m with a maximum moment of wL²/8 = 180 kN·m. Practical designers therefore compare the predicted settlement with this threshold; here 15 mm is only one sixth of it, so contact is retained.

Answer: 90 mm

Problem 5 [A1-025] Reactions and free-body diagrams of determinate beams and frames

A temporary work platform girder at a transmission-tower site near Sudbury is 11.5 m long. It rests on a pin support at A and a roller support at B, 9.0 m from A, and overhangs 2.5 m beyond B to a free end C. The girder weighs 5 kN/m along its full length. A hoist hung from C lifts equipment weighing 80 kN, and this load acts vertically downward at C. The crew finds that with the hoist loaded, the girder tends to lift off the pin at A. They propose adding a ballast block, treated as a point load, set 1.5 m from A. Treat all supports as frictionless and horizontal loads as zero. Use reactions positive when upward.

  1. (a) Find the vertical reaction at A with the 80 kN hoist load applied and no ballast. A negative result means uplift. [4]
  2. (b) Find the ballast weight W, placed 1.5 m from A, that makes the reaction at A equal to +10 kN. [5]
  3. (c) With that ballast in place, find the reaction at B. [3]
  4. (d) Find the smallest ballast weight at the same position that just prevents uplift at A. [3]
  5. (e) With no ballast, find the largest hoist load at C for which the reaction at A remains non-negative. [5]
(a)

Isolate the girder and take moments about B, the roller, so that the unknown R_B drops out. The span AB carries 5(9.0) = 45 kN acting 4.5 m from B, the overhang carries 5(2.5) = 12.5 kN acting 1.25 m beyond B, and the hoist load is 80 kN acting 2.5 m beyond B. Counterclockwise positive about B, with the loads left of B counterclockwise: -R_A(9.0) + 45(4.5) - 12.5(1.25) - 80(2.5) = 0. So 9R_A = 202.5 - 15.625 - 200 = -13.125, giving R_A = -1.458 kN. The negative sign means the pin must pull down by 1.46 kN, so the girder is trying to lift off A and needs a tie-down or ballast.

Answer: -1.46 kN (uplift)

(b)

Add the ballast W at 1.5 m from A, which is 7.5 m to the left of B. Its moment about B is W(7.5), and it acts in the same direction as the span weight. Moments about B: -R_A(9.0) + 202.5 + 7.5W - 15.625 - 200 = 0. Setting R_A = +10 kN gives -90 + 202.5 + 7.5W - 215.625 = 0, so 7.5W = 103.125 and W = 13.75 kN. The ballast has the leverage advantage of the long arm: it is placed far from the roller, so a small weight resists a large overturning moment from the overhang. The ballast weight is only 17 percent of the hoist load, which keeps the platform practical to assemble.

Answer: 13.75 kN

(c)

Use vertical equilibrium for the whole girder with the ballast in place. The total downward load is the girder weight 5(11.5) = 57.5 kN, plus the hoist load 80 kN, plus the ballast 13.75 kN, which sums to 151.25 kN. The upward reactions R_A and R_B must equal this. With R_A = +10 kN, R_B = 151.25 - 10 = 141.25 kN upward. Check by moments about A, counterclockwise positive: R_B(9.0) - 45(4.5) - 12.5(10.25) - 80(11.5) - 13.75(1.5) = 1271.25 - 202.5 - 128.125 - 920 - 20.625 = 0. The roller therefore carries 93 percent of the load, which controls the bearing check.

Answer: 141.25 kN

(d)

The limiting case for no uplift is R_A = 0. Set R_A = 0 in the moment equation about B with the ballast included: 202.5 + 7.5W - 15.625 - 200 = 0. This gives 7.5W = 13.125 and W = 1.75 kN. A ballast of at least 1.75 kN just leaves the pin unloaded, so the girder would be on the verge of rotating about B. That is not acceptable practice because any dynamic effect from the hoist would cause a lift-off; this is why part (b) chose a positive reaction of 10 kN. The minimum is a useful lower bound for the ballast, and any real design would apply a safety factor above it.

Answer: 1.75 kN

(e)

With no ballast, let the hoist load be P at C, 2.5 m from B. Moments about B with R_A = 0 give 202.5 - 15.625 - 2.5P = 0, so P = 186.875/2.5 = 74.75 kN. Any hoist load above 74.75 kN produces uplift at A. The actual load of 80 kN exceeds this threshold by 5.25 kN, which agrees with the small negative reaction found in part (a): 5.25(2.5)/9.0 = 1.46 kN. The crew can therefore either limit the hoist capacity to 74.75 kN, with a margin, or add ballast. Working in loads rather than reactions shows directly how close the platform is to its stability limit.

Answer: 74.75 kN

A1 Practice Paper 6

Problem 1 [A1-026] Shear and bending moment diagrams for beams with point and distributed loads

A steel runway beam in a fabrication shop in Oshawa spans 10.0 m between a pin support at A and a roller support at B, both at the same level. Stored plate stock produces a uniformly distributed downward load of 18 kN/m acting only on the first 6.0 m measured from A. A hoist rail clamp at 8.0 m from A delivers a downward point load of 45 kN. Self-weight is already included in the 18 kN/m. The fabricator must select a rolled section and the design is governed by bending, with an allowable bending stress of 160 MPa. Draw the shear and moment diagrams mentally, and use them to find the quantities below. Take sagging moment as positive and ignore shear stress.

  1. (a) Find the vertical reaction at A. [3]
  2. (b) Find the distance from A at which the shear force is zero. [4]
  3. (c) Find the maximum bending moment in the beam. [5]
  4. (d) Find the bending moment directly under the 45 kN point load. [3]
  5. (e) Find the minimum elastic section modulus required, in 10³ mm³. [5]
(a)

Take moments about B to find R_A, because the roller reaction then drops out. The distributed load has a resultant of 18(6.0) = 108 kN, acting at the centre of its loaded length, 3.0 m from A, which is 7.0 m from B. The point load is 2.0 m from B. Counterclockwise positive about B: R_A(10.0) - 108(7.0) - 45(2.0) = 0, so R_A = (756 + 90)/10.0 = 84.6 kN upward. For checking, R_B = 108 + 45 - 84.6 = 68.4 kN. A moment check about A gives 68.4(10) = 108(3.0) + 45(8.0) = 324 + 360 = 684, which is true. Both reactions are upward, so no uplift occurs.

Answer: 84.6 kN

(b)

Draw the shear diagram from the left. At A the shear jumps up to +84.6 kN. Within the loaded length 0 to 6.0 m the shear falls linearly at 18 kN per metre: V(x) = 84.6 - 18x. Beyond x = 6.0 m there is no distributed load, and the shear is constant at 84.6 - 108 = -23.4 kN until x = 8.0 m, where it drops by 45 kN to -68.4 kN, the negative of R_B, which closes the diagram. The zero crossing lies in the loaded zone: 84.6 - 18x = 0 gives x = 4.70 m. The moment is a maximum where the shear changes sign, so the critical section is 4.70 m from A, inside the loaded length as required.

Answer: 4.70 m

(c)

The maximum moment occurs at the zero-shear section. Cut the beam at x = 4.70 m and take moments of the forces on the left piece: M = R_A x - w x²/2 = 84.6(4.70) - 18(4.70²)/2. The first term is 397.62 kN·m and the second is 18(22.09)/2 = 198.81 kN·m, so M_max = 397.62 - 198.81 = 198.81 kN·m, sagging. The equality of the two terms is a property of a uniform load with a linear shear: the area under the shear diagram from A to the zero point is (1/2)(84.6)(4.70) = 198.81. That equality gives a useful independent check, since the moment equals the area of the shear triangle.

Answer: 198.8 kN·m

(d)

Continue the moment diagram past the loaded region by adding shear areas. The moment at x = 6.0 m, where the distributed load ends, is M = 84.6(6.0) - 18(6.0²)/2 = 507.6 - 324 = 183.6 kN·m. Between x = 6.0 and x = 8.0 m the shear is -23.4 kN, so the moment falls by 23.4(2.0) = 46.8 kN·m to 136.8 kN·m at the point load. Check from the right: M = R_B(2.0) = 68.4(2.0) = 136.8 kN·m, which agrees. The moment at the load is lower than the maximum by 62 kN·m, so the point load does not control the design, though the diagram shows a slope change at that section.

Answer: 136.8 kN·m

(e)

Bending stress is σ = M/S, so the required elastic section modulus is S = M_max/σ_allow. Use M_max = 198.81 kN·m = 198.81 × 10⁶ N·mm and σ_allow = 160 N/mm². S = 198.81 × 10⁶/160 = 1.2426 × 10⁶ mm³ = 1243 × 10³ mm³. A designer would then look in a section table for a rolled beam with S not less than this value. The result is a minimum; because the allowable stress is a working-stress limit, no further factors are applied. If the beam were also checked for deflection or lateral-torsional buckling, a heavier section might be needed, but the bending requirement alone sets this lower bound.

Answer: 1243 × 10³ mm³

Problem 2 [A1-027] Member forces in determinate trusses by joints and sections

A steel pedestrian truss bridge near Peterborough spans 12.0 m and has three equal panels of 4.0 m. The bottom chord joints are L0, L1, L2 and L3 from left to right. The top chord joints are U1 above L1 and U2 above L2, both 3.0 m above the bottom chord. The members are the bottom chord members L0L1, L1L2 and L2L3, the top chord member U1U2, the inclined end posts L0U1 and L3U2, the vertical members L1U1 and L2U2, and a single diagonal L1U2 in the middle panel. L0 is a pin and L3 is a roller. Deck loads of 90 kN at L1 and 60 kN at L2 act downward. Tension is positive. The bottom chord member L1L2 is made of steel with an allowable tensile stress of 150 MPa.

  1. (a) Find the vertical reaction at the pin L0. [3]
  2. (b) Find the magnitude of the force in the end post L0U1. [4]
  3. (c) By the method of sections, find the magnitude of the force in the top chord U1U2. [5]
  4. (d) Find the force in the diagonal L1U2, with tension positive. [4]
  5. (e) Find the minimum net area of the bottom chord member L1L2, in mm². [4]
(a)

Take moments about the roller L3, so the unknown reaction there is eliminated. The distances from L3 are 8.0 m to L1 and 4.0 m to L2. Counterclockwise positive: R_L0(12.0) - 90(8.0) - 60(4.0) = 0, so R_L0 = (720 + 240)/12.0 = 80 kN upward. Then vertical equilibrium gives R_L3 = 150 - 80 = 70 kN. Check by moments about L0: R_L3(12) = 90(4) + 60(8) = 360 + 480 = 840, so R_L3 = 70 kN, which agrees. The loads are applied only at the panel points, so every member is a two-force member and carries axial force only.

Answer: 80 kN

(b)

Use the method of joints at L0. The end post runs from L0 up to U1, a horizontal distance of 4.0 m and a vertical rise of 3.0 m, so its length is √(4² + 3²) = 5.0 m, with direction cosines 0.8 horizontal and 0.6 vertical. The only vertical force at L0 besides the end post is the reaction of 80 kN, so the vertical component of the end post must be 80 kN downward on the joint. F(0.6) = 80 gives F = 133.3 kN. It pushes the joint toward the support, so it is in compression. The horizontal component is 133.3(0.8) = 106.7 kN, which the bottom chord L0L1 must balance in tension.

Answer: 133.3 kN (compression)

(c)

Cut the truss through the middle panel, passing through U1U2, L1U2 and L1L2, and examine the left part. The unknown diagonal and bottom chord both pass through L1, so take moments about L1. Forces on the left piece: R_L0 = 80 kN up at 4.0 m to the left of L1, and the top chord force acting 3.0 m above L1. Moments about L1: 80(4.0) - F_top(3.0) = 0, because the load at L1 acts through the point. F_top = 320/3.0 = 106.7 kN. The top chord is pushing toward the left part, so it is in compression. This matches the horizontal component found at joint L0 in part (b), which is a consistency check on the end post force.

Answer: 106.7 kN (compression)

(d)

Use the same section and sum the vertical forces on the left piece. Upward 80 kN from the reaction acts against the 90 kN load at L1, which acts on the left piece because L1 lies within it. The net 80 - 90 = -10 kN must be balanced by the vertical component of the diagonal, which therefore acts upward and equals 10 kN. The diagonal slopes at 3.0 m of rise per 4.0 m of run, so its vertical component is 0.6 of the force: F = 10/0.6 = 16.67 kN. The diagonal pulls on the left piece, upward and to the right toward U2, so it is in tension, +16.67 kN. The end post and the diagonal have different roles; here the diagonal carries only the shear difference.

Answer: 16.67 kN (tension)

(e)

Find the force in bottom chord L1L2 by taking moments about U2 for the same left piece, which eliminates the top chord and the diagonal. The reaction 80 kN acts 8.0 m to the left of U2 and the load 90 kN acts 4.0 m to the left of U2. The chord force T acts 3.0 m below U2. Counterclockwise positive: 80(8.0) clockwise = 640, and 90(4.0) counterclockwise = 360, so the net is 280 kN·m clockwise, balanced by T(3.0). T = 280/3.0 = 93.3 kN tension. Required area = T/σ_allow = 93 333 N/150 N/mm² = 622 mm². This is the minimum net area after deduction of bolt holes at any splice.

Answer: 622 mm²

Problem 3 [A1-028] Three-hinged arches and cables

A pedestrian suspension bridge crosses a gorge in the Bruce Peninsula. Its main cable runs between two towers at the same elevation, 60 m apart horizontally. At midspan the cable hangs 6.0 m below the tower tops. The deck and hangers apply a uniformly distributed vertical load of 4.0 kN/m measured along the horizontal span, and the cable self-weight is included in that value. Treat the cable as perfectly flexible and parabolic. The designer must size the cable steel and consider a cheaper alternative with a deeper sag. The allowable tensile stress in the cable steel is 500 MPa. Use the series approximation for cable length given in part (e), which is accurate for a flat parabola.

  1. (a) Find the horizontal component of cable tension. [4]
  2. (b) Find the maximum cable tension, at the tower. [4]
  3. (c) Find the minimum cross-sectional area of the cable steel, in mm². [4]
  4. (d) Find the sag that would limit the horizontal tension to 250 kN. [4]
  5. (e) For the original 6.0 m sag, find the cable length using L_c = L[1 + (8/3)(h/L)²]. [4]
(a)

For a parabolic cable under uniform load per horizontal metre, take moments about midspan for half the cable. The left half carries the load w(L/2) = 4.0(30) = 120 kN acting 15 m from the midspan section, and the cable tension at midspan is purely horizontal, H, acting at the lowest point. The moment arm of H about the left tower is the sag h = 6.0 m. Moments about the tower: H(6.0) = 120(15) gives H = 300 kN. The general formula is H = wL²/(8h) = 4.0(3600)/(8 × 6.0) = 300 kN. This horizontal pull must be resisted by the tower tops or back-stays, so it also sets the foundation design.

Answer: 300 kN

(b)

The maximum tension occurs where the slope is greatest, at the towers. The vertical component at each tower equals half the total load: V = wL/2 = 4.0(60)/2 = 120 kN. The horizontal component is H = 300 kN throughout. The resultant is T_max = √(H² + V²) = √(300² + 120²) = √(90 000 + 14 400) = √104 400 = 323.1 kN. The cable slope at the tower is tan θ = V/H = 0.4, so θ = 21.8° from horizontal. At the lowest point the tension is only 300 kN, so the tension rises by less than 8 percent from midspan to the tower. A flat cable thus carries almost its whole force as horizontal pull.

Answer: 323.1 kN

(c)

The cable must carry its largest tension, the value at the tower, so the stress check uses T_max = 323.1 kN = 323 110 N. Required area A = T_max/σ_allow = 323 110/500 = 646 mm². This corresponds to a solid round bar of diameter √(4 × 646/π) = 28.7 mm, or an equivalent area of strand. Working stress is used here because the problem gives an allowable stress, so no load or resistance factors are applied. The tension along the cable varies, so a designer could in principle taper the cable, but practical cables use a constant area, governed by the tower end where the force is greatest.

Answer: 646 mm²

(d)

Because H = wL²/(8h), a deeper sag lowers the horizontal tension in inverse proportion. To limit H to 250 kN, h = wL²/(8H) = 4.0(3600)/(8 × 250) = 14 400/2000 = 7.2 m. The sag must therefore increase from 6.0 m to 7.2 m, a 20 percent increase, which cuts the horizontal force by one sixth. The cost is a longer cable and lower deck clearance if the towers are kept at the same height, so the designer must balance cable steel against the extra geometry. At 7.2 m the sag-to-span ratio is 1:8.33, still flat enough for the parabola formulas to hold with good accuracy.

Answer: 7.2 m

(e)

Using the given series expansion for a parabolic cable, the length is L_c = L[1 + (8/3)(h/L)²], with L = 60 m and h = 6.0 m. The ratio h/L = 0.10, and its square is 0.01. Then L_c = 60[1 + (8/3)(0.01)] = 60[1 + 0.026667] = 61.6 m. The cable is therefore only 2.7 percent longer than the straight chord between the tower tops, 1.6 m extra. The extra length matters for ordering steel and for temperature movement, because a change in the cable length of a few millimetres changes the sag noticeably. The expansion has dropped higher-order terms, which are tiny at this ratio.

Answer: 61.6 m

Problem 4 [A1-029] Axial force, shear and moment diagrams of determinate frames

A portal-type steel frame supports a loading canopy at a transit maintenance yard in Mississauga. Columns AB and CD are 4.5 m high and the beam BC is 7.0 m long, with rigid joints at B and C. The frame is pinned to its footing at A and rests on a roller at D that allows horizontal movement, so the frame is statically determinate. A wind-driven horizontal force of 24 kN acts to the right at joint B. A uniformly distributed downward load of 15 kN/m, from snow, acts over the full length of BC. The beam is to be a rolled section with an allowable bending stress of 165 MPa. Work in kN and m, with reactions positive when acting upward or to the right as appropriate.

  1. (a) Find the vertical reaction at the roller D. [4]
  2. (b) Find the vertical reaction at the pin A. [3]
  3. (c) Find the magnitude of the bending moment in the column AB at joint B. [3]
  4. (d) Find the maximum bending moment in beam BC. [5]
  5. (e) Find the minimum elastic section modulus of the beam, in 10³ mm³. [5]
(a)

Take moments about the pin A for the whole frame, because the pin reactions then drop out. The horizontal 24 kN acts 4.5 m above A. The snow load has a resultant of 15(7.0) = 105 kN acting 3.5 m from A horizontally. The roller reaction R_D is at 7.0 m. Both the wind force and the snow load turn the frame clockwise about A, so the upward roller reaction must supply the counterclockwise moment: R_D(7.0) - 24(4.5) - 105(3.5) = 0. Then R_D = (108 + 367.5)/7.0 = 475.5/7.0 = 67.93 kN upward. The roller carries more than half of the snow load because the wind adds to the overturning moment about the pin.

Answer: 67.93 kN

(b)

Apply vertical equilibrium to the entire frame. The total vertical load is the snow load of 105 kN. The vertical reactions are R_A and R_D, so R_A = 105 - 67.93 = 37.07 kN upward. For horizontal equilibrium, the pin must resist the entire wind force because the roller at D has no horizontal capacity, so H_A = 24 kN acting to the left. The column AB therefore carries an axial compression of 37.07 kN and a constant shear of 24 kN along its height. The column CD carries axial compression of 67.93 kN and no shear at all, so its bending moment is zero throughout its height.

Answer: 37.07 kN

(c)

Cut column AB just below joint B and take moments of the forces below the cut about the cut section. The only force producing moment is the horizontal reaction H_A = 24 kN, acting at a lever arm equal to the column height 4.5 m. M_B = 24(4.5) = 108 kN·m. The vertical reaction acts along the column axis and contributes nothing to bending. The moment varies linearly from zero at the pin to 108 kN·m at the joint, because the shear is constant. The beam must carry that same 108 kN·m across the rigid joint, which can be checked from the beam side in the next part.

Answer: 108 kN·m

(d)

Examine beam BC from the right end C, where the moment is zero because column CD has no shear, so no moment is delivered at C. Measure x from C. The beam receives a vertical shear of R_D = 67.93 kN from the column, so V(x) = 67.93 - 15x, and M(x) = 67.93x - 7.5x². At x = 7.0 m, M = 475.5 - 367.5 = 108 kN·m, which matches the column moment at B. Shear is zero at x = 67.93/15 = 4.529 m from C. Mmax = 67.93²/(2 × 15) = 4614.5/30 = 153.8 kN·m. That is 42 percent more than the joint moment.

Answer: 153.8 kN·m

(e)

The required elastic section modulus is S = M_max/σ_allow. With M_max = 153.81 kN·m = 153.81 × 10⁶ N·mm and σ_allow = 165 N/mm², S = 153.81 × 10⁶/165 = 932 200 mm³ = 932 × 10³ mm³. This is the minimum value for strength in bending. The beam would be chosen from a section table with at least this modulus, and then checked for shear at the joint, deflection under snow and the lateral bracing of the compression flange. Because the maximum moment occurs 4.5 m from C and not at the joint, the critical section for bending is mid-beam, while the joint is critical for the connection.

Answer: 932 × 10³ mm³

Problem 5 [A1-030] Influence lines for reactions of beams

A steel service bridge at an airport baggage facility near Toronto is modelled as a beam with a pin support at A and a roller support at B, 12.0 m from A. The beam overhangs 4.0 m beyond B to a free end C, so the deck extends 16.0 m from A. A two-axle maintenance tug crosses the deck, and may travel in either direction. Its front axle load is 120 kN, its rear axle load is 80 kN, and the axles are 3.0 m apart. Both axles must remain on the deck. The anchor bolts at A must be designed for uplift, and the designer applies a load factor of 1.5 to the unfactored uplift. Use influence lines for the reactions R_A and R_B, with x measured from A.

  1. (a) Find the influence line ordinate for R_B when a unit load is at the free end C. [3]
  2. (b) Find the influence line ordinate for R_A when a unit load is at the free end C. [3]
  3. (c) Find the maximum possible reaction at B due to the tug. [5]
  4. (d) Find the maximum possible downward-load reaction at A due to the tug. [4]
  5. (e) Find the factored design uplift force on the anchor bolts at A. [5]
(a)

Place a unit load at distance x from A and take moments about A for the whole beam: R_B(12.0) = 1.0(x), so the influence line for R_B is x/12.0, a straight line from zero at A, through 1.0 at B, continuing in the same straight line along the overhang. At the free end, x = 16.0 m, the ordinate is 16/12 = 1.333. A value above one is expected: a load on the overhang is lever-armed about the pin, so the roller carries more than the load itself. Equilibrium in the vertical direction then shows that the pin must pull down, which is checked in part (b).

Answer: 1.333

(b)

By vertical equilibrium for a unit load at x, R_A + R_B = 1.0, so R_A = 1 - x/12.0. The influence line starts at 1.0 above A and falls linearly to zero at the roller B. It then continues below the baseline along the overhang. At the free end, x = 16.0 m, the ordinate is 1 - 16/12 = -0.333. The negative sign means a load at C produces a downward reaction at A, which is uplift on the bearing and the anchor bolts. At the roller (x = 12.0 m) the ordinate crosses zero, so any load directly over B has no effect on A at all.

Answer: -0.333

(c)

R_B is the load multiplied by the ordinate x/12.0, summed over the axles. The ordinate grows with x, so the greatest R_B occurs when the tug is as far out on the overhang as it can be, with the heavy front axle at the free end, x = 16.0 m, and the rear axle 3.0 m behind it, x = 13.0 m. R_B = 120(16/12) + 80(13/12) = 160.0 + 86.67 = 246.7 kN. The opposite arrangement, with the 80 kN axle at C, gives 80(1.333) + 120(1.083) = 106.7 + 130 = 236.7 kN, which is smaller. The tug therefore places 246.7 kN on the roller, about 23 percent more than its own weight of 200 kN.

Answer: 246.7 kN

(d)

R_A has ordinate 1 - x/12.0, which is greatest at x = 0, directly over the pin. With the tug able to travel either way, the heaviest axle can be placed over A, at x = 0, with the lighter axle 3.0 m inward at x = 3.0. R_A = 120(1.0) + 80(1 - 3/12) = 120 + 80(0.75) = 120 + 60 = 180 kN. The reverse arrangement with the 80 kN axle at A gives 80 + 120(0.75) = 170 kN, which is smaller. The pin at A therefore sees 90 percent of the tug weight, and the live-load check on its bearing uses 180 kN. Dead load of the deck would be added separately.

Answer: 180 kN

(e)

Uplift at A is produced by loads on the overhang, where the ordinate for R_A is negative. The most negative combination puts the heavy front axle at the free end, x = 16.0 m, and the 80 kN axle at x = 13.0 m. R_A = 120(1 - 16/12) + 80(1 - 13/12) = 120(-0.3333) + 80(-0.0833) = -40.0 - 6.67 = -46.67 kN. This is an unfactored uplift of 46.67 kN. The reverse arrangement gives only -26.67 - 10 = -36.67 kN. Applying the load factor of 1.5, the design uplift is 1.5(46.67) = 70.0 kN. Dead load of the deck would reduce this, but because it is not given the check is conservative.

Answer: 70 kN

A1 Practice Paper 7

Problem 1 [A1-031] Influence lines for shear and moment in beams

A fabrication shop in Hamilton supports a travelling hoist and a stack of loose plate on a simply supported steel runway beam. The beam spans 12.0 m between a pin at A and a roller at B. Section X lies 4.0 m from A. The hoist and its lifted load act together as a single 90 kN downward point load that can stand at any position on the beam. Plate stock can be stacked on any length of the beam, in any position, as a uniformly distributed load of 18 kN/m. Both loads are live loads, and the beam self weight is handled separately. The shop wants the runway checked at section X and then wants to know how much plate load the shop may allow if the permitted shear at X is limited.

  1. (a) Using the influence line for shear at X, find the maximum positive shear at X caused by the 90 kN point load acting with the 18 kN/m load placed in the most severe way. [6]
  2. (b) Find the magnitude of the maximum negative shear at X from the same two live loads. [4]
  3. (c) Using the influence line for bending moment at X, find the maximum bending moment at X. [5]
  4. (d) The 90 kN point load stays, but the shop limits the maximum positive shear at X to 100 kN. Find the largest uniformly distributed plate load w, in kN/m, that is allowed. [5]
(a)

For a unit load at distance x from A, to the right of X, the shear at X equals R_A = (12 − x)/12. Just right of X the ordinate is (12 − 4)/12 = +0.667, and it falls in a straight line to zero at B. For a unit load left of X the shear is −R_B = −x/12, which reaches −0.333 at X. The positive region is therefore a triangle with base 8.0 m and height 0.667, area ½ × 8.0 × 0.667 = 2.667 m. The distributed load is placed over this whole positive region: 18 × 2.667 = 48.0 kN. The point load is placed at the peak ordinate just right of X: 90 × 0.667 = 60.0 kN. Adding the two contributions gives V = 48.0 + 60.0 = 108.0 kN.

Answer: 108.0 kN

(b)

The negative part of the influence line lies left of X. It is a triangle with base 4.0 m, running from zero at A to −0.333 at X, because the shear at X for a unit load at x on the left is −R_B = −x/12 and x = 4 gives −4/12. Its area is ½ × 4.0 × 0.333 = 0.667 m. The distributed load is placed only over A to X: 18 × 0.667 = 12.0 kN. The point load stands just left of X on the peak ordinate: 90 × 0.333 = 30.0 kN. The total negative shear is 12.0 + 30.0 = 42.0 kN in magnitude. The positive shear governs the design, but the beam must still be checked for this reversal, which is smaller by a factor of about 2.6.

Answer: 42.0 kN

(c)

For a unit load at x from A the moment at X is R_B × 8 = 8x/12 when x ≤ 4, and R_A × 4 = 4(12 − x)/12 when x ≥ 4. Both expressions give the peak ordinate a(L − a)/L = 4 × 8/12 = 2.667 m at x = 4, and the influence line is a triangle spanning the whole beam. Its area is ½ × 12.0 × 2.667 = 16.0 m². Every ordinate is positive, so the distributed load covers the entire span: 18 × 16.0 = 288.0 kN·m. The point load stands directly over X at the peak ordinate: 90 × 2.667 = 240.0 kN·m. The maximum moment is 288.0 + 240.0 = 528.0 kN·m. Because the influence line has no negative region, placing the uniform load everywhere is correct.

Answer: 528.0 kN·m

(d)

From part a the point load at the peak ordinate contributes 90 × 0.667 = 60.0 kN to the positive shear at X, and this contribution does not depend on the plate load. The allowable shear is 100 kN, so the plate load may add at most 100 − 60.0 = 40.0 kN. The distributed plate load must cover the positive region of the influence line, whose area is 2.667 m, in order to be critical. The condition is w × 2.667 = 40.0, so w = 40.0/2.667 = 15.0 kN/m. This is below the 18 kN/m first assumed, so the shop must restrict stacking to about 83 percent of its original plan. Stacking plate on the short length from A to X does not raise the positive shear, so it needs no restriction for this check.

Answer: 15.0 kN/m

Problem 2 [A1-032] Influence lines for truss member forces

A pedestrian and service-vehicle bridge in northern Ontario uses a Pratt truss of four equal panels, each 4.0 m wide, giving a 16.0 m span between a pin at the left bottom joint L0 and a roller at the right bottom joint L4. The bottom chord joints are L0, L1, L2, L3, L4 from left to right. The top chord joints U1, U2, U3 sit 3.0 m directly above L1, L2, L3. Verticals join each U to the L below it, end posts join L0 to U1 and L4 to U3, and the two diagonals run from U1 down to L2 and from U3 down to L2. Live load reaches the truss through floor beams at the bottom chord joints only. The live load is a 30 kN/m uniform load of any length and a single 120 kN axle load. Diagonal U1L2 is made from a steel flat of allowable stress 150 MPa in tension.

  1. (a) Using a section through the second panel, find the influence ordinate for the force in diagonal U1L2 when a unit load is at L2 (positive for tension). [4]
  2. (b) Find the largest tensile force in U1L2 from the 30 kN/m load and the 120 kN axle load placed together in the worst way. [6]
  3. (c) Find the largest compressive force in U1L2 from the same live loads. [5]
  4. (d) Find the minimum cross-sectional area of the flat needed to carry the maximum tension at the allowable stress. [5]
(a)

Cut the truss through the second panel, between L1 and L2, so the cut passes through U1U2, U1L2 and L1L2. For a unit load right of the cut, at L2 or beyond, the left part has only the reaction R_A acting upward as the external force, so the panel shear is V = R_A. With the unit load at x = 8.0 m, R_A = (16 − 8)/16 = 0.500. The diagonal U1L2 runs 4.0 m across and 3.0 m down, so its length is 5.0 m and its vertical component is 3/5 of its force. Vertical equilibrium of the left part gives R_A − (3/5)F = 0, so F = (5/3) × 0.500 = +0.833, tension. The positive sign shows the diagonal is stretched when the load is on L2.

Answer: 0.833

(b)

The influence line for F is (5/3) times the panel shear. At L1 the unit load gives panel shear −R_B = −0.250, so F = −0.417. At L2 F = +0.833, at L3 F = (5/3)(0.250) = +0.417, and it is zero at L0 and L4. Between L1 and L2 the line is straight, so it crosses zero at 4.0 + 4.0 × (0.417/1.250) = 5.333 m. The positive area is a triangle from 5.333 to 8.0 m of height 0.833, plus a triangle from 8.0 to 16.0 m of height 0.833: ½ × 2.667 × 0.833 + ½ × 8.0 × 0.833 = 1.111 + 3.333 = 4.444 m. Uniform load: 30 × 4.444 = 133.3 kN. Axle at L2: 120 × 0.833 = 100.0 kN. Maximum tension = 233.3 kN.

Answer: 233.3 kN

(c)

The negative part of the influence line lies between x = 0 and x = 5.333 m, with a lowest ordinate of −0.417 at L1. It is a triangle of base 5.333 m and height 0.417, so its area is ½ × 5.333 × 0.417 = 1.111 m. The uniform load, placed over this region only, gives 30 × 1.111 = 33.3 kN of compression. The 120 kN axle is placed at L1 over the lowest ordinate: 120 × 0.417 = 50.0 kN. The maximum compressive force is therefore 33.3 + 50.0 = 83.3 kN. The flat is slender and cannot carry compression, which suggests that a stress reversal this size requires either a counter diagonal or a stiffer section. The tension case governs the area but this reversal governs the choice of detail.

Answer: 83.3 kN

(d)

The member is designed for the largest tension found in part b, which is 233.3 kN. The allowable stress is 150 MPa, which equals 150 N/mm². The required area follows from stress = force/area, so A = F/σ. Converting the force to newtons gives 233.3 kN = 233 300 N. Then A = 233 300 N / 150 N/mm² = 1555.6 mm². A flat of 1556 mm² is the least area; a practical flat of 100 mm width and 16 mm thickness gives 1600 mm², which is just above the requirement. Net area at the bolt holes must be checked separately, because the gross area found here is not reduced for holes. Dead load tension in the diagonal would add to this demand and must be included in a full design.

Answer: 1556 mm²

Problem 3 [A1-033] Maximum shear and moment envelope under a moving wheel train

A mine-site maintenance gantry in the Sudbury basin is a simply supported steel girder of 15.0 m span. A three-axle service carriage rolls along it. Measured along the carriage, the axle loads are 70 kN, then 110 kN at 3.0 m behind it, then 110 kN at a further 4.5 m behind that. The carriage can cross in either direction, and the girder self weight is ignored for this question. Axles may roll on or off the span, so both full and partial loading must be considered. Girder steel is designed for an allowable bending stress of 160 MPa in the elastic range, and the contractor needs the shear at the supports, the single worst bending moment anywhere, and the required elastic section modulus.

  1. (a) Locate the resultant of the three axle loads, measured from the 70 kN axle toward the rear. [4]
  2. (b) Find the absolute maximum bending moment in the girder. [7]
  3. (c) Find the maximum shear force at a support. [4]
  4. (d) Find the minimum elastic section modulus needed, in 10³ mm³, at the allowable stress. [5]
(a)

The total of the three axle loads is R = 70 + 110 + 110 = 290 kN. To locate the resultant, take moments about the 70 kN axle, measuring distance toward the rear. The 110 kN axles are at 3.0 m and 7.5 m behind it, so ΣP·d = 70 × 0 + 110 × 3.0 + 110 × 7.5 = 330 + 825 = 1155 kN·m. Then the resultant sits at x̄ = 1155/290 = 3.983 m behind the 70 kN axle. The resultant lies 0.983 m beyond the first 110 kN axle, between the two heavy axles and nearer the first. This distance is the key to the absolute maximum moment, because the moment peaks under the load that is closest to the resultant when the midspan bisects that gap.

Answer: 3.983 m

(b)

The absolute maximum moment occurs under a heavy axle when the centreline of the span bisects the distance between that axle and the resultant. Try the first 110 kN axle, which is 0.983 m from the resultant. Place that axle 0.491 m to one side of midspan, at 7.009 m from the near support, and the resultant 0.491 m on the other side. The 70 kN axle then stands at 4.009 m and the second 110 kN axle at 11.509 m. Taking moments about the far support gives the near reaction R_A = [70 × (15 − 4.009) + 110 × (15 − 7.009) + 110 × (15 − 11.509)]/15 = (769.4 + 879.0 + 384.0)/15 = 135.5 kN. Moment under the axle: M = 135.5 × 7.009 − 70 × 3.0 = 739.7 kN·m. The other two axles give smaller moments, so this is the absolute maximum.

Answer: 739.7 kN·m

(c)

The maximum support shear equals the largest reaction. It occurs with as much load as possible on the span and the heaviest load right over the support. Place a 110 kN axle directly on support A with the carriage heading in from that end, so the loads on the span are 110 kN at 0, 110 kN at 4.5 m and 70 kN at 7.5 m. Taking moments about B: R_B = (110 × 4.5 + 70 × 7.5)/15 = (495 + 525)/15 = 68.0 kN. Then R_A = 290 − 68.0 = 222.0 kN. The opposite order, with the 70 kN axle at the support, gives only 213.0 kN, and the carriage with one axle off the span gives less, so 222.0 kN is the maximum shear at a support.

Answer: 222.0 kN

(d)

The elastic section modulus needed is Z = M/σ_allow, with the moment in N·mm and the stress in N/mm². The maximum moment is 739.7 kN·m = 739.7 × 10⁶ N·mm, and the allowable stress is 160 MPa = 160 N/mm². Therefore Z = 739.7 × 10⁶/160 = 4.623 × 10⁶ mm³, which is 4623 × 10³ mm³. A rolled wide-flange beam with at least this section modulus about its major axis can carry the carriage, and since the self weight of the girder was ignored, the chosen section should have a margin of several percent for it. The maximum shear of 222 kN is then checked separately against the web area of the chosen shape.

Answer: 4623 ×10³ mm³

Problem 4 [A1-034] Beam deflection by double integration

A steel bracket beam projects 3.2 m horizontally from a concrete wall at a loading dock in Windsor. It is fully fixed at the wall and free at the other end. It carries a uniformly distributed load of 12 kN/m over its whole length, from a conveyor deck, and a downward point load of 8 kN at the free end from a hanging hoist. The material is steel with E = 200 GPa and the beam has constant flexural rigidity. The cross-section initially chosen has I = 85 × 10⁶ mm⁴. The owner requires that the free-end deflection stay within the span divided by 180, to avoid damage to the conveyor, and the designer must find whether the first section works and size one that does.

  1. (a) By double integration, find the free-end deflection for the section with I = 85 × 10⁶ mm⁴. [6]
  2. (b) Find the slope at the free end. [4]
  3. (c) Find the deflection at 1.6 m from the free end. [5]
  4. (d) Find the least moment of inertia, in 10⁶ mm⁴, for which the free-end deflection does not exceed L/180. [5]
(a)

Measure s from the free end. The bending moment at s is M = −(P s + w s²/2), hogging. The curvature equation is EI y'' = P s + w s²/2 with deflection y taken downward. Integrating once gives EI y' = P s²/2 + w s³/6 + C1, and the fixed end gives y' = 0 at s = L, so C1 = −(P L²/2 + w L³/6). Integrating again gives EI y = P s³/6 + w s⁴/24 + C1 s + C2, and y = 0 at s = L gives C2 = P L³/3 + w L⁴/8. At s = 0 the first three terms vanish, so EI y = C2 = P L³/3 + w L⁴/8 = 8(32.768)/3 + 12(104.858)/8 = 87.38 + 157.29 = 244.67 kN·m³. EI = 200 × 10⁶ kPa × 85 × 10⁻⁶ m⁴ = 17 000 kN·m². Then y = 244.67/17 000 = 14.39 mm.

Answer: 14.39 mm

(b)

Slope is the first integral. At the free end s = 0 the term P s²/2 + w s³/6 vanishes, so EI y' = C1, which has magnitude P L²/2 + w L³/6. Substituting, P L²/2 = 8 × 10.24/2 = 40.96 kN·m² and w L³/6 = 12 × 32.768/6 = 65.54 kN·m². Their sum is 106.50 kN·m². With EI = 17 000 kN·m² the slope is 106.50/17 000 = 0.006264 rad, about 0.36 degrees. The tip rotates downward in the direction of the deflection. The slope is a useful check on part a, because for a cantilever the deflection at the tip is always of the order of two thirds of the length times the slope, and 0.6667 × 3.2 × 0.006264 = 13.4 mm lies close to 14.4 mm.

Answer: 0.00626 rad

(c)

Using the integration constants, at s = 1.6 m from the free end, EI y = P s³/6 + w s⁴/24 + C1 s + C2. With the values from parts a and b, C1 = −106.496 kN·m² and C2 = +244.67 kN·m³. The terms are P s³/6 = 8 × 4.096/6 = 5.461, w s⁴/24 = 12 × 6.5536/24 = 3.277, C1 s = −106.496 × 1.6 = −170.39, giving EI y = 5.461 + 3.277 − 170.39 + 244.67 = 83.02 kN·m³. Dividing by EI = 17 000 kN·m² gives y = 4.883 mm. This is about one third of the tip deflection, as expected for a cantilever, where deflection grows rapidly toward the free end.

Answer: 4.88 mm

(d)

The limit is L/180 = 3200/180 = 17.78 mm. The first section gave 14.39 mm, which is within this limit, so it works, and this part asks for the least section that just meets the limit. The tip deflection is 244.67 kN·m³/(E I), so I = 244.67/(E × 0.017778). With E = 200 × 10⁶ kPa, I = 244.67/(200 × 10⁶ × 0.017778) = 6.881 × 10⁻⁵ m⁴. This equals 68.8 × 10⁶ mm⁴. The 85 × 10⁶ mm⁴ section therefore has a 24 percent reserve in stiffness. A lighter section with I of about 69 × 10⁶ mm⁴ would just pass, but bending strength must be checked too.

Answer: 68.8 ×10⁶ mm⁴

Problem 5 [A1-035] Beam deflection by the moment-area method

A steel crane-rail beam in a Thunder Bay paper mill is simply supported over a span of 10.0 m with a pin at A and a roller at B. A single trolley wheel load of 80 kN acts at 4.0 m from A. Self weight is small enough to ignore here. The section trial has E = 200 GPa and I = 240 × 10⁶ mm⁴, constant along the span. The rail supplier asks that the midspan deflection stay within span/360 so that the trolley does not creep downhill toward the load. Use the moment-area theorems, not tables, to find the deflection, and then size the beam for the limit.

  1. (a) Find the slope at A for the trial section. [5]
  2. (b) Find the deflection at midspan for the trial section. [7]
  3. (c) Find the least moment of inertia, in 10⁶ mm⁴, so the midspan deflection does not exceed span/360. [5]
  4. (d) State whether the trial section passes, giving the ratio of provided I to required I. [3]
(a)

Reactions: R_A = 80 × 6/10 = 48 kN and R_B = 32 kN. The moment peaks under the load at M = 48 × 4 = 192 kN·m. The M/EI diagram is a triangle with base 10 m. Use the second moment-area theorem: the deviation of B from the tangent at A is t_B/A = moment of the M/EI area about B. The left piece has area ½ × 4 × 192 = 384 and its centroid is 6 + 4/3 = 7.333 m from B, giving 2816. The right piece has area ½ × 6 × 192 = 576, and its centroid lies two thirds of the way from the zero end at B toward the peak, so 4.0 m from B, giving 2304. Total 5120 kN·m³ divided by EI. The slope at A is t_B/A divided by L: θ_A = 5120/(10 EI) = 512/EI. With EI = 200 × 10⁶ × 240 × 10⁻⁶ = 48 000 kN·m², θ_A = 0.010667 rad.

Answer: 0.01067 rad

(b)

Midspan is at 5.0 m, where M = 48 × 5 − 80 × 1 = 160 kN·m. The deflection below the tangent at A is the deviation t_mid/A, the moment of the M/EI area between A and midspan about the midspan section. The triangle from A to the load has area 384 and centroid 2/3 × 4 = 2.667 m from A, so 5 − 2.667 = 2.333 m from midspan, giving 896. The trapezoid from 4 to 5 m has a rectangle 160 × 1 = 160 at 0.5 m and a triangle ½ × 1 × 32 = 16 at 0.667 m, giving 80 + 10.67 = 90.67. So t = 986.67 kN·m³/EI. The tangent line at A drops θ_A × 5 = 2560/EI at midspan, so the deflection is (2560 − 986.67)/EI = 1573.33/EI = 1573.33/48 000 = 32.78 mm. The closed form Pa(L−x)(2Lx−x²−a²)/(6EIL) gives the same value.

Answer: 32.78 mm

(c)

The limit is span/360 = 10 000 mm/360 = 27.78 mm. The midspan deflection in kN·m³ is 1573.33 divided by EI, a result that came from the moment-area work in part b and is independent of the section. Setting 1573.33/(E I) = 0.027778 m gives I = 1573.33/(200 × 10⁶ × 0.027778). The denominator is 5.5556 × 10⁶ kN/m, so I = 2.832 × 10⁻⁴ m⁴, or 283.2 × 10⁶ mm⁴. This is the stiffness needed for the deflection limit alone. Strength and web shear are not considered here, and the self weight of the beam adds a few more millimetres of deflection that the final selection must allow for.

Answer: 283.2 ×10⁶ mm⁴

(d)

The trial section has I = 240 × 10⁶ mm⁴ and the required value from part c is 283.2 × 10⁶ mm⁴. The ratio is 240/283.2 = 0.847. Because the ratio is below 1.0, the trial section does not pass the span/360 deflection limit, which is consistent with part b, where the computed 32.78 mm exceeds the 27.78 mm limit; indeed 27.78/32.78 = 0.847. A larger section is needed, with at least 283.2 × 10⁶ mm⁴ of inertia, and more again to absorb the beam's own weight, which adds deflection of a few millimetres at midspan. Any replacement shape must also check for shear and bending strength.

Answer: 0.85, the trial section does not pass

A1 Practice Paper 8

Problem 1 [A1-036] Beam deflection by the conjugate beam method

A pedestrian bridge stringer in Kingston is simply supported over 8.0 m with a pin at A and a roller at B. Cover plates were welded to the right half only, so the left half, from A to midspan, has flexural rigidity EI and the right half, from midspan to B, has 2EI. For the left half, E = 200 GPa and I = 120 × 10⁶ mm⁴. A uniformly distributed load of 16 kN/m acts over the whole span. The municipality sets a limit of 20 mm on the largest deflection anywhere along the stringer, and the designer must work out how stiff the left half has to be, keeping the right half at exactly twice the left. Use the conjugate beam method, with the M/EI diagram as the load.

  1. (a) Find the slope of the stringer at A. [5]
  2. (b) Find the deflection at midspan. [5]
  3. (c) Find the maximum deflection along the stringer. [5]
  4. (d) Find the left-half moment of inertia, in 10⁶ mm⁴, that holds the maximum deflection to 20 mm if the right half stays at twice the left. [5]
(a)

The real beam has M = 8x(8 − x) kN·m, from R_A = 64 kN. The conjugate beam is simply supported and carries M/EI, which is M/EI over the left half and M/2EI over the right half. Its loads, in units of 1/EI, are: left half area = ∫ 8x(8 − x) dx from 0 to 4 = 341.3, with centroid moment ∫ x·8x(8 − x) dx = 853.3 about A; right half area = 341.3/2 = 170.7, with moment about A of 938.7. The conjugate reaction at B is (853.3 + 938.7)/8 = 224.0, so at A it is 341.3 + 170.7 − 224.0 = 288.0. The real slope equals the conjugate shear: θ_A = 288.0/EI = 288.0/24 000 = 0.0120 rad, using EI = 200 × 10⁶ kPa × 120 × 10⁻⁶ m⁴ = 24 000 kN·m².

Answer: 0.0120 rad

(b)

Deflection equals the conjugate bending moment, so cut the conjugate beam at midspan, x = 4 m, and take moments of the forces on its left part. The conjugate reaction 288.0/EI acts up at A with an arm of 4 m, giving 1152.0/EI. The conjugate load on the left half has area 341.3 with centroid at 2.5 m from A, so its moment about the cut is 341.3 × (4 − 2.5) = 512.0. Therefore the conjugate moment at midspan is (1152.0 − 512.0)/EI = 640.0/EI. The real deflection is y = 640.0/24 000 = 0.02667 m = 26.67 mm. The sign is downward because the conjugate moment is positive. A uniform beam of rigidity EI would deflect 5wL⁴/(384EI) = 35.6 mm at midspan, so the stiffer right half reduces this, but it also pushes the point of largest deflection toward the softer left half.

Answer: 26.67 mm

(c)

The maximum deflection is where the real slope is zero, which is where the conjugate shear is zero. The maximum lies in the softer left half. In the left half the conjugate shear is 288.0 − 8(4x² − x³/3) = 0, so 4x² − x³/3 = 36, or x³ − 12x² + 108 = 0. Solving by trial gives x = 3.582 m, since at 3.58 the left side is 45.9 − 153.8 + 108 = 0.1, very close to zero. The conjugate moment there is M' = 288.0x − 8(4x³/3 − x⁴/12) with x = 3.582: 1031.6 − 8(47.55) = 1031.6 − 380.4 = 651.2/EI. Then y = 651.2/24 000 = 27.13 mm. This exceeds the 20 mm limit by 36 percent, so the stringer fails as built and the left half must be stiffened.

Answer: 27.13 mm

(d)

For a fixed ratio of 2 between the two halves, the deflection is inversely proportional to the left-half rigidity. Changing I changes every conjugate load by the same factor, so the shape of the deflected curve is the same and only its size scales with 1/I. At 120 × 10⁶ mm⁴ the maximum deflection is 27.13 mm. To reach 20 mm, I must be multiplied by 27.13/20 = 1.3565. The required left-half value is 120 × 1.3565 = 162.8 × 10⁶ mm⁴, and the right half needs 325.6 × 10⁶ mm⁴. The location of the maximum, at 3.58 m, stays where it is. In practice the extra stiffness is easiest to add by thickening the cover plates and extending them over the left half.

Answer: 162.8 ×10⁶ mm⁴

Problem 2 [A1-037] Truss deflection by virtual work (unit load)

A roof truss over an arena concourse in Ottawa has bottom joints A, B and C at 0, 6.0 m and 12.0 m along a horizontal line, and top joints D and E at 3.0 m and 9.0 m along, each 4.0 m above the bottom line. The members are AB, BC, DE, AD, DB, BE and EC. Joint A is a pin and joint C is a roller. A mechanical unit hanging at B applies 90 kN downward, and a wind gust applies 36 kN horizontally to the right at D. All members have the same cross-sectional area and E = 200 GPa. A trial area of 2500 mm² is proposed, but the vertical movement of B must not exceed 2.0 mm so that a rigid duct below it is not stressed.

  1. (a) Find the vertical reaction at C. [4]
  2. (b) Find the force in member BE, positive for tension. [5]
  3. (c) By the unit load method, find the vertical deflection of B for the trial area of 2500 mm². [6]
  4. (d) Find the least common area, in mm², that holds the vertical movement of B to 2.0 mm. [5]
(a)

Treat the whole truss as a rigid body on the pin at A and the roller at C. The roller gives only a vertical reaction C_y. Take moments about A, counterclockwise positive. The 90 kN load at B has an arm of 6.0 m and the 36 kN wind load at D acts at a height of 4.0 m above A. The vertical load turns the truss clockwise about A, and so does the wind force pushing right at a height above A. So C_y × 12 = 90 × 6 + 36 × 4 = 540 + 144 = 684 kN·m, giving C_y = 57.0 kN upward. Then A_y = 90 − 57 = 33.0 kN and A_x = 36 kN to the left. The wind adds 12 kN to the right-hand reaction compared with gravity alone.

Answer: 57.0 kN

(b)

Use the method of joints, starting at C where only two members meet. Member EC runs 3 m across and 4 m up, length 5 m, so its vertical component is 4/5 of its force. Vertically at C: 57.0 = 0.8 F_EC, so F_EC = 71.25 kN, compression because it pushes down on the joint. Horizontally, the horizontal component 0.6 × 71.25 = 42.75 kN pushes C to the right, so BC is in tension at 42.75 kN. At joint E, member EC pushes up with 0.8 × 71.25 = 57.0 kN. Member BE, if in tension, pulls E toward B, down and to the left with vertical component 0.8 F_BE. Vertical balance gives 57.0 = 0.8 F_BE, so F_BE = 71.25 kN tension.

Answer: 71.25 kN

(c)

Apply a unit downward load at B on the unloaded truss. By symmetry the reactions are 0.5 each, and the member forces f are: AB 0.375 T, BC 0.375 T, DE 0.750 C, AD 0.625 C, DB 0.625 T, BE 0.625 T and EC 0.625 C. The real forces F are AB 60.75 T, BC 42.75 T, DE 85.5 C, AD 41.25 C, DB 41.25 T, BE 71.25 T and EC 71.25 C. Compression is negative, so the products F·f·L, in kN²·m, are AB 136.7, BC 96.2, DE 384.8, AD 128.9, DB 128.9, BE 222.7 and EC 222.7. Their sum is 1320.8. With AE = 2500 × 10⁻⁶ m² × 200 × 10⁶ kPa = 500 000 kN, Δ_B = 1320.8/500 000 = 2.64 mm downward.

Answer: 2.64 mm

(d)

With all members the same, the deflection is Δ = ΣFfL/(A E), so it is inversely proportional to A. The sum ΣFfL = 1320.75 kN²·m does not depend on A. Set Δ = 0.0020 m and solve: A = 1320.75/(200 × 10⁶ × 0.0020) = 1320.75/400 000 = 3.302 × 10⁻³ m² = 3302 mm². The trial 2500 mm² therefore gives 2.64 mm, which is 32 percent over the limit, and a common area of 3302 mm² is the least that meets it. A designer would round up to a standard tube or angle pair, and might also use bigger sections only in the high-stress members, DE, BE and EC, which contribute the most to the sum.

Answer: 3302 mm²

Problem 3 [A1-038] Beam and frame deflection by virtual work

A steel support frame carries a signal mast on a rooftop in Kingston. It is an L-shaped rigid frame. Column AB is vertical, 4.0 m high, and fully fixed at its base A. Beam BC runs horizontally 3.0 m from the top of the column at B to the free end C, with a rigid joint at B. At C, the mast base applies a downward force of 20 kN and a wind force of 10 kN horizontally, pointing away from the column. The material is steel with E = 200 GPa and the frame has constant I = 150 × 10⁶ mm⁴ throughout. Neglect axial and shear deformation. The owner limits horizontal sway at C to the column height divided by 300 so that the mast stays aligned.

  1. (a) Find the moment reaction at the fixed base A. [4]
  2. (b) By virtual work, find the horizontal deflection of C. [7]
  3. (c) By virtual work, find the vertical deflection of C. [5]
  4. (d) Find the moment of inertia, in 10⁶ mm⁴, needed to hold the horizontal sway at C to H/300 with the same loads. [4]
(a)

Take moments of the applied loads about the base A. The 20 kN vertical load is 3.0 m from the column axis, so it gives 20 × 3.0 = 60 kN·m. The 10 kN horizontal load acts at the level of the beam, 4.0 m above A, so it gives 10 × 4.0 = 40 kN·m. Both tend to turn the frame the same way, clockwise as the loads are drawn, so the fixed-end moment at A that balances them is 60 + 40 = 100 kN·m counterclockwise. The base also carries a vertical reaction of 20 kN and a horizontal reaction of 10 kN. This moment is also the maximum bending moment in the column, which is a check on strength.

Answer: 100.0 kN·m

(b)

Apply a virtual unit horizontal load at C, in the direction of the real horizontal force. In the beam it passes along the beam axis and produces no bending moment, so only the column counts. Measure u down the column from joint B, so u = 4 − y where y is the height above A. Real moment in the column M = 60 + 10u. Virtual moment m = u. Then Δ_h = (1/EI) ∫₀⁴ (60 + 10u) u du = (1/EI)(30 × 16 + 10 × 64/3) = (480 + 213.3)/EI = 693.3 kN·m³/EI. EI = 200 × 10⁶ kPa × 150 × 10⁻⁶ m⁴ = 30 000 kN·m². Δ_h = 693.3/30 000 = 0.02311 m = 23.11 mm, to the right, the way the wind force acts.

Answer: 23.11 mm

(c)

Apply a virtual unit vertical load at C acting downward. In the beam, at distance s from C, the virtual moment is m = s and the real moment is M = 20 s, since the wind load acts along the beam axis. In the column the virtual moment is constant at 3.0, and the real moment is 60 + 10u. The beam contributes ∫₀³ 20 s × s ds = 20 × 9 = 180. The column contributes ∫₀⁴ (60 + 10u) × 3.0 du = 3.0 × (240 + 80) = 960. The total is 1140 kN·m³. Dividing by EI = 30 000 kN·m² gives Δ_v = 0.0380 m = 38.0 mm downward, with the sign positive because it matches the virtual load direction.

Answer: 38.0 mm

(d)

The limit is H/300 = 4000/300 = 13.33 mm. The horizontal deflection varies inversely with EI, and the virtual work integral 693.3 kN·m³ does not depend on the section. So I = 693.3/(E × 0.013333) with E in kPa. This gives I = 693.3/(200 × 10⁶ × 0.013333) = 693.3/2.6667 × 10⁶ = 2.600 × 10⁻⁴ m⁴, which is 260.0 × 10⁶ mm⁴. The present frame has 150 × 10⁶ mm⁴, so the stiffness must rise by a factor of 1.73. The vertical deflection would then be 1140/(200 × 10⁶ × 2.6 × 10⁻⁴) = 21.9 mm. A deeper column, which carries most of the sway demand, is the efficient way to gain stiffness.

Answer: 260.0 ×10⁶ mm⁴

Problem 4 [A1-039] Deflection by strain energy and Castigliano's theorem

A wall bracket carries an illuminated sign outside a transit station in Mississauga. Two pin-jointed bars meet at joint B. Bar AB is horizontal, 2.4 m long, and pinned to the wall at A. Bar CB runs from a wall pin at C, which is 1.8 m directly below A, up to B, so its length is 3.0 m. A sign applies a downward load P = 45 kN at B. Bar AB has area 800 mm² and bar CB has area 1500 mm². Both are steel with E = 200 GPa. Use strain energy and Castigliano's theorem, adding a small horizontal dummy load Q at B where needed. The designer must keep the vertical movement of B to 2.0 mm by changing only the area of AB.

  1. (a) Find the force in the strut CB for P = 45 kN, as a positive compression. [3]
  2. (b) Using Castigliano's theorem, find the vertical deflection of B. [6]
  3. (c) Using a dummy horizontal load Q at B, find the horizontal deflection of B, positive away from the wall. [6]
  4. (d) With the area of CB unchanged, find the least area of AB that limits the vertical deflection of B to 2.0 mm. [5]
(a)

Resolve the forces at joint B. Let T be the tension in AB, pulling B toward the wall, and C the compression in CB, pushing B up and away from C. The strut runs 2.4 m across and 1.8 m up, so its direction cosines are 0.8 horizontally and 0.6 vertically. Vertical equilibrium of B gives 0.6 C = P, so C = 45/0.6 = 75.0 kN. Horizontal equilibrium gives T = 0.8 C = 60.0 kN, so the tie AB is in tension at 60.0 kN. With the dummy load Q to be added later, the strut force stays 1.6667 P, because Q has no vertical component, while the tie force becomes 1.3333 P + Q.

Answer: 75.0 kN

(b)

The strain energy of the pair is U = F_AB² L_AB/(2 A_AB E) + F_CB² L_CB/(2 A_CB E). Castigliano's theorem gives the vertical deflection as ∂U/∂P = Σ F (∂F/∂P) L/(A E). With F_AB = 1.3333 P and F_CB = 1.6667 P, ∂F_AB/∂P = 1.3333 and ∂F_CB/∂P = 1.6667. For AB: 60.0 × 1.3333 × 2.4/(800 × 10⁻⁶ × 200 × 10⁶) = 192.0/160 000 = 1.20 × 10⁻³ m. For CB: 75.0 × 1.6667 × 3.0/(1500 × 10⁻⁶ × 200 × 10⁶) = 375.0/300 000 = 1.25 × 10⁻³ m. The sum is 2.45 × 10⁻³ m = 2.45 mm downward.

Answer: 2.45 mm

(c)

Add a horizontal dummy load Q at B, acting away from the wall. The joint equations become 0.6 C = P and T = 0.8 C + Q, so C is unchanged at 1.6667 P and T = 1.3333 P + Q. Then ∂F_AB/∂Q = 1 and ∂F_CB/∂Q = 0. Castigliano gives Δ_h = ∂U/∂Q = F_AB (∂F_AB/∂Q) L_AB/(A_AB E), evaluated at Q = 0, because the strut term is multiplied by zero. This is 60.0 × 1 × 2.4/(800 × 10⁻⁶ × 200 × 10⁶) = 144.0/160 000 = 0.90 × 10⁻³ m. The deflection is positive, so B moves 0.90 mm away from the wall, because the tie lengthens. The strut does not contribute since its force does not depend on Q.

Answer: 0.90 mm

(d)

From part b the strut term of the vertical deflection is fixed at 1.25 mm, because the area of CB is unchanged. The tie term must then supply no more than 2.0 − 1.25 = 0.75 mm. The tie term is F_AB (∂F_AB/∂P) L/(A_AB E) = 60.0 × 1.3333 × 2.4/(A_AB × 200 × 10⁶) = 192.0/(200 × 10⁶ A_AB). Set it equal to 0.75 × 10⁻³ m: A_AB = 192.0/(200 × 10⁶ × 0.75 × 10⁻³) = 192.0/150 000 = 1.28 × 10⁻³ m² = 1280 mm². The stress in the tie then falls to 60 000/1280 = 46.9 MPa, well within yield. The trial area of 800 mm² was therefore too small for the stiffness limit even though it was ample for strength.

Answer: 1280 mm²

Problem 5 [A1-040] Force method for one-degree indeterminate beams

A steel girder on an overpass near Barrie is built into the south abutment at A, which acts as a fixed support, and rests on a roller bearing on a pier at B, 8.0 m from A. A single heavy wheel load of 96 kN acts 5.0 m from A. The girder has E = 200 GPa and I = 1200 × 10⁶ mm⁴ along its length. Use the force method, taking the roller reaction at B as the redundant. The pier bearing may settle after construction because of soft soil, and the owner wants to know how much settlement the abutment connection can tolerate if the fixed-end moment at A is not to exceed 150 kN·m.

  1. (a) Find the reaction at B if the pier does not move. [5]
  2. (b) Find the magnitude of the fixed-end moment at A if the pier does not move. [4]
  3. (c) Find the reaction at B if the pier settles 12.0 mm. [5]
  4. (d) Find the settlement of B, in mm, at which the fixed-end moment at A reaches 150 kN·m. [6]
(a)

Remove the roller at B to leave a cantilever fixed at A. The redundant is R_B. Compatibility requires the net deflection at B to be zero. The load P = 96 kN at a = 5.0 m from the fixed end gives a deflection at B of Δ_BP = P a²(3L − a)/(6EI) = 96 × 25 × 19/(6 × 240 000) = 45 600/1 440 000 = 0.03167 m, using EI = 200 × 10⁶ × 1.2 × 10⁻³ = 240 000 kN·m². A unit upward force at B gives a flexibility f_BB = L³/(3EI) = 512/720 000 = 0.000711 m/kN. Compatibility: Δ_BP − f_BB R_B = 0, so R_B = 0.03167/0.000711 = 44.53 kN upward. The reaction is 46 percent of the load.

Answer: 44.53 kN

(b)

With R_B known, statics gives the rest. Take moments about A for the whole girder. The load produces P a = 96 × 5.0 = 480 kN·m, which the roller reaction partly offsets with R_B L = 44.53 × 8.0 = 356.25 kN·m. The fixed-end moment is M_A = 480 − 356.25 = 123.75 kN·m, hogging at the abutment. The vertical reaction at A is R_A = 96 − 44.53 = 51.47 kN. A check against the cantilever solution for the same load, with no pier, would give a fixed-end moment of 480 kN·m, so the pier removes nearly three quarters of it. The moment under the load is 51.47 × 5 − 123.75 = 133.6 kN·m sagging, which is slightly larger than the fixed-end value.

Answer: 123.75 kN·m

(c)

Settlement lowers the support, so the cantilever tip need only be pushed up by the amount that it deflects minus the settlement. The compatibility equation becomes Δ_BP − f_BB R_B = δ, where δ = 0.012 m is the downward settlement of B. Then R_B = (Δ_BP − δ)/f_BB = (0.03167 − 0.01200)/0.000711 = 0.01967/0.000711 = 27.66 kN. A settlement of 12 mm therefore removes 16.9 kN of the pier reaction, shedding load onto the abutment. The fixed-end moment goes up to 480 − 8.0 × 27.66 = 258.7 kN·m, more than double its no-settlement value. This shows why a continuous or propped member is more sensitive to support movement than a determinate one.

Answer: 27.66 kN

(d)

The fixed-end moment is M_A = P a − R_B L, so for M_A = 150 kN·m we need R_B L = 480 − 150 = 330, giving R_B = 41.25 kN. Now use compatibility: δ = Δ_BP − f_BB R_B = 0.03167 − 0.000711 × 41.25 = 0.03167 − 0.02933 = 0.00233 m. The settlement at which the moment reaches the limit is therefore 2.33 mm. Settlement larger than this makes M_A exceed 150 kN·m, because every extra millimetre lowers R_B by about 1.41 kN and raises M_A by about 11.3 kN·m. The abutment connection is thus very sensitive; a pier on soft soil should be piled or the connection designed for a bigger moment.

Answer: 2.33 mm

A1 Practice Paper 9

Problem 1 [A1-041] Force method for indeterminate trusses

A bracing panel in a steel gantry used to lift formwork at a Sudbury mine headframe is modelled as a pin-jointed rectangular truss ABCD, 4.0 m wide (A to B along the bottom chord) and 3.0 m high (A to D up the left post). Joint A is a pin and joint B is a roller that restrains vertical movement only. Members AB, BC, CD and DA form the outer frame, and two diagonals AC and BD cross inside the panel without being connected where they cross. A horizontal wind force of 60 kN acts at D, pointing toward the right side of the panel (the direction from A toward B). Every member except AC has a cross-sectional area of 1200 mm², and E = 200 GPa for all members. The designer may choose the area of diagonal AC.

  1. (a) Take the force in diagonal AC as the redundant and remove AC. Find the force in diagonal BD in the remaining determinate truss (magnitude, in kN). [5]
  2. (b) With AC also of area 1200 mm², find the force X in AC in the real truss (kN, tension positive). [6]
  3. (c) Find the magnitude of the force in diagonal BD in the real truss. [4]
  4. (d) The designer wants AC to carry exactly 40 kN of tension. Find the required cross-sectional area of AC, in mm², with all other members unchanged. [5]
(a)

The truss is externally determinate (three reactions) and has one extra bar internally, so it is indeterminate to the first degree. Reactions: moments about A give By × 4.0 = 60 × 3.0, so By = 45 kN upward; ΣFy gives Ay = 45 kN downward; ΣFx gives Ax = 60 kN toward the left. With AC removed, joint C joins only BC and CD, which are not collinear and carry no load, so both are zero. At joint D the bars are CD (zero), DA (vertical) and BD (slope 3 to 4, length 5.0 m). ΣFx at D: 60 + 0.8 F_BD = 0, so F_BD = −75.0 kN, which means 75.0 kN of compression. DA then carries 45 kN tension from the vertical balance.

Answer: 75.0 kN compression

(b)

Apply a unit tension pair along AC and solve the joints. Joint C gives f_CD = −0.8 and f_BC = −0.6; joint A gives f_AB = −0.8 and f_DA = −0.6; joint B then gives f_BD = +1.0. The primary forces (AC removed) are F_AB = 60 and F_DA = 45 tension and F_BD = −75, all others zero. Compatibility needs zero relative movement of the cut ends of AC: X Σf²L/AE + Σf F0 L/AE = 0. Σ f F0 L = (−0.8)(60)(4) + (−0.6)(45)(3) + (1)(−75)(5) = −192 − 81 − 375 = −648. Σ f² L = 0.64×4 + 0.36×3 + 0.64×4 + 0.36×3 + 5 + 5 = 17.28, and AE is the same in every bar so it cancels. X = 648 / 17.28 = 37.5 kN tension.

Answer: 37.5 kN tension

(c)

Superpose the primary state and X times the unit state: F = F0 + X f. For BD: F_BD = −75.0 + 37.5 × 1.0 = −37.5 kN, so BD carries 37.5 kN of compression, half what it carried when AC was removed. The remaining bars follow the same way: AB = 60 − 30 = 30 kN tension, DA = 45 − 22.5 = 22.5 kN tension, BC = −22.5 kN, CD = −30 kN. Check at joint D: ΣFx = 60 + F_CD + 0.8 F_BD = 60 − 30 − 30 = 0, and ΣFy = −F_DA − 0.6 F_BD = −22.5 + 22.5 = 0. Both balance, so the redundant force and the superposition are consistent.

Answer: 37.5 kN compression

(d)

Let the area of AC be A_c (mm²) while the other five bars stay at 1200 mm². In the compatibility equation the common factor E and the 1200 mm² unit cancel, so X = 648 / [12.28 + 5.0 × (1200 / A_c)]. The number 12.28 is the sum of f²L for the five bars other than AC: 2.56 + 1.08 + 2.56 + 1.08 + 5.0. Setting X = 40 kN gives 12.28 + 6000 / A_c = 648 / 40 = 16.2, so 6000 / A_c = 3.92 and A_c = 1530.6 mm². The force in AC can never exceed 648 / 12.28 = 52.8 kN however large the area is made, so the 40 kN target sits inside the achievable range.

Answer: 1531 mm²

Problem 2 [A1-042] Slope-deflection method for continuous beams

A continuous steel girder on an Ottawa pedestrian overpass has two spans, AB = 6.0 m and BC = 5.0 m. End A is fully fixed into an abutment, B rests on a pier and C is a roller at an expansion end where the bending moment is zero. Flexural rigidity is EI = 12 000 kN·m² throughout, and there is no support settlement. Span AB carries a uniformly distributed load of 24 kN/m, and span BC carries a single 80 kN point load 2.0 m from B. The pier cap at B was detailed for a hogging moment of no more than 100 kN·m. Use the slope-deflection method with the modified stiffness for the pinned end C.

  1. (a) Find the rotation of joint B in milliradians (magnitude). [5]
  2. (b) Find the hogging moment at B. [5]
  3. (c) Find the vertical reaction at A. [4]
  4. (d) With the 80 kN load unchanged, find the largest uniformly distributed load on AB for which the hogging moment at B stays within 100 kN·m. [6]
(a)

Counter-clockwise end moments and rotations are taken as positive. Only θB is unknown, since θA = 0 and the settlements are zero. Fixed-end moments: AB carries wL²/12 = 24(36)/12 = 72, so FEM_AB = +72 and FEM_BA = −72. BC with the point load has FEM_BC = Pab²/L² = 80(2)(9)/25 = +57.6 and FEM_CB = −Pa²b/L² = −38.4. Because the moment at C is zero, use the modified form M_BC = (3EI/5)θB + FEM_BC − FEM_CB/2 = 0.6 EIθB + 57.6 + 19.2. Also M_BA = (4EI/6)θB − 72. Joint equilibrium M_BA + M_BC = 0 gives (0.6667 + 0.6) EIθB + 4.8 = 0, so EIθB = −3.789 kN·m². Then θB = −3.789 / 12 000 = −0.316 × 10⁻³ rad, a clockwise rotation of 0.316 mrad.

Answer: 0.316 mrad clockwise

(b)

Substitute EIθB = −3.789 into the end-moment equations. M_BA = 0.6667(−3.789) − 72 = −74.53 kN·m; the negative sign means a clockwise end moment on the left span at B, which is hogging. Check from the right span: M_BC = 0.6(−3.789) + 76.8 = +74.53 kN·m, equal and opposite, so joint B is in balance. The hogging moment at the pier is 74.5 kN·m, inside the 100 kN·m detailed capacity. At the fixed end the moment is M_AB = (2EI/6)θB + 72 = 0.3333(−3.789) + 72 = +70.74 kN·m, counter-clockwise on the member, which is also hogging at the abutment.

Answer: 74.5 kN·m

(c)

Isolate span AB as a free body, with end moments M_AB = +70.74 and M_BA = −74.53 (counter-clockwise positive), the 144 kN resultant of the 24 kN/m load acting 3.0 m from either end, and the unknown vertical reaction V_A at A. Take moments about B, counter-clockwise positive: 70.74 − 74.53 − 6.0 V_A + 144 × 3.0 = 0. The reaction acting up at 6.0 m to the left of B turns clockwise about B, hence the minus sign, while the load turns counter-clockwise. Then 6.0 V_A = 432 − 3.79 = 428.21, so V_A = 71.4 kN upward. That is slightly less than the fixed-fixed value of 72 kN because the hogging at B (74.5 kN·m) is a little larger than the hogging at A (70.7 kN·m), so (70.7 − 74.5)/6 = −0.63 kN is taken off.

Answer: 71.4 kN

(d)

Moment at B is linear in the unknown load w, so write it in terms of w. FEM_BA = −3w and the joint equation becomes 1.2667 EIθB + (−3w + 76.8) = 0, so EIθB = −(76.8 − 3w)/1.2667 = −60.63 + 2.368w. Then M_BA = 0.6667 EIθB − 3w = −40.42 + 1.579w − 3w = −40.42 − 1.421w. At w = 24 this gives −74.5, matching part (b). Setting |M_BA| = 100 gives 40.42 + 1.421w = 100, so w = 59.58 / 1.421 = 41.9 kN/m. The 80 kN load alone already produces 40.4 kN·m of hogging at B, and each kN/m on span AB adds 1.42 kN·m, so the allowable load is limited.

Answer: 41.9 kN/m

Problem 3 [A1-043] Slope-deflection method with support settlement

A two-span reinforced concrete girder on a Thunder Bay highway overpass is continuous over a pin at A, an interior pier at B and a roller at C, with AB = 6.0 m and BC = 8.0 m. It carries a uniformly distributed load of 20 kN/m along its full length, and EI = 60 000 kN·m² is constant. The pier bearing at B sits on jacks so that the engineer can lower it deliberately to relieve the hogging moment over the pier. Assume the supports at A and C stay level. Apply the slope-deflection method with modified stiffness 3EI/L for the pinned ends A and C, taking clockwise moments, rotations and chord rotations as positive.

  1. (a) Bearing B is lowered by 15 mm. Find the rotation of joint B, in milliradians (clockwise). [5]
  2. (b) Find the hogging moment at B after the 15 mm settlement. [5]
  3. (c) Find the vertical reaction at A after the settlement. [4]
  4. (d) Find the settlement of B, in mm, that would reduce the moment at B to zero. [6]
(a)

Clockwise-positive fixed-end moments: span AB, wL²/12 = 60, so FEM_AB = −60 and FEM_BA = +60; span BC, wL²/12 = 106.67, so FEM_BC = −106.67 and FEM_CB = +106.67. With A and C pinned, modify the end at B: FEM_BA' = 60 + 60/2 = 90 and FEM_BC' = −106.67 − 53.33 = −160. Stiffnesses are k1 = 3(60 000)/6 = 30 000 and k2 = 3(60 000)/8 = 22 500 kN·m/rad. Dropping B by 0.015 m turns chord AB clockwise, ψ1 = 0.015/6 = +0.0025 rad, and chord BC counter-clockwise, ψ2 = −0.015/8 = −0.001875 rad. M_BA = 30 000(θB − 0.0025) + 90 and M_BC = 22 500(θB + 0.001875) − 160. Setting the sum to zero: 52 500θB − 75 + 42.19 − 70 = 0, so θB = 102.81/52 500 = 1.958 × 10⁻³ rad.

Answer: 1.958 mrad clockwise

(b)

Put θB = 0.0019583 rad into the left-hand member: M_BA = 30 000(0.0019583 − 0.0025) + 90 = −16.25 + 90 = +73.75 kN·m. A positive clockwise end moment acting on the left span at the pier is a hogging moment. Check from the right span: M_BC = 22 500(0.0019583 + 0.001875) − 160 = 86.25 − 160 = −73.75 kN·m, equal and opposite, so the joint balances. Without settlement the same equations give θB = 1.333 mrad and a hogging moment of 130 kN·m, so the 15 mm drop of the pier has removed 56.25 kN·m, or 43 percent of the original pier moment.

Answer: 73.75 kN·m

(c)

Free body of span AB: the end at A has no moment (pin), the end at B carries the clockwise end moment 73.75 kN·m, and the load is 20 × 6 = 120 kN acting 3.0 m from either end. Take moments about B with counter-clockwise positive. The clockwise end couple counts −73.75, the downward load 120 kN at 3.0 m to the left of B counts +360, and the upward reaction V_A at 6.0 m to the left counts −6.0 V_A. So −73.75 + 360 − 6.0 V_A = 0, and V_A = 286.25 / 6.0 = 47.7 kN upward. A simply supported span would give 60 kN, so the hogging at B has shed 12.3 kN from A onto the pier.

Answer: 47.7 kN

(d)

Keep the settlement Δ (in metres) as a variable. ψ1 = Δ/6 and ψ2 = −Δ/8, so k1ψ1 + k2ψ2 = 5000Δ − 2812.5Δ = 2187.5Δ. The joint equation gives 52 500θB = 2187.5Δ + 70, so θB = 0.0013333 + 0.041667Δ. Then M_BA = 30 000θB − 30 000(Δ/6) + 90 = 40 + 1250Δ − 5000Δ + 90 = 130 − 3750Δ. Setting M_BA = 0 gives Δ = 130 / 3750 = 0.03467 m = 34.7 mm. At Δ = 0 the formula returns 130 kN·m and at 15 mm it returns 73.75 kN·m, matching parts (a) and (b); each millimetre of lowering removes 3.75 kN·m of hogging.

Answer: 34.7 mm

Problem 4 [A1-044] Moment distribution for continuous beams

A three-span continuous concrete beam ABCD carries a mezzanine floor in a Regina distribution warehouse. End A is built into a shear wall (fixed), B and C are interior columns acting as rollers, and D is a simple roller end. The spans are AB = 5.0 m, BC = 6.0 m and CD = 4.0 m, and EI is the same for all spans. Span AB carries 18 kN/m, span BC carries a uniformly distributed load w, and a single 60 kN load acts at the midspan of CD. Analyse by moment distribution using the modified stiffness for the simple end D, with w = 30 kN/m in parts (a) to (c). Counter-clockwise end moments are positive.

  1. (a) Find the distribution factor of member BA at joint B. [4]
  2. (b) Find the final hogging moment at B. [5]
  3. (c) Find the final hogging moment at C. [5]
  4. (d) The hogging moment at C must not exceed 100 kN·m. Find the largest w on span BC that satisfies this, with the other loads unchanged. [6]
(a)

Relative stiffnesses with EI constant. At B: member BA has a fixed far end, so k = 4EI/5.0 = 0.8000 EI; member BC also uses full stiffness since C is a continuous joint, so k = 4EI/6.0 = 0.6667 EI. The sum is 1.4667 EI. The distribution factor of BA is 0.8000 / 1.4667 = 0.5455, and for BC it is 0.4545. At C the factors are, for CB, 0.6667 / (0.6667 + 0.75) = 0.4706, and for CD with its simple far end the modified stiffness 3EI/4.0 = 0.7500 EI gives 0.5294. The factors at each joint sum to 1.000, as they must.

Answer: 0.545

(b)

Fixed-end moments: AB ±wL²/12 = ±37.5; BC ±30(36)/12 = ±90; CD with the simple end released, PL/8 = 30 and the modified FEM_CD = 30 + 30/2 = 45, with no carry-over to D. Joint B starts with FEM_BA + FEM_BC = −37.5 + 90 = 52.5 unbalanced, so the balancing moments are −28.64 to BA and −23.86 to BC, carrying −14.32 to A and −11.93 to C. Joint C starts with −90 + 45 = −45, balancing +21.18 to CB and +23.82 to CD, carrying +10.59 to B. Repeating balance and carry-over until the changes are below 0.1 kN·m converges to M_BA = −73.86 and M_BC = +73.86 kN·m. The hogging moment at B is 73.9 kN·m. The cycles agree with the exact slope-deflection solution.

Answer: 73.9 kN·m

(c)

Continuing the same distribution table to convergence, the end moments at C settle at M_CB = −76.84 and M_CD = +76.84 kN·m, equal and opposite so joint C balances. The negative sign on M_CB is a clockwise moment on the left span at its right end, which is hogging. The hogging moment at C, 76.8 kN·m, is larger than at B because the heavy span BC and the 60 kN load on CD both act on joint C. At the fixed end A the moment is the fixed-end value plus half of the total change at B: M_AB = 37.5 + 0.5(−73.86 + 37.5) = 19.32 kN·m, counter-clockwise on the member. All three support moments are hogging, so the top steel at C is governed by 76.8 kN·m.

Answer: 76.8 kN·m

(d)

Moments from moment distribution are linear in the loads, so the moment at C can be written as a constant from the other loads plus a term proportional to w. Running the same distribution with w = 0 gives M_CB = −15.06 kN·m, and with w = 30 it gives −76.84, so the slope is (76.84 − 15.06)/30 = 2.059 kN·m of hogging per kN/m. Hence |M_CB| = 15.06 + 2.059w. Setting this equal to the 100 kN·m limit gives w = (100 − 15.06)/2.059 = 41.2 kN/m. At that load the hogging at B is 97.9 kN·m, so C governs. Loads above 41.2 kN/m on span BC would push the moment at C beyond what the section was designed to carry.

Answer: 41.2 kN/m

Problem 5 [A1-045] Moment distribution for frames without sidesway

Part of a braced steel frame in a Barrie parking garage is idealised as a single rigid joint B where three members meet. Column AB runs 4.0 m down from B to a fixed base A. Column BD runs 3.0 m up from B to D, which is held against rotation and movement by a stiff transfer girder. Beam BC extends 6.0 m horizontally from B to a pinned end C on a wall bracket. The beam carries 30 kN/m over its full length and has a second moment of area I_b = 2 I_c, where I_c is that of both columns. E is the same everywhere. Joint B cannot translate, so there is no sidesway. Use moment distribution with the modified stiffness for the pinned end C.

  1. (a) Find the distribution factor of column AB at joint B. [4]
  2. (b) Find the final end moment of the beam at B. [5]
  3. (c) Find the moment at the fixed base A. [5]
  4. (d) The designer wants column AB to take only 36 kN·m at its top. Find the required ratio I_b / I_c. [6]
(a)

Stiffness of each member at joint B, written in terms of E I_c. Column AB has a fixed far end, so k = 4EI_c/4.0 = 1.000 E I_c. Column BD also has a fixed far end, so k = 4EI_c/3.0 = 1.333 E I_c. Beam BC has a pinned far end, so the modified stiffness is 3E(2 I_c)/6.0 = 1.000 E I_c. The sum at the joint is 3.333 E I_c. The distribution factor for AB is 1.000 / 3.333 = 0.300, for BC it is also 0.300 and for BD it is 0.400, and the three add to 1.000. A beam stiffer than the columns would pull a larger share of the unbalanced moment into itself, so the factors depend on the ratio I_b / I_c, which is used in part (d).

Answer: 0.300

(b)

With the far end C pinned, the fixed-end moment at B is wL²/8 = 30(36)/8 = 135 kN·m. This already includes the release of the moment at C, so the carry-over from C to B is not used again. Joint B has only this one unbalanced moment of 135 kN·m, so a single balancing step finishes the analysis. The columns take 0.300 × 135 = 40.5 (AB) and 0.400 × 135 = 54.0 (BD), a total of 94.5 kN·m. The final beam end moment at B is 135 − 0.300 × 135 = 94.5 kN·m hogging, which equals the sum of the two column moments, so joint B is in equilibrium: 94.5 = 40.5 + 54.0.

Answer: 94.5 kN·m

(c)

The balancing moment given to column AB at joint B is 0.300 × 135 = 40.5 kN·m. A fixed far end receives half of this by carry-over, so M_AB = 0.5 × 40.5 = 20.25 kN·m at the base. The carry-over from A back to B would only matter if joint B were unbalanced again, which it is not because all other joints are fixed or pinned. The base moment is therefore 20.25 kN·m, half the top moment, with the same curvature sense. The base footing and holding-down bolts at A must be designed for this moment, along with the axial load from the beam reaction and column self weight.

Answer: 20.25 kN·m

(d)

Let r = I_b / I_c. Beam stiffness becomes 3E(r I_c)/6.0 = 0.5 r E I_c, so the stiffness sum at B is 1.000 + 1.333 + 0.5r. The fixed-end moment at B stays 135 kN·m because it does not depend on I. The top moment in column AB is DF_AB × 135, and we need this to equal 36 kN·m, so DF_AB = 36 / 135 = 0.2667. Then 1.000 / (2.333 + 0.5r) = 0.2667, so 2.333 + 0.5r = 3.750 and 0.5r = 1.4167, giving r = 2.83. A stiffer beam than the original 2.0 attracts more of the 135 kN·m at the joint and so shields the columns from moment.

Answer: 2.83

A1 Practice Paper 10

Problem 1 [A1-046] Stiffness, carry-over and fixed-end moments including modified stiffness

At the top of a stair core in a Calgary office tower, three members meet at a rigid joint O, and a heavy cantilevered canopy applies a clockwise moment of 240 kN·m directly to the joint.
