Member OA is 5.0 m long with second moment of area I and a fixed far end A. Member OB is 4.0 m long with the same I and a pinned far end B. Member OC is 6.0 m long with second moment of area 1.5 I and a fixed far end C. Take E = 200 GPa and I = 8.0 × 10⁻⁴ m⁴. The joint can rotate but cannot translate, and no member carries span loading.

  1. (a) Find the rotation of joint O, in milliradians. [5]
  2. (b) Find the moment resisted by member OB at the joint. [4]
  3. (c) Find the moment carried over to the fixed end A. [5]
  4. (d) The designer wants member OA to take only 25 percent of the applied moment. Find the required second moment of area of member OC as a multiple of I. [6]
(a)

Flexural rigidity EI = 200 × 10⁶ × 8.0 × 10⁻⁴ = 160 000 kN·m². Rotational stiffness of each member at O: OA fixed far end, K = 4EI/L = 4(160 000)/5.0 = 128 000 kN·m/rad. OB pinned far end, so the modified stiffness 3EI/L = 3(160 000)/4.0 = 120 000. OC fixed far end with 1.5 EI, K = 4(240 000)/6.0 = 160 000. The members share the same joint rotation, so the sum is K_total = 408 000 kN·m/rad. Since no span loads act, all fixed-end moments are zero and θ = M / ΣK = 240 / 408 000 = 5.882 × 10⁻⁴ rad = 0.588 mrad, in the clockwise sense of the applied moment.

Answer: 0.588 mrad

(b)

Each member resists a share of the applied moment equal to its stiffness times the common joint rotation. For OB: M_OB = K_OB θ = 120 000 × 5.882 × 10⁻⁴ = 70.59 kN·m. The same result comes from the distribution factor: DF_OB = 120 000 / 408 000 = 0.2941, and 0.2941 × 240 = 70.59 kN·m. Because B is pinned, nothing is carried over to B and the whole of this moment is resisted at the joint end. Member OB uses its reduced stiffness 3EI/L rather than 4EI/L, which is why a pinned far end attracts less moment than a fixed one of the same size, 25 percent less here.

Answer: 70.6 kN·m

(c)

Member OA has a fixed far end, so it takes M_OA = K_OA θ = 128 000 × 5.882 × 10⁻⁴ = 75.29 kN·m at O. Check by distribution factor: 128 000 / 408 000 = 0.3137, and 0.3137 × 240 = 75.29. The carry-over factor to a fixed far end is one half, so the moment developed at A is 0.5 × 75.29 = 37.65 kN·m, with the same direction of rotation as at O. The fixed support at A must therefore be designed for a reaction moment of 37.6 kN·m, in addition to any load effects from the other loading cases acting on the frame.

Answer: 37.6 kN·m

(d)

The share taken by OA is DF_OA = K_OA / ΣK, and the target is 0.25. In units of EI: K_OA = 4/5 = 0.800, K_OB = 3/4 = 0.750, and K_OC = 4(nEI)/6 = 0.6667n, where n is the multiple of I. Then 0.800 / (0.800 + 0.750 + 0.6667n) = 0.25, so 1.550 + 0.6667n = 3.200 and 0.6667n = 1.650. Thus n = 2.475, which means OC needs a second moment of area of 2.475 I, or 2.475 × 8.0 × 10⁻⁴ = 1.98 × 10⁻³ m⁴. It is 1.65 times the current value of 1.5 I. A stiffer member OC draws moment away from OA, and OA's share falls from 31 to 25 percent.

Answer: 2.48 I

Problem 2 [A1-047] Least work and energy methods for indeterminate structures

A steel cantilever girder AB, 6.0 m long, supports a crane runway outside a Hamilton steel plant. It is fixed at A and its free end B is held up by a vertical steel tie rod, 4.0 m long, hanging from a rigid roof truss. The rod has area 400 mm² and E = 200 GPa; the girder has EI = 50 000 kN·m². The girder carries a uniformly distributed load of 18 kN/m over its full length, and the rod is exactly taut with no pretension before the load is applied. Treat the girder as bending only, and take the tie force T as the redundant. The anchor-bolt group at A is rated for a moment of 100 kN·m.

  1. (a) Use the theorem of least work to find the tie force T. [6]
  2. (b) Find the hogging moment at the fixed end A. [4]
  3. (c) Find the downward deflection of end B, in mm. [4]
  4. (d) Find the smallest rod area, in mm², for which the moment at A does not exceed the rated 100 kN·m. [6]
(a)

Measure x from B toward A. With the tie force T upward at B, the bending moment is M = Tx − wx²/2, so ∂M/∂T = x. The strain energy is U = ∫M² dx/(2EI) + T²h/(2AE), where h = 4.0 m is the rod length. Least work says ∂U/∂T = 0 because the rod top is on a rigid support: ∫₀ᴸ (Tx − wx²/2) x dx / EI + Th/AE = 0, which gives T L³/(3EI) − wL⁴/(8EI) + Th/AE = 0. Numbers: wL⁴/(8EI) = 18(1296)/(400 000) = 0.05832 m; L³/(3EI) = 216/150 000 = 0.00144 m/kN; h/AE = 4.0/(400 × 10⁻⁶ × 200 × 10⁶) = 5.0 × 10⁻⁵ m/kN. T = 0.05832 / (0.00144 + 0.00005) = 39.14 kN.

Answer: 39.1 kN

(b)

The moment at the fixed end is the value of M at x = L = 6.0 m: M_A = TL − wL²/2 = 39.14(6.0) − 18(36)/2 = 234.85 − 324.0 = −89.15 kN·m. The negative sign means tension on the top face, a hogging moment of 89.2 kN·m. Without the tie rod the cantilever would have developed 324 kN·m at the support, so the rod removes 72 percent of it. Against the anchor rating of 100 kN·m the margin is 10.8 kN·m. The rod force of 39.14 kN also gives a rod stress of 39 140 / 400 = 97.9 MPa, well under yield for typical structural steel.

Answer: 89.2 kN·m

(c)

The deflection of B equals the stretch of the rod, since B hangs from it: δ = T h / (AE) = 39.14 × 5.0 × 10⁻⁵ = 1.957 × 10⁻³ m = 1.96 mm. Cross-check with the girder alone: free-end deflection under the uniform load is wL⁴/(8EI) = 0.05832 m downward, and the upward effect of T is TL³/(3EI) = 39.14 × 0.00144 = 0.05636 m. The net downward movement is 0.05832 − 0.05636 = 0.00196 m = 1.96 mm. Both routes give the same value, which confirms compatibility between rod and girder and a correct value of T.

Answer: 1.96 mm

(d)

To have M_A = 100 kN·m the tie must carry T = (wL²/2 − 100)/L = (324 − 100)/6.0 = 37.33 kN. Put this into the least-work equation T [L³/(3EI) + h/AE] = wL⁴/(8EI). The bracket must equal 0.05832 / 37.33 = 0.0015621 m/kN. Subtracting the girder term 0.00144 leaves h/AE = 0.0001221 m/kN, so AE = 4.0 / 0.0001221 = 32 750 kN. With E = 200 × 10⁶ kN/m², A = 1.637 × 10⁻⁴ m² = 163.7 mm². A rod smaller than this is more flexible, takes less load and lets M_A rise above 100 kN·m. The limit with a rigid support would be T = 3wL/8 = 40.5 kN.

Answer: 164 mm²

Problem 3 [A1-048] Indeterminate structure with settlement or temperature change, comparing methods

A reinforced concrete beam AB, 8.0 m long, carries a heated roof slab in a Windsor foundry. It is fixed at A and rests on a roller prop at B. The section is 0.40 m wide and 0.60 m deep, with E = 30 GPa, so EI = 216 000 kN·m². The top face is held 30 °C warmer than the bottom face, with a linear temperature variation through the depth and a coefficient of thermal expansion of 1.2 × 10⁻⁵ per °C. The prop at B has settled downward by 8.0 mm. Ignore self weight and all other loads. Solve with the force method first, then check the rotation at B with the slope-deflection method.

  1. (a) Find the upward reaction at the prop B using the force method. [6]
  2. (b) Find the moment at the fixed end A. [4]
  3. (c) Using slope-deflection, find the rotation of the beam at B in milliradians. [6]
  4. (d) Find the prop settlement, in mm, at which the prop reaction would fall to zero. [4]
(a)

The temperature gradient gives a free curvature κ = αΔT/h = 1.2 × 10⁻⁵ × 30 / 0.60 = 6.0 × 10⁻⁴ per metre, with the top fibre longer, so the free cantilever curves downward. Release the prop and let R be the redundant upward force at B. The thermal drop of the free end is κL²/2 = 6.0 × 10⁻⁴ × 64 / 2 = 0.0192 m. The force R lifts the end by RL³/(3EI) = R × 512 / 648 000 = 7.901 × 10⁻⁴ R. The end must finish 0.008 m below the original level, where the prop now is, so 0.0192 − 7.901 × 10⁻⁴ R = 0.008. This gives R = 0.0112 / 7.901 × 10⁻⁴ = 14.18 kN, acting upward on the beam at B.

Answer: 14.2 kN

(b)

Thermal curvature alone produces no bending moment in the released cantilever, because it is free to curve. So the only moment at A comes from the prop reaction: M_A = R L = 14.175 × 8.0 = 113.4 kN·m, causing tension in the top face, which is hogging. The thermal strain therefore only creates stress because the prop restrains the end. Compare the settlement effect: if the prop had not settled, R would be 3 EI κ/(2L) = 3 × 216 000 × 6.0 × 10⁻⁴ / 16 = 24.3 kN and the moment at A would be 194.4 kN·m, so the 8 mm settlement has relieved about 42 percent of the restraint moment.

Answer: 113.4 kN·m

(c)

Use clockwise positive and the span with θA = 0. The chord rotation is ψ = Δ/L = 0.008 / 8.0 = 0.001 rad clockwise, since B has moved down relative to A. A fully restrained member with the top 30 °C warmer needs end moments EIκ = 216 000 × 6.0 × 10⁻⁴ = 129.6 kN·m, so FEM_AB = +129.6 and FEM_BA = −129.6 in the clockwise-positive convention. With the moment at B equal to zero: M_BA = (2EI/L)(2θB − 3ψ) + FEM_BA = 54 000 (2θB − 0.003) − 129.6 = 0. So 2θB − 0.003 = 0.0024 and θB = 0.0027 rad = 2.70 mrad clockwise. The force method gives the same: θB = κL − RL²/(2EI) = 0.0048 − 14.175 × 64 / 432 000 = 0.0027 rad.

Answer: 2.70 mrad

(d)

The prop reaction is zero when the prop moves down by exactly the amount the free end would drop on its own, so that the beam just touches it with no force. From part (a), the free thermal drop is κL²/2 = 6.0 × 10⁻⁴ × 64 / 2 = 0.0192 m = 19.2 mm. At 8 mm of settlement the prop still has to lift the beam by 11.2 mm, which takes 14.2 kN. The reaction is linear in the settlement: R = 3EI(0.0192 − Δ)/L³ = 1.266 kN per mm × (19.2 − Δ in mm), which gives 14.18 kN at 8 mm and falls by 1.27 kN for each extra millimetre. Beyond 19.2 mm the beam would sag clear of the prop, which cannot pull down, so it would lose contact.

Answer: 19.2 mm

Problem 4 [A1-049] Reactions and free-body diagrams of determinate beams and frames

A boat-storage shed near Kingston is framed by a portal ABCDE. The two columns, AB at the left and ED at the right, are 5.0 m high and pinned to their footings at A and E, which are 12.0 m apart. The roof beam BD joins the column tops and carries a uniform downward load of 15 kN/m over its full 12.0 m length. An internal hinge C in the beam is located 4.0 m from B, so the frame is statically determinate. A steady wind applies a horizontal force of 20 kN at B toward D. Take the x-axis positive from A toward E and use equilibrium of the whole frame and of the part of the frame to the right of the hinge.

  1. (a) Find the vertical reaction at E. [5]
  2. (b) Find the horizontal reaction at A (positive toward E). [5]
  3. (c) Find the bending moment in column AB just below joint B. [4]
  4. (d) What if the hinge is moved to 6.0 m from B? Find the new horizontal reaction at A (positive toward E). [6]
(a)

Draw the whole frame as a free body with unknowns Ax, Ay, Ex, Ey, the 180 kN resultant of the roof load acting at 6.0 m from either column, and the 20 kN wind force at the height of 5.0 m. Take moments about A, counter-clockwise positive: Ey(12.0) − 20(5.0) − 180(6.0) = 0. The wind pushes toward E at height 5.0 m, which is clockwise about A, and the roof load is clockwise as well. So 12.0 Ey = 100 + 1080 = 1180 and Ey = 98.33 kN upward. Moments about A involve neither Ex nor the hinge, so this reaction cannot depend on where the hinge is placed, a fact that is used again in part (d).

Answer: 98.3 kN upward

(b)

Separate the frame at hinge C, which transmits force but no moment. Take the right-hand part, from C to E, with 8.0 m of roof load (120 kN acting 4.0 m from C), the reaction Ey = 98.33 kN at 8.0 m from C, and Ex at the base, 5.0 m below the beam. Moments about C, counter-clockwise positive: Ey(8.0) + 5.0 Ex − 120(4.0) = 0, so 786.7 + 5.0 Ex − 480 = 0 and Ex = −61.33 kN, meaning it acts toward A. Whole-frame ΣFx: Ax + Ex + 20 = 0, so Ax = 61.33 − 20 = 41.33 kN toward E. Check ΣFy: Ay = 180 − 98.33 = 81.67 kN upward.

Answer: 41.3 kN toward E

(c)

Column AB is pinned at A, so the moment at its base is zero and the only horizontal force on the column below B is Ax, with no load along the column. The moment therefore grows linearly from zero at A to Ax × 5.0 just below B: M = 41.33 × 5.0 = 206.7 kN·m. The wind force acts at joint B itself, so it does not change the moment on the column section just under the joint. This moment is carried through the rigid joint into the roof beam, which must be checked at B for 206.7 kN·m together with an axial thrust of 41.3 kN and the 81.7 kN vertical reaction going down the column.

Answer: 206.7 kN·m

(d)

Repeat the right-hand free body with C now 6.0 m from B, so the part from C to E is 6.0 m long, carrying 90 kN at 3.0 m from C. Moments about C: Ey(6.0) + 5.0 Ex − 90(3.0) = 0. Ey is still 98.33 kN, because the whole-frame moment equation does not contain the hinge position. So 590.0 + 5.0 Ex − 270 = 0, giving Ex = −64.0 kN. Then Ax = 64.0 − 20 = 44.0 kN toward E. Moving the hinge toward the middle raises the horizontal thrust at A by 2.67 kN, about 6.5 percent, because the shorter right-hand segment has to resist its own load with a smaller lever arm for Ey.

Answer: 44.0 kN

Problem 5 [A1-050] Shear and bending moment diagrams for beams with point and distributed loads

A timber stringer on a logging bridge near Timmins is a beam ABCD, 12.0 m long. It has a pin support at A and a roller support at C, 9.0 m from A, so the part CD is a 3.0 m overhang with a free end at D. A stockpile of bark applies a uniformly distributed load of 20 kN/m on the first 4.0 m, from A to a point 4.0 m from A. A truck wheel group applies a single 50 kN downward load 6.0 m from A. The overhang carries no load at first. Later a barrier post is bolted to the free end and adds a 35 kN downward load at D. Draw the shear and bending moment diagrams in your working, using sagging moment as positive.

  1. (a) Find the reaction at C for the original loading. [4]
  2. (b) Find the distance from A at which the shear force is zero for the original loading. [3]
  3. (c) Find the maximum sagging bending moment for the original loading. [4]
  4. (d) After the 35 kN barrier post is added at D, find the hogging moment at C. [4]
  5. (e) With the post in place, find the new maximum sagging moment. [5]
(a)

Replace the 20 kN/m load by its resultant of 80 kN acting 2.0 m from A. Take moments about A, counter-clockwise positive: R_C(9.0) − 80(2.0) − 50(6.0) = 0. Then 9.0 R_C = 160 + 300 = 460 and R_C = 51.11 kN upward. Vertical equilibrium: R_A + R_C = 80 + 50 = 130 kN, so R_A = 78.89 kN upward. Check by moments about C: R_A(9.0) − 80(7.0) − 50(3.0) = 710.0 − 560.0 − 150.0 = 0, which agrees. Both reactions are upward, so no uplift occurs at either support. The overhang carries no load, so the shear and moment there are both zero.

Answer: 51.1 kN

(b)

Take shear as the sum of upward forces to the left of a section. In the loaded length 0 ≤ x ≤ 4.0 m, V(x) = 78.89 − 20x, falling linearly from +78.89 kN at A. It reaches zero where 20x = 78.89, so x = 3.944 m, which lies inside the loaded length, so it is valid. At x = 4.0 m the shear is 78.89 − 80 = −1.11 kN, and it stays −1.11 kN to the 50 kN load, where it jumps to −51.11 kN. At C the reaction of +51.11 kN brings the shear back to zero, and the shear is zero on the overhang. So the only zero crossing is at 3.94 m from A.

Answer: 3.94 m

(c)

The bending moment is greatest where the shear changes sign, at x = 3.944 m. M = R_A x − w x²/2 = 78.89(3.944) − 20(3.944²)/2 = 311.1 − 155.6 = 155.6 kN·m, or equivalently R_A² / (2w) = 78.89² / 40 = 155.59 kN·m. Check the other candidate point under the truck: M at x = 6.0 m is the moment at 4.0 m, which is 78.89(4.0) − 80(2.0) = 155.56, less 1.11 kN × 2.0 m, so 153.33 kN·m, smaller than the peak. The moment then falls linearly at 51.11 kN/m to zero at C, since 153.33 − 51.11(3.0) = 0. The governing sagging moment is 155.6 kN·m near the stockpile.

Answer: 155.6 kN·m

(d)

A 35 kN load at the free end creates a hogging moment over the support equal to the load times the overhang length, because the overhang is a cantilever from C and nothing else acts on it. M_C = −35(3.0) = −105 kN·m, so the hogging moment at C is 105 kN·m. This is new: in the original loading the moment at C was zero. The moment diagram on the overhang is a straight line from zero at D to −105 kN·m at C, and the shear on the overhang is a constant −35 kN. The hogging moment will need top reinforcement or a deeper section over the pier-side support.

Answer: 105 kN·m

(e)

Recompute the reactions. Moments about A: R_C(9.0) = 80(2.0) + 50(6.0) + 35(12.0) = 160 + 300 + 420 = 880, so R_C = 97.78 kN, and R_A = 165 − 97.78 = 67.22 kN. Zero shear still lies in the loaded length: x = 67.22 / 20 = 3.361 m, which is below 4.0 m. Maximum sagging moment: R_A² / (2w) = 67.22² / 40 = 112.97 kN·m. Under the truck, M at 6.0 m is 67.22(6.0) − 80(4.0) = 83.3 kN·m, which is smaller. The post reduced the peak sagging moment from 155.6 to 113.0 kN·m by taking 11.7 kN away from R_A, yet created a 105 kN·m hogging moment, so the hogging moment over the support is now nearly as large as the sagging peak.

Answer: 113.0 kN·m

A1 Practice Paper 11

Problem 1 [A1-051] Member forces in determinate trusses by joints and sections

A pedestrian bridge over a rail corridor in Hamilton is carried by two identical Warren trusses, and one truss is analysed as a pin-jointed plane frame. The bottom chord has joints A, B and C at 0 m, 6 m and 12 m along a horizontal line. The top chord has joints D and E, 3 m and 9 m from A, and lies 3 m above the bottom chord. Members are AB, BC, DE, AD, DB, BE and EC. Joint A is pinned and joint C is on a roller. A snow drift gives a 60 kN downward joint load at B and a maintenance cart gives a 30 kN downward joint load at D. Self weight may be ignored. Tension is positive.

  1. (a) Find the vertical reaction at A. [3]
  2. (b) Using a vertical section through members DE, DB and AB, find the force in AB. [5]
  3. (c) From the same section, find the force in DE. Give compression as a negative number. [4]
  4. (d) Find the force in diagonal DB. [4]
  5. (e) The 30 kN cart is moved from joint D to joint E. Find the new force in AB, and state whether the force in DE changes. [4]
(a)

Treat the whole truss as a rigid body and take moments about C, where the roller reaction acts, so that only Ay appears. Counter-clockwise positive: Ay(12) - 60(6) - 30(9) = 0. The 60 kN load at B is 6 m from C and the 30 kN load at D is 9 m from C. Ay = (360 + 270)/12 = 52.5 kN upward. Check with the vertical reaction at C: Cy(12) = 60(6) + 30(3) = 450, so Cy = 37.5 kN, and 52.5 + 37.5 = 90 kN equals the total applied load. There is no horizontal load, so Ax = 0.

Answer: 52.5 kN

(b)

Pass a vertical cut between x = 3 m and x = 6 m so that it severs DE, DB and AB, and keep the left piece containing A and D. Take moments about joint D, which removes DE and DB because both pass through D. The 30 kN load acts at D and drops out as well. Moment of Ay about D is 52.5(3) clockwise, and the bottom chord force F_AB acts 3 m below D. For equilibrium F_AB(3) = Ay(3), so F_AB = 52.5 kN. A pull on the cut face is a positive force, so AB is in tension.

Answer: 52.5 kN (tension)

(c)

Use the same left piece and take moments about joint B, which removes AB and DB since both pass through B. Forces about B: Ay = 52.5 kN acts upward 6 m to the left of B and the 30 kN load acts downward 3 m to the left of B. The top chord DE is 3 m above B. Moment equilibrium gives 52.5(6) - 30(3) + F_DE(3) = 0, with F_DE taken positive as a pull on the cut face. Then F_DE(3) = -(315 - 90) = -225, so F_DE = -75.0 kN. The negative sign shows the top chord is in compression, as expected for a chord in the sagging zone.

Answer: -75.0 kN (compression)

(d)

Apply vertical equilibrium to the same left piece. The vertical forces are Ay = 52.5 kN upward, the 30 kN load downward at D, and the vertical component of the force in DB. Member DB runs from D down to B, 3 m horizontal and 3 m vertical, so it makes 45 degrees with the horizontal and its vertical component is F_DB sin45°. A tensile force pulls the piece toward B, which is downward. So 52.5 - 30 - F_DB(0.7071) = 0. F_DB = 22.5/0.7071 = 31.8 kN, positive and therefore in tension.

Answer: 31.8 kN (tension)

(e)

With the 30 kN at E the left piece for the same section carries only Ay. Moments about C give Ay(12) = 60(6) + 30(3) = 450, so Ay = 37.5 kN. Moments about D for the cut through DE, DB and AB give F_AB(3) = 37.5(3), so F_AB = 37.5 kN tension, down from 52.5 kN. For DE take moments about B: 37.5(6) + F_DE(3) = 0 gives F_DE = -75.0 kN, identical to before. The reason is that the net moment about B of everything left of the cut is 225 kN·m in both cases: moving the load to E removes 30(3) = 90 kN·m of counter-moment, but Ay also falls by 15 kN, which removes 15(6) = 90 kN·m.

Answer: 37.5 kN; DE unchanged at -75.0 kN

Problem 2 [A1-052] Three-hinged arches and cables

A parabolic three-hinged arch carries a park footbridge deck. The arch has pinned supports A and B at the same level, 30 m apart, and a hinge C at the crown, 6.0 m above the line AB and midway between the supports. The arch axis follows y = 4h x(L - x)/L², with x measured from A, L = 30 m and h = 6.0 m. The deck puts a uniformly distributed load of 18 kN/m on the left half of the span only, from A to C. A maintenance truck wheel group acts as a single downward load of 80 kN at x = 22.5 m. Ignore the self weight of the arch ribs.

  1. (a) Find the vertical reaction at A. [3]
  2. (b) Find the horizontal thrust at the supports. [5]
  3. (c) Find the bending moment in the arch rib at x = 7.5 m. [5]
  4. (d) The designer raises the crown to h = 8.0 m, keeping the same loads. Find the new horizontal thrust. [3]
  5. (e) For the h = 8.0 m arch, find the bending moment at x = 7.5 m and explain in one sentence why it differs or not from part (c). [4]
(a)

The supports are pins at equal levels, so the vertical reactions come from moments for the whole arch, which acts like a simply supported beam for vertical loads. Moments about B, counter-clockwise positive: Ay(30) - 18(15)(22.5) - 80(7.5) = 0. The resultant of the distributed load is 270 kN at x = 7.5 m, which is 22.5 m from B, and the wheel load is 7.5 m from B. Ay = (6075 + 600)/30 = 222.5 kN upward. Then By = 270 + 80 - 222.5 = 127.5 kN, a useful check for the next step.

Answer: 222.5 kN

(b)

The crown hinge C cannot carry moment, so take moments about C for the right-hand half, from C to B. Forces on it are By = 127.5 kN upward at 15 m horizontal distance, the 80 kN wheel load 7.5 m from C, and the thrust H acting horizontally at the pin B, 6.0 m below C. Moment equilibrium: By(15) - 80(7.5) - H(6.0) = 0. So H = (1912.5 - 600)/6.0 = 218.75 kN, directed inward at each support. Check with the left half: 222.5(15) - 218.75(6) - 270(7.5) = 3337.5 - 1312.5 - 2025 = 0, which confirms it.

Answer: 218.75 kN

(c)

Locate the rib at x = 7.5 m: y = 4(6)(7.5)(22.5)/30² = 4.5 m. Cut the arch there and take moments of everything to the left about the cut. Forces are Ay = 222.5 kN at 7.5 m horizontal lever arm, H = 218.75 kN acting at 4.5 m vertical lever arm, and the distributed load over the 7.5 m, equal to 135 kN acting 3.75 m from the cut. M = 222.5(7.5) - 218.75(4.5) - 135(3.75) = 1668.75 - 984.375 - 506.25 = 178.1 kN·m. The positive result means sagging, with tension on the inner face of the rib.

Answer: 178.1 kN·m

(d)

The vertical reactions do not depend on the rise because the supports are still 30 m apart and the loads have not moved, so Ay = 222.5 kN and By = 127.5 kN. Only the lever arm of the thrust at the crown changes. Moments about C for the right half now give By(15) - 80(7.5) - H(8.0) = 0, so H = 1312.5/8.0 = 164.06 kN. This is the reduction of 25 percent that follows from the ratio 6/8, because the thrust is inversely proportional to the rise for a given set of loads.

Answer: 164.1 kN

(e)

The new rib height at x = 7.5 m is y = 4(8)(7.5)(22.5)/900 = 6.0 m. The bending moment is M = 222.5(7.5) - 164.06(6.0) - 135(3.75) = 1668.75 - 984.38 - 506.25 = 178.1 kN·m, the same as before. The product H times y is 1312.5(0.75), independent of h, because H is proportional to 1/h while y is proportional to h. So raising a parabolic arch of this type cuts the thrust and the foundation load but does nothing to the moment in the rib under this unsymmetrical loading, which still equals the beam moment minus the H y term.

Answer: 178.1 kN·m, unchanged

Problem 3 [A1-053] Axial force, shear and moment diagrams of determinate frames

A single-bay portal frame supports the roof of a loading dock in Sudbury. Columns AB and DC are 5.0 m high. The beam BC is 8.0 m long and rigidly connected to the column tops. Joint A is a pin at the base of the left column and joint D is a roller at the base of the right column, free to move horizontally. A wind load pushes a horizontal force of 15 kN to the right at B. The roof carries 10 kN/m of snow and roofing weight across the full beam length BC. Treat the frame as a rigid body with moment-resisting corners.

  1. (a) Find the vertical reaction at D. [5]
  2. (b) Find the bending moment at the top of the left column, joint B. [3]
  3. (c) Find the distance from B at which the beam moment is a maximum. [3]
  4. (d) Find the maximum sagging moment in the beam. [4]
  5. (e) Wind strengthens and the horizontal force at B doubles to 30 kN. Find the new maximum sagging moment in the beam. [5]
(a)

Whole frame as a free body. The roller at D gives only a vertical reaction, the pin at A gives Ax and Ay. Take moments about A, counter-clockwise positive: Dy(8) - 10(8)(4) - 15(5) = 0. The roof load of 80 kN acts 4 m from A horizontally, and the wind force acts 5 m above A. Dy = (320 + 75)/8 = 49.4 kN upward. The wind overturns the frame about A and increases the load on the roller side. Horizontal equilibrium gives Ax = 15 kN to the left, and Ay = 80 - 49.375 = 30.6 kN.

Answer: 49.4 kN

(b)

Cut the left column just below B and look at the piece below the cut, which has the pin reaction Ax = 15 kN acting horizontally at the base. At the cut the column carries axial force Ay = 30.6 kN compression and a shear force of 15 kN. The bending moment at B equals the horizontal reaction times the column height, M_B = 15(5) = 75.0 kN·m. This moment is carried around the rigid corner into the beam, where it produces tension on the inside face, matching a sagging beam moment of +75 kN·m at x = 0.

Answer: 75.0 kN·m

(c)

Take the beam moment as sagging positive and measure x from B. For a free body to the left of a section at x, the moment is M(x) = 75 + Ay x - 10x²/2, since the corner moment of 75 kN·m is carried across the joint into the beam. With Ay = 30.625 kN, M(x) = 75 + 30.625x - 5x². The maximum moment is where the shear is zero: dM/dx = 30.625 - 10x = 0, so x = 3.0625 m. This lies inside the beam, 3.06 m from B. Check M(8) = 75 + 245 - 320 = 0 at the roller, as required.

Answer: 3.06 m

(d)

Substitute x = 3.0625 m into M(x) = 75 + 30.625x - 5x². The linear term is 30.625(3.0625) = 93.79 and the quadratic term is 5(3.0625)² = 5(9.379) = 46.89. M_max = 75 + 93.79 - 46.89 = 121.9 kN·m. A simply supported beam of the same span would see only wL²/8 = 80 kN·m, so the frame beam moment is about 52 percent higher. The extra comes from the wind overturning moment carried through the rigid corner, and the corner moment of 75 kN·m is most of that increase.

Answer: 121.9 kN·m

(e)

With 30 kN of wind, moments about A give Dy(8) = 320 + 30(5) = 470, so Dy = 58.75 kN and Ay = 80 - 58.75 = 21.25 kN. The corner moment is now 30(5) = 150 kN·m. The beam moment is M(x) = 150 + 21.25x - 5x², with zero shear at x = 21.25/10 = 2.125 m. M_max = 150 + 21.25(2.125) - 5(2.125)² = 150 + 45.16 - 22.58 = 172.6 kN·m. Doubling the wind force raised the maximum beam moment by about 42 percent, because the corner term doubled. At x = 8 the moment is 150 + 170 - 320 = 0, which checks.

Answer: 172.6 kN·m

Problem 4 [A1-054] Influence lines for reactions of beams

A timber boardwalk girder 17.0 m long rests on two supports at an Ontario lakeshore park. Support B is 3.0 m from the left end and support C is 13.0 m from the left end, so the girder overhangs 3.0 m beyond B and 4.0 m beyond C. Distances x are measured from the left end. The girder carries a permanent load of 12 kN/m over its whole length. The live load from crowds is a uniformly distributed load of 25 kN/m that can be placed over any length of the girder. Use the influence line for the reaction at C, with upward reaction positive.

  1. (a) Find the ordinate of the influence line for the reaction at C at the left end of the girder (x = 0). [3]
  2. (b) Find the ordinate at the right end (x = 17.0 m). [3]
  3. (c) Find the maximum reaction at C from the permanent load plus the live load. [5]
  4. (d) Find the minimum reaction at C. [4]
  5. (e) The right overhang is shortened to 2.0 m (total length 15.0 m, supports unchanged). Find the new maximum reaction at C. [5]
(a)

A unit load at position x produces a reaction at C found from moments about B: R_C(10) = 1(x - 3), so R_C = (x - 3)/10, valid for the whole girder because the overhangs behave as extensions of the simple span. The influence line is therefore a straight line that is zero at B (x = 3), equal to 1.0 at C (x = 13) and linear beyond. At the left end, x = 0: R_C = (0 - 3)/10 = -0.30. The negative sign means a load on the left overhang pulls the right support down, as a seesaw does.

Answer: -0.30

(b)

Using R_C = (x - 3)/10, put x = 17.0 m at the right free end. R_C = (17 - 3)/10 = 1.40. A unit load at the end of the 4 m right overhang produces a reaction at C that is larger than the load itself, because C is carrying both the load and the moment balance about B. The straight line passes through 0 at B, 1 at C and 1.4 at the tip. Because the influence line is a straight line over the whole girder, only these three points are needed to draw it.

Answer: 1.40

(c)

Permanent load acts over the whole length, so it uses the net area under the line. Net area = ((17)²/2 - 3(17))/10 = (144.5 - 51)/10 = 9.35 m, giving 12(9.35) = 112.2 kN. The live load for the greatest reaction is placed only where the ordinates are positive, from B to the right tip: positive area = ½(14)(1.40) = 9.8 m, giving 25(9.8) = 245 kN. The sum is R_C,max = 112.2 + 245 = 357.2 kN. Placing live load on the left overhang as well would subtract from the result, so it stays off.

Answer: 357.2 kN

(d)

For the minimum reaction the live load goes only where the ordinates are negative, which is the left overhang from x = 0 to x = 3 m. The area there is ½(3)(0.30) = 0.45 m, taken as negative, so the live contribution is 25(-0.45) = -11.25 kN. The permanent load reaction is the same 112.2 kN as in part (c). R_C,min = 112.2 - 11.25 = 100.95 kN, about 101 kN. The reaction at C never goes negative, so no uplift anchor is needed for this load combination at C.

Answer: 101.0 kN

(e)

With total length 15.0 m the influence line is still R_C = (x - 3)/10, now ending at x = 15 where the ordinate is 1.20. Net area for permanent load = (15²/2 - 3(15))/10 = (112.5 - 45)/10 = 6.75 m, so 12(6.75) = 81 kN. Positive area for live load = ½(12)(1.20) = 7.2 m, so 25(7.2) = 180 kN. R_C,max = 81 + 180 = 261.0 kN. Shortening the right overhang by 2 m cut the maximum reaction by about 27 percent, because both the loaded length and the lever arm about B dropped.

Answer: 261.0 kN

Problem 5 [A1-055] Influence lines for shear and moment in beams

A runway girder in a Windsor fabrication shop is simply supported over a 20.0 m span between supports A and B. A trolley hoist rolls along the girder and can park anywhere, imposing a single downward load of 90 kN. A service walkway adds a live load of 15 kN/m that may be placed over any part of the span. Ignore the self weight of the girder. Section S lies 8.0 m from support A. Use influence lines to find the extreme effects at S, treating the hoist load and the walkway load as independent live loads that may both take their worst positions together.

  1. (a) Find the peak ordinate of the influence line for bending moment at S. [3]
  2. (b) Find the maximum positive shear at S. [5]
  3. (c) Find the maximum negative shear at S, as a magnitude. [3]
  4. (d) Find the maximum bending moment at S. [5]
  5. (e) The inspector proposes checking the section at midspan instead. Find the maximum moment there and say how it compares with part (d). [4]
(a)

The influence line for bending moment at a section a from the left support on a span L is a triangle with its peak under the section. The peak ordinate is a(L - a)/L. Here a = 8.0 m and L = 20.0 m, so the peak is 8(12)/20 = 4.8 m. It has the unit of length because the moment caused by a unit load is expressed per kN of load. The ordinate falls linearly to zero at A and at B. The area under the whole line is ½(20)(4.8) = 48 m², which is needed for the walkway load.

Answer: 4.8 m

(b)

The shear influence line at S has a jump of 1.0 at the section. To the right of S the ordinate is (L - ξ)/L, which equals +0.6 immediately right of the section and falls to zero at B. To the left it is -ξ/L, which equals -0.4 just left of S. For the maximum positive shear, place the hoist just right of S: 90(0.6) = 54 kN. Load the walkway from S to B: area = ½(12)(0.6) = 3.6 m, so 15(3.6) = 54 kN. V_max = 54 + 54 = 108 kN.

Answer: 108 kN

(c)

The negative ordinates lie to the left of the section, where the influence line runs from 0 at A to -0.4 just left of S (that is, -8/20). Park the hoist just left of S: 90(-0.4) = -36 kN. Put the walkway load over A to S only: area = ½(8)(-0.4) = -1.6 m, so 15(-1.6) = -24 kN. The total is -36 - 24 = -60 kN, a magnitude of 60 kN. A load right of S would reduce this negative shear, so no live load is placed beyond S. The net swing in shear through the section is therefore 108 + 60 = 168 kN.

Answer: 60 kN

(d)

All the ordinates of the moment influence line are positive, so the worst case loads the whole span and puts the hoist at the peak, above S. Walkway: area 48 m², so 15(48) = 720 kN·m. Hoist: 90(4.8) = 432 kN·m. M_max = 720 + 432 = 1152 kN·m. The hoist belongs at S because the line peaks there. A hoist anywhere else gives a smaller ordinate and therefore less moment at S. The walkway load covers the whole span for the same reason: every ordinate is positive, so no part of the span can reduce the moment at S.

Answer: 1152 kN·m

(e)

At midspan a = 10 m, so the peak ordinate is 10(10)/20 = 5.0 m and the area is ½(20)(5.0) = 50 m². Walkway load: 15(50) = 750 kN·m. Hoist at midspan: 90(5.0) = 450 kN·m. M_max = 1200 kN·m. Compared with 1152 kN·m at S the moment is higher by 48 kN·m, or 4.2 percent. The check at midspan governs the flexural design of the girder, and the section at 8 m is only critical for shear or for a section change such as a flange cut-off.

Answer: 1200 kN·m, 4.2 percent higher

A1 Practice Paper 12

Problem 1 [A1-056] Influence lines for truss member forces

A Pratt through-truss carries a farm-access road over a creek near Guelph. It has four panels of 4.0 m, bottom joints L0 to L4 on a horizontal line at 0, 4, 8, 12 and 16 m, and top joints U1, U2 and U3 directly above L1, L2 and L3, 3.0 m higher. Members are the chords, the verticals at U1L1, U2L2 and U3L3, the end posts L0U1 and L4U3, and diagonals U1L2 and U3L2. Moving loads reach the truss only at bottom joints through floor beams. Dead load is 20 kN/m and live load is 30 kN/m, both taken as uniform along the span. Support L0 is a pin and L4 is a roller.

  1. (a) Draw the influence line for the force in bottom chord member L1L2 by a section through panel L1 to L2. Give its ordinate for a unit load at L2. [4]
  2. (b) Find the maximum tension in bottom chord member L1L2 from dead plus live load. [5]
  3. (c) Find the maximum tension in diagonal U1L2. [5]
  4. (d) Find the minimum force in diagonal U1L2 (tension positive), and state whether a counter diagonal is needed. [3]
  5. (e) The designer deepens the truss to 4.0 m with the same panel length and loads. Find the new maximum tension in L1L2. [3]
(a)

Cut through panel L1 to L2, severing U1U2, U1L2 and L1L2. Moments about U1 remove the two members that meet there. For a unit load at or right of L2 the left piece is analysed: F(3) = R_A(4), so F = 4R_A/3. At L2 R_A = 0.5, giving F = 0.667. For a unit load at or left of L1 use the right piece: F(3) = R_B(12), so F = 4R_B, which gives 1.0 at L1 where R_B = 0.25. The ordinates are 0 at L0, 1.0 at L1, 0.667 at L2, 0.333 at L3 and 0 at L4, joined by straight lines.

Answer: 0.667

(b)

All ordinates of the line in part (a) are positive, so both loads act over the whole span. The area is the sum of four trapezoids with width 4 m: ½(4)(1.0) = 2.0, 4(1.0 + 0.667)/2 = 3.333, 4(0.667 + 0.333)/2 = 2.0 and ½(4)(0.333) = 0.667. The total area is 8.0 m. Force = (20 + 30)(8.0) = 400 kN tension. This is the greatest tension because every ordinate adds to it, and the chord is in tension for downward load as a bottom chord of a simply supported truss must be.

Answer: 400 kN

(c)

The diagonal U1L2 is sloped with horizontal 4 m and vertical 3 m, so its length is 5 m and sin θ = 0.6. The panel shear controls it. For a unit load right of the panel the left piece gives F(0.6) = R_A, so F = R_A/0.6 in tension: 0.833 at L2 and 0 at L4. For a load left of the panel F = -R_B/0.6, giving -0.417 at L1. The line crosses zero at 5.33 m. Positive area is ½(2.667)(0.833) + ½(8)(0.833) = 1.111 + 3.333 = 4.444 m. Maximum tension = 20(3.333) + 30(4.444) = 66.7 + 133.3 = 200 kN, where 3.333 is the net area.

Answer: 200 kN

(d)

The most compressive case loads only the negative part of the line with live load, which has area ½(4)(-0.417) + ½(1.333)(-0.417) = -0.833 - 0.278 = -1.111 m. Dead load gives a net area of 4.444 - 1.111 = 3.333 m, so 20(3.333) = 66.7 kN tension. Live load gives 30(-1.111) = -33.3 kN. The minimum force is 66.7 - 33.3 = 33.3 kN, still tension. Dead load alone outweighs the worst live compression, so the diagonal never reverses and no counter diagonal is needed in this panel. It is a safe conclusion only for these load intensities.

Answer: 33.3 kN tension; no counter needed

(e)

With a depth of 4.0 m the moment equation about U1 becomes F(4) = R_A(4), so F = R_A for load right of the panel, and F = 12R_B/4 = 3R_B for load left of it. Every ordinate of the line is therefore scaled by 3/4: the ordinate at L2 is 0.5 and the peak at L1 is 0.75. The area drops from 8.0 m to 6.0 m. Force = 50(6.0) = 300 kN. The chord force fell by 25 percent for a 33 percent increase in depth, since chord force is inversely proportional to the lever arm between the chords.

Answer: 300 kN

Problem 2 [A1-057] Maximum shear and moment envelope under a moving wheel train

A simply supported steel crane runway beam spans 16.0 m between supports A and B in a Cambridge foundry. A three-wheel bridge crane truck crosses it and may travel in either direction. The wheel loads are 70 kN, 110 kN and 110 kN. The 70 kN wheel is 3.5 m ahead of the first 110 kN wheel, and the second 110 kN wheel is 1.5 m behind that first 110 kN wheel, so the 70 kN wheel is 5.0 m ahead of the last wheel. Call the loads P1 (70 kN), P2 (the first 110 kN) and P3 (the second 110 kN). Ignore impact and self weight.

  1. (a) Find the distance of the resultant of the three loads from P1. [3]
  2. (b) Find the largest possible reaction (shear) at support A while the truck is on the span. [5]
  3. (c) Find the absolute maximum bending moment in the beam. [7]
  4. (d) The span is replaced by a 12.0 m span with the same truck. Find the new absolute maximum moment. [5]
(a)

The resultant equals the sum of the loads: 70 + 110 + 110 = 290 kN. Take moments of the loads about P1, measuring distance backward along the truck: 110(3.5) + 110(5.0) = 385 + 550 = 935 kN·m. The resultant location is x̄ = 935/290 = 3.224 m behind P1. This is 0.276 m ahead of P2 on the side toward P1, because P2 is 3.5 m behind P1. The resultant lies very close to P2, which is why P2 is the load that will govern the absolute maximum moment.

Answer: 3.224 m

(b)

The reaction at A is largest when the heaviest group of loads is nearest A and the whole truck is on the span. Place P3 directly over A and let the truck extend along the span with P2 at 1.5 m and P1 at 5.0 m. Moments about B: R_A(16) = 110(16) + 110(14.5) + 70(11). R_A = (1760 + 1595 + 770)/16 = 257.8 kN. The reverse arrangement with P1 at A gives (70(16) + 110(12.5) + 110(11))/16 = 231.6 kN, which is smaller. So the maximum shear at A is 257.8 kN.

Answer: 257.8 kN

(c)

The absolute maximum moment occurs under a load when that load and the resultant are placed equally on either side of midspan. Use P2, the load closest to the resultant, which lies 0.276 m from it. Put P2 at 8.0 + 0.138 = 8.138 m from A, so the resultant is at 7.862 m and P1 at 4.638 m, P3 at 9.638 m, all on the span. R_A = 290(16 - 7.862)/16 = 147.5 kN. M under P2 = 147.5(8.138) - 70(3.5) = 1200.4 - 245.0 = 955.4 kN·m. The moment is 955 kN·m, only slightly more than the 955.0 kN·m found with P2 exactly at midspan, which shows how flat the maximum is.

Answer: 955 kN·m

(d)

Repeat the rule for L = 12 m. Place P2 and the resultant symmetrically about midspan at 6.0 m: P2 at 6.138 m from A, resultant at 5.862 m, P1 at 2.638 m and P3 at 7.638 m, all on the span. R_A = 290(12 - 5.862)/12 = 148.3 kN. M under P2 = 148.3(6.138) - 70(3.5) = 910.3 - 245.0 = 665.4 kN·m. Shortening the span by 25 percent lowered the absolute maximum moment by 30 percent, because the moment scales roughly with span, while the truck stays whole on the shorter beam.

Answer: 665 kN·m

Problem 3 [A1-058] Beam deflection by double integration

A cantilever steel canopy beam projects from a concrete wall at a transit station in Ottawa. It is 4.0 m long, fixed at the wall and free at the tip. Rainwater and ballast produce a distributed downward load that varies linearly from 24 kN/m at the wall to zero at the free tip. The modulus of elasticity is 200 GPa and the second moment of area is 3.2 × 10⁸ mm⁴, so EI = 64 000 kN·m². Use x measured from the wall and apply the boundary conditions at the fixed support. Work with the differential equation EI v'' = M(x), downward deflection positive in your final answers.

  1. (a) Find the bending moment at the wall. [3]
  2. (b) Find the slope at the free tip by double integration. [4]
  3. (c) Find the deflection at the free tip. [5]
  4. (d) The projection is lengthened to 5.0 m with the same peak intensity and EI. Find the new tip deflection. [4]
  5. (e) For the 5.0 m cantilever, find the smallest second moment of area, in 10⁶ mm⁴, that keeps the tip deflection within span/240. Use E = 200 GPa. [4]
(a)

Let s be the distance from the free tip, so the intensity is w(s) = 24 s/4 = 6s kN/m. The shear at a section is the area of the load beyond it, V = 3s². The moment is the integral of the shear: M = s³. At the wall s = 4, so M = 64 kN·m, hogging, with tension in the top fibre. This agrees with the closed form w0L²/6 = 24(16)/6 = 64 kN·m. In terms of x from the wall, the moment magnitude is M(x) = (4 - x)³, which is zero at the tip as it should be.

Answer: 64.0 kN·m

(b)

With hogging moment, the governing equation is EI v'' = -(4 - x)³ for upward-positive deflection v. Integrating once: EI v' = (4 - x)⁴/4 + C1. The wall is fixed, so v'(0) = 0, which gives C1 = -256/4 = -64. At the tip x = 4 the first term vanishes, so EI v' = -64 kN·m², and v' = -64/64 000 = -0.0010 rad. The negative sign means the tip rotates downward. The magnitude 0.0010 rad matches the standard result w0L³/(24EI) = 24(64)/(24 × 64 000).

Answer: 0.0010 rad

(c)

Integrate the slope equation again: EI v = -(4 - x)⁵/20 + C1 x + C2 with C1 = -64. At the wall v(0) = 0 gives 0 = -1024/20 + C2, so C2 = 51.2. At the tip x = 4: EI v = 0 - 64(4) + 51.2 = -256 + 51.2 = -204.8 kN·m³. Then v = -204.8/64 000 = -0.0032 m, so the tip deflects downward by 3.2 mm. The result equals w0L⁴/(30EI) = 24(256)/(30 × 64 000) = 0.0032 m, which verifies the integration.

Answer: 3.2 mm

(d)

The tip deflection follows w0L⁴/(30EI), so it varies with the fourth power of length when w0 and EI are fixed. With L = 5.0 m: δ = 24(625)/(30 × 64 000) = 15 000/1 920 000 = 0.0078125 m = 7.81 mm. Equivalently δ = 3.2(5/4)⁴ = 3.2(2.441) = 7.81 mm. A 25 percent longer cantilever deflects 144 percent more, and the wall moment also rises to 24(25)/6 = 100 kN·m. The deflection limit would likely govern before strength does.

Answer: 7.81 mm

(e)

The limit is 5000/240 = 20.83 mm = 0.020833 m. The deflection is δ = w0L⁴/(30EI), so the required stiffness is EI = w0L⁴/(30δ) = 24(625)/(30 × 0.020833) = 15 000/0.625 = 24 000 kN·m². This is well below the 64 000 kN·m² of the 4 m beam because the allowable deflection of 20.8 mm is much looser than the 3.2 mm the 4 m beam actually shows. Then I = 24 000/(200 × 10⁶ kN/m²) = 1.2 × 10⁻⁴ m⁴ = 120 × 10⁶ mm⁴.

Answer: 120 × 10⁶ mm⁴

Problem 4 [A1-059] Beam deflection by the moment-area method

A stepped steel girder in an industrial mezzanine near Kitchener is simply supported over 8.0 m. The end 2.0 m lengths have flexural rigidity EI0 = 30 000 kN·m², while the central 4.0 m is reinforced with cover plates so that its rigidity is 2EI0. A single concentrated load of 60 kN acts at midspan. Ignore self weight. The girder supports a machinery platform whose serviceability limit is a midspan deflection of span/360. Use the moment-area theorems, and remember that the sections change rigidity at 2.0 m and 6.0 m from A, with the tangent at midspan horizontal by symmetry, and report downward deflection as positive.

  1. (a) Find the maximum bending moment. [3]
  2. (b) Find the slope of the girder at support A. [5]
  3. (c) Find the midspan deflection. [6]
  4. (d) Find the midspan deflection if the girder had uniform rigidity EI0 over the full length. [3]
  5. (e) Find the percentage reduction in midspan deflection achieved by the cover plates. [3]
(a)

Each support carries half the load, 30 kN. The bending moment grows linearly from the support, M = 30x, up to midspan where x = 4 m. M_max = 30(4) = 120 kN·m, sagging. At x = 2 m, where the section stiffens, the moment is 60 kN·m. Because EI changes at that point, the diagram of M/EI has a jump: in the end segments M/EI0 rises from 0 to 60/EI0, and in the central segment it begins at 60/(2EI0) = 30/EI0 and rises to 120/(2EI0) = 60/EI0. These ordinates are used in part (b).

Answer: 120 kN·m

(b)

By the first moment-area theorem the slope change between A and midspan C equals the area of the M/EI diagram between them. Because the tangent at C is horizontal, this change equals the slope at A. End segment: ½(2)(60) = 60/EI0. Central half-segment, x from 2 to 4 m: a rectangle 30 × 2 = 60 plus a triangle ½(2)(30) = 30, so 90/EI0. Sum = 150/EI0. θA = 150/30 000 = 0.0050 rad. The jump in the diagram at x = 2 m is the reason the central region contributes less area than an unstiffened one.

Answer: 0.0050 rad

(c)

By the second theorem the deviation of A from the tangent at C equals the first moment of the M/EI area between A and C about A, and by symmetry this is the midspan deflection. End triangle 60/EI0 acts at 2(2)/3 = 1.333 m from A, so its moment is 80. Rectangle 60/EI0 acts at 3.0 m: 180. Triangle 30/EI0 acts at 2 + (2/3)(2) = 3.333 m: 100. Sum = 360/EI0. δ = 360/30 000 = 0.0120 m = 12.0 mm. The result is less than the 21.3 mm of an unplated girder, as expected.

Answer: 12.0 mm

(d)

With uniform EI0 the diagram of M/EI0 is a single triangle from 0 to 120/EI0 over 4 m. Its area is ½(4)(120) = 240/EI0 and it acts at 2(4)/3 = 2.667 m from A, giving a first moment of 640/EI0. δ = 640/30 000 = 0.02133 m = 21.3 mm. This agrees with the closed form PL³/(48EI0) = 60(512)/(48 × 30 000) = 0.02133 m, which confirms the method. So a girder with no plates deflects 21.3 mm, which is just inside a span/360 = 22.2 mm limit, so the plated girder has a comfortable margin.

Answer: 21.3 mm

(e)

The reduction is the difference between the uniform and the stepped deflections, expressed as a fraction of the uniform value: (21.333 - 12.000)/21.333 = 9.333/21.333 = 0.4375, or 43.75 percent. The cover plates are only 4 m long and sit where the moment is largest, which is why they are effective. They double the rigidity over half of the span and still cut deflection by nearly half, because the central region contributes most of the curvature area to the deviation. Plates on the outer 2 m lengths would have done much less.

Answer: 43.8 percent

Problem 5 [A1-060] Beam deflection by the conjugate beam method

A simply supported laboratory test beam of 12.0 m span between pins A and B carries two equal concentrated loads of 50 kN, one 4.0 m from A and the other 4.0 m from B, so the loads are 4.0 m apart in the middle third. The beam has constant flexural rigidity EI = 1.0 × 10⁵ kN·m². Ignore self weight. Solve with the conjugate beam method: load a conjugate beam of the same span with the real M/EI diagram, so that conjugate shear gives real slope and conjugate moment gives real deflection. Report downward deflection and take slopes as magnitudes.

  1. (a) Find the slope of the real beam at support A. [4]
  2. (b) Find the deflection under the load 4.0 m from A. [5]
  3. (c) Find the midspan deflection. [5]
  4. (d) The loads are moved outward, toward the supports, so that each is 3.0 m from its nearest support. Find the new midspan deflection. [3]
  5. (e) For the original loading, find the EI that would limit the midspan deflection to 20 mm. [3]
(a)

Each reaction is 50 kN, so the real moment is 50x from each end, reaching 200 kN·m at x = 4 m and staying constant at 200 kN·m between the loads. The conjugate beam has the same span and ends, with the M/EI diagram as a downward load: two triangles of area ½(4)(200) = 400/EI each and a rectangle 4(200) = 800/EI. Total load = 1600/EI. By symmetry the conjugate reaction at A is 800/EI. The real slope equals the conjugate shear at A: θA = 800/100 000 = 0.0080 rad. A simple support in the real beam stays a simple support in the conjugate.

Answer: 0.0080 rad

(b)

The deflection under the load equals the conjugate moment at x = 4 m. Take the part of the conjugate beam from A to this section. It contains the left triangle, 400/EI acting 2.667 m from A, which is 1.333 m from the section. Conjugate moment M' = 800(4) - 400(1.333) = 3200 - 533.3 = 2666.7/EI. δ = 2666.7/100 000 = 0.02667 m = 26.7 mm. The result is positive, which means the real deflection is downward. A check by the formula Pa(3L² - 4a²)/(24EI) at midspan will follow in the next part.

Answer: 26.7 mm

(c)

At midspan x = 6 m the conjugate moment is taken from the left. The conjugate reaction 800/EI acts at 6 m. The triangle of 400/EI has its centroid 2.667 m from A, so 3.333 m from the section. The half rectangle from 4 m to 6 m has area 2(200) = 400/EI with its centroid at 5 m, 1 m from the section. M' = 800(6) - 400(3.333) - 400(1) = 4800 - 1333.3 - 400 = 3066.7/EI. δ = 3066.7/100 000 = 30.67 mm. The formula Pa(3L² - 4a²)/(24EI) gives 50(4)(432 - 64)/24 = 3066.7 / EI, which confirms it.

Answer: 30.7 mm

(d)

Now a = 3.0 m. The moment is 150 kN·m between the loads. The conjugate load is two triangles of ½(3)(150) = 225/EI and a rectangle 6(150) = 900/EI, total 1350/EI, so the conjugate reaction is 675/EI. Evaluating the conjugate moment at midspan gives M' = 675(6) - 225(4) - 450(1.5) = 4050 - 900 - 675 = 2475/EI. This matches the closed form δ = Pa(3L² - 4a²)/(24EI) = 50(3)(432 - 36)/(24 × 100 000) = 0.02475 m. The midspan deflection falls to 24.75 mm, a drop of 19 percent, because the loads moved nearer the supports.

Answer: 24.75 mm

(e)

The deflection scales as 1/EI, and with the present EI of 100 000 kN·m² the deflection is 30.67 mm. For a limit of 20 mm, the required rigidity is EI = (30.67/20)(100 000) = 153 333 kN·m². Equivalently, EI = 3066.7/0.020 = 153 333 kN·m², since the conjugate moment of 3066.7 does not depend on EI. The beam needs 53 percent more rigidity. With a fixed E, this means the second moment of area must increase by the same factor, or the section must be deepened.

Answer: 1.53 × 10⁵ kN·m²

A1 Practice Paper 13

Problem 1 [A1-061] Truss deflection by virtual work (unit load)

A steel canopy bracket at a school entrance in Barrie is a two-bar pin-jointed truss fixed to a masonry wall. Support A is on the wall. Support C is on the wall 3.0 m directly below A. Joint B lies 4.0 m horizontally out from A, level with A. Bar AB is horizontal and has area 1200 mm². Bar CB joins C to B and has area 2000 mm². Both bars have E = 200 GPa. A snow and equipment load of 60 kN acts vertically downward at joint B. Neglect self-weight and treat the joints as frictionless pins. The architect wants the bracket tip to move as little as possible, so the engineer must understand how each bar contributes to the movement of B.

  1. (a) Find the axial force in bar CB (magnitude, compression positive). [4]
  2. (b) Use the unit-load method to find the vertical deflection of joint B. [7]
  3. (c) Use a unit horizontal load to find the horizontal deflection of joint B. [4]
  4. (d) The designer doubles the area of bar AB only. Find the new vertical deflection of B and say which bar governs. [5]
(a)

Isolate joint B. Bar CB runs from C, 3.0 m below A, up to B, 4.0 m out, so its length is √(4² + 3²) = 5.0 m with direction cosines 0.8 horizontal and 0.6 vertical. Vertical equilibrium at B: the 60 kN load is carried by the vertical component of CB, so F_CB × 0.6 = 60, giving F_CB = 100 kN. CB lies below B and pushes up and away from the wall, so it is in compression. Horizontal equilibrium: the outward push of CB is 100 × 0.8 = 80 kN, and AB must pull B back toward the wall, so F_AB = 80 kN tension. Check by resolving along AB: 80 - 80 = 0, so the joint is in equilibrium.

Answer: 100 kN compression

(b)

Virtual work: Δ = Σ F f L / (EA), where f is the bar force from a 1 kN vertical load at B. Scaling part (a) by 1/60 gives f_AB = +80/60 = +4/3 (tension) and f_CB = -100/60 = -5/3 (compression). For AB, EA = 200 × 10⁶ kPa × 1200 × 10⁻⁶ m² = 240 000 kN, so its term is 80 × (4/3) × 4.0 / 240 000 = 1.778 × 10⁻³ m. For CB, EA = 400 000 kN, so the term is (-100)(-5/3)(5.0)/400 000 = 2.083 × 10⁻³ m. Both terms are positive because force and virtual force have the same sign, so Δv = 1.778 + 2.083 = 3.861 mm downward. Bar CB contributes more, since it is longer and carries more force.

Answer: 3.86 mm downward

(c)

Apply a 1 kN horizontal virtual load at B pointing away from the wall. Vertical equilibrium at B with no vertical load requires the vertical component of CB to be zero, so f_CB = 0. Horizontal equilibrium then gives f_AB = +1 (tension). Only AB contributes: Δh = F_AB × f_AB × L_AB / (EA)_AB = 80 × 1 × 4.0 / 240 000 = 1.333 × 10⁻³ m = 1.33 mm. The sign is positive, so B moves in the direction of the virtual load, away from the wall, which agrees with the physical picture of AB stretching under 80 kN tension while the compressed bar CB shortens without moving B sideways on its own.

Answer: 1.33 mm away from the wall

(d)

The virtual-work sum is unchanged except for the AB term. With A_AB = 2400 mm², EA = 480 000 kN and the AB term becomes 80 × (4/3) × 4.0 / 480 000 = 0.889 × 10⁻³ m. The CB term stays at 2.083 mm. New Δv = 0.889 + 2.083 = 2.972 mm, a reduction of 0.889 mm or 23 percent from 3.861 mm. After the change CB governs, contributing 70 percent of the deflection. This shows that stiffening the tension bar gives only a modest gain and the compression diagonal should be enlarged next, subject to buckling checks, which are not part of this problem.

Answer: 2.97 mm

Problem 2 [A1-062] Beam and frame deflection by virtual work

A signal-head support on a Highway 401 overpass is a steel L-shaped frame. A vertical post 4.0 m high is fixed at its base. At the top it joins a horizontal arm rigidly, and the arm projects 3.0 m to one side. The signal head applies a 15 kN downward load at the free end of the arm. The post and the arm both have EI = 160 000 kN·m² (E = 200 GPa and I = 8.0 × 10⁻⁴ m⁴). Neglect axial and shear deformation and the self-weight of the members. The municipality wants to know how far the signal head moves in service and whether stiffening only the post is worth the cost.

  1. (a) Find the constant bending moment in the post. [3]
  2. (b) Find the vertical deflection of the arm tip using virtual work. [6]
  3. (c) Find the horizontal deflection of the arm tip. [5]
  4. (d) Only the post is replaced by a section with twice the I. Find the new vertical tip deflection. [6]
(a)

Cut the post at any height above the base and take the free body above the cut. The only load on that free body is the 15 kN force at the arm tip, which acts at a horizontal lever arm of 3.0 m from the axis of the post. Moment about the cut = 15 × 3.0 = 45 kN·m. The lever arm does not change with the height of the cut, so the moment is constant over the full 4.0 m of the post. It causes tension on the side away from the arm. In the arm itself the moment varies linearly from zero at the tip to 45 kN·m at the corner, M = 15x with x measured from the tip.

Answer: 45 kN·m

(b)

Apply a 1 kN virtual vertical load at the tip. The virtual moments are m = x in the arm (x from the tip) and m = 3.0 in the post, in the same sense as the real moments. Δv = ∫ M m dx / EI. Arm: ∫₀³ (15x)(x) dx = 15 × 27/3 = 135 kN²·m³. Post: (45)(3.0)(4.0) = 540 kN²·m³. Sum = 675. Δv = 675 / 160 000 = 4.219 × 10⁻³ m = 4.22 mm downward, in the direction of the virtual load. The post supplies 80 percent of the movement even though the arm is the member that carries the load, because a constant moment acts over the longer length.

Answer: 4.22 mm downward

(c)

Apply a 1 kN virtual horizontal load at the tip, acting outward along the line of the arm. It passes through the axis of the arm, so m = 0 in the arm. In the post it has moment arm y measured down from the corner, m = y, in the same sense as the real moment. Δh = ∫₀⁴ (45)(y) dy / EI = 45 × 16/2 / 160 000 = 360 / 160 000 = 2.25 × 10⁻³ m. The positive sign means the tip moves outward, away from the post, in the direction of the virtual load. This sideways drift comes entirely from bending of the post, since the arm does not bend under a force along its own axis.

Answer: 2.25 mm outward

(d)

Doubling I in the post halves its flexibility, so its integral contribution is divided by two: 540 / 2 = 270 kN²·m³. The arm is unchanged at 135. Δv = (135 + 270) / 160 000 = 405 / 160 000 = 2.531 × 10⁻³ m = 2.53 mm. This is a 40 percent reduction from 4.22 mm. The horizontal deflection would also halve to 1.13 mm. Stiffening the post is more effective than stiffening the arm because the post carries a large constant moment over a long length. Doubling the arm instead would reduce Δv by only 135/2 / 675 = 10 percent.

Answer: 2.53 mm

Problem 3 [A1-063] Deflection by strain energy and Castigliano's theorem

A timber-and-steel viewing platform at a conservation area is supported by a steel girder ABC. The girder has a pin support at A and a roller support at B, 6.0 m from A, and overhangs 2.0 m beyond B to a free end C. EI = 15 000 kN·m² throughout. A uniformly distributed load of 8 kN/m acts downward on span AB only. A guard-post connection applies a 20 kN downward load at the free end C. The platform designer must check how much the cantilever tip drops and how far the girder end at A rotates, and whether adding a heavier load at the tip would be acceptable. Use Castigliano's theorem with fictitious loads and ignore shear and axial energy.

  1. (a) Find the vertical reaction at A. [3]
  2. (b) Find the vertical deflection at C using Castigliano's theorem. [7]
  3. (c) Find the rotation of the girder at A (milliradians, clockwise positive). [5]
  4. (d) The tip load is doubled to 40 kN. Find the new vertical deflection at C and comment on the result. [5]
(a)

Take moments about B for the whole girder. Let the tip load be Q, which equals 20 kN for the real loading. The UDL resultant is 8 × 6 = 48 kN, acting 3.0 m from B on the A side. Moments about B: A_y × 6 - 48 × 3 + Q × 2 = 0 for the left span and overhang combined, giving A_y = (144 - 2Q)/6 = 24 - Q/3. With Q = 20: A_y = 24 - 6.667 = 17.33 kN upward. The reaction at B follows from vertical equilibrium, B_y = 48 + 20 - 17.33 = 50.67 kN. The overhang load reduces the reaction at A because it hogs the girder over B.

Answer: 17.33 kN

(b)

Treat the tip load as Q and differentiate before substituting Q = 20. With x from A, in AB: M = (24 - Q/3)x - 4x², so ∂M/∂Q = -x/3. In BC, using the distance u = 8 - x from the free end, M = Qu, so ∂M/∂Q = u. Δ_C = (1/EI)[∫₀⁶ M(∂M/∂Q)dx + ∫₀² M u du]. In AB with Q = 20, M = 17.333x - 4x²: ∫₀⁶ (17.333x - 4x²)(-x/3) dx = -(17.333 × 72 - 4 × 324)/3 = -(1248 - 1296)/3 = +16 kN²·m³. In BC: ∫₀² 20u × u du = 20 × 8/3 = 53.33. Sum = 69.33. Δ_C = 69.33 / 15 000 = 4.622 mm downward, in the direction of Q.

Answer: 4.62 mm downward

(c)

Add a fictitious clockwise couple M₀ at A. It changes the reaction at A and gives ∂M/∂M₀ = 1 - x/6 in AB; it adds no moment in the overhang, so that part contributes nothing. Then set M₀ = 0. θ_A = (1/EI) ∫₀⁶ M (1 - x/6) dx with M = 17.333x - 4x². ∫₀⁶ M dx = 17.333 × 18 - 4 × 72 = 312 - 288 = 24. ∫₀⁶ M x/6 dx = (17.333 × 72 - 4 × 324)/6 = (1248 - 1296)/6 = -8. So the integral is 24 - (-8) = 32 kN²·m³. θ_A = 32 / 15 000 = 2.133 × 10⁻³ rad = 2.13 mrad. The positive sign shows A rotates clockwise, in the direction of M₀, as expected for a sagging span.

Answer: 2.13 mrad clockwise

(d)

Deflection at C is linear in the loads, so split it. UDL alone (Q = 0): A_y = 24, M = 24x - 4x², and Δ_C = (1/EI)∫₀⁶ (24x - 4x²)(-x/3)dx = -(24 × 72 - 4 × 324)/(3 × 15 000) = -432/(3 × 15 000) = -9.6 mm, which is an upward lift of the tip. The tip load alone contributes (Q × 10.667)/15 000 where 10.667 is the integral of (∂M/∂Q)², so 20 kN gives 14.22 mm and 40 kN gives 28.44 mm. Total = -9.6 + 28.44 = 18.84 mm downward. Doubling the tip load multiplies the deflection by 4.08, not 2, because the UDL was lifting the tip by 9.6 mm and cancelled part of the tip load effect at the lower load. The designer should not extrapolate linearly from the 20 kN case.

Answer: 18.84 mm downward

Problem 4 [A1-064] Force method for one-degree indeterminate beams

A reinforced concrete transfer beam in a Hamilton parkade is cast monolithically into a shear wall at A, which can be treated as a fixed support. The beam spans 7.0 m to a steel column at B, which provides a vertical roller support only. The beam carries a uniformly distributed load of 15 kN/m over its full length and a 40 kN point load acting downward 3.0 m from A. EI = 40 000 kN·m² and is constant. Use the force method with the reaction at B as the redundant. The owner also asks what happens if the column footing at B later settles by 15 mm, since the soil there is softer than at the wall.

  1. (a) Remove the support at B and find the deflection at B of the released cantilever under the real loads. [4]
  2. (b) Find the reaction at B. [6]
  3. (c) Find the fixed-end moment at A (hogging, magnitude). [4]
  4. (d) Find the reaction at B if the support at B settles 15 mm downward. [6]
(a)

Release the redundant by removing the roller at B. The primary structure is a cantilever fixed at A. Its tip deflection at B comes from two loads. For the UDL, δ = wL⁴/(8EI) = 15 × 7⁴/(8 × 40 000) = 15 × 2401/320 000 = 0.11255 m. For the point load P = 40 kN at a = 3.0 m from the fixed end, the tip deflection is δ = Pa²(3L - a)/(6EI) = 40 × 9 × (21 - 3)/(240 000) = 40 × 9 × 18/240 000 = 0.0270 m. The two add because both push B downward: δ₁₀ = 0.11255 + 0.0270 = 0.13955 m = 139.5 mm. This is the gap the real support at B must close by pushing upward.

Answer: 139.5 mm

(b)

Apply a unit upward load at B on the cantilever. Its flexibility is δ₁₁ = L³/(3EI) = 343 / 120 000 = 2.858 × 10⁻³ m per kN. Compatibility at B requires zero net deflection: δ₁₀ - R_B δ₁₁ = 0, with δ₁₀ measured downward and R_B upward. R_B = 0.13955 / 2.858 × 10⁻³ = 48.82 kN. The sign is positive, so the roller carries 48.8 kN upward. Sense check: the total load is 15 × 7 + 40 = 145 kN. A simply supported beam would put roughly 70 kN on each end, but a fixed end draws load toward itself, so a propped cantilever puts a smaller share on the prop, and 48.8 kN is consistent with that.

Answer: 48.8 kN

(c)

Take moments about A for the whole beam. The UDL resultant is 105 kN at 3.5 m, giving 367.5 kN·m. The point load gives 40 × 3.0 = 120 kN·m. The roller reaction R_B = 48.82 kN at 7.0 m gives 341.7 kN·m upward-acting relief. The fixed-end moment M_A = 367.5 + 120 - 341.75 = 145.75 kN·m, hogging (tension in the top fibre at the wall). Vertical equilibrium gives A_y = 145 - 48.82 = 96.18 kN. As a check, the moment at the 40 kN load is A_y × 3 - 15 × 9/2 - M_A = 288.5 - 67.5 - 145.75 = 75.3 kN·m sagging, which is plausible for the largest positive moment.

Answer: 145.8 kN·m

(d)

A settlement of Δ = 0.015 m at B moves the support away from the beam, so the compatibility condition becomes δ₁₀ - R_B δ₁₁ = Δ, meaning the beam tip can now deflect 15 mm before the support catches it. R_B = (0.13955 - 0.015) / 2.858 × 10⁻³ = 0.12455 / 2.858 × 10⁻³ = 43.57 kN. The reaction falls by 5.25 kN, about 11 percent. The load shifts to the wall: M_A rises to 367.5 + 120 - 43.57 × 7 = 182.5 kN·m, an increase of 25 percent. The owner should know that settlement here reduces the support load at B but hogs the wall connection harder, so the top reinforcement at A is the part at risk.

Answer: 43.6 kN

Problem 5 [A1-065] Force method for indeterminate trusses

A rectangular bay of a steel warehouse in Mississauga is braced by a pin-jointed panel ABCD. Joint A is at the bottom left, B is 4.0 m to the right of A, C is 3.0 m directly above B and D is 3.0 m directly above A. The panel has members AB, BC, CD and DA around the edge, plus two diagonals AC and BD that cross without being connected to each other. A is a pin support and B is a roller support allowing horizontal movement. A wind-load transfer force of 50 kN acts horizontally to the right at joint D. All six members have the same EA = 400 000 kN. Take the force in diagonal AC as the redundant. Use the force method for the trusses.

  1. (a) With diagonal AC removed, find the force in diagonal BD (magnitude, compression positive). [4]
  2. (b) Find the force in diagonal AC for the complete truss (tension positive). [7]
  3. (c) Find the horizontal deflection of joint D in the complete truss. [5]
  4. (d) Find the horizontal deflection of D if diagonal AC were absent (the primary structure), and state the ratio to the answer in part (c). [4]
(a)

Remove AC to leave a statically determinate truss. Reactions: moments about A give B_y × 4.0 = 50 × 3.0, so B_y = 37.5 kN upward, A_y = 37.5 kN downward and A_x = 50 kN toward the left. Joint C now has only two members, BC and CD, at right angles and no load, so both carry zero force. At joint D, members DC (zero), DA (vertical) and DB (inclined, length 5.0 m, direction cosines 0.8 and 0.6) meet with the 50 kN load. Horizontal equilibrium at D gives 0.8 F_DB = 50, so F_DB = 62.5 kN. DB pushes D away from B, so it is in compression. DA then carries 0.6 × 62.5 = 37.5 kN in tension, and AB carries 50 kN in tension.

Answer: 62.5 kN compression

(b)

Cut AC and apply a pair of unit tension forces along AC at A and C. Joint analysis gives f: AB = -0.8, BC = -0.6, CD = -0.8, DA = -0.6, BD = +1.0 and AC = +1. Primary forces F⁰: AB = +50, DA = +37.5, BD = -62.5, BC = CD = 0. Σ F⁰ f L over the primary members = 50(-0.8)(4) + 37.5(-0.6)(3) + (-62.5)(1.0)(5) = -160 - 67.5 - 312.5 = -540. Σ f² L over all six members = 2.56 + 1.08 + 2.56 + 1.08 + 5 + 5 = 17.28. Compatibility: the cut must not open, so -540 + X × 17.28 = 0 in units where EA is constant. X = 540 / 17.28 = 31.25 kN. The positive sign means AC is in tension, and the perimeter members are relieved: AB = 50 - 0.8(31.25) = 25 kN.

Answer: 31.25 kN tension

(c)

The final member forces are AB = +25.0, BC = -18.75, CD = -25.0, DA = +18.75, BD = -31.25 and AC = +31.25 kN. For the deflection of D, a unit horizontal virtual load at D can be placed on the primary truss, which is a legitimate determinate structure. Its member forces are AB = +1.0, DA = +0.75, BD = -1.25 and zero elsewhere. Δ = Σ F f L / EA = [25(1.0)(4) + 18.75(0.75)(3) + (-31.25)(-1.25)(5)] / 400 000 = (100 + 42.19 + 195.31)/400 000 = 337.5 / 400 000 = 0.844 mm to the right, in the direction of the 50 kN load.

Answer: 0.844 mm

(d)

If AC is absent, the real forces are the primary forces: AB = +50, DA = +37.5, BD = -62.5, with BC and CD zero. Using the same unit-load forces as in part (c), Δ = [50(1.0)(4) + 37.5(0.75)(3) + (-62.5)(-1.25)(5)] / 400 000 = (200 + 84.375 + 390.625)/400 000 = 675 / 400 000 = 1.6875 mm. The ratio to the complete truss is 1.6875 / 0.84375 = 2.00. The ratio of exactly two follows because the forces everywhere in the primary truss are twice the redundant-structure forces in the members that contribute, so adding the second diagonal halves the sway. In practice, however, the compression diagonal BD may buckle and is often designed as slack, which would make AC take the full load.

Answer: 1.69 mm

A1 Practice Paper 14

Problem 1 [A1-066] Slope-deflection method for continuous beams

A two-span continuous steel girder carries a pedestrian bridge deck near Kingston. The girder is rigidly fixed into an abutment at A, rests on a roller at pier B 6.0 m from A, and rests on a roller at end support C 5.0 m beyond B. EI is constant. Span AB carries a uniformly distributed load of 20 kN/m. Span BC carries a single 60 kN point load at its midspan. The supports do not settle. Use the slope-deflection method with clockwise end moments positive. The bridge owner also wants to know how a load doubled on span BC changes the pier moment, since a heavy maintenance vehicle may stand there.

  1. (a) Find the fixed-end moment at B on span BC (magnitude). [3]
  2. (b) Find the rotation of joint B as EI × θ_B (clockwise positive). [5]
  3. (c) Find the hogging moment at B. [4]
  4. (d) Find the reaction at B. [4]
  5. (e) Recompute the hogging moment at B with the point load on BC doubled to 120 kN. [4]
(a)

For a point load at midspan of a fixed-fixed member, the fixed-end moments are PL/8 in magnitude at each end. With P = 60 kN and L = 5.0 m, PL/8 = 60 × 5.0 / 8 = 37.5 kN·m. By the clockwise-positive convention a downward load makes the left end moment anticlockwise and the right end moment clockwise, so FEM_BC = -37.5 kN·m and FEM_CB = +37.5 kN·m. For the UDL on AB the fixed-end moments are wL²/12 = 20 × 36 / 12 = 60 kN·m, with FEM_AB = -60 and FEM_BA = +60. These are the moments that would exist if both ends of every span were clamped against rotation.

Answer: 37.5 kN·m

(b)

The slope-deflection equation is M = (2EI/L)(2θ_near + θ_far) + FEM, with no chord rotations since supports do not settle and θ_A = 0. Then M_BA = (4EI/6)θ_B + 60 = 0.6667 EIθ_B + 60. M_BC = (4EI/5)θ_B + (2EI/5)θ_C - 37.5 = 0.8 EIθ_B + 0.4 EIθ_C - 37.5. M_CB = 0.4 EIθ_B + 0.8 EIθ_C + 37.5 = 0 since C is a simple end. Joint B: M_BA + M_BC = 0 gives 1.4667 EIθ_B + 0.4 EIθ_C = -22.5. From M_CB: EIθ_C = -46.875 - 0.5 EIθ_B. Substituting: 1.2667 EIθ_B = -3.75, so EIθ_B = -2.9605 kN·m². The negative sign means B rotates anticlockwise.

Answer: -2.96 kN·m² (anticlockwise)

(c)

With EIθ_B = -2.9605 and EIθ_C = -46.875 + 1.4803 = -45.395, M_BA = 0.6667(-2.9605) + 60 = 58.03 kN·m, clockwise on the end of member BA, which means hogging at B for span AB. Check from span BC: M_BC = 0.8(-2.9605) + 0.4(-45.395) - 37.5 = -2.368 - 18.158 - 37.5 = -58.03, anticlockwise on the left end of BC, again hogging. The two members meet with equal and opposite end moments, so the joint is in equilibrium. M_AB = 0.3333(-2.9605) - 60 = -60.99, so the abutment hogging moment is 60.99 kN·m, close to the pier moment because the loads are similar in effect.

Answer: 58.0 kN·m

(d)

Span AB: moments about B with hogging 60.99 at A and 58.03 at B give A_y = (20 × 36/2 + 60.99 - 58.03)/6 = (360 + 2.96)/6 = 60.49 kN, so the shear at B on the left is 120 - 60.49 = 59.51 kN. Span BC: moments about C with hogging 58.03 at B and zero at C give C_y = (60 × 2.5 - 58.03)/5 = 91.97/5 = 18.39 kN, so the shear at B on the right is 60 - 18.39 = 41.61 kN. Reaction at B = 59.51 + 41.61 = 101.11 kN. Check: total load 120 + 60 = 180 kN equals A_y + B_y + C_y = 60.49 + 101.11 + 18.39 = 179.99 kN.

Answer: 101.1 kN

(e)

Doubling P to 120 kN doubles the fixed-end moment on BC to 75 kN·m. The equations become 1.4667 EIθ_B + 0.4 EIθ_C = +15 (since 60 - 75 = -15 unbalanced) and 0.4 EIθ_B + 0.8 EIθ_C = -75. Solving: EIθ_C = -93.75 - 0.5 EIθ_B, then 1.2667 EIθ_B = 52.5, so EIθ_B = 41.45. M_BA = 0.6667(41.45) + 60 = 87.63 kN·m hogging. The pier moment rose from 58.03 to 87.63, an increase of 51 percent for a 100 percent increase in load on BC. The increase is smaller than the load increase because span AB's heavy UDL already carries much of the moment at B, so the pier moment responds less than proportionally, and the sense of B's rotation also reverses.

Answer: 87.6 kN·m

Problem 2 [A1-067] Slope-deflection method with support settlement

A two-span continuous reinforced concrete bridge slab in Ottawa is fixed into an abutment at A, passes over an intermediate pier at B 6.0 m from A, and ends on a roller at C, 5.0 m beyond B. EI = 30 000 kN·m² is constant. Both spans carry a uniformly distributed load of 25 kN/m. The pier at B stands on Leda clay and the geotechnical engineer predicts it will settle 12 mm relative to the abutments, while A and C do not move. Use the slope-deflection method with clockwise moments and clockwise chord rotations positive. The contractor wants to compare conditions with and without the settlement before deciding on top reinforcement over the pier.

  1. (a) Find the rotation of joint B including settlement, in milliradians (clockwise positive). [4]
  2. (b) Find the hogging moment at the abutment A. [4]
  3. (c) Find the hogging moment over the pier B. [4]
  4. (d) Find the reaction at pier B after settlement. [5]
  5. (e) The reaction at B before settlement is 153.2 kN. Find the percentage reduction caused by settlement. [3]
(a)

Chord rotations: B drops 12 mm below A, so span AB rotates clockwise, ψ_AB = +0.012/6 = +0.0020 rad. Span BC has C higher than B by 12 mm, so ψ_BC = -0.012/5 = -0.0024 rad. Fixed-end moments: wL²/12 gives 25 × 36/12 = 75 kN·m on AB and 25 × 25/12 = 52.08 kN·m on BC. With k₁ = 2EI/6 = 10 000 and k₂ = 2EI/5 = 12 000, M_BA = 10 000(2θ_B - 0.006) + 75 = 20 000θ_B + 15; M_BC = 12 000(2θ_B + θ_C + 0.0072) - 52.08 = 24 000θ_B + 12 000θ_C + 34.32; M_CB = 12 000θ_B + 24 000θ_C + 138.48 = 0. Joint B: 44 000θ_B + 12 000θ_C + 49.32 = 0. Eliminating θ_C = -0.005770 - 0.5θ_B gives 38 000θ_B = 19.92, so θ_B = 5.243 × 10⁻⁴ rad = 0.524 mrad.

Answer: 0.524 mrad

(b)

At the fixed end A the slope-deflection equation has θ_A = 0: M_AB = 10 000(θ_B - 3ψ_AB) - 75 = 10 000(5.243 × 10⁻⁴ - 0.006) - 75 = 5.24 - 60 - 75 = -129.76 kN·m. The negative sign means anticlockwise on the end of the member, which at a left-hand support is hogging, with tension in the top fibre. The abutment moment is 129.76 kN·m, compared with 74.18 kN·m before the settlement. Settlement raises the abutment moment by 75 percent because the beam is forced to follow an S-shaped chord in which the end at A has to resist the 12 mm downward drop at B.

Answer: 129.8 kN·m

(c)

Substitute θ_B into the equation for M_BA: M_BA = 20 000(5.243 × 10⁻⁴) + 15 = 10.49 + 15 = 25.49 kN·m, clockwise on the right end of AB, which is hogging at B. Check with span BC: M_BC = 24 000(5.243 × 10⁻⁴) + 12 000(-6.032 × 10⁻³) + 34.32 = 12.58 - 72.39 + 34.32 = -25.49, so the moments on the two sides of the pier are equal and opposite and the joint balances. Without settlement the pier moment was 76.64 kN·m, so settlement removes about two thirds of the hogging at B, because the pier is partly unloaded when it drops away.

Answer: 25.5 kN·m

(d)

Span AB: moments about B give M(6) = A_y × 6 - 25 × 36/2 - 129.76 = -25.49, so A_y = (450 + 129.76 - 25.49)/6 = 92.38 kN, and the shear on AB at B is 150 - 92.38 = 57.62 kN. Span BC: moments about C with hogging 25.49 at B and none at C give C_y = (25 × 25/2 - 25.49)/5 = (312.5 - 25.49)/5 = 57.40 kN, so the shear on BC at B is 125 - 57.40 = 67.60 kN. Reaction at B = 57.62 + 67.60 = 125.22 kN. Check: the total load 150 + 125 = 275 kN equals 92.38 + 125.22 + 57.40 = 275.0 kN.

Answer: 125.2 kN

(e)

Repeat the analysis with ψ = 0. The equations become M_BA = 20 000θ_B + 75, M_BC = 24 000θ_B + 12 000θ_C - 52.08 and M_CB = 12 000θ_B + 24 000θ_C + 52.08 = 0. Then θ_C = -0.002170 - 0.5θ_B, and joint B gives 38 000θ_B = 3.125, so θ_B = 8.22 × 10⁻⁵ rad. M_BA = 76.64 kN·m hogging, A_y = (450 + 74.18 - 76.64)/6 = 74.59 kN, B on the left = 75.41 kN, C_y = (312.5 - 76.64)/5 = 47.17 kN, B on the right = 77.83 kN, so R_B = 153.24 kN. Reduction = (153.24 - 125.22)/153.24 = 18.28 percent. The beam did not lose much support at B, so the pier still carries most of its original share.

Answer: 18.3 percent

Problem 3 [A1-068] Moment distribution for continuous beams

A three-span continuous concrete slab strip in a Windsor parking structure is fixed into end walls at A and D and rests on interior supports B and C. The spans are AB = 4.0 m, BC = 6.0 m and CD = 5.0 m, all with the same EI. Span AB carries a uniformly distributed load of 18 kN/m. Span BC carries a single 90 kN point load acting 2.0 m from B. Span CD carries 10 kN/m uniformly. There is no settlement. Use moment distribution, with clockwise end moments positive and joint balancing followed by carry-over of one half. The engineer will use the converged values to place top reinforcement and to size the interior supports.

  1. (a) Find the distribution factor of member CB at joint C. [4]
  2. (b) Find the fixed-end moment of span BC at end B (magnitude). [3]
  3. (c) Carry the distribution to convergence and state the hogging moment at B. [6]
  4. (d) State the hogging moment at C after convergence. [3]
  5. (e) Find the reaction at support B. [4]
(a)

Far ends A and D are fixed, so every member has relative stiffness 4EI/L. With EI common, the relative stiffnesses are k_BA = 1/4 = 0.25, k_BC = 1/6 = 0.1667 and k_CD = 1/5 = 0.20. At joint B the total is 0.25 + 0.1667 = 0.4167, so DF_BA = 0.60 and DF_BC = 0.40. At joint C the total is 0.1667 + 0.20 = 0.3667, so DF_CB = 0.1667/0.3667 = 0.4545 and DF_CD = 0.2/0.3667 = 0.5455. Each pair sums to 1.00 as required. The fixed supports A and D have no distribution, since they are rigid against rotation and simply absorb whatever is carried over to them.

Answer: 0.4545

(b)

For a point load P at distance a from one end and b from the other, the fixed-end moments are Pab²/L² at the near end (distance a) and Pa²b/L² at the far end. Here P = 90 kN, a = 2.0 m from B, b = 4.0 m, L = 6.0 m. M_BC = 90 × 2 × 16/36 = 80.0 kN·m anticlockwise, and M_CB = 90 × 4 × 4/36 = 40.0 kN·m clockwise. The larger moment sits at the end nearer the load. The other fixed-end moments are wL²/12: AB gives ∓24.0 kN·m (18 × 16/12), and CD gives ∓20.83 kN·m (10 × 25/12). Signs are anticlockwise at the left end and clockwise at the right end.

Answer: 80 kN·m

(c)

Cycle 1, joint B: M_BA = +24 and M_BC = -80 give an unbalance of -56, so add +56: BA +33.6 to reach 57.6 and BC +22.4 to reach -57.6. Carry over half: AB +16.8 and CB +11.2. Joint C: CB = 40 + 11.2 = 51.2 and CD = -20.83, unbalance +30.37, so add -30.37: CB -13.81 to reach 37.39 and CD -16.56 to reach -37.39. Carry: BC -6.90 and DC -8.28.
