Cycle 2, joint B: unbalance 57.6 - 64.5 = -6.9, add +6.9: BA +4.14 to reach 61.74. The process converges quickly because the carry-over factor is 0.5 and DFs are below 1. Continuing five cycles gives M_BA = 61.94 kN·m clockwise on the end of AB, hogging at B, and M_BC = -61.94, anticlockwise on the left end of BC. The joint balances exactly.

Answer: 61.9 kN·m

(d)

Continuing the same table, the moments at C converge to M_CB = +38.19 kN·m (clockwise on the right end of span BC) and M_CD = -38.19 kN·m (anticlockwise on the left end of span CD). The moment at the interior support is the hogging value, 38.19 kN·m. As a check, the exact slope-deflection solution for this beam gives EIθ_B = 37.94 and EIθ_C = -21.69, which produce the same joint moments: M_CB = (2/6)(37.94) + (4/6)(-21.69) + 40 = 38.19. The distribution sum is therefore confirmed by an independent method. The remote-end moments are 5.03 kN·m at A and 12.16 kN·m at D, both hogging, much smaller than at the interior supports.

Answer: 38.2 kN·m

(e)

Treat spans AB and BC as free bodies using the converged end moments. Span AB: hogging 5.03 at A and 61.94 at B. Moments about B: V_A × 4 = 18 × 16/2 + 5.03 - 61.94 gives V_A = (144 - 56.91)/4 = 21.77 kN, so the shear at B on the left is 72 - 21.77 = 50.23 kN. Span BC: hogging 61.94 at B and 38.19 at C. Moments about C for this span, with the load 4.0 m from C, give V_B,right × 6 = 90 × 4 + 61.94 - 38.19 = 383.75 kN·m, so V_B,right = 63.96 kN. Reaction at B = 50.23 + 63.96 = 114.19 kN.

Answer: 114.2 kN

Problem 4 [A1-069] Moment distribution for frames without sidesway

At a floor level of a parking garage in London, Ontario, a rigid joint B connects three members of a concrete frame. Column BA extends 4.0 m below B and is fixed into its footing at A. Column BD extends 3.0 m above B and is fixed into the roof slab beam at D. A floor beam BC runs 6.0 m horizontally from B to a bearing wall at C, which acts as a pin and prevents any sideways movement of the frame. All members have the same EI. The floor beam carries 20 kN/m over its full length. Joint B is the only joint that can rotate, so no sidesway occurs. Analyse with moment distribution using the modified stiffness for the pinned end of BC.

  1. (a) Find the distribution factor of member BC at joint B. [3]
  2. (b) Find the final hogging moment at B in beam BC. [5]
  3. (c) Find the moment at the fixed top of column BD, at D (magnitude). [4]
  4. (d) Find the vertical reaction at the bearing C. [4]
  5. (e) The upper column BD is removed. Find the new hogging moment at B in beam BC. [4]
(a)

Rotational stiffness depends on the far-end condition. Column BA has a fixed far end, so k_BA = 4EI/4.0 = 1.000 EI. Column BD also has a fixed far end, so k_BD = 4EI/3.0 = 1.333 EI. Beam BC has a pinned far end at the bearing, so the modified stiffness is used, k_BC = 3EI/6.0 = 0.500 EI. The sum is 2.833 EI. The distribution factors are DF_BA = 1.000/2.833 = 0.3529, DF_BD = 1.333/2.833 = 0.4706 and DF_BC = 0.500/2.833 = 0.1765. They add to 1.0000. Using the 3EI/L stiffness for BC means the carry-over from B to C is zero, so no moment is passed to the pin and one balancing is enough.

Answer: 0.1765

(b)

With a pinned far end, the fixed-end moment at B is the modified value wL²/8 = 20 × 36/8 = 90 kN·m, anticlockwise on the end of BC (hogging). It is the only unbalanced moment at the joint, since the columns carry no load. Joint B must therefore be balanced by adding +90 kN·m clockwise, distributed in proportion to the DFs: BA +31.76, BD +42.35 and BC +15.88. The final end moment in BC is -90 + 15.88 = -74.12 kN·m, so the hogging moment at B is 74.12 kN·m. Joint check: 31.76 + 42.35 - 74.12 = 0.0, so the three members meeting at B are in moment equilibrium.

Answer: 74.1 kN·m

(c)

The distributed moment in BD is 42.35 kN·m at B. For a prismatic member with a fixed far end the carry-over factor is one half, so the moment developed at D is 42.35/2 = 21.18 kN·m. The carry-over has the same sense, so D carries a clockwise moment of 21.18 kN·m on the member. The same rule gives M_AB = 31.76/2 = 15.88 kN·m at the footing. Column BD is therefore stressed more than BA, because its shorter length makes it stiffer and so attracts more of the joint moment. The designer should detail the D connection for 21.2 kN·m.

Answer: 21.2 kN·m

(d)

Beam BC is simply supported at C, so take moments about B with the end moment applied. The hogging moment at B is 74.12 kN·m. The UDL resultant is 20 × 6 = 120 kN acting 3.0 m from either end. The hogging end moment at B reduces the bearing reaction, so R_C = (wL²/2 - M_B)/L = (360 - 74.12)/6 = 47.65 kN upward. The shear at B in the beam is the remainder, 120 - 47.65 = 72.35 kN, which is passed down into the columns as axial load. The reaction at the pin is smaller than half the load, 60 kN, because the stiff joint takes extra load through hogging.

Answer: 47.65 kN

(e)

With BD removed, joint B has only BA (k = 1.000 EI) and BC (k = 0.500 EI), a total of 1.500 EI. DF_BA = 1.000/1.500 = 0.6667 and DF_BC = 0.3333. The unbalanced moment is still 90 kN·m, from the modified fixed-end moment of the beam. Distribution to BC is 0.3333 × 90 = 30.0 kN·m, so M_BC = -90 + 30 = -60.0 kN·m and the hogging moment at B falls to 60.0 kN·m. The moment in BA is 0.6667 × 90 = 60.0 kN·m, now larger than before at 31.76 kN·m. Removing the upper column reduces the restraint at B, so the beam hogging falls by 19 percent and its midspan sagging moment rises.

Answer: 60.0 kN·m

Problem 5 [A1-070] Stiffness, carry-over and fixed-end moments including modified stiffness

A floor joist AB in a Peterborough office building is a prismatic steel beam of span 6.0 m with EI = 48 000 kN·m². An engineer is setting up a moment distribution analysis and needs its stiffness properties and fixed-end moments before assembling the frame. A single 70 kN load acts downward on the member 2.0 m from A. The engineer must compare the member behaviour when the far end B is clamped against rotation and when B is released to act as a simple pin. Use clockwise end moments positive. The comparison will show why the modified stiffness 3EI/L is used when a far end is a pin.

  1. (a) Find the rotational stiffness of end A when the far end B is fixed. [3]
  2. (b) Find the fixed-end moment at A (magnitude) due to the 70 kN load with both ends fixed. [4]
  3. (c) With B fixed, find the moment needed at A to rotate A by 0.002 rad. [4]
  4. (d) With B pinned, find the moment needed at A to rotate A by 0.002 rad. [4]
  5. (e) Find the modified fixed-end moment at A (magnitude) when B is a pin. [5]
(a)

For a prismatic member with the far end fixed against rotation and translation, the moment required to give unit rotation at the near end is K = 4EI/L. Here K = 4 × 48 000 / 6.0 = 32 000 kN·m per radian. This is the stiffness that appears in the distribution factors. The same moment at the near end induces a moment at the far end equal to half of it, the carry-over factor of 0.5 for a prismatic member. So a clockwise moment M at A rotates A by M/32 000 radians and induces M/2 at B in the same sense.

Answer: 32 000 kN·m/rad

(b)

With both ends fixed, a point load P at distance a from A and b from B gives M_AB = Pab²/L² at the near end and M_BA = Pa²b/L² at the far end. Here P = 70 kN, a = 2.0 m, b = 4.0 m and L = 6.0 m. M_AB = 70 × 2.0 × 16 / 36 = 62.22 kN·m, anticlockwise, which is hogging at A. M_BA = 70 × 4.0 × 4.0 / 36 = 31.11 kN·m, clockwise. As a check, the fixed-fixed reactions are V_A = Pb²(3a + b)/L³ = 70 × 16 × 10 / 216 = 51.85 kN and V_B = 18.15 kN, which add to the 70 kN load. The near end gets the larger moment because the load is closer to A.

Answer: 62.2 kN·m

(c)

The moment required is M = K θ with K = 32 000 kN·m per radian and θ = 0.002 rad. M = 32 000 × 0.002 = 64 kN·m. Because the far end is fixed, it develops a carry-over moment of half that value, 32 kN·m, in the same sense. This second moment is a reaction supplied by the fixity at B, and it must be resisted by whatever clamps B. The prismatic member has constant EI along its length, which is the condition under which the carry-over factor equals exactly one half. A haunched member would have a different factor.

Answer: 64 kN·m

(d)

With B pinned, the far end cannot resist any moment, so the member behaves with the modified stiffness K' = 3EI/L = 3 × 48 000 / 6.0 = 24 000 kN·m per radian. The moment required for the same rotation is M = 24 000 × 0.002 = 48 kN·m. This is 25 percent lower than the fixed-far-end value of 64 kN·m, so a pinned far end is more flexible and attracts less moment in a distribution. There is no carry-over to B at all, since the pin has zero moment. Using 3EI/L directly means the far end need not be balanced and carried over in later cycles, which saves effort in frame analysis.

Answer: 48 kN·m

(e)

If B is a pin, the fixed-end moment at B must be released. Releasing M_BA = +31.11 clockwise transfers half of it to A with the same sign, so the modified fixed-end moment is M'_AB = M_AB - ½ M_BA = -62.22 - ½(31.11) = -77.78 kN·m, anticlockwise, which is hogging at A. The pinned member has no moment at B. Check with the propped cantilever formula M_A = Pab(L + b) / (2L²) = 70 × 2.0 × 4.0 × 10 / 72 = 77.78 kN·m, which matches. The hogging at A rises by 25 percent compared with the fixed-fixed value, because releasing the far end pushes more of the restraint onto A.

Answer: 77.8 kN·m

A1 Practice Paper 15

Problem 1 [A1-071] Least work and energy methods for indeterminate structures

A 6.0 m long steel crane-rail girder at a mill in Hamilton is fixed against rotation and translation at end A and rests on a roller at end B. It carries a uniformly distributed load of 18 kN/m over the full length, and its flexural rigidity is EI = 40 000 kN·m². Ignore axial and shear deformation. The designer first treats the roller at B as rigid and uses the theorem of least work, taking the vertical reaction at B as the redundant. A site inspection then finds that the roller bearing has been replaced by an elastomeric support that behaves as a linear spring of stiffness k = 5000 kN/m, and the engineer must judge how this changes the load path into the fixed end.

  1. (a) Using the theorem of least work (Castigliano's second theorem with zero deflection at B), find the reaction at B when the support is rigid. [5]
  2. (b) Find the fixed-end moment magnitude at A for the rigid-support case. [3]
  3. (c) Find the reaction at B when the support is the linear spring. [5]
  4. (d) Find the fixed-end moment magnitude at A with the spring support. [3]
  5. (e) Find the vertical movement of the spring support at B. [4]
(a)

Take the vertical reaction R at B as the redundant and measure x from B toward A. The bending moment in the released beam is M = R x - w x²/2, and ∂M/∂R = x. Because B does not move, ∂U/∂R = ∫(M/EI)(∂M/∂R)dx = 0 over the length L. That gives ∫0..L (R x² - w x³/2)dx = R L³/3 - w L⁴/8 = 0, so R = 3wL/8. With w = 18 kN/m and L = 6.0 m, R = 3(18)(6)/8 = 40.5 kN upward. The result does not depend on EI because EI is constant, which is why least work gives the redundant from geometry alone. This is the well known propped cantilever answer, and it is a useful check on the later spring case.

Answer: 40.5 kN

(b)

Equilibrium of the whole girder now gives the fixed-end quantities. Taking moments about A with the rigid reaction R = 40.5 kN: MA = wL²/2 - R L = 18(36)/2 - 40.5(6) = 324 - 243 = 81.0 kN·m. The vertical reaction at A is wL - R = 108 - 40.5 = 67.5 kN. The moment at A is hogging, with tension on the top fibre, and it is the largest moment in the span. Compare it with a cantilever carrying the same load and no prop, where the root moment would be 324 kN·m: the prop at B removes three quarters of the root moment. Check that wL²/8 = 18(36)/8 = 81.0 kN·m, which agrees with the standard result.

Answer: 81.0 kN·m

(c)

With the spring, B is no longer fixed and the compatibility condition changes: the downward deflection of the beam at B must equal the compression of the spring, R/k. Use the energy method for deflection with the released beam: the deflection at B due to w alone is wL⁴/(8EI) = 18(1296)/(8×40 000) = 0.0729 m, and the deflection due to an upward R at B is R L³/(3EI) = R(216)/(120 000) = 0.0018 R. Compatibility: 0.0729 - 0.0018 R = R/5000 = 0.0002 R. So 0.0729 = 0.002 R and R = 36.45 kN. The spring attracts less load than the rigid roller because it gives way under it.

Answer: 36.45 kN

(d)

Return to equilibrium of the girder with the new reaction R = 36.45 kN at B. Moments about A give MA = wL²/2 - R L = 324 - 36.45(6) = 324 - 218.7 = 105.3 kN·m, hogging at the fixed end. The vertical reaction at A becomes wL - R = 108 - 36.45 = 71.55 kN, up from 67.5 kN. Moment at the fixed end therefore rises by 105.3 - 81.0 = 24.3 kN·m, about 30 percent. This is the point of the what-if: a flexible support does not make the structure safer. It shifts demand toward the stiff fixed end, so the root connection and anchor bolts governed by MA must be checked for the larger value, not the rigid-roller one.

Answer: 105.3 kN·m

(e)

The spring support compresses by the reaction divided by its stiffness. Using the reaction found in part (c), δ = R/k = 36.45 kN / 5000 kN/m = 0.00729 m = 7.29 mm downward. Check against the beam: the free-end deflection of the cantilever from w is 72.9 mm, and the upward reaction removes 0.0018 × 36.45 = 0.0656 m = 65.6 mm, leaving 72.9 - 65.6 = 7.3 mm, which matches the spring movement. A 7 mm settlement at B is small against the 6 m span, but it is what lets the root moment grow, so in the report the spring stiffness should be stated and not assumed infinite.

Answer: 7.29 mm

Problem 2 [A1-072] Indeterminate structure with settlement or temperature change, comparing methods

A continuous steel stringer on an Ottawa pedestrian overpass has two equal spans of 5.0 m, with simple supports at A, B and C, where B is the centre support. It is lightly loaded during erection, and its self-weight may be neglected. The contractor discovers that the top of the centre bearing at B was built 12 mm higher than the line joining the tops of the bearings at A and C, and the girder has been forced onto it. Take EI = 30 000 kN·m² and treat the material as linear elastic. The engineer compares the force method with the slope-deflection method and also asks what happens if concrete topping cracks and EI of the section falls to 18 000 kN·m².

  1. (a) Using the force method with the reaction at B as the redundant, find the force at B caused by the misfit. [6]
  2. (b) Find the magnitude of the vertical reaction at each end support, and say whether it acts up or down. [3]
  3. (c) Find the maximum bending moment magnitude in the girder. [4]
  4. (d) Find the new maximum moment if EI falls to 18 000 kN·m², the misfit remaining 12 mm. [4]
  5. (e) Explain why the slope-deflection method gives the same moment at B, and what would change if the 12 mm were a downward settlement of B beneath a loaded girder. [3]
(a)

Release the redundant at B so the girder is a simple beam of span 2L = 10.0 m. A force P applied upward at mid-span of that beam gives a deflection δ = P(2L)³/(48EI). The compatibility condition is that the girder must be pushed up by the 12 mm misfit, so δ = 0.012 m. Then P = 48EIδ/(2L)³ = 48(30 000)(0.012)/1000 = 17.28 kN. The bearing at B pushes upward on the girder with 17.28 kN. No load is applied, so this force arises entirely from the geometric misfit, and it is proportional to EI: a stiffer girder resists the forced shape more strongly and carries a larger force.

Answer: 17.28 kN

(b)

The girder is in equilibrium under the upward force at B and the two end reactions. Symmetry makes the end reactions equal. Vertical equilibrium gives Ay + Cy + 17.28 = 0, so each end reaction is -8.64 kN, and the magnitude is 8.64 kN acting downward. The end bearings are therefore held down on the pier tops, not pushed up. A bearing detail with no hold-down or an anchor of low capacity could lift off, and this is the check a reviewer should make for an uplift reaction that arises with no applied load. Moment equilibrium about A confirms it: 17.28(5) - Cy(10) = 0 gives Cy = 8.64 kN downward.

Answer: 8.64 kN downward

(c)

The bending moment is greatest at the centre support, where the shear changes sign. Take the left half: the end reaction of 8.64 kN acts downward at A, so the moment at distance x is M = -8.64 x, hogging with tension in the top. At B, x = 5.0 m, M = -8.64(5) = -43.2 kN·m. The check is the simple-beam result PL/4 for a central point load on 2L = 10 m: 17.28(10)/4 = 43.2 kN·m, the same value. The sagging moment in the spans is zero because there is no downward load. The section at B must resist 43.2 kN·m on top of any gravity moment, which is what the misfit adds to the design.

Answer: 43.2 kN·m

(d)

If cracking lowers EI to 18 000 kN·m² the same misfit produces less force, because the force needed for a fixed displacement is proportional to stiffness. P = 48(18 000)(0.012)/1000 = 10.368 kN. The maximum moment is then PL/4 with the span 2L = 10 m: 10.368(10)/4 = 25.92 kN·m, which is 60 percent of 43.2 kN·m. The ratio 18 000/30 000 = 0.6 confirms the scaling. This is the useful lesson: forced-displacement effects are self-relieving, and a cracked section sheds the stress that an uncracked analysis predicts. For loads the opposite is true, so the designer should not carry the same stiffness assumption into every load case.

Answer: 25.92 kN·m

(e)

The slope-deflection method writes each end moment from the joint rotations and the chord rotation ψ = Δ/L of the span. Span BA has its far end A pinned, so the modified form is M = (3EI/L)(θB - ψ). By symmetry θB = 0 and ψ = 0.012/5 = 0.0024, so |M| = 3(30 000)(0.0024)/5 = 43.2 kN·m, the same as the force method, because both enforce equilibrium plus the same compatibility. If B were instead a downward settlement beneath a loaded girder, ψ reverses sign, the support moves away from the beam, the reaction at B falls and the hogging moment at B drops. Settlement helps the middle support but loads the ends.

Answer: Same compatibility; settlement relieves B

Problem 3 [A1-073] Reactions and free-body diagrams of determinate beams and frames

A simple L-shaped steel frame supports a roof walkway outside a research building in Kingston. Column AB is vertical, 5.0 m tall, with a pin support at its base A. Beam BC runs horizontally from the top of the column at B for 8.0 m to C, where a roller support provides only a vertical reaction. The beam carries a uniformly distributed downward load of 15 kN/m over its full length and a 30 kN downward point load 3.0 m from B. A wind load of 20 kN acts horizontally to the right on the column 3.0 m above A. Treat all members as rigid joined at B, and neglect member self-weight. This is a frame problem in which the bending in the column and the beam must be linked through the joint at B.

  1. (a) Find the vertical reaction at C. [5]
  2. (b) Find the vertical reaction at A. [3]
  3. (c) Find the bending moment in the column at B, using the free body of the column. [4]
  4. (d) Find the maximum bending moment in beam BC. [5]
  5. (e) Find the distance from C to the section of maximum moment. [3]
(a)

Draw the free body of the whole frame with Ax and Ay at A and Cy at C. The loads are the 120 kN resultant of the distributed load acting 4.0 m from B, the 30 kN point load 3.0 m from B and the 20 kN horizontal wind load at 3.0 m height. Take moments about the pin A, counter-clockwise positive. The roller at C is 8.0 m from A horizontally: 8 Cy - 120(4) - 30(3) - 20(3) = 0. The wind load acts to the right, 3.0 m above A, so its moment about A is clockwise. Therefore 8 Cy = 480 + 90 + 60 = 630 and Cy = 78.75 kN upward. Moments about A eliminate both reactions at the pin in a single step.

Answer: 78.75 kN

(b)

Apply vertical equilibrium to the whole frame. The total vertical load is 15(8) + 30 = 150 kN, so Ay + Cy = 150. Using Cy = 78.75 kN gives Ay = 150 - 78.75 = 71.25 kN upward. For the horizontal reaction, ΣFx = 0 gives Ax + 20 = 0, so Ax = 20 kN acting to the left. Check with moments about C, counter-clockwise positive: the 120 kN resultant is 4.0 m from C and the 30 kN load is 5.0 m from C, so taking clockwise moments positive, with Ax = 20 kN acting left at 5.0 m below beam level and the wind load acting right at 2.0 m below it, 8Ay - 120(4) - 30(5) + 20(5) - 20(2) = 0 gives Ay(8) = 480 + 150 - 100 + 40 = 570, and Ay = 71.25 kN, which agrees. The wind load, acting to the right above the base, adds to the load carried at C and relieves A, which is why Cy exceeds Ay.

Answer: 71.25 kN

(c)

Cut the column just below B and consider the free body below the cut, which contains A and the wind load. The column carries the pin reactions Ax = 20 kN (left) and Ay = 71.25 kN (up). Take moments about the cut at B, 5.0 m above A. The vertical force at A passes through the column axis and has no moment. The horizontal Ax acts 5.0 m below B, and the wind load acts 2.0 m below B: M = 20(5) - 20(2) = 60 kN·m. Above the wind load level the shear in the column is zero, so the moment is constant at 60 kN·m up to B. The column bends outward, with tension on the left face. The joint at B transfers this 60 kN·m into the beam.

Answer: 60 kN·m

(d)

Take beam BC with C as origin and x measured toward B. For 0 ≤ x ≤ 5.0 m, before reaching the point load, M = 78.75 x - 15x²/2. For x > 5.0 m, M = 78.75 x - 7.5x² - 30(x - 5). The shear is V = 78.75 - 15x up to x = 5, giving V = 3.75 kN at x = 5 just before the 30 kN load and -26.25 kN after it. Shear changes sign under the point load, so the maximum moment is there: M = 78.75(5) - 7.5(25) = 393.75 - 187.5 = 206.25 kN·m. At B, x = 8, the same formula returns 630 - 480 - 90 = 60 kN·m, matching the column moment from part (c), which confirms the joint is in equilibrium.

Answer: 206.25 kN·m

(e)

Maximum bending moment occurs where the shear passes through zero. Starting at C, V = 78.75 - 15x for x < 5.0 m. Setting V = 0 would give x = 5.25 m, which lies beyond the 30 kN point load, so the zero cannot occur there. At x = 5.0 m the shear is still +3.75 kN just before the load, then drops by 30 kN to -26.25 kN. The sign change is therefore exactly at the point load, 5.0 m from C and 3.0 m from B. Because the shear never reaches zero in a smooth region, the peak is a kink in the diagram, not a smooth maximum, and the location is 5.0 m from C.

Answer: 5.0 m

Problem 4 [A1-074] Shear and bending moment diagrams for beams with point and distributed loads

A timber glulam beam in a barn roof near Guelph is simply supported over a clear span of 10.0 m, with a pin at A on the west wall and a roller at B on the east wall. A partial snow drift places a uniformly distributed load of 8 kN/m on the beam from A to a point 6.0 m from A. A hanging hoist adds a 40 kN downward point load 8.0 m from A. The beam has a solid rectangular section 250 mm wide and 500 mm deep. Neglect self-weight. Draw the shear and moment diagrams mentally by section, then answer the questions below, treating a bending stress check as the final link from the diagrams to a design decision.

  1. (a) Find the vertical reaction at A. [3]
  2. (b) Find the distance from A to the section where the shear is zero. [4]
  3. (c) Find the maximum bending moment in the beam. [5]
  4. (d) Find the largest shear force magnitude in the beam. [3]
  5. (e) Find the maximum bending stress in the section. [5]
(a)

Replace the distributed load with its resultant: 8 kN/m over 6.0 m is 48 kN acting at its centroid, 3.0 m from A. The point load is 40 kN at 8.0 m. Take moments about B, 10.0 m from A, to find Ay: Ay(10) - 48(7) - 40(2) = 0, so Ay = (336 + 80)/10 = 41.6 kN upward. The reaction at B follows from vertical equilibrium, By = 88 - 41.6 = 46.4 kN, and a moment check about A gives By(10) = 48(3) + 40(8) = 464, again 46.4 kN. Both reactions are positive, so the beam is held down nowhere. A free body with the two reactions and the 88 kN of total load is the starting point for every later cut.

Answer: 41.6 kN

(b)

Shear at a section x from A, within the loaded length 0 ≤ x ≤ 6.0 m, is V = 41.6 - 8x. Setting V = 0 gives x = 41.6/8 = 5.2 m, which lies inside the loaded segment, so this is a valid zero. Past x = 6.0 m the distributed load ends, and the shear stays at 41.6 - 48 = -6.4 kN until the point load at 8.0 m. It then drops by 40 kN to -46.4 kN, which equals minus By. The shear diagram therefore crosses zero once, at 5.2 m, so the moment diagram has one smooth peak there and a kink at the point load. A single sign change means a single local moment maximum on the span.

Answer: 5.2 m

(c)

The bending moment at the zero-shear section is the area under the shear diagram from A: M = 41.6(5.2) - 8(5.2)²/2 = 216.32 - 108.16 = 108.16 kN·m. Equivalently, the area of the triangle in the shear diagram is 0.5(5.2)(41.6) = 108.16 kN·m. Compare it with the moment under the point load, M(8) = 46.4(2) = 92.8 kN·m, taken from the B side. The value at 5.2 m is greater, so the governing moment is 108.16 kN·m, sagging. The moment under the hoist is a local kink and is 15 kN·m smaller, a fact worth noting before sizing the hanger bracket location.

Answer: 108.16 kN·m

(d)

Read the shear at the critical points. At A the shear is +41.6 kN. At x = 6.0 m it is -6.4 kN. Just left of the hoist load it is still -6.4 kN, and just right of it, V = -6.4 - 40 = -46.4 kN, which persists to B. The largest magnitude is therefore 46.4 kN, equal to the reaction at B and slightly above the 41.6 kN at A. Shear governs the design of the end bearing and the shear stress in the web region near B. For a rectangular section the peak shear stress is 1.5V/A = 1.5(46.4 × 1000)/(250 × 500) = 0.557 MPa, which is far lower than the bending stress and is not critical here.

Answer: 46.4 kN

(e)

The section modulus of the rectangle is S = b h²/6 = 250(500)²/6 = 10.417 × 10⁶ mm³. The extreme fibre stress is σ = M/S with M = 108.16 kN·m = 108.16 × 10⁶ N·mm: σ = 108.16 × 10⁶ / 10.417 × 10⁶ = 10.38 MPa, compression in the top fibre and tension in the bottom, because the moment is sagging. The result belongs to the same cross section at x = 5.2 m. A designer would compare it with the factored bending resistance given by the project, which is not needed here. The point load location moves the peak only slightly, so the beam depth is controlled by this moment.

Answer: 10.38 MPa

Problem 5 [A1-075] Member forces in determinate trusses by joints and sections

A Pratt-type steel truss carries a rail platform at a Sudbury maintenance yard. The bottom chord joints are A, B, C, D and E, spaced 4.0 m apart, with a pin at A and a roller at E. The top chord joints G, H and I are 3.0 m above B, C and D respectively. Vertical members GB, HC and ID join the chords. Diagonal members run from A to G, G to C, C to I and I to E. The top chord runs G to H to I. Gravity loads of 50 kN at B, 80 kN at C and 50 kN at D act downward at the bottom chord joints. All joints are pins. The top chord member GH is a hollow section with I = 15 × 10⁶ mm⁴, pinned at both ends, with E = 200 GPa.

  1. (a) Find the vertical reaction at each support. [2]
  2. (b) Using the method of sections, find the force in top chord member GH as a positive magnitude. [5]
  3. (c) Find the force in bottom chord member BC. [4]
  4. (d) Find the force in diagonal member GC. [3]
  5. (e) Find the factor of safety of member GH against Euler buckling in its length of 4.0 m. [6]
(a)

The truss and loading are symmetric about C, so the reactions are equal. Total load is 50 + 80 + 50 = 180 kN, and each support takes 90 kN. A moment check about A confirms it: E(16) = 50(4) + 80(8) + 50(12) = 200 + 640 + 600 = 1440, so E = 90 kN. The horizontal reaction at A is zero because there is no horizontal load. The structure is statically determinate: 13 members, 8 joints and 3 reactions satisfy m + r = 2j, so the method of sections and joints applies directly. Both reactions are upward and no uplift occurs at either support.

Answer: 90 kN

(b)

Cut through members GH, GC and BC and take the left portion containing A, B and G. Moments about joint C eliminate GC and BC, which both pass through C. The 90 kN reaction at A acts 8.0 m left of C, the 50 kN load at B acts 4.0 m left, and GH acts at 3.0 m above C. Taking tension in GH positive: 90(8) - 50(4) + F_GH(3) = 0 with the sign set so that a compressive GH balances the net sagging moment. Then 720 - 200 = 520, so F_GH = -520/3 = -173.3 kN. The negative sign means compression, as expected for a top chord in a simply supported truss.

Answer: 173.3 kN compression

(c)

Take moments about joint G on the same left portion, which eliminates GH and GC. G is 4.0 m from A horizontally and 3.0 m above the bottom chord. The 90 kN reaction acts 4.0 m left of G and the 50 kN load at B is directly below G, with zero lever arm. The bottom chord force BC acts 3.0 m below G. Taking tension positive: BC(3) - 90(4) = 0, so BC = 360/3 = 120 kN tension. A horizontal equilibrium check on the cut portion: F_GH + BC + 0.8 F_GC = -173.3 + 120 + 53.3 = 0, which is satisfied when F_GC = +66.7 kN, confirming all three forces together.

Answer: 120 kN tension

(d)

Use vertical equilibrium of the same left portion. The vertical forces are the 90 kN reaction up, the 50 kN load at B down, and the vertical component of GC. GC runs from G (4.0 m, 3.0 m) to C (8.0 m, 0), so its slope length is 5.0 m and the vertical component is 3/5 of the member force. For a tension force the member pulls G toward C, downward on the cut portion: 90 - 50 - 0.6 F_GC = 0, so F_GC = 40/0.6 = 66.7 kN tension. The horizontal check in part (c) used the same value, so the three section forces satisfy both vertical and horizontal equilibrium and the section moment equations.

Answer: 66.7 kN tension

(e)

For a pinned-pinned column the Euler load is Pcr = π²EI/L². With E = 200 000 N/mm², I = 15 × 10⁶ mm⁴ and L = 4000 mm, EI = 3.0 × 10¹² N·mm², and Pcr = 9.8696(3.0 × 10¹²)/(4000)² = 1.8505 × 10⁶ N = 1850.5 kN. The factor of safety is Pcr divided by the applied force of 173.3 kN: 1850.5/173.33 = 10.68. This is high, so Euler buckling about the weak axis is not governing the chord. In practice local buckling, end eccentricity and the compound effect of the unbraced length out of plane must also be checked, so 10.7 is an upper bound on the true margin.

Answer: 10.7

A1 Practice Paper 16

Problem 1 [A1-076] Three-hinged arches and cables

A pedestrian suspension bridge crosses a river gorge near Thunder Bay. Two main cables each span 60.0 m between towers of equal height, with the cable sag at mid-span of 5.0 m. The deck load is 4.0 kN/m of horizontal span carried by each cable, and the deck is supported by closely spaced hangers so the load may be treated as uniformly distributed along the horizontal. The cable weight is small and is neglected, and the cable shape is a parabola. The steel cable has a linear coefficient of thermal expansion of 12 × 10⁻⁶ per °C. The engineer must also look at what happens when the temperature rises by 30 °C on a summer day while the towers remain fixed.

  1. (a) Find the horizontal component of cable tension. [4]
  2. (b) Find the maximum cable tension. [4]
  3. (c) Find the length of the parabolic cable using the standard two-term approximation. [4]
  4. (d) Find the increase in mid-span sag caused by a 30 °C temperature rise. [5]
  5. (e) Find the resulting reduction in horizontal tension. [3]
(a)

Take the free body of half the cable from the low point at mid-span to the tower. The only horizontal force at the low point is H, and the vertical force there is zero by symmetry. Moments about the tower top give H f = w(L/2)²/2, so H = wL²/(8f). With w = 4.0 kN/m, L = 60.0 m and f = 5.0 m, H = 4(3600)/(8 × 5) = 14 400/40 = 360 kN. Horizontal equilibrium of the full cable then requires the same horizontal pull at both towers. This horizontal component is the same at every point along the cable because there are no horizontal loads, so only the vertical component changes along the span.

Answer: 360 kN

(b)

The tension is greatest at the towers, where the vertical component is greatest. The vertical component at each tower is half the total load on the span, V = wL/2 = 4(60)/2 = 120 kN. The maximum tension is the resultant of the horizontal and vertical components: T = √(H² + V²) = √(360² + 120²) = √(129 600 + 14 400) = √144 000 = 379.5 kN. The slope of the cable at the tower is tan θ = V/H = 120/360 = 0.333, about 18.4°, which matches the parabola end slope 4f/L = 4(5)/60 = 0.333. This tension fixes the cable size and the anchorage design, and it is only 5.4 percent above H, so the cable is shallow.

Answer: 379.5 kN

(c)

For a parabola of span L and sag f, the length is approximately S = L + 8f²/(3L), valid when the sag-to-span ratio is small. Here f/L = 5/60 = 1/12, so the series is accurate. S = 60 + 8(25)/(3 × 60) = 60 + 200/180 = 61.11 m. The cable is therefore 1.11 m longer than the horizontal span. This extra length matters because a change in length, such as from temperature, produces a larger change in sag than the length change would suggest: the sag is very sensitive to the cable length, and this is the geometric reason for part (d). The approximate formula is within 0.05 percent of the exact parabolic arc length for this ratio.

Answer: 61.11 m

(d)

The cable length increases by ΔS = α S ΔT = (12 × 10⁻⁶)(61.11)(30) = 0.0220 m = 22.0 mm. Differentiating S = L + 8f²/(3L) with the towers fixed gives ΔS = 16 f Δf/(3L), so Δf = 3 L ΔS/(16 f) = 3(60)(0.0220)/(16 × 5) = 3.96/80 = 0.0495 m = 49.5 mm. The 22 mm of expansion therefore produces about 50 mm more sag, a magnification of 2.25 times, because a small change in length is spread over a very shallow curve. The new sag is 5.0495 m. In design the hanger clearances and the clearance above the river must allow for this additional lowering of the deck.

Answer: 49.5 mm

(e)

With the new sag f' = 5.0495 m the horizontal tension is H' = wL²/(8f') = 14 400/(8 × 5.0495) = 14 400/40.396 = 356.47 kN. The reduction is 360 - 356.47 = 3.53 kN, about 1 percent. The fall is small because H varies inversely with the sag, and the sag changes only 1 percent. Hot weather therefore slackens the cable slightly and a cold snap of the same size would raise H by a similar amount, which is a check on the anchorage and tower base moment.

Answer: 3.53 kN

Problem 2 [A1-077] Axial force, shear and moment diagrams of determinate frames

A signal gantry at a rail crossing near Windsor is modelled as a cantilever frame. A vertical steel column AB, 4.0 m tall, is fixed at its base A. At its top B, a horizontal arm BC extends 5.0 m to a free end C. The arm carries a uniformly distributed downward load of 10 kN/m from B to C, including the signal heads, and a 20 kN downward point load at C. A wind load of 12 kN acts horizontally to the right on the column 2.0 m above A. The column is a solid square section 300 mm by 300 mm. Neglect self-weight. The designer needs the member-end actions that feed the diagrams, and the resulting stresses at the base.

  1. (a) Find the magnitude of the fixed-end moment at A. [5]
  2. (b) Find the bending moment in the arm at B, which must also act on the top of the column. [3]
  3. (c) Find the maximum compressive stress at the base of the column. [5]
  4. (d) Find the maximum tensile stress at the base of the column. [4]
  5. (e) Describe the shape of the axial, shear and moment diagrams in the column and the arm. [3]
(a)

Draw the free body of the whole frame and cut at the base. The reactions are Ax, Ay and the fixed-end moment MA. Vertical equilibrium gives Ay = 10(5) + 20 = 70 kN upward, and horizontal equilibrium gives Ax = 12 kN to the left. Take moments about A, counter-clockwise positive. The distributed load has a 50 kN resultant acting 2.5 m from the column axis, the point load acts 5.0 m out, and the wind load acts 2.0 m up. MA - 50(2.5) - 20(5) - 12(2) = 0, so MA = 125 + 100 + 24 = 249 kN·m. The wind and the gravity moments add at the base, since the arm load and the wind both rotate the frame in the same sense about A.

Answer: 249 kN·m

(b)

Cut the arm just to the right of B and take the free body of the overhanging part. The moment at that section is produced by the distributed load and the point load, both acting downward at distances from B. M = 10(5)²/2 + 20(5) = 125 + 100 = 225 kN·m, hogging, which puts tension in the top face of the arm. Joint B has only two members and no external moment, so the column must deliver the same 225 kN·m at its top. This is confirmed from the column side in part (a): the column moment at B is 249 - 12(2) = 225 kN·m, since the wind load at 2.0 m removes 24 kN·m from the base value and the moment is constant above that level.

Answer: 225 kN·m

(c)

At the base of the column, the actions are an axial compression of 70 kN and a bending moment of 249 kN·m. The area is A = 300 × 300 = 90 000 mm² and the section modulus is S = bh²/6 = 300(300)²/6 = 4.5 × 10⁶ mm³. Axial stress P/A = 70 000/90 000 = 0.778 MPa. Bending stress M/S = 249 × 10⁶/4.5 × 10⁶ = 55.33 MPa. On the compression face the two add: σ = 0.778 + 55.33 = 56.11 MPa. The compression face is the one on the side the wind pushes toward. The result is an elastic stress, not a design check.

Answer: 56.11 MPa

(d)

On the opposite face the bending stress is tensile and the axial stress is still compressive, so the net tensile stress is the bending stress minus the axial stress: σ = 55.33 - 0.778 = 54.56 MPa. The axial load reduces the tension only slightly, by about 1.4 percent, because the bending is overwhelmingly dominant. For anchor bolt design this tensile face is where the bolts pull in the base plate, and the designer would use the resultant tension of the section, not the axial load alone. The neutral axis sits close to the compression face centreline, about 2 mm off centre.

Answer: 54.56 MPa

(e)

Column AB: the axial force is a constant compression of 70 kN, because no vertical load is applied along its height. The shear is 12 kN from A to the wind level at 2.0 m, then zero up to B, a step diagram. The moment varies linearly from 249 kN·m at A down to 225 kN·m at 2.0 m, then remains constant at 225 kN·m to B. Arm BC: the axial force is zero. The shear is 70 kN at B, decreasing linearly under the distributed load to 20 kN just before C, then dropping to zero at the free end. The moment is 225 kN·m at B, falling as a parabola to zero at C.

Answer: Described in working

Problem 3 [A1-078] Influence lines for reactions of beams

A highway ramp girder at a Mississauga interchange is a beam ABC of total length 17.0 m. It has a pin support at A and a roller support at B, 12.0 m from A, and an overhang of 5.0 m from B to the free end C. Vehicles may travel over the full length of the deck, including the overhang. The design check uses a two-axle service vehicle with a rear axle load of 120 kN and a front axle load of 80 kN, spaced 4.0 m apart, which may travel in either direction, together with a uniform lane load of 10 kN/m. Wheel loads on the girder are treated as concentrated forces and the girder self-weight is ignored.

  1. (a) Draw the influence line for the reaction at B: find its ordinate when the unit load is at C. [4]
  2. (b) Find the maximum reaction at B from the service vehicle. [6]
  3. (c) Find the most negative reaction at A (greatest uplift) from the service vehicle. [5]
  4. (d) Find the reaction at B when the lane load covers the full length of the girder. [5]
(a)

Place a unit load at distance x from A and find the reaction at B by moments about A. For 0 ≤ x ≤ 17, the equilibrium equation is By(12) = 1(x), so By = x/12, valid on the whole beam including the overhang because the pin at A is the moment centre. The influence line is a straight line rising from zero at A to 1.0 at B (x = 12) and continuing to 17/12 = 1.4167 at the free end C. The ordinate above 1 at C reflects the lever action of the overhang: a load placed beyond the roller is carried by B with magnification. This ordinate is the greatest value and fixes the position of the heavy axle.

Answer: 1.4167

(b)

The influence line is positive everywhere and increases toward C, so the heaviest axle goes at C. Put the 120 kN axle at x = 17.0 m, and the 80 kN axle 4.0 m behind it at x = 13.0 m. Ordinates: 17/12 = 1.4167 at the rear axle, 13/12 = 1.0833 at the front axle. By = 120(1.4167) + 80(1.0833) = 170.0 + 86.67 = 256.67 kN. Moving the vehicle back so that the light axle is at C would give 80(1.4167) + 120(1.0833) = 243.3 kN, which is lower, so the heavy axle at the free end governs. Both axles are on the overhang, so the girder is critical in bearing at B and in negative moment over that support.

Answer: 256.7 kN

(c)

The influence line for Ay, from vertical equilibrium or moments about B, is Ay = 1 - x/12. It is positive over AB, zero at B, and negative on the overhang, falling to 1 - 17/12 = -0.4167 at C. Uplift occurs when loads are on the overhang. Place the 120 kN axle at C, ordinate -0.4167, and the 80 kN axle at x = 13.0 m, ordinate 1 - 13/12 = -0.0833. Ay = 120(-0.4167) + 80(-0.0833) = -50.0 - 6.67 = -56.67 kN. This is the downward force that the support at A must provide: a hold-down anchor or counterweight of at least 56.7 kN, which is not obvious from the dead load case alone.

Answer: -56.67 kN

(d)

For a uniform load, the reaction equals the load intensity times the area under the influence line over the loaded length. The area has two parts: triangle from A to B, 0.5(12)(1) = 6.0 m, and a trapezoid from B to C with ordinates 1.0 and 1.4167 over 5.0 m, 0.5(5)(1 + 1.4167) = 6.0417 m. Total area = 12.0417 m. By = 10(12.0417) = 120.42 kN. Check by statics: the load is 170 kN with its centroid at 8.5 m from A, so moments about A give By = 170(8.5)/12 = 120.4 kN, which agrees exactly. A lane load covering only part of the length would give less, so the full length is the governing case for By.

Answer: 120.4 kN

Problem 4 [A1-079] Influence lines for shear and moment in beams

A simply supported steel crane runway beam in a Brantford fabrication shop spans 15.0 m between a pin at A and a roller at B. The designer examines the section at C, 6.0 m from A. The beam carries a movable uniform live load of 20 kN/m, which can be placed over any length of the span, and a movable concentrated load of 100 kN, which can be placed at any point. Both loads may act together or separately, and each is placed to produce the worst effect at C. Reactions are found with unit loads and then the influence lines for shear and moment at section C are used. Self-weight is neglected for this problem.

  1. (a) Find the peak ordinate of the influence line for moment at C. [3]
  2. (b) Find the maximum positive shear at C. [5]
  3. (c) Find the maximum negative shear at C, as a signed value. [4]
  4. (d) Find the maximum bending moment at C. [5]
  5. (e) Explain why the live load is placed over different lengths for the maximum shear and maximum moment cases. [3]
(a)

Put a unit load at distance x from A and find the moment at C, a = 6.0 m from A and b = 9.0 m from B. For x ≤ 6, M_C = RB-based: M_C = (x/15)(9) from the right reaction taken to the left, giving 9x/15. For x ≥ 6, M_C = (1 - x/15)(6). Both expressions meet at x = 6, where the ordinate is ab/L = 6(9)/15 = 3.6 m. The influence line for moment is a triangle with peak 3.6 m directly under C and zero ordinate at both supports. Because it is positive everywhere, a sagging moment at C is increased by every load placed anywhere on the span.

Answer: 3.6 m

(b)

The shear influence line at C has a jump of 1.0 at the section. For a load left of C, V_C = -x/15, falling to -6/15 = -0.4 just left of C. For a load right of C, V_C = 1 - x/15, which is +0.6 just right of C and falls to zero at B. Maximum positive shear uses the positive part, from C to B, which is 9.0 m long. The distributed load covers that length: area = 0.5(9)(0.6) = 2.7 m, giving 20(2.7) = 54 kN. The 100 kN point load goes just right of C at ordinate 0.6, giving 60 kN. V_max = 54 + 60 = 114 kN.

Answer: 114 kN

(c)

Maximum negative shear uses the negative part of the influence line, from A to C, which is 6.0 m long with a peak ordinate of -0.4 at the section. The uniform load covers 0 to 6 m: area = 0.5(6)(0.4) = 1.2 m, so 20(1.2) = 24 kN in the negative sense. The 100 kN point load is placed just left of C where the ordinate is -0.4, contributing -40 kN. V_min = -24 - 40 = -64 kN. The positive shear (+114 kN) is larger in magnitude than the negative shear, so the positive case governs shear design at C, but the sign reversal means the section must resist both directions of shear in a connection.

Answer: -64 kN

(d)

The moment influence line is a triangle of base 15 m and peak 3.6 m, so its area is 0.5(15)(3.6) = 27 m². The uniform live load covers the entire span, because all ordinates are positive: 20(27) = 540 kN·m. The 100 kN concentrated load is placed directly at C where the ordinate is 3.6 m: 100(3.6) = 360 kN·m. M_max = 540 + 360 = 900 kN·m, sagging. As a check, the same loading on a simple span gives a reaction at A of 20(15)/2 + 100(9/15) = 150 + 60 = 210 kN, and M at C is 210(6) - 20(6)²/2 - 0 = 1260 - 360 = 900 kN·m, in agreement.

Answer: 900 kN·m

(e)

Placement of a movable load always follows the sign of the influence-line ordinates, because a load adds to an effect only where the ordinate has the same sign as the effect sought. The moment influence line at C is positive across the whole span, so the live load must cover the full length for the maximum sagging moment. The shear influence line changes sign at C, with positive ordinates to the right and negative ordinates to the left. For the largest positive shear the load covers only the right segment CB, and for the largest negative shear only AC. Loading the entire span for shear would let the opposing signs cancel and understate the demand.

Answer: Placement follows sign of ordinates

Problem 5 [A1-080] Influence lines for truss member forces

A Warren through-truss carries a farm access bridge in Perth County. The bottom chord joints are A, C, E and G at 0, 8, 16 and 24 m, with a pin at A and a roller at G. The top chord joints B, D and F lie 4.0 m above the bottom chord at 4, 12 and 20 m. Members are AB, BC, CD, DE, EF, FG, AC, CE, EG, BD and DF, all pinned. Moving loads reach the trusses only at bottom chord joints through floor beams, with stringers spanning each panel. The design vehicle has axle loads of 150 kN and 90 kN spaced 6.0 m apart, which may travel in either direction. A lane load of 30 kN/m may cover any length.

  1. (a) Find the influence line ordinate for the force in bottom chord member CE when the unit load is at joint C. [3]
  2. (b) Find the maximum tension in CE caused by the lane load. [4]
  3. (c) Find the maximum tension in CE caused by the design vehicle. [4]
  4. (d) Find the maximum tension in diagonal CD caused by the lane load. [5]
  5. (e) Find the maximum tension in diagonal CD caused by the design vehicle. [4]
(a)

Cut the truss through BD, CD and CE and take the left portion. Moments about joint D eliminate BD and CD, leaving CE as the only unknown. D is 12 m from A and 4.0 m above the bottom chord, so the lever arm for CE is 4.0 m. For a unit load at joint C (x = 8 m), RA = 1 - 8/24 = 0.6667 and the load itself lies to the left of the cut: tension positive, 4 F_CE = RA(12) - 1(12 - 8) = 8.0 - 4.0 = 4.0, so F_CE = 1.0. For a unit load at A the ordinate is zero. Joint C therefore carries an ordinate of exactly 1.0, and the influence line is a trapezoid: zero at A, 1.0 at C and E, and zero at G.

Answer: 1.0

(b)

For a unit load right of the panel (x ≥ 16) the left portion carries no load, so F_CE = RA(12)/4 = 3(1 - x/24), giving 1.0 at E and zero at G. Between C and E the stringer transfers the load to the two joints, so the influence line is straight at 1.0. All ordinates are positive, so the lane load covers the full 24 m. Area of the trapezoid = 0.5(24 + 8)(1.0) = 16.0 m. F_CE = 30(16.0) = 480 kN tension. The central bottom chord panel is the most heavily stressed chord member, and the flat top of the influence line is the reason the force is the same wherever a load sits inside the panel.

Answer: 480 kN

(c)

The influence line is flat at 1.0 between C and E, a distance of 8.0 m. The two axles are 6.0 m apart, so both can sit on the plateau at the same time, each with an ordinate of 1.0. Place them anywhere inside the plateau, for example the 150 kN axle at 9 m and the 90 kN axle at 15 m. F_CE = 150(1.0) + 90(1.0) = 240 kN tension. Any other position puts at least one axle on a sloping part where the ordinate is less than 1.0, and so reduces the force. The flat plateau means that the vehicle result is just the total axle weight, 240 kN, and the lane load controls CE by a factor of two.

Answer: 240 kN

(d)

Take the shear in the panel CE. For loads left of C the panel shear is -x/24 and for loads right of E it is 1 - x/24, varying linearly between joints C and E. At x = 8 the shear is -0.3333 and at x = 16 it is +0.3333, crossing zero at x = 12. The diagonal CD slopes at 45°, so its force is √2 times the panel shear with the sign reversed, giving ordinates +0.4714 at C, 0 at x = 12 and -0.4714 at E. The positive area is the triangle 0 to 8 m, 0.5(8)(0.4714) = 1.886 m, plus the triangle 8 to 12 m, 0.5(4)(0.4714) = 0.943 m, total 2.828 m. F_CD = 30(2.828) = 84.85 kN tension.

Answer: 84.85 kN

(e)

The tension ordinates are largest at C, 0.4714, falling to 0.1178 at x = 2 m from A. Place the 150 kN axle at C, x = 8 m, and the 90 kN axle 6.0 m behind it at x = 2 m, where the ordinate is 0.4714(2/8) = 0.1179. F_CD = 150(0.4714) + 90(0.1179) = 70.71 + 10.61 = 81.32 kN. The alternative, 90 kN at C with 150 kN at x = 2, gives 42.43 + 17.68 = 60.1 kN, smaller. A forward position of the light axle at x = 14 m would add a negative ordinate and reduce the force. The vehicle result is slightly below the lane result, so the lane load governs the diagonal design in tension.

Answer: 81.3 kN

A1 Practice Paper 17

Problem 1 [A1-081] Maximum shear and moment envelope under a moving wheel train

A steel runway girder in a Hamilton foundry spans 16.0 m between a pin support at A and a roller support at B. A three-wheel maintenance carriage rolls along the girder from A toward B, leading wheel first. The leading wheel carries 90 kN, the middle wheel carries 150 kN and sits 3.2 m behind the leading wheel, and the trailing wheel carries 150 kN and sits 4.4 m behind the middle wheel. Ignore the self-weight of the girder and the impact allowance. A wheel that has rolled off either end of the girder, or has not yet entered it, applies no load. The carriage may stop at any position on its travel. Find the extreme effects of the moving load on the girder.

  1. (a) Find the largest vertical reaction that can occur at support A and state where the trailing wheel is when it happens. [5]
  2. (b) Find the absolute maximum bending moment in the girder. [6]
  3. (c) Find the distance from support A to the wheel under which the absolute maximum moment occurs. [4]
  4. (d) Find the largest positive shear force that can occur at a section 5.0 m from A. [5]
(a)

The reaction at A is the sum of each wheel load times its influence ordinate (L - x)/L, where x is the wheel position measured from A. Every ordinate is largest when the wheel is near A, so the reaction grows as the carriage moves in, until the trailing wheel reaches the support. Put the trailing wheel directly over A (x = 0). The middle wheel is then at 4.4 m and the leading wheel at 7.6 m, so all three are on the span. RA = 150(16)/16 + 150(11.6)/16 + 90(8.4)/16 = 150 + 108.75 + 47.25 = 306.0 kN. Moving the carriage further would carry the trailing wheel off the girder and lose 150 kN of load, so 306.0 kN is the maximum.

Answer: 306.0 kN, with the trailing wheel directly over A

(b)

The absolute maximum moment occurs under a wheel that lies close to the resultant of the train. Resultant R = 90 + 150 + 150 = 390 kN. Take moments about the leading wheel: 390 d = 150(3.2) + 150(7.6) = 1620, so d = 4.154 m behind the leading wheel. The middle wheel is 3.2 m behind the leading wheel, so the resultant lies 0.954 m behind the middle wheel. Place the middle wheel and the resultant equally either side of midspan, so the middle wheel is 0.477 m past midspan, at 8.477 m from A. The resultant is then at 7.523 m. RA = 390(16 - 7.523)/16 = 206.6 kN. The leading wheel is 3.2 m ahead of the middle wheel, at 11.677 m, so it lies to the right of the section and does not enter the moment. Moment under the middle wheel = 206.6(8.477) - 150(4.4) = 1751.5 - 660.0 = 1091.5 kN·m. The other wheels give smaller values.

Answer: 1091.5 kN·m

(c)

The rule for absolute maximum moment is that midspan bisects the distance between the critical wheel and the resultant of all loads on the span. The resultant of the 390 kN train lies 0.954 m behind the middle wheel, as found in part (b). Half of that gap is 0.477 m. Midspan is at 8.0 m from A, and the critical wheel must sit on the side of midspan away from the resultant, so the middle wheel is at 8.0 + 0.477 = 8.477 m from A. The resultant is 0.954 m back from it, at 7.523 m, which is the same distance from midspan on the other side. A check with the trailing wheel as the candidate gives a lower moment because it is lighter in position relative to the resultant. The governing wheel is therefore the middle 150 kN wheel.

Answer: 8.48 m from A

(d)

Positive shear just to the right of a section at c = 5.0 m equals RA minus all wheel loads to the left of the section. It is largest when no load is left of the section and the reaction RA is as big as possible. Place the trailing wheel just to the right of the section, at 5.0 m. The middle wheel is then at 9.4 m and the leading wheel at 12.6 m, so all three wheels are on the span and all are to the right of the section. RA = 150(11)/16 + 150(6.6)/16 + 90(3.4)/16 = 103.125 + 61.875 + 19.125 = 184.125 kN. With no wheel to the left, V = RA = 184.1 kN. Shifting the carriage forward only adds a wheel to the left of the section, which subtracts load.

Answer: 184.1 kN

Problem 2 [A1-082] Beam deflection by double integration

A timber-framed mezzanine in a Thunder Bay warehouse is supported by a steel beam AB that spans 5.0 m between a pin at A and a roller at B. The beam carries a uniformly distributed load of 18 kN/m over its whole length. At the roller end B, a stub column framed rigidly to the beam applies a pure clockwise couple of 40 kN·m to the beam. The beam has constant flexural rigidity, with E = 200 GPa and I = 5.0 × 10⁷ mm⁴. Use double integration of the moment equation with x measured from A, taking deflection positive upward. A mid-span serviceability limit of span/360 applies to the maximum deflection.

  1. (a) Find the vertical reaction at A. [3]
  2. (b) Find the slope of the beam at A in radians, by double integration. [4]
  3. (c) Find the deflection at mid-span. [5]
  4. (d) Find the maximum downward deflection in the span. [4]
  5. (e) Find the minimum I, in units of 10⁷ mm⁴, that would keep the maximum deflection within span/360. [4]
(a)

Draw the free body of the whole beam. Taking moments about B, with anticlockwise positive, the upward reaction at A lies 5.0 m to the left of B and produces a clockwise moment, -RA(5.0). The 90 kN resultant of the uniform load acts 2.5 m to the left of B and produces an anticlockwise moment, +90(2.5). The applied couple is clockwise, so it contributes -40. Then -5RA + 225 - 40 = 0, so RA = 185/5 = 37.0 kN upward. The reaction at B follows from vertical equilibrium, RB = 90 - 37 = 53 kN. The couple helps reduce the load carried at A.

Answer: 37.0 kN upward

(b)

Cut the beam at x from A and take the left part. The sagging moment is M(x) = 37x - 18x²/2 = 37x - 9x², in kN·m, which does not contain the couple because the couple acts at B. Then EI y'' = 37x - 9x². Integrate once: EI y' = 18.5x² - 3x³ + C1. Integrate again: EI y = 6.1667x³ - 0.75x⁴ + C1 x + C2. At A, y = 0 gives C2 = 0. At B, y = 0 at x = 5: 6.1667(125) - 0.75(625) + 5 C1 = 0, so 770.83 - 468.75 + 5C1 = 0 and C1 = -60.417 kN·m². EI = 200 × 10⁶ × 5.0 × 10⁻⁵ = 1.0 × 10⁴ kN·m². The slope at A is C1/EI = -60.417/10⁴ = -6.04 × 10⁻³ rad, a clockwise rotation.

Answer: 6.04 × 10⁻³ rad, clockwise

(c)

Use the deflection function from part (b), EI y = 6.1667x³ - 0.75x⁴ - 60.417x, and evaluate it at mid-span, x = 2.5 m. The cubic term is 6.1667(15.625) = 96.35. The quartic term is 0.75(39.0625) = 29.30. The linear term is 60.417(2.5) = 151.04. So EI y = 96.35 - 29.30 - 151.04 = -83.99 kN·m³. Dividing by EI = 1.0 × 10⁴ kN·m² gives y = -8.399 × 10⁻³ m, or 8.40 mm downward. The negative sign confirms the beam sags below the chord between supports at mid-span, as expected for a beam whose loading is mostly gravity.

Answer: 8.40 mm downward

(d)

The maximum deflection occurs where the slope is zero. Set the slope function to zero: 18.5x² - 3x³ - 60.417 = 0. Solve by trial. At x = 2.0, 74 - 24 - 60.42 = -10.4. At x = 2.5, 115.6 - 46.9 - 60.4 = 8.3. At x = 2.27, 95.3 - 35.1 - 60.4 = -0.2. Refining gives x = 2.275 m, which is slightly nearer A than mid-span, because the couple at B pushes the low point toward A. Substitute into the deflection function: 6.1667(11.774) - 0.75(26.78) - 60.417(2.275) = 72.61 - 20.09 - 137.45 = -84.93 kN·m³. Then y = -84.93/10⁴ = -8.49 mm. The mid-span value is only 1.1 percent smaller.

Answer: 8.49 mm at x = 2.27 m from A

(e)

The limit is span/360 = 5000/360 = 13.89 mm = 0.013889 m. The shape of the deflected curve does not depend on EI, so the product EI·y_max = 84.93 kN·m³ stays the same whatever section is used. Required EI = 84.93/0.013889 = 6115 kN·m². With E = 200 × 10⁶ kN/m², I = 6115/(200 × 10⁶) = 3.057 × 10⁻⁵ m⁴ = 3.057 × 10⁷ mm⁴. The given section has I = 5.0 × 10⁷ mm⁴, so it passes with a margin of about 39 percent, giving a deflection of 8.49 mm against the 13.89 mm limit. Strength and local buckling would still need separate checks.

Answer: I = 3.06 × 10⁷ mm⁴ minimum

Problem 3 [A1-083] Beam deflection by the moment-area method

A cantilever steel bracket arm AB projects 6.0 m from a rigid concrete wall at A, with the free tip at B. The arm is built up from two sections welded end to end. From the wall to a point 3.0 m out, the second moment of area is 8.0 × 10⁸ mm⁴. From 3.0 m out to the tip B, a lighter section is used with I = 4.0 × 10⁸ mm⁴. The modulus of elasticity is 200 GPa. The arm carries a downward point load of 30 kN at the tip B and a uniformly distributed downward load of 8 kN/m acting over the outer 3.0 m only, from the change of section to the tip. Use the moment-area theorems and measure distances from the tip B where convenient.

  1. (a) Find the bending moment at the wall A. [3]
  2. (b) Find the vertical deflection of the tip B. [8]
  3. (c) Find the rotation of the tip B. [5]
  4. (d) Find the vertical deflection of the section at the change of section, 3.0 m from A. [4]
(a)

Take the free body from the tip B back to a cut at the wall. The tip load of 30 kN acts 6.0 m from the wall, giving 30(6) = 180 kN·m. The uniform load of 8 kN/m over 3.0 m has a resultant of 24 kN acting at the middle of the loaded length, which is 1.5 m from the tip and therefore 4.5 m from the wall. Its moment is 24(4.5) = 108 kN·m. The moment at A is the sum, 180 + 108 = 288 kN·m, hogging, with tension in the top fibres. It is also the largest moment in the arm, so the weld at the wall governs the strength check.

Answer: 288 kN·m hogging

(b)

The wall is fixed, so the tangent to the elastic curve at A is horizontal. The second moment-area theorem then says the tip deflection equals the moment, about B, of the area of the M/EI diagram between A and B. Let s be the distance from B. For 0 ≤ s ≤ 3: M = 30s + 4s², with EI = 200 × 10⁶ × 4.0 × 10⁻⁴ = 8.0 × 10⁴ kN·m². For 3 ≤ s ≤ 6: M = 30s + 24(s - 1.5) = 54s - 36, with EI = 200 × 10⁶ × 8.0 × 10⁻⁴ = 1.6 × 10⁵ kN·m². Outer part: ∫(30s + 4s²)s ds from 0 to 3 = 10(27) + 81 = 351, divided by 8.0 × 10⁴ gives 4.388 × 10⁻³ m. Inner part: ∫(54s² - 36s)ds from 3 to 6 = [18s³ - 18s²] = 3240 - 324 = 2916, divided by 1.6 × 10⁵ gives 18.225 × 10⁻³ m. Sum = 22.61 mm downward.

Answer: 22.6 mm downward

(c)

The first moment-area theorem says the rotation of B relative to the tangent at A equals the area of the M/EI diagram between A and B. Since the tangent at the wall does not rotate, this area is the tip rotation. Outer part, 0 ≤ s ≤ 3: ∫(30s + 4s²)ds = 15s² + 1.3333s³ = 135 + 36 = 171 kN·m², divided by 8.0 × 10⁴ gives 2.1375 × 10⁻³ rad. Inner part, 3 ≤ s ≤ 6: ∫(54s - 36)ds = 27s² - 36s, evaluated as (972 - 216) - (243 - 108) = 756 - 135 = 621 kN·m², divided by 1.6 × 10⁵ gives 3.881 × 10⁻³ rad. The tip rotation is 2.1375 × 10⁻³ + 3.881 × 10⁻³ = 6.02 × 10⁻³ rad, with the tip turning downward.

Answer: 6.02 × 10⁻³ rad

(d)

The same theorem now applies between A and the change of section J, 3.0 m from A. Only the inner segment is needed, where EI = 1.6 × 10⁵ kN·m². The moment at A is 288 kN·m. At J, s = 3, M = 54(3) - 36 = 126 kN·m. The M/EI diagram is a trapezoid because the moment varies linearly with a straight line in this part. Its area is (288 + 126)/2 × 3.0 = 621 kN·m², divided by EI is 3.881 × 10⁻³ rad. The centroid of the trapezoid is at 3.0(126 + 2 × 288)/(3 × (126 + 288)) = 1.696 m from J. The deflection of J below the tangent at A is 3.881 × 10⁻³ × 1.696 = 6.58 × 10⁻³ m, or 6.58 mm.

Answer: 6.58 mm downward

Problem 4 [A1-084] Beam deflection by the conjugate beam method

A pedestrian boardwalk girder ABC in a Niagara conservation area is simply supported by a pin at A and a roller at B, 6.0 m apart, and overhangs 2.0 m past B to a free end C. A uniformly distributed load of 10 kN/m acts on the span AB only. A downward point load of 40 kN, from a lookout railing post, acts at the free end C. The girder has E = 200 GPa and I = 3.0 × 10⁸ mm⁴ throughout. Solve by the conjugate beam method. Report deflections in millimetres and rotations in radians, and treat the self weight of the girder as negligible.

  1. (a) Find the reaction at the roller B. [4]
  2. (b) Find the rotation of the girder at B. [5]
  3. (c) Find the deflection at the middle of span AB, stating whether it is up or down. [5]
  4. (d) Find the downward deflection at the free end C. [6]
(a)

Take moments about A, anticlockwise positive. The uniform load gives a resultant of 10(6) = 60 kN acting 3.0 m from A, so its moment is -60(3) = -180 kN·m. The point load at C is 8.0 m from A, so its moment is -40(8) = -320 kN·m. The reaction RB acts upward at 6.0 m, so its moment is +6RB. Equilibrium gives 6RB - 180 - 320 = 0 and RB = 500/6 = 83.33 kN. Then RA = 60 + 40 - 83.33 = 16.67 kN. The moment at B comes entirely from the overhang, 40(2) = 80 kN·m hogging, which is the largest moment in the girder.

Answer: RB = 83.3 kN (RA = 16.7 kN)

(b)

The bending moment in AB is M = 16.667x - 5x², sagging, reaching -80 kN·m at B. The M/EI diagram is the load on the conjugate beam, with EI = 200 × 10⁶ × 3.0 × 10⁻⁴ = 6.0 × 10⁴ kN·m². Cut the conjugate segment A'B' at the hinge B'. Its total load is the integral of M over 0 to 6, which is 8.333(36) - 1.6667(216) = 300 - 360 = -60 kN·m² (net downward). Moments about the hinge B' must vanish, and the moment of the load about B' is ∫M(6 - x)dx = 60 kN·m³. This gives the reaction at A', and A'y(6) = -60, so A'y = -10 (units kN·m²). The shear at B', which equals the real rotation, is -10 - 60 = -70, so θB = -70/6.0 × 10⁴ = -1.167 × 10⁻³ rad, clockwise.

Answer: 1.17 × 10⁻³ rad clockwise

(c)

The deflection at mid-span is the bending moment in the conjugate beam at x = 3 m. Use the free body from A' to the section. The reaction at A' is -10 kN·m² (found in part b), acting at 3.0 m, so its moment about the section is -30. The load on the first 3 m is M/EI with M = 16.667x - 5x². Its moment about the section is ∫(16.667x - 5x²)(3 - x)dx from 0 to 3 = 25(9) - 10.556(27) + 1.25(81) = 225 - 285.0 + 101.25 = 41.25. Conjugate moment = -30 + 41.25 = 11.25 kN·m³. Deflection = 11.25/6.0 × 10⁴ = 1.875 × 10⁻⁴ m = 0.1875 mm. A positive conjugate moment means the girder deflects upward. The overhang load hogs the span enough to lift it.

Answer: 0.1875 mm upward

(d)

The conjugate beam has a fixed end at C', so the deflection at C is the conjugate moment at the fixed end, taken on the cantilever B'C' that is 2.0 m long. The loads on it are the vertical force from the hinge and the M/EI loading of the overhang. The hinge force equals the shear at B' found in part (b), -70 kN·m², and acts 2.0 m from C', giving a moment contribution of -140. The overhang moment is M = -40s, with s measured from C, a triangle of area -40(2)(2)/2 = -80 kN·m² with its centroid 1.333 m from C'. That load contributes -80(1.333) = -106.7. The conjugate moment at C' is -140 - 106.7 = -246.7 kN·m³. Then yC = -246.7/6.0 × 10⁴ = -4.11 × 10⁻³ m. The tip deflects 4.11 mm downward.

Answer: 4.11 mm downward

Problem 5 [A1-085] Truss deflection by virtual work (unit load)

A pin-jointed steel truss carries a service walkway over a rail yard. The bottom chord runs from pin support A, through joint D at mid-span, to roller support B, with AD = DB = 4.0 m. The apex joint C sits 3.0 m directly above D. The members are AC and CB (top chords), AD and DB (bottom chords), and the vertical CD. Cross-sectional areas are 2400 mm² for AC and CB, 1800 mm² for AD and DB, and 1200 mm² for CD. E = 200 GPa for all members. A vehicle fixture hangs from D and applies a downward load of 48 kN at D. The roller at B restrains vertical movement only. Use the method of virtual work (unit load).

  1. (a) Find the axial force in member AC, giving its magnitude and whether it is tension or compression. [4]
  2. (b) Find the vertical deflection of joint D under the 48 kN load. [8]
  3. (c) Find the horizontal movement of the roller at B. [4]
  4. (d) During fabrication, member CD was cut 6.0 mm too short and was forced into place before the 48 kN load was applied. Find the net upward movement of D once the 48 kN load acts. [4]
(a)

Joint D is the simplest place to start. The only members meeting at D are AD, DB and CD, and the two bottom chords are horizontal, so vertical equilibrium at D gives the force in CD alone: CD = 48 kN in tension, holding the load up to C. By symmetry the support reactions are Ay = By = 24 kN. At joint A, member AC runs up and to the right at a slope of 3 in 5 (length 5.0 m, sine = 0.6, cosine = 0.8). Vertical equilibrium: 24 + FAC(0.6) = 0, taking FAC as tension positive, so FAC = -40.0 kN. The negative sign shows compression. Horizontal equilibrium at A gives FAD + FAC(0.8) = 0, so FAD = +32.0 kN tension. Members CB and DB follow by symmetry.

Answer: AC = 40.0 kN compression

(b)

Apply a unit vertical load downward at D with no real loads. The joint results are the same as in part (a) scaled by 1/48: n(CD) = +1.0, n(AC) = n(CB) = -0.8333, n(AD) = n(DB) = +0.6667. The virtual work equation is 1.0 × Δ = Σ n N L/(AE). With E = 200 × 10⁶ kN/m²: AC and CB: 2 × (-0.8333)(-40)(5)/(2400 × 10⁻⁶ × 200 × 10⁶) = 2 × 166.67/4.8 × 10⁵ = 6.944 × 10⁻⁴ m. AD and DB: 2 × (0.6667)(32)(4)/(1800 × 10⁻⁶ × 200 × 10⁶) = 2 × 85.33/3.6 × 10⁵ = 4.741 × 10⁻⁴ m. CD: (1.0)(48)(3)/(1200 × 10⁻⁶ × 200 × 10⁶) = 144/2.4 × 10⁵ = 6.000 × 10⁻⁴ m. The total is 1.7685 × 10⁻³ m, or 1.77 mm downward, since the result is positive in the direction of the unit load.

Answer: 1.77 mm downward

(c)

Apply a unit horizontal load at B, directed away from A, with no other loads. The pin at A resists the horizontal force, so the horizontal reaction at A is -1.0 and the vertical reactions are zero. At joint B the only members are DB and CB. CB is inclined and no vertical force exists to resist, so n(CB) = 0, and DB carries the full unit force in tension, n(DB) = +1.0. Joint D then gives n(AD) = +1.0, and joint C gives n(AC) = n(CD) = 0. The movement is Σ n N L/(AE) over members carrying n: AD and DB each give (1.0)(32)(4)/(3.6 × 10⁵) = 3.556 × 10⁻⁴ m. Sum = 7.111 × 10⁻⁴ m = 0.711 mm. The tension in the bottom chord lengthens it, so B moves away from A. Only tension in the bottom chord matters here.

Answer: 0.711 mm away from A

(d)

A lack of fit is treated as an initial length change in the member. With the unit load at D from part (b), the virtual work equation includes the term n × ΔL for the misfit member. CD is 6.0 mm too short, so ΔL = -6.0 mm, and n(CD) = +1.0. This term contributes 1.0 × (-6.0) = -6.0 mm to the vertical movement at D, which means D rises 6.0 mm because the short member pulls D up toward C. The truss is statically determinate, so the misfit induces no member forces before the load is applied. The loaded deflection from part (b) is +1.77 mm downward. Net movement = 1.77 - 6.0 = -4.23 mm, so D ends 4.23 mm above its theoretical unloaded position.

Answer: 4.23 mm upward

A1 Practice Paper 18

Problem 1 [A1-086] Beam and frame deflection by virtual work

A conveyor drive bracket in a Sudbury ore plant is an L-shaped steel frame. Column AB is vertical, 4.0 m high, and fixed at its base A. Arm BC is horizontal, 3.0 m long, and joined rigidly to the top of the column at B, with C the free end projecting to the right. The arm carries a downward vertical load of 20 kN at C. A belt tensioner applies a horizontal force of 10 kN at B acting to the right. The frame has constant EI = 4.0 × 10⁴ kN·m² (E = 200 GPa, I = 2.0 × 10⁸ mm⁴). Neglect axial and shear deformation and use virtual work with the bending moment only.

  1. (a) Find the bending moment at the fixed base A. [3]
  2. (b) Find the vertical deflection of the free end C. [7]
  3. (c) Find the horizontal deflection of the free end C. [6]
  4. (d) Find the rotation of the joint at C. [4]
(a)

Cut the column just above the base and take the free body above the cut, which contains the whole arm and both loads. The 20 kN vertical load acts 3.0 m horizontally from the column axis, so it produces a moment of 20(3) = 60 kN·m. The 10 kN horizontal force acts at B, 4.0 m above the base, so it produces 10(4) = 40 kN·m. Both tend to rotate the frame clockwise about A, so the moments add: M = 60 + 40 = 100 kN·m. At a section a distance d below B on the column, the same reasoning gives M = 60 + 10d. In the arm, a distance x from C, M = 20x only, because the horizontal force acts along the line of BC and has no lever arm there.

Answer: 100 kN·m at A

(b)

Apply a unit downward load at C alone. In the arm, m = x (distance from C), 0 to 3 m. In the column, m = 3.0 (the lever arm) for the full 4.0 m. The virtual work equation is 1 × Δ = ∫ M m dx/EI. Arm: ∫0..3 (20x)(x)dx = 20(27)/3 = 180. Column: ∫0..4 (60 + 10d)(3)dd = 3[60(4) + 5(16)] = 3(320) = 960. The sum is 1140 kN·m³. Then Δ = 1140/(4.0 × 10⁴) = 0.0285 m = 28.5 mm downward. About 84 percent of it comes from the column, because the 3.0 m lever arm of the vertical load bends the column over its full height.

Answer: 28.5 mm downward

(c)

Apply a unit horizontal load at C, directed to the right. In the arm the line of the unit load passes through the axis of BC, so m = 0 in the arm and the arm contributes nothing. In the column, the unit load acts at the level of the arm, so its lever arm about a section a distance d below B is d, and the sense of the moment is clockwise, the same as the real moments, so m = d. Then ∫ M m dd = ∫0..4 (60 + 10d)(d)dd = 30(16) + (10/3)(64) = 480 + 213.33 = 693.33 kN·m³. Δ = 693.33/(4.0 × 10⁴) = 0.017333 m = 17.3 mm. The positive sign means the deflection is in the direction of the unit load, so C moves 17.3 mm to the right.

Answer: 17.3 mm to the right

(d)

Apply a unit clockwise couple at C. A pure couple produces the same moment, m = 1.0, at every section of the frame, in both the arm and the column, and the sense is clockwise, matching the real moments. The virtual work equation gives θ = ∫ M m dx/EI = (1/EI)[∫ arm M dx + ∫ column M dd]. Arm: ∫0..3 20x dx = 10(9) = 90 kN·m². Column: ∫0..4 (60 + 10d)dd = 240 + 80 = 320 kN·m². The sum is 410 kN·m². θ = 410/(4.0 × 10⁴) = 0.01025 rad, about 0.59 degrees, clockwise. The arm bends under the vertical tip load, and the column bends under both loads, so both contribute to this joint rotation.

Answer: 0.01025 rad clockwise

Problem 2 [A1-087] Deflection by strain energy and Castigliano's theorem

A steel cantilever beam AB, 4.0 m long, is built into a concrete abutment at A. Its free end B rests on an elastomeric bearing pad that behaves as a linear spring of stiffness k = 3000 kN/m, supported on rigid ground. A uniformly distributed load of 10 kN/m acts downward over the full length of the beam. The beam has EI = 2.0 × 10⁴ kN·m² (E = 200 GPa, I = 1.0 × 10⁸ mm⁴) and its own weight is included in the 10 kN/m. Neglect the axial and shear strain energy. Use Castigliano's second theorem, with the strain energy of the beam and of the spring, and measure s from the free end B toward the abutment.

  1. (a) Find the force R carried by the spring at B. [7]
  2. (b) Find the downward deflection of the tip B. [3]
  3. (c) Find the bending moment at the abutment A. [3]
  4. (d) Using a dummy load Q at the mid-length of the beam, find the downward deflection at mid-length. [7]
(a)

The spring force R is the redundant. For a section a distance s from B, the beam moment is M = w s²/2 - R s = 5s² - Rs (hogging positive), with ∂M/∂R = -s. The total strain energy is U = ∫0..L M²/(2EI) ds + R²/(2k), the second term being the energy stored in the spring. The far end of the spring rests on rigid ground, so the system as a whole does not move at the point where R acts, and Castigliano's theorem gives ∂U/∂R = 0. That is ∫ M(∂M/∂R)/EI ds + R/k = 0, or -(1/EI)[w L⁴/8 - R L³/3] + R/k = 0. With L = 4: wL⁴/8 = 10(256)/8 = 320, and L³/3 = 21.333. So -(320 - 21.333R)/(2.0 × 10⁴) + R/3000 = 0, which gives 21.333R/(2.0 × 10⁴) + R/3000 = 320/(2.0 × 10⁴), so R(0.0010667 + 0.0003333) = 0.016, R = 11.43 kN.

Answer: R = 11.43 kN

(b)

The spring is attached to the tip, so the tip deflection equals the spring compression. For a linear spring, the compression is the force divided by the stiffness: δB = R/k = 11.4286/3000 = 3.8095 × 10⁻³ m, or 3.81 mm downward. As a check, the beam alone would deflect wL⁴/(8EI) = 320/(2.0 × 10⁴) = 16.0 mm at the tip with no support. The spring force pushing up reduces this by R L³/(3EI) = 11.4286(64)/(3 × 2.0 × 10⁴) = 12.19 mm, which leaves 16.0 - 12.19 = 3.81 mm. The two routes agree, which confirms that compatibility between beam and spring is satisfied.

Answer: 3.81 mm downward

(c)

The moment at the abutment follows from the moment function at s = L = 4.0 m. Take the free body from the tip to the abutment, with the downward load resultant of 10(4) = 40 kN acting 2.0 m from the tip (80 kN·m) and the spring force R = 11.4286 kN acting upward at the tip, 4.0 m from the abutment (45.714 kN·m). The load tends to produce hogging, and the spring force opposes it. MA = 5(16) - 11.4286(4) = 80 - 45.714 = 34.29 kN·m, hogging. This is less than half of the 80 kN·m that an unsupported cantilever would develop. The abutment reaction is 40 - 11.43 = 28.57 kN, which can be checked by taking vertical equilibrium of the whole beam.

Answer: 34.3 kN·m hogging

(d)

Add a dummy downward load Q at the mid-length, 2.0 m from B. For s from 0 to 2, the moment is unchanged: M = 5s² - Rs, and ∂M/∂Q = 0. For s from 2 to 4, M = 5s² - Rs + Q(s - 2), with ∂M/∂Q = (s - 2). Because the actual structure has no load at this point, set Q = 0 after differentiating. Since ∂U/∂R = 0 in the full system, the change in R caused by Q does not add anything to the mid-length deflection, so only the explicit dependence on Q is needed. δ = (1/EI)∫2..4 (5s² - 11.4286s)(s - 2)ds. Expanding: 5s³ - 21.4286s² + 22.857s. The antiderivative is 1.25s⁴ - 7.1429s³ + 11.4286s². At s = 4: 320 - 457.14 + 182.86 = 45.714. At s = 2: 20 - 57.14 + 45.71 = 8.571. Difference = 37.143. δ = 37.143/(2.0 × 10⁴) = 1.857 × 10⁻³ m, which is 1.86 mm downward.

Answer: 1.86 mm downward

Problem 3 [A1-088] Force method for one-degree indeterminate beams

A reinforced concrete grade beam AB, 6.0 m long, is cast into a pile cap at A, which can be taken as a fixed support, and rests on a bearing pier at B, modelled as a roller. It carries a uniformly distributed load of 15 kN/m over its full length, including self-weight. The flexural rigidity is EI = 4.5 × 10⁴ kN·m² (E = 25 GPa, I = 1.8 × 10⁹ mm⁴), constant along the beam. After construction, the pier at B settles by 12 mm because of soft clay below it, and the beam stays in contact with the pier. Use the force method with the reaction at B as the redundant, and compare the cases without and with the settlement.

  1. (a) Find the reaction at B if the pier does not settle. [4]
  2. (b) Find the reaction at B after the 12 mm settlement. [6]
  3. (c) Find the hogging moment at the fixed support A after the settlement. [4]
  4. (d) After the settlement, find the maximum sagging moment in the beam. [6]
(a)

The beam has 4 reaction components (3 at the fixed end, 1 at the roller) and only 3 equations of statics, so it is indeterminate to the first degree. Remove the roller at B to get the released structure, a cantilever fixed at A. Under the load, the released tip deflects downward by Δ10 = wL⁴/(8EI) = 15(1296)/(8 × 45 000) = 19 440/360 000 = 0.0540 m. A unit upward load at B gives a flexibility f11 = L³/(3EI) = 216/135 000 = 0.0016 m/kN. Compatibility says the deflection at B is zero when the pier does not move: Δ10 - RB f11 = 0, so RB = 0.0540/0.0016 = 33.75 kN upward. This equals 3wL/8, the textbook result for a propped cantilever.

Answer: RB = 33.75 kN

(b)

The settlement changes only the compatibility condition. The pier moves down by 12 mm and the beam stays on it, so the deflection at B of the released cantilever is not zero but 0.012 m downward. Using the same released structure: Δ10 - RB f11 = 0.012. Then RB = (0.0540 - 0.012)/0.0016 = 0.0420/0.0016 = 26.25 kN. The 12 mm settlement removes 7.5 kN, or 22 percent, of the pier reaction, and the load is shed to the abutment end. As a check, a 12 mm settlement alone with no load would require a reaction of 0.012/0.0016 = 7.5 kN downward, hence 33.75 - 7.5 = 26.25 kN when it is combined with the load.

Answer: RB = 26.25 kN

(c)

With RB known, the remaining reactions follow from equilibrium of the whole beam. The total load is 15(6) = 90 kN, so the vertical reaction at A is 90 - 26.25 = 63.75 kN upward. Taking moments about A, the load resultant acts 3.0 m from A and produces 90(3) = 270 kN·m, while RB acts 6.0 m from A and produces 26.25(6) = 157.5 kN·m in the opposite sense. The fixed-end moment is MA = 270 - 157.5 = 112.5 kN·m, hogging (tension on the top face). With no settlement it would have been 270 - 33.75(6) = 67.5 kN·m, so the settlement increases the demand at the fixed support by about 67 percent. The reinforcement at A is therefore the critical design item.

Answer: MA = 112.5 kN·m hogging

(d)

Measure x from B toward A. The sagging moment is M(x) = RB x - w x²/2 = 26.25x - 7.5x². The shear is zero where dM/dx = 26.25 - 15x = 0, so x = 26.25/15 = 1.75 m from B. At that point, M = 26.25(1.75) - 7.5(3.0625) = 45.94 - 22.97 = 22.97 kN·m, sagging. This is a modest sagging peak compared with the 112.5 kN·m hogging at A, which governs the design. At x = 6.0 m the formula gives 157.5 - 270 = -112.5 kN·m, which agrees with the support moment found in part (c), a useful check on the arithmetic.
