The point of contraflexure lies at x = 3.5 m from B, where M = 0.

Answer: 22.97 kN·m sagging, at 1.75 m from B

Problem 4 [A1-089] Force method for indeterminate trusses

A rectangular braced bay on the side of a mill building is idealised as a pin-jointed truss with joints A (bottom left), B (bottom right), C (top right) and D (top left). The bay is 4.0 m wide and 3.0 m high. The members are AB and CD (horizontal), AD and BC (vertical), and two crossed diagonals AC and BD. The bay is supported by a pin at A and a roller at B that resists vertical movement only. A wind load of 60 kN acts horizontally to the right at joint D. All members have the same area A = 2500 mm² and E = 200 GPa, except where stated. The truss is internally indeterminate to the first degree. Take the force in diagonal BD as the redundant, tension positive.

  1. (a) Find the vertical reaction at the roller B. [3]
  2. (b) Find the force in diagonal BD. [8]
  3. (c) Find the force in the bottom chord AB, stating whether it is in tension or compression. [4]
  4. (d) The diagonal BD is replaced by a member of twice the area (5000 mm²). Find the new magnitude of the force in BD. [5]
(a)

Draw the free body of the whole truss. The only horizontal load is the 60 kN force at D, which is 3.0 m above the base line AB. The pin at A can resist horizontal force, and the roller at B cannot, so the horizontal reaction is at A. Take moments about A, anticlockwise positive. The wind load acts to the right at a height of 3.0 m, so it gives -60(3) = -180 kN·m. The roller reaction By acts upward at 4.0 m from A and gives +4By. Then 4By - 180 = 0, so By = 45.0 kN upward. Vertical equilibrium gives Ay = -45.0 kN, meaning A is pulled downward 45 kN, and horizontal equilibrium gives Ax = 60 kN acting to the left.

Answer: By = 45.0 kN upward

(b)

Cut diagonal BD to get the primary structure. Joint D then has three forces: the 60 kN load, member DA and member DC, giving DC = -60 kN (compression) and DA = 0. Joint C gives AC = +75 kN (tension, since 0.8 AC must balance the 60 kN pushed in) and BC = -45 kN. Joint B gives AB = 0, so these N0 forces are statically correct. Now apply a unit tension pair in BD. This produces n(AC) = +1.0, n(AB) = n(CD) = -0.8 and n(BC) = n(DA) = -0.6. Compatibility says the relative movement of the cut ends is zero: Σ(N0 n L) + X Σ(n² L) = 0 for constant EA. Σ N0 n L = (-45)(-0.6)(3) + (-60)(-0.8)(4) + (75)(1)(5) = 81 + 192 + 375 = 648. Σ n² L = 2(0.64)(4) + 2(0.36)(3) + 2(1.0)(5) = 17.28. X = -648/17.28 = -37.5 kN, so BD carries 37.5 kN in compression.

Answer: BD = 37.5 kN compression

(c)

The final force in each member is N = N0 + X n, with X = -37.5 kN from part (b). For the bottom chord AB, N0 = 0 and n = -0.8, so N = 0 + (-37.5)(-0.8) = +30.0 kN, tension. As a check, take horizontal equilibrium at joint B. The compressive diagonal BD pushes B with a horizontal component 37.5(0.8) = 30 kN, directed to the right and away from D. The chord AB pulls on B toward A with 30 kN in tension, to the left. The two balance, and the vertical members are consistent as well: BC (-22.5 kN) and the vertical component of BD (22.5 kN) together equal By = 45 kN. This confirms both the chord force and the reaction.

Answer: AB = 30.0 kN tension

(d)

Doubling the area of BD only changes the flexibility term for that member. Σ(n² L/EA) now carries BD with half of its former weight: the terms are 2(0.64)(4) + 2(0.36)(3) + 5 = 12.28 for the five original members of AB, CD, BC, DA and AC, plus 5/2 = 2.5 for BD, so the sum becomes 14.78 in units of m per EA. The numerator is unchanged at 648, since N0 in BD is zero. X = -648/14.78 = -43.84 kN. The stiffer diagonal attracts more of the shear, 43.8 kN against 37.5 kN, an increase of 17 percent. The other diagonal AC drops from 37.5 kN to 75 - 43.84 = 31.16 kN, and the thicker diagonal now carries 0.8 × 43.84 = 35.1 kN of the 60 kN horizontal shear, about 58 percent.

Answer: BD = 43.8 kN compression

Problem 5 [A1-090] Slope-deflection method for continuous beams

A two-span continuous bridge deck girder ABC in northern Ontario is fixed against rotation at the abutment A and rests on rollers at the pier B and the abutment C. Span AB is 6.0 m and span BC is 8.0 m. The girder has constant EI = 6.0 × 10⁴ kN·m² (E = 200 GPa, I = 3.0 × 10⁸ mm⁴). Span AB carries a uniformly distributed load of 20 kN/m. Span BC carries a concentrated load of 80 kN at its mid-span. After construction, the pier at B settles 10 mm downward relative to A and C, which stay at their original levels. Use the slope-deflection method with clockwise end moments and clockwise rotations positive, and treat the rotation at A as zero and the moment at C as zero.

  1. (a) Find the rotation of the girder at pier B. [4]
  2. (b) Find the hogging moment at the fixed support A. [4]
  3. (c) Find the hogging moment over the pier B. [4]
  4. (d) Find the vertical reaction at the abutment C. [4]
  5. (e) Find the vertical reaction at the abutment A. [4]
(a)

Unknowns are θB and θC, with θA = 0. Fixed-end moments (clockwise positive): AB, uniform load: ±wL²/12 = ±60, so FAB = -60 and FBA = +60. BC, central point load: ±PL/8 = ±80, so FBC = -80 and FCB = +80. Chord rotations: B settles 10 mm, so chord AB turns clockwise by ψ1 = 0.010/6.0 = 1.667 × 10⁻³ rad, and chord BC turns anticlockwise by ψ2 = -0.010/8.0 = -1.25 × 10⁻³ rad. With 2EI/L = 2.0 × 10⁴ for AB and 1.5 × 10⁴ for BC: MBA = 2.0 × 10⁴(2θB - 3ψ1) + 60 = 4.0 × 10⁴θB - 40. MBC = 1.5 × 10⁴(2θB + θC - 3ψ2) - 80 = 3.0 × 10⁴θB + 1.5 × 10⁴θC - 23.75. MCB = 1.5 × 10⁴(2θC + θB - 3ψ2) + 80 = 3.0 × 10⁴θC + 1.5 × 10⁴θB + 136.25 = 0. Joint B: MBA + MBC = 0 gives 7.0 × 10⁴θB + 1.5 × 10⁴θC = 63.75. From MCB = 0, θC = -0.5θB - 4.542 × 10⁻³. Then 6.25 × 10⁴θB = 131.875 and θB = 2.11 × 10⁻³ rad clockwise.

Answer: θB = 2.11 × 10⁻³ rad clockwise

(b)

The slope-deflection equation at the near end A of span AB, with θA = 0, is MAB = (2EI/L)(θB - 3ψ1) + FAB = 2.0 × 10⁴(2.11 × 10⁻³ - 5.0 × 10⁻³) - 60. The term 3ψ1 = 3(1.667 × 10⁻³) = 5.0 × 10⁻³. So MAB = 2.0 × 10⁴(-2.89 × 10⁻³) - 60 = -57.8 - 60 = -117.8 kN·m. The negative sign means the moment acting on the girder end at A is anticlockwise, which produces tension in the top fibres of the girder at A, that is, hogging. The settlement term alone contributes -3(2.0 × 10⁴)(1.667 × 10⁻³) = -100 kN·m to this moment, which is why the settlement matters so much at a fixed support. This is the governing design moment at the abutment.

Answer: 117.8 kN·m hogging

(c)

The moment at the near end B of span AB is MBA = 4.0 × 10⁴θB - 40 = 4.0 × 10⁴(2.11 × 10⁻³) - 40 = 84.4 - 40 = 44.4 kN·m, clockwise on the end of the span AB, which means the girder is hogging at B. As a check, use the other span: MBC = 3.0 × 10⁴(2.11 × 10⁻³) + 1.5 × 10⁴(-5.5967 × 10⁻³) - 23.75 = 63.3 - 83.95 - 23.75 = -44.4 kN·m. The two end moments at joint B sum to zero, which is the equilibrium condition used to solve for the rotations, so the hogging moment over the pier is 44.4 kN·m. The pier moment is the combined result of both spans' loads and the 10 mm settlement.

Answer: 44.4 kN·m hogging

(d)

Isolate span BC as a free body with the end moment MBC = -44.4 kN·m (anticlockwise, 44.4 kN·m) at B, zero moment at C, and the 80 kN point load at mid-span. Take moments about B with anticlockwise positive: the end moment contributes +44.4, the load at 4.0 m to the right of B contributes -80(4) = -320, and the reaction RC at 8.0 m contributes +8RC. Then 44.4 - 320 + 8RC = 0, so RC = 275.6/8 = 34.45 kN upward. Compared with a simple span, which would give 40 kN, the hogging moment at B relieves the abutment C by 5.55 kN. This is also the shear force in the right-hand end of the span BC, a useful value for checking bearing capacity at the abutment.

Answer: RC = 34.45 kN

(e)

Isolate span AB as a free body. The moments at the ends are MAB = -117.8 (anticlockwise 117.8 at A) and MBA = +44.4 (clockwise 44.4 at B). The uniform load resultant is 20(6) = 120 kN at 3.0 m from B. Take moments about B with anticlockwise positive: end moment at A contributes +117.8, end moment at B contributes -44.4, the load, acting downward at 3.0 m to the left of B, contributes +120(3) = +360, and the reaction RA, acting upward at 6.0 m to the left of B, contributes -6RA. Then 117.8 - 44.4 + 360 - 6RA = 0, giving RA = 433.4/6 = 72.23 kN upward. The reaction at the pier is the remainder, 120 + 80 - 72.23 - 34.45 = 93.32 kN, by vertical equilibrium of the whole girder.

Answer: RA = 72.23 kN

A1 Practice Paper 19

Problem 1 [A1-091] Slope-deflection method with support settlement

A continuous steel walkway girder ABC carries a service pipe over a drainage channel in Hamilton. The girder is rigidly built into a concrete abutment at A, rests on a roller pier at B, 6.0 m from A, and on a roller seat at C, 5.0 m beyond B. The flexural rigidity EI is constant at 40 000 kN·m² for both spans. Span AB carries a uniformly distributed load of 20 kN/m. Span BC carries a single 30 kN point load at its midspan. The pier at B was founded on soft clay and has settled 15 mm below its original level, while A and C have not moved. Analyse the girder by the slope-deflection method with clockwise end moments and clockwise rotations taken as positive, and treat the end at C as free to rotate.

  1. (a) Find the rotation of joint C, in milliradians (clockwise positive). [4]
  2. (b) Find the end moment M_BA acting on span AB at B, in kN·m (clockwise positive). [4]
  3. (c) Find the magnitude of the fixed-support moment at A. [4]
  4. (d) Find the vertical reaction at the settled pier B. [4]
  5. (e) Find how much the reaction at B is reduced by the settlement, compared with the same girder on unyielding supports. [4]
(a)

Slope-deflection form with clockwise positive: M_ij = (2EI/L)(2θi + θj - 3ψ) + FEM_ij. The stiffness factors are 2EI/L = 13 333.3 kN·m/rad for AB and 16 000 kN·m/rad for BC. The settlement of B tilts chord AB clockwise, ψ_AB = +0.015/6.0 = +0.0025, and tilts chord BC counter-clockwise, ψ_BC = -0.015/5.0 = -0.0030. Fixed-end moments are -60 and +60 kN·m on AB (wL²/12) and -18.75 and +18.75 kN·m on BC (PL/8). With θA = 0 the unknowns are θB and θC. Joint B, M_BA + M_BC = 0, gives 58 666.7θB + 16 000θC = -85.25. The free end C, M_CB = 0, gives 16 000θB + 32 000θC = -162.75. Solving, θB = -0.0000765 rad and θC = -0.005048 rad, so C turns 5.05 mrad counter-clockwise.

Answer: -5.05 mrad

(b)

Using θB = -0.0000765 rad from part (a), the end moment of span AB at B is M_BA = (2EI/L)(2θB + θA - 3ψ_AB) + FEM_BA = 13 333.3(2(-0.0000765) - 3(0.0025)) + 60. The bracket is -0.007653, so the first term is -102.04 kN·m and M_BA = -102.04 + 60 = -42.04 kN·m. The negative sign means the moment on the member end at B is counter-clockwise, which at the right-hand end of a span is sagging. Without settlement this moment would be a hogging +43.2 kN·m, so the 15 mm movement has not only removed the hogging at B but reversed it. As a check, M_BC = 16 000(2θB + θC - 3ψ_BC) - 18.75 = +42.04 kN·m, which balances M_BA at the joint as it must.

Answer: -42.0 kN·m

(c)

The moment at the built-in support is M_AB = (2EI/L)(2θA + θB - 3ψ_AB) + FEM_AB = 13 333.3(0 - 0.0000765 - 0.0075) - 60. The bracket is -0.007576, so the first term is -101.02 kN·m and M_AB = -101.02 - 60 = -161.02 kN·m. The magnitude is 161.0 kN·m, hogging at A. Without settlement the same moment is only 68.4 kN·m, so the abutment connection must now be designed for more than double its original moment. The reason is that A is held against rotation while B drops, and the chord rotation ψ_AB adds to the hogging already produced by the 20 kN/m load. This is the most critical effect of the settlement in design terms.

Answer: 161.0 kN·m

(d)

Use member equilibrium. For span AB take moments about B, clockwise positive: 6.0R_A + M_AB + M_BA - 120(3.0) = 0, because the 120 kN resultant of the UDL acts 3.0 m left of B. R_A = (360 + 161.02 + 42.04)/6.0 = 93.84 kN. For span BC take moments about B: M_BC + M_CB + 30(2.5) - 5.0R_C = 0, so R_C = (42.04 + 0 + 75)/5.0 = 23.41 kN. The total load is 120 + 30 = 150 kN, so R_B = 150 - 93.84 - 23.41 = 32.75 kN. Global moments about A, 150 kN loads and reactions together with M_AB, also balance, which confirms the member moments and signs are consistent with each other.

Answer: 32.7 kN

(e)

Repeat the analysis with the settlement set to zero, so ψ_AB = ψ_BC = 0. Joint B gives 58 666.7θB + 16 000θC = -60 + 18.75 = -41.25, and joint C gives 16 000θB + 32 000θC = -18.75. Solving, θB = -0.000629 rad and θC = -0.000271 rad. Then M_AB = -68.39 kN·m, M_BA = +43.22 kN·m and M_BC = -43.22 kN·m. Span AB gives R_A = (360 + 68.39 - 43.22)/6.0 = 64.19 kN, span BC gives R_C = (-43.22 + 75)/5.0 = 6.36 kN, and R_B = 150 - 64.19 - 6.36 = 79.45 kN. The reduction is 79.45 - 32.75 = 46.70 kN, which the abutment A and seat C pick up instead.

Answer: 46.7 kN

Problem 2 [A1-092] Moment distribution for continuous beams

A continuous reinforced concrete conveyor beam ABCD in a Windsor parts warehouse is fixed against rotation at A, rests on rollers at B and C, and ends on a simple roller at D. The spans are AB = 5.0 m, BC = 6.0 m and CD = 4.0 m. The flexural rigidity of AB is 60 000 kN·m², and that of BC and CD is 30 000 kN·m² each. Span AB carries a 60 kN point load at midspan. Span BC carries a uniformly distributed load of 18 kN/m over its whole length. Span CD carries a 40 kN point load 1.5 m from C. The supports do not settle. Analyse the beam by moment distribution, treat the far end D as a free pin so that no carry-over to D is wanted, and take clockwise end moments as positive.

  1. (a) Find the distribution factor for member BA at joint B. [3]
  2. (b) Find the distribution factor for member CB at joint C. [3]
  3. (c) Find the final end moment M_BA. [5]
  4. (d) Find the final end moment M_CB. [4]
  5. (e) Find the total vertical reaction at B. [5]
(a)

Member stiffness is 4EI/L when the far end is restrained against translation and can carry a moment. For BA the far end A is fixed, so K_BA = 4(60 000)/5.0 = 48 000 kN·m/rad. For BC the far end C is a continuous joint, so K_BC = 4(30 000)/6.0 = 20 000 kN·m/rad. The distribution factor is the member stiffness divided by the sum at the joint, so DF_BA = 48 000/(48 000 + 20 000) = 0.7059, and DF_BC = 20 000/68 000 = 0.2941. The two factors sum to 1.000, which is the check at every joint. The stiffer member AB, with double the EI and a shorter span, takes about 71 percent of any moment applied at B.

Answer: 0.706

(b)

At C the member CD ends on a simple roller, so its far-end moment is zero and the modified stiffness K_CD = 3EI/L = 3(30 000)/4.0 = 22 500 kN·m/rad is used. This removes the need to balance and carry over from D. The member CB has its far end B continuous, so K_CB = 4(30 000)/6.0 = 20 000 kN·m/rad. Then DF_CB = 20 000/(20 000 + 22 500) = 0.4706 and DF_CD = 22 500/42 500 = 0.5294. Because the modified stiffness is used, the fixed-end moment of CD must also be modified: FEM_CD = -Pab²/L² = -40(1.5)(2.5²)/4.0² = -23.44, FEM_DC = +Pa²b/L² = +14.06, so the modified value at C is -23.44 - 14.06/2 = -30.47 kN·m.

Answer: 0.471

(c)

Fixed-end moments are FEM_AB = -PL/8 = -37.5 and FEM_BA = +37.5 kN·m, and FEM_BC = -wL²/12 = -54 and FEM_CB = +54 kN·m, with FEM_CD = -30.47 as modified. Cycle 1 at B: unbalance = 37.5 - 54 = -16.5, so BA gains 0.7059(16.5) = +11.65 to 49.15, BC gains +4.85 to -49.15. Carry-over gives AB +5.82 and CB +2.43 to 56.43. At C: unbalance = 56.43 - 30.47 = +25.96, so CB falls by 0.4706(25.96) = 12.22 to 44.21, CD falls to -44.21, and BC receives a carry-over of -6.11 to -55.25. Cycle 2 at B: unbalance -6.10 gives BA = 53.46. Cycle 3 gives 53.61, and further cycles change nothing visible. M_BA = 53.61 kN·m, hogging at B.

Answer: 53.6 kN·m

(d)

The same distribution table gives M_CB. After cycle 1 it is 44.21 kN·m. In cycle 2 the balance at B sends a carry-over of +0.90 to CB, so the unbalance at C is +0.90 and balancing removes 0.42, leaving M_CB = 44.69. Cycle 3 brings it to 44.70 kN·m. The corresponding value M_CD = -44.70 kN·m balances it at C, so M_CB + M_CD = 0 as joint equilibrium requires. At the final iteration joint B also checks, since 53.61 + (-53.61) = 0. M_CB is positive clockwise at the right-hand end of BC, which is hogging at C, so span BC is hogging at both ends and the sagging moment at midspan is correspondingly reduced from the simple-beam value.

Answer: 44.7 kN·m

(e)

Find the shear contributions on each side of B. Span AB, moments about B: 5.0R_A + M_AB + M_BA - 60(2.5) = 0 with M_AB = -29.44 and M_BA = +53.61, so R_A = (150 + 29.44 - 53.61)/5.0 = 25.17 kN, and the part of the 60 kN load taken at B is 60 - 25.17 = 34.83 kN. Span BC, moments about B: M_BC + M_CB + 108(3.0) - 6.0R_C = 0, so R_C(from BC) = (324 - 53.61 + 44.70)/6.0 = 52.52 kN, and the part of the 108 kN load taken at B is 108 - 52.52 = 55.48 kN. R_B = 34.83 + 55.48 = 90.32 kN. The total of all four reactions equals 208 kN, the full load, which checks the working.

Answer: 90.3 kN

Problem 3 [A1-093] Moment distribution for frames without sidesway

A single-bay portal frame ABCD supports a mezzanine slab in a Kingston workshop. Column AB is 4.0 m high with a fixed base at A. Column CD is 5.0 m high with a pinned base at D. Beam BC is 7.0 m long and joins the column tops rigidly at B and C. The flexural rigidity is 30 000 kN·m² for each column and 60 000 kN·m² for the beam. The beam carries a uniformly distributed load of 24 kN/m over its full length, and the columns carry no transverse load. A rigid horizontal link at beam level prevents the frame from swaying, so every joint rotates but none translates. Analyse the frame by moment distribution with clockwise end moments positive, using the modified stiffness for the pinned column base.

  1. (a) Find the distribution factor for member BA at joint B. [3]
  2. (b) Find the final end moment M_BA at the top of column AB. [4]
  3. (c) Find the final end moment M_CB at the right end of the beam. [4]
  4. (d) Find the horizontal reaction at the fixed base A, in kN, positive to the right. [4]
  5. (e) Find the horizontal force carried by the sway-preventing link. [5]
(a)

At joint B the two members are the column BA, whose far end A is fixed, and the beam BC, whose far end C is continuous. Both use 4EI/L. K_BA = 4(30 000)/4.0 = 30 000 kN·m/rad and K_BC = 4(60 000)/7.0 = 34 286 kN·m/rad. The distribution factor DF_BA = 30 000/(30 000 + 34 286) = 0.4667 and DF_BC = 0.5333. The sum is 1.000, which is the joint check. Because sway is prevented, no chord rotation terms enter and the stiffness values apply directly. The beam is slightly stiffer than the column, so it receives a slightly larger share of any unbalanced moment at B.

Answer: 0.467

(b)

Fixed-end moments for the beam are FEM_BC = -wL²/12 = -24(49)/12 = -98.0 kN·m and FEM_CB = +98.0 kN·m. At C the column CD has a pinned base, so K_CD = 3EI/L = 3(30 000)/5.0 = 18 000 kN·m/rad and K_CB = 34 286, giving DF_CB = 0.6557 and DF_CD = 0.3443. Cycle 1: unbalance at B is -98, so BA = +45.73 and BC = -98 + 52.27 = -45.73; carry-over gives AB +22.87 and CB 98 + 26.13 = 124.13, which is balanced at C to 42.73 with carry-over -40.7 back to B. Continuing, M_BA = 45.73, 64.73, 66.39, 66.53, then 66.55 kN·m. Joint B closes with M_BC = -66.55, so M_BA + M_BC = 0.

Answer: 66.5 kN·m

(c)

Continue the table from part (b). Cycle 1 at C: unbalance = 124.13 kN·m (the 98 plus the carry-over of 26.13 from B), so CB falls by 0.6557(124.13) = 81.4 to 42.73 and CD becomes -42.73. The carry-over to BC is -40.7. Cycle 2 at B balances -40.7, and the C balance of the returned carry-over moves CB to 46.47. Later cycles give 46.80, 46.83, then 46.83 kN·m. At joint C the column end moment is M_CD = -46.83 kN·m, which cancels M_CB, so M_CB + M_CD = 0 as joint equilibrium requires. M_CB is clockwise at the right end of a beam, which is hogging at C, with a magnitude 46.83 kN·m.

Answer: 46.8 kN·m

(d)

Column AB is a vertical member with its base at A. Its final moments are M_AB = +33.27 kN·m (half of M_BA, the carry-over to the fixed base) and M_BA = +66.55 kN·m. Take moments about the base A for the column alone: M_AB + M_BA + 4.0 H_B = 0, where H_B is the horizontal force the joint applies on the column top, positive to the right. This gives H_B = -(33.27 + 66.55)/4.0 = -24.95 kN. The column is in horizontal equilibrium, so the base reaction at A is H_A = +24.95 kN to the right. Both end moments are clockwise, so the column bends in double curvature and carries a constant shear of 24.95 kN.

Answer: 24.9 kN

(e)

Column CD has the pinned base D, so M_DC = 0 and M_CD = -46.83 kN·m. Moments about D for this column alone give 5.0 H_C + M_CD = 0 if H_C is the horizontal force on the top, so H_C = +9.37 kN to the right, and the base reaction at D is H_D = -9.37 kN, i.e. 9.37 kN to the left. The two base reactions are +24.95 and -9.37, a net 15.59 kN to the right. There are no applied horizontal loads, so total horizontal equilibrium demands that the link supply 15.59 kN acting to the left on the beam level. If the link were removed, the frame would sway to the right, which is why sway analysis would also be required.

Answer: 15.6 kN

Problem 4 [A1-094] Stiffness, carry-over and fixed-end moments including modified stiffness

A two-span steel beam ABC in an Oshawa loading bay has a prismatic member AB and a prismatic member BC. Member AB is 6.0 m long with I = 8.0 × 10⁸ mm⁴, fixed at A. Member BC is 8.0 m long with I = 4.0 × 10⁸ mm⁴, and its far end C is a frictionless pin. E = 200 GPa throughout. Member BC carries a uniformly distributed load of 15 kN/m over the first 5.0 m measured from B, and member AB is unloaded. A mechanical equipment plinth applies a concentrated couple of 80 kN·m, clockwise, directly to joint B. Joint B may rotate but not translate. Use the standard stiffness definitions, with clockwise end moments positive.

  1. (a) Find the distribution factor of member BA at B, using the modified stiffness for BC. [3]
  2. (b) Find the modified fixed-end moment at B for member BC, accounting for the pinned far end. [5]
  3. (c) Find the final end moment M_BA. [4]
  4. (d) Find the carry-over moment M_AB at the fixed support. [4]
  5. (e) Find the rotation of joint B, in milliradians. [4]
(a)

Convert to flexural rigidities: EI_BC = 200 × 10⁶ kPa × 4.0 × 10⁸ × 10⁻¹² m⁴ = 80 000 kN·m², and EI_AB is twice that, 160 000 kN·m². Member BA has a fixed far end, so K_BA = 4EI/L = 4(160 000)/6.0 = 106 667 kN·m/rad, with carry-over factor 1/2. Member BC has a pinned far end, so the modified stiffness K_BC = 3EI/L = 3(80 000)/8.0 = 30 000 kN·m/rad, with no carry-over. The total is 136 667, so DF_BA = 106 667/136 667 = 0.7805 and DF_BC = 0.2195. Using the modified stiffness is correct only because the pin at C releases the far-end moment completely.

Answer: 0.780

(b)

For a load of intensity w over a length a = 5.0 m from the left end of a span L = 8.0 m, the fixed-fixed end moments are FEM_BC = -wa²(6L² - 8aL + 3a²)/(12L²) and FEM_CB = +wa³(4L - 3a)/(12L²). Substituting, FEM_BC = -15(25)(384 - 320 + 75)/(12 × 64) = -15(25)(139)/768 = -67.87 kN·m. FEM_CB = 15(125)(32 - 15)/768 = +41.50 kN·m. Because C is a pin, release it: the modified moment at B is FEM'_BC = FEM_BC - FEM_CB/2 = -67.87 - 20.75 = -88.62 kN·m. The half of the C moment is carried to B before being removed, which is why the sign adds to the hogging value.

Answer: -88.6 kN·m

(c)

With joint B clamped, member BA carries no moment and BC carries -88.62 kN·m. The joint has an external clockwise couple of 80 kN·m, and the members must together supply M_BA + M_BC = +80 kN·m. The balancing moment to be distributed is therefore 80 - (-88.62) = +168.62 kN·m. Member BA takes DF_BA × 168.62 = 0.7805(168.62) = +131.61 kN·m. Hence M_BA = 131.61 kN·m. Member BC takes 0.2195(168.62) = 37.01 kN·m, so M_BC = -88.62 + 37.01 = -51.61 kN·m. Check: 131.61 - 51.61 = 80.00, which equals the applied couple.

Answer: 131.6 kN·m

(d)

The far end of BA is fixed, so half of the moment applied at B is carried over to A with the same sign: M_AB = 0.5 × M_BA = 0.5(131.61) = +65.80 kN·m. No fixed-end moment exists on AB because it is unloaded. The sign is positive (clockwise at A), meaning the wall pushes back on the beam with a clockwise moment as the couple tries to rotate the joint clockwise. Both end moments are clockwise, so AB bends in double curvature, with the sign change of moment somewhere along the span. The magnitude at A is exactly half of that at B because the member is prismatic and the far end is fixed.

Answer: 65.8 kN·m

(e)

The joint rotation follows from the distributed moment and the combined stiffness: θB = M_balance / ΣK = 168.62 / 136 667 = 0.0012338 rad = 1.234 mrad clockwise. Check with member BA alone: M_BA = K_BA θB = 106 667 × 0.0012338 = 131.6 kN·m, which agrees with part (c), and M_BC' = 30 000 × 0.0012338 = 37.0 kN·m, the rotation-induced part of M_BC. The rotation is small, about 0.07 degrees, which is typical for a stiff beam joint under this size of couple. The positive sign means clockwise, the same sense as the applied couple, and the modified stiffness is valid because the far end of BC is a pin.

Answer: 1.234 mrad

Problem 5 [A1-095] Least work and energy methods for indeterminate structures

A steel ceiling-mounted utility platform in a Sudbury mine shaft house hangs from a single pin joint D carried by three rods that meet at D and are fixed to the rock above. Two identical inclined rods are each inclined 35 degrees to the vertical, with a cross-sectional area of 600 mm² and a length equal to the vertical rod's height divided by cos 35°. A central vertical rod is 3.0 m long with an area of 900 mm². All rods are steel with E = 200 GPa. A vertical load of 150 kN is hung from D. The upper ends are rigid and the rods are pinned at both ends, so each carries axial force only. Analyse the system by the least-work method, treating the force in the central rod as the redundant and neglecting the weight of the rods.

  1. (a) Find the force in the central vertical rod. [5]
  2. (b) Find the force in each inclined rod. [4]
  3. (c) Find the vertical displacement of joint D, in millimetres. [4]
  4. (d) Find the total strain energy stored in the three rods, in joules. [3]
  5. (e) Find the displacement of D, in millimetres, if the central rod were absent. [4]
(a)

Let R be the tension in the central rod. Vertical equilibrium of joint D gives 2F cos 35° + R = 150, so each inclined rod has F = (150 - R)/(2 cos 35°). The inclined rod length is L1 = 3.0/cos 35° = 3.662 m. Strain energy U = 2F²L1/(2A1E) + R²Lv/(2A2E) = (150 - R)²L1/(4cos²35° A1E) + R²Lv/(2A2E). Least work requires dU/dR = 0, because the rock support at the top of the central rod does not move, so the redundant force does no external work. With A1E = 120 000 kN and A2E = 180 000 kN: -(150 - R)(2.2741 × 10⁻⁵) + R(1.6667 × 10⁻⁵) = 0, so R = 150(2.2741)/(2.2741 + 1.6667) = 86.56 kN, tension.

Answer: 86.6 kN

(b)

Back-substitute R = 86.56 kN into the equilibrium equation. The load shared by the two inclined rods is 150 - 86.56 = 63.44 kN vertically. Each rod carries half of that vertical component, divided by cos 35° = 0.81915 to obtain the axial force: F = 63.44/(2 × 0.81915) = 38.72 kN, tension. The vertical rod, which is shorter and stiffer in axial terms than the inclined pair, attracts the larger share of the load, 57.7 percent. Axial stresses are F/A1 = 38 722/600 = 64.5 MPa in the inclined rods and R/A2 = 86 561/900 = 96.2 MPa in the vertical rod, both well below yield for ordinary structural steel.

Answer: 38.7 kN

(c)

The displacement of D equals the elongation of the vertical rod, since it hangs vertically: δ = R Lv/(A2E) = 86.56 × 3.0/180 000 = 1.4427 × 10⁻³ m = 1.443 mm downward. Check through the inclined rods: their elongation is F L1/(A1E) = 38.72 × 3.662/120 000 = 1.1816 × 10⁻³ m, and the vertical displacement is the elongation divided by cos 35°, 1.1816/0.81915 = 1.4426 mm, which agrees. The agreement confirms that the redundant force from the least-work equation satisfies compatibility, which is the physical meaning of dU/dR = 0 here.

Answer: 1.443 mm

(d)

Strain energy of the system is U = Σ F²L/(2AE). For the two inclined rods, U = 2 × 38.72² × 3.662/(2 × 120 000) = 0.04576 kN·m. For the vertical rod, U = 86.56² × 3.0/(2 × 180 000) = 0.06244 kN·m. Total U = 0.10820 kN·m = 108.2 J. Check by external work: the load rises linearly with the deflection, so U = ½Pδ = 0.5 × 150 × 1.4427 × 10⁻³ = 0.1082 kN·m, the same value. This is Clapeyron's theorem and gives an independent confirmation that all the member forces and the displacement are consistent with each other.

Answer: 108.2 J

(e)

Without the central rod the problem is statically determinate. Each inclined rod carries F0 = 150/(2 cos 35°) = 91.56 kN. Elongation of each inclined rod is F0 L1/(A1E) = 91.56 × 3.662/120 000 = 2.794 × 10⁻³ m. The joint moves vertically by this elongation divided by cos 35°, 2.794/0.81915 = 3.411 mm. The central rod therefore reduces the deflection from 3.411 mm to 1.443 mm, a reduction of 58 percent, and the peak stress in the inclined rods falls from 152.6 MPa to 64.5 MPa. It shows that the redundant rod carries a large share of the load because it is a direct, stiff load path.

Answer: 3.411 mm

A1 Practice Paper 20

Problem 1 [A1-096] Indeterminate structure with settlement or temperature change, comparing methods

A steel crane-runway beam in a Thunder Bay mill is a propped cantilever AB, 8.0 m long, with EI = 50 000 kN·m². It is fixed at A and rests on a bearing at the free end B. It carries a uniformly distributed load of 10 kN/m over its full length. The beam is 400 mm deep and the top surface is exposed to the sun, so the top is 30 °C warmer than the bottom, with a linear variation through the depth. The coefficient of thermal expansion is 11 × 10⁻⁶ per °C. Over the years the pier under B has settled 20 mm. Treat the bearing at B as the redundant and find its reaction by the force method, then verify one result by the slope-deflection method.

  1. (a) Find the reaction at B for the uniform load alone on unyielding supports. [3]
  2. (b) Find the reaction at B for the uniform load with the 20 mm settlement. [4]
  3. (c) Find the reaction at B for the load, the settlement and the temperature gradient together. [5]
  4. (d) For the combined case, find the magnitude of the hogging moment at A. [4]
  5. (e) Find the settlement at B, in millimetres, that would reduce the combined-case reaction at B to zero. [4]
(a)

Release the support at B. The cantilever deflection at B under the UDL is Δ_B0 = wL⁴/(8EI) = 10(8.0⁴)/(8 × 50 000) = 0.1024 m downward. A unit upward force at B produces a flexibility f_BB = L³/(3EI) = 512/150 000 = 3.4133 × 10⁻³ m per kN. Compatibility with an unmoving support requires R_B f_BB = Δ_B0, so R_B = 0.1024/0.0034133 = 30.0 kN, the familiar 3wL/8 for a propped cantilever. The remaining reaction at A is 80 - 30 = 50 kN, and the fixed-end moment is wL²/8 = 80 kN·m. These are the benchmark values against which the effects of settlement and temperature are measured.

Answer: 30.0 kN

(b)

With the support at B 20 mm lower than the original level, the compatibility condition is that the final deflection of B equals 0.020 m downward. The free deflection from the load is 0.1024 m downward, and the redundant lifts the beam by R_B f_BB. So 0.1024 - R_B(0.0034133) = 0.020, giving R_B = 0.0824/0.0034133 = 24.14 kN. Settlement of 20 mm has therefore relieved the bearing of 5.86 kN, about 20 percent of its original reaction. The sign is intuitive: a support that moves away from the beam attracts less load. The load carried by the fixed support A rises correspondingly to 80 - 24.14 = 55.86 kN.

Answer: 24.1 kN

(c)

Thermal curvature is κ = αΔT/h = (11 × 10⁻⁶)(30)/0.400 = 8.25 × 10⁻⁴ per metre. A warmer top fibre lengthens the top more than the bottom, so the beam curves with its centre of curvature below it, the same hogging sense as the load. A cantilever fixed at A therefore has its free end move down, by κL²/2 = 8.25 × 10⁻⁴ × 64/2 = 0.0264 m. The free downward deflection at B is 0.1024 + 0.0264 = 0.1288 m. Compatibility with the 20 mm settlement requires 0.1288 − R_B(0.0034133) = 0.020, so R_B = 0.1088/0.0034133 = 31.88 kN. The gradient therefore pushes the beam harder onto the bearing and raises the reaction by a further 7.7 kN over the settlement case. Thermal effects like this one are often ignored in routine checks, yet here they matter as much as the settlement.

Answer: 31.9 kN

(d)

From statics on the cantilever with R_B = 31.875 kN, the moment at A is M_A = R_B L − wL²/2 = 31.875(8.0) − 10(64)/2 = 255.0 − 320 = −65.0 kN·m, so the hogging magnitude is 65.0 kN·m. Verify with slope-deflection: k = 2EI/L = 12 500, ψ = 0.020/8.0 = 0.0025. Fixed-end moments from load are FEM_AB = −53.33 and FEM_BA = +53.33 kN·m. The gradient restraint moments EIκ = 41.25 act the opposite way, so the combined FEM_AB = −53.33 + 41.25 = −12.08 and FEM_BA = +12.08 kN·m. The condition M_BA = 0 gives 12 500(2θB − 0.0075) + 12.08 = 0, so θB = 3.267 × 10⁻³ rad, and M_AB = 12 500(θB − 0.0075) − 12.08 = −65.0 kN·m. Both methods agree.

Answer: 65.0 kN·m

(e)

The reaction at B vanishes when the beam no longer touches the bearing. Then the redundant is zero and the compatibility equation reduces to the free deflection: the final deflection of B equals the free deflection of the cantilever under the load and gradient together. That is 0.1024 + 0.0264 = 0.1288 m = 128.8 mm, since the warm top bends the tip downward as well. Any settlement larger than 128.8 mm would leave the beam hanging on A alone with an 80 kN reaction and a moment of 320 kN·m, and the beam would be unsupported at B. In practice an engineer would check the bearing for uplift and the pier for further movement before that state is reached. The reaction depends linearly on settlement, falling by 0.293 kN for each additional millimetre.

Answer: 128.8 mm

Problem 2 [A1-097] Reactions and free-body diagrams of determinate beams and frames

A steel maintenance gantry beam ABC on a hospital roof in Ottawa has a pin support at A and a roller support at B, 10.0 m from A. The beam continues 3.0 m past B to the free end C. Self-weight and a light walkway grating add 4 kN/m over the full 13.0 m. A monorail hoist trolley with its lifted load, totalling 70 kN, can be parked at any point from A to C. The bearing at B is rated for a service reaction of 110 kN. The pin at A has no anchor to resist uplift. The facility manager wants a single posted maximum trolley load that is safe at every position. Treat the trolley as a point load and the supports as frictionless.

  1. (a) Find the reaction at B under the distributed load alone. [4]
  2. (b) Find the reaction at B when the 70 kN trolley is parked at C. [4]
  3. (c) Find the reaction at A for that trolley position, taking upward as positive. [4]
  4. (d) Find the largest trolley load that can be parked at C before the pin at A lifts. [4]
  5. (e) Find the single trolley load to post, so that neither the uplift at A nor the 110 kN rating at B is exceeded anywhere. [4]
(a)

Treat the whole 13.0 m beam as the free body. The distributed load has a resultant of 4(13.0) = 52 kN acting 6.5 m from A. Moments about A, counter-clockwise positive, with the reaction R_B at 10.0 m upward: R_B(10.0) - 52(6.5) = 0, so R_B = 338/10.0 = 33.8 kN. Vertical equilibrium gives R_A = 52 - 33.8 = 18.2 kN upward. No horizontal load acts, so the pin carries no horizontal reaction. The distributed load alone therefore keeps both supports in compression with a margin of 18.2 kN at A, and this small margin is what the trolley load will use up when it is parked on the overhang.

Answer: 33.8 kN

(b)

Add the trolley at C, 13.0 m from A. Its moment about A is 70(13.0) = 910 kN·m, so the extra reaction at B is 910/10.0 = 91.0 kN. The total is R_B = 33.8 + 91.0 = 124.8 kN. This is the largest value this trolley can cause at B, because the influence of a unit load on R_B is x/10.0, which grows linearly with x and reaches its maximum of 1.3 at the free end. The reaction exceeds the 110 kN bearing rating by 14.8 kN, a 13 percent excess, so the full 70 kN trolley cannot be parked at C. The designer must either strengthen the bearing or limit the trolley load.

Answer: 124.8 kN

(c)

The influence of a unit load at x metres from A on the reaction at A is (10.0 - x)/10.0, which becomes negative beyond B. At C, x = 13.0, the influence is -0.3. The trolley therefore changes R_A by 70(-0.3) = -21.0 kN. With the dead-load reaction of 18.2 kN, R_A = 18.2 - 21.0 = -2.8 kN. The negative sign means the beam tries to lift off the pin by 2.8 kN, a small value, but the pin has no anchor so the beam is not in equilibrium as described. Either a hold-down of at least 2.8 kN must be provided or the trolley load must be limited, with a margin for dynamic effects of the hoist.

Answer: -2.8 kN

(d)

Let the trolley load be P at C. Then R_A = 18.2 - 0.3P. Uplift begins when R_A = 0, so P = 18.2/0.3 = 60.67 kN. Any load below 60.67 kN leaves A in compression, and any load above it lifts the pin. The 70 kN full load exceeds this by 9.3 kN. It is also worth noting that the critical position is the extreme of the overhang, because the influence line for R_A is a straight line, so the least reaction always occurs at the end of the range. No position between A and B can cause uplift because the influence there is positive.

Answer: 60.7 kN

(e)

Two limits apply, both governed by the trolley at C. For the bearing at B, 33.8 + 1.3P ≤ 110, so P ≤ 76.2/1.3 = 58.6 kN. For the pin at A, P ≤ 60.67 kN from part (d). The lower value governs, so the posted trolley load is 58.6 kN. At that load R_B is exactly 110 kN, and R_A is 18.2 - 0.3(58.6) = +0.6 kN, still in compression. Because both limiting influences are straight lines in the trolley position, the extreme position C governs and no other position needs checking. A prudent engineer would post a rounded value of 55 kN to leave a margin for dynamic amplification.

Answer: 58.6 kN

Problem 3 [A1-098] Shear and bending moment diagrams for beams with point and distributed loads

A simply supported steel girder AB with a span of 10.0 m carries the floor of a parking structure in London, Ontario. It rests on a pin at A and a roller at B. The girder carries a uniformly distributed load of 20 kN/m over its entire span. A column from the level above delivers a 90 kN concentrated downward load at 3.0 m from A. The fabricator needs to place a bolted field splice, and the designer will only allow it where the bending moment is no more than half of the maximum moment in the girder. Draw the shear and bending moment diagrams in your working, using the usual sign convention for a simply supported beam, and answer the following.

  1. (a) Find the reaction at A. [3]
  2. (b) Find the distance from A to the section of zero shear. [4]
  3. (c) Find the maximum bending moment. [5]
  4. (d) Find the distance from B within which the moment is no more than half of the maximum. [5]
  5. (e) State, with the bending moment at midspan, whether a splice at midspan would be acceptable. [3]
(a)

Find the reactions from equilibrium of the whole girder. The distributed load has a resultant of 20(10.0) = 200 kN at 5.0 m, and the point load is 90 kN at 3.0 m. Moments about A: R_B(10.0) = 200(5.0) + 90(3.0) = 1000 + 270 = 1270, so R_B = 127 kN. Vertical equilibrium: R_A = 200 + 90 - 127 = 163 kN. As a check, take moments about B: R_A(10.0) = 200(5.0) + 90(7.0) = 1000 + 630 = 1630, so R_A = 163 kN, in agreement. Both reactions are upward and positive, so the girder is in compression on both bearings, as expected for gravity loads on a simple span.

Answer: 163 kN

(b)

Draw the shear diagram from the left. At A the shear jumps to +163 kN and then falls at 20 kN/m. At 3.0 m, just before the point load, V = 163 - 20(3.0) = 103 kN. The 90 kN load drops the shear to 103 - 90 = 13 kN just after it. Shear continues to fall at 20 kN/m and passes through zero when 13 - 20s = 0, where s is the distance past the load, so s = 0.65 m. The zero-shear section is therefore at x = 3.0 + 0.65 = 3.65 m from A. At B the shear reaches 13 - 20(7.0) = -127 kN, equal in magnitude to R_B, which is the closing check on the diagram.

Answer: 3.65 m

(c)

The maximum moment occurs where shear is zero, at x = 3.65 m. Take moments of the forces to the left of the section: M = R_A x - 90(x - 3.0) - 20x²/2 = 163(3.65) - 90(0.65) - 10(3.65²). That is 594.95 - 58.50 - 133.23 = 403.2 kN·m, sagging. Check from the right: M = 127(6.35) - 20(6.35²)/2 = 806.45 - 403.23 = 403.2 kN·m, which agrees. For reference, the moment at the point load is 163(3.0) - 10(9.0) = 399 kN·m, only 4.2 kN·m less than the peak, because the shear just to the right of the load is small (13 kN).

Answer: 403.2 kN·m

(d)

Half the maximum moment is 201.6 kN·m. On the right of the peak the moment diagram is a parabola, and it is simplest to measure from B, where M = 127y - 20y²/2 = 127y - 10y², with y the distance from B. Set 127y - 10y² = 201.6, i.e. 10y² - 127y + 201.6 = 0. Then y = [127 - √(127² - 4(10)(201.6))]/20 = [127 - √8063.6]/20 = (127 - 89.80)/20 = 1.86 m. The other root, 10.8 m, lies outside the span. So any section within 1.86 m of B has a moment no more than half the maximum. A similar zone exists near A, but the load at 3.0 m means the left zone is much shorter, only about 1.35 m.

Answer: 1.86 m

(e)

At midspan, x = 5.0 m, the moment is M = 163(5.0) - 90(2.0) - 10(25.0) = 815 - 180 - 250 = 385 kN·m. This is 385/403.2 = 95.5 percent of the maximum, far above the 50 percent allowed for a splice. The girder is nearly at its maximum moment across a wide central region, from about 2.9 m to 5.1 m, since the shear is small there and the moment diagram is flat-topped. So midspan is the worst place for a splice, and the splice must instead be located within 1.86 m of the roller end B, where the moment is much lower. The designer should also check the shear at that location, which is as high as 127 kN near B.

Answer: No, 385 kN·m is 95.5 percent of the maximum

Problem 4 [A1-099] Member forces in determinate trusses by joints and sections

A pin-jointed steel roof truss over a curling rink in Barrie spans 16.0 m with a pin at joint L0 and a roller at joint L4. The bottom chord joints L0, L1, L2, L3 and L4 are 4.0 m apart. Top chord joints U1, U2 and U3 sit 3.0 m above L1, L2 and L3. The members are the bottom chord, the top chord segments U1U2 and U2U3, the end posts L0U1 and L4U3, the verticals L1U1, L2U2 and L3U3, and two diagonals L1U2 and L3U2. Ceiling and lighting loads act vertically downward at the bottom joints: 50 kN at L1, 80 kN at L2 and 30 kN at L3. Self-weight is neglected. The diagonals are slender and are rated for a compression of 90 kN each.

  1. (a) Find the reaction at the pin L0. [3]
  2. (b) Find the force in bottom chord member L1L2 (tension positive). [5]
  3. (c) Find the force in diagonal L1U2 (tension positive). [5]
  4. (d) Find the force in top chord member U1U2 (tension positive). [4]
  5. (e) With the other loads unchanged, find the largest load at L2 that keeps the compression in diagonal L1U2 within its 90 kN rating. [3]
(a)

Take moments about the roller L4 for the whole truss, counter-clockwise positive: R_A(16.0) - 50(12.0) - 80(8.0) - 30(4.0) = 0, so R_A = (600 + 640 + 120)/16.0 = 85 kN upward. Vertical equilibrium gives R_B = 160 - 85 = 75 kN. There is no horizontal load, so the pin has no horizontal reaction. As a check, moments about L0 give R_B(16.0) = 50(4.0) + 80(8.0) + 30(12.0) = 200 + 640 + 360 = 1200, so R_B = 75 kN. The reactions are positive, so the truss does not lift at either support under the load case, and the load is carried to the supports by the members.

Answer: 85 kN

(b)

Cut through panel L1L2 to isolate the left piece, cutting U1U2, L1U2 and L1L2. Take moments about U2, the intersection of the other two cut members, so only L1L2 appears. Left piece, taking the 85 kN reaction at x = 0 and the 50 kN load at x = 4.0, with U2 at x = 8.0 and height 3.0 m: the reaction produces a clockwise moment 85(8.0) = 680 kN·m, the 50 kN load a counter-clockwise 50(4.0) = 200 kN·m, and a tensile F in the bottom chord, 3.0 m below U2, a counter-clockwise 3.0F. Equilibrium: 680 = 200 + 3.0F, so F = 160 kN, tension. The positive sign confirms the bottom chord is stretched, as expected for gravity loads on a bridge-type truss.

Answer: +160 kN

(c)

Use the same cut and sum vertical forces on the left piece. The diagonal L1U2 runs from (4, 0) to (8, 3), so its length is 5.0 m and its vertical component is 3/5 of its force. The chord forces are horizontal and do not enter. Vertical equilibrium: 85 - 50 + 0.6F_d = 0, so F_d = -35/0.6 = -58.33 kN. The negative sign means compression: the diagonal pushes against the left piece. This is a feature of this layout, where the diagonals slope upward toward the centre. Compare with the rating of 90 kN: the demand is 65 percent of the rating, a comfortable margin at this loading, but the check on the slenderness of a 5.0 m member still has to be done separately.

Answer: -58.3 kN

(d)

Cut the same panel and take moments about the bottom joint L2 at (8, 0). On the left piece the 85 kN reaction gives a clockwise 680 kN·m and the 50 kN load a counter-clockwise 200 kN·m. The diagonal force line passes through U2, at 3.0 m directly above L2, with horizontal component 0.8F_d = -46.67 kN, so its moment about L2 is a counter-clockwise 3.0(46.67) = 140 kN·m. The top chord force F_t acts at height 3.0 m: a compression C contributes 3.0C counter-clockwise. Equilibrium: 680 = 200 + 140 + 3.0C, so C = 113.33 kN compression, F = -113.33 kN. The top chord is in compression, the usual role for the upper chord of a simply supported truss.

Answer: -113.3 kN

(e)

Leave the loads at L1 and L3 as they are and write the left reaction as a function of the load P at L2: R_A = [50(12.0) + P(8.0) + 30(4.0)]/16.0 = 45 + 0.5P. The cut vertical balance gives the diagonal force F_d = -(R_A - 50)/0.6 = -(0.5P - 5)/0.6. The compression equals 90 kN when 0.5P - 5 = 54, so P = 118 kN. At the present 80 kN the compression is 58.3 kN, so there is room to increase the load at L2 by 38 kN. Because the relation is linear, doubling the load beyond this would double the compression, which is why the upper limit of 118 kN is reliable. The chord forces would be checked separately.

Answer: 118 kN

Problem 5 [A1-100] Three-hinged arches and cables

A three-hinged parabolic arch spans a pedestrian passage in a Niagara Falls park building, 24.0 m between the abutment hinges at A and B, which are at the same level. The crown hinge C is 6.0 m above the abutment hinges at midspan. The arch carries a snow drift load of 15 kN/m on the left half of the span, measured on the horizontal projection, and a 60 kN equipment load 20.0 m from A. The abutments are tied together by a steel tie rod at the level of the hinges, and the hinge at B rests on a roller so that the tie rod is the only horizontal restraint and carries the full horizontal thrust. The designer is checking whether a standard bar of 700 mm² is adequate, using an allowable tensile stress of 150 MPa and the service loads given here. Neglect the weight of the arch itself.

  1. (a) Find the vertical reaction at A. [3]
  2. (b) Find the horizontal thrust H at the abutments. [5]
  3. (c) Find the bending moment at the section 6.0 m from A. [4]
  4. (d) Find the axial compression in the arch at that section. [4]
  5. (e) Find the tie rod area required for the allowable stress, in mm², and decide whether the 700 mm² bar is adequate. [4]
(a)

Take moments about B for the whole arch, clockwise positive: V_A(24.0) - (15 × 12)(18.0) - 60(4.0) = 0. The distributed load has a resultant of 180 kN at 6.0 m from A, which is 18.0 m from B, and the 60 kN load is 4.0 m from B. So V_A = (3240 + 240)/24.0 = 145 kN. Vertical equilibrium: V_B = 180 + 60 - 145 = 95 kN. As a check, moments about A: V_B(24.0) = 180(6.0) + 60(20.0) = 1080 + 1200 = 2280, so V_B = 95 kN. The horizontal reactions are equal and opposite because no horizontal load is applied, and they are found in the next part using the crown hinge.

Answer: 145 kN

(b)

The hinge at C carries no moment, so the moment of all forces on one side of C about C is zero. Using the left segment, 12.0 m long: V_A(12.0) - 15(12.0)(6.0) - H(6.0) = 0. That is 145(12.0) - 1080 - 6.0H = 0, so H = (1740 - 1080)/6.0 = 110 kN. The check from the right segment: V_B(12.0) - 60(8.0) - 6.0H = 0 gives 1140 - 480 = 660, so H = 110 kN, the same. The thrust acts inward at both abutments, 110 kN on each. The three-hinge condition is what makes the arch statically determinate: the extra equation from the crown hinge supplies the horizontal reaction.

Answer: 110 kN

(c)

The arch axis is the parabola y = 4fx(L - x)/L² with f = 6.0 m and L = 24.0 m. At x = 6.0 m, y = 4(6.0)(6.0)(18.0)/576 = 4.5 m. Take moments of the forces on the left of the section about the point on the axis: M = V_A x - w x²/2 - H y = 145(6.0) - 15(36)/2 - 110(4.5) = 870 - 270 - 495 = 105 kN·m. The positive value is the sagging-type moment of the equivalent beam, reduced by the thrust times the rise. For comparison, the simple-beam moment is 600 kN·m and the thrust removes 495 kN·m of it, which is why an arch is efficient: the bending is small compared with an equivalent beam.

Answer: 105 kN·m

(d)

At x = 6.0 m the arch slope is dy/dx = 4f(L - 2x)/L² = 4(6.0)(12.0)/576 = 0.500, so the tangent angle is 26.57° with cos = 0.8944 and sin = 0.4472. The shear force in the equivalent beam at this section is V = V_A - wx = 145 - 90 = 55 kN. The axial force normal to the section is N = H cos θ + V sin θ = 110(0.8944) + 55(0.4472) = 98.39 + 24.60 = 122.99 kN, compression. The horizontal thrust and the vertical shear both resolve along the tangent to compress the section. The radial shear in the arch is V cos θ - H sin θ = 49.2 - 49.2 = 0, which shows the shear at this section vanishes, so the section is dominated by axial force.

Answer: 123.0 kN

(e)

The tie rod must carry the thrust, which is H = 110 kN, if it replaces the abutment's horizontal restraint. Required area A = H/σ_allow = 110 000 N/150 N/mm² = 733.3 mm². The available bar of 700 mm² gives only 700 × 150 = 105 kN, which is 4.5 percent short of the 110 kN demand. The bar's stress under the full thrust would be 110 000/700 = 157 MPa, 4.8 percent over the allowable value. The designer should choose the next standard size above 733 mm², and also recognise that the thrust will rise if snow drifts over more of the span or if the equipment load moves toward the crown. A sound judgement would allow some margin for that.

Answer: 733 mm², the 700 mm² bar is not adequate

A1 Practice Paper 21

Problem 1 [A1-101] Axial force, shear and moment diagrams of determinate frames

A lifting frame in a pump house in Sudbury is modelled as a determinate plane frame. Column AB is vertical, 4.0 m high, with a pin at its base A. Beam BC is horizontal and 6.0 m long, rigidly joined to the column top at B, and its far end C rests on a roller that can resist vertical force only. A uniformly distributed load of 12 kN/m acts downward over the full length of BC from a ventilation duct and its supports. A wind-driven door impact applies a horizontal force of 20 kN at joint B, directed from B toward C. Self-weight of the members is ignored and axial deformation does not change the geometry. The designer needs the member end actions for the reaction check and for the connection design at B.

  1. (a) Find the vertical reaction at the roller C. [4]
  2. (b) Find the axial force in column AB, stating tension or compression. [4]
  3. (c) Find the largest sagging bending moment in beam BC and its distance from C. [6]
  4. (d) The 20 kN door impact is replaced by a gust that acts the other way, from B back toward A. Find the new largest sagging moment in beam BC, and state what happens to the sign of the moment at joint B. [6]
(a)

Only three reaction components exist: Ax and Ay at the pin and Cy at the roller, so statics alone is enough. Take moments about A, counterclockwise positive. The roller reaction Cy acts upward 6.0 m from A. The beam load is 12 × 6 = 72 kN, centred 3.0 m from A, and gives a clockwise moment of 72 × 3 = 216 kN·m. The 20 kN horizontal force acts to the right at a height of 4.0 m above A and also gives a clockwise moment of 20 × 4 = 80 kN·m. Then 6Cy - 216 - 80 = 0, so Cy = 296/6 = 49.33 kN upward. Horizontal equilibrium gives Ax = 20 kN acting to the left.

Answer: Cy = 49.33 kN

(b)

Vertical equilibrium of the whole frame gives Ay + Cy = 72 kN, so Ay = 72 - 49.33 = 22.67 kN upward. Cut the column just above A. The only vertical force acting on the free body below the cut is the pin reaction Ay, so the column carries an axial force of 22.67 kN, pushing on the column from below, which is compression. The horizontal reaction Ax is perpendicular to the column axis and therefore produces shear of 20 kN along the full column height, not axial force. The column moment grows from zero at A to 20 × 4 = 80 kN·m at B, which is the moment that must be carried round the joint into the beam.

Answer: N_AB = 22.67 kN compression

(c)

Measure s from C along the beam. The beam sees no axial force because the roller cannot resist horizontal force, so shear is V(s) = Cy - 12s = 49.33 - 12s, and the moment is M(s) = 49.33s - 6s². The shear is zero where s = 49.33/12 = 4.111 m from C, which is inside the 6.0 m beam. The moment there is M = Cy²/(2w) = 49.33²/(2 × 12) = 2433.8/24 = 101.4 kN·m, sagging. Check the joint: at s = 6.0, M = 296 - 216 = 80 kN·m, which equals the column-top moment found from the 20 kN force, so the joint is in moment equilibrium.

Answer: M_max = 101.4 kN·m at 4.11 m from C

(d)

Reverse the horizontal force so it acts to the left at B. Moments about A now give 6Cy - 216 + 80 = 0, so Cy = 136/6 = 22.67 kN, and Ay = 72 - 22.67 = 49.33 kN. In the beam, shear is zero at s = 22.67/12 = 1.889 m from C, and the maximum sagging moment is Cy²/(2w) = 22.67²/24 = 21.41 kN·m. The moment at B from the beam side is 22.67 × 6 - 216 = -80 kN·m, so the sign changes from the earlier +80 to -80: the beam side of the joint now has the opposite curvature and the tension face switches. The designer must therefore check the connection at B for both directions of wind.

Answer: M_max = 21.41 kN·m; joint moment sign reverses

Problem 2 [A1-102] Influence lines for reactions of beams

A cantilevered edge of a highway overpass near Kingston is idealized as a beam ABC. A is a pin and B a roller, 10.0 m apart, and the beam continues 4.0 m beyond B to a free end C. Distances x are measured from A toward C. Dead load is a uniform 15 kN/m over the full 14.0 m. A two-axle maintenance truck can travel in either direction along the deck: the heavy axle carries 80 kN and the light axle carries 40 kN, 3.0 m behind it. A designer is checking whether the bearing at A could ever lift off, because that bearing has no hold-down device. Use influence lines throughout, treat the axles as point loads, and ignore lane loading and impact.

  1. (a) State the ordinate of the influence line for the reaction at B when a unit load is at the free end C. [3]
  2. (b) Find the largest upward reaction at B produced by the truck. [5]
  3. (c) Find the reaction at A caused by the dead load. [5]
  4. (d) Load factors of 0.9 on dead load and 1.5 on live load are used when checking uplift. With the truck placed to give the most negative reaction at A, find the factored minimum reaction at A. State whether the bearing lifts. [7]
(a)

For a unit load at position x, moments about A give RB × 10 = 1 × x, so RB = x/10. This straight line applies along the whole beam, including the overhang, because moment equilibrium about A does not care where the load sits. At x = 10 the ordinate is 1.0, at x = 0 it is 0, and at the free end x = 14 it is 14/10 = 1.40. The ordinate above 1.0 means a load on the cantilever pulls more than its own weight into the roller. This also tells us RA = 1 - RB = 1 - x/10, which becomes negative past B, so a load on the overhang tends to lift the pin at A.

Answer: 1.40

(b)

Because the ordinate rises steadily toward C, the heavy axle goes at the tip, x = 14, and the 40 kN axle sits 3.0 m behind it at x = 11. The truck is as far toward the end as it can get, and both axles are on the positive part of the line. RB = 80(14/10) + 40(11/10) = 112 + 44 = 156 kN. If the truck were turned around so the light axle led, the sum would be 40(1.4) + 80(1.1) = 56 + 88 = 144 kN, which is smaller. So the heavy axle leads and the maximum is 156 kN upward.

Answer: 156 kN

(c)

The influence line for RA is RA = 1 - x/10, which has ordinate +1.0 at A, zero at B, and -0.4 at C. The reaction from a uniform load is the load intensity times the net area under the line. The positive triangle from A to B has area ½(10)(1.0) = 5.0 m. The negative triangle on the overhang has area ½(4)(-0.4) = -0.8 m. The net area is 4.2 m, so RA(dead) = 15 × 4.2 = 63 kN upward. As a check, simple statics: the total load is 15 × 14 = 210 kN at 7.0 m from A, so RB = 210 × 7/10 = 147 kN and RA = 210 - 147 = 63 kN.

Answer: 63 kN

(d)

The most negative RA comes from the heavy axle at the tip and the light axle 3.0 m behind it. The ordinates are RA = -0.4 at x = 14 and 1 - 11/10 = -0.1 at x = 11. Live reaction = 80(-0.4) + 40(-0.1) = -32 - 4 = -36 kN, which is an uplift tendency. Factored: 0.9 × 63 - 1.5 × 36 = 56.7 - 54.0 = 2.7 kN, still upward. The bearing does not lift, but only by 2.7 kN, which is a very thin margin; an engineer would flag it and either add a hold-down or ballast, because a small error in dead load, such as a lighter wearing surface, would reverse the sign.

Answer: +2.7 kN, no lift-off, marginal

Problem 3 [A1-103] Influence lines for shear and moment in beams

A floor beam in a distribution warehouse in Mississauga spans 16.0 m between simple supports A and B. Section S lies 6.0 m from A. A forklift crosses the beam in either direction. Its front axle carries 45 kN and its rear axle carries 15 kN, 2.4 m apart, and the forklift may be travelling forwards or in reverse, so either axle can lead. The floor also carries a uniform lane load of 8 kN/m that may be placed over any length of the span for the check. Treat the axles as point loads and ignore impact and the beam's own weight. Use influence lines to find the extreme actions at section S, and note which load arrangement governs the beam's design, not just the numeric answer.

  1. (a) Find the largest positive shear at section S caused by the forklift alone. [5]
  2. (b) Find the largest bending moment at section S caused by the forklift alone. [5]
  3. (c) Find the moment at S caused by the lane load over the full span. [4]
  4. (d) Find the largest positive shear at S when the lane load covers only the part of the span to the right of S while the forklift is in its worst position. State why the lane load is not placed to the left of S. [6]
(a)

Shear at S for a unit load at x: for x < 6 it is -x/16, reaching -0.375 just left of S, and for x > 6 it is 1 - x/16, which is +0.625 just right of S and falls to zero at B. For positive shear the loads go to the right of S. Put the 45 kN axle just right of S (ordinate 0.625) and the 15 kN axle 2.4 m further right at x = 8.4 (ordinate 1 - 8.4/16 = 0.475). V = 45(0.625) + 15(0.475) = 28.125 + 7.125 = 35.25 kN. The reverse order gives 15(0.625) + 45(0.475) = 30.75 kN, which is smaller, so the front axle must lead.

Answer: 35.25 kN

(b)

The moment influence line is a triangle with peak ordinate ab/L = 6 × 10/16 = 3.75 m at S, falling to zero at both supports. At x = 8.4 the ordinate is 3.75 × (16 - 8.4)/10 = 2.85 m, and at x = 3.6 it is 3.75 × 3.6/6 = 2.25 m. Put the heavy axle at S, with the light axle at 8.4: M = 45(3.75) + 15(2.85) = 168.75 + 42.75 = 211.5 kN·m. Putting the light axle behind at 3.6 gives 168.75 + 33.75 = 202.5 kN·m, so the forward position is higher. The 45 kN axle sits at the peak because that gives the largest ordinate to the largest load.

Answer: 211.5 kN·m

(c)

A uniform load causes the intensity times the area under the influence line. The moment triangle has base 16.0 m and height 3.75 m, so its area is ½ × 16 × 3.75 = 30 m². The moment at S is therefore 8 × 30 = 240 kN·m. A direct check: with full uniform load RA = 8 × 16/2 = 64 kN, so the moment at 6.0 m is 64 × 6 - 8 × 6 × 3 = 384 - 144 = 240 kN·m, which agrees. The lane load alone gives a larger moment than the forklift alone, so a design that checked only the forklift would be unsafe by a wide margin.

Answer: 240 kN·m

(d)

Positive shear at S needs positive ordinates, which exist only to the right of S. The area of the positive part of the line is a triangle of base 10.0 m and height 0.625, giving ½ × 10 × 0.625 = 3.125 m. The lane load contributes 8 × 3.125 = 25 kN. The forklift in its worst position adds 35.25 kN, so V = 25 + 35.25 = 60.25 kN. Loading the part to the left of S would add load where the ordinate is negative (down to -0.375), subtracting from the shear we are maximizing. The lane load is therefore deliberately left off that segment, which is the usual rule of loading only where the influence line has the same sign.

Answer: 60.25 kN

Problem 4 [A1-104] Influence lines for truss member forces

A Warren-type footbridge truss over a creek in Peterborough spans 16.0 m between a pin at L0 and a roller at L4. The bottom chord has joints L0, L1, L2, L3 and L4 at 4.0 m spacing, and the top chord has joints U1, U2, U3 and U4 located 2.0 m, 6.0 m, 10.0 m and 14.0 m from L0. The truss is 3.0 m deep and has no vertical members. The diagonals are L0U1, U1L1, L1U2, U2L2, L2U3, U3L3, L3U4 and U4L4. The deck is carried by floor beams at the bottom joints, so all loads enter at L1, L2 and L3. Dead load is 30 kN at each of L1, L2 and L3. A heavy service vehicle axle of 120 kN may be placed at any bottom joint.

  1. (a) Find the influence-line ordinates for the force in diagonal U2L2 at joints L1 and L2, taking tension as positive. [4]
  2. (b) Find the influence-line ordinate for the force in bottom chord L1L2 when the unit load is at L2. [4]
  3. (c) Find the force in bottom chord L1L2 from the dead load. [5]
  4. (d) With the 120 kN axle at L1, find the net force in U2L2, including dead load. State the nature of the force and any design consequence. [7]
(a)

A section cutting U2U3, U2L2 and L1L2 passes between joints L1 and L2, so the shear carried through the panel equals the diagonal's vertical component. The diagonal rises 3.0 m over a horizontal distance of 2.0 m, so its length is √13 = 3.606 m and sinθ = 3.0/3.606 = 0.832. For the unit load at L1, which is left of the panel, panel shear = -RB = -4/16 = -0.25. At L2 the load is right of the panel, so shear = RA = 1 - 8/16 = 0.50. Tension in U2L2 = shear/sinθ, so the ordinates are -0.25/0.832 = -0.300 at L1 and 0.50/0.832 = 0.601 at L2.

Answer: -0.300 at L1, 0.601 at L2

(b)

Cut the same section and take moments about top joint U2, which lies 6.0 m from L0 and 3.0 m above the bottom chord. This removes the diagonal and top chord from the moment equation, leaving only the bottom chord force acting with a 3.0 m lever arm. With a unit load at L2 (8.0 m from A), RA = 0.50 and RB = 0.50. Considering the left side, moment about U2 = RA × 6.0 = 0.50 × 6.0 = 3.00. The load itself is right of U2 so it is not on the left piece. Then F(L1L2) × 3.0 = 3.00 gives F = 1.000, tension. This is the largest ordinate on the line for this member.

Answer: 1.000

(c)

The same moment approach gives the other ordinates. At L1 the unit load is left of U2, so the moment about U2 of the left forces is RA × 6 - 1 × (6 - 4) with RA = 0.75: 4.50 - 2.00 = 2.50, so the force ordinate is 2.50/3.0 = 0.833. At L3 the load is right of U2 and RA = 0.25, so the moment is 0.25 × 6 = 1.50, and the ordinate is 0.500. The dead load is 30 kN at each joint, so F = 30(0.833 + 1.000 + 0.500) = 30 × 2.333 = 70.0 kN tension. The ordinates sum to 2.333 because the chord force carries the full panel moment.

Answer: 70.0 kN tension

(d)

With the axle at L1 the live contribution is 120 × (-0.300) = -36.06 kN (compression). The dead load contribution is 30 × (-0.300 + 0.601 + 0.300) = 30 × 0.601 = 18.03 kN tension. Net = 18.03 - 36.06 = -18.03 kN, so the diagonal changes from tension to compression of 18.0 kN. Because the member is designed as a tension diagonal, the sign reversal means it must be checked for buckling over its 3.606 m length, or a counter-diagonal must be provided. Without this check a slender tension bar could buckle. The reversal arises only when the heavy axle stands at L1, which the influence line makes easy to identify.

Answer: -18.0 kN (compression), reversal

Problem 5 [A1-105] Maximum shear and moment envelope under a moving wheel train

An overhead crane runway girder in a steel fabrication shop in Hamilton is a simply supported beam with a span of 12.0 m. The crane delivers three wheel loads in a fixed order along the girder: 60 kN, 60 kN and 30 kN, with 3.0 m between the first and second wheels and 2.0 m between the second and third. The crane can travel either way along the runway, so either end of the train can lead. The girder self-weight is small and is ignored. The designer must find the governing actions for the girder and then apply an impact allowance of 25 percent on the wheel loads and a load factor of 1.5.

  1. (a) Find the distance of the resultant of the three wheel loads from the first (60 kN) wheel. [4]
  2. (b) Find the absolute maximum bending moment in the girder and state where the wheel train must be placed. [7]
  3. (c) Find the maximum support shear and compare the absolute maximum moment with the moment under the second wheel placed at midspan. [5]
  4. (d) Find the factored design moment, applying the 25 percent impact allowance and the 1.5 load factor. [4]
(a)

The resultant of the three loads is R = 60 + 60 + 30 = 150 kN. Take moments of the loads about the first wheel, treating that wheel as the origin. The second wheel is 3.0 m away and the third is 3.0 + 2.0 = 5.0 m away. Σ(P × distance) = 60(0) + 60(3.0) + 30(5.0) = 0 + 180 + 150 = 330 kN·m. The location of the resultant is 330/150 = 2.20 m from the first wheel, toward the other wheels. This sits 0.80 m before the second wheel. That small offset matters, because the absolute maximum moment appears under the load nearest the resultant when the load and resultant are placed symmetrically about midspan.

Answer: 2.20 m

(b)

The load nearest the resultant is the second wheel, 0.80 m beyond it. Place midspan halfway between them, so the resultant is 0.40 m to the left of midspan at x = 5.6 m, and the second wheel is 0.40 m to the right at x = 6.4 m. The first wheel is at 3.4 m and the third at 8.4 m, all within the span. The reaction at A is RA = 150 × (12 - 5.6)/12 = 80 kN. Take moments of the left-hand forces about the second wheel: M = 80(6.4) - 60(3.0) = 512 - 180 = 332 kN·m. This is the absolute maximum; the train sits with the second wheel 0.40 m from midspan.

Answer: 332 kN·m

(c)

For maximum support shear, put the 60 kN first wheel directly at A so the other wheels are as far onto the span as possible, at 3.0 m and 5.0 m. RA = (60 × 12 + 60 × 9 + 30 × 7)/12 = (720 + 540 + 210)/12 = 122.5 kN. With the train reversed so the 30 kN wheel leads (wheels at 0, 2.0 and 5.0 m), RA = (360 + 600 + 420)/12 = 115.0 kN, which is smaller. Moment comparison: second wheel at midspan gives RA = (60 × 9 + 60 × 6 + 30 × 4)/12 = 85 kN, so M = 85 × 6 - 60 × 3 = 330 kN·m. The absolute maximum of 332 kN·m is only 0.6 percent larger.

Answer: 122.5 kN; midspan case 330 kN·m

(d)

The unfactored absolute maximum moment of 332 kN·m is multiplied by the impact allowance of 1.25 and then by the load factor of 1.5. First, 332 × 1.25 = 415 kN·m. Then 415 × 1.5 = 622.5 kN·m. Both multipliers apply because the wheel loads are the only source of this moment, with self-weight neglected. In practice a designer would add the factored girder self-weight moment to this figure, and the small difference between 330 and 332 kN·m shows why many designers simply use the midspan case with the heaviest wheel, as the error is below the accuracy of the wheel load data.

Answer: 622.5 kN·m

A1 Practice Paper 22

Problem 1 [A1-106] Beam deflection by double integration

A cantilevered entrance canopy at a school in Thunder Bay is idealized as a prismatic beam 4.0 m long, built into a wall at its fixed end and free at the other. A snow drift loads the canopy so that the intensity varies linearly from zero at the free end to 12 kN/m at the wall. The flexural rigidity is EI = 8000 kN·m², constant along the length, and shear deformation is ignored. The architect has asked that the free-end deflection not exceed L/360. Use double integration, with x measured from the free end, and report downward deflections as positive magnitudes. The structural steel has E = 200 GPa.

  1. (a) Find the bending moment at the wall. [3]
  2. (b) Find the slope at the free end. [5]
  3. (c) Find the deflection at a point 2.0 m from the free end. [6]
  4. (d) Find the smallest second moment of area of the canopy section that meets the L/360 limit at the free end. [6]
(a)

The total load is the area of the triangle, ½ × 4.0 × 12 = 24 kN. Its centroid lies one third of the base from the large end, which is 4.0/3 = 1.333 m from the wall. The fixed-end moment is therefore 24 × 1.333 = 32.0 kN·m, hogging. The same result comes from the closed form w0L²/6 = 12 × 16/6 = 32 kN·m. With x from the free end, the load intensity is w(x) = 12x/4 = 3x, and the moment is M(x) = -w0x³/(6L) = -0.5x³. At x = 4 this equals -0.5 × 64 = -32 kN·m, which confirms the equation used in part (b).

Answer: 32 kN·m hogging

(b)

The differential equation is EI v'' = M(x) = -w0x³/(6L). Integrating once gives EI v' = -w0x⁴/(24L) + C1. The wall is rigid, so the slope is zero at x = L = 4: C1 = w0L³/24 = 12 × 64/24 = 32. At the free end x = 0, EI v' = 32, so v' = 32/8000 = 0.004 rad. Because x is measured back from the free end, the sign flips relative to the usual convention, so the slope is read as a magnitude: the tip rotates downward as the canopy droops. The slope is small, which justifies the small-angle form v'' = M/EI.

Answer: 0.004 rad

(c)

Integrating again, EI v = -w0x⁵/(120L) + C1x + C2. The wall also has zero deflection at x = L: 0 = -12(1024)/(480) + 32(4) + C2 = -25.6 + 128 + C2, so C2 = -102.4. At x = 2.0, EI v = -12(32)/480 + 32(2) - 102.4 = -0.8 + 64.0 - 102.4 = -39.2. Then v = -39.2/8000 = -0.0049 m, a downward deflection of 4.9 mm. At the free end x = 0, EI v = C2 = -102.4, so the tip deflection is 102.4/8000 = 12.8 mm, which is more than the 11.1 mm limit needed in part (d).

Answer: 4.9 mm down

(d)

The L/360 limit for a 4.0 m cantilever is 4000/360 = 11.11 mm. The tip deflection is w0L⁴/(30EI), so EI must be at least 12 × 256/(30 × 0.011111) = 3072/0.33333 = 9216 kN·m². With E = 200 GPa = 200 × 10⁶ kN/m², I = 9216/(200 × 10⁶) = 4.608 × 10⁻⁵ m⁴ = 46.08 × 10⁶ mm⁴. The present I = 8000/(200 × 10⁶) = 40 × 10⁶ mm⁴ falls about 13 percent short. Because deflection is inversely proportional to I, a section about 15 percent stiffer is needed. Remember that the available catalogue sections come in steps, so the next standard size up will be selected.

Answer: 46.08 × 10⁶ mm⁴

Problem 2 [A1-107] Beam deflection by the moment-area method

A conveyor support beam in a recycling plant in Windsor is a simply supported steel beam with a span of 8.0 m, pinned at A and on a roller at B. A single 60 kN machine skid bears on the beam at a point 3.0 m from A. The beam has a constant flexural rigidity of EI = 60 000 kN·m² (E = 200 GPa, I = 3.0 × 10⁻⁴ m⁴). The plant engineer wants to know whether the midspan deflection is a fair stand-in for the true maximum deflection when positioning a laser alignment sensor. Use the moment-area theorems with the M/EI diagram, and give deflections as downward magnitudes.

  1. (a) Find the reaction at A. [3]
  2. (b) Use the moment-area theorems to find the slope of the beam at A. [6]
  3. (c) Use the second moment-area theorem to find the deflection at midspan. [6]
  4. (d) Find the maximum deflection and its distance from A. Say whether midspan is an acceptable sensor location. [5]
(a)

Take moments about B. The skid is 5.0 m from B, so RA × 8.0 = 60 × 5.0 = 300, giving RA = 37.5 kN upward. Then RB = 60 - 37.5 = 22.5 kN. The bending moment under the load is RA × 3.0 = 112.5 kN·m, which is the peak of the M diagram. The M/EI diagram is a triangle with base 8.0 m and peak 112.5/60 000 = 0.001875 m⁻¹ under the load. Its area is ½ × 8.0 × 112.5/EI = 450/EI, a value used in the next part, along with the first moment of area about A.

Answer: RA = 37.5 kN

(b)

The tangent at A and the tangent at B form a chord relation: the deflection of B from the tangent at A is zero, because both supports are at the same level. By the second theorem, t(B/A) = (area of M/EI between A and B) × (distance from B to the centroid). The triangle's apex is under the load at 3.0 m, so its centroid is (0 + 3 + 8)/3 = 3.667 m from A, which is 4.333 m from B. t(B/A) = (450/EI)(4.333) = 1950/EI. Then θA = t(B/A)/L = 1950/(8 EI) = 243.75/60 000 = 0.0040625 rad. This is the slope of the beam at A, downward clockwise. The second theorem supplies t(B/A), and the slope then follows from the geometry of the tangent, θA = t(B/A)/L, since the first theorem alone cannot fix an absolute slope here.

Answer: 0.0040625 rad

(c)

At midspan x = 4.0 m, find the offset of the beam from the tangent at A: t = (area under M/EI from A to midspan) × (distance to its centroid from midspan). The M diagram rises to 112.5 at 3.0 m, then falls to 37.5 × 4 - 60 × 1 = 90 at 4.0 m. Left triangle: area ½ × 3 × 112.5 = 168.75, centroid 2.0 m from A, which is 2.0 m from midspan, moment 337.5. Piece from 3.0 to 4.0: rectangle 90 × 1 at 0.5 m plus triangle 11.25 at 0.667 m gives 45 + 7.5 = 52.5. Total 390. The tangent drop is θA × 4 = 0.01625 m, and the deflection is 0.01625 - 390/60 000 = 0.01625 - 0.0065 = 0.00975 m, or 9.75 mm.

Answer: 9.75 mm

(d)

The maximum deflection occurs where the slope is zero. From B, with a = 3.0 m, that point is at x' = √((L² - a²)/3) = √(55/3) = 4.282 m from B, so 3.718 m from A. Using the known deflection formula for a point load, v = P a x'(L² - a² - x'²)/(6 EI L) = 60 × 3 × 4.282 × (55 - 18.33)/(6 × 60 000 × 8) = 9.81 mm. This is only 0.6 percent above the midspan value of 9.75 mm, and the sensor can sit at midspan with an error well below typical measurement noise. Midspan is therefore an acceptable location.

Answer: 9.81 mm at 3.72 m from A

Problem 3 [A1-108] Beam deflection by the conjugate beam method

A concrete balcony slab strip in a Toronto condominium is analysed as a beam ABC. The beam is supported on a pin at A and a roller at B, 6.0 m apart, and overhangs 2.0 m beyond B to a free tip C. A railing connection delivers a 45 kN point load downward at C. The flexural rigidity of the strip is EI = 30 000 kN·m², constant over the length. The consultant plans to use the conjugate beam method, and later to check how much the tip deflection would change if the overhang were shortened to 1.0 m by cutting back the slab while the moment at B stays at the same value. Express deflections as downward magnitudes.

  1. (a) Find the magnitude of the reaction at A and state its direction. [3]
  2. (b) Describe the conjugate beam supports and loads, then find the rotation of the real beam at A. [5]
  3. (c) Find the deflection of the tip C. [7]
  4. (d) The overhang is shortened to 1.0 m and the tip load is raised to 90 kN so the moment at B is unchanged. Find the new tip deflection. [5]
(a)

Take moments about B, with the load 2.0 m from B on the overhang. Ay × 6.0 acting at A has to balance 45 × 2.0 = 90 kN·m, so |Ay| = 90/6 = 15 kN. The load at C rotates the beam about B, trying to lift A, so the support at A must pull the beam down. The reaction at A is a 15 kN downward force. The reaction at B is then 45 + 15 = 60 kN upward. The moment diagram is zero at A, falls linearly to -90 kN·m at B (hogging), and decreases linearly to zero at C. This shape is what the conjugate beam will carry as its load.

Answer: 15 kN downward

(b)

The conjugate beam has the same length. Its supports transform as follows: a pin at A stays a pin, the interior roller at B becomes a hinge, and the free tip at C becomes a fixed end. It is loaded with M/EI, which is hogging and so acts downward on the conjugate beam. Over AB the load is a triangle with area ½ × 6 × 90/EI = 270/EI, centroid 4.0 m from A. For the free body AB with a hinge at B (zero conjugate moment), RA' × 6 = (270/EI)(2.0), so RA' = 90/EI. The conjugate shear at A is the real rotation: θA = 90/30 000 = 0.003 rad.

Answer: θA = 0.003 rad

(c)

The tip deflection equals the conjugate bending moment at the fixed end C. From the equilibrium of AB, the hinge at B transmits a force of 270/EI - 90/EI = 180/EI downward to the cantilever BC. The overhang also carries its own triangular load: area ½ × 2 × 90/EI = 90/EI, with its centroid 2/3 m from B, which is 1.333 m from C. Take moments at C: M = (180/EI)(2.0) + (90/EI)(1.333) = 360/EI + 120/EI = 480/EI. The tip deflection is 480/30 000 = 0.016 m, or 16.0 mm downward. A check with P a²(L + a)/(3EI) = 45 × 4 × 8/(3EI) = 480/EI agrees.

Answer: 16.0 mm down

(d)

The moment at B must stay at 90 kN·m, so with a = 1.0 m the tip load is 90 kN. The closed form for the tip of an overhang beam is δ = P a²(L + a)/(3EI), and it can be derived with the same conjugate beam as above. Substituting the new geometry: δ = 90 × 1.0² × (6.0 + 1.0)/(3 × 30 000) = 630/90 000 = 0.007 m, or 7.0 mm. Cutting the overhang in half reduces the tip movement by 56 percent, because at constant support moment the tip deflection is M a (L + a)/(3EI), which falls from 16.0 mm to 7.0 mm. The consultant could therefore meet a tighter railing limit simply by trimming the slab.

Answer: 7.0 mm

Problem 4 [A1-109] Truss deflection by virtual work (unit load)

A roadside sign bracket near Barrie is a three-member pin-jointed truss. Members AB, AC and BC form a triangle: A is a pin support and B is a roller on the same level, 6.0 m apart horizontally. Joint C is the apex, 3.0 m horizontally from A and 4.0 m above AB, so that AC and BC are each 5.0 m long. The sign delivers a 40 kN downward load at C. Every member is steel with A = 800 mm² and E = 200 GPa, so EA = 160 000 kN. Member AB was fabricated 2.0 mm shorter than its design length. Use the unit load method, with tension positive.

  1. (a) Find the force in member AB. [4]
  2. (b) Find the vertical deflection of joint C caused by the 40 kN load. [6]
  3. (c) Find the horizontal movement of the roller at B caused by the load. [5]
  4. (d) Find the net vertical deflection at C when the fabrication error in AB is combined with the load. State the direction. [5]
(a)

The loading is symmetric, so each support carries 20 kN upward. At joint A, members AC rise at an angle with sin = 4/5 = 0.8 and cos = 3/5 = 0.6. Vertical equilibrium at A: the vertical component of AC's force must balance the 20 kN reaction, so F_AC sin = 20, and AC is in compression with 20/0.8 = 25 kN. Horizontal equilibrium at A: AB must pull toward B to balance the horizontal part of AC's push, so F_AB = 25 × 0.6 = 15 kN. A positive result means AB is in tension. Member BC is the mirror image of AC and carries 25 kN compression.
