Answer: F_AB = 15 kN tension

(b)

Apply a unit downward load at C. The member forces are in proportion to the real case: f_AC = f_BC = -25/40 = -0.625 and f_AB = 15/40 = 0.375. The deflection is δ = Σ F f L/(EA), summing over all three members. For AC: (-25)(-0.625)(5.0) = 78.125. For BC the same, 78.125. For AB: (15)(0.375)(6.0) = 33.75. The sum is 190.0 kN²·m per kN. Dividing by EA: 190.0/160 000 = 0.0011875 m, or 1.1875 mm, downward since the result has the same sign as the unit load. Compression members shorten and the tension chord lengthens, both of which lower C.

Answer: 1.188 mm down

(c)

To find the horizontal movement of B, apply a unit horizontal load at B pointing to the right and ignore the real load. The roller gives no horizontal reaction, so the pin at A must provide 1 kN to the left, and with the load and A on the same level there is no moment, so the vertical reactions are zero. At joint B the vertical forces must balance without a reaction, so member BC carries nothing. Member AB then carries 1 kN of tension (f_AB = 1). Then δ = (15)(1)(6.0)/160 000 = 90/160 000 = 0.0005625 m = 0.5625 mm, directed to the right. Only the bottom chord stretches, so B moves away from A.

Answer: 0.5625 mm to the right

(d)

A member fabricated short by an amount ΔL contributes f × ΔL to the virtual work equation, where f comes from a unit load in the desired direction. With the unit load down at C, f_AB = +0.375, and AB is 2.0 mm short, so the contribution is 0.375 × (-2.0) = -0.75 mm. A negative result means C moves upward relative to the load case. The net deflection is 1.1875 - 0.75 = 0.4375 mm downward. The error therefore cancels almost two thirds of the load deflection. Because the truss is statically determinate (three members, three reactions, three joints), the misfit causes no member forces; it only changes the geometry, so the stresses are those of the load case.

Answer: 0.4375 mm down

Problem 5 [A1-110] Beam and frame deflection by virtual work

An L-shaped signal mast arm on a road in Guelph is idealized as a plane frame, rigidly jointed at B. Column AB is vertical, 3.0 m high, and fixed at its base A. Beam BC is horizontal, 4.0 m long, and free at C. The signal head hangs from C and weighs 20 kN, treated as a point load acting downward at C. Both members have the same flexural rigidity, EI = 25 000 kN·m², and axial and shear deformations are neglected. Use the virtual work (unit load) method with the bending moment integral ∫ M m dx/EI. Give deflections as magnitudes, and assume the frame is linear elastic.

  1. (a) Find the bending moment at the base A of the column. [4]
  2. (b) Find the vertical deflection of C. [6]
  3. (c) Find the horizontal deflection of C. [5]
  4. (d) The column is replaced by one with double the flexural rigidity (2EI) while the beam is unchanged. Find the new vertical deflection of C. [5]
(a)

The signal head weight of 20 kN acts at C, 4.0 m horizontally from the line of the column. A fixed base resists the load with a vertical reaction of 20 kN, a zero horizontal reaction, and a moment equal to the load times its horizontal distance: M_A = 20 × 4.0 = 80 kN·m. The beam moment grows linearly from zero at C to 80 kN·m at B, given by M = -20x measured from C, while the column moment is constant at 80 kN·m over its full height, since the load line stays 4.0 m away from the column axis all the way down. The column carries 20 kN of axial compression but the problem neglects its effect on the deflection.

Answer: 80 kN·m

(b)

Put a unit vertical load at C. The virtual moment in the beam is m = -x (x from C), and in the column it is constant at -4.0. The real moments are M = -20x in the beam and -80 in the column. Beam: ∫0⁴ (20x)(x) dx = 20 × 64/3 = 426.67. Column: 80 × 4.0 × 3.0 = 960. The total is 1386.67 kN²·m³, and dividing by EI = 25 000 gives 0.055467 m, or 55.47 mm downward. The column contributes about 69 percent of the deflection, because its moment is large over the whole height and its virtual moment is large too, which is why the column should be the first member to stiffen.

Answer: 55.47 mm down

(c)

For the horizontal deflection, apply a unit horizontal load at C pointing to the right. Its line of action runs along the beam axis, so it produces no virtual moment in the beam, and the beam contributes nothing. In the column, at height y above A, the virtual moment arm is 3.0 - y, so m = 3.0 - y, with the same sense as the real moment of 80 kN·m. The integral is ∫0³ 80(3 - y) dy = 80 × 9/2 = 360. Then δh = 360/25 000 = 0.0144 m = 14.4 mm to the right. The combined movement of C is √(55.47² + 14.4²) = 57.3 mm, inclined at about 14.6 degrees from vertical.

Answer: 14.4 mm to the right

(d)

Doubling the column rigidity halves the column part of the integral but leaves the beam part alone. The beam term is 426.67/EI, as before. The column term is 960/(2EI) = 480/EI. The sum is (426.67 + 480)/25 000 = 906.67/25 000 = 0.036267 m, or 36.27 mm. The deflection drops by 34.6 percent for a doubling of one member's stiffness. Doubling the beam instead would give (213.33 + 960)/25 000 = 46.9 mm, so stiffening the column is the more effective change here, which is a useful rule: stiffen the member contributing most of the virtual work.

Answer: 36.27 mm

A1 Practice Paper 23

Problem 1 [A1-111] Deflection by strain energy and Castigliano's theorem

A steel canopy beam projects as a cantilever from the concrete wall of a school gymnasium in Kingston, Ontario. The fixed support is at A and the free end is at B, 3.2 m from the wall. The beam has a constant flexural rigidity EI = 12 000 kN·m². It carries a uniformly distributed load of 8.0 kN/m over its full length (snow plus self-weight) and a downward point load of 15 kN at the free end from a hung sign. The architect's note says the tip deflection must not exceed span/240 under this service load. Use strain energy methods, not tabulated deflection formulas, and neglect shear and axial deformation. Treat bending strain energy as U = ∫M²/(2EI) dx.

  1. (a) Use Castigliano's second theorem to find the vertical deflection of the free end B. [6]
  2. (b) Use a dummy moment at B to find the rotation of the free end, in radians. [5]
  3. (c) Evaluate the total bending strain energy stored in the beam under the real loads. [4]
  4. (d) Decide whether the beam meets the span/240 limit. If not, find the flexural rigidity EI that would just meet it. [5]
(a)

Castigliano's second theorem gives the displacement in the direction of a load as Δ = ∂U/∂P. Measure x from the free end B. The moment is M = -(P x + w x²/2), hogging, so ∂M/∂P = -x. The tip load already acts at the point and in the direction wanted, so no dummy force is needed. Δ = (1/EI)∫0 to L of (P x + w x²/2)(x) dx = (1/EI)(P L³/3 + w L⁴/8). Numbers: L³ = 32.768 m³ and L⁴ = 104.858 m⁴. P L³/3 = 15 × 32.768/3 = 163.84 kN·m³. w L⁴/8 = 8 × 104.858/8 = 104.86 kN·m³. The sum is 268.70 kN·m³. Divide by EI = 12 000 kN·m²: Δ = 0.02239 m, or 22.4 mm downward.

Answer: 22.4 mm

(b)

To get a rotation, apply a fictitious moment M' at B and write ∂U/∂M' before setting M' to zero. With M' acting, the bending moment gains a term M', so ∂M/∂M' = 1 in magnitude and the same sense as the hogging moment. Then θ = (1/EI)∫0 to L of (P x + w x²/2)(1) dx = (1/EI)(P L²/2 + w L³/6). Numbers: P L²/2 = 15 × 10.24/2 = 76.80 kN·m². w L³/6 = 8 × 32.768/6 = 43.69 kN·m². The sum is 120.49 kN·m². Dividing by 12 000 gives θ = 0.01004 rad, about 0.58 degrees, rotating in the same sense as the downward deflection. The dummy moment has no effect on the answer once it is set to zero.

Answer: 0.01004 rad

(c)

Expand the squared moment: M² = (P x + w x²/2)² = P²x² + P w x³ + w²x⁴/4. Integrate from 0 to L: P²L³/3 + P w L⁴/4 + w²L⁵/20. With L⁵ = 335.544 m⁵ the terms are 225 × 32.768/3 = 2457.6, then 15 × 8 × 104.858/4 = 3145.7, then 64 × 335.544/20 = 1073.7, all in kN²·m³. The sum is 6677.1 kN²·m³. Strain energy U = 6677.1/(2 × 12 000) = 0.2782 kN·m, which is 0.278 kJ. Note that the cross term P w L⁴/4 is the interaction between the two loads, so the energy of the combined loading is more than the sum of the two cases taken separately. This is why superposition applies to deflections but not to energy.

Answer: 0.278 kJ

(d)

The limit is L/240 = 3200/240 = 13.3 mm. The computed deflection of 22.4 mm exceeds it by 68 percent, so the beam as specified does not comply. Deflection is inversely proportional to EI for fixed loading, so the required rigidity is EI_req = EI × (22.39/13.33). Working directly from the energy result, EI_req = 268.70 kN·m³ / 0.013333 m = 20 152 kN·m², about 20 150. That is 1.68 times the present value. Because I grows with depth cubed for a similar shape, the section depth must rise by about 1.681/3 = 1.19, roughly 19 percent deeper, or the designer can add a tie-back or a stiffening bracket at the tip to shorten the effective span.

Answer: 20 150 kN·m²

Problem 2 [A1-112] Force method for one-degree indeterminate beams

A reinforced concrete transfer beam in a Mississauga parking structure is built monolithically into a column at A and is held at B by a slender steel prop column, 6.0 m away. Treat A as a fixed support and B as a vertical support that resists only vertical force. The beam has constant EI = 40 000 kN·m², and it carries a uniformly distributed load of 10 kN/m over its whole length and a 30 kN downward point load at 3.0 m from A. Use the force method with the prop reaction at B as the redundant. The designer also wants to know what happens if the prop column shortens and B drops 15 mm after the structure is loaded. Use only standard cantilever deflection results in your working.

  1. (a) Find the reaction at B, treating it as the redundant. [7]
  2. (b) Find the fixed-end moment at A, as a hogging magnitude. [5]
  3. (c) Find the new reaction at B if B settles 15 mm downward. [5]
  4. (d) Find the new fixed-end moment at A for part c and state how much it has changed. [3]
(a)

Remove the support at B to leave a cantilever fixed at A. The compatibility condition is that the deflection at B equals zero. Deflection at the tip from the UDL is wL⁴/(8EI) = 10 × 1296/8 = 1620/EI. Deflection at the tip from the 30 kN load at a = 3 m is P a²(3L - a)/(6EI) = 30 × 9 × 15/6 = 675/EI. The total downward deflection is 2295/EI. A unit upward force at B gives a flexibility f = L³/(3EI) = 72/EI. Setting 2295/EI - 72 By/EI = 0 gives By = 31.875 kN upward. The flexural rigidity cancels, so the reaction does not depend on EI when the support does not move.

Answer: 31.9 kN

(b)

With By known, take moments about A on the free body of the whole beam. The loads give a clockwise moment (taking the beam as drawn with A on the left) of wL²/2 = 10 × 36/2 = 180 kN·m plus P × 3 = 90 kN·m, a total of 270 kN·m. The prop reaction gives a counter-clockwise relief of By × 6 = 191.25 kN·m. The fixed end must provide the difference: MA = 270 - 191.25 = 78.75 kN·m, hogging. Without the prop, the cantilever would have to resist 270 kN·m, so the prop has removed about 71 percent of the support moment. Vertical equilibrium then gives Ay = 60 + 30 - 31.875 = 58.125 kN upward.

Answer: 78.75 kN·m

(c)

If B drops 15 mm, the redundant force no longer needs to hold the beam at zero deflection. The compatibility equation becomes: deflection from loads at B minus deflection from the redundant equals the settlement, so 2295/EI - 72 By/EI = 0.015 m. With EI = 40 000 kN·m², 2295/EI = 0.057375 m, and the flexibility is 72/40 000 = 0.0018 m per kN. Then By = (0.057375 - 0.015)/0.0018 = 23.54 kN. The prop picks up about 26 percent less force than when it was rigid (31.875 kN), because part of the beam's deflection is now allowed to occur at B rather than being resisted there.

Answer: 23.5 kN

(d)

Repeat the moment equation with the new reaction: MA = 270 - 6 × 23.54 = 270 - 141.25 = 128.75 kN·m hogging. This is 50 kN·m more than the 78.75 kN·m found with an unyielding prop, a rise of about 63 percent. The settlement therefore moves load from the prop into the fixed end. The designer should check the column-side reinforcement at A for the larger moment rather than rely on the original value, and should not assume the prop is stiff enough to treat as rigid.

Answer: 128.75 kN·m

Problem 3 [A1-113] Force method for indeterminate trusses

A small plant-room walkway in Hamilton hangs from a transfer girder by three steel rods that meet at a single pin joint D beneath the girder. One rod is vertical and 4.0 m long. The other two rods are identical, lie in the same vertical plane on opposite sides of the vertical rod, and each makes 30° with the vertical. All three rods are attached to the girder at the same level, and all have a cross-sectional area of 800 mm² and a modulus of 200 GPa. The walkway applies a 60 kN downward load at joint D. Treat the rods as pin-ended and the girder as rigid. Take the force in the vertical rod as the redundant and consider only axial deformation.

  1. (a) Find the force in the vertical rod. [6]
  2. (b) Find the force in each inclined rod. [4]
  3. (c) Find the vertical displacement of joint D, in millimetres. [4]
  4. (d) The vertical rod was fabricated 1.0 mm short and was forced into place before any load was applied. Find the force it carries from this lack of fit alone. [6]
(a)

Cut the vertical rod and call its force Fc, tension. The two inclined rods alone carry the rest, each with force F. Vertical equilibrium of the joint is Fc + 2F cos30° = 60. For compatibility, joint D must move down by the same amount as the vertical rod stretches. An inclined rod of length L/cosθ with force F stretches by F L/(AE cosθ), and joint D moves down by that stretch divided by cosθ, which is F L/(AE cos²θ). Substituting F = (60 - Fc)/(2cosθ) and setting the movement equal to the vertical rod stretch Fc L/AE gives 2Fc cos³θ = 60 - Fc, so Fc = P/(1 + 2cos³θ). With cos30° = 0.8660, cos³θ = 0.6495, so Fc = 60/2.2990 = 26.10 kN tension.

Answer: 26.1 kN

(b)

Use vertical equilibrium of joint D with the redundant now known: Fc + 2 F cos30° = 60 kN. Then F = (60 - 26.10)/(2 × 0.8660) = 33.90/1.7321 = 19.57 kN tension in each inclined rod. As a check on the horizontal equilibrium, the two inclined rods pull equal and opposite horizontal components, 19.57 sin30° = 9.79 kN each, which cancel by symmetry. The vertical rod therefore carries 43.5 percent of the load, even though it is shorter than the inclined rods. This is because it is the stiffest load path, since it deflects least per kN. The inclined rods share the other 56.5 percent.

Answer: 19.6 kN

(c)

The displacement of D follows from the elongation of any one rod, and the vertical rod is the simplest. AE = 800 × 10⁻⁶ m² × 200 × 10⁶ kN/m² = 160 000 kN. Then δ = Fc L/(AE) = 26.10 × 4.0/160 000 = 6.52 × 10⁻⁴ m = 0.652 mm downward. Check with an inclined rod: its length is 4.0/cos30° = 4.619 m and its elongation is 19.57 × 4.619/160 000 = 5.65 × 10⁻⁴ m. The vertical component of D's movement is this elongation divided by cos30°, which gives 6.52 × 10⁻⁴ m. The two routes agree, which confirms compatibility.

Answer: 0.652 mm

(d)

With no external load, the short rod pulls joint D upward by an amount u. The vertical rod, short by Δ = 1.0 mm, ends up stretched by Δ - u. Each inclined rod is shortened by u cosθ and so is in compression. Equilibrium requires the vertical rod tension T to equal 2C cosθ. With the rod stiffnesses this becomes (Δ - u)AE/L = 2u cos³θ AE/L, so u = Δ/(1 + 2cos³θ) = 1.0/2.299 = 0.435 mm. Then T = (1.0 - 0.435) × 10⁻³ × 160 000/4.0 = 22.6 kN tension in the vertical rod, balanced by 13.05 kN compression in each inclined rod. This is an indeterminate-structure effect: a fabrication error alone produces force.

Answer: 22.6 kN

Problem 4 [A1-114] Slope-deflection method for continuous beams

A two-span steel stringer under a pedestrian bridge approach in Thunder Bay is built into the abutment at A, rests on a pier at B, and ends on a roller bearing at C. Span AB is 6.0 m long and carries a uniformly distributed load of 20 kN/m. Span BC is 5.0 m long and carries a single 50 kN load at its midpoint. The flexural rigidity EI is the same in both spans. The supports do not settle. Use the slope-deflection equations with end moments positive clockwise on the member end. The unknown joint rotations are those at B and at C, and the rotation at the fixed support A is zero.

  1. (a) Find EIθB, the joint rotation at B multiplied by EI (negative if counter-clockwise). [5]
  2. (b) Find the support moment at B, as a hogging magnitude. [5]
  3. (c) Find the fixed-end moment at A, as a hogging magnitude. [5]
  4. (d) Find the vertical reaction at C. [5]
(a)

Fixed-end moments: span AB, wL²/12 = 20 × 36/12 = 60, so FEM_AB = -60 and FEM_BA = +60 kN·m. Span BC, PL/8 = 50 × 5/8 = 31.25, so FEM_BC = -31.25 and FEM_CB = +31.25. With θA = 0 and no chord rotation, M_AB = (2EI/6)θB - 60, M_BA = (2EI/6)(2θB) + 60, M_BC = (2EI/5)(2θB + θC) - 31.25, M_CB = (2EI/5)(θB + 2θC) + 31.25. The roller at C carries no moment, so M_CB = 0, giving EIθC = -39.06 - 0.5 EIθB. Joint B requires M_BA + M_BC = 0, which gives 1.4667 EIθB + 0.4 EIθC + 28.75 = 0. Substituting, 1.2667 EIθB = -13.125, so EIθB = -10.36 kN·m², counter-clockwise.

Answer: -10.36 kN·m²

(b)

Substitute EIθB = -10.36 into the end-moment equation for the left side of the joint: M_BA = (2EI/6)(2θB) + 60 = (2/3)(-10.36) + 60 = -6.91 + 60 = 53.09 kN·m. Check with the right side: EIθC = -39.06 + 5.18 = -33.88, so M_BC = 0.4 × (2 × (-10.36) + (-33.88)) - 31.25 = 0.4 × (-54.60) - 31.25 = -53.09 kN·m. The two ends sum to zero, which confirms joint equilibrium. The sign shows the beam is hogging at B (tension on top), and 53.1 kN·m is the design moment at the pier support. The value is smaller than the 60 kN·m that would act if B were fully fixed, since B is free to rotate.

Answer: 53.1 kN·m

(c)

The moment at the built-in end follows from the first equation: M_AB = (2EI/6)θB - 60 = (1/3)(-10.36) - 60 = -3.45 - 60 = -63.45 kN·m. The negative sign means counter-clockwise on the member end at A, which is hogging for a beam whose fixed end is on the left. The magnitude, 63.45 kN·m, exceeds the 60 kN·m that a fully fixed span would carry, because rotation at B pushes extra moment back to A. The carry-over from B to A is half the distributed moment at B, which is the usual 0.5 carry-over factor for a prismatic member, consistent with the -3.45 kN·m added here.

Answer: 63.5 kN·m

(d)

Take span BC as a free body with the end moment M_BC = -53.09 kN·m (counter-clockwise on the member at B) and zero moment at C. Moments about B, clockwise positive, are M_BC + 50 × 2.5 - Cy × 5 = 0, so Cy = (-53.09 + 125)/5 = 14.38 kN upward. A check on shears: Cy as a simple span would be 25 kN, and the hogging moment at B reduces it by 53.09/5 = 10.62 kN, giving 14.38 kN. The reaction at B from this span is then 50 - 14.38 = 35.62 kN upward, so the pier carries the larger share of the point load because it is the stiffer, restrained side.

Answer: 14.4 kN

Problem 5 [A1-115] Slope-deflection method with support settlement

A two-span continuous steel girder carries an access road over a drainage channel near Ottawa. Both spans are 7.0 m long and carry a uniformly distributed load of 12 kN/m. The girder is pin-supported at A, supported on a pier at B, and on a roller at C. EI is 60 000 kN·m² throughout. The pier at B rests on soft clay. Geotechnical staff think it could settle, so the engineer must see how the support moment changes. Use the slope-deflection equations, with the modified (pin-end) form for the outer spans. Settlement is downward and is measured at B relative to the ends A and C, which do not move.

  1. (a) Find the hogging moment at B when no settlement occurs. [4]
  2. (b) Find the hogging moment at B if the pier settles 12 mm. [6]
  3. (c) Find the vertical reaction at B after the 12 mm settlement. [5]
  4. (d) Find the settlement of B, in millimetres, at which the moment at B becomes exactly zero. [5]
(a)

Because the loading, spans and supports are symmetric about B, the rotation at B is zero. With the far ends pinned, use the modified slope-deflection form for the member end at B: M_BA = (3EI/L)(θB - ψ_AB) + FEM_BA - FEM_AB/2. For a UDL, FEM_AB = -wL²/12 = -49 and FEM_BA = +49 kN·m. With θB = 0 and ψ = 0 this gives M_BA = 49 + 24.5 = 73.5 kN·m, which equals wL²/8 = 12 × 49/8, the well-known value for a propped span with a fixed end at B. The same result arises on the other side, so the joint is in equilibrium (M_BA + M_BC = 0 in sign convention, since BC gives -73.5). The moment is hogging.

Answer: 73.5 kN·m

(b)

With B settling by δ = 0.012 m, the chord of span AB rotates clockwise by ψ_AB = δ/L = 0.012/7 = 0.001714 rad, and span BC rotates counter-clockwise by the same amount. The loading and settlement remain symmetric, so θB is still zero. Then M_BA = (3EI/L)(0 - ψ_AB) + 73.5 = 73.5 - 3EIδ/L². Numbers: 3 × 60 000 × 0.012/49 = 44.08 kN·m. So M_BA = 73.5 - 44.08 = 29.42 kN·m, still hogging. The settlement lets the girder sag at the middle support and so relieves the hogging moment, but at the cost of load moving to the outer supports.

Answer: 29.4 kN·m

(c)

For each span, the shear at the interior support is wL/2 plus the moment effect: with a hogging moment M at B and zero moment at the pin end, the end reaction at B is wL/2 + M/L. For one span that is 42 + 29.42/7 = 42 + 4.20 = 46.20 kN. Both spans contribute equally, so R_B = 2 × 46.20 = 92.41 kN. The end reactions are R_A = R_C = 42 - 4.20 = 37.80 kN. Check equilibrium: 92.41 + 2 × 37.80 = 168.0 kN, which equals the total load of 12 × 14 = 168 kN. Compared with 105 kN before settlement, the pier now carries about 12 percent less.

Answer: 92.4 kN

(d)

The moment varies linearly with settlement, M_B = 73.5 - (3EI/L²)δ. The slope is 3 × 60 000/49 = 3673.5 kN·m per metre. Setting M_B = 0 gives δ = 73.5/3673.5 = 0.02001 m, about 20.0 mm. At that point the girder behaves like two simply supported spans with no continuity moment. A settlement larger than this reverses the sign of the moment at B and produces sagging at the pier, which the section would need to be designed for. Because 20 mm is a realistic clay settlement, the designer should treat the continuity moment as unreliable.

Answer: 20.0 mm

A1 Practice Paper 24

Problem 1 [A1-116] Moment distribution for continuous beams

A three-span continuous steel girder in a Barrie parking structure is built into a wall at A, rests on rollers at B and C, and ends on a pin support at D. Span AB is 6.0 m with flexural rigidity EI and carries 15 kN/m uniformly distributed. Span BC is 8.0 m with rigidity 2EI and carries a 60 kN point load 3.0 m from B. Span CD is 5.0 m with rigidity EI and carries a 40 kN point load at midspan. No support settles. Analyse the girder by moment distribution, using the modified stiffness for the span next to the pinned end D. Use as many cycles as are needed for the unbalanced moments to fall below 0.05 kN·m.

  1. (a) Find the distribution factor for member BC at joint B. [3]
  2. (b) Find the distribution factor for member CB at joint C, using the modified stiffness of CD. [3]
  3. (c) Find the final hogging moment at B in span AB (end BA). [7]
  4. (d) Find the final hogging moment at the fixed support A. [7]
(a)

Stiffness for a member with a far end continuous or fixed is 4EI/L. At B, member BA has 4EI/6 = 0.6667 EI. Member BC has 4(2EI)/8 = 1.000 EI. The sum is 1.6667 EI. The distribution factor for BC is 1.000/1.6667 = 0.600, and for BA is 0.400. The two factors sum to one, as they must. Member BC takes the larger share of any unbalanced moment at B because its rigidity is twice that of AB, even though it is longer. A long, stiff span attracts more moment than a short, flexible one only when the I/L ratio is higher, and here 2/8 = 0.25 exceeds 1/6 = 0.167.

Answer: 0.600

(b)

At joint C, the far end of CD is a pin, so the stiffness of CD is 3EI/L = 3EI/5 = 0.600 EI rather than 4EI/L. This is the modified stiffness, which also removes the carry-over from D. Member CB has 4(2EI)/8 = 1.000 EI. The total at C is 1.600 EI. DF_CB = 1.000/1.600 = 0.625 and DF_CD = 0.600/1.600 = 0.375. Using the full stiffness 4EI/5 = 0.8 EI for CD would give 0.556 and 0.444, which would overstate the moment taken by CD. The correct treatment uses the modified fixed-end moment as well: CD's fixed-end moment is 25 kN·m, and it becomes 25 + 25/2 = 37.5 kN·m after the pin end is released.

Answer: 0.625

(c)

Fixed-end moments: AB ±45 kN·m; BC from Pab²/L² = 60 × 3 × 25/64 = 70.31 at B and Pa²b/L² = 42.19 at C; CD modified 37.5 at C. Cycle 1 at B: unbalanced 45 - 70.31 = -25.31, so BA receives +10.12 and BC +15.19, with half carried to A (5.06) and to C (7.59). At C: unbalanced 42.19 + 7.59 - 37.5 = 12.28, so CB receives -7.68 and CD -4.60, carrying -3.84 back to B. After cycle 1, M_BA = 55.12. Cycles 2 to 4 give 56.66, 56.80 and 56.82, and the unbalance falls below 0.05 kN·m. The final end moment M_BA is 56.82 kN·m hogging, the support moment on the left of B.

Answer: 56.8 kN·m

(d)

The moment at A comes only from the carry-over from B plus its fixed-end moment of -45 kN·m. After cycle 1 the moment at A is -45 + 5.06 = -39.94 kN·m. Each later cycle adds half the distributed amount at B: cycle 2 gives -39.17, cycle 3 gives -39.10 and cycle 4 gives -39.09. The result is M_AB = 39.09 kN·m hogging at the wall. Note that it is smaller than the fixed-end value of 45 kN·m because the joint at B rotates under the heavier span BC, which relieves A. This fixed-end moment is the one that governs the wall connection and the anchor design.

Answer: 39.1 kN·m

Problem 2 [A1-117] Moment distribution for frames without sidesway

A braced steel frame in an Oshawa industrial building has one rigid joint B where three members meet. Column BA is 4.0 m high with its base A fixed to a concrete footing. Beam BC extends 6.0 m to the right to a fixed connection at C and carries a uniformly distributed load of 20 kN/m. Beam BD extends 5.0 m to the left to a bearing D that acts as a pin, and carries a 30 kN load at its midpoint. EI is the same for all members. The stiff floor diaphragm prevents B from translating, so there is no sidesway. Use the slope-deflection or moment distribution method with the modified stiffness for the pinned member BD.

  1. (a) Find EIθB, the rotation of joint B multiplied by EI. [4]
  2. (b) Find the end moment in beam BD at B (hogging magnitude). [5]
  3. (c) Find the end moment in beam BC at B (hogging magnitude). [5]
  4. (d) Find the moment at the column base A. [3]
  5. (e) Find the moment at the fixed end C of beam BC. [3]
(a)

Member stiffnesses are K_BA = 4EI/4 = 1.000 EI for the column with a fixed base, K_BC = 4EI/6 = 0.6667 EI, and K_BD = 3EI/5 = 0.600 EI since D is a pin. Fixed-end moments: BC gives -wL²/12 = -60 kN·m at B. Beam BD fixed-end value is PL/8 = 18.75 kN·m at B; releasing the pin at D raises it to 18.75 + 18.75/2 = 28.125 kN·m. Moment equilibrium of the joint says the sum of member end moments at B is zero: (1.000 + 0.6667 + 0.600) EIθB - 60 + 28.125 = 0, so 2.2667 EIθB = 31.875 and EIθB = 14.06 kN·m². Positive means clockwise rotation of the joint.

Answer: 14.06 kN·m²

(b)

The end moment on BD at B is its modified fixed-end moment plus its stiffness times the rotation: M_BD = 0.600 × 14.0625 + 28.125 = 8.44 + 28.125 = 36.56 kN·m. For beam DB with B at its right end, a clockwise moment on the member end is hogging, so this is 36.6 kN·m hogging in the beam. Because D is a pin, there is no moment at D and no carry-over to it. As a check, the joint sum is M_BA + M_BC + M_BD = 14.06 - 50.63 + 36.56 = 0, which proves equilibrium at B and confirms the earlier arithmetic.

Answer: 36.6 kN·m

(c)

For beam BC, M_BC = (4EI/6)θB - wL²/12 = 0.6667 × 14.0625 - 60 = 9.375 - 60 = -50.63 kN·m. The negative sign means counter-clockwise on the member end at B, which is hogging for a beam whose B end is on the left. So 50.6 kN·m of hogging acts at B in beam BC. This is the moment that governs the top reinforcement or the flange stress over the joint. The fixed-end value was 60 kN·m, so rotation of the joint relieves it by 9.4 kN·m, passing that amount partly into the column and the left beam.

Answer: 50.6 kN·m

(d)

The column carries M_BA = (4EI/4)θB = 14.06 kN·m at the joint, and the far end is fixed, so half of this carries over to the base: M_AB = 0.5 × 14.06 = 7.03 kN·m. Directly from the slope-deflection equation, M_AB = (2EI/4)θB = 0.5 × 14.0625 = 7.03 kN·m, which agrees. The base of the column is therefore lightly loaded in bending compared with the beams, which is expected because the column is much stiffer relative to the unbalance it receives. The footing must still be designed for this moment plus the axial load from the frame.

Answer: 7.03 kN·m

(e)

At the far fixed end C, M_CB = (2EI/6)θB + wL²/12 = 0.3333 × 14.0625 + 60 = 4.69 + 60 = 64.69 kN·m. Equivalently, the fixed-end moment of 60 kN·m is increased by the carry-over from B, which is half of the 9.375 kN·m change distributed to member BC at B (the distributed amount is +9.375, and half is 4.69). The sign is clockwise on the member end at C, which is hogging for a beam whose C end is on the right. The wall connection at C therefore has to resist 64.7 kN·m, the largest moment in the frame.

Answer: 64.7 kN·m

Problem 3 [A1-118] Stiffness, carry-over and fixed-end moments including modified stiffness

A prismatic concrete beam segment AB, 5.0 m long with flexural rigidity EI = 45 000 kN·m², forms one member of a rigid-jointed floor frame in a Sudbury community centre. The analyst needs the basic quantities that feed a moment distribution analysis. Rotation of end A is the only displacement allowed in parts a to c, while end B is either fully fixed or free to rotate on a pin, as stated in each part. In part d, the member carries a single 40 kN load acting downward at 2.0 m from A, end A is fixed, and end B is a pin that has no moment resistance. Moment values are magnitudes in kN·m.

  1. (a) Find the rotational stiffness at A when B is fixed (moment per radian). [4]
  2. (b) Find the modified rotational stiffness at A when B is a pin. [4]
  3. (c) With B fixed, end A is rotated by 0.004 rad. Find the carry-over moment induced at B. [4]
  4. (d) For the loaded member of part d, find the hogging moment at A. [8]
(a)

Rotational stiffness is the moment needed at A to produce a unit rotation there when the far end is held. For a prismatic member with the far end fixed, K = 4EI/L. Here K = 4 × 45 000/5.0 = 36 000 kN·m per radian. This is the stiffness used in distribution factors for members whose far end is fixed or continuous. A moment of 36 000 kN·m would rotate A by one radian, which is far outside the elastic range, so the figure is used as a ratio. The distribution factor at a joint is this value divided by the sum of the stiffnesses of all members meeting there.

Answer: 36 000 kN·m/rad

(b)

With the far end a pin, the member cannot develop any moment at B, so the stiffness drops to the modified value K' = 3EI/L = 3 × 45 000/5.0 = 27 000 kN·m per radian. This is exactly 3/4 of the fixed-far-end value, as 3/4 = 27 000/36 000. The pin also removes the carry-over to B, since a pin cannot take moment. Using K' in a distribution table saves one carry-over step and shortens the iteration. Treating a pinned end as if it were fixed would overstate this member's share of the joint moment by 33 percent (36 000 against 27 000), which is a serious error in the sharing of moment at a joint.

Answer: 27 000 kN·m/rad

(c)

Rotating A by 0.004 rad with B fixed requires a moment at A of K θ = 36 000 × 0.004 = 144 kN·m. The moment induced at the far fixed end B is the carry-over moment, equal to the carry-over factor times the applied moment. For a prismatic member the factor is 1/2, so the moment at B is 0.5 × 144 = 72 kN·m. Direct check using slope-deflection: M_BA = (2EI/L)θA = 2 × 45 000/5.0 × 0.004 = 72 kN·m, which agrees. The carried moment has the same sign (same sense) as the applied moment, so a clockwise rotation at A produces a clockwise end moment at both ends.

Answer: 72 kN·m

(d)

First, the fixed-fixed end moments for a 40 kN load at a = 2.0 m, b = 3.0 m: FEM_AB = P a b²/L² = 40 × 2 × 9/25 = 28.8 kN·m and FEM_BA = P a² b/L² = 40 × 4 × 3/25 = 19.2 kN·m. Releasing the pin at B means cancelling the 19.2 kN·m at B, which carries over half, 9.6 kN·m, to A in the same sense. The final moment at A is 28.8 + 9.6 = 38.4 kN·m hogging. Check with the propped-cantilever formula P a b (L + b)/(2L²) = 40 × 2 × 3 × 8/(2 × 25) = 38.4 kN·m, which agrees. Compared with the fully fixed value of 28.8 kN·m, the pin raises the moment at A by a third.

Answer: 38.4 kN·m

Problem 4 [A1-119] Least work and energy methods for indeterminate structures

A two-span timber floor beam in a Sault Ste. Marie recreation centre has simply supported ends at A and C and a middle support at B. Each span is 6.0 m long, EI is constant, and the supports are rigid and level. A single downward point load of 48 kN, from a stage platform, acts on span AB at 3.0 m from A. Apply the principle of least work: treat the reaction at B as the redundant, write the bending strain energy as U = ∫M²/(2EI) dx, and require ∂U/∂R_B = 0. Measure x from A in span AB and from C in span BC. Keep R_B as a symbol until the minimisation, then substitute.

  1. (a) Find the reaction at B by least work. [7]
  2. (b) Find the magnitude of the reaction at C. State in your working which direction it acts. [5]
  3. (c) Find the bending moment under the 48 kN load. [4]
  4. (d) Find the total strain energy, multiplied by EI, at the least-work solution. [4]
(a)

Equilibrium in terms of R_B: moments about C give 12 R_A + 6 R_B - 48 × 9 = 0, so R_A = 36 - 0.5 R_B, and R_C = 48 - R_A - R_B = 12 - 0.5 R_B. Moments: in AB for 0 ≤ x ≤ 3, M = R_A x; for 3 ≤ x ≤ 6, M = R_A x - 48(x - 3); in BC, measured from C, M = R_C x. In each segment ∂M/∂R_B = -0.5x. Least work requires ∂U/∂R_B = (1/EI)∫M(∂M/∂R_B)dx = 0. The three segment integrals are 2.25 R_B - 162, then 15.75 R_B - 594, then 18 R_B - 432. Their sum is 36 R_B - 1188 = 0, so R_B = 33.0 kN upward. The flexural rigidity drops out, so the answer holds for any constant EI.

Answer: 33.0 kN

(b)

With R_B = 33.0 kN, R_A = 36 - 16.5 = 19.5 kN upward and R_C = 12 - 16.5 = -4.5 kN. The negative sign means the end support at C must pull the beam downward with 4.5 kN, so a hold-down is needed there. Check vertical equilibrium: 19.5 + 33.0 - 4.5 = 48 kN, equal to the applied load. A check using moments about A: 33.0 × 6 - 4.5 × 12 = 198 - 54 = 144 kN·m, and the load gives 48 × 3 = 144 kN·m, so the beam is in equilibrium. The load on span AB lifts the far end of BC, which is why the roller at C is in uplift.

Answer: 4.5 kN (downward)

(c)

The largest sagging moment is under the load, at x = 3.0 m from A, where M = R_A × 3.0 = 19.5 × 3.0 = 58.5 kN·m. Comparison points: at B, from the left, M = 19.5 × 6 - 48 × 3 = 117 - 144 = -27 kN·m, and from the right M = -4.5 × 6 = -27 kN·m, a match that confirms continuity of moment over the support. So the hogging moment over B is 27 kN·m, and the design sagging moment is 58.5 kN·m. A simply supported 6 m span with this load would have 72 kN·m, so continuity reduces the sagging moment by about 19 percent.

Answer: 58.5 kN·m

(d)

The strain energy is the sum of ∫M²dx/(2EI) over the three segments. Segment 1 (0 to 3 m): M = 19.5x, so ∫M²dx = 19.5² × 27/3 = 3422.25, then half of it gives 1711.1. Segment 2 (3 to 6 m): M = 19.5x - 48(x - 3) = 144 - 28.5x, and ∫M²dx = 2571.75, half 1285.9. Segment 3 (BC): M = -4.5x', ∫M²dx = 20.25 × 72 = 1458, half 729.0. The sum is 1711.1 + 1285.9 + 729.0 = 3726 kN²·m³, so U = 3726/EI. Any other value of R_B would give a larger total, which is the meaning of least work.

Answer: 3726 kN²·m³

Problem 5 [A1-120] Indeterminate structure with settlement or temperature change, comparing methods

A precast concrete beam spans 8.0 m between two stiff abutments in a Sarnia road underpass, and both ends are built in rigidly. The section is 250 mm wide and 600 mm deep, so A = 0.15 m², and E = 20 GPa gives EI = 90 000 kN·m². The coefficient of thermal expansion is 10 × 10⁻⁶ per kelvin. Over a summer day the top face is 30 K warmer than the bottom face, with the temperature varying linearly through the depth. In a separate check, abutment B settles 12 mm below A. Consider each effect on its own first, and then judge the worst combination. In part d, the beam is also heated uniformly by 25 K, and the abutments are assumed rigid against axial movement.

  1. (a) Find the restraint moment caused by the 30 K temperature gradient (constant along the beam). [5]
  2. (b) Find the end moment caused by the 12 mm settlement of B. [5]
  3. (c) Find the larger end moment when both effects act together in the least favourable combination. [5]
  4. (d) Find the axial force induced by the uniform 25 K temperature rise with both ends fully restrained axially. [5]
(a)

A temperature gradient ΔT between top and bottom faces over depth h gives a free curvature α ΔT/h. With both ends fixed, the beam cannot rotate at the ends, so the restraint must remove that curvature. Force method: release the rotation at one end, find the free end rotation αΔT L/h, and remove it with M L/(EI) = αΔT L/h. The result is a constant moment M = EI α ΔT/h along the whole beam. Slope-deflection gives the same through fixed-end moments of that size. Numbers: M = 90 000 × 10 × 10⁻⁶ × 30/0.6 = 45.0 kN·m. It is a uniform moment of that size over the full span, tension on the cooler face.

Answer: 45.0 kN·m

(b)

A settlement δ of one fixed end relative to the other gives a chord rotation ψ = δ/L, and slope-deflection with zero joint rotations gives M = 6EIψ/L = 6EIδ/L². Numbers: 6 × 90 000 × 0.012/64 = 6480/64 = 101.25 kN·m. This moment is hogging at A and sagging at B (opposite signs at the two ends), with a constant shear of 12EIδ/L³ = 12 × 90 000 × 0.012/512 = 25.3 kN. A force-method check releases the support at B, gives the tip deflection under the unit force and the end rotation, and arrives at the same value. This is more than twice the thermal moment, even for a small movement of 12 mm.

Answer: 101.25 kN·m

(c)

The thermal restraint moment is the same at both ends (uniform along the beam), 45 kN·m, whereas the settlement moments have opposite signs at the two ends, +101.25 at one end and -101.25 at the other. At one end the effects add: 101.25 + 45 = 146.25 kN·m. At the other end they partly cancel: 101.25 - 45 = 56.25 kN·m. The larger end moment is therefore 146.25 kN·m. This is the figure for design of the supporting section, and it is 3.25 times the thermal moment alone. Because the two effects have different sign patterns, they cannot simply be added with the same sign at both ends.

Answer: 146.25 kN·m

(d)

A uniform temperature rise changes length, not curvature, so no bending moment arises. If both ends are fully restrained against axial movement, the free expansion α ΔT L must be suppressed, and the axial force is N = EA α ΔT. Numbers: EA = 20 × 10⁶ kN/m² × 0.15 m² = 3.0 × 10⁶ kN, so N = 3.0 × 10⁶ × 10 × 10⁻⁶ × 25 = 750 kN compression. Axial restraint is rarely complete, because abutments move a little, but this is the upper bound. It acts together with the bending effects, so the designer would check combined axial compression and moment, and may add an expansion joint to reduce the force.

Answer: 750 kN

Exam A2: Elementary Structural Design

A2 Practice Paper 1

Problem 1 [A2-001] Limit states design: factored loads and load combinations

An interior column of a three-level parking structure in Ottawa is a square hollow steel section with a gross area of 9 680 mm² and a yield strength Fy = 350 MPa. The column is braced so that buckling is not a concern, so treat it as a short compression member with factored axial resistance Cr = φ A Fy, where φ = 0.90. Specified axial loads from the tributary area are: dead load D = 980 kN, parking live load L = 620 kN and snow load S = 310 kN. Wind effects on this column are negligible. Check the following limit states combinations: 1.4D; 1.25D + 1.5L + 0.5S; and 1.25D + 1.5S + 0.5L. The largest factored effect from any combination is compared with Cr.

  1. (a) Calculate the factored axial load from the combination 1.4D. [3]
  2. (b) Calculate the factored axial load from 1.25D + 1.5L + 0.5S. [4]
  3. (c) Calculate the factored axial load from 1.25D + 1.5S + 0.5L. [4]
  4. (d) Determine the factored axial resistance Cr of the column. [4]
  5. (e) Find the governing factored load and the ratio of governing load to Cr, and state whether the column is adequate. [5]
(a)

The dead load alone is the only variable in this combination, and the factor 1.4 covers the case where permanent load dominates and live effects are small. Pf = 1.4 × 980 = 1 372 kN. This value is the smallest of the three combinations because the live and snow loads, which are large here, are left out entirely. It matters in design mainly for structures where dead load is a very high share of the total, such as heavy concrete frames, and here it is a check only. Units are kN because the loads are already specified as axial forces on the column.

Answer: 1 372 kN

(b)

In this combination live load L is the principal variable load and snow S acts as a companion load with the reduced factor 0.5, because it is unlikely that the maximum parking live load and the maximum snow load occur together. Pf = 1.25 × 980 + 1.5 × 620 + 0.5 × 310 = 1 225 + 930 + 155 = 2 310 kN. The dead load factor of 1.25 is used instead of 1.4 because dead load is accompanied by a principal live load here. This combination gives the largest result of the three, which is checked in part e.

Answer: 2 310 kN

(c)

Here the roles are reversed: snow is the principal variable load with factor 1.5, and the parking live load becomes the companion load with factor 0.5. Pf = 1.25 × 980 + 1.5 × 310 + 0.5 × 620 = 1 225 + 465 + 310 = 2 000 kN. This is lower than part b because the snow load of 310 kN is half the live load of 620 kN, so swapping which load takes the full factor reduces the total by 310 kN. A designer should always try each load as the principal load in turn, because the governing case is not obvious in advance.

Answer: 2 000 kN

(d)

The column is treated as a short compression member, so its factored resistance is the factored squash load: Cr = φ A Fy = 0.90 × 9 680 mm² × 350 MPa. Multiplying, 9 680 × 350 = 3 388 000 N, and times 0.90 gives 3 049 200 N, or 3 049 kN. Using MPa with mm² gives newtons, which are divided by 1 000 to give kN. The resistance factor of 0.90 reduces the nominal capacity to account for variability in material strength, member dimensions and workmanship.

Answer: 3 049 kN

(e)

The governing factored load is the largest of the three: max(1 372, 2 310, 2 000) = 2 310 kN, from the 1.25D + 1.5L + 0.5S combination. The ratio is 2 310 / 3 049 = 0.758. Since the factored load is less than the factored resistance, Pf ≤ Cr is satisfied and the column is adequate, with about 24 percent reserve in capacity. The design is controlled by live load, not snow, so any increase in parking live load would erode the margin faster than a heavier snow load.

Answer: 0.758, adequate

Problem 2 [A2-002] Resistance factors and reliability in limit states design

A tension hanger in an Ontario industrial building is being calibrated for reliability. Its specified (nominal) load effect is Qn = 420 kN. The design requirement is φ Rn ≥ α Qn, where the single combined load factor is α = 1.45 and the resistance factor is φ = 0.85. Statistical studies give a mean resistance of 1.08 Rn with a coefficient of variation VR = 0.13, and a mean load effect of 0.88 Qn with a coefficient of variation VQ = 0.22. Assume both are lognormal. Use the simplified reliability index β = ln(Rm / Qm) / √(VR² + VQ²), where Rm and Qm are the mean values, and the failure probability Pf = Φ(−β), where Φ is the standard normal cumulative distribution function.

  1. (a) Determine the nominal resistance Rn needed to just satisfy φ Rn = α Qn. [4]
  2. (b) Calculate the mean resistance Rm and mean load effect Qm. [3]
  3. (c) Calculate the reliability index β. [5]
  4. (d) Calculate the probability of failure Pf, expressed in units of 10⁻³. [4]
  5. (e) Find the resistance factor φ that would be required to achieve a target β = 3.5, holding α and the statistical data constant. [4]
(a)

Set the design equation to equality: φ Rn = α Qn, so Rn = α Qn / φ. Substituting, Rn = 1.45 × 420 / 0.85 = 609 / 0.85 = 716.5 kN. The factored load α Qn = 609 kN is what the factored resistance must at least equal. Dividing by φ shows how the nominal resistance must be larger than the factored load, in this case by the factor 1/0.85 = 1.176. This is the value that the designer would provide when sizing the hanger.

Answer: 716.5 kN

(b)

The statistics are expressed relative to nominal values, so the means are found by scaling. Rm = 1.08 × Rn = 1.08 × 716.5 = 773.8 kN. The bias factor above 1.0 reflects the fact that real members are on average stronger than their nominal rating. Qm = 0.88 × Qn = 0.88 × 420 = 369.6 kN, a bias below 1.0 because specified loads are set at conservative upper values. The ratio Rm / Qm = 773.8 / 369.6 = 2.094 is the central safety factor used in the next part.

Answer: Rm = 773.8 kN, Qm = 369.6 kN

(c)

For lognormal variables the reliability index is β = ln(Rm/Qm) / √(VR² + VQ²). The numerator is ln(2.094) = 0.7389. The denominator is √(0.13² + 0.22²) = √(0.0169 + 0.0484) = √0.0653 = 0.2555. Hence β = 0.7389 / 0.2555 = 2.89. The index measures how many combined standard deviations separate the mean margin from zero. A value near 2.9 is close to the usual member target of about 3.0, while part e asks what φ a higher target of 3.5 would need.

Answer: 2.89

(d)

The failure probability is Pf = Φ(−β) = Φ(−2.891). The standard normal tail beyond 2.891 is about 0.00192, which can be read from tables or computed with the error function. Pf ≈ 1.92 × 10⁻³, or roughly 1 in 520. This is the probability that load exceeds resistance over the reference period used in the calibration. It is a notional value, since lognormal tails and independent variables are assumed, but it lets designers compare options consistently. Moving to β = 3.5 would cut this probability by roughly a factor of ten.

Answer: 1.92 × 10⁻³

(e)

For β = 3.5, ln(Rm/Qm) = 3.5 × 0.2555 = 0.8943, so Rm/Qm = e0.8943 = 2.446 and Rm = 2.446 × 369.6 = 903.9 kN. Rn = Rm / 1.08 = 836.9 kN. Since φ = α Qn / Rn = 609 / 836.9, φ = 0.728. The factor falls from 0.85 to about 0.73, meaning that a more severe target reliability needs a lower resistance factor, equivalent to a member 17 percent larger for the same load. The designer should weigh that extra material against the consequence of failure of a hanger that is not redundant.

Answer: 0.728

Problem 3 [A2-003] Specified live, snow and rain loads on roofs and floors

A three-storey school in Barrie, Ontario has an interior column supporting a tributary bay of 6.5 m by 7.2 m at the roof and at each of the two floors below. Roof snow load is S = Is[Ss(Cb Cw Cs Ca) + Sr] with Is = 1.0, ground snow Ss = 2.7 kPa, associated rain Sr = 0.4 kPa, and Cb = 0.8, Cw = 1.0, Cs = 1.0, Ca = 1.0. Dead loads are 0.9 kPa at the roof and 3.1 kPa at each floor. The specified floor live load is 2.4 kPa, reducible by the factor 0.3 + √(9.8 / AT) where AT is the total tributary floor area carried by the column (the factor is not less than 0.5). Use combinations 1.25D + 1.5L + 0.5S and 1.25D + 1.5S + 0.5L.

  1. (a) Calculate the specified roof snow load S in kPa. [4]
  2. (b) Calculate the factored roof pressure 1.25D + 1.5S in kPa. [3]
  3. (c) Calculate the live load reduction factor for the column. [4]
  4. (d) Calculate the governing factored axial load at the base of the column, in kN. [6]
  5. (e) Calculate the reduction in specified live load on the column, in kN, due to the reduction factor. [3]
(a)

Substitute into S = Is[Ss(Cb Cw Cs Ca) + Sr]. The product of the coefficients is 0.8 × 1.0 × 1.0 × 1.0 = 0.8, so Ss × 0.8 = 2.7 × 0.8 = 2.16 kPa. Adding the rain load, 2.16 + 0.4 = 2.56 kPa, and multiplying by the importance factor Is = 1.0 for a normal building leaves S = 2.56 kPa. The basic roof factor Cb = 0.8 reflects wind sweeping part of the snow from a large roof, and the Sr term is added because rain can fall on snow and increase the weight.

Answer: 2.56 kPa

(b)

The roof pressure is the area load before it is multiplied by the tributary area. Dead load factored at 1.25 gives 1.25 × 0.9 = 1.125 kPa. Snow as the principal load at 1.5 gives 1.5 × 2.56 = 3.84 kPa. Their sum is 1.125 + 3.84 = 4.965 kPa. This is the design pressure for roof framing under snow-dominated loading. The live load is not included because there is no floor occupancy on the roof, and no companion live load is considered here.

Answer: 4.965 kPa

(c)

The column carries two floors, so AT = 2 × (6.5 × 7.2) = 2 × 46.8 = 93.6 m². The reduction factor is 0.3 + √(9.8 / AT) = 0.3 + √(9.8 / 93.6) = 0.3 + √0.1047 = 0.3 + 0.3236 = 0.6236. This exceeds the lower limit of 0.5, so it governs. The reduction recognises that it is very unlikely every square metre of a large tributary area carries full design occupancy at the same moment. About 38 percent of the specified live load can be removed for this column.

Answer: 0.624

(d)

Per level the tributary area is 46.8 m². Total dead load D = 46.8 × (0.9 + 3.1 + 3.1) = 46.8 × 7.1 = 332.3 kN. Reduced live load L = 2 × 46.8 × 2.4 × 0.6236 = 140.1 kN. Snow S = 46.8 × 2.56 = 119.8 kN. First combination: 1.25 × 332.3 + 1.5 × 140.1 + 0.5 × 119.8 = 415.4 + 210.1 + 59.9 = 685.4 kN. Second combination: 415.4 + 1.5 × 119.8 + 0.5 × 140.1 = 415.4 + 179.7 + 70.1 = 665.2 kN. The first governs, so the factored load is about 685 kN.

Answer: 685 kN

(e)

Without reduction the specified live load on the column is 2 × 46.8 × 2.4 = 224.6 kN. With reduction it is 224.6 × 0.6236 = 140.1 kN. The difference is 224.6 − 140.1 = 84.6 kN. Using the reduced value lowers the factored column load by 1.5 × 84.6 = 127 kN in the live-load-governed combination, a direct saving in column size and foundation, justified by the statistical improbability of full loading everywhere. The reduction applies to live load only, never to dead or snow load, which act over the whole area at once.

Answer: 84.6 kN

Problem 4 [A2-004] Wind load on a building from reference pressure and coefficients

A six-storey hotel in Windsor, Ontario is 21 m tall, with a plan 32 m wide normal to the wind and 18 m deep. The design wind pressure on a surface is p = Iw q Ce Cg Cp, with importance factor Iw = 1.0, reference velocity pressure q = 0.52 kPa, gust factor Cg = 2.0, and exposure factor Ce = (h / 10)0.2 but not less than 0.9, where h is the height above ground in metres. Use external pressure coefficients Cp = +0.8 on the windward wall and Cp = −0.5 on the leeward wall, so the combined coefficient on the building is 1.3. For overall forces, evaluate Ce at mid-height and apply the resulting uniform net pressure over the full windward elevation. The wind load factor is 1.4.

  1. (a) Calculate Ce at the roof, h = 21 m. [3]
  2. (b) Calculate the uniform net pressure on the building, using Ce at mid-height, in kPa. [4]
  3. (c) Calculate the total specified wind base shear in kN. [5]
  4. (d) Calculate the specified overturning moment at the base, in kN·m, assuming the uniform pressure acts at mid-height. [4]
  5. (e) The shear is resisted by four identical shear walls in this direction. Calculate the factored shear in each wall, in kN. [4]
(a)

Apply the given expression with h = 21 m. Ce = (21 / 10)0.2 = 2.10.2. Taking logarithms, ln 2.1 = 0.7419, and multiplying by 0.2 gives 0.14839, so Ce = e0.14839 = 1.160. This exceeds the lower limit of 0.9, so it is used as calculated. The exposure factor grows with height because wind speed increases with elevation above the ground, and the roof of this building sees about 16 percent more pressure than the reference height of 10 m.

Answer: 1.160

(b)

At mid-height h = 10.5 m, so Ce = (1.05)0.2 = 1.0098. The combined pressure coefficient is 0.8 − (−0.5) = 1.3 because the pressure pushes on the windward wall while suction pulls on the leeward wall, and both load the frame in the same direction. Then p = Iw q Ce Cg (Cp1 − Cp2) = 1.0 × 0.52 × 1.0098 × 2.0 × 1.3 = 1.365 kPa. Evaluating Ce at mid-height is a simplification of the true height-varying pressure and is stated in the problem.

Answer: 1.365 kPa

(c)

The wind acts on the 32 m wide, 21 m tall windward elevation, so the area is 32 × 21 = 672 m². The base shear equals the net pressure times that area: V = 1.3653 kPa × 672 m² = 917.5 kN. kPa multiplied by m² gives kN directly. The result is a specified (unfactored) load and is the total horizontal force that the lateral system and foundations must transfer to the ground in the wind direction considered. The load factor of 1.4 is applied later, when the member forces are compared with resistances.

Answer: 917 kN

(d)

With uniform pressure, the resultant acts at mid-height, 21 / 2 = 10.5 m above the base. The overturning moment is M = V × 10.5 = 917.45 × 10.5 = 9 633 kN·m. The footprint depth in the wind direction is 18 m, and the resisting moment from dead weight would be taken about the leeward edge. A real pressure profile increases with height, so the resultant would act slightly above mid-height, and this simple answer is slightly low. A more refined analysis would integrate the pressure storey by storey.

Answer: 9 633 kN·m

(e)

The factored base shear is 1.4 × 917.45 = 1 284.4 kN. If the four identical walls share the load equally, each carries 1 284.4 / 4 = 321.1 kN. Equal sharing assumes a rigid floor diaphragm and no torsion, since a centre of rigidity displaced from the line of wind action would increase the load on the walls farthest from it. Each wall and its connections to the foundation must be designed for at least this factored shear. The 1.4 factor is applied because wind is a variable load with a large uncertainty.

Answer: 321 kN

Problem 5 [A2-005] Equivalent static seismic base shear and its vertical distribution

A five-storey hospital in Ontario has a reinforced concrete shear wall system with a height hn = 36 m, with storey heights of 7.2 m. Seismic weights are 11 800 kN at each of levels 1 to 4 and 9 600 kN at the roof, level 5. Use the empirical period Ta = 0.05 hn0.75 s. Design spectral acceleration is S(0.5) = 0.52 and S(1.0) = 0.31, interpolated linearly for periods between. Take Mv = 1.0, importance factor IE = 1.5, ductility-related factor Rd = 2.0 and overstrength factor Ro = 1.5. The base shear is V = S(Ta) Mv IE W / (Rd Ro). A top concentrated force Ft = 0.07 Ta V applies at the roof when Ta > 0.7 s. The remainder (V − Ft) is distributed as Fx = (V − Ft) Wx hx / Σ(Wi hi).

  1. (a) Calculate the period Ta in seconds. [3]
  2. (b) Determine S(Ta) by linear interpolation. [3]
  3. (c) Calculate the base shear V in kN. [4]
  4. (d) Calculate the top force Ft in kN. [3]
  5. (e) Calculate the lateral force Fx at level 3, in kN. [7]
(a)

The total weight is W = 4 × 11 800 + 9 600 = 56 800 kN, used later. For the period, hn0.75 = 360.75 = e0.75 × ln 36 = e0.75 × 3.5835 = e2.6876 = 14.70. Then Ta = 0.05 × 14.70 = 0.735 s. This is above 0.7 s, so the top force Ft will apply. The empirical formula gives a conservative period for a shear wall building and avoids needing a dynamic analysis at this design stage.

Answer: 0.735 s

(b)

The period 0.735 s lies between 0.5 s and 1.0 s, so interpolate. The fraction along the interval is (0.735 − 0.5) / (1.0 − 0.5) = 0.4696. The spectral acceleration falls from 0.52 to 0.31, a drop of 0.21. So S(Ta) = 0.52 − 0.4696 × 0.21 = 0.52 − 0.0986 = 0.421. Linear interpolation between tabulated periods is the usual method, and a longer period gives smaller acceleration because the building is more flexible and responds less to the ground motion.

Answer: 0.421

(c)

Substitute the values: V = S(Ta) Mv IE W / (Rd Ro) = 0.4214 × 1.0 × 1.5 × 56 800 / (2.0 × 1.5). The numerator is 0.4214 × 1.5 = 0.6320, times 56 800 = 35 900 kN, and the denominator is 3.0. So V = 11 967 kN. This is about 21 percent of the seismic weight. The importance factor raises the force for a hospital that must remain operational, while Rd Ro lowers it to reflect ductile inelastic behaviour.

Answer: 11 967 kN

(d)

Because Ta = 0.735 s exceeds 0.7 s, the top force is Ft = 0.07 × Ta × V = 0.07 × 0.7348 × 11 966.7 = 615.6 kN. It is applied at the roof level in addition to its share of the distributed force. The extra force accounts for higher modes of vibration in flexible, longer-period structures, which add to roof-level accelerations beyond what a purely linear distribution suggests. The remainder to distribute is V − Ft = 11 351 kN.

Answer: 616 kN

(e)

Compute weights times heights: levels 1 to 4 have Wx hx = 11 800 × (7.2, 14.4, 21.6, 28.8) = 84 960, 169 920, 254 880, 339 840 kN·m, and the roof has 9 600 × 36 = 345 600. The sum is 1 195 200 kN·m. At level 3, Fx = (11 966.7 − 615.6) × 254 880 / 1 195 200 = 11 351.1 × 0.21325 = 2 420.7 kN. The share is proportional to weight times height, so upper levels attract larger forces, giving an inverted triangular shape.

Answer: 2 421 kN

A2 Practice Paper 2

Problem 1 [A2-006] Timber beam design for bending, shear and bearing

A glued-laminated timber beam, 175 mm wide by 380 mm deep, spans 5.6 m simply supported between two masonry pilasters over a community-hall stage in Peterborough. It carries a factored uniformly distributed load of 26 kN/m, including self-weight, and bears 100 mm on each support. Use specified strengths fb = 24.0 MPa, fv = 2.0 MPa and fcp = 7.0 MPa, resistance factor φ = 0.90, and load duration factor KD = 1.15, with all other modification factors equal to 1.0. Resistances are Mr = φ fb KD S, Vr = φ fv KD (2/3) A, and Qr = φ fcp KD Ab. Take the critical shear section at a distance d from the face of the support, with d equal to the beam depth, and neglect the pilaster width.

  1. (a) Calculate the maximum factored bending moment Mf in kN·m. [3]
  2. (b) Calculate the factored bending resistance Mr in kN·m. [4]
  3. (c) Calculate the factored shear Vf at the critical section, in kN. [3]
  4. (d) Calculate the factored shear resistance Vr in kN. [4]
  5. (e) Calculate the minimum bearing length at a support so that the bearing resistance equals the factored reaction, in mm. [6]
(a)

The maximum moment for a uniformly loaded simple span occurs at midspan: Mf = wf L² / 8 = 26 × 5.6² / 8 = 26 × 31.36 / 8 = 101.9 kN·m. The beam supports a stage platform, so the loads are assumed to be uniform over the whole span and the moment diagram is a parabola with zero at each support. This is the demand to compare with the factored bending resistance of the section in the next part.

Answer: 101.9 kN·m

(b)

First find the section modulus of the rectangle: S = b d² / 6 = 175 × 380² / 6 = 175 × 144 400 / 6 = 4.212 × 10⁶ mm³. Then Mr = φ fb KD S = 0.90 × 24.0 × 1.15 × 4.212 × 10⁶ N·mm = 104.6 × 10⁶ N·mm = 104.6 kN·m. The factor 1.15 is allowed because the load acts for a short time compared with the standard term. Since Mr > Mf, bending is adequate with a margin of about 2.6 percent, which is thin.

Answer: 104.6 kN·m

(c)

The reaction is wf L / 2 = 26 × 2.8 = 72.8 kN. Shear at a distance d = 0.38 m from the support face is reduced by the load acting between the support and that section: Vf = wf (L/2 − d) = 26 × (2.8 − 0.38) = 26 × 2.42 = 62.9 kN. Taking the critical section at d is permitted because loads within that distance are transferred directly to the support through compression struts in the timber, not through shear on the full section.

Answer: 62.9 kN

(d)

Shear resistance of a rectangular section is Vr = φ fv KD (2/3) A, with A = 175 × 380 = 66 500 mm². Then Vr = 0.90 × 2.0 × 1.15 × (2/3) × 66 500 = 2.07 × 44 333 = 91 770 N = 91.8 kN. The 2/3 factor arises because the maximum shear stress in a rectangle is 1.5 times the average. Since Vr = 91.8 kN exceeds Vf = 62.9 kN, shear does not control, and the utilization is 0.69.

Answer: 91.8 kN

(e)

The factored reaction is Rf = wf L / 2 = 72.8 kN. Bearing resistance is Qr = φ fcp KD b lb, where Ab = b × lb. Setting Qr = Rf gives lb = Rf / (φ fcp KD b) = 72 800 / (0.90 × 7.0 × 1.15 × 175) = 72 800 / 1 267.9 = 57.4 mm. The provided 100 mm exceeds this, so bearing is satisfactory. Bearing is perpendicular to the grain, where timber is weakest in compression, which is why the plate length is checked separately.

Answer: 57.4 mm

Problem 2 [A2-007] Timber column design and slenderness

A free-standing 190 mm by 190 mm sawn timber post carries the porch roof of a heritage house in Kingston. Its effective length is Le = Ke L, where L = 3.9 m and Ke = 1.0 (pinned at both ends). Axial resistance is Pr = φ Fc A KZc Kc, with φ = 0.80, A the gross area, Fc = 11.5 MPa, and KZc = 1.0. The slenderness factor is Kc = [1 + Fc KZc Cc³ / (35 E05 KSE KT)]−1, with Cc = Le / d, E05 = 6 500 MPa, KSE = 1.0 and KT = 1.0. The slenderness ratio Cc must not exceed 50. After inspection, the owner proposes to fix the base into a concrete pier so that Ke becomes 0.8, with the other quantities unchanged.

  1. (a) Calculate the slenderness ratio Cc for the existing pinned post. [3]
  2. (b) Calculate the slenderness factor Kc. [5]
  3. (c) Calculate the axial resistance Pr in kN. [5]
  4. (d) Calculate the axial resistance Pr after the base is fixed (Ke = 0.8), in kN. [4]
  5. (e) Calculate the percentage increase in resistance from fixing the base. [3]
(a)

The post is square, so the least dimension is d = 190 mm. With Ke = 1.0, Le = 1.0 × 3 900 = 3 900 mm. Then Cc = Le / d = 3 900 / 190 = 20.5. This is below the limit of 50, so the member is permitted. A slenderness near 20 is intermediate: the post will not fail by pure crushing, but buckling reduces capacity noticeably, which the factor Kc will show in part b.

Answer: 20.5

(b)

Compute Cc³ = 20.526³ = 8 648 (20.526² = 421.3, times 20.526 = 8 648). The numerator term is Fc KZc Cc³ = 11.5 × 1.0 × 8 648 = 99 450. The denominator is 35 E05 KSE KT = 35 × 6 500 × 1.0 × 1.0 = 227 500. The ratio is 0.4371, so Kc = 1 / (1 + 0.4371) = 1 / 1.4371 = 0.696. The factor means the post develops only about 70 percent of its crushing strength because of buckling effects.

Answer: 0.696

(c)

The gross area is A = 190 × 190 = 36 100 mm². Then Pr = φ Fc A KZc Kc = 0.80 × 11.5 × 36 100 × 1.0 × 0.6958. First 0.80 × 11.5 = 9.2 MPa, times 36 100 gives 332 120 N, and times 0.6958 gives 231 100 N = 231 kN. This is the factored resistance, so compare it with factored roof loads only. Small porch loads are far below this value, so the post has a large reserve.

Answer: 231 kN

(d)

With Ke = 0.8, Le = 0.8 × 3 900 = 3 120 mm and Cc = 3 120 / 190 = 16.42. Cc³ = 4 428. Then Fc Cc³ = 11.5 × 4 428 = 50 920, divided by 227 500 gives 0.2238, so Kc = 1 / 1.2238 = 0.8171. Pr = 332 120 × 0.8171 = 271 400 N = 271 kN. Fixing the base shortens the effective buckling length and cuts the slenderness, so more of the section's strength is available.

Answer: 271 kN

(e)

The increase is (Pr,fixed − Pr,pinned) / Pr,pinned × 100 = (271.38 − 231.09) / 231.09 × 100 = 40.29 / 231.09 × 100 = 17.4 percent. This is worthwhile but modest, because the post was already fairly stocky. The pier connection must also resist moments at its base, and detailing a true fixed support in rot-prone wood near grade is difficult, so the designer might take a Ke value between 0.8 and 1.0 for safety. The base fixity also needs a tested detail, such as a standoff steel shoe, to keep the end grain dry.

Answer: 17.4 percent

Problem 3 [A2-008] Timber tension members and net section

The bottom chord of a roof truss on a curling rink in Orillia is a single sawn timber, 140 mm wide by 190 mm deep, spliced to a steel gusset with 16 mm diameter bolts. The bolt holes are drilled 2 mm oversize, so the hole diameter is 18 mm. At the critical section two bolts sit in the same cross-section, one above the other across the depth, so two holes reduce the depth. Tension resistance is Tr = φ Ft KD KZt An, with φ = 0.90, Ft = 5.5 MPa, KD = 1.15 and KZt = 1.0. The truss analysis gives a factored chord tension Tf = 165 kN.

  1. (a) Calculate the gross cross-sectional area of the chord in mm². [2]
  2. (b) Calculate the net area at the critical section with two holes. [4]
  3. (c) Calculate the factored tension resistance Tr in kN, and state whether the chord carries Tf = 165 kN. [4]
  4. (d) Calculate Tr if the connection were redesigned with three holes across the depth, in kN. [4]
  5. (e) Find the minimum depth of the 140 mm wide member that carries Tf = 165 kN with two holes, in mm. [6]
(a)

The gross area is the full rectangle: Ag = b d = 140 × 190 = 26 600 mm². It is not used directly in the tension resistance equation here, because tension failure in timber occurs through the weakest section where the wood fibres are cut by the bolt holes, but it is the reference from which the net area is obtained and the starting point for any check of how much section has been lost. Here the gross area is 26 600 mm², which also lets the net-to-gross ratio be reported as a quick measure of connection efficiency.

Answer: 26 600 mm²

(b)

At a section through the bolts the holes remove material across the depth. Two 18 mm holes remove 2 × 18 = 36 mm of depth, so the net depth is 190 − 36 = 154 mm and An = 140 × 154 = 21 560 mm². That is 81 percent of the gross area. Holes drilled 2 mm over the bolt diameter are included, because the actual wood removed is the hole, not the bolt. Stagger of bolts would reduce the loss, but here the bolts are in line.

Answer: 21 560 mm²

(c)

Tr = φ Ft KD KZt An = 0.90 × 5.5 × 1.15 × 1.0 × 21 560 = 5.6925 × 21 560 = 122 730 N = 122.7 kN. This is less than the applied Tf = 165 kN, so the chord is inadequate as drawn; the ratio Tf / Tr = 1.34. The member would fail at the bolt holes by net-section tension rather than in the clear length. Hence either the depth must increase or fewer, larger holes with a different bolt layout must be used.

Answer: 122.7 kN, inadequate

(d)

With three holes, the removed depth is 3 × 18 = 54 mm, so the net depth is 190 − 54 = 136 mm and An = 140 × 136 = 19 040 mm². Then Tr = 5.6925 × 19 040 = 108 390 N = 108.4 kN. Adding a hole costs 14 kN, more than 11 percent of the capacity, so a connection layout with three bolts in the same section is poor practice. Bolts should be staggered along the length where possible to avoid weakening a single section.

Answer: 108.4 kN

(e)

The required net area is An = Tf / (φ Ft KD KZt) = 165 000 / 5.6925 = 28 985 mm². Dividing by the width gives the net depth 28 985 / 140 = 207.0 mm. Add back the two holes: d = 207.0 + 36 = 243.0 mm. A standard 140 × 241 mm member would almost do, but is slightly under, so the designer selects the next available size, such as 140 × 292 mm. The hole allowance has to be added because the net depth, not the gross depth, carries the force.

Answer: 243 mm

Problem 4 [A2-009] Timber connections with bolts and nails

A tension splice in a glulam arch at a Guelph arena uses two steel side plates and a single timber member, so each bolt acts in double shear (two shear planes). Eight 12.7 mm bolts are arranged in two rows of four. The basic lateral resistance of one bolt in one shear plane is given as qu = 6.2 kN. The factored resistance of a bolt group is Nr = φ ns qu KD nF n, where φ = 0.80, ns = 2 shear planes, KD = 1.15, n is the number of bolts and nF = 0.88 is the group action factor for this layout. The factored tension in the splice is Tf = 72 kN. As an alternative, a nailed splice uses nails each having a basic lateral resistance of 1.24 kN per nail, with Nr = φ n qn KD and the same φ and KD, with no group reduction.

  1. (a) Calculate the factored resistance of a single bolt in double shear, φ ns qu KD, in kN. [3]
  2. (b) Calculate the factored resistance Nr of the eight-bolt group. [4]
  3. (c) Calculate the ratio Tf / Nr and state whether the bolted splice is adequate. [3]
  4. (d) Calculate the factored resistance of the nailed alternative if 40 nails are used, in kN. [4]
  5. (e) Calculate the minimum whole number of nails needed to carry Tf = 72 kN. [6]
(a)

The side plates make each bolt act in double shear, so there are two shear planes per bolt and the capacity doubles in principle. The factored resistance of one bolt is φ ns qu KD = 0.80 × 2 × 6.2 × 1.15 = 11.41 kN. The load duration factor KD of 1.15 applies to short-term loads such as snow or wind. The result is the strength before the reduction for group action, which accounts for uneven load sharing between bolts in a row.

Answer: 11.41 kN

(b)

Multiply by the number of bolts and the group factor: Nr = 8 × 11.408 × 0.88 = 80.31 kN. The group factor of 0.88 reduces the capacity by 12 percent because bolts in a row do not all reach their ultimate load at the same time; the end bolts attract more than the middle ones, and the timber splits sooner as a result. Without the factor the group would show 91.3 kN, so ignoring group action would overstate the splice by roughly 14 percent.

Answer: 80.3 kN

(c)

The ratio is Tf / Nr = 72 / 80.31 = 0.897. Since Tf is less than Nr, the splice satisfies the requirement and about 10 percent of resistance is spare. The bolt layout should still be checked for edge, end and spacing distances and for tear-out or row shear in the timber, which are separate limit states not asked for here. A utilization close to 0.9 is acceptable but leaves little room for future changes of load. The group factor raises the ratio from 0.79 to 0.90, so the designer should confirm that 0.88 applies to this exact bolt spacing.

Answer: 0.897, adequate

(d)

For the nailed alternative the factored resistance is Nr = φ n qn KD = 0.80 × 40 × 1.24 × 1.15 = 45.63 kN. Each nail carries only 0.80 × 1.24 × 1.15 = 1.14 kN, which is why nailed splices need many fasteners. 40 nails give just 63 percent of the factored tension of 72 kN, so this number of nails is inadequate. Nails are cheap and ductile but they are suitable only for light loads. Predrilling would not change this basic comparison with the bolted splice.

Answer: 45.6 kN

(e)

The resistance per nail is 0.80 × 1.24 × 1.15 = 1.1408 kN. Dividing the required tension gives n = 72 / 1.1408 = 63.1. Fasteners are discrete, so round up to 64 nails. Check: 64 × 1.1408 = 73.0 kN, which exceeds 72 kN. Packing 64 nails into the side members may require long plates and careful spacing, which is why the eight-bolt splice with 80.3 kN capacity is generally the better choice for this load. Fewer fasteners also mean less drilling and less risk of splitting the member.

Answer: 64 nails

Problem 5 [A2-010] Steel tension members: gross section, net section and block shear

A single angle L127 × 89 × 9.5, used as a hanger brace in a gymnasium roof in Brantford, is bolted through its 127 mm leg to a gusset plate by a single line of three 20 mm bolts, with 22 mm holes. Its gross area is Ag = 2 020 mm², Fy = 300 MPa and Fu = 450 MPa. Resistance factors are φ = 0.90 (yielding) and φu = 0.75 (fracture). Use Tr = φ Ag Fy for gross yielding; Tr = 0.85 φu An Ut Fu for net fracture with shear lag factor Ut = 0.8; and for block shear Tr = φu [Ut Ant Fu + 0.6 Agv (Fy + Fu)/2] with Ut = 1.0. The leg thickness is t = 9.5 mm. The block has a gross shear length of 175 mm (end distance 35 mm plus two 70 mm pitches) and a tension face of 40 mm from the bolt line to the leg edge, reduced by half a hole. Use the 22 mm hole diameter as given for all net areas, with no additional allowance for hole damage.

  1. (a) Calculate the gross-section yielding resistance in kN. [4]
  2. (b) Calculate the net-section fracture resistance in kN. [4]
  3. (c) Calculate the block shear resistance in kN. [6]
  4. (d) State the governing tension resistance in kN. [2]
  5. (e) Recalculate the block shear resistance if the end distance is increased to 55 mm, with the shear length becoming 195 mm. [4]
(a)

Gross yielding is a ductile limit state over the whole length of the member. Tr = φ Ag Fy = 0.90 × 2 020 × 300 = 545 400 N = 545.4 kN. The resistance factor is 0.90 because yielding gives warning by large deformations before any rupture. This result is the highest of the three limit states, which is typical: the net section and the bolted end generally control, since the holes remove material and the load must flow through a smaller area.

Answer: 545.4 kN

(b)

The net area removes one 22 mm hole across the 9.5 mm leg: An = 2 020 − 22 × 9.5 = 2 020 − 209 = 1 811 mm². Because only one leg is bolted, shear lag applies, with Ut = 0.8. Then Tr = 0.85 × 0.75 × 1 811 × 0.8 × 450 = 0.6375 × 1 811 × 0.8 × 450 = 415 600 N = 415.6 kN. Fracture is brittle, so φu is lower, and the extra 0.85 factor adds margin. This is 24 percent below the yield resistance.

Answer: 415.6 kN

(c)

Gross shear area Agv = 175 × 9.5 = 1 662.5 mm². Net tension area Ant = (40 − 22/2) × 9.5 = 29 × 9.5 = 275.5 mm². Then Tr = 0.75 [1.0 × 275.5 × 450 + 0.6 × 1 662.5 × (300 + 450)/2] = 0.75 [123 975 + 0.6 × 1 662.5 × 375] = 0.75 [123 975 + 374 063] = 0.75 × 498 038 = 373 530 N = 373.5 kN. Block shear tears out a block of steel at the end of the angle, with fracture on the tension face and yielding on the shear faces.

Answer: 373.5 kN

(d)

The governing resistance is the smallest of the three: min(545.4, 415.6, 373.5) = 373.5 kN, from block shear. The result shows why a connection must be checked separately from the member. The angle itself could carry 545 kN in yield, but the bolted end limits it to 373.5 kN, about 68 percent of the gross capacity. Lengthening the end distance would raise the block shear resistance, and part e shows by how much. In design the connection is therefore proportioned after the member, with the end distance and pitch chosen to bring all three limit states close together.

Answer: 373.5 kN

(e)

With a 55 mm end distance the gross shear length is 55 + 140 = 195 mm, so Agv = 195 × 9.5 = 1 852.5 mm². The tension term is unchanged at 123 975 N. The shear term is 0.6 × 1 852.5 × 375 = 416 813 N. Then Tr = 0.75 × (123 975 + 416 813) = 0.75 × 540 788 = 405 590 N = 405.6 kN. This now sits just below the net-fracture value of 415.6 kN, so block shear still governs, but only by 2.4 percent.

Answer: 405.6 kN

A2 Practice Paper 3

Problem 1 [A2-011] Laterally supported steel beam flexural resistance

Roof beams for a new warehouse in Sudbury, Ontario are rolled wide-flange shapes simply supported over a clear span of 7.5 m. The compression flange of each beam is fully restrained against lateral movement by the steel deck welded along the whole span, so lateral-torsional buckling does not govern. The section is Class 1 for bending, with plastic section modulus Zx = 1 060 × 10³ mm³ and elastic section modulus Sx = 940 × 10³ mm³. Use Fy = 350 MPa and a resistance factor φ = 0.90, so that for a laterally supported Class 1 section the factored moment resistance is Mr = φ Zx Fy. Self-weight is already included in the factored uniformly distributed line load quoted below. The owner is considering a heavier roof-top unit that will raise the factored load to 52 kN/m.

  1. (a) Calculate the factored moment resistance Mr of the beam in kN·m. [5]
  2. (b) Calculate the shape factor Zx/Sx and state in one sentence what it tells you about the reserve of strength beyond first yield. [3]
  3. (c) Find the largest factored uniformly distributed load w, in kN/m, the beam can carry on the 7.5 m span. [6]
  4. (d) For the heavier roof-top unit (w = 52 kN/m factored) the beam is no longer adequate. Find the minimum plastic section modulus, in mm³, that a replacement beam of the same steel must have. [6]
(a)

For a Class 1 section that is fully laterally supported, the section can develop its full plastic moment Mp = Zx Fy. The factored resistance is Mr = φ Zx Fy = 0.90 × 1 060 × 10³ mm³ × 350 MPa. The product 1 060 × 10³ × 350 = 371.0 × 10⁶ N·mm, and multiplying by 0.90 gives 333.9 × 10⁶ N·mm = 333.9 kN·m. No reduction for lateral-torsional buckling is applied because the deck restrains the compression flange continuously, and no local buckling reduction is needed because the section is Class 1. This value is the benchmark for the remaining parts.

Answer: 333.9 kN·m

(b)

The shape factor is the ratio of the plastic moment to the yield moment, Zx/Sx = 1 060 × 10³ / 940 × 10³ = 1.128, about 1.13. The yield moment My = Sx Fy corresponds to the outer fibre just reaching Fy, while Mp = Zx Fy corresponds to the whole section yielded. A value of 1.13 means the beam can carry about 13 percent more moment after first yield before a plastic hinge forms. Wide-flange shapes bent about the strong axis typically fall between 1.10 and 1.18, so this value is ordinary and the reserve is modest compared with a rectangular section, whose shape factor is 1.5.

Answer: 1.13

(c)

For a simply supported beam with a uniformly distributed factored load, the maximum moment at midspan is Mf = w L² / 8. Setting Mf equal to the resistance gives w = 8 Mr / L². With Mr = 333.9 kN·m and L = 7.5 m, w = 8 × 333.9 / 7.5² = 2 671.2 / 56.25 = 47.5 kN/m. This is a bending-controlled limit only. Shear resistance and deflection must be checked separately, but with a stocky span of 7.5 m they rarely govern a roof beam that is fully braced. The load of 47.5 kN/m is already factored, so it is compared directly with the factored demand, not with service loads.

Answer: 47.5 kN/m

(d)

The factored moment for the heavier load is Mf = w L² / 8 = 52 × 7.5² / 8 = 52 × 56.25 / 8 = 365.6 kN·m. Since 365.6 exceeds the present Mr of 333.9, the beam is overstressed by about 9.5 percent. The replacement section must satisfy φ Zx Fy ≥ Mf, so Zx required = Mf / (φ Fy) = 365.6 × 10⁶ N·mm / (0.90 × 350 MPa) = 365.6 × 10⁶ / 315 = 1.161 × 10⁶ mm³. A shape with a plastic modulus of at least 1 161 × 10³ mm³ is needed, and the next heavier standard section in the catalogue above this value would be selected. Because the same deck bracing applies, no buckling reduction enters the choice.

Answer: 1.161 × 10⁶ mm³

Problem 2 [A2-012] Lateral torsional buckling of steel beams

A crane-runway girder in a Hamilton fabrication shop is a doubly symmetric Class 1 wide-flange section with Zx = 1 300 × 10³ mm³, Iy = 20.0 × 10⁶ mm⁴, torsional constant J = 380 × 10³ mm⁴ and warping constant Cw = 480 × 10⁹ mm⁶. Take Fy = 350 MPa, E = 200 000 MPa, G = 77 000 MPa and φ = 0.90. The girder is braced against twist and lateral movement only at the ends of a segment of unbraced length Lu = 5.0 m. For Lu beyond the fully plastic range the critical elastic moment is Mu = (ω₂ π / Lu) √(E Iy G J + (π E / Lu)² Iy Cw). When Mu > 0.67 Mp, the resistance is Mr = 1.15 φ Mp (1 − 0.28 Mp / Mu) but not more than φ Mp; Mp = Zx Fy.

  1. (a) Calculate the upper limit φ Mp of the resistance, in kN·m. [3]
  2. (b) Calculate the critical elastic moment Mu for uniform bending moment over the segment (ω₂ = 1.00). [6]
  3. (c) Calculate the factored moment resistance Mr for ω₂ = 1.00, and confirm which equation applies. [5]
  4. (d) The actual moment diagram is not uniform and gives ω₂ = 1.30 for the segment. Recalculate Mr, and comment briefly on how much of the plastic capacity is now available. [6]
(a)

The plastic moment is Mp = Zx Fy = 1 300 × 10³ mm³ × 350 MPa = 455.0 × 10⁶ N·mm = 455.0 kN·m. Multiplying by the resistance factor, φ Mp = 0.90 × 455.0 = 409.5 kN·m.
