This is the ceiling on the moment resistance of any laterally supported or partially supported segment of this section: no amount of bracing can make the beam resist more than the full plastic capacity reduced by φ. Parts c and d will show how far the unbraced length of 5.0 m pulls the resistance below this ceiling, and the ceiling is also used to cap the equation if the result exceeds it.

Answer: 409.5 kN·m

(b)

Work in N and mm with Lu = 5 000 mm. The St. Venant term is E Iy G J = 200 000 × 20.0 × 10⁶ × 77 000 × 380 × 10³ = 1.1704 × 10²³. The warping term uses π E / Lu = π × 200 000 / 5 000 = 125.66 N/mm², so (π E / Lu)² Iy Cw = 15 791 × 20.0 × 10⁶ × 480 × 10⁹ = 1.5159 × 10²³. The sum is 2.6863 × 10²³, and its square root is 5.183 × 10¹¹. With ω₂ = 1.00, Mu = (π / 5 000) × 5.183 × 10¹¹ = 6.2832 × 10⁻⁴ × 5.183 × 10¹¹ = 3.257 × 10⁸ N·mm = 325.7 kN·m. Both the torsion and the warping terms contribute almost equally here, so ignoring warping would understate Mu noticeably.

Answer: 325.7 kN·m

(c)

The test is whether Mu exceeds 0.67 Mp. Here 0.67 × 455.0 = 304.9 kN·m, and Mu = 325.7 kN·m is larger, so the inelastic equation applies: Mr = 1.15 φ Mp (1 − 0.28 Mp / Mu). The ratio Mp / Mu = 455.0 / 325.7 = 1.397, so the bracket is 1 − 0.28 × 1.397 = 0.6088. Then Mr = 1.15 × 409.5 × 0.6088 = 286.7 kN·m. This is below the cap φ Mp = 409.5 kN·m, so the cap does not control. The beam develops only 70 percent of its fully braced capacity because the 5.0 m unbraced length lets the compression flange buckle laterally before the section yields completely.

Answer: 286.7 kN·m

(d)

The factor ω₂ accounts for a moment gradient: where the moment varies along the segment, the compression flange is less heavily stressed over most of the length, so the critical moment rises in proportion. With ω₂ = 1.30, Mu = 1.30 × 325.7 = 423.4 kN·m. Then Mp / Mu = 455.0 / 423.4 = 1.0747 and the bracket is 1 − 0.28 × 1.0747 = 0.6991. Mr = 1.15 × 409.5 × 0.6991 = 329.2 kN·m, still under the 409.5 kN·m cap. The girder therefore reaches about 80 percent of φ Mp. A 15 percent gain in resistance results from a moment gradient alone, with no extra steel, which is why the shape of the moment diagram must always be examined.

Answer: 329.2 kN·m

Problem 3 [A2-013] Steel beam shear resistance and web bearing

A transit-station mezzanine in Ottawa is framed with simply supported rolled steel beams spanning 6.0 m between the centres of their end supports. The beam is 410 mm deep with flange thickness tf = 12.8 mm and web thickness w = 7.7 mm, and carries a factored uniformly distributed load of 100 kN/m including self-weight. Take Fy = 350 MPa and φ = 0.90 for shear. The clear web depth is h = d − 2 tf. When h/w ≤ 1014/√Fy (Fy in MPa) the web shear strength is Fs = 0.66 Fy, and the shear resistance is Vr = φ Aw Fs with Aw = h w. At each end the beam bears on a steel plate over a bearing length N. The web bearing (yielding) resistance at an end support is Br = φbr w (N + 4 tf) Fy with φbr = 0.80.

  1. (a) Check that the web is stocky enough for Fs = 0.66 Fy and calculate the shear resistance Vr in kN. [5]
  2. (b) Calculate the factored end shear Vf and the ratio Vf / Vr. [4]
  3. (c) Calculate the bearing resistance Br at an end support when the bearing length is N = 90 mm, in kN. [5]
  4. (d) Find the minimum bearing length N, in mm, for which Br equals the factored end reaction. [6]
(a)

The clear web depth is h = 410 − 2 × 12.8 = 384.4 mm, so h / w = 384.4 / 7.7 = 49.9. The limit is 1014 / √350 = 1014 / 18.71 = 54.2. Since 49.9 is below 54.2, the web yields in shear before it buckles and Fs = 0.66 × 350 = 231 MPa. The web area is Aw = h w = 384.4 × 7.7 = 2 960 mm². Then Vr = φ Aw Fs = 0.90 × 2 960 × 231 = 615 400 N = 615 kN. The flanges are ignored in carrying shear, which is the standard assumption, and the comparison with the limit confirms that no stiffeners or tension-field action are needed for this part.

Answer: 615 kN

(b)

For a simply supported beam under a uniformly distributed load, each reaction and the end shear equal half of the total load, Vf = w L / 2 = 100 × 6.0 / 2 = 300 kN. The utilisation ratio is Vf / Vr = 300 / 615.4 = 0.4875, or about 0.49. The beam therefore uses less than half its shear capacity. This is typical: on a 6 m span carrying 100 kN/m, bending would normally govern the design well before shear does, so shear is a check rather than the controlling limit state. The end shear of 300 kN is the demand that the bearing check of the next parts must also resist, since the end reaction equals the end shear.

Answer: Vf = 300 kN, ratio 0.49

(c)

The bearing resistance at an end support is Br = φbr w (N + 4 tf) Fy. With N = 90 mm and tf = 12.8 mm, the effective length is N + 4 tf = 90 + 51.2 = 141.2 mm. Then Br = 0.80 × 7.7 × 141.2 × 350 = 304 430 N = 304 kN. The end support uses N + 4 tf rather than N + 10 tf because only one side of the load point has web available to spread the force. Compare with the reaction of 300 kN: the resistance of 304 kN just exceeds it, so the 90 mm plate is barely adequate with a utilisation of about 0.99, which leaves almost no margin.

Answer: 304 kN

(d)

Set Br equal to the factored reaction of 300 kN and solve for N. Writing Br = φbr w (N + 4 tf) Fy = 300 000 N gives N + 4 tf = 300 000 / (0.80 × 7.7 × 350) = 300 000 / 2 156 = 139.1 mm. Subtract 4 tf = 51.2 mm to find N = 139.1 − 51.2 = 87.9 mm. A designer would round up to a practical plate, for example 100 mm, which gives a margin. The result agrees with part c, where N = 90 mm just exceeded the demand. If a smaller bearing length were physically required by the support detail, bearing stiffeners would be added to the web instead of lengthening the plate.

Answer: 87.9 mm

Problem 4 [A2-014] Steel beam deflection and serviceability

A simply supported steel floor beam in a university laboratory in Waterloo spans 9.0 m. Its second moment of area is Ix = 216 × 10⁶ mm⁴ and E = 200 000 MPa. The unfactored loads are a dead load of 6 kN/m uniformly distributed (including self-weight), a live load of 12 kN/m uniformly distributed, and a 20 kN live load from a fixed instrument acting at midspan. Serviceability requires that the deflection due to live load alone not exceed span/360. Deflection of a simply supported beam is 5 w L⁴ / (384 E I) under a uniform load and P L³ / (48 E I) for a central point load. Superposition may be used, and all loads in this problem are specified (unfactored) service loads.

  1. (a) Calculate the midspan deflection due to the full live load (distributed plus point load), in mm. [6]
  2. (b) Find the minimum second moment of area Ix, in mm⁴, needed to satisfy the span/360 limit. [5]
  3. (c) Calculate the dead-load midspan deflection of the original 216 × 10⁶ mm⁴ beam, in mm, which the fabricator could remove by cambering. [4]
  4. (d) The designer substitutes a beam with Ix = 270 × 10⁶ mm⁴. Find its live-load deflection and its value as a fraction of the span/360 limit. [5]
(a)

Convert units first: L = 9 000 mm, and 12 kN/m equals 12 N/mm. The distributed live load gives Δ1 = 5 × 12 × 9 000⁴ / (384 × 200 000 × 216 × 10⁶). The numerator is 60 × 6.561 × 10¹⁵ = 3.937 × 10¹⁷ and the denominator is 1.659 × 10¹⁶, so Δ1 = 23.73 mm. The 20 kN point load gives Δ2 = 20 000 × 9 000³ / (48 × 200 000 × 216 × 10⁶) = 1.458 × 10¹⁶ / 2.074 × 10¹⁵ = 7.03 mm. Both loads sag the beam downward at midspan, so by superposition the live deflection is 23.73 + 7.03 = 30.76 mm, about 30.8 mm. This is the quantity compared with the limit.

Answer: 30.8 mm

(b)

The allowable live deflection is L / 360 = 9 000 / 360 = 25.0 mm. The computed value of 30.8 mm exceeds it by about 23 percent, so the existing beam fails serviceability even though it may pass strength. Deflection is inversely proportional to I for fixed loads and span, so the required Ix equals the present Ix times the ratio of computed to allowed deflection: Ix,req = 216 × 10⁶ × 30.76 / 25.0 = 265.8 × 10⁶ mm⁴, or 2.66 × 10⁸ mm⁴. Any replacement section must have at least this second moment of area, regardless of its strength, which is why floor beams are frequently governed by stiffness.

Answer: 2.66 × 10⁸ mm⁴

(c)

Only the dead load acts, 6 kN/m or 6 N/mm. The formula for a uniform load gives Δ = 5 w L⁴ / (384 E I) = 5 × 6 × 9 000⁴ / (384 × 200 000 × 216 × 10⁶) = 1.9683 × 10¹⁷ / 1.659 × 10¹⁶ = 11.87 mm. This is exactly half the deflection from the 12 kN/m live load because the dead load is half as large and the beam is linear. A fabricator can camber the beam upward by about this amount so the beam is level when the permanent loads are on it. Camber does not alter the live-load deflection, which is why part b is still needed in addition.

Answer: 11.9 mm

(d)

The live-load deflection scales inversely with I, so the new deflection is 30.76 × 216 / 270 = 24.61 mm. Compared with the allowable 25.0 mm, the ratio is 24.61 / 25.0 = 0.984, so the beam passes but with only a 1.6 percent margin. The substitution with Ix = 270 × 10⁶ mm⁴ exceeds the minimum found in part b of 265.8 × 10⁶ mm⁴, which confirms the check. Because the margin is so thin, a designer would normally choose a section with a larger Ix or confirm that the 20 kN instrument load has been given with a realistic dynamic allowance, since small load increases would cause failure.

Answer: 24.6 mm, 0.98 of the limit

Problem 5 [A2-015] Steel column compressive resistance and effective length

A 6.0 m high interior column in a Thunder Bay maintenance garage is a rolled wide-flange shape with gross area A = 7 230 mm², radius of gyration rx = 111 mm about the strong axis and ry = 48.0 mm about the weak axis. It is pinned at both ends against rotation about both axes (effective length factor K = 1.0), and wall girts brace the weak axis at mid-height, so the weak-axis unbraced length is 3.0 m. Take Fy = 350 MPa, E = 200 000 MPa and φ = 0.90. The factored compressive resistance of a Class 1, 2 or 3 section is Cr = φ A Fy (1 + λ2n)−1/n with n = 1.34, where λ = (KL/r) √(Fy / (π² E)), and the governing axis is the one with the larger KL/r.

  1. (a) Calculate KL/r about each axis and state which axis governs; give the governing value. [4]
  2. (b) Calculate the non-dimensional slenderness ratio λ for the governing axis. [4]
  3. (c) Calculate the factored compressive resistance Cr of the column, in kN. [7]
  4. (d) The girts remain at mid-height, and the column base is now also fixed about the weak axis, so the weak-axis effective length factor becomes K = 0.80 on the 3.0 m length. Recalculate the column resistance and explain which axis now governs. [5]
(a)

For the strong axis, K L / rx = 1.0 × 6 000 / 111 = 54.05. For the weak axis, the unbraced length is only 3 000 mm because of the girts, so K L / ry = 1.0 × 3 000 / 48.0 = 62.5. The larger value controls the buckling strength, which is the weak axis at 62.5. This shows that bracing at mid-height does not remove weak-axis governing: the radius of gyration is much smaller about the weak axis (48 mm against 111 mm), so even half the length leaves it more slender. The same logic is why designers brace wide-flange columns about the weak axis whenever they can.

Answer: Strong 54.1, weak 62.5; weak governs, 62.5

(b)

Use λ = (KL/r) √(Fy / (π² E)). The square root is √(350 / (9.8696 × 200 000)) = √(1.7731 × 10⁻⁴) = 0.013316. Multiplying by the governing slenderness of 62.5 gives λ = 62.5 × 0.013316 = 0.832. A value below about 0.2 would mean the column crushes without buckling, and a value above 2.0 would mean elastic Euler buckling controls, so 0.83 lies in the intermediate range where residual stresses and initial imperfections reduce the capacity below both limits. This is the case the empirical curve with n = 1.34 was calibrated to represent.

Answer: 0.832

(c)

Evaluate the curve with λ = 0.8322 and n = 1.34. First λ2n = 0.83222.68 = e2.68 × ln 0.8322 = e2.68 × (−0.18348) = e−0.4917 = 0.6118. Then 1 + 0.6118 = 1.6118 and (1.6118)−1/1.34 = e−0.7463 × 0.47737 = e−0.3563 = 0.7003. The squash load is φ A Fy = 0.90 × 7 230 × 350 = 2 277.5 kN. Thus Cr = 2 277.5 × 0.7003 = 1 595 kN. The factor 0.70 shows the buckling reduction, about 30 percent of the full yield capacity, and the column should be used only when the factored axial load is below 1 595 kN.

Answer: 1 595 kN

(d)

With K = 0.80 on the 3.0 m weak-axis length, KL/ry = 0.80 × 3 000 / 48.0 = 50.0, which is now smaller than the strong-axis value of 54.05. The strong axis therefore governs, with λ = 54.05 × 0.013316 = 0.7198. Then λ2.68 = e2.68 × ln 0.7198 = e−0.8815 = 0.4141, 1.4141−0.7463 = e−0.7463 × 0.34612 = e−0.2583 = 0.7724, and Cr = 2 277.5 × 0.7724 = 1 758 kN. The resistance rises by about 10 percent. Further improvement to the weak axis would give nothing more, because the strong axis now limits the column, so any extra bracing would be wasted.

Answer: 1 758 kN, strong axis governs

A2 Practice Paper 4

Problem 1 [A2-016] Steel beam-columns under combined axial load and bending

A braced-frame column in a school gymnasium in Guelph is a wide-flange member with strong-axis second moment of area Ix = 222 × 10⁶ mm⁴ and an effective length of 4.2 m about the strong axis. A roof purlin load applied between the ends makes the member carry transverse load, so the equivalent-moment factor is ω₁ = 1.00. Take E = 200 000 MPa. The member's factored axial compressive resistance (with its governing slenderness already included) is Cr = 2 150 kN and its factored moment resistance is Mrx = 240 kN·m. The factored forces are Cf = 900 kN and Mfx = 110 kN·m. The member is checked with Cf / Cr + 0.85 U₁ₓ Mfx / Mrx ≤ 1.0, where U₁ₓ = ω₁ / (1 − Cf / Ce) and U₁ₓ is not taken below 1.0. Ce = π² E Ix / (K L)².

  1. (a) Calculate the Euler buckling load Ce about the strong axis, in kN. [4]
  2. (b) Calculate the amplification factor U₁ₓ. [4]
  3. (c) Evaluate the interaction expression and state whether the member is adequate. [6]
  4. (d) Holding Cf = 900 kN, find the largest factored moment Mfx, in kN·m, that the member can carry before the expression reaches 1.0. [6]
(a)

The Euler load is Ce = π² E Ix / (K L)². With E = 200 000 MPa, Ix = 222 × 10⁶ mm⁴ and K L = 4 200 mm, the numerator is 9.8696 × 200 000 × 222 × 10⁶ = 4.3822 × 10¹⁴ N·mm². The denominator is 4 200² = 1.764 × 10⁷ mm². Therefore Ce = 2.484 × 10⁷ N = 24 842 kN. This is the elastic buckling load of a perfect pin-ended strut and it is far larger than the applied 900 kN, which tells you the second-order effect will be modest. Ce uses the elastic modulus only, without any yield strength, so it is independent of the steel grade.

Answer: 24 842 kN

(b)

The amplification factor accounts for the extra bending moment produced when the axial force acts on the deflected shape (the P-delta effect). It is U₁ₓ = ω₁ / (1 − Cf / Ce) = 1.00 / (1 − 900 / 24 842). The ratio Cf / Ce = 0.03623, so the denominator is 0.96377 and U₁ₓ = 1.0376. Since this exceeds the lower limit of 1.0, it is used as calculated. The result shows that the axial load amplifies the first-order moment by only 3.8 percent, because the column is stocky relative to its Euler load. For a slender member, where Cf approaches Ce, the factor grows rapidly and becomes the dominant influence.

Answer: 1.038

(c)

The axial term is Cf / Cr = 900 / 2 150 = 0.4186. The bending term is 0.85 U₁ₓ Mfx / Mrx = 0.85 × 1.0376 × 110 / 240 = 0.85 × 1.0376 × 0.4583 = 0.4042. Adding the two gives 0.4186 + 0.4042 = 0.8228. Since 0.823 is below 1.0, the member is adequate, with about 18 percent of its interaction capacity unused. The 0.85 factor in the bending term reflects the fact that the strengths in axial compression and bending cannot both be fully used at once, and the equation is a linear interaction that is conservative for stocky members. The member should also be checked at the cross-section level, but that is not requested here.

Answer: 0.823, adequate

(d)

Set the interaction expression equal to 1.0 with Cf fixed. The axial term remains 0.4186, so the bending term can be at most 1 − 0.4186 = 0.5814. Writing 0.85 U₁ₓ Mfx / Mrx = 0.5814 gives Mfx = 0.5814 × Mrx / (0.85 × U₁ₓ) = 0.5814 × 240 / (0.85 × 1.0376) = 139.5 / 0.8820 = 158.2 kN·m. This is about 44 percent above the present 110 kN·m, so there is considerable reserve. U₁ₓ is held constant since it depends only on Cf, which is fixed. If Cf were increased the allowable moment would fall twice: once because the axial term rises, and again because U₁ₓ grows.

Answer: 158 kN·m

Problem 2 [A2-017] Bolted steel connections in bearing

A tension splice in the bottom chord of a roof truss at a Kingston arena joins two 16 mm thick main plates, each of ultimate strength Fu = 450 MPa, using two 10 mm thick cover plates, one on each face, with the bolts in double shear. The bolts are 20 mm diameter high-strength bolts (Ab = 314.2 mm²) with Fu = 830 MPa, installed snug-tight with the threads excluded from the shear planes. Assume that edge distance and spacing requirements are satisfied and that block shear and net section fracture have been checked elsewhere. Use φb = 0.80 for bolt shear and φbr = 0.80 for bearing. The shear resistance of one bolt is Vr = 0.60 φb n m Ab Fu, where m is the number of shear planes, and the bearing resistance is Br = 3 φbr n t d Fu, taken on the main plate. Here n = 1 for a single bolt.

  1. (a) Calculate the factored shear resistance of one bolt in double shear, in kN. [5]
  2. (b) Calculate the factored bearing resistance of one bolt on the 16 mm main plate, in kN, and state whether bolt shear or bearing governs a single bolt. [4]
  3. (c) A splice has six bolts on each side of the joint line. Calculate the factored resistance of the connection, in kN. [5]
  4. (d) The truss chord must carry a factored tension of 1 600 kN. Find the minimum number of bolts required on each side of the joint. [6]
(a)

The shear resistance for one bolt is Vr = 0.60 φb n m Ab Fu. With φb = 0.80, n = 1, m = 2 shear planes, Ab = 314.2 mm² and Fu = 830 MPa, Vr = 0.60 × 0.80 × 1 × 2 × 314.2 × 830. Multiply: 0.60 × 0.80 = 0.48, then 0.48 × 2 = 0.96, and 314.2 × 830 = 260 786 N, so Vr = 0.96 × 260 786 = 250 355 N, about 250.3 kN. The two shear planes arise because the main plate sits between the cover plates, so the bolt shank is cut in two places when the plates slide apart. Using single shear would halve this resistance, which is why symmetrical splices with cover plates are preferred.

Answer: 250.3 kN

(b)

Bearing is checked on the thinner of the load-bearing material. The main plate is 16 mm thick, while the two cover plates together provide 2 × 10 = 20 mm, so the 16 mm main plate governs. Br = 3 φbr n t d Fu = 3 × 0.80 × 1 × 16 × 20 × 450 = 3 × 0.80 × 144 000 = 345 600 N = 345.6 kN. Comparing the two, bolt shear (250.3 kN) is lower than bearing (345.6 kN), so shear governs for a single bolt. The factor 3 in the bearing equation reflects the high bearing stress allowed when the hole is far from an edge, which is why the edge-distance assumption in the statement matters.

Answer: 345.6 kN; shear governs

(c)

Each bolt can resist the lesser of its shear and bearing values, which is 250.3 kN from part b. With six bolts sharing the load equally, the connection resistance is 6 × 250.3 = 1 501.9 kN. Equal sharing is a reasonable assumption for a short splice with a small number of bolts in line, because yielding of the plate around the holes redistributes force. For very long connections with many bolts in line, the end bolts would take more load, and the code reduces the resistance. That reduction is not required for six bolts at normal spacing. The result, about 1 502 kN, is the capacity to compare with the chord tension.

Answer: 1 502 kN

(d)

The required number of bolts is the factored tension divided by the resistance of one bolt: 1 600 / 250.3 = 6.39. Bolts must be provided in whole numbers, so the number is rounded up to 7. Check: seven bolts give 7 × 250.3 = 1 752 kN, which exceeds 1 600 kN, while six give 1 502 kN, which is less than 1 600 kN, so six is insufficient. Using seven bolts, the utilisation is 1 600 / 1 752 = 0.91. The designer could alternatively select a larger bolt diameter, for example 22 mm, to keep six bolts, but that would change the bearing and spacing checks.

Answer: 7 bolts

Problem 3 [A2-018] Eccentrically loaded bolt groups and slip-critical connections

A steel bracket supporting a conveyor at a Windsor plant is bolted to a column flange with six 20 mm diameter high-strength bolts in two vertical lines of three. The lines are 100 mm apart and the bolts in each line are at a pitch of 90 mm, so the bolts lie at x = ±50 mm and y = −90, 0 and +90 mm from the centroid of the group. A vertical load of 120 kN acts downward at a horizontal distance of 200 mm from the centroid, on the right side. Use the elastic method: each bolt takes an equal share P/6 of the direct load, plus a torsional force proportional to its distance from the centroid. Ab = 314.2 mm² and Fu = 830 MPa. The slip resistance of one bolt in single shear is Vs = 0.53 μ ks m Ab Fu with slip coefficient μ = 0.30, ks = 1.0 and m = 1.

  1. (a) Calculate the polar moment of the bolt group, Σ(x² + y²), in mm². [4]
  2. (b) Calculate the resultant force on the most heavily loaded bolt, in kN. [7]
  3. (c) Calculate the slip resistance of one bolt, in kN. [4]
  4. (d) The connection is slip-critical, so no bolt may slip. Find the largest load P, in kN, that the bracket may carry at the same eccentricity. [5]
(a)

Sum the squares of the coordinates over all six bolts. The x-contribution is six bolts each at x = ±50 mm, so Σx² = 6 × 50² = 15 000 mm². For y, the middle row contributes zero, while the top and bottom rows each hold two bolts at y = ±90 mm, so Σy² = 4 × 90² = 32 400 mm². The polar moment is therefore J = 15 000 + 32 400 = 47 400 mm². This is the property that resists the twisting moment, in the same way that a polar moment of area resists torque in a circular shaft, except that each bolt is treated as a unit area. It is used to share the moment among the bolts in proportion to their distance from the centroid.

Answer: 47 400 mm²

(b)

The moment about the centroid is Mf = P e = 120 kN × 200 mm = 24 000 kN·mm. The direct vertical share is P / 6 = 20 kN per bolt. The critical bolt is the lower right or upper right corner bolt, farthest from the centroid with x = 50, y = 90, on the side nearer the load. Torsion components are Fx = Mf y / J = 24 000 × 90 / 47 400 = 45.57 kN horizontal, and Fy = Mf x / J = 24 000 × 50 / 47 400 = 25.32 kN vertical, in the same direction as the direct load on that side. The vertical total is 20 + 25.32 = 45.32 kN, so the resultant is √(45.57² + 45.32²) = √(2 076.6 + 2 054.0) = 64.27 kN.

Answer: 64.3 kN

(c)

The slip resistance of one bolt is Vs = 0.53 μ ks m Ab Fu. With μ = 0.30, ks = 1.0, m = 1, Ab = 314.2 mm² and Fu = 830 MPa, Vs = 0.53 × 0.30 × 1.0 × 1 × 314.2 × 830. The product 314.2 × 830 = 260 786 N, and 0.53 × 0.30 = 0.159, so Vs = 0.159 × 260 786 = 41 465 N, about 41.5 kN. Slip resistance relies on friction between the connected surfaces, generated by the high clamping force from pretensioning the bolts, so it is much smaller than the shear resistance of the bolt shank itself. It is the governing limit when slip would be unacceptable, such as with reversing or vibrating loads from machinery.

Answer: 41.5 kN

(d)

The present resultant on the critical bolt is 64.27 kN under P = 120 kN, but the slip resistance is only 41.46 kN, so the connection would slip, with a ratio of 64.27 / 41.46 = 1.55. Because the elastic bolt forces are directly proportional to P at a fixed eccentricity, the allowable load scales linearly: Pmax = 120 × 41.46 / 64.27 = 77.4 kN. At this load the critical bolt just reaches its slip resistance. To carry the full 120 kN, the designer could add bolts, increase the group depth to lower the torsional force, or move the bracket so that the eccentricity is smaller. The lever arm effects make eccentricity the most efficient parameter to reduce.

Answer: 77.4 kN

Problem 4 [A2-019] Fillet weld resistance and weld length

A 10 mm thick, 120 mm wide flat-bar tie (Fy = 350 MPa) in a Barrie farm-implement frame is lapped on to a gusset plate and joined by fillet welds made with E49 electrodes, Xu = 490 MPa. The largest fillet size permitted along the edge of a 10 mm plate is 8 mm, and this size is to be used throughout. Use the resistance factor φw = 0.67. The factored resistance of a fillet weld is Vr = 0.67 φw Aw Xu (1.00 + 0.50 sin1.5 θ), where Aw = 0.707 D L is the effective throat area for a weld of size D and length L, and θ is the angle between the line of the applied force and the longitudinal axis of the weld. The tie must carry a factored tensile force of 360 kN, and full penetration of the weld metal into the base metal is assumed. For the combined-weld case, the resistances of longitudinal and transverse welds may be added directly.

  1. (a) Calculate the factored resistance of the 8 mm fillet weld per millimetre of length when the force is parallel to the weld axis (θ = 0°), in kN/mm. [4]
  2. (b) Calculate the resistance per millimetre when the force is perpendicular to the weld axis (θ = 90°), in kN/mm. [4]
  3. (c) If only two longitudinal fillet welds (one along each edge of the bar) are used, find the required length of each, in mm. [6]
  4. (d) A transverse weld across the full 120 mm width at the end of the bar is added to the two longitudinal welds. Find the required length of each longitudinal weld, in mm. [6]
(a)

For a force parallel to the weld axis, θ = 0° and sin θ = 0, so the directional factor is 1.00. Per millimetre of length, the throat area is Aw = 0.707 D = 0.707 × 8 = 5.656 mm²/mm. Then Vr = 0.67 φw Aw Xu = 0.67 × 0.67 × 5.656 × 490. Multiply: 0.67 × 0.67 = 0.4489, then 0.4489 × 5.656 = 2.539, and 2.539 × 490 = 1 244 N/mm = 1.244 kN/mm. The first 0.67 is the factor applied to the ultimate strength of the weld metal, and the second is the resistance factor φw. This result is the weakest direction for a fillet weld, so it is the conservative value to use when direction is unknown.

Answer: 1.244 kN/mm

(b)

For θ = 90°, sin θ = 1, so the factor becomes 1.00 + 0.50 × 11.5 = 1.50. The transverse resistance is therefore 1.50 × 1.244 = 1.866 kN/mm. A fillet weld loaded perpendicular to its length is stronger than one loaded along its length, because the failure plane carries the load in a direction that engages more of the throat in bearing and less in pure shear, and the weld metal is also more ductile in the longitudinal direction. The 50 percent gain is applied in the code for any angle between 0° and 90°, but it is only available when the weld is actually inclined to the load.

Answer: 1.866 kN/mm

(c)

With two longitudinal welds, both are loaded parallel to the force, so each millimetre resists 1.244 kN. The total resistance is 2 L × 1.244 kN/mm, where L is the length of each weld. Set this equal to the factored force: 2 L × 1.244 = 360, so L = 360 / (2 × 1.244) = 360 / 2.488 = 144.7 mm. Since 144.7 mm is longer than the 120 mm width of the bar, the lap would need to extend past the bar width, which is acceptable because the requirement is that the length of each side weld be at least the perpendicular distance between the welds. In practice the designer rounds the length up to, for example, 160 mm.

Answer: 144.7 mm

(d)

Add the transverse weld first. Its length equals the bar width of 120 mm and each millimetre resists 1.866 kN, so it carries 120 × 1.866 = 223.9 kN. The remaining force is 360 − 223.9 = 136.1 kN, which the two longitudinal welds must resist. They resist 2 L × 1.244 = 136.1, so L = 136.1 / 2.488 = 54.7 mm. The combination shortens each longitudinal weld from 144.7 mm to 54.7 mm. Adding resistances of welds in different directions assumes that they deform enough to share load, which is acceptable for ductile welds. The statement allows the resistances to be added directly, so no reduction factor is applied to the combined welds. The bar itself can carry 0.90 × 1 200 × 350 = 378 kN in gross yielding, which is above the 360 kN design force, so the welds and not the bar govern.

Answer: 54.7 mm

Problem 5 [A2-020] Eccentric weld groups and simple beam connections

A bracket plate carrying a platform at a Peterborough water-treatment plant is welded to a column flange by two parallel vertical fillet welds. Each weld is 250 mm long, and the welds are 100 mm apart. A vertical factored load of 90 kN acts on the bracket at a horizontal distance of 175 mm from the centroid of the weld group. Use the elastic method with the welds treated as lines of unit throat. Force per millimetre is found from the direct shear plus the torsional force proportional to distance from the centroid. Use the weld resistance per millimetre 0.67 φw (0.707 D) Xu with φw = 0.67 and Xu = 490 MPa, ignoring the directional strength increase, and take D = 8 mm for parts a to c.

  1. (a) Calculate the polar moment of the weld group treated as two lines, J = Σ(L³/12 + L d²), in mm³. [4]
  2. (b) Calculate the resultant force per millimetre of weld at the most heavily loaded end of the weld group, in N/mm. [7]
  3. (c) Calculate the resistance per millimetre of the 8 mm weld, and the ratio of the demand to the resistance. [4]
  4. (d) Find the smallest theoretical fillet size D, in mm, that carries the load. [5]
(a)

Each weld is a line of length L = 250 mm whose centre is d = 50 mm from the centroid of the group, which lies midway between the two welds. For a vertical line the polar moment about the centroid is L³/12 + L d², where L³/12 is the line's own moment about its centre (for a vertical line of unit thickness, the horizontal offset appears in the second term). L³/12 = 250³ / 12 = 15 625 000 / 12 = 1 302 083 mm³ and L d² = 250 × 2 500 = 625 000 mm³, so one weld gives 1 927 083 mm³. For two welds, J = 2 × 1 927 083 = 3 854 167 mm³. The units are mm³ because each weld has unit throat, so J is a polar moment of line length.

Answer: 3.854 × 10⁶ mm³

(b)

The moment about the centroid is Mf = 90 000 N × 175 mm = 15.75 × 10⁶ N·mm. The direct shear per millimetre is P / (2L) = 90 000 / 500 = 180 N/mm downward. The critical point is the top or bottom end of the weld on the load side, at x = 50 mm and y = 125 mm. The torsional components are horizontal fx = Mf y / J = 15.75 × 10⁶ × 125 / 3.854 × 10⁶ = 510.8 N/mm, and vertical fy = Mf x / J = 15.75 × 10⁶ × 50 / 3.854 × 10⁶ = 204.3 N/mm. The vertical torsional component adds to direct shear on this side, giving 384.3 N/mm. The resultant is √(510.8² + 384.3²) = √(260 917 + 147 690) = 639 N/mm.

Answer: 639 N/mm

(c)

The resistance per millimetre of an 8 mm weld is 0.67 φw (0.707 D) Xu = 0.67 × 0.67 × 0.707 × 8 × 490. Compute 0.707 × 8 = 5.656 mm, then 0.67 × 0.67 = 0.4489, and 0.4489 × 5.656 × 490 = 1 244 N/mm. The demand from part b is 639.2 N/mm, so the ratio is 639.2 / 1 244 = 0.514. The weld therefore uses about half of its capacity. Ignoring the directional strength gain is conservative, as in a real design the vertical and inclined segments could be a little stronger. The ratio below 1.0 confirms that the 8 mm weld is adequate for the load, and part d asks how much smaller it could be.

Answer: 1 244 N/mm, ratio 0.51

(d)

Resistance is proportional to D, so the smallest size follows from the demand: D = 639.2 / (0.67 × 0.67 × 0.707 × 490) = 639.2 / 155.5 = 4.11 mm. In practice, the designer would not use this value. A minimum fillet size depends on the thickness of the thicker plate joined, and most codes require at least 5 or 6 mm for plates of this kind, so the practical choice would be 5 mm or 6 mm. The minimum weld size also reflects heat input, because a tiny weld on a thick plate cools too quickly and cracks. Here, the theoretical 4.11 mm is therefore a lower bound, and the governing requirement is probably the code minimum rather than the strength.

Answer: 4.11 mm

A2 Practice Paper 5

Problem 1 [A2-021] Singly reinforced concrete beam flexure

A simply supported rectangular reinforced concrete floor beam in a parking garage near Kingston, Ontario, spans 7.0 m. The cross-section has width b = 300 mm, effective depth d = 520 mm and overall depth h = 600 mm. The tension steel is four 25M bars, total area As = 2000 mm², placed in one layer. Use f'c = 30 MPa, fy = 400 MPa, material resistance factors φc = 0.65 and φs = 0.85, maximum concrete strain εcu = 0.0035, Es = 200 000 MPa, stress-block factors α1 = 0.85 − 0.0015 f'c and β1 = 0.97 − 0.0025 f'c. The beam is checked as singly reinforced with a rectangular stress block. Compression steel is ignored and the member carries no axial load.

  1. (a) Find the depth a of the equivalent rectangular stress block. [4]
  2. (b) Find the strain in the tension steel at ultimate and state whether the steel has yielded (yield strain = fy/Es). [4]
  3. (c) Find the factored moment resistance Mr. [6]
  4. (d) The beam also carries its own weight in the factored load. Find the maximum total factored uniform load wf, in kN/m, that the beam can resist over the 7.0 m span. [3]
  5. (e) Find the minimum tension steel area As,min = 0.2 √f'c b h / fy and state whether the provided steel satisfies it. [3]
(a)

Equilibrium of the section requires the tension force to equal the compression force, φs As fy = α1 φc f'c b a. First α1 = 0.85 − 0.0015 × 30 = 0.805. Then a = φs As fy / (α1 φc f'c b) = 0.85 × 2000 × 400 / (0.805 × 0.65 × 30 × 300) = 680 000 / 4709.3 = 144.4 mm. The resistance factors are applied to the two forces separately, which is why φs appears in the numerator and φc in the denominator. The block depth is the starting point for both the strain check and the lever arm, so an error here carries into every later part.

Answer: a = 144 mm

(b)

The neutral axis depth is c = a / β1, with β1 = 0.97 − 0.0025 × 30 = 0.895, so c = 144.4 / 0.895 = 161.3 mm. By similar triangles on the linear strain profile, εs = εcu (d − c) / c = 0.0035 × (520 − 161.3) / 161.3 = 0.0035 × 2.224 = 0.00778. The yield strain is fy / Es = 400 / 200 000 = 0.0020. Because 0.00778 is almost four times the yield strain, the steel has yielded before the concrete crushes. This confirms the assumption used in part (a), where the steel stress was taken as fy, and shows the failure would be ductile with plenty of warning.

Answer: εs = 0.00778 (yielded)

(c)

The resisting couple is the steel force times the lever arm between the steel and the centroid of the stress block. Steel force T = φs As fy = 0.85 × 2000 × 400 = 680 000 N = 680 kN. The lever arm is d − a/2 = 520 − 144.4/2 = 447.8 mm. Mr = 680 × 0.4478 = 304.5 kN·m. Moments are taken about the steel centroid or the block centroid, which gives the same result for a pure couple with no axial load. The factored resistance already includes φc and φs, so it is compared directly with the factored moment from the load combination.

Answer: Mr = 304.5 kN·m

(d)

For a simply supported beam under uniform load, the maximum moment at midspan is Mf = wf L² / 8. Setting Mf equal to the resistance Mr gives wf = 8 Mr / L² = 8 × 304.5 / 7.0² = 2436 / 49 = 49.7 kN/m. This total already has to cover the factored self-weight of the beam, which is about 1.25 × 0.30 × 0.60 × 24 = 5.4 kN/m, so the remaining factored capacity for the floor load is near 44 kN/m. Shear and deflection would be checked separately and could govern before this bending limit is reached.

Answer: wf = 49.7 kN/m

(e)

The minimum steel prevents a brittle failure where the beam cracks and the steel snaps before any warning. As,min = 0.2 √f'c b h / fy = 0.2 × √30 × 300 × 600 / 400. Here √30 = 5.477, so As,min = 0.2 × 5.477 × 300 × 600 / 400 = 197 178 / 400 = 493 mm². The provided area of 2000 mm² is about four times this minimum, so the requirement is satisfied easily. The steel ratio is 2000 / (300 × 520) = 1.28 percent, a normal value for a beam of this type, well above the minimum and well below the balanced ratio.

Answer: As,min = 493 mm², satisfied

Problem 2 [A2-022] Doubly reinforced and T-section concrete beams

A cast-in-place floor in a hospital addition in Ottawa has T-beams. Each T-beam has an effective flange width bf = 900 mm, flange thickness hf = 90 mm, web width bw = 320 mm and effective depth d = 560 mm to the tension steel. The tension steel is four 35M bars, As = 4000 mm² in total, placed in one layer. Use f'c = 25 MPa, fy = 400 MPa, φc = 0.65, φs = 0.85, εcu = 0.0035, Es = 200 000 MPa, α1 = 0.85 − 0.0015 f'c and β1 = 0.97 − 0.0025 f'c. The beam is in positive bending so the flange is in compression. Treat the section as a T-beam whenever the rectangular block would extend below the underside of the flange.

  1. (a) Compute the stress block depth a assuming the section behaves as a rectangular beam of width bf, and state whether the section must be treated as a T-beam. [4]
  2. (b) Find the steel area Asf needed to balance the compression in the overhanging parts of the flange. [5]
  3. (c) Find the stress block depth aw acting on the web using the remaining steel Asw = As − Asf. [4]
  4. (d) Find the strain in the tension steel at ultimate load. [3]
  5. (e) Find the factored moment resistance Mr of the T-beam. [4]
(a)

Assume first that the whole flange width carries compression in a rectangular block. With α1 = 0.85 − 0.0015 × 25 = 0.8125, a = φs As fy / (α1 φc f'c bf) = 0.85 × 4000 × 400 / (0.8125 × 0.65 × 25 × 900) = 1 360 000 / 11 883 = 114.5 mm. This block is deeper than the flange thickness of 90 mm, so part of the compressed concrete would lie in the web, where the width is only 320 mm. The assumption of full width is therefore wrong and the section must be analysed as a true T-beam, with the flange overhangs and the web treated separately.

Answer: a = 114.5 mm > 90 mm, T-beam

(b)

Split the compression into two parts: the two overhanging flange wings, and the web rectangle of width bw. The wings have an area (bf − bw) hf = (900 − 320) × 90 = 52 200 mm² carrying stress α1 φc f'c. Their force is 0.8125 × 0.65 × 25 × 52 200 = 689 250 N. The steel area that balances this force is Asf = 689 250 / (φs fy) = 689 250 / (0.85 × 400) = 689 250 / 340 = 2027 mm². This is just over half of the 4000 mm² provided, so the web has to be balanced by the remaining steel, found in the next part.

Answer: Asf = 2027 mm²

(c)

The steel left to work with the web is Asw = As − Asf = 4000 − 2027 = 1973 mm². The web is a rectangle of width bw = 320 mm, so aw = φs Asw fy / (α1 φc f'c bw) = 0.85 × 1973 × 400 / (0.8125 × 0.65 × 25 × 320) = 670 820 / 4225 = 158.8 mm. The depth a is measured from the top of the flange, so it covers the 90 mm flange plus about 69 mm of web. It is the depth of the block in the web part of the model, where the wings are already accounted for and do not add to it.

Answer: aw = 158.8 mm

(d)

The neutral axis depth is c = aw / β1, where β1 = 0.97 − 0.0025 × 25 = 0.9075, so c = 158.8 / 0.9075 = 175.0 mm. From similar triangles, εs = εcu (d − c) / c = 0.0035 × (560 − 175.0) / 175.0 = 0.0035 × 2.2 = 0.00770. The yield strain is 400 / 200 000 = 0.002, so the steel has yielded with a large margin, which confirms the assumption fs = fy used in the earlier parts. The ratio c/d = 0.31 is also well below the balanced value, so this is a ductile, tension-controlled T-beam.

Answer: εs = 0.0077

(e)

The resistance has two couples. Flange wings: Cf = 689 250 N acting at a lever arm of d − hf/2 = 560 − 45 = 515 mm gives 355.0 kN·m. Web: the force is φs Asw fy = 0.85 × 1973 × 400 = 670 820 N at a lever arm d − aw/2 = 560 − 79.4 = 480.6 mm giving 322.4 kN·m. Mr = 355.0 + 322.4 = 677.3 kN·m. Check on equilibrium: the flange force 689.25 kN plus the web force 670.82 kN is 1360.07 kN, which equals the full steel force 0.85 × 4000 × 400 = 1360 kN.

Answer: Mr = 677 kN·m

Problem 3 [A2-023] Concrete beam shear and stirrup design

A simply supported transfer beam in a mid-rise residential building in Mississauga has web width bw = 350 mm and effective shear depth dv = 540 mm. At the critical section a distance dv from the support, the factored shear is Vf = 420 kN. Use the simplified shear method: the concrete contribution is Vc = φc λ β √f'c bw dv with φc = 0.65, λ = 1.0, β = 0.18 and f'c = 30 MPa. The steel contribution is Vs = φs Av fy dv cot θ / s with φs = 0.85, fy = 400 MPa and θ = 42°. Closed two-leg 10M stirrups are used, Av = 200 mm². The maximum stirrup spacing is the smaller of 0.7 dv and 600 mm when Vf ≤ 0.125 φc f'c bw dv, and half of that otherwise. The minimum stirrup area is Av,min = 0.06 √f'c bw s / fy.

  1. (a) Find the concrete shear resistance Vc. [4]
  2. (b) Find the shear force Vs that the stirrups must carry. [3]
  3. (c) Find the largest stirrup spacing s that provides this steel contribution. [6]
  4. (d) Find the maximum permitted spacing for this beam from the code limit stated above. [3]
  5. (e) A contractor proposes 150 mm spacing instead. Find Av,min at that spacing and state whether the 10M stirrups meet it and whether 150 mm is acceptable for strength. [4]
(a)

Vc = φc λ β √f'c bw dv. The square root of f'c is √30 = 5.477 (MPa units). Then Vc = 0.65 × 1.0 × 0.18 × 5.477 × 350 × 540 = 0.65 × 0.18 × 5.477 × 189 000 N. Evaluating, 0.65 × 0.18 = 0.117; 0.117 × 5.477 = 0.6408; 0.6408 × 189 000 = 121 118 N, which is 121.1 kN. This is the shear carried by the concrete through aggregate interlock, the compression zone and dowel action, and it is only about 29 percent of the factored shear, so stirrups are clearly required.

Answer: Vc = 121.1 kN

(b)

The factored shear resistance must at least equal the factored shear, Vr = Vc + Vs ≥ Vf. So the stirrups must supply Vs = Vf − Vc = 420 − 121.1 = 298.9 kN. Because Vc is already reduced by φc and the steel term includes φs, both are directly comparable with the factored force with no further factor. The result is about 71 percent of the demand, a heavy stirrup requirement for this beam. A check on the upper limit of shear (crushing of the web) would also be done, and 420 kN is modest compared with the web crushing capacity of a 350 × 540 mm web at 30 MPa.

Answer: Vs = 298.9 kN

(c)

Rearrange Vs = φs Av fy dv cot θ / s for the spacing: s = φs Av fy dv cot θ / Vs. With θ = 42°, cot 42° = 1.1106. Then s = 0.85 × 200 × 400 × 540 × 1.1106 / 298 880 N. The numerator is 0.85 × 200 = 170; 170 × 400 = 68 000; 68 000 × 540 = 36 720 000; 36 720 000 × 1.1106 = 40 781 000. Dividing by 298 880 gives s = 136.4 mm. Stirrup spacing must not exceed this value. In practice the spacing is rounded down to a convenient dimension such as 130 mm, which gives a slight excess capacity.

Answer: s = 136 mm

(d)

First decide which limit applies by comparing Vf with 0.125 φc f'c bw dv = 0.125 × 0.65 × 30 × 350 × 540 = 460 688 N = 460.7 kN. Since Vf = 420 kN is less than 460.7 kN, the beam is not in the high shear range and the full limit applies, smax = min(0.7 dv, 600) = min(0.7 × 540, 600) = min(378, 600) = 378 mm. The calculated spacing of 136 mm is far below this, so the strength requirement governs the design, not the spacing limit. The maximum spacing exists to ensure every potential diagonal crack is crossed by at least one stirrup.

Answer: smax = 378 mm

(e)

At s = 150 mm, Av,min = 0.06 √f'c bw s / fy = 0.06 × 5.477 × 350 × 150 / 400 = 17 253 / 400 = 43.1 mm². The two-leg 10M stirrup has Av = 200 mm², far more than this minimum, so minimum reinforcement is satisfied. For strength, the larger spacing reduces Vs to 298.9 × 136.4 / 150 = 271.8 kN. Then Vc + Vs = 121.1 + 271.8 = 392.9 kN, below 420 kN. So 150 mm is acceptable for the minimum steel and the spacing limit but is too wide for strength, and the proposal must be rejected.

Answer: Av,min = 43.1 mm²; 150 mm is too wide for strength

Problem 4 [A2-024] Reinforced concrete short columns, tied and spiral, with interaction

A short tied column in a warehouse in Hamilton is 450 mm × 450 mm with six 25M bars (As = 500 mm² each), three along each of two opposite faces, with the steel centroids 65 mm from the nearest face, so d = 385 mm. Use f'c = 35 MPa, fy = 400 MPa, φc = 0.65, φs = 0.85, α1 = 0.85 − 0.0015 f'c, β1 = 0.97 − 0.0025 f'c, εcu = 0.0035 and Es = 200 000 MPa. For tied columns the factored axial resistance is limited to Pr,max = 0.80 Pr0, and for spiral columns to 0.85 Pr0, where Pr0 = α1 φc f'c (Ag − Ast) + φs fy Ast. Bending acts about the axis for which three bars sit on each face. In the balanced-point work of parts c and d, neglect the small area of concrete displaced by the compression bars, although part a subtracts the steel area from the gross area. Compare also with a circular spiral column of diameter 500 mm with 4000 mm² of longitudinal steel.

  1. (a) Find the pure axial factored resistance Pr0 of the tied column. [3]
  2. (b) Find the maximum axial resistance Pr,max allowed for the tied column. [3]
  3. (c) At the balanced point (εs = fy/Es at the tension face at the same time as εcu), find the neutral axis depth cb and the axial resistance Pr,b. [5]
  4. (d) Find the balanced moment resistance Mr,b about the centreline of the section. [6]
  5. (e) For the circular spiral column, find Pr,max. [3]
(a)

The pure axial resistance has a concrete part and a steel part. Ag = 450 × 450 = 202 500 mm² and Ast = 6 × 500 = 3000 mm². With α1 = 0.85 − 0.0015 × 35 = 0.7975, the concrete term is 0.7975 × 0.65 × 35 × (202 500 − 3000) = 18.143 × 199 500 = 3 619 600 N. The steel term is 0.85 × 400 × 3000 = 1 020 000 N. Pr0 = 3 619.6 + 1 020 = 4639.6 kN. The area of concrete displaced by steel is subtracted so it is not counted twice. This value cannot be reached in practice because some eccentricity always exists.

Answer: Pr0 = 4640 kN

(b)

Real columns always have some accidental eccentricity from construction tolerances and unbalanced loads, so the code does not allow the full concentric resistance. For a tied column, Pr,max = 0.80 Pr0 = 0.80 × 4639.6 = 3711.6 kN. This cap is the top of the interaction diagram, the horizontal line that cuts off the curve before it reaches the theoretical pure compression point. Any column design with a factored axial load above this limit would need a larger section, higher strength concrete or more steel, and no amount of moment capacity check could make up for it.

Answer: Pr,max = 3712 kN

(c)

At the balanced condition the tension steel just reaches εy = 400 / 200 000 = 0.002 as the extreme concrete fibre reaches 0.0035. Then cb = 0.0035 d / (0.0035 + 0.002) = 0.0035 × 385 / 0.0055 = 245.0 mm. The block depth is ab = β1 cb, with β1 = 0.97 − 0.0025 × 35 = 0.8825, so ab = 216.2 mm. Compression steel strain is 0.0035 × (245 − 65) / 245 = 0.00257, larger than 0.002, so it also yields. Its force φs As' fy equals the tension steel force, so they cancel in the axial balance. Pr,b = α1 φc f'c b ab = 0.7975 × 0.65 × 35 × 450 × 216.2 = 1765 kN.

Answer: cb = 245 mm; Pr,b = 1765 kN

(d)

Take moments about the section centreline, which lies 225 mm from each face. The concrete force Cc = 1765.2 kN acts at ab/2 = 108.1 mm from the compression face, so its arm about the centreline is 225 − 108.1 = 116.9 mm, giving 1765.2 × 0.1169 = 206.4 kN·m. The compression steel force is φs As' fy = 0.85 × 1500 × 400 = 510 kN, acting 225 − 65 = 160 mm from the centreline on the compression side, giving 81.6 kN·m. The tension steel force is also 510 kN, acting 385 − 225 = 160 mm from the centreline on the tension side, giving another 81.6 kN·m. All three moments act in the same sense, so Mr,b = 206.4 + 81.6 + 81.6 = 369.6 kN·m. The axial forces of the two steel layers cancel, which is why Pr,b equals Cc.

Answer: Mr,b = 369.6 kN·m

(e)

For the circular column, Ag = π × 500² / 4 = 196 350 mm² and Ast = 4000 mm². Pr0 = α1 φc f'c (Ag − Ast) + φs fy Ast = 18.143 × (196 350 − 4000) + 0.85 × 400 × 4000 = 18.143 × 192 350 + 1 360 000 = 3 489 600 + 1 360 000 = 4 849.6 kN. A spiral column confines the core better and gives a more ductile failure, so the code allows a higher cap: Pr,max = 0.85 Pr0 = 0.85 × 4849.8 = 4122 kN. Compared with the tied column's 3712 kN the spiral column is stronger by about 11 percent, from the larger area, extra steel and the higher cap factor.

Answer: Pr,max = 4122 kN

Problem 5 [A2-025] Limit states design: factored loads and load combinations

A simply supported steel roof beam over a mechanical storage deck in a Sudbury industrial building spans 9.0 m. The specified uniform loads on the beam are dead D = 6.0 kN/m, live (storage) L = 8.0 kN/m, snow S = 4.0 kN/m, and a net wind effect W = 5.0 kN/m acting upward. Use these limit states load combinations: 1.4D; 1.25D + 1.5L + 0.5S; 1.25D + 1.5S + 0.5L; and, for wind, 0.9D + 1.4W with W taken as upward (negative gravity). Resistance factor φ = 0.90 and yield strength Fy = 350 MPa. The compact beam is fully laterally braced in the downward case, so its moment resistance is Mr = φ Z Fy where Z is the plastic section modulus.

  1. (a) Find the governing factored downward uniform load wf from the three gravity combinations. [4]
  2. (b) Find the factored midspan moment Mf. [4]
  3. (c) Find the net factored uniform load from the wind combination 0.9D + 1.4W and the magnitude of the resulting midspan moment. [4]
  4. (d) Find the minimum plastic section modulus Z required, in 10³ mm³. [5]
  5. (e) Explain which flange of the beam is in compression under the wind combination and why this matters for the bracing design. [3]
(a)

Evaluate each gravity combination with the stated factors. 1.4D = 1.4 × 6.0 = 8.4 kN/m. 1.25D + 1.5L + 0.5S = 7.5 + 12.0 + 2.0 = 21.5 kN/m. 1.25D + 1.5S + 0.5L = 7.5 + 6.0 + 4.0 = 17.5 kN/m. The largest is the second combination, so live load is the principal load and snow is the companion at half value. wf = 21.5 kN/m. Notice that the principal load gets the full 1.5 factor while the companion gets a reduced factor because it is unlikely that two variable loads reach their maximum together. The permanent load carries a smaller factor since its variability is lower.

Answer: wf = 21.5 kN/m

(b)

For a simply supported beam under uniform load, the maximum bending moment occurs at midspan and equals Mf = wf L² / 8. With wf = 21.5 kN/m and L = 9.0 m, Mf = 21.5 × 9.0² / 8 = 21.5 × 81 / 8 = 1741.5 / 8 = 217.7 kN·m. The self-weight of the steel section is assumed to be included in the dead load of 6.0 kN/m. If the final section were heavier than assumed the dead load would have to be updated and the design repeated. The moment is calculated from the governing combination only, since that combination controls the strength design of the member.

Answer: Mf = 217.7 kN·m

(c)

Wind can reduce the net downward load because it pulls the roof up, so the dead load is multiplied by the smaller factor 0.9 when it is helping to resist wind. Taking downward as positive, the net load is 0.9 × 6.0 − 1.4 × 5.0 = 5.4 − 7.0 = −1.6 kN/m, so the net factored load is 1.6 kN/m upward. The midspan moment magnitude is 1.6 × 9.0² / 8 = 1.6 × 81 / 8 = 16.2 kN·m, and it is a reversed (hogging) moment. This is far smaller than the gravity moment, so it does not control the size of the member, but it reverses the compressed flange.

Answer: Net 1.6 kN/m upward; M = 16.2 kN·m

(d)

The required moment resistance equals the governing factored moment, so φ Z Fy ≥ Mf. Solve for Z = Mf / (φ Fy). Use consistent units with Mf = 217.7 × 10⁶ N·mm: Z = 217.7 × 10⁶ / (0.90 × 350) = 217.7 × 10⁶ / 315 = 691 100 mm³ = 691 × 10³ mm³. A compact section with Z of at least this value would be chosen from the section tables, and the next heavier standard shape above 691 × 10³ mm³ is then checked for shear, deflection under specified loads and lateral-torsional buckling spacing. This calculation sets the minimum strength size only.

Answer: Z = 691 × 10³ mm³

(e)

Under gravity loading the top flange is in compression and the roof deck usually braces it continuously. Under the wind combination the net load is upward, so the moment reverses: the top flange goes into tension and the bottom flange goes into compression. The bottom flange has no deck attached to it, so it is unbraced between the supports unless bracing is added. The design must therefore check the lateral-torsional buckling resistance of the beam in uplift with the bottom flange as the compression flange, even though the moment is small (16.2 kN·m), using the actual unbraced length. Light struts or bottom-flange bracing to the purlins are typical remedies.

Answer: The bottom flange is in compression, so it needs lateral bracing in uplift

A2 Practice Paper 6

Problem 1 [A2-026] Resistance factors and reliability in limit states design

A tension connection in a small pedestrian bridge near Barrie is designed so that the factored resistance φ Rn equals the factored load 1.25 Dn + 1.5 Ln, where the nominal dead load is Dn = 40 kN and the nominal live load is Ln = 60 kN. The proposed resistance factor is φ = 0.80. Statistics: dead load bias (mean/nominal) 1.05, COV 0.10; live load bias 1.00, COV 0.25; resistance bias 1.10, COV VR = 0.12. All variables are independent and lognormal. For the total load Q = D + L, take the mean as the sum of the means and the standard deviation from the root sum of squares. Use the simplified reliability index β = ln(Rm/Qm) / √(VR² + VQ²), where m denotes mean.

  1. (a) Find the mean total load Qm. [3]
  2. (b) Find the coefficient of variation VQ of the total load. [4]
  3. (c) Find the reliability index β achieved with φ = 0.80. [5]
  4. (d) The owner requires β = 4.0 for this brittle connection. Find the nominal resistance Rn needed, and hence the resistance factor φ that should be used with the same factored load. [6]
  5. (e) Explain in words why a brittle failure mode justifies a higher target β than a ductile one. [2]
(a)

The mean of each load is bias times nominal. Mean dead load is 1.05 × 40 = 42.0 kN. Mean live load is 1.00 × 60 = 60.0 kN. For the total load Q = D + L the means add, Qm = 42.0 + 60.0 = 102.0 kN. The factored design load, 1.25 × 40 + 1.5 × 60 = 140 kN, is greater than this mean by a margin that becomes the safety margin between the mean load and the design value. The ratio 140/102 = 1.37 is the part of the margin that sits on the load side of the equation, with the rest in φ and the resistance bias.

Answer: Qm = 102 kN

(b)

Standard deviations are mean times COV. Dead: σD = 0.10 × 42.0 = 4.2 kN. Live: σL = 0.25 × 60.0 = 15.0 kN. Independent loads combine by root sum of squares, σQ = √(4.2² + 15.0²) = √(17.64 + 225.0) = √242.64 = 15.58 kN. Then VQ = σQ / Qm = 15.58 / 102.0 = 0.1527. The live load dominates the variability, contributing 225 of the 242.6 in the sum of squared deviations (93 percent), even though it is only 59 percent of the mean load. This is why live load carries the larger load factor of 1.5.

Answer: VQ = 0.153

(c)

With φ = 0.80 the nominal resistance is Rn = 140 / 0.80 = 175 kN, so the mean resistance is Rm = 1.10 × 175 = 192.5 kN. The ratio Rm/Qm = 192.5 / 102.0 = 1.887 and ln(1.887) = 0.6350. The combined scatter is √(VR² + VQ²) = √(0.12² + 0.1527²) = √(0.0144 + 0.02332) = √0.03772 = 0.1942. Then β = 0.6350 / 0.1942 = 3.27. This is the number of standard deviations (of ln R/Q) separating the mean from failure. A β of 3.27 corresponds to a failure probability of roughly 5 in 10 000, typical of ordinary ductile members but low for brittle details.

Answer: β = 3.27

(d)

Solve the reliability equation backwards. For β = 4.0, ln(Rm/Qm) = 4.0 × 0.1942 = 0.7768, so Rm/Qm = e0.7768 = 2.175 and Rm = 2.175 × 102.0 = 221.9 kN. The nominal resistance is Rn = Rm / 1.10 = 221.9 / 1.10 = 201.7 kN. The resistance factor that links this nominal value to the unchanged factored load is φ = 140 / 201.7 = 0.694. So the factor drops from 0.80 to about 0.69, which means the connection must have about 15 percent more nominal capacity (201.7 against 175 kN) for the higher reliability.

Answer: Rn = 201.7 kN; φ = 0.694

(e)

A ductile member gives visible warning, such as large deflection or yielding, and can redistribute load to other parts of the structure before collapse, so the consequences of the nominal failure probability are limited. A brittle connection, such as a bolt fracture or a weld failing in tension, fails suddenly with no warning and no redistribution, and the failure of one such element can trigger progressive collapse. Because the consequences are severe and there is no second chance, the code authors accept a smaller failure probability, meaning a higher target β, for brittle modes. The same logic applies to elements whose failure endangers many people, such as the connections of a public pedestrian bridge.

Answer: Brittle failures give no warning or redistribution, so a lower failure probability is required

Problem 2 [A2-027] Specified live, snow and rain loads on roofs and floors

A community recreation centre in Thunder Bay has a pitched roof sloping at 45° over a gymnasium, and a three-storey office wing with reinforced concrete floors. Use these relations: roof snow load S = Is [Ss (Cb Cw Cs Ca) + Sr] with Is = 1.0, Ss = 2.3 kPa, Sr = 0.4 kPa, Cb = 0.8, Cw = 1.0, Ca = 1.0; slope factor Cs = 1.0 for slope α ≤ 30° and Cs = (70 − α)/40 for 30° < α < 70° (non-slippery surface). Floor live load reduction: for a tributary area AT ≥ 20 m² the reduced load is L0 (0.3 + √(9.8/AT)), where L0 = 2.4 kPa for offices. Rain load on a flat roof area is Sr,flat = ρg (ds + dh) with ρg = 9.81 kN/m³. A purlin spacing of 1.5 m, measured in plan (the horizontal projection, not along the slope), is used on the pitched roof.

  1. (a) Find the slope factor Cs for the 45° roof. [4]
  2. (b) Find the specified roof snow load S in kPa. [4]
  3. (c) Find the specified snow line load on each purlin, in kN/m, assuming S acts on the plan area between purlins spaced 1.5 m. [4]
  4. (d) Find the reduced live load for an office floor beam with a tributary area of 54 m², in kPa. [4]
  5. (e) On an adjacent flat roof the static head ds to the drain inlet is 70 mm and the hydraulic head dh above the inlet when the drain is overloaded is 45 mm. Find the specified rain load. [4]
(a)

The slope factor depends on the roof angle. The given roof slope α = 45° lies between 30° and 70°, so the intermediate expression applies: Cs = (70 − α)/40 = (70 − 45)/40 = 25/40 = 0.625. The result is reasonable because a steep roof sheds snow by sliding, so less snow remains, and the factor decreases from 1.0 at 30° to zero at 70°. If the roof had a slippery surface such as unobstructed metal, a different, more favourable relation would apply, but the problem states a non-slippery surface. This factor multiplies the ground snow load inside the bracket, along with the basic and exposure factors.

Answer: Cs = 0.625

(b)

Substitute into S = Is [Ss (Cb Cw Cs Ca) + Sr]. The bracket factor product is Cb Cw Cs Ca = 0.8 × 1.0 × 0.625 × 1.0 = 0.500. So Ss × 0.500 = 2.3 × 0.500 = 1.15 kPa. Adding the associated rain load, Sr = 0.4 kPa, gives 1.55 kPa, and Is = 1.0 for a normal-importance building leaves it unchanged. S = 1.55 kPa. Note that the rain term Sr is not reduced by the slope factor, because rain that falls with the snow is assumed to be absorbed in the snowpack and stays on the roof regardless of slope. The load acts on the horizontal projection of the roof.

Answer: S = 1.55 kPa

(c)

Snow is specified per square metre of horizontal plan area, so the load tributary to one purlin is S times the plan width between purlins. Taking the stated 1.5 m spacing as the plan spacing, w = S × 1.5 = 1.55 × 1.5 = 2.325 kN/m, and this is a load per metre of purlin length. When the purlin is designed, this vertical line load is resolved into a component normal to the roof, w cos 45° = 1.64 kN/m, and a component along the slope, w sin 45° = 1.64 kN/m, since the purlin is a sloping member. The value of 2.33 kN/m is the specified (unfactored) load. The limit states factor of 1.5 for snow would be applied afterwards, together with the dead load of the roof deck and purlin.

Answer: w = 2.33 kN/m

(d)

Live load reduction recognises that it is improbable that the full specified load acts over a large tributary area at once. With AT = 54 m², which exceeds 20 m², the factor is 0.3 + √(9.8 / 54) = 0.3 + √0.18148 = 0.3 + 0.4260 = 0.7260. The reduced load is L = 2.4 × 0.7260 = 1.742 kPa. This is a reduction of about 27 percent. The reduction applies to the live load only and never to the dead load, and it is not allowed for assembly areas or storage floors where full loading is likely. The reduced value is then carried into the load combinations for the floor beam.

Answer: L = 1.74 kPa

(e)

The rain load is the weight of the water that can accumulate on a flat roof if the primary drain blocks or is overwhelmed. It equals the unit weight of water times the total depth of ponded water: Sr,flat = ρg (ds + dh) = 9.81 × (0.070 + 0.045) = 9.81 × 0.115 = 1.128 kPa. Here ds is the static head, the depth to the inlet, and dh the extra head needed to push the design flow through the inlet. If this depth is deep enough to deflect the roof further, extra ponding makes the load larger, so the roof stiffness must be checked. Compared with the pitched roof snow load of 1.55 kPa, the rain load is about three quarters as large.

Answer: Sr = 1.13 kPa

Problem 3 [A2-028] Wind load on a building from reference pressure and coefficients

A light steel-framed distribution building near Windsor, Ontario, stands 24 m high with a plan 12 m deep in the wind direction and 40 m long across it. Use the static procedure: external pressure p = Iw q Ce Cg Cp, with Iw = 1.0, reference velocity pressure q = 0.45 kPa, exposure factor Ce = (h/10)0.2 evaluated at the building height h and applied uniformly over the full height, gust factor Cg = 2.0, and external pressure coefficients Cp = +0.8 on the windward wall and −0.5 on the leeward wall (suction). The total dead load of the building is W = 3600 kN, acting at mid-depth. Overturning is checked with load factors 1.4 on wind and 0.9 on dead load. Anchors are placed along the windward and leeward wall lines, 12 m apart, and overturning is taken about the leeward line.

  1. (a) Find Ce at the building height. [3]
  2. (b) Find the net pressure (windward plus leeward) acting across the building, in kPa. [4]
  3. (c) Find the base shear V and the specified (unfactored) overturning moment M about the base, taking the resultant of the uniform pressure at mid-height. Report M. [4]
  4. (d) Find the net uplift tension T carried by the windward anchor line using 1.4 M for overturning and 0.9 W for resistance, taking the dead load to act at 6 m from the leeward line. [4]
  5. (e) Each anchor has a factored tensile resistance of 95 kN. Find the minimum number of anchors in the windward line. [5]
(a)

The exposure factor Ce raises the reference pressure to account for the wind speeding up with height above ground. With h = 24 m, Ce = (h/10)0.2 = (2.4)0.2. Take the natural logarithm: ln 2.4 = 0.8755, multiplied by 0.2 gives 0.1751, and e0.1751 = 1.191. So Ce = 1.19. The code procedure also applies a minimum value for open terrain, but 1.19 is larger than that minimum, so the computed value governs. Applying one value over the whole height is conservative for the lower half of the wall, where the true factor is smaller, and it keeps the hand calculation short.

Answer: Ce = 1.19

(b)

Windward wall: p = Iw q Ce Cg Cp = 1.0 × 0.45 × 1.1914 × 2.0 × 0.8 = 0.858 kPa pushing on the wall. Leeward wall: p = 1.0 × 0.45 × 1.1914 × 2.0 × 0.5 = 0.536 kPa of suction pulling the wall outward, which acts in the same direction as the windward push. The net pressure against the building as a whole is the sum, 0.858 + 0.536 = 1.394 kPa. Equivalent to 1.0 × 0.45 × 1.1914 × 2.0 × (0.8 + 0.5) = 1.394 kPa. Summing the two walls gives the total horizontal force on the structure because pressure and suction both push the building downwind.

Answer: p = 1.39 kPa

(c)

The wind acts on the 40 m wide by 24 m high face. The base shear is V = p × width × height = 1.394 × 40 × 24 = 1338.1 kN. With a uniform pressure over the height, the resultant acts at mid-height, 12 m above the base, so the overturning moment about the base is M = V × h/2 = 1338.1 × 12 = 16 057.6 kN·m. This is the specified (unfactored) moment. The load factor of 1.4 is applied in the next part when the moment is compared with the stabilizing moment of the dead load. The base shear is also needed for sliding, which would be checked against friction on the foundation.

Answer: M = 16 060 kN·m

(d)

Take moments about the leeward anchor line. Factored overturning moment = 1.4 × 16 057.6 = 22 480.6 kN·m. Resisting moment from dead load alone, with the load factor of 0.9 because dead load helps, is 0.9 × 3600 × 6.0 = 19 440 kN·m, since W acts at mid-depth, 6 m from the leeward line. The shortfall, 22 480.6 − 19 440 = 3040.6 kN·m, must be provided by the anchors on the windward line. The lever arm between the two anchor lines is 12 m, so the anchor force is T = 3040.6 / 12 = 253.4 kN. If the shortfall had been negative the building would be stable by its weight and anchors would only be nominal.

Answer: T = 253 kN

(e)

Compare the factored demand of 253.4 kN with the factored tensile resistance of each anchor. The number required is n = T / 95 = 253.4 / 95 = 2.67. Anchors are discrete, so round up to the next whole number, n = 3. With three anchors the capacity is 285 kN, which is 12 percent above the demand, a reasonable margin since the load factors are already included. A designer would usually add one extra anchor in the line for symmetry and for uneven load sharing among the bolts. The anchors also need an embedment check and a check of the concrete breakout, which is not part of this question.

Answer: 3 anchors

Problem 4 [A2-029] Equivalent static seismic base shear and its vertical distribution

A four-storey steel office building in Ottawa has a roof at hn = 15.0 m. Storey weights are 3200 kN at levels 1, 2 and 3 (heights 4.5 m, 8.0 m and 11.5 m above the base) and 2600 kN at the roof. Use the equivalent static procedure: V = S(Ta) Mv IE W / (Rd Ro), with Mv = 1.0, IE = 1.0, Rd = 2.0, Ro = 1.3. The fundamental period is Ta = 0.05 hn3/4 s. The design spectral acceleration S(Ta) varies linearly between S(0.2 s) = 0.55 and S(0.5 s) = 0.32. Because Ta is less than 0.7 s, no top force Ft is added, and the lateral force at level x is Fx = V Wx hx / Σ(Wi hi).

  1. (a) Find the fundamental period Ta. [3]
  2. (b) Find S(Ta) by linear interpolation. [3]
  3. (c) Find the design base shear V. [5]
  4. (d) Find the lateral force F at the roof level. [5]
  5. (e) The owner wants the design base shear limited to 10 percent of W. With Ro = 1.3 unchanged, find the ductility factor Rd that would be required, and comment on its practicality. [4]
(a)

The empirical period formula stated in the problem, Ta = 0.05 hn3/4, is used as given here; it is not offered as the NBCC steel moment-frame equation. With hn = 15.0 m, 150.75 = e0.75 × ln 15 = e0.75 × 2.7081 = e2.0311 = 7.623. Then Ta = 0.05 × 7.623 = 0.3811 s. This is a short period, typical for a low-rise building, and it sits on the falling branch of the spectrum between 0.2 s and 0.5 s, where the structure still attracts large accelerations. Since the period is below 0.7 s, higher mode effects are small and the whole lateral force can be distributed over height without a concentrated top force, as the problem states.

Answer: Ta = 0.381 s

(b)

Ta = 0.381 s lies between 0.2 s and 0.5 s, so interpolate linearly. The spectrum drops from 0.55 to 0.32 across 0.3 s, a slope of (0.55 − 0.32) / 0.3 = 0.7667 per second. At 0.381 s the drop from the 0.2 s value is 0.7667 × (0.3811 − 0.2) = 0.7667 × 0.1811 = 0.1388. So S(Ta) = 0.55 − 0.1388 = 0.4112. This acceleration is about 41 percent of gravity before any reduction for ductility and overstrength. The interpolation is only valid inside the stated range; outside it the code spectrum would be read from different ordinates.

Answer: S(Ta) = 0.411

(c)

First the total seismic weight is W = 3 × 3200 + 2600 = 12 200 kN. The elastic base shear is S(Ta) Mv IE W = 0.41116 × 1.0 × 1.0 × 12 200 = 5016.1 kN. It is reduced by the force reduction factors for ductility and overstrength, Rd Ro = 2.0 × 1.3 = 2.6. So V = 5016.1 / 2.6 = 1929.3 kN, which is about 15.8 percent of the weight. Rd = 2.0 is a moderately ductile system, and a higher Rd would permit a lower shear but would then require stricter detailing of connections and members.

Answer: V = 1929 kN

(d)

Compute the weight-height products: level 1, 3200 × 4.5 = 14 400; level 2, 3200 × 8.0 = 25 600; level 3, 3200 × 11.5 = 36 800; roof, 2600 × 15.0 = 39 000. The sum is Σ Wi hi = 115 800 kN·m. The roof force is F = V × 39 000 / 115 800 = 1929.3 × 0.3368 = 649.8 kN. The forces at levels 1, 2 and 3 are 239.9, 426.5 and 613.1 kN, which sum with the roof force to the base shear. The forces increase with height, following the first-mode shape of the building as a triangle, so the roof carries the largest share even though it is the lightest floor.

Answer: F = 650 kN

(e)

Set V = 0.10 W, which means S(Ta) Mv IE / (Rd Ro) = 0.10. With S(Ta) = 0.4112 and Ro = 1.3 held fixed, Rd = S(Ta) Mv IE / (0.10 Ro) = 0.4112 / (0.10 × 1.3) = 0.4112 / 0.13 = 3.16. A required Rd of 3.16 is higher than the 2.0 assumed, and it is not itself a tabulated NBCC value: code Rd values are discrete, so a system with Rd = 3.0 would give V = 0.4112 / (3.0 × 1.3) = 0.105 W, still just above the 10 percent limit, and the designer would have to move to a more ductile system with an Rd above 3.16 and its stricter detailing, such as the ductile steel systems with Rd up to 5.0. The request is therefore achievable only with ductile detailing, and the reduction in shear comes at the price of larger inelastic drift demand, so deflection limits could become the governing check.

Answer: Rd = 3.16

Problem 5 [A2-030] Timber beam design for bending, shear and bearing

A sawn Douglas fir-larch joist beam in a lakeside cottage near Parry Sound spans 3.6 m simply supported and carries a factored uniform load, including its own weight. The section is 191 mm wide by 292 mm deep (actual dimensions). Use specified strengths already adjusted for service and treatment: fb = 11.8 MPa for bending, fv = 1.5 MPa for shear and fcp = 7.0 MPa for compression perpendicular to grain. Resistance factor φ = 0.90. The beam is fully laterally supported, so the lateral stability factor is 1.0, and size and load duration factors are included in the strengths. Shear resistance is Vr = φ fv (2/3) A, where A = b d; bending resistance is Mr = φ fb S; bearing resistance is Qr = φ fcp Ab, with Ab = b × lb. Ignore the shear reduction near the supports.

  1. (a) Find the factored bending resistance Mr. [4]
  2. (b) Find the factored shear resistance Vr. [4]
  3. (c) Find the maximum factored uniform load w the beam can carry, and state which effect governs. [6]
  4. (d) Find the minimum bearing length lb required at each support for the reaction produced by that load. [6]
(a)

For a rectangular section, the elastic section modulus is S = b d² / 6 = 191 × 292² / 6. Now 292² = 85 264, and 191 × 85 264 = 16 285 424, so S = 2 714 237 mm³. The factored bending resistance is Mr = φ fb S = 0.90 × 11.8 × 2 714 237 N·mm = 28.83 × 10⁶ N·mm = 28.83 kN·m. All other adjustment factors have been taken as one or included in fb, which means the result applies only to a laterally braced, dry, standard-term member. Larger depth-to-width ratios would bring a lateral stability factor into the equation, but the continuous bracing here avoids it.

Answer: Mr = 28.8 kN·m

(b)

For a rectangular beam the maximum shear stress is 1.5 V / A, which is why the resistance uses the factor two-thirds on area. The gross area is A = 191 × 292 = 55 772 mm². Then Vr = φ fv (2/3) A = 0.90 × 1.5 × 0.6667 × 55 772 = 50 195 N = 50.2 kN. Sawn timber is weak in shear along the grain because the fibres can slide past each other in the horizontal plane, and splits or checks near the ends reduce this further. That is why shear can govern short, heavily loaded beams, even though it does not govern this longer span.

Answer: Vr = 50.2 kN

(c)

Convert each resistance to a uniform load. Bending: Mf = w L² / 8 = Mr gives w = 8 Mr / L² = 8 × 28.83 / 3.6² = 230.6 / 12.96 = 17.79 kN/m. Shear: the end reaction is w L / 2 = Vr, which gives w = 2 Vr / L = 2 × 50.19 / 3.6 = 27.89 kN/m. The smaller value controls, so w = 17.8 kN/m, and bending governs. The shear limit is about 57 percent larger than the bending limit, so there is a reserve in shear. Deflection under the specified service load would be checked next, and for a 3.6 m span in timber that check could govern before the strength limit.

Answer: w = 17.8 kN/m, governed by bending

(d)

The end reaction at the governing load is R = w L / 2 = 17.79 × 3.6 / 2 = 32.03 kN. The bearing resistance is Qr = φ fcp b lb, so the required length is lb = R / (φ fcp b) = 32 030 / (0.90 × 7.0 × 191) = 32 030 / 1203.3 = 26.6 mm. Compressing the wood perpendicular to the grain crushes the cells rather than splitting them, and it is a strength limit state in CSA O86, checked with the factored resistance Qr = φ fcp Ab, not a serviceability check. A bearing length of 27 mm is theoretically enough, but practical details use at least 40 to 90 mm, such as a seat angle or a bearing plate, to resist movement and to ensure the support is not damaged by construction tolerances.

Answer: lb = 26.6 mm

A2 Practice Paper 7

Problem 1 [A2-031] Timber column design and slenderness

A free-standing sawn timber column of square cross-section supports a canopy over the loading dock of a cold-storage building in Sudbury, Ontario. The column is 4.2 m long, pinned at both ends so that its effective length equals its full length, and carries a factored axial compression of 220 kN. The timber is Spruce-Pine-Fir, and the problem gives the adjusted compressive strength parallel to grain Fc = 9.0 MPa and the adjusted modulus of elasticity E05 = 6000 MPa, with a resistance factor of 0.80. Use the slenderness ratio Cc = Le/d, valid up to 50, the stability factor Kc = 1 / (1 + Fc Cc³ / (35 E05)), and the factored resistance Pr = 0.80 Fc A Kc. Available square sizes (actual dimensions) are 140, 184, 235 and 286 mm.

  1. (a) Calculate the slenderness ratio Cc for the 184 mm square column. [5]
  2. (b) Calculate the stability factor Kc for the 184 mm column. [5]
  3. (c) Calculate the factored compressive resistance Pr of the 184 mm column and state whether it carries 220 kN. [5]
  4. (d) Select the smallest of the four available sizes that carries 220 kN, and give its Pr. [5]
(a)

The slenderness ratio compares the effective length with the least cross-sectional dimension, because a square section buckles about either axis equally and the least dimension is simply the side length d. Cc = Le / d = 4200 mm / 184 mm = 22.83. This is below the limit of 50 stated for sawn columns, so the section is permitted, and it is in the intermediate range where both crushing and buckling matter. A ratio near 23 means the column will be noticeably less strong than a short block of the same area, which is why the stability factor in the next part is needed before any strength comparison is made.

Answer: Cc = 22.83

(b)

The stability factor reduces the crushing strength to account for buckling. Substitute the given values: Fc Cc³ = 9.0 × 22.83³. Since 22.83³ = 11 897, the product is 107 070. The denominator is 35 E05 = 35 × 6000 = 210 000. The fraction is 107 070 / 210 000 = 0.510. Therefore Kc = 1 / (1 + 0.510) = 1 / 1.510 = 0.662. A value of 0.662 says that about one third of the squash capacity is lost to slenderness effects. Kc must lie between 0 and 1, which it does, so the arithmetic is credible.

Answer: Kc = 0.662

(c)

Area A = 184 × 184 = 33 856 mm². Pr = 0.80 × Fc × A × Kc = 0.80 × 9.0 MPa × 33 856 mm² × 0.6624. First 0.80 × 9.0 = 7.2 MPa; 7.2 × 33 856 = 243 763 N; multiplying by 0.6624 gives 161 464 N, which is 161.5 kN. Because the factored axial load is 220 kN and 161.5 kN is smaller, the demand-to-resistance ratio is 220 / 161.5 = 1.36, so the 184 mm column is inadequate. A larger section is needed; the next size up has both more area and a smaller slenderness ratio, so it gains strength twice over.

Answer: Pr = 161.5 kN < 220 kN, inadequate

(d)

Try 235 mm. Cc = 4200 / 235 = 17.87, A = 235² = 55 225 mm². Kc = 1 / (1 + 9.0 × 17.87³ / 210 000). 17.87³ = 5708, so the fraction is 51 372 / 210 000 = 0.2446 and Kc = 0.8034. Pr = 7.2 × 55 225 × 0.8034 = 319 460 N = 319.5 kN, which exceeds 220 kN (ratio 0.69). Since the 184 mm size failed and 235 mm passes, 235 mm is the smallest adequate size. The 286 mm column would work but is heavier and dearer for no need. Selecting 235 mm gives a comfortable reserve for accidental impact at a dock.

Answer: 235 mm square; Pr = 319.5 kN

Problem 2 [A2-032] Timber tension members and net section

The bottom chord of a roof truss over a community arena in Thunder Bay, Ontario is a single piece of sawn Douglas Fir-Larch, 89 mm thick, loaded in pure tension by a factored force Tf = 65 kN. At each bolted joint the chord is drilled for two 19 mm bolts placed side by side across the depth, so both holes lie in the same cross-section and each hole is taken as 21 mm diameter. The adjusted tensile strength parallel to grain is Ft = 5.5 MPa and the resistance factor is 0.90, giving Tr = 0.90 Ft An. Available depths are 140, 184 and 235 mm. Ignore any reduction for the distance between the bolt rows and treat the holes as passing through the full 89 mm thickness.

  1. (a) Calculate the net area An required to carry 65 kN. [5]
  2. (b) Calculate the net area of the 89 × 235 mm chord at a bolted joint. [5]
  3. (c) Calculate Tr for the 89 × 235 mm chord and the ratio Tf / Tr. [5]
  4. (d) Select the smallest depth from the list that provides the required net area, and give that depth in mm. [5]
(a)

Tension members fail by rupture at the section weakened most by holes, so the design starts from the net area. Rearranging Tr = 0.90 Ft An and setting Tr equal to Tf gives An = Tf / (0.90 Ft). Convert 65 kN to 65 000 N and use Ft = 5.5 N/mm²: An = 65 000 / (0.90 × 5.5) = 65 000 / 4.95 = 13 131 mm². That is the minimum net area that gives exactly a factored resistance of 65 kN. Any real member must exceed it, and the gross area will be larger by the area removed by the two holes, which is calculated in the next part.

Answer: An required = 13 131 mm²

(b)

Gross area of the member is 89 × 235 = 20 915 mm². The two holes lie in the same cross-section, so the width removed is the hole diameter multiplied by the number of holes: 2 × 21 mm = 42 mm over the 89 mm thickness. Area removed = 42 × 89 = 3738 mm². Net area An = 20 915 − 3738 = 17 177 mm². This is larger than the required 13 131 mm², so the section has enough material left after drilling. Note that the holes are deducted at their full drilled size, not the bolt diameter, because the drilled hole is the material actually removed.

Answer: An = 17 177 mm²

(c)

Use Tr = 0.90 Ft An = 0.90 × 5.5 N/mm² × 17 177 mm². First 0.90 × 5.5 = 4.95 N/mm². Then 4.95 × 17 177 = 85 026 N, which is 85.0 kN. Compare with the applied load: Tf / Tr = 65 / 85.0 = 0.765. A utilization of 76 percent means the chord is adequate with a reserve of about 24 percent. The reserve is useful because tension capacity in timber is sensitive to knots near the connection, which design values only partly reflect. The member also needs separate checks for the bolt group, which are outside this question.

Answer: Tr = 85.0 kN; Tf / Tr = 0.765

(d)
