Test each depth for net area with two 21 mm holes: An = 89 d − 2 × 21 × 89 = 89 (d − 42). For d = 140: 89 × 98 = 8722 mm², below 13 131. For d = 184: 89 × 142 = 12 638 mm², still short by about 3.8 percent. For d = 235: 89 × 193 = 17 177 mm², which exceeds the requirement. The smallest adequate depth is therefore 235 mm. The 184 mm piece looks close but fails, which shows why the holes must be deducted before a size is chosen; selecting by gross area (16 376 mm²) would have wrongly accepted it.

Answer: 235 mm

Problem 3 [A2-033] Timber connections with bolts and nails

A tension splice in a glued-laminated stair stringer of a lookout tower near Algonquin Park uses a single row of 19 mm diameter bolts in double shear through a steel side plate arrangement, loading the timber parallel to grain. The factored tensile force transferred is 48 kN. For this problem, the unfactored lateral resistance of one bolt per shear plane is given as 6.2 kN, there are two shear planes per bolt, and the resistance factor is 0.80. A group factor for n bolts in a line is Jg = 1 − 0.03 (n − 1). The factored resistance of the row is Pr = 0.80 × (6.2 × 2) × n × Jg. Required spacings are 4d between bolts along the grain and 7d end distance in tension, where d is the bolt diameter.

  1. (a) Calculate the factored resistance of one bolt in double shear, before the group factor. [5]
  2. (b) Determine the minimum number of bolts in the row for 48 kN, applying the group factor. [5]
  3. (c) Calculate the factored resistance of that row. [5]
  4. (d) Calculate the distance from the end of the member to the centre of the last bolt. [5]
(a)

A bolt in double shear transfers load through two shear planes, so its capacity is twice the single-plane value. The given unfactored value per plane is 6.2 kN. Multiplying by two planes gives 12.4 kN per bolt. Applying the resistance factor of 0.80 gives 0.80 × 12.4 = 9.92 kN. This is the capacity of an isolated bolt. When several bolts share load along the grain, load is not shared perfectly because the end bolts take more than the middle ones, and the group factor handled in the next part removes that optimism.

Answer: 9.92 kN per bolt

(b)

The row resistance is n × 9.92 × Jg with Jg = 1 − 0.03 (n − 1). Try n = 5: Jg = 0.88, Pr = 5 × 9.92 × 0.88 = 43.6 kN, below 48. Try n = 6: Jg = 1 − 0.03 × 5 = 0.85, Pr = 6 × 9.92 × 0.85 = 50.6 kN, which is above 48. Therefore six bolts is the minimum. Notice the group factor falls as bolts are added, so the capacity does not grow in proportion to n: going from five to six bolts adds only 7.0 kN, not the 9.92 kN that a naive count would suggest. Seven bolts would be wasteful.

Answer: n = 6 bolts

(c)

With n = 6 the group factor is Jg = 1 − 0.03 × (6 − 1) = 0.85. Row resistance Pr = 0.80 × (6.2 × 2) × 6 × 0.85 = 9.92 × 6 × 0.85 = 50.59 kN, rounded to 50.6 kN. Compare with the applied 48 kN: the ratio is 48 / 50.6 = 0.949, so the splice is adequate and about 5 percent of capacity is spare. The spare capacity is modest but acceptable, since the loads are factored already. Bolt bending and the capacity of the steel plates and of the net timber section would still need separate checks in a full design.

Answer: Pr = 50.6 kN

(d)

Bolt diameter d = 19 mm. The end distance in tension is 7d = 7 × 19 = 133 mm to the first bolt. Five spaces separate six bolts, and each is 4d = 4 × 19 = 76 mm, so the spaces total 5 × 76 = 380 mm. Distance from the member end to the last bolt centre = 133 + 380 = 513 mm. The splice therefore needs at least 513 mm of member beyond the face of the joint on this side. Meeting these spacings prevents the timber splitting between bolts or shearing out ahead of the end bolt, which are brittle failures that the group factor does not cover.

Answer: 513 mm

Problem 4 [A2-034] Steel tension members: gross section, net section and block shear

A hanger plate 150 mm wide in a pedestrian bridge at a conservation area in Guelph, Ontario is bolted to a gusset through two lines of three 22 mm bolts. The holes are 24 mm diameter, the gauge between the two lines is 70 mm, the bolt pitch is 65 mm and the end distance from the plate end to the first bolt is 40 mm. Steel has Fy = 350 MPa and Fu = 450 MPa. Use Tr = 0.90 Ag Fy (gross), Tr = 0.85 × 0.75 An Fu (net), and block shear Tr = 0.75 [An Fu + 0.6 Agv (Fy + Fu)/2], where An is the net area of the tension face of the block and Agv is the gross area of both shear faces. Plate thicknesses available are 10, 12 and 16 mm. The factored tension is 400 kN.

  1. (a) Calculate the gross-section resistance of a 12 mm plate. [5]
  2. (b) Calculate the net-section resistance of a 12 mm plate, counting two holes across the width. [5]
  3. (c) Calculate the block shear resistance of a 12 mm plate (tension face between the lines, two shear faces). [5]
  4. (d) Select the smallest listed thickness that carries 400 kN in all three modes and give it in mm. [5]
(a)

Gross yielding along the member length is the ductile limit state, so it uses the full width. Ag = 150 × 12 = 1800 mm². Tr = 0.90 × Ag × Fy = 0.90 × 1800 × 350 = 567 000 N = 567 kN. This is the largest of the three resistances here and it is a gentle failure, since yielding gives visible stretching before collapse. Because the plate is designed so that yielding would occur only well above the net section rupture load, gross yielding is not expected to control, and the following parts show which mode actually does.

Answer: Tr = 567 kN

(b)

Net section rupture occurs through the line of holes. The two bolt lines place two holes across the critical section, so the width is reduced by 2 × 24 = 48 mm, leaving 150 − 48 = 102 mm. An = 102 × 12 = 1224 mm². Net resistance Tr = 0.85 × 0.75 × An × Fu = 0.6375 × 1224 × 450 = 351 135 N = 351 kN. The factor 0.85 allows for shear lag and uneven stress at the holes. This value is much less than the 567 kN yield value, because rupture is brittle and the code purposely demands a lower design capacity.

Answer: Tr = 351 kN

(c)

The block that tears out is bounded by two shear faces along the outer bolt lines and one tension face across the plate between them. Each shear face runs from the plate end past the last bolt: 40 + 2 × 65 = 170 mm. The gross shear area of both faces is Agv = 2 × 170 × 12 = 4080 mm². The tension face lies between the two bolt lines: gauge 70 mm less one 24 mm hole = 46 mm, so An = 46 × 12 = 552 mm². Then Tr = 0.75 [552 × 450 + 0.6 × 4080 × 400] = 0.75 [248 400 + 979 200] = 920.7 kN. This is far above the net section value, so block shear does not control here.

Answer: Tr = 921 kN

(d)

Check each thickness against 400 kN using the net section, which governs. Net resistance is proportional to thickness: 0.6375 × 102 × 450 = 29.26 kN per mm. For 10 mm: 292.6 kN, below 400. For 12 mm: 351.1 kN, below 400. For 16 mm: 468.2 kN, above 400. Gross yielding for 16 mm is 756 kN and block shear is far higher, so both are satisfied. The smallest adequate listed thickness is 16 mm. The 12 mm plate looks adequate if only gross yielding and block shear are checked, but net rupture fails, which is why all three modes are required.

Answer: 16 mm

Problem 5 [A2-035] Laterally supported steel beam flexural resistance

A simply supported steel beam spans 7.2 m in a storage mezzanine at a distribution warehouse in Hamilton, Ontario. It carries a specified dead load of 4.5 kN/m (including self-weight) and a specified live load of 7.0 kN/m, both uniformly distributed, plus two stacked equipment racks that impose specified live point loads of 36 kN each, located at the third points of the span, 2.4 m from each support. Use load factors 1.25 for dead and 1.5 for live load. The beam is laterally supported along its entire length and every candidate section is Class 1, so Mr = 0.90 Zx Fy with Fy = 350 MPa. Candidate sections have plastic section moduli Zx of 0.76 × 10⁶, 0.94 × 10⁶ and 1.20 × 10⁶ mm³.

  1. (a) Calculate the maximum factored bending moment Mf at midspan. [5]
  2. (b) Calculate the minimum plastic section modulus required. [5]
  3. (c) Calculate Mr for the smallest candidate section that is adequate. [5]
  4. (d) Calculate the ratio Mf / Mr for the selected section. [5]
(a)

Factor the loads first. Uniform load wf = 1.25 × 4.5 + 1.5 × 7.0 = 5.625 + 10.5 = 16.125 kN/m. Each rack point load is live only, so Pf = 1.5 × 36 = 54 kN. For a simply supported beam the midspan moment from the uniform load is wf L² / 8 = 16.125 × 7.2² / 8 = 16.125 × 51.84 / 8 = 104.49 kN·m. For two equal loads at the third points, the moment anywhere between them is constant and equals Pf × L/3 = 54 × 2.4 = 129.6 kN·m. Adding the two effects gives Mf = 104.49 + 129.6 = 234.09 kN·m, which is the design moment at midspan.

Answer: Mf = 234.1 kN·m

(b)

For a laterally supported Class 1 section the moment resistance is Mr = 0.90 Zx Fy. Setting Mr equal to Mf and solving for Zx gives Zx = Mf / (0.90 Fy). Convert the moment to N·mm: 234.09 kN·m = 234.09 × 10⁶ N·mm. Then Zx = 234.09 × 10⁶ / (0.90 × 350) = 234.09 × 10⁶ / 315 = 743 143 mm³. This is the smallest plastic modulus that works. Comparing with the candidates: 0.76 × 10⁶ mm³ is the first to exceed 743 143 mm³, so it is the lightest adequate section; 0.94 × 10⁶ and 1.20 × 10⁶ are larger than needed.

Answer: Zx required = 743 143 mm³

(c)

The smallest adequate candidate is the one with Zx = 0.76 × 10⁶ mm³. Its factored resistance is Mr = 0.90 × 0.76 × 10⁶ mm³ × 350 MPa = 0.90 × 266 × 10⁶ N·mm = 239.4 × 10⁶ N·mm = 239.4 kN·m. This is greater than the demand of 234.1 kN·m, so the section passes in bending. Shear should be checked as well: the maximum factored shear at a support is wf L/2 + Pf = 16.125 × 3.6 + 54 = 112.05 kN, which is modest for a section of this size. Lateral support is assumed continuous, so no reduction for lateral torsional buckling applies.

Answer: Mr = 239.4 kN·m

(d)

The utilization ratio is demand over resistance: Mf / Mr = 234.09 / 239.4 = 0.978. A ratio of 0.978 is below 1.0, so the section is adequate, but only 2.2 percent of capacity is spare. This is a tight selection and a designer would consider whether future changes, such as heavier racks, justify choosing the 0.94 × 10⁶ mm³ section (Mr = 296.1 kN·m, ratio 0.79) at the price of additional weight. The decision would also account for deflection of the mezzanine, which often governs warehouse floors before strength does, and which is checked separately.

Answer: Mf / Mr = 0.978

A2 Practice Paper 8

Problem 1 [A2-036] Lateral torsional buckling of steel beams

A rolled I-shaped steel beam in a pump-house roof in Windsor, Ontario is a Class 1 section with Zx = 1.0 × 10⁶ mm³, Iy = 4.2 × 10⁶ mm⁴, torsional constant J = 1.4 × 10⁵ mm⁴ and warping constant Cw = 1.9 × 10¹¹ mm⁶. Fy = 350 MPa, E = 200 000 MPa and G = 77 000 MPa. It is braced against lateral movement and twist at points 3.0 m apart and carries a factored moment of 170 kN·m. Use the elastic critical moment Mu = ω2 (π/L) √(E Iy G J + (πE/L)² Iy Cw), with ω2 = 1.0 for uniform moment. With Mp = Zx Fy and φ = 0.90: if Mu ≤ 0.67 Mp then Mr = φ Mu; otherwise Mr = 1.15 φ Mp (1 − 0.28 Mp / Mu) but not more than φ Mp.

  1. (a) Calculate the elastic critical moment Mu for the 3.0 m unbraced length with ω2 = 1.0. [5]
  2. (b) Calculate the factored moment resistance Mr at 3.0 m. [5]
  3. (c) Calculate the largest unbraced length, in mm, for which Mr is at least 170 kN·m with ω2 = 1.0. [5]
  4. (d) If the moment diagram over the 3.0 m segment has ω2 = 1.30, calculate the new Mr. [5]
(a)

Evaluate the two terms under the root. E Iy G J = 200 000 × 4.2 × 10⁶ × 77 000 × 1.4 × 10⁵ = 9.055 × 10²¹ N²mm². The second term uses πE/L = π × 200 000 / 3000 = 209.4 N/mm³, whose square is 43 865; multiplied by Iy Cw = 4.2 × 10⁶ × 1.9 × 10¹¹ = 7.98 × 10¹⁷ gives 3.500 × 10²². The sum is 4.406 × 10²², and its square root is 2.099 × 10¹¹. Multiply by π/L = 1.0472 × 10⁻³ mm⁻¹ to get 2.198 × 10⁸ N·mm = 219.8 kN·m. St. Venant torsion supplies about one fifth of the quantity under the root and warping the rest.

Answer: Mu = 219.8 kN·m

(b)

First find the plastic moment: Mp = Zx Fy = 1.0 × 10⁶ × 350 = 350 × 10⁶ N·mm = 350 kN·m. The threshold is 0.67 Mp = 234.5 kN·m. Because Mu = 219.8 kN·m is below 234.5 kN·m, the beam buckles elastically, and the rule gives Mr = φ Mu = 0.90 × 219.8 = 197.8 kN·m. The inelastic expression does not apply. Since 197.8 kN·m exceeds the factored moment of 170 kN·m, the beam is adequate at a 3.0 m bracing spacing, with a utilization of 170 / 197.8 = 0.86. The resistance is only 63 percent of φ Mp = 315 kN·m, showing that lateral buckling controls over section strength.

Answer: Mr = 197.8 kN·m

(c)

Because the resistance is in the elastic range, set φ Mu = 170 kN·m, so Mu must be at least 170 / 0.90 = 188.9 kN·m, and this is below 0.67 Mp so the elastic branch is the right one. Mu falls as L increases, so find the length at which Mu = 188.9 kN·m. Trial values: at L = 3000 mm, Mu = 219.8; at L = 3500 mm the root terms give about 168; interpolating and refining by repeated evaluation of the full expression gives L ≈ 3267 mm, where Mu = 188.9 kN·m. Thus bracing may be spaced up to about 3.27 m; practically one would select 3.2 m or a spacing that matches the framing.

Answer: L max ≈ 3267 mm

(d)

A larger ω2 recognizes that a moment gradient along the segment makes lateral buckling less likely than under uniform moment. Mu = 1.30 × 219.8 = 285.75 kN·m. This now exceeds 0.67 Mp = 234.5 kN·m, so the inelastic expression applies: Mr = 1.15 × 0.90 × 350 × (1 − 0.28 × 350 / 285.75) = 362.25 × (1 − 0.3430) = 362.25 × 0.6570 = 238.0 kN·m. The cap φ Mp = 315 kN·m is not reached. The gain from 197.8 to 238.0 kN·m is 20 percent, showing why the moment shape matters. The value of ω2 must come from the actual moment diagram and cannot be assumed.

Answer: Mr = 238.0 kN·m

Problem 2 [A2-037] Steel beam shear resistance and web bearing

A welded plate girder of small size supports a conveyor gallery floor at a paper mill in Thunder Bay, Ontario. Its web is 400 mm deep between flanges and 7.5 mm thick, with Fy = 350 MPa, and the distance k from the outside of the flange to the web toe of the fillet is 20 mm. At the end support, the beam rests on a steel bearing plate of length N and carries a factored end reaction of 560 kN. Use Vr = 0.90 Aw Fs with Aw = h w and Fs = 0.66 Fy when h/w ≤ 439 √(kv/Fy) with kv = 5.34 (unstiffened web), and web bearing resistance Br = 0.80 w (N + 4 k) Fy, the end-reaction form of the bearing rule. Assume no web stiffeners and no web crippling check beyond the bearing formula given.

  1. (a) Calculate the factored shear resistance Vr, after checking the web slenderness limit. [5]
  2. (b) Calculate the web bearing resistance Br for a bearing length N = 50 mm. [5]
  3. (c) Calculate the minimum bearing length N required for the 560 kN reaction. [5]
  4. (d) Calculate the maximum factored end reaction the web can carry if N = 75 mm. [5]
(a)

The shear formula Fs = 0.66 Fy applies only if the web is stocky enough that it yields before it buckles in shear. Compute h/w = 400 / 7.5 = 53.3. The limit is 439 √(5.34 / 350) = 439 × 0.1235 = 54.2. Since 53.3 is below 54.2, the web yields in shear and Fs = 0.66 × 350 = 231 MPa. Web area Aw = 400 × 7.5 = 3000 mm². Then Vr = 0.90 × 3000 × 231 = 623 700 N = 623.7 kN. The slenderness is just under the limit, so a slightly thinner web would have required the lower buckling stress. Vr exceeds the reaction of 560 kN, giving a shear utilization of 0.90.

Answer: Vr = 623.7 kN

(b)

Web bearing, sometimes called web yielding under a concentrated reaction, assumes the load spreads at a 1 to 2.5 slope through the flange and fillet into the web. At an end support the spread is possible on one side only, so the effective length is N plus 4 k. With N = 50 mm and k = 20 mm: N + 4 k = 50 + 80 = 130 mm. Br = 0.80 × 7.5 × 130 × 350 = 6.0 × 130 × 350 = 273 000 N = 273 kN. This is well below the 560 kN reaction, so a 50 mm plate fails badly. The result shows that a narrow bearing plate, not the shear capacity, is the weak link at the support, and the plate must be lengthened or stiffeners added.

Answer: Br = 273 kN

(c)

Set Br equal to the reaction and solve for N. Br = 0.80 w (N + 4k) Fy gives N + 4k = Vf / (0.80 w Fy) = 560 000 / (0.80 × 7.5 × 350) = 560 000 / 2100 = 266.7 mm. Hence N = 266.7 − 4 × 20 = 186.7 mm. The bearing plate must be at least about 187 mm long measured along the beam, which is long for a small girder, so a designer would probably add a pair of bearing stiffeners instead and round any plate up to a convenient size such as 200 mm. Providing exactly 186.7 mm would leave zero reserve, which is not prudent because the seating of the plate is not perfectly controlled.

Answer: N min = 186.7 mm

(d)

With N = 75 mm the effective length is 75 + 80 = 155 mm and Br = 0.80 × 7.5 × 155 × 350 = 6.0 × 155 × 350 = 325 500 N = 325.5 kN. The end reaction is also limited by shear, Vr = 623.7 kN. The smaller of the two governs, so the maximum end reaction is 325.5 kN, controlled by web bearing. This is only 58 percent of the required 560 kN, so a 75 mm plate is not acceptable without web stiffeners. Note the two limits are quite different failure modes, local yielding under the load against overall web shear, so both must be checked and the lesser used.

Answer: Maximum end reaction = 325.5 kN

Problem 3 [A2-038] Steel beam deflection and serviceability

A steel girder carries pedestrians over a drainage channel in a municipal park in Barrie, Ontario. It is simply supported on a span of 8.0 m. The specified live loads are a uniform pedestrian load of 11 kN/m over the full span and a maintenance cart wheel load of 40 kN acting at midspan. The serviceability limit under live load alone is span/360. Take E = 200 000 MPa. The mid-span deflection of a simple beam is 5 w L⁴ / (384 E I) for a uniform load w and P L³ / (48 E I) for a central point load P, and the two effects add. Three candidate sections have strong-axis second moments of area of 1.9 × 10⁸, 2.4 × 10⁸ and 3.1 × 10⁸ mm⁴.

  1. (a) Calculate the live-load midspan deflection of the section with I = 1.9 × 10⁸ mm⁴. [5]
  2. (b) Calculate the allowable deflection span/360. [5]
  3. (c) Calculate the minimum required I, in units of 10⁶ mm⁴. [5]
  4. (d) Calculate the deflection of the smallest adequate candidate section. [5]
(a)

Use consistent units of newtons and millimetres. The uniform load is 11 kN/m = 11 N/mm, L = 8000 mm, and P = 40 000 N. Uniform part: 5 × 11 × 8000⁴ / (384 × 200 000 × 1.9 × 10⁸). 8000⁴ = 4.096 × 10¹⁵, so the numerator is 2.2528 × 10¹⁷ and the denominator is 1.4592 × 10¹⁶, which gives 15.44 mm. Point part: 40 000 × 8000³ / (48 × 200 000 × 1.9 × 10⁸); 8000³ = 5.12 × 10¹¹, so the numerator is 2.048 × 10¹⁶ and the denominator is 1.824 × 10¹⁵, giving 11.23 mm. Total = 15.44 + 11.23 = 26.67 mm.

Answer: δ = 26.7 mm

(b)

The serviceability limit for live-load deflection is span/360, which keeps floors and walkways from feeling bouncy and protects finishes. Allowable δ = L / 360 = 8000 / 360 = 22.2 mm. Compare with the 26.7 mm found for the lightest section: 26.7 is larger than 22.2, so that section violates the limit by about 20 percent even though it may easily be strong enough. Serviceability checks use specified, unfactored loads, so no load factors enter this comparison. The check shows that a stiffness limit, not strength, can set the size of a pedestrian girder.

Answer: δ allowable = 22.2 mm

(c)

Deflection is inversely proportional to I, so write δ = (5 w L⁴ / (384 E) + P L³ / (48 E)) / I and set δ equal to 22.22 mm. The load terms are 5 × 11 × 4.096 × 10¹⁵ / (384 × 200 000) = 2.933 × 10⁹ N·mm² per mm⁴-unit, and 40 000 × 5.12 × 10¹¹ / (48 × 200 000) = 2.133 × 10⁹. Their sum is 5.067 × 10⁹. Then I required = 5.067 × 10⁹ / 22.22 = 228.0 × 10⁶ mm⁴. Any section with I below this value breaks the limit, so the 1.9 × 10⁸ section is eliminated and the next candidate, 2.4 × 10⁸, must be tested.

Answer: I required = 228.0 × 10⁶ mm⁴

(d)

The candidates are 190, 240 and 310 million mm⁴. Only 240 × 10⁶ and 310 × 10⁶ exceed the required 228.0 × 10⁶, so the smallest adequate one is 2.4 × 10⁸ mm⁴. Its deflection is δ = 5.067 × 10⁹ / 2.4 × 10⁸ = 21.11 mm, which is below 22.22 mm, a utilization of 0.95. This section meets the limit with only 5 percent to spare. If designers wanted a margin for dynamic comfort under walking, as is common for pedestrian structures, they would consider the 3.1 × 10⁸ section (δ = 16.3 mm), and would check natural frequency separately.

Answer: δ = 21.1 mm

Problem 4 [A2-039] Steel column compressive resistance and effective length

A square hollow steel section column supports a rooftop air-handling unit at a hospital in London, Ontario. The section has gross area A = 6990 mm², radius of gyration r = 77.8 mm (the same about both axes) and Fy = 350 MPa, with E = 200 000 MPa. The column is 5.2 m between its base and the roof beam. Use Cr = φ A Fy (1 + λ2n)−1/n, where λ = (KL/r) √(Fy/E) / π, n = 2.24 and φ = 0.90. The factored axial load from the unit and snow is 1250 kN. In the finished building the column is pinned at both ends, for which K = 1.0. During erection, before the roof beam is connected, it acts as a cantilever with a free top, for which K = 2.0.

  1. (a) Calculate the slenderness ratio KL/r for the finished condition, K = 1.0. [5]
  2. (b) Calculate the compressive resistance Cr for the finished condition. [5]
  3. (c) Calculate Cr for the erection condition, K = 2.0, and state by what percentage it is lower than the finished-condition resistance of part b. [5]
  4. (d) With K = 1.0, calculate the greatest column length, in mm, for which Cr is at least 1500 kN. [5]
(a)

The effective length is the product of the effective length factor and the actual length: KL = 1.0 × 5200 = 5200 mm. Dividing by the radius of gyration gives KL/r = 5200 / 77.8 = 66.84. A slenderness near 67 puts this column in the intermediate range, where buckling reduces capacity noticeably but does not govern outright. Because the section is square and hollow, r is the same about both axes, so no separate check about a weak axis is needed. Slenderness ratios above 200 are not permitted for compression members, and this value is far below that.

Answer: KL/r = 66.8

(b)

First convert slenderness to the non-dimensional ratio: λ = (66.84 / π) × √(350 / 200 000) = 21.28 × 0.04183 = 0.890. Then λ2n = 0.8904.48 = 0.593, and 1 + 0.593 = 1.593. Raising to the power −1/2.24: 1.593−0.4464 = 0.812. The squash load factor is φ A Fy = 0.90 × 6990 × 350 = 2 201 850 N = 2202 kN. Therefore Cr = 2202 × 0.812 = 1788 kN. This exceeds the factored load of 1250 kN, so the pinned-pinned column is adequate, with a utilization ratio of 1250 / 1788 = 0.70.

Answer: Cr = 1788 kN

(c)

For the cantilever case KL = 2.0 × 5200 = 10 400 mm, so KL/r = 133.7. Then λ = (133.7 / π) × 0.04183 = 1.780 and λ4.48 = 13.2, giving 1 + 13.2 = 14.2. Raising to −0.4464: 14.2−0.4464 = 0.3055. Cr = 2202 × 0.3055 = 672.7 kN. This is 62 percent lower than the finished-condition resistance of 1788 kN. During erection the column carries only its own weight and temporary loads, not the full 1250 kN of roof and unit loads, so a low resistance is not by itself a failure of the design. It does show why the column needs temporary bracing or a quick connection to the roof beam before the unit is placed. The free-top condition cuts strength by 62 percent.

Answer: Cr = 672.7 kN, 62 percent lower than the finished condition

(d)

Cr must be at least 1500 kN with K = 1.0, so the required reduction factor is 1500 / 2202 = 0.681, which requires (1 + λ4.48)−0.4464 = 0.681, giving 1 + λ4.48 = 0.681−2.24 = 2.362 and λ4.48 = 1.362, so λ = 1.3621/4.48 = 1.0714. Then KL/r = λ π / 0.04183 = 1.0714 × 3.1416 / 0.04183 = 80.5, and L = 80.5 × 77.8 = 6260 mm. Checking by substitution gives Cr ≈ 1500 kN. The column can therefore be lengthened from 5.2 m to about 6.26 m if the target is raised to 1500 kN. Solving the equation was done by inverting it, and a trial and error check confirms the answer.

Answer: L max = 6260 mm

Problem 5 [A2-040] Steel beam-columns under combined axial load and bending

A steel column in a single-storey braced frame at a machine shop in Oshawa, Ontario is a square hollow section with A = 6990 mm², Ix = 4.23 × 10⁷ mm⁴, plastic modulus Zx = 0.50 × 10⁶ mm³, Fy = 350 MPa and E = 200 000 MPa. The column is 4.0 m high, pinned at both ends in the braced frame, so K = 1.0. A crane bracket applies a factored axial compression Cf = 900 kN together with a factored bending moment Mf = 70 kN·m, uniform over the height (ω1 = 1.0). Use Cr = φ A Fy (1 + λ2n)−1/n with λ = (KL/r) √(Fy/E)/π, r = √(I/A), n = 2.24, φ = 0.90, and Mrx = φ Zx Fy. Euler load Cex = π² E I / (KL)². The interaction check is Cf/Cr + 0.85 U1x Mf/Mrx ≤ 1.0, with U1x = ω1 / (1 − Cf/Cex) and U1x not less than 1.0.

  1. (a) Calculate the axial compressive resistance Cr. [4]
  2. (b) Calculate the Euler buckling load Cex. [4]
  3. (c) Calculate the amplification factor U1x. [4]
  4. (d) Calculate the interaction value and state whether the column is adequate. [4]
  5. (e) With the axial load held at 900 kN, calculate the largest Mf that the interaction equation permits. [4]
(a)

The radius of gyration is r = √(Ix / A) = √(4.23 × 10⁷ / 6990) = √6051 = 77.8 mm. With K = 1.0 and L = 4000 mm, KL/r = 51.4 and λ = (51.4 / π) × √(350 / 200 000) = 16.37 × 0.04183 = 0.6847. Then λ4.48 = 0.1832, so 1 + λ4.48 = 1.1832. The squash load is φ A Fy = 0.90 × 6990 × 350 = 2201.9 kN. Evaluating the root, 1.1832−0.4464 = e−0.4464 × 0.1682 = e−0.0751 = 0.9277, so Cr = 2201.9 × 0.9277 = 2042.7 kN, which agrees to rounding with 2042.5 kN.

Answer: Cr = 2042.5 kN

(b)

Euler buckling load is a theoretical elastic limit used only to measure how much the bending moment is amplified by the axial load acting through the lateral deflection. Cex = π² E I / (KL)² = 9.8696 × 200 000 × 4.23 × 10⁷ / 4000². Numerator: 9.8696 × 200 000 = 1.9739 × 10⁶, times 4.23 × 10⁷ = 8.350 × 10¹³. Denominator = 1.6 × 10⁷. Cex = 5.219 × 10⁶ N = 5219 kN. Because the Euler load is about 5.8 times the factored axial load, the amplification will be modest. A load closer to Cex would give a rapidly rising amplification.

Answer: Cex = 5219 kN

(c)

The amplification factor accounts for the second-order moment P-delta effect. Cf / Cex = 900 / 5218.6 = 0.1725. Then 1 − 0.1725 = 0.8275, and U1x = ω1 / 0.8275 = 1.0 / 0.8275 = 1.208. This is not less than 1.0, so it governs and the moment is increased by about 21 percent. If the moment gradient made ω1 as low as 0.6, the factor would be 0.725, which is below 1.0, and U1x would be taken as 1.0 instead. In this problem the uniform moment is the most severe case, with ω1 = 1.0, so the full amplification applies.

Answer: U1x = 1.208

(d)

First the moment resistance: Mrx = 0.90 × 0.50 × 10⁶ × 350 = 157.5 × 10⁶ N·mm = 157.5 kN·m. Substituting into the interaction equation: Cf/Cr = 900 / 2042.5 = 0.4406. The bending term is 0.85 × U1x × Mf/Mrx = 0.85 × 1.208 × 70 / 157.5 = 1.0268 × 0.4444 = 0.4563. The sum is 0.4406 + 0.4563 = 0.897. Since 0.897 is less than 1.0, the column is adequate under combined loading, with about 10 percent reserve. Axial load takes 49 percent of the interaction capacity and bending the remainder, so neither effect can be ignored.

Answer: Interaction = 0.897, adequate

(e)

Rearrange the interaction equation for Mf, keeping Cf at 900 kN and U1x at 1.208. The share of capacity left for bending is 1 − Cf/Cr = 1 − 0.4406 = 0.5594. Then 0.85 U1x Mf / Mrx = 0.5594 gives Mf = 0.5594 × Mrx / (0.85 × 1.208) = 0.5594 × 157.5 / 1.0268 = 88.1 / 1.0268 = 85.8 kN·m. The column could therefore carry up to 85.8 kN·m with the given axial load, 23 percent more than the applied 70 kN·m. If the axial load increased, U1x would also increase, so the allowable moment would fall faster than a linear estimate predicts.

Answer: Mf max = 85.8 kN·m

A2 Practice Paper 9

Problem 1 [A2-041] Bolted steel connections in bearing

A tension splice in a steel gusset system for a conveyor support frame in Hamilton, Ontario joins a 250 mm wide by 18 mm thick main plate to two 12 mm cover plates, one on each face, using 22 mm diameter high-strength bolts in standard 24 mm holes. The bolts are arranged in rows of two across the plate width, with the threads excluded from nothing (assume threads may lie in the shear planes). Each bolt therefore acts in double shear. The factored tension to be transferred is Tf = 960 kN. Use these resistance formulas, all stated here: bolt shear Vr = 0.60 φb n m Ab Fu with φb = 0.80, n = 1 bolt, m = 2 shear planes, Fu(bolt) = 830 MPa; bearing Br = 3 φbr t d Fu(plate) with φbr = 0.80 and Fu(plate) = 450 MPa; net section tension Tr = 0.85 φu An Fu(plate) with φu = 0.75. Gross bolt area Ab = π d²/4.

  1. (a) Calculate the factored shear resistance of one bolt, in kN. [5]
  2. (b) Calculate the factored bearing resistance of one bolt on the 18 mm main plate, in kN. [5]
  3. (c) Determine the smallest whole number of bolts that carries Tf, keeping the rows of two. [4]
  4. (d) Calculate Tr for the main plate at the first bolt row, where two 24 mm holes cut the section, and state whether the plate is adequate. [6]
(a)

The bolts are in double shear, so each bolt has two shear planes. The area is Ab = π × 22² / 4 = 380.1 mm². Applying Vr = 0.60 φb n m Ab Fu gives Vr = 0.60 × 0.80 × 1 × 2 × 380.1 × 830 = 302 890 N, or 302.9 kN. The factor 0.60 already allows for the possibility that a thread runs through a shear plane, which is why no separate reduction is applied here. The result is the capacity of one bolt for the shear failure mode only. Bearing is checked next, because the smaller of the two values for the bolt governs how many bolts are needed. Each bolt carries this resistance irrespective of its row position, since the bolts are assumed to share load equally in a concentrically loaded splice.

Answer: 302.9 kN

(b)

Bearing is governed by the main plate, not the cover plates, because the 18 mm main plate is thinner than the combined 24 mm of the two covers and carries the whole bolt force at its hole. Using Br = 3 φbr t d Fu: Br = 3 × 0.80 × 18 × 22 × 450 = 427 680 N = 427.7 kN. This is larger than the shear resistance of 302.9 kN, so bearing does not control the bolt value. The design capacity per bolt is the smaller of the two resistances, 302.9 kN, which comes from shear. If the plate had been thin enough to push Br below 302.9 kN, the bearing equation would have set the number of bolts instead. Edge distance and spacing are assumed adequate so that tear-out does not govern.

Answer: 427.7 kN

(c)

The resistance per bolt is the lesser of shear and bearing, so 302.9 kN. The number required is n = Tf / Vr = 960 / 302.9 = 3.17. Rounding up gives four bolts. Because the layout calls for rows of two across the plate width, three bolts would leave an unbalanced row, and four bolts give two complete rows with a group resistance of 4 × 302.9 = 1211.6 kN, which exceeds 960 kN. The utilization of the bolt group is 960 / 1211.6 = 0.79, so there is spare capacity. This is acceptable for a splice, where the bolt count is set by the whole-number and symmetry requirement rather than by the strength alone.

Answer: 4 bolts

(d)

At the first row the section passes through two holes. The net width is 250 - 2 × 24 = 202 mm, so An = 202 × 18 = 3636 mm². Net section tension resistance is Tr = 0.85 φu An Fu = 0.85 × 0.75 × 3636 × 450 = 1 043 078 N, which is 1043 kN. Since 1043 kN exceeds the factored load of 960 kN, the plate is adequate at the net section, with a ratio of 960 / 1043 = 0.92. The ratio is high enough that the plate thickness should not be reduced. At the second row, part of the load has already passed into the cover plates through the first row of bolts, so the first row is the critical section for the main plate. Gross-section yielding would also be checked in practice, but it is not asked here.

Answer: 1043 kN, adequate

Problem 2 [A2-042] Eccentrically loaded bolt groups and slip-critical connections

A steel bracket is bolted to the flange of a column in a parking structure using six 22 mm high-strength bolts in a slip-critical connection. The bolts sit in two vertical lines, 100 mm apart, with three bolts in each line at a vertical pitch of 75 mm, so the group is symmetric about its centroid. A downward factored load of P = 90 kN acts in the plane of the group at a horizontal eccentricity e = 250 mm from the centroid of the bolt group. Use the elastic method, in which the load is carried equally by all bolts and the moment P e is resisted by forces proportional to distance from the centroid. The slip resistance of one bolt on one faying surface is Vs = 0.53 ks m Ab Fu, with ks = 0.33, m = 1 slip plane, Ab = π d²/4 and Fu = 830 MPa. Treat Vs as the limit for the resultant force on any bolt.

  1. (a) Calculate the slip resistance Vs of one bolt, in kN. [4]
  2. (b) Calculate the polar moment Σ(x² + y²) of the bolt group about its centroid, in mm². [4]
  3. (c) Calculate the resultant force on the most heavily loaded bolt, in kN. [6]
  4. (d) Determine the largest load P, at the same eccentricity, for which no bolt exceeds Vs, in kN. [6]
(a)

The bolt area is Ab = π × 22² / 4 = 380.1 mm². Using the stated formula Vs = 0.53 ks m Ab Fu, we have Vs = 0.53 × 0.33 × 1 × 380.1 × 830 = 55 183 N, which is 55.2 kN. This is the load a single bolt can transfer by friction between the plies before the connection slips. In a slip-critical design, slip is the serviceability limit that governs, so the resultant force on each bolt is compared with this value rather than with the larger shear or bearing capacity. Because the connection is a single lap with one faying surface per bolt, m is 1. The result is kept as the limiting force for the group in the next parts.

Answer: 55.2 kN

(b)

Place the origin at the centroid of the group. The bolts are at x = ±50 mm and y = -75, 0 and +75 mm, two bolts at each y level. The sum of x² over six bolts is 6 × 2500 = 15 000 mm². The sum of y² is 2 × (5625 + 0 + 5625) = 22 500 mm². The polar moment is therefore J = Σx² + Σy² = 15 000 + 22 500 = 37 500 mm². This is the sum of the squared distances of all bolts from the centroid and is the stiffness term in the elastic torsion formula, so it is required before any bolt force can be found.

Answer: 37 500 mm²

(c)

The eccentric load is equivalent to the same load at the centroid plus a moment T = P e = 90 × 250 = 22 500 kN·mm. The direct force is P / 6 = 15 kN vertically on each bolt. The moment adds a force at each bolt perpendicular to its radius with components Fx = T y / J and Fy = T x / J. The ratio T / J is 22 500 / 37 500 = 0.60 kN/mm. For the corner bolt on the load side, at x = 50 and y = 75, Fx = 0.60 × 75 = 45 kN and Fy = 15 + 0.60 × 50 = 45 kN. The resultant is √(45² + 45²) = 63.6 kN. The other corner on the load side is equally critical, and the far bolts carry less because the direct and torsional vertical components subtract.

Answer: 63.6 kN

(d)

The elastic forces are proportional to P, so the largest bolt force scales linearly with P. The present maximum is 63.6 kN for P = 90 kN, so the force per kN of load is 63.64 / 90 = 0.707 kN per kN. Setting this equal to the slip limit Vs = 55.18 kN gives P = 55.18 / 0.707 = 78.0 kN. The connection with the 90 kN load fails the slip check, since 63.6 exceeds 55.2 by about 15 percent. To work with 90 kN the designer could add a column of bolts, use a larger pitch, reduce the eccentricity, or increase the bolt diameter. The allowable P of 78.0 kN is the practical maximum for this layout.

Answer: 78.0 kN

Problem 3 [A2-043] Fillet weld resistance and weld length

A flat steel tension plate of a roof truss in Sudbury, Ontario is lapped onto a gusset plate and joined by fillet welds of leg size w = 8 mm made with an electrode of ultimate strength Xu = 490 MPa. The welds are made by a shielded process in the shop. Use the factored resistance of a fillet weld Vr = 0.67 φw Aw Xu (1.0 + 0.50 sin1.5 θ), where φw = 0.67, Aw = 0.707 w L is the throat area, L is the weld length, and θ is the angle between the weld axis and the line of force. The plate is 150 mm wide and carries a factored tension of 360 kN. Two longitudinal welds, one along each edge of the plate, are available (θ = 0°). A transverse weld across the end of the plate (θ = 90°) may also be added. Ignore base-metal checks and minimum length rules.

  1. (a) Calculate the factored resistance per millimetre of a longitudinal 8 mm fillet weld, in kN/mm. [5]
  2. (b) With longitudinal welds only, determine the length of each of the two welds needed for 360 kN, in mm. [5]
  3. (c) Calculate the resistance per millimetre of the 8 mm transverse weld, in kN/mm. [4]
  4. (d) If a 150 mm transverse end weld is added, determine the length of each longitudinal weld still needed, in mm. [6]
(a)

For a longitudinal weld θ = 0°, so sin θ = 0 and the bracket (1.0 + 0.50 sin1.5 θ) equals 1.0. The throat area per millimetre of length is Aw / L = 0.707 × 8 = 5.656 mm. The resistance per millimetre is then 0.67 × 0.67 × 5.656 × 490 = 1244 N/mm, which is 1.244 kN/mm. The two factors of 0.67 are distinct: one is the shear strength factor on the electrode strength and the other is the resistance factor φw, so both must appear in the product. The result is the strength of weld per unit length that will be used to size the lap.

Answer: 1.244 kN/mm

(b)

With only two longitudinal welds, the total length required is Lt = Tf / (resistance per mm) = 360 / 1.244 = 289.4 mm. The load is shared equally by the two edge welds, so each weld must be 289.4 / 2 = 144.7 mm long. In practice the length is rounded up to the next convenient value such as 150 mm, which also satisfies the common rule that longitudinal welds on a plate should not be shorter than the plate width, here 150 mm. The weld length is the essential variable, because the leg size is fixed and the base metal checks are ignored by the statement. Equal division assumes the load line passes through the centroid of the two welds.

Answer: 144.7 mm

(c)

For the transverse weld θ = 90°, so sin 90° = 1 and (1.0 + 0.50 × 1) = 1.50. The resistance per millimetre is therefore 1.50 times the longitudinal value: 1.50 × 1.244 = 1.866 kN/mm. The strength increase arises because a transverse fillet loaded perpendicular to its axis is stronger and stiffer than one loaded along its length. Repeating the arithmetic in full gives 0.67 × 0.67 × 5.656 × 490 × 1.5 = 1866 N/mm, confirming the factor of 1.5 applied to part (a). This transverse resistance is applied only to the length of weld that lies across the force direction.

Answer: 1.866 kN/mm

(d)

The end weld across the 150 mm plate carries 150 × 1.866 = 279.9 kN. The remaining demand is 360 - 279.9 = 80.1 kN, which the two longitudinal welds must resist. The length per weld is 80.1 / (2 × 1.244) = 32.2 mm. A weld this short is not practical, because the resistance formulas assume a minimum length, so the designer would instead choose a standard minimum such as the plate width or use only the longitudinal welds. The calculation shows that the transverse weld does most of the work. Combining longitudinal and transverse welds in one joint requires a more careful treatment than simply adding the two resistances, so this is a simplified check.

Answer: 32.2 mm

Problem 4 [A2-044] Eccentric weld groups and simple beam connections

A short steel bracket supporting a crane runway hanger in a mill building in Windsor, Ontario is attached to the face of a column by two parallel vertical fillet welds, each 200 mm long and 150 mm apart. There are no horizontal welds. A factored vertical load of 60 kN acts in the plane of the welds at a horizontal distance of 300 mm from the centroid of the weld group. Use the elastic method with the welds treated as lines of unit throat: the polar moment of the line group is Ip, the direct shear is shared equally over the total weld length, and the torsional force per millimetre at a point is T r / Ip. The factored resistance of a fillet weld per millimetre of length is Vr = 0.67 φw (0.707 w) Xu with φw = 0.67, Xu = 490 MPa and w = 6 mm, applying equally in every direction.

  1. (a) Calculate the polar moment Ip of the two-line weld group about its centroid, in mm³. [5]
  2. (b) Calculate the maximum resultant force per millimetre of weld, at the end of a weld, in kN/mm. [6]
  3. (c) Calculate the factored resistance per millimetre of the 6 mm weld, in kN/mm. [4]
  4. (d) Determine the minimum weld leg size, assuming resistance is proportional to size, in mm. [5]
(a)

With the origin at the group centroid, each vertical line is 200 mm long and lies 75 mm from the vertical axis. For one line the polar moment of a line of length L about its own centre is L³ / 12 = 200³ / 12 = 666 667 mm³, and the transfer term is L d² = 200 × 75² = 1 125 000 mm³. Their sum for one line is 1 791 667 mm³. For two lines Ip = 2 × 1 791 667 = 3 583 333 mm³. The unit of mm³ arises because the weld is treated as a line with no thickness; force per millimetre will then result when torque in kN·mm is divided by it. Both lines contribute equally.

Answer: 3.583 × 10⁶ mm³

(b)

The torque is T = P e = 60 × 300 = 18 000 kN·mm. The direct shear per millimetre is P / (2 × 200) = 60 / 400 = 0.150 kN/mm, acting vertically. The critical point is the top or bottom end of a weld on the load side, where x = 75 mm and y = 100 mm. The torsional components are Fx = T y / Ip = 18 000 × 100 / 3 583 333 = 0.502 kN/mm and Fy = T x / Ip = 18 000 × 75 / 3 583 333 = 0.377 kN/mm. Adding the direct shear to the vertical component gives Fy = 0.377 + 0.150 = 0.527 kN/mm. The resultant is √(0.502² + 0.527²) = 0.728 kN/mm.

Answer: 0.728 kN/mm

(c)

The throat per millimetre of weld length is 0.707 × 6 = 4.242 mm. The resistance per millimetre is Vr = 0.67 × 0.67 × 4.242 × 490 = 933 N/mm, which is 0.933 kN/mm. Because the statement tells us to apply this value in every direction, no directional strength factor is used, which is a simplification of real weld behaviour in which transverse loading is stronger. The comparison of this value with the demand of 0.728 kN/mm from part (b) shows that the 6 mm weld has a utilisation of about 0.78, so the weld is adequate with some reserve. Resistance for other sizes follows in proportion.

Answer: 0.933 kN/mm

(d)

Resistance is proportional to the leg size, so the weld must provide at least 0.728 kN/mm. The resistance per millimetre of leg is 0.933 / 6 = 0.1555 kN/mm per mm of leg. The minimum leg is therefore 0.728 / 0.1555 = 4.68 mm. In practice the leg is rounded up to the next standard size, 5 mm, but welding codes also set a minimum size according to the thickness of the thicker plate joined, which could govern. The calculation shows the 6 mm weld has about 28 percent more capacity than the minimum required, so a 5 mm weld could be considered if code minima permit.

Answer: 4.7 mm

Problem 5 [A2-045] Singly reinforced concrete beam flexure

A rectangular reinforced concrete beam forms part of a school gymnasium roof in London, Ontario. It has a width b = 300 mm, an effective depth d = 520 mm to the centroid of the tension steel and a total depth of 600 mm. The tension steel is four 25M bars (area 500 mm² each) in one layer. Concrete strength is fc' = 30 MPa and reinforcement yield strength is fy = 400 MPa. Use resistance factors φc = 0.65 and φs = 0.85, a stress block factor α1 = 0.85 - 0.0015 fc' and depth factor β1 = 0.97 - 0.0025 fc'. The equivalent rectangular stress block depth is a = φs As fy / (α1 φc fc' b) and the factored moment resistance is Mr = φs As fy (d - a/2). The balanced neutral axis depth is cb = 700 d / (700 + fy). The beam spans 6.5 m simply supported.

  1. (a) Calculate the stress block depth a, in mm. [5]
  2. (b) Calculate the ratio c / d and compare it to cb / d. State whether the steel yields at failure. [5]
  3. (c) Calculate the factored moment resistance Mr, in kN·m. [5]
  4. (d) Calculate the total factored uniform load, in kN/m including self weight, that the beam can carry over the 6.5 m span. [5]
(a)

The steel area is As = 4 × 500 = 2000 mm². The stress block factor is α1 = 0.85 - 0.0015 × 30 = 0.805. The compression force equals the tension force, so a = φs As fy / (α1 φc fc' b) = 0.85 × 2000 × 400 / (0.805 × 0.65 × 30 × 300). The numerator is 680 000 N. The denominator is 0.805 × 0.65 × 30 × 300 = 4709.3 N/mm. So a = 680 000 / 4709.3 = 144.4 mm. This is the depth of the equivalent rectangular compression zone measured from the top of the beam. It is about 28 percent of the effective depth, which suggests a lightly to moderately reinforced section.

Answer: 144.4 mm

(b)

The depth factor is β1 = 0.97 - 0.0025 × 30 = 0.895. The neutral axis depth is c = a / β1 = 144.4 / 0.895 = 161.3 mm, giving c / d = 161.3 / 520 = 0.310. The balanced value is cb = 700 × 520 / (700 + 400) = 330.9 mm, so cb / d = 0.636. Since the actual c / d of 0.310 is well below 0.636, the neutral axis is above the balanced position, so the steel yields before the concrete crushes. The failure is ductile with ample warning, as desired. The assumption of yielding in the first stress block equation is therefore justified and no iteration is needed.

Answer: 0.310 against 0.636

(c)

With yielding confirmed, the resisting couple has a lever arm of d - a / 2 = 520 - 144.4 / 2 = 447.8 mm. The tension force is φs As fy = 0.85 × 2000 × 400 = 680 000 N = 680 kN. The moment resistance is Mr = 680 × 447.8 = 304 504 kN·mm, or 304.5 kN·m. The compression force in the concrete equals the same 680 kN, as confirmed by the stress block of 144.4 mm. The value is a factored resistance and may be compared directly with the factored moment from the loads. Minimum steel and spacing checks are separate and are not required here.

Answer: 304.5 kN·m

(d)

For a simply supported beam under uniform load the maximum moment is wf L² / 8. Setting this equal to Mr gives wf = 8 Mr / L² = 8 × 304.5 / 6.5² = 2436 / 42.25 = 57.66 kN/m. The load includes the self weight of the beam, which for a section 300 mm by 600 mm at 24 kN/m³ is 4.3 kN/m before factoring, so the usable superimposed factored load is smaller than 57.7 kN/m by the factored self weight. Shear and deflection must also be checked, because flexure alone does not determine the capacity of a beam. The value gives the flexural limit only.

Answer: 57.7 kN/m

A2 Practice Paper 10

Problem 1 [A2-046] Doubly reinforced and T-section concrete beams

A reinforced concrete floor in a parking garage in Ottawa, Ontario is built monolithically, so the beams act as T-sections. One interior beam has an effective flange width bf = 600 mm, a flange thickness hf = 90 mm, a web width bw = 300 mm and an effective depth d = 500 mm. The tension steel is four 30M bars, total area As = 2800 mm². Use fc' = 25 MPa, fy = 400 MPa, φc = 0.65 and φs = 0.85, with α1 = 0.85 - 0.0015 fc'. The equivalent rectangular stress block depth for a rectangular section of width b is a = φs As fy / (α1 φc fc' b). For a T-section whose block extends below the flange, treat the overhanging flange as one resisting couple and the web as a second rectangular section carrying the balance of the steel. Assume the steel yields and that compression steel is not provided.

  1. (a) Compute the stress block depth a assuming the section behaves as a rectangle of width bf, in mm, and state whether it falls inside the flange. [4]
  2. (b) Calculate the compression force Cf in the overhanging flanges, in kN. [4]
  3. (c) Calculate the stress block depth a for the web portion, in mm, using the steel area remaining after the flange couple. [6]
  4. (d) Calculate the factored moment resistance Mr of the T-beam, in kN·m. [6]
(a)

First α1 = 0.85 - 0.0015 × 25 = 0.8125. With a rectangular section of width bf = 600 mm, a = 0.85 × 2800 × 400 / (0.8125 × 0.65 × 25 × 600) = 952 000 / 7921.9 = 120.2 mm. Because this exceeds the flange thickness of 90 mm, the compression zone extends into the web and the assumption of a rectangular section is wrong. The beam must be analysed as a true T-section, with the flange overhangs and web treated separately. The test is simple and guards against overestimating the moment capacity, since a wide rectangular block would assign too much compression area at full strength.

Answer: 120.2 mm

(b)

The overhanging flange parts have width bf - bw = 600 - 300 = 300 mm and thickness 90 mm, so the area in compression is 300 × 90 = 27 000 mm². The stress is α1 φc fc' = 0.8125 × 0.65 × 25 = 13.203 MPa. The compression force is Cf = 13.203 × 27 000 = 356 484 N, or 356.5 kN. This force must be balanced by tension in a portion of the steel. The area of steel needed for that is As1 = Cf / (φs fy) = 356 484 / (0.85 × 400) = 1048.5 mm². The rest of the steel, 2800 - 1048.5 = 1751.5 mm², works with the web rectangle.

Answer: 356.5 kN

(c)

The remaining steel As2 = 1751.5 mm² is balanced by a rectangular block of width bw = 300 mm. Its depth is a = φs As2 fy / (α1 φc fc' bw) = 0.85 × 1751.5 × 400 / (13.203 × 300) = 595 510 / 3960.9 = 150.3 mm. This is measured from the top of the beam and includes the flange thickness, since the web block extends from the top surface through the flange and into the stem. The depth of 150.3 mm is well above the neutral axis limit for yielding of the steel, which is about 0.64 d, so the assumption of yielding is satisfied by a wide margin.

Answer: 150.3 mm

(d)

The moment resistance is the sum of the two couples. The flange couple has force 356.5 kN at lever arm d - hf / 2 = 500 - 45 = 455 mm, giving 356.5 × 0.455 = 162.2 kN·m. The web couple has force φs As2 fy = 0.85 × 1751.5 × 400 = 595.5 kN at lever arm d - a / 2 = 500 - 75.2 = 424.8 mm, giving 595.5 × 0.4248 = 253.0 kN·m. The total is Mr = 162.2 + 253.0 = 415.2 kN·m. This is more than a rectangular beam of width 300 mm with the same steel could provide, and the flange is the reason for the extra capacity.

Answer: 415.2 kN·m

Problem 2 [A2-047] Concrete beam shear and stirrup design

A rectangular concrete transfer beam in an office building in Mississauga, Ontario has a web width bw = 350 mm and an effective depth d = 600 mm. At the critical section near the support the factored shear is Vf = 420 kN. Concrete strength is fc' = 30 MPa and stirrup yield strength is fy = 400 MPa. Use the simplified method with the effective shear depth dv = 0.9 d, resistance factors φc = 0.65 and φs = 0.85, concrete shear resistance Vc = φc λ β √fc' bw dv with λ = 1.0 and β = 0.18, stirrup resistance Vs = φs Av fy dv cot θ / s with θ = 42° and a limiting total shear Vr,max = 0.25 φc fc' bw dv. Stirrups are two-leg 10M, with Av = 200 mm² for the pair. Take fc' in MPa so that √fc' is in MPa as well.

  1. (a) Calculate the concrete contribution Vc, in kN. [5]
  2. (b) Calculate the shear that the stirrups must carry, Vs required, in kN. [4]
  3. (c) Calculate the maximum stirrup spacing s, in mm. [6]
  4. (d) Calculate the maximum shear resistance Vr,max that limits the section, in kN. [5]
(a)

The effective shear depth is dv = 0.9 × 600 = 540 mm. With λ = 1.0 and β = 0.18, the concrete shear resistance is Vc = 0.65 × 1.0 × 0.18 × √30 × 350 × 540. Here √30 = 5.477, so Vc = 0.65 × 0.18 × 5.477 × 350 × 540 = 121 118 N, or 121.1 kN. The term √fc' is capped at 8 MPa in code practice, which is not reached here. The concrete carries only about 29 percent of the factored shear, so the beam clearly needs stirrups, and shear reinforcement cannot be omitted even though the section depth is generous.

Answer: 121.1 kN

(b)

The shear to be carried by the stirrups is the factored shear less the concrete contribution. Vs required = Vf - Vc = 420 - 121.1 = 298.9 kN. This is the factored force that the stirrups crossing a diagonal crack must resist. The result is positive, which confirms stirrups are needed. The value of Vs gives a reasonably high demand, about 71 percent of the total, and next the spacing needed to supply this resistance will be found from the stirrup equation. The check against maximum shear follows afterward so the web does not crush before the stirrups yield.

Answer: 298.9 kN

(c)

Rearranging Vs = φs Av fy dv cot θ / s gives s = φs Av fy dv cot θ / Vs. The cotangent of 42° is 1.1106. The numerator is 0.85 × 200 × 400 × 540 × 1.1106 = 40 779 000 N·mm, using Av = 200 mm². Dividing by Vs = 298 900 N gives s = 136.4 mm. A practical choice is 125 mm to be safe on spacing. The code limit on spacing, 0.7 dv = 378 mm, is not governing here, so the strength requirement sets the spacing. Closer spacing would simply give more shear capacity than needed. At sections farther from the support the demand decreases and the spacing can be relaxed.

Answer: 136 mm

(d)

The upper limit on shear is Vr,max = 0.25 φc fc' bw dv = 0.25 × 0.65 × 30 × 350 × 540 = 921 375 N, or 921.4 kN. This is far above the factored shear of 420 kN, so the web is in no danger of crushing and the section dimensions are adequate. The limit protects against diagonal compression failure in the concrete struts of the truss analogy regardless of how much steel is placed. Because the demand is only 46 percent of Vr,max, the concrete section could be reduced somewhat if other criteria such as flexure allowed.

Answer: 921.4 kN

Problem 3 [A2-048] Reinforced concrete short columns, tied and spiral, with interaction

A ground-floor column in a warehouse in Barrie, Ontario is a short, braced column and is to be designed as concentrically loaded with the minimum eccentricity accounted for by the usual reduction factor. Two alternatives are considered. Option T is a tied column, 400 mm square, with eight 25M bars (500 mm² each). Option S is a spiral column, 450 mm in diameter, also with eight 25M bars. Use fc' = 30 MPa, fy = 400 MPa, φc = 0.65, φs = 0.85 and α1 = 0.85 - 0.0015 fc' = 0.805. The factored axial resistance with no eccentricity is Pr0 = α1 φc fc' (Ag - Ast) + φs fy Ast. The maximum permitted resistance is 0.80 Pr0 for a tied column and 0.85 Pr0 for a spiral column. The factored axial load from the floors above is Pf = 3200 kN.

  1. (a) Calculate Pr0 for the tied column, in kN. [4]
  2. (b) Calculate the maximum permitted factored axial resistance of the tied column, in kN, and state whether it carries Pf. [4]
  3. (c) Calculate the maximum permitted factored axial resistance of the 450 mm spiral column, in kN. [6]
  4. (d) Determine the longitudinal steel area needed in the 400 mm square tied column so that its maximum resistance equals Pf, in mm². [6]
(a)

The gross area of the tied column is Ag = 400 × 400 = 160 000 mm², and the steel area is Ast = 8 × 500 = 4000 mm². The concrete area is 160 000 - 4000 = 156 000 mm². Concrete term: 0.805 × 0.65 × 30 × 156 000 = 2 448 810 N. Steel term: 0.85 × 400 × 4000 = 1 360 000 N. The sum is Pr0 = 3 808 810 N, or 3809 kN. This is the pure axial capacity, which assumes perfectly centred loading. Since real columns always have some accidental eccentricity, the code reduces this value, and the next part applies that reduction. The steel ratio is 2.5 percent, within the permitted range for longitudinal reinforcement.

Answer: 3809 kN

(b)

For a tied column the maximum factored axial resistance is 0.80 Pr0 = 0.80 × 3809 = 3047 kN. This is the largest axial load the column may be assigned, because the reduction factor of 0.80 covers a minimum eccentricity and the lower ductility of tied columns. Comparing with the applied Pf = 3200 kN, the demand exceeds the resistance by 153 kN, or about 5 percent, so the 400 mm tied column with eight 25M bars does not carry the load. The shortfall can be fixed by more steel, a bigger section or higher strength concrete, and part (d) takes the first route.

Answer: 3047 kN

(c)

The spiral column has Ag = π × 450² / 4 = 159 043 mm². The steel area is again 4000 mm², so the concrete area is 155 043 mm². Concrete term: 0.805 × 0.65 × 30 × 155 043 = 2 433 800 N. Steel term is 1 360 000 N as before. So Pr0 = 3 793 800 N, or 3794 kN. The reduction for a spiral column is 0.85 because it has better confinement and more ductile behaviour, so the maximum resistance is 0.85 × 3794 = 3225 kN. This exceeds Pf = 3200 kN, and so the spiral column carries the load with the same steel while using slightly less concrete area than the tied one.

Answer: 3225 kN

(d)

Set 0.80 Pr0 = Pf, so Pr0 = 3200 / 0.80 = 4000 kN. The equation is 4 000 000 = α1 φc fc' (Ag - Ast) + φs fy Ast. Write the concrete stress as k = 0.805 × 0.65 × 30 = 15.698 MPa. Then 4 000 000 = k Ag + Ast (φs fy - k) = 15.698 × 160 000 + Ast (340 - 15.698). The first term is 2 511 700 N. So Ast = (4 000 000 - 2 511 700) / 324.30 = 4589.5 mm². This is a steel ratio of 2.87 percent, below the usual limit of 4 percent, so ten 25M bars would be a reasonable choice, giving 5000 mm² with a margin.

Answer: 4590 mm²

Problem 4 [A2-049] Limit states design: factored loads and load combinations

A steel roof girder over a curling rink in Thunder Bay, Ontario spans 12 m, simply supported. The specified uniformly distributed loads on the girder are dead load D = 6.5 kN/m, snow load S = 8.0 kN/m, wind pressure acting inward W(in) = 2.5 kN/m, and wind suction acting upward W(up) = 5.5 kN/m. Wind pressure and suction are separate load cases that never act together. Use these combinations, which are all stated here: 1.4 D; 1.25 D + 1.5 S + 0.4 W(in); 1.25 D + 1.4 W(in) + 0.5 S; and, for uplift, 0.9 D - 1.4 W(up), with downward loads positive. A designer asks what happens if a revised snow study raises the snow load by 20 percent to 9.6 kN/m, with everything else unchanged.

  1. (a) Determine the governing factored downward load, in kN/m, with S = 8.0 kN/m. [5]
  2. (b) Calculate the factored net load for the uplift case, in kN/m, and state its direction. [5]
  3. (c) With S = 9.6 kN/m, find the percentage increase in the governing factored downward load. [5]
  4. (d) Calculate the maximum factored bending moment in the girder for the revised snow load, in kN·m. [5]
(a)

Evaluate each downward combination. Combination 1: 1.4 × 6.5 = 9.10 kN/m. Combination 2: 1.25 × 6.5 + 1.5 × 8.0 + 0.4 × 2.5 = 8.125 + 12.0 + 1.0 = 21.125 kN/m. Combination 3: 1.25 × 6.5 + 1.4 × 2.5 + 0.5 × 8.0 = 8.125 + 3.5 + 4.0 = 15.625 kN/m. The largest is combination 2 at 21.125 kN/m, in which snow is the principal load and wind pressure the companion. Combination 1 is only relevant where dead load alone dominates, and combination 3 has wind as principal load, but the wind pressure is small compared with the snow here, so it does not govern.

Answer: 21.125 kN/m

(b)

The uplift case checks whether the girder, or its connections, see a net upward force when the dead load is least favourable. The dead load is reduced to 0.9 D because it helps resist the uplift, while wind suction is factored up. Net load = 0.9 × 6.5 - 1.4 × 5.5 = 5.85 - 7.70 = -1.85 kN/m. The negative sign means the net factored load is upward, so there is a net uplift of 1.85 kN/m that the girder bottom flange, bracing and anchorage would have to be checked for. Snow is not included because it may not be present when the wind blows at its design value.

Answer: -1.85 kN/m (upward)

(c)

With S = 9.6 kN/m the combinations change. Combination 2 becomes 8.125 + 1.5 × 9.6 + 1.0 = 8.125 + 14.4 + 1.0 = 23.525 kN/m. Combination 3 becomes 8.125 + 3.5 + 4.8 = 16.425 kN/m, and combination 1 is unchanged. Combination 2 still governs at 23.525 kN/m. The increase is (23.525 - 21.125) / 21.125 = 0.1136, or 11.4 percent. This is smaller than the 20 percent rise in snow load because the dead load term of 8.125 kN/m is unchanged and only the 1.5 S term grows, by 1.5 × 1.6 = 2.4 kN/m. The finding tells the designer that moderate snow revisions have a damped effect on the design load.

Answer: 11.4 percent

(d)

The girder is simply supported and carries a uniform factored load, so the maximum moment at midspan is Mf = wf L² / 8. With wf = 23.525 kN/m and L = 12 m, Mf = 23.525 × 144 / 8 = 3387.6 / 8 = 423.45 kN·m. With the original snow load the moment would have been 21.125 × 144 / 8 = 380.25 kN·m, so the revision adds about 43 kN·m, or 11.4 percent, matching the load increase. The designer would then check whether the selected section has Mr at least equal to this moment, and also check deflection under the unfactored snow load.

Answer: 423.5 kN·m

Problem 5 [A2-050] Resistance factors and reliability in limit states design

A reliability study for a steel tension hanger in a Toronto pedestrian bridge compares the effect of the resistance factor on safety. The nominal dead load effect is Dn = 80 kN and the nominal live load effect is Ln = 120 kN. The factored load is 1.25 Dn + 1.5 Ln, and the member is sized so that φ Rn equals that factored load exactly. Treat the actual dead load as normal with mean 1.05 Dn and coefficient of variation 0.10, and the actual live load as normal with mean 0.80 Ln and coefficient of variation 0.25, independent of one another. The resistance is lognormal with mean 1.10 Rn and coefficient of variation VR = 0.12. Use the first-order estimate of the reliability index β = ln(μR / μQ) / √(VR² + VQ²), where μQ is the mean total load and VQ its coefficient of variation.

  1. (a) Calculate the nominal resistance Rn required for φ = 0.90, in kN. [4]
  2. (b) Calculate the mean total load μQ, in kN. [3]
  3. (c) Calculate the coefficient of variation VQ of the total load. [4]
  4. (d) Calculate the reliability index β for φ = 0.90. [5]
  5. (e) Recalculate β if φ is lowered to 0.80 and the member is resized so that φ Rn again equals the factored load. [4]
(a)

The factored load is 1.25 × 80 + 1.5 × 120 = 100 + 180 = 280 kN. Sizing so that φ Rn equals this value means Rn = 280 / 0.90 = 311.1 kN. This is the nominal resistance, the value a designer would compute from the specified yield strength and the member area before applying the factor. The actual strength will differ because of material overstrength and fabrication variation, which is the reason a mean bias of 1.10 and a coefficient of variation are given for the resistance. The nominal value itself is deterministic and is the starting point for the statistical comparison with the mean resistance.

Answer: 311.1 kN

(b)

The mean dead load is 1.05 × 80 = 84 kN, because dead load is usually well controlled and slightly above nominal. The mean live load is 0.80 × 120 = 96 kN, because the maximum lifetime live load is rarely reached in a given hanger and the mean is below nominal. The mean total load is the sum, μQ = 84 + 96 = 180 kN. This is much smaller than the factored load of 280 kN, which shows how much margin the load factors contain before resistance is considered. The mean is used in the logarithm of the reliability index.

Answer: 180 kN

(c)

The standard deviations are σD = 0.10 × 84 = 8.4 kN and σL = 0.25 × 96 = 24.0 kN. Because the loads are independent, the variances add: σQ² = 8.4² + 24.0² = 70.56 + 576 = 646.56, so σQ = 25.43 kN. Then VQ = σQ / μQ = 25.43 / 180 = 0.1413. The live load contributes about 90 percent of the variance, since its coefficient of variation is more than twice that of the dead load and it is a larger fraction of the total. This explains why the live load factor is larger than the dead load factor in the combination.

Answer: 0.141

(d)

The mean resistance is 1.10 × 311.1 = 342.2 kN. The ratio μR / μQ = 342.2 / 180 = 1.901 and its natural logarithm is 0.6425. The combined variability is √(0.12² + 0.1413²) = √(0.0144 + 0.01996) = 0.1853. So β = 0.6425 / 0.1853 = 3.47. A reliability index of this size corresponds to a probability of failure of roughly 3 in 10 000 over the reference period under the normal approximation, which is typical of the safety level aimed for in limit states codes for ordinary structural members.

Answer: 3.47

(e)

With φ = 0.80 the required Rn = 280 / 0.80 = 350 kN, so the mean resistance is 1.10 × 350 = 385 kN. The mean load and VQ are unchanged. Then ln(385 / 180) = ln 2.139 = 0.7603 and β = 0.7603 / 0.1853 = 4.10. Reducing φ from 0.90 to 0.80 raised Rn by 12.5 percent and raised β from 3.47 to 4.10, so the member is safer but heavier. The what-if shows that the resistance factor trades economy against reliability: it can be calibrated until β reaches the target value chosen by the code writers.

Answer: 4.10

A2 Practice Paper 11

Problem 1 [A2-051] Specified live, snow and rain loads on roofs and floors

A community recreation centre near Sudbury, Ontario has a flat-profile low-slope roof carried by steel purlins spaced 1.5 m apart and spanning 7.2 m, simply supported. Specified snow load is S = Is [Ss (Cb Cw Cs Ca) + Sr]. The 1-in-50-year ground snow load is Ss = 2.4 kPa and the associated rain load is Sr = 0.40 kPa. Use basic roof snow load factor Cb = 0.8, wind exposure factor Cw = 1.0, slope factor Cs = 1.0, accumulation factor Ca = 1.0 and importance factor Is = 1.0. The specified roof dead load is D = 0.90 kPa. Use the factored combination 1.25D + 1.5S for the purlins, and take the load on a purlin as the factored pressure times its spacing.

  1. (a) Calculate the specified roof snow load S in kPa for the stated conditions. [3]
  2. (b) Determine the factored roof pressure from 1.25D + 1.5S, in kPa. [3]
  3. (c) Calculate the maximum factored bending moment Mf in a purlin, in kN·m. [4]
  4. (d) Part of the site is later found to be fully exposed to wind, so Cw is reduced to 0.75 with everything else unchanged. Find the new snow load S and the percentage reduction in Mf compared with part (c). [5]
  5. (e) The owner reclassifies the building to the High importance category, which raises the importance factor to Is = 1.15 (Cw back to 1.0). Find the new factored purlin moment and explain in one sentence why the change in Mf differs from the 15 percent change in Is. [5]
(a)

The specified snow load multiplies the ground snow load by the basic roof factor and the other modifying factors, then adds the rain load, and the whole bracket is scaled by the importance factor. S = Is [Ss (Cb Cw Cs Ca) + Sr] = 1.0 × [2.4 × (0.8 × 1.0 × 1.0 × 1.0) + 0.40]. The product inside the first bracket is 2.4 × 0.8 = 1.92 kPa. Adding the rain load gives 1.92 + 0.40 = 2.32 kPa. Because Is = 1.0 for a normal-importance building, S = 2.32 kPa. The 0.8 basic factor reflects the fact that snow on a large flat roof is typically lighter than on the ground, since some is blown off, while the rain term allows for rain falling on the snowpack.

Answer: 2.32 kPa

(b)

Apply the stated limit states combination to the specified dead and snow pressures. Factored pressure = 1.25 × 0.90 + 1.5 × 2.32. The dead-load term is 1.125 kPa and the snow term is 3.480 kPa, so the sum is 4.605 kPa. For this roof the dead load acts downward together with snow, so both add and no counteracting 0.9D case matters for the gravity check. The snow load clearly dominates the combination because it is more than twice the dead load and carries the larger load factor of 1.5. This 4.605 kPa value is the pressure acting on the horizontal roof area and is the basis for the purlin load in the next part.

Answer: 4.605 kPa

(c)

Convert the roof pressure to a line load on one purlin using the 1.5 m spacing: wf = 4.605 kPa × 1.5 m = 6.9075 kN/m. For a simply supported member under uniform load the maximum moment is at midspan, Mf = wf L² / 8. Substituting L = 7.2 m gives Mf = 6.9075 × 7.2² / 8 = 6.9075 × 51.84 / 8 = 44.76 kN·m. The moment diagram is parabolic with zero at each support. Because the load is already factored, this value is compared directly with the factored bending resistance of the chosen purlin section, which is not requested here. The result is the reference case against which the two what-if changes below are compared.

Answer: 44.76 kN·m

(d)

The exposure factor Cw multiplies only the snowfall term, not the rain term. New S = 1.0 × [2.4 × (0.8 × 0.75) + 0.40] = 2.4 × 0.6 + 0.40 = 1.44 + 0.40 = 1.84 kPa. The factored pressure becomes 1.125 + 1.5 × 1.84 = 3.885 kPa, so wf = 3.885 × 1.5 = 5.8275 kN/m. Then Mf = 5.8275 × 51.84 / 8 = 37.76 kN·m. The reduction relative to part (c) is (44.76 − 37.76) / 44.76 = 0.156, or 15.6 percent. A 25 percent reduction in Cw gives only about a 16 percent reduction in moment because the dead load and the rain load are unaffected by wind exposure, which dilutes the effect.

Answer: 15.6 percent reduction in Mf

(e)

The importance factor multiplies the whole bracket including the rain term. New S = 1.15 × 2.32 = 2.668 kPa. Factored pressure = 1.125 + 1.5 × 2.668 = 1.125 + 4.002 = 5.127 kPa, so wf = 5.127 × 1.5 = 7.6905 kN/m and Mf = 7.6905 × 51.84 / 8 = 49.83 kN·m. This is an 11.3 percent rise over 44.76 kN·m. It is less than the 15 percent increase in Is because only the snow term in the combination is scaled by Is; the dead load of 0.90 kPa, carrying a 1.125 kPa share of the factored pressure, is unchanged, so the total moment rises by a smaller fraction than the snow load alone does.

Answer: 49.83 kN·m

Problem 2 [A2-052] Wind load on a building from reference pressure and coefficients

A single-storey steel-framed warehouse near Windsor, Ontario is 24 m long and 12 m wide in plan, with a flat roof and an eave height of 12 m. Wind blows perpendicular to the 24 m long wall. The external pressure on a surface is p = Iw q Ce Cg Cp, with Iw = 1.0, reference velocity pressure q = 0.45 kPa, gust effect factor Cg = 2.0 for the wall cladding and frame check, and external pressure coefficients Cp = +0.8 on the windward wall and Cp = −0.5 on the leeward wall. For the open terrain site the exposure factor is given as Ce = 0.90, uniform over the wall height, and the rougher site in part d is likewise given as Ce = 0.50; both are site exposure data supplied for this problem and are not looked up from the code. Treat the pressures as uniform over the wall height and use a wind load factor of 1.4. Internal pressure is ignored.

  1. (a) Calculate the windward wall pressure in kPa. [4]
  2. (b) Calculate the magnitude of the leeward wall suction in kPa. [3]
  3. (c) Find the total horizontal wind force on the 24 m long wall pair in kN, and the factored value using 1.4. [5]
  4. (d) A new road makes the surroundings rougher, so the exposure factor falls to Ce = 0.50 with everything else unchanged. Find the new specified force and the percentage reduction. [4]
  5. (e) For the original open-terrain case, find the minimum total dead load of the building, acting at the centre of its 12 m width, needed to resist overturning about the leeward base edge, using 1.4W against 0.9D. Take the factored wind force at 6 m height. [4]
(a)

Apply p = Iw q Ce Cg Cp with the windward coefficient Cp = +0.8. The product is p = 1.0 × 0.45 × 0.90 × 2.0 × 0.8. Multiplying the first three factors gives 0.45 × 0.90 = 0.405 kPa, then × 2.0 gives 0.810 kPa, and the coefficient 0.8 reduces this to 0.648 kPa. The positive sign means pressure acting toward the wall surface. Ce accounts for the wind speed increase with height and terrain roughness, Cg amplifies the pressure for gusts on an element or a small structure, and Cp converts the free stream pressure to the pressure on this particular face of the building. The result is uniform over the wall height by the stated assumption.

Answer: 0.648 kPa

(b)

On the leeward wall Cp = −0.5. So p = 1.0 × 0.45 × 0.90 × 2.0 × (−0.5) = 0.810 × (−0.5) = −0.405 kPa. The negative sign means suction, a pressure acting away from the wall surface, so the magnitude is 0.405 kPa. Both the windward push and the leeward pull act in the same global direction, which is the direction of the wind. This is why the frame resists their sum rather than their difference. The magnitude is smaller than the windward value because the separated wake behind the building is less intense than the stagnation zone in front of it.

Answer: 0.405 kPa

(c)

The net pressure across the building is the windward push plus the leeward suction magnitude: 0.648 + 0.405 = 1.053 kPa. The face area exposed to wind is 24 m × 12 m = 288 m². Specified horizontal force = 1.053 × 288 = 303.3 kN. Multiplying by the load factor, the factored force is 1.4 × 303.3 = 424.6 kN. This is the force that the bracing system or the rigid frames must carry in the direction of the wind and deliver to the foundations. The pressures were treated as uniform over height, so the resultant acts at mid-height, 6 m above the base, which is used in the overturning checks below.

Answer: 303.3 kN specified

(d)

Every pressure scales directly with Ce, so the force scales by 0.50 / 0.90. New specified force = 303.3 × 0.50 / 0.90 = 168.5 kN. The reduction is (303.3 − 168.5) / 303.3 = 0.444, which is 44.4 percent. Expressed directly, the ratio 0.50 / 0.90 = 0.556 means that the force is 55.6 percent of the open-terrain value. A rougher surrounding terrain slows the wind near the ground through friction, which lowers the gust-weighted velocity pressure at wall height. Note that this ratio holds only because Ce is uniform over the height and every other factor is unchanged, so all pressures change by the same factor.

Answer: 44.4 percent reduction

(e)

Overturning about the downwind base edge: the factored wind force 424.6 kN acts 6 m above the base, giving an overturning moment of 424.6 × 6 = 2547 kN·m. The dead load acts through the centre of the 12 m plan width, which is 6 m from the downwind edge, with the stabilizing load factor 0.9. Setting 0.9 D × 6 = 2547 gives D = 2547 / 5.4 = 471.7 kN. A lightweight warehouse commonly weighs less than this, so the design relies on anchors and foundation uplift resistance, a practical conclusion. The same check for the rough-terrain site needs only 55.6 percent of this dead load, showing how strongly exposure drives anchorage design.

Answer: 471.7 kN

Problem 3 [A2-053] Equivalent static seismic base shear and its vertical distribution

A four-storey office building in Ottawa, Ontario has a steel braced-frame system. The seismic weights are 3200 kN at each of the three floor levels, located 4 m, 8 m and 12 m above the base, and 2600 kN at the roof, located 16 m above the base. Use the equivalent static base shear V = S(Ta) Mv IE W / (Rd Ro) with S(Ta) = 0.38, Mv = 1.0, IE = 1.0, ductility modifier Rd = 2.0 and overstrength modifier Ro = 1.3. The fundamental period is below 0.7 s so no top concentrated force is added, and the minimum and maximum limits on V are not governing. Distribute V by Fx = V Wx hx / Σ(Wi hi).

  1. (a) Find the total seismic weight W in kN. [3]
  2. (b) Calculate the design base shear V in kN. [4]
  3. (c) Calculate the lateral forces at the roof and at the 4 m level. [5]
  4. (d) Calculate the base overturning moment of the lateral forces in kN·m. [4]
  5. (e) Conventional construction detailing is chosen instead, so Rd = 1.5 with Ro = 1.3 unchanged. Find the new V and the new roof force, and state the percentage change in V. [4]
(a)

The seismic weight is the sum of the weights assigned to all levels, since the base shear is calculated for the whole structure acting as a system. W = 3200 + 3200 + 3200 + 2600 = 12 200 kN. The roof weight is lower than the typical floor weight because it does not carry partitions or occupant-related loads. Seismic weight in practice includes the full dead load plus a portion of snow and any storage load, but here the question provides the totals, so no further adjustment is needed. This W is carried through both the base shear and the distribution formula, so an error here propagates to every later result.

Answer: 12200 kN

(b)

Use V = S(Ta) Mv IE W / (Rd Ro). The denominator is Rd Ro = 2.0 × 1.3 = 2.6. The numerator is 0.38 × 1.0 × 1.0 × 12 200 = 4636 kN. So V = 4636 / 2.6 = 1783.1 kN. This is about 14.6 percent of the building weight. The division by Rd Ro captures the inelastic energy dissipation and overstrength: the structure is designed for a force well below the elastic demand because it is assumed to yield in a ductile way. If the frame detailing were less ductile, Rd would fall and the design force would rise, as shown in part (e).

Answer: 1783 kN

(c)

First find Σ(Wi hi) = 3200 × 4 + 3200 × 8 + 3200 × 12 + 2600 × 16 = 12 800 + 25 600 + 38 400 + 41 600 = 118 400 kN·m. The roof force is F = 1783.1 × (2600 × 16) / 118 400 = 1783.1 × 41 600 / 118 400 = 626.5 kN. The force at the 4 m level is F = 1783.1 × 12 800 / 118 400 = 192.8 kN. The distribution is triangular-like because the weight times height product grows with height, which mimics the first-mode shape of a regular building. The roof level, with the least weight, still attracts the largest force because it is the highest. The sum of all four forces must equal V as a check.

Answer: 626.5 kN at the roof

(d)

Compute each level force from Fx = V Wx hx / 118 400: F(4 m) = 192.8 kN, F(8 m) = 385.5 kN, F(12 m) = 578.3 kN, F(16 m) = 626.5 kN. Their sum is 1783.1 kN, which confirms V. The overturning moment at the base is Σ Fx hx = 192.8 × 4 + 385.5 × 8 + 578.3 × 12 + 626.5 × 16 = 771 + 3084 + 6940 + 10 024 = 20 819 kN·m. The effective height of the resultant is 20 819 / 1783.1 = 11.7 m. This is the moment the foundation and the braced-frame columns must resist before the factor for foundation rocking reductions that some codes allow, which is not applied here.

Answer: 20819 kN·m

(e)

The denominator becomes Rd Ro = 1.5 × 1.3 = 1.95. V = 4636 / 1.95 = 2377.4 kN. The distribution fractions do not depend on V, so the roof force is 2377.4 × 41 600 / 118 400 = 835.3 kN. The ratio of the new to the old base shear is 2.6 / 1.95 = 1.333, a 33.3 percent increase. Choosing less ductile detailing therefore costs a third more design force, and every member and connection would be sized for it. The trade-off is that the simpler detailing is cheaper to fabricate, but the larger design force usually erases much of that saving in heavier braces and foundations.

Answer: V = 2377 kN, roof force 835.3 kN

Problem 4 [A2-054] Timber beam design for bending, shear and bearing

A glued-laminated timber beam, 130 mm wide by 380 mm deep, forms a floor beam in a lakeside cottage near Muskoka, Ontario. It is simply supported on a clear span of 4.4 m, laterally braced by the floor sheathing, and carries a factored uniformly distributed load of wf = 24 kN/m. Use the following design data. Bending: Mr = φ Fb S KZbg KL with φ = 0.90, Fb = 24.0 MPa, volume (size) factor KZbg = 1.0, taken conservatively with no allowance for beam volume, and KL = 1.0. Shear: Vr = φ Fv (2 Ag / 3) with Fv = 2.0 MPa, checked at a distance equal to the beam depth from the support face. Bearing perpendicular to the grain: Qr = φ Fcp Ab with Fcp = 7.0 MPa and Kzcp = 1.0. Each support has a bearing length of 100 mm.

  1. (a) Calculate the factored bending resistance Mr in kN·m. [4]
  2. (b) Calculate the factored bending moment Mf and the ratio Mf / Mr. [4]
  3. (c) Calculate Vr, the factored shear force Vf at a distance d from the support face, and the ratio Vf / Vr. [4]
  4. (d) Find the minimum bearing length required at each support in mm. [4]
  5. (e) The cottage owner wants the span increased with the same wf = 24 kN/m and the same section. Find the maximum span at which bending is just satisfied, and the Mf / Mr ratio for a span of 5.0 m. [4]
(a)

The section modulus of the rectangle is S = b d² / 6 = 130 × 380² / 6 = 130 × 144 400 / 6 = 3.1287 × 10⁶ mm³. Then Mr = φ Fb S KZbg KL = 0.90 × 24.0 × 3.1287 × 10⁶ × 1.0 × 1.0. Multiplying 0.90 × 24.0 gives 21.6 MPa; times S gives 67.58 × 10⁶ N·mm = 67.58 kN·m.
