  4. (d) Calculate the ratio Mr / Mcr and state whether it is adequate to avoid a sudden failure on first cracking. [3]
  5. (e) Find the maximum factored uniform load, in kN/m, that the beam can carry over the 6.5 m span. [4]
(a)

Horizontal equilibrium requires the concrete compression to equal the steel tension. The steel tension is φs As fy = 0.85 × 1500 × 400 = 510 000 N. The stress block intensity uses α1 = 0.85 - 0.0015 × 30 = 0.805, so the concrete stress is 0.805 × 0.65 × 30 = 15.70 MPa. Setting 15.70 × a × 300 = 510 000 gives a = 510 000 / (15.70 × 300) = 108.3 mm. The block depth is about 20 percent of the effective depth, which means the section is comfortably under-reinforced and the steel will yield before the concrete crushes. That is the failure mode the design method aims for, because yielding gives visible warning. The answer is a = 108.3 mm.

Answer: 108.3 mm

(b)

The internal lever arm is the effective depth less half the block depth, d - a/2 = 540 - 108.3/2 = 485.8 mm. Using the steel force already found, Mr = φs As fy (d - a/2) = 510 000 × 485.8 = 247.8 × 10⁶ N·mm = 247.8 kN·m. The same value is obtained from the concrete side because the two forces are equal and the lever arm is the same. The resistance is a factored value that already contains the reduction factors for both materials, so it is compared directly with factored moments from the load combination. A designer should also confirm that the steel area is not below the minimum needed for cracking control, which part c and d examine. The answer is Mr = 247.8 kN·m.

Answer: 247.8 kN·m

(c)

The modulus of rupture is fr = 0.6 √30 = 3.286 MPa. The gross moment of inertia of the rectangle is Ig = b h³ / 12 = 300 × 600³ / 12 = 5.4 × 10⁹ mm⁴. The tension face is at yt = h/2 = 300 mm from the centroid, so Mcr = fr Ig / yt = 3.286 × 5.4 × 109 / 300 = 59.15 × 10⁶ N·mm = 59.2 kN·m. This ignores the small effect of the transformed steel, which is acceptable for a first estimate. At this moment the tension face begins to crack and the tension that the concrete carried is transferred suddenly to the steel, so the steel must be large enough to take it. The answer is Mcr = 59.2 kN·m.

Answer: 59.2 kN·m

(d)

The ratio is Mr / Mcr = 247.8 / 59.15 = 4.19. A common rule is that the factored resistance should exceed the cracking moment by a margin, with 1.2 being the usual minimum, so that when the section cracks the steel can carry the transferred tension without immediately yielding or fracturing. A ratio of 4.19 is far above that minimum, so the steel is more than enough and the beam will crack gradually, with the steel taking the load, rather than failing suddenly. For lightly reinforced beams the ratio can be below 1.0, and a brittle failure on first cracking is then a real danger. The answer is 4.19, which is adequate.

Answer: 4.19, adequate

(e)

For a simply supported beam under a uniform load the maximum moment is wf L² / 8. Setting this equal to the resistance Mr gives wf = 8 Mr / L² = 8 × 247.8 / 6.5² = 1982.3 / 42.25 = 46.9 kN/m. This is the largest total factored load per metre that the flexural resistance can support, including the beam's own factored weight, so the factored superimposed load must be smaller. Shear, deflection and the support conditions have not been checked in this question, and in a real design any of them can govern before flexure does. The span is the centre-to-centre distance assumed here, and a longer effective span would reduce this value quickly because it varies with the inverse of the span squared. The answer is 46.9 kN/m.

Answer: 46.9 kN/m

Problem 4 [A2-094] Doubly reinforced and T-section concrete beams

A precast inverted-tee style floor beam in an Ottawa transit maintenance building acts as a T-beam with the slab in compression. The effective flange width is b = 1000 mm, the flange thickness is hf = 90 mm, the web width is bw = 320 mm and the effective depth is d = 560 mm. Tension steel is seven 30M bars of 700 mm² each, and there is no compression steel. Use f'c = 30 MPa, fy = 400 MPa, φc = 0.65, φs = 0.85 and stress block intensity α1 φc f'c with α1 = 0.805. Take β1 = 0.97 - 0.0025 f'c = 0.895. Where the block is deeper than the flange, treat the compression as the sum of a flange-overhang force Cf acting over (b - bw) × hf and a web force Cw acting over bw × a, and take moments about the tension steel.

  1. (a) Assume first that the section behaves as a rectangle of width 1000 mm and calculate the block depth a. State whether T-beam behaviour applies. [3]
  2. (b) Calculate the flange-overhang compression force Cf. [4]
  3. (c) Calculate the web compression force Cw and the depth a of the web stress block. [5]
  4. (d) Calculate the factored moment resistance Mr. [5]
  5. (e) Calculate c / d (neutral axis depth over effective depth) and comment on ductility. [3]
(a)

The steel tension is φs As fy = 0.85 × 4900 × 400 = 1 666 000 N. If the beam behaved as a rectangle 1000 mm wide, the concrete compression would be 0.805 × 0.65 × 30 × a × 1000 = 15 698 a newtons. Equating gives a = 1 666 000 / 15 698 = 106.1 mm. This is greater than the flange thickness of 90 mm, so the stress block would extend below the flange into the narrow web, and the rectangular assumption is false. The beam must be analysed as a true T-section, in which the web carries the compression below the flange with a width of only 320 mm. The answer is a = 106.1 mm, so T-beam behaviour applies.

Answer: 106.1 mm, T-beam behaviour applies

(b)

The flange overhangs are the parts of the flange outside the web, with a combined width of b - bw = 1000 - 320 = 680 mm. They are fully stressed over the whole thickness of 90 mm, so the area is 680 × 90 = 61 200 mm². The concrete stress is α1 φc f'c = 0.805 × 0.65 × 30 = 15.70 MPa. The force is therefore Cf = 15.70 × 61 200 = 960 690 N = 960.7 kN. This force is a fixed quantity because the overhangs are always fully compressed once the block passes the underside of the flange. It uses part of the steel tension, and the web must supply the remainder. The answer is Cf = 960.7 kN.

Answer: 960.7 kN

(c)

The steel tension of 1666.0 kN is balanced by Cf plus the web force, so Cw = 1666.0 - 960.7 = 705.3 kN. The web compression acts over the web width bw = 320 mm, so the block depth follows from Cw = 15.70 × a × 320. That gives a = 705 313 / (15.70 × 320) = 140.4 mm. The depth is measured from the top face, so the web stress block extends 50.4 mm below the underside of the flange. The assumption that the flange overhang is fully stressed over 90 mm is consistent, because a is greater than hf. If a had come out smaller than hf the T-beam model would have been inconsistent. The answer is a = 140.4 mm.

Answer: a = 140.4 mm

(d)

Moments are taken about the tension steel. The flange-overhang force Cf acts at the middle of the flange, a distance d - hf/2 = 560 - 45 = 515 mm above the steel. The web force Cw acts at the centroid of its block, a distance d - a/2 = 560 - 70.2 = 489.8 mm above the steel. Then Mr = 960.7 × 0.515 + 705.3 × 0.4898 = 494.8 + 345.5 = 840.2 kN·m. Both terms are positive and the sum is the factored resistance. The flange overhangs carry a bit more than half of the total moment even though they are only part of the cross-section, which shows why a wide flange makes the beam efficient. The answer is Mr = 840.2 kN·m.

Answer: 840.2 kN·m

(e)

The neutral axis depth is c = a / β1 = 140.4 / 0.895 = 156.9 mm. The ratio to the effective depth is c / d = 156.9 / 560 = 0.280. A ratio well below the balanced value, which for 400 MPa steel is about 0.64 at the limit of ductile behaviour, means the steel yields long before the concrete reaches its crushing strain. The beam will therefore show wide cracks and large deflection before it fails, which is the warning behaviour designers want. The assumed yielding of the steel is confirmed, so the equations used are valid. The answer is c / d = 0.280, a ductile section.

Answer: 0.280

Problem 5 [A2-095] Concrete beam shear and stirrup design

A simply supported transfer beam in a Barrie condominium podium has a clear and effective span of 7.0 m measured between support centrelines. It carries a factored uniform load of 48 kN/m (including its own weight) and a single factored concentration of 240 kN at midspan. The section is 350 mm wide and 700 mm deep with an effective depth d = 640 mm. The supports are 300 mm wide. Use f'c = 30 MPa, φc = 0.65, φs = 0.85, fy = 400 MPa. For this problem the shear depth is dv = max(0.9 d, 0.72 h). Concrete contribution Vc = φc × 0.18 √f'c × bw dv. Steel contribution Vs = φs Av fy dv cot θ / s with θ = 35°. Maximum Vr = 0.25 φc f'c bw dv. Maximum spacing is the smaller of 0.7 dv and 600 mm. Stirrups are two-leg 10M, total Av = 200 mm².

  1. (a) Find the factored shear Vf at the critical section, taken a distance dv from the face of the support. [4]
  2. (b) Calculate the concrete contribution Vc. [4]
  3. (c) Find the shear that must be carried by stirrups, Vs required. [3]
  4. (d) Calculate the spacing of 10M two-leg stirrups required by strength. [5]
  5. (e) Calculate the maximum permitted spacing and state the spacing you would adopt, with the check on maximum Vr. [4]
(a)

The support reaction is half of the total factored load: 48 × 7.0 / 2 + 240 / 2 = 168 + 120 = 288 kN. The dv value is the larger of 0.9 × 640 = 576 mm and 0.72 × 700 = 504 mm, so dv = 576 mm. The support is 300 mm wide, so the face of the support is 150 mm from the centreline, and the critical section is 150 + 576 = 726 mm = 0.726 m from the centreline. The concentrated load at midspan is far away, so it does not enter. The distributed load between the support centreline and the section reduces the shear: Vf = 288 - 48 × 0.726 = 288 - 34.85 = 253.2 kN. The answer is 253.2 kN.

Answer: 253.2 kN

(b)

Using the stated simplified expression, Vc = φc × 0.18 × √f'c × bw × dv. Here √30 = 5.477, so Vc = 0.65 × 0.18 × 5.477 × 350 × 576 N. Multiplying: 0.65 × 0.18 = 0.117; 0.117 × 5.477 = 0.6408; 0.6408 × 350 = 224.3; 224.3 × 576 = 129 190 N, which is 129.2 kN. The factor 0.18 is a simplified value that stands for the shear that cracked concrete can still transfer through aggregate interlock and the compression zone, and it is stated rather than looked up. Because this is a resistance already including φc, it is compared directly with Vf. The answer is Vc = 129.2 kN.

Answer: 129.2 kN

(c)

The total factored shear is 253.2 kN and the concrete supplies 129.2 kN, so the stirrups must supply the difference: Vs = Vf - Vc = 253.2 - 129.2 = 124.0 kN. This difference is a factored force, so it already includes the resistance factor φs inside the stirrup equation that follows and is set equal to the left side directly. If Vf were smaller than Vc the beam would need only minimum stirrups, but here the stirrups share the load roughly equally with the concrete, which is typical for a transfer beam carrying a heavy point load. The answer is Vs = 124.0 kN.

Answer: 124.0 kN

(d)

Rearranging Vs = φs Av fy dv cot θ / s gives s = φs Av fy dv cot θ / Vs. The cotangent of 35° is 1.428. Substituting, s = 0.85 × 200 × 400 × 576 × 1.428 / 124 000. The numerator is 0.85 × 200 = 170; 170 × 400 = 68 000; 68 000 × 576 = 39.17 × 10⁶; 39.17 × 106 × 1.428 = 55.93 × 10⁶. Dividing by 124 000 N gives s = 451 mm. This is the largest spacing that gives enough steel strength, but spacing limits for crack control can be stricter, which is why part e is required. The answer is s = 451 mm.

Answer: 451 mm

(e)

The maximum spacing is the smaller of 0.7 dv = 0.7 × 576 = 403.2 mm and 600 mm, so it is 403.2 mm. This is smaller than the 451 mm required by strength, so the spacing limit governs, and a bar spacing of 400 mm is adopted, rounding down to a convenient dimension. The upper limit on shear is Vr,max = 0.25 × 0.65 × 30 × 350 × 576 = 982 800 N = 982.8 kN, which is far greater than Vf = 253.2 kN, so the section is not crushed in the web and the dimensions are adequate. Spacing at the limit is acceptable here because Vf is well below the maximum. The answer is a maximum spacing of 403 mm, adopt 400 mm.

Answer: 403 mm; adopt 400 mm

A2 Practice Paper 20

Problem 1 [A2-096] Reinforced concrete short columns, tied and spiral, with interaction

A structural designer for a Thunder Bay parkade compares two short column options carrying the same load. Option T is a tied square column, 450 mm by 450 mm, with eight 25M bars (500 mm² each). Option S is a round spiral column of 500 mm diameter with the same eight 25M bars. Use f'c = 30 MPa, fy = 400 MPa, φc = 0.65, φs = 0.85 and α1 = 0.805. The maximum axial resistance for design is Pr,max = 0.80 [α1 φc f'c (Ag - Ast) + φs fy Ast] for a tied column and 0.85 [same bracket] for a spiral column. For Option T, the pure-bending resistance is given as Mro = 290 kN·m, and a simplified straight-line interaction Mr = Mro (1 - Pf / Pr,max) may be used for axial loads up to Pr,max.

  1. (a) Calculate Pr,max for Option T. [5]
  2. (b) Calculate the steel ratio ρ = Ast / Ag for Option T, as a percentage. [2]
  3. (c) Calculate Pr,max for Option S. [5]
  4. (d) For Option T, calculate the moment resistance available together with a factored axial load Pf = 1800 kN. [5]
  5. (e) Calculate the ratio of Pr,max per unit gross area for Option S to that of Option T, and comment. [3]
(a)

For the tied column, Ag = 450 × 450 = 202 500 mm² and Ast = 8 × 500 = 4000 mm². The concrete term is α1 φc f'c (Ag - Ast) = 0.805 × 0.65 × 30 × (202 500 - 4000) = 15.70 × 198 500 = 3 116 000 N. The steel term is φs fy Ast = 0.85 × 400 × 4000 = 1 360 000 N. The sum is 4 476 000 N, and multiplying by 0.80 for the tied column gives Pr,max = 3 581 000 N = 3581 kN. The factor 0.80 caps the capacity to allow for unavoidable accidental eccentricity, so the column is never designed for a purely concentric load. The answer is Pr,max = 3581 kN.

Answer: 3581 kN

(b)

The steel ratio is the area of steel divided by the gross area of the column section: ρ = Ast / Ag = 4000 / 202 500 = 0.01975, which is 1.98 percent. This is inside the usual limits, which require at least about 1 percent so that the column has some ductility and the long-term creep of the concrete does not shift all the load onto the steel, and at most 8 percent under CSA A23.3, with 4 percent or less preferred so the bars can be placed and the concrete can be consolidated. Eight bars in a square column give one bar at each corner and one at the middle of each face, a standard arrangement for tie support. The answer is 1.98 percent.

Answer: 1.98 percent

(c)

The round column has a gross area of π × 500² / 4 = 196 350 mm², and Ast is still 4000 mm². The concrete term is 15.70 × (196 350 - 4000) = 15.70 × 192 350 = 3 020 000 N. Adding the same steel term of 1 360 000 N gives 4 380 000 N. The spiral column uses the larger factor 0.85, so Pr,max = 0.85 × 4 380 000 = 3 722 000 N = 3722 kN. The higher factor is allowed because a continuous spiral confines the core and gives the column more ductility after the cover spalls than separate ties do. The answer is Pr,max = 3722 kN.

Answer: 3722 kN

(d)

The stated interaction line connects the pure-bending point (P = 0, M = Mro) to the maximum axial point (P = Pr,max, M = 0). At Pf = 1800 kN the available moment is Mr = Mro (1 - Pf / Pr,max) = 290 × (1 - 1800 / 3581) = 290 × (1 - 0.5026) = 290 × 0.4974 = 144.2 kN·m. This is a simplification, because the true interaction curve is bulged and the balanced point carries more moment than a straight line suggests, so the line is conservative at moderate axial loads. A moment larger than 144.2 kN·m together with 1800 kN would need a larger section or more steel. The answer is Mr = 144.2 kN·m.

Answer: 144.2 kN·m

(e)

The capacity per unit of gross area is 3722 kN / 196 350 mm² = 0.018957 kN/mm² for the spiral column and 3581 / 202 500 = 0.017684 kN/mm² for the tied column. The ratio is 0.018957 / 0.017684 = 1.072. The spiral column is therefore about 7 percent more efficient per unit of section area, even though it uses the same bars, because of the higher 0.85 factor and the smaller area. The spiral costs more to fabricate and the round form costs more to build, so the saving in section size has to be weighed against labour. The answer is a ratio of 1.07.

Answer: 1.07

Problem 2 [A2-097] Limit states design: factored loads and load combinations

A column in a Windsor distribution centre supports a mezzanine floor and a lightweight roof platform for rooftop equipment. The specified (unfactored) axial effects at the base are: dead load D = 210 kN compression, floor live load L = 120 kN compression, snow load S = 65 kN compression, and wind W = 260 kN of uplift (tension). The load combinations to be used are: (1) 1.4 D; (2) 1.25 D + 1.5 L + 0.5 S; (3) 1.25 D + 1.5 S + 0.5 L; (4) 0.9 D + 1.4 W, with compression taken as positive. The load factors are stated here and are not to be looked up. The designer is uncertain about the floor use and wants to see how sensitive the design is to the live load.

  1. (a) Calculate the factored compression for combinations 1, 2 and 3, and state the governing factored compression Pf. [4]
  2. (b) Calculate the factored axial force from combination 4 and give the design tension force for the anchor bolts. [4]
  3. (c) If the floor use changes so that L doubles to 240 kN, calculate the new governing factored compression. [4]
  4. (d) Calculate the percentage increase in governing factored load caused by doubling L, and compare it with the 100 percent increase in L. [4]
  5. (e) Explain, in words, why the dead load factor is 1.25 in combination 2 but 0.9 in combination 4. [4]
(a)

Combination 1 gives 1.4 × 210 = 294 kN. Combination 2 gives 1.25 × 210 + 1.5 × 120 + 0.5 × 65 = 262.5 + 180 + 32.5 = 475 kN. Combination 3 gives 1.25 × 210 + 1.5 × 65 + 0.5 × 120 = 262.5 + 97.5 + 60 = 420 kN. The largest value governs, so Pf = 475 kN from combination 2, where the floor live load is the principal variable load and snow is the companion load. Combination 1 is the dead-load-only case and is nearly always lower when a live load is present, which is the situation here. Each combination is a separate check, and all must be run because the principal load changes. The answer is Pf = 475 kN.

Answer: 475 kN (combination 2)

(b)

In combination 4 the dead load is a stabilizing action that opposes uplift, so it is factored down to 0.9 of its specified value, and the wind uplift is factored up to 1.4. With compression positive and uplift negative, 0.9 × 210 - 1.4 × 260 = 189 - 364 = -175 kN. The negative sign means a net tension of 175 kN at the column base. The anchor bolts and base plate must therefore be designed for a factored tension of 175 kN, which is a different design case from the compression in part a. The column and footing must be checked for uplift resistance as well, using the same combination, and the sign of the result is the point of the exercise. The answer is 175 kN tension.

Answer: 175 kN tension

(c)

With L = 240 kN, combination 2 becomes 1.25 × 210 + 1.5 × 240 + 0.5 × 65 = 262.5 + 360 + 32.5 = 655 kN. Combination 3 becomes 262.5 + 97.5 + 0.5 × 240 = 480 kN, and combination 1 is still 294 kN, so combination 2 continues to govern. The governing factored compression is 655 kN. This is the number the column would have to be designed for if the mezzanine were later used for heavy storage, which is exactly the kind of change of use that an owner might make without realizing the structural consequence. The answer is 655 kN.

Answer: 655 kN

(d)

The increase in governing load is (655 - 475) / 475 = 180 / 475 = 0.379, which is 37.9 percent. The live load itself went up by 100 percent, but the factored column load rose by much less, because the dead load of 210 kN and the snow load are unchanged and make up a large part of the total. Only the live term, 1.5 × 120 = 180 kN, moved, and it moved by 180 kN. The sensitivity is therefore 0.379 / 1.00 = 0.38 percent of design load per percent of live load. For a heavily dead-loaded column the margin hides some uncertainty, but a column that is dominated by live load would respond much more strongly. The answer is 37.9 percent.

Answer: 37.9 percent

(e)

Limit states design uses different load factors depending on whether a load helps or hurts the check being made. In combination 2 the column is checked for compression, so the dead load adds to the demand, and it carries a factor of 1.25 to cover the possibility that the dead load is heavier than the specified value. In combination 4 the check is for uplift, and the dead load now acts against the wind and helps the column stay down. A higher dead load would make the case safer, so the unfavourable direction is that the dead load is smaller than specified. The factor is therefore reduced to 0.9, which covers the chance that some of the dead load, such as removable finishes or equipment, is absent when the wind blows.

Answer: Dead load helps resist uplift, so its factor is reduced for that case.

Problem 3 [A2-098] Resistance factors and reliability in limit states design

A steel hanger rod in a Peterborough arena roof is designed so that φ Rn = 1.25 Dn + 1.5 Ln, where the nominal dead load is Dn = 40 kN and the nominal live load is Ln = 60 kN, with φ = 0.90. Statistics for the loads: dead load has mean 1.05 Dn and coefficient of variation 0.10; live load has mean 0.90 Ln and coefficient of variation 0.25. Resistance has mean 1.10 Rn and coefficient of variation VR = 0.12. Treat the loads as independent, add their variances, and use the lognormal reliability index β = ln(Rm / Sm) / √(VR² + VS²), where Rm and Sm are the mean resistance and mean total load effect and VS is the coefficient of variation of the total load effect. The target reliability index for this member is β = 3.5.

  1. (a) Calculate the mean total load effect Sm and its coefficient of variation VS. [4]
  2. (b) Calculate the nominal resistance Rn and the reliability index β achieved with φ = 0.90. [6]
  3. (c) Find the resistance factor φ that would make β = 3.5 exactly for this load ratio. [5]
  4. (d) If a poorer fabrication quality raises VR to 0.18 while the design stays as in part b, calculate the new β and comment. [5]
(a)

The mean dead load is 1.05 × 40 = 42 kN and the mean live load is 0.90 × 60 = 54 kN, so the mean total is Sm = 42 + 54 = 96 kN. The standard deviations are 0.10 × 42 = 4.2 kN for the dead load and 0.25 × 54 = 13.5 kN for the live load. Independent variances add: 4.2² + 13.5² = 17.64 + 182.25 = 199.89 kN², and the standard deviation of the total is 14.14 kN. Dividing by the mean gives VS = 14.14 / 96 = 0.1473. The live load supplies about 91 percent of the variance even though it is only 56 percent of the mean, which is why live-load uncertainty dominates reliability in many structures. The answer is Sm = 96 kN and VS = 0.147.

Answer: Sm = 96 kN, VS = 0.1473

(b)

The design equation gives φ Rn = 1.25 × 40 + 1.5 × 60 = 50 + 90 = 140 kN, so Rn = 140 / 0.90 = 155.6 kN. The mean resistance is Rm = 1.10 × 155.6 = 171.1 kN. Then ln(Rm / Sm) = ln(171.1 / 96) = ln(1.7824) = 0.5780. The combined coefficient of variation is √(0.12² + 0.1473²) = √(0.0144 + 0.0217) = √0.0361 = 0.1900. The reliability index is β = 0.5780 / 0.1900 = 3.04. This is below the target of 3.5 for this member, so the design as written is less reliable than the target for this particular ratio of live to dead load, even though it satisfies the design equation. The answer is Rn = 155.6 kN and β = 3.04.

Answer: Rn = 155.6 kN, β = 3.04

(c)

To obtain β = 3.5 the mean resistance must satisfy Rm = Sm exp(β √(VR² + VS²)) = 96 × exp(3.5 × 0.1900) = 96 × exp(0.665) = 96 × 1.9446 = 186.7 kN. The nominal resistance is Rm / 1.10 = 169.7 kN. The factored load is still 140 kN, so the resistance factor needed is φ = 140 / 169.7 = 0.825. The factor 0.825 is lower than 0.90, and it shows that a higher target index must be bought with a lower resistance factor, which means more material for the same load. A single φ for all members can only be an average, so members dominated by live load are under-designed relative to the target. The answer is φ = 0.825.

Answer: 0.825

(d)

The design is unchanged, so Rm remains 171.1 kN and ln(Rm / Sm) remains 0.5780. The combined coefficient of variation becomes √(0.18² + 0.1473²) = √(0.0324 + 0.0217) = √0.0541 = 0.2326. Then β = 0.5780 / 0.2326 = 2.49. The reliability index fell from 3.04 to 2.49, which is a large drop for a change in a single scatter parameter, and 2.49 is well below the target of 3.5. In practical terms the probability of failure rises by a factor of about five, from roughly 1.2 × 10-3 to 6.4 × 10-3. This demonstrates why resistance factors are tied to a stated level of quality control, and why poor workmanship cannot be fixed afterwards by calculation alone. The answer is β = 2.49.

Answer: 2.49

Problem 4 [A2-099] Specified live, snow and rain loads on roofs and floors

A school gymnasium in Timmins has a flat roof carried by steel beams spaced 3.0 m apart and spanning 9.0 m simply supported. The specified roof snow load is S = Is [Ss (Cb Cw Cs Ca) + Sr], with importance factor Is = 1.0, ground snow load Ss = 2.4 kPa, associated rain load Sr = 0.4 kPa, basic roof snow load factor Cb = 0.8, wind exposure factor Cw = 1.0, slope factor Cs = 0.85 and accumulation factor Ca = 1.0. The roof dead load is 1.1 kPa. The roof beam uses the combination 1.25 D + 1.5 S. For a column supporting floor area in the same school, the specified floor live load is 4.8 kPa and the reduction factor for a tributary area A (in m²) larger than 20 m² is R = 0.3 + √(9.8 / A).

  1. (a) Calculate the specified roof snow load S. [4]
  2. (b) Calculate the maximum factored bending moment in one roof beam under 1.25 D + 1.5 S. [6]
  3. (c) A floor column has a tributary area of 85 m². Calculate the reduction factor R and the reduced specified live load. [5]
  4. (d) The designer asks what happens if the roof is treated as fully exposed with Cb = 1.0 instead of 0.8. Calculate the new S and the percentage change. [5]
(a)

The snow load has two parts: the snow that sits on the roof, which is the ground snow load adjusted by the roof factors, and the rain that falls with it. The adjusted snow is Ss Cb Cw Cs Ca = 2.4 × 0.8 × 1.0 × 0.85 × 1.0 = 1.632 kPa. Adding the associated rain load gives 1.632 + 0.4 = 2.032 kPa. Multiplying by the importance factor of 1.0 leaves S = 2.032 kPa, or 2.03 kPa. The basic factor Cb of 0.8 reflects the fact that wind sweeps snow off a large flat roof, so the roof carries less than the ground does. The slope factor of 0.85 is the allowance for slipperiness or slope given in the statement. The answer is S = 2.03 kPa.

Answer: 2.03 kPa

(b)

The factored area load on the roof is 1.25 × 1.1 + 1.5 × 2.032 = 1.375 + 3.048 = 4.423 kPa. A beam collects load from a strip equal to its spacing, 3.0 m, so the line load is 4.423 × 3.0 = 13.27 kN/m. For a simply supported beam under uniform load, the maximum moment at midspan is Mf = w L² / 8 = 13.27 × 9.0² / 8 = 13.27 × 81 / 8 = 134.3 kN·m. This uses the tributary width of 3.0 m for every beam, an acceptable assumption for interior beams with equal spacing. It neglects the beam's own weight, which would add a little to the dead load and so to the moment. The answer is Mf = 134.3 kN·m.

Answer: 134.3 kN·m

(c)

The tributary area is 85 m², which is greater than 20 m², so the stated reduction applies. The factor is R = 0.3 + √(9.8 / 85) = 0.3 + √0.1153 = 0.3 + 0.3396 = 0.640. The reduced live load is 0.640 × 4.8 = 3.07 kPa. The reduction exists because it is unlikely that every square metre of a large floor area carries its full specified load at the same moment, so the average over a big area is lower. The reduction does not apply to the load on a small area such as a single slab panel. A column collecting load from several floors would also have a floor-count reduction in a code, but that is not part of this question. The answer is 3.07 kPa.

Answer: R = 0.640, 3.07 kPa

(d)

With Cb = 1.0 the adjusted snow is 2.4 × 1.0 × 1.0 × 0.85 × 1.0 = 2.04 kPa, and adding the rain load gives S = 2.04 + 0.4 = 2.44 kPa. The change from the original 2.032 kPa is (2.44 - 2.032) / 2.032 = 0.408 / 2.032 = 0.201, an increase of 20.1 percent. This applies to the snow load alone, and the effect on the roof beam moment would be smaller because dead load is unchanged. The comparison is informative because Cb = 0.8 is only allowed where the roof is wide and exposed, so a designer should confirm the surroundings of the school before relying on it. If trees or taller buildings shelter the roof, the full factor of 1.0 is appropriate. The answer is S = 2.44 kPa, a 20.1 percent increase.

Answer: 2.44 kPa, increase of 20.1 percent

Problem 5 [A2-100] Wind load on a building from reference pressure and coefficients

A 30 m tall rectangular building in open terrain near Chatham has a plan of 24 m width facing the wind and a depth of 40 m. The reference velocity pressure is q = 0.48 kPa. The external pressure p = q Ce Cg Cp, with gust factor Cg = 2.0, exposure factor for open terrain Ce = (h / 10)0.2 with h in metres (not less than 0.9), windward wall Cp = +0.8 and leeward wall Cp = -0.5. As a simplification, use Ce evaluated at the full building height H for the entire height, giving uniform pressures, and treat the building as a rigid block. The wind load factor is 1.4, and the total wind force acts at mid-height. Ignore roof forces and internal pressure.

  1. (a) Calculate Ce at the building height of 30 m. [3]
  2. (b) Calculate the windward wall pressure p. [3]
  3. (c) Calculate the total (unfactored) base shear on the building, adding the windward pressure and the leeward suction. [5]
  4. (d) Calculate the factored overturning moment at the base, taking the resultant at mid-height. [4]
  5. (e) If the building were 36 m tall with the same plan, calculate the percentage change in unfactored base shear and explain why it is not proportional to the height ratio. [5]
(a)

The exposure factor for open terrain is given as Ce = (h / 10)0.2. For h = 30 m, h / 10 = 3.0, so Ce = 3.00.2. Taking logarithms, ln 3.0 = 1.0986, multiplying by 0.2 gives 0.2197, and exp(0.2197) = 1.2457. The result is greater than the stated lower limit of 0.9, so it is used as calculated. The factor is greater than 1 because wind speed rises with height above ground, and the value at 30 m is about 25 percent higher than the reference at 10 m. Using the top value over the full height, as the question instructs, is conservative because lower floors in reality see lower wind. The answer is Ce = 1.246.

Answer: 1.246

(b)

The windward wall pressure is p = q Ce Cg Cp = 0.48 × 1.2457 × 2.0 × 0.8. Multiplying step by step: 0.48 × 1.2457 = 0.5979; 0.5979 × 2.0 = 1.1958; 1.1958 × 0.8 = 0.9567 kPa. The pressure is positive, meaning it pushes against the wall. The gust factor of 2.0 raises the average pressure to account for short, strong gusts that a rigid building responds to almost instantly. This is a uniform pressure over the 30 m height by the simplification stated, so the windward wall load is 0.957 kPa on every square metre. The answer is p = 0.957 kPa.

Answer: 0.957 kPa

(c)

The leeward suction is p = 1.1958 × 0.5 = 0.598 kPa, taken as a magnitude, because Cp is negative and acts away from the wall, in the same direction as the windward push on the building as a whole. The sum of windward and leeward pressures is 0.957 + 0.598 = 1.555 kPa. The area facing the wind is the width times the height, 24 × 30 = 720 m². Base shear is V = 1.555 × 720 = 1119 kN. The side walls and the roof also feel wind, but the question tells us to neglect roof forces, and side walls carry no force in the direction of the wind in this simple model. The answer is V = 1119 kN.

Answer: 1119 kN

(d)

The factored base shear is 1.4 × 1119.4 = 1567.1 kN. The total force acts at mid-height, 30 / 2 = 15 m above the base, because the pressure is uniform over the height. The factored overturning moment at the base is Mf = 1567.1 × 15 = 23 507 kN·m. This moment must be resisted by the combined dead-load restoring moment and the foundation, using the dead load factor of 0.9 for the stabilizing action, which is the check that governs the uplift at the windward edge of the foundation. A real wind load would vary with height, so the true resultant would act a little higher than mid-height. The answer is 23 507 kN·m.

Answer: 23 507 kN·m

(e)

For H = 36 m, Ce = 3.60.2 = exp(0.2 × ln 3.6) = exp(0.2 × 1.2809) = exp(0.2562) = 1.2920. The combined coefficient is 0.8 + 0.5 = 1.3, so the pressure sum is 0.48 × 1.2920 × 2.0 × 1.3 = 1.6124 kPa. The area is 24 × 36 = 864 m², so V = 1.6124 × 864 = 1393 kN. The change is (1393 - 1119.4) / 1119.4 = 0.2446, an increase of 24.5 percent. The height ratio is 36 / 30 = 1.20, which gives only 20 percent more area, but the exposure factor also rises with height by 1.292 / 1.2457 = 1.037, and the two effects multiply: 1.20 × 1.037 = 1.245. The load therefore grows faster than height alone. The answer is a 24.5 percent increase.

Answer: 24.5 percent increase

A2 Practice Paper 21

Problem 1 [A2-101] Equivalent static seismic base shear and its vertical distribution

A four-storey steel moment-frame library in Ottawa has a roof height hn = 18.0 m, with storeys 4.5 m high. Seismic weights are W1 = W2 = W3 = 3200 kN at levels 1 to 3 and W4 = 2600 kN at the roof. Use the equivalent static force method with V = S(Ta) Mv Ie W / (Rd Ro), where Mv = 1.0, Ie = 1.3 (high importance category), Rd = 3.5 and Ro = 1.3, where the Rd and Ro values are given for this exercise only. The period is Ta = 0.085 hn3/4 s. The design spectral acceleration S(T) is linear between S(0.2) = 0.60, S(0.5) = 0.45, S(1.0) = 0.25 and S(2.0) = 0.12. V need not exceed (2/3) S(0.2) Ie W/(Rd Ro) and shall not be less than S(2.0) Ie W/(Rd Ro). The top-level force is Ft = 0.07 Ta V if Ta > 0.7 s (maximum 0.25 V), and Fx = (V − Ft) Wx hx / Σ(Wi hi).

  1. (a) Find the period Ta and the interpolated S(Ta). [4]
  2. (b) Find the design base shear V, checking both limits. [5]
  3. (c) Find Ft and the total design force F4 at the roof level. [6]
  4. (d) The owner proposes a less ductile system with Rd = 2.0 and Ro = 1.3. Find the new base shear and comment on cost against the ductile choice. [5]
(a)

Ta = 0.085 × 180.75 = 0.085 × 8.739 = 0.743 s. Because 0.5 s < Ta < 1.0 s, I interpolate linearly between S(0.5) = 0.45 and S(1.0) = 0.25: S = 0.45 + (0.25 − 0.45)(0.743 − 0.5)/(1.0 − 0.5) = 0.45 − 0.4 × 0.243 = 0.45 − 0.097 = 0.353 g. The slope of the spectrum is negative here, so a period longer than 0.5 s lowers the demand. The period exceeds 0.7 s, which will matter later because it triggers the whiplash top force Ft. Checking the sign of the interpolation, S must lie between 0.25 and 0.45, and 0.353 does.

Answer: Ta = 0.743 s, S = 0.353 g

(b)

Total weight W = 3 × 3200 + 2600 = 12 200 kN. The unlimited base shear is V = S Mv Ie W/(Rd Ro) = 0.353 × 1.0 × 1.3 × 12 200/(3.5 × 1.3) = 5598/4.55 = 1230 kN. Upper limit: (2/3) × 0.60 × 1.3 × 12 200/4.55 = 1394 kN. Lower limit: 0.12 × 1.3 × 12 200/4.55 = 418 kN. Since 418 < 1230 < 1394, neither limit governs and the calculated value stands. The limits matter for long-period or very stiff buildings; here the building is in the descending part of the spectrum so the formula result is accepted. V ≈ 1230 kN is about 10.1 percent of the seismic weight.

Answer: V = 1230 kN

(c)

Since Ta = 0.743 s > 0.7 s, Ft = 0.07 × 0.743 × 1230 = 64.0 kN, which is below the cap 0.25 V = 307 kN. Σ Wi hi = 3200 × 4.5 + 3200 × 9.0 + 3200 × 13.5 + 2600 × 18.0 = 14 400 + 28 800 + 43 200 + 46 800 = 133 200 kN·m. The roof share of the remaining shear is (V − Ft) W4 h4/Σ = (1230 − 64.0) × 46 800/133 200 = 1166 × 0.3514 = 409.7 kN. Total roof force F4 = Ft + 409.7 = 473.7 kN. Ft is added at the roof only, representing higher-mode response in a flexible building, so the force at the top is largest and forces increase linearly in height elsewhere.

Answer: F4 = 474 kN

(d)

With Rd = 2.0 and Ro = 1.3 the divisor falls to 2.6 so V = 0.353 × 1.3 × 12 200/2.6 = 2153 kN. Limits become 732 kN and 2440 kN, so the calculated value again governs. The ratio 2153/1230 = 1.75 means the frame must resist 75 percent more lateral force. Less ductile detailing is cheaper per connection, but members, bases and foundations would all be sized for the larger force, and the saving in detailing rarely offsets the extra steel and foundation cost. A ductile system (Rd = 3.5) lets the frame yield in a controlled way, so I would recommend it unless the connections cannot be detailed to deliver that ductility.

Answer: V = 2150 kN

Problem 2 [A2-102] Timber beam design for bending, shear and bearing

A simply supported No. 1 spruce floor beam of rectangular section 140 mm wide by 300 mm deep spans 4.80 m in a storage mezzanine in a Sudbury warehouse. It carries a factored uniform load of 9.5 kN/m including self-weight. Design values in this problem: φ = 0.90, specified bending strength fb = 16.5 MPa, shear strength fv = 1.5 MPa, compression perpendicular to grain fcp = 5.3 MPa. All modification factors for load duration, service condition, size and lateral support equal 1.0. Factored bending resistance Mr = φ fb S, shear resistance Vr = φ fv (2/3) A, and bearing resistance Qr = φ fcp b lb. Design shear is taken at a distance d from the face of each support. The beam bears 90 mm on each support.

  1. (a) Find Mr and state whether the beam passes in bending. [5]
  2. (b) Find Vr and the factored shear at distance d from the support, and state the ratio Vf/Vr. [5]
  3. (c) Find the minimum bearing length needed at each support. [4]
  4. (d) Find the largest factored uniform load w the beam can carry, and state which check governs. [6]
(a)

Section modulus S = b d²/6 = 140 × 300²/6 = 2.10 × 10⁶ mm³. Resistance Mr = φ fb S = 0.90 × 16.5 × 2.10 × 10⁶ = 31.19 × 10⁶ N·mm = 31.2 kN·m. The factored moment is Mf = w L²/8 = 9.5 × 4.8²/8 = 27.4 kN·m. Because Mr > Mf (utilisation 0.88), the beam passes in bending. All modification factors are 1.0 as instructed, so no reduction for size or lateral stability enters. In practice the 300 mm depth to 140 mm width ratio of 2.1 would need no lateral bracing beyond the floor sheathing, which supports the factor of 1.0.

Answer: Mr = 31.2 kN·m, passes

(b)

Area A = 140 × 300 = 42 000 mm². Vr = φ fv (2/3) A = 0.90 × 1.5 × (2/3) × 42 000 = 37 800 N = 37.8 kN. The reaction is R = wL/2 = 9.5 × 4.8/2 = 22.8 kN. Shear is evaluated at d = 0.30 m from the support face, giving Vf = w (L/2 − d) = 9.5 × (2.40 − 0.30) = 19.95 kN. The ratio Vf/Vr = 19.95/37.8 = 0.53, so shear is not critical. Taking shear at d is a standard allowance for the compression strut that forms near a support; the load within d goes directly into the bearing rather than being resisted as shear in the member.

Answer: Vr = 37.8 kN, Vf = 19.95 kN

(c)

Reaction R = 22.8 kN. The bearing resistance per unit length is φ fcp b = 0.90 × 5.3 × 140 = 667.8 N/mm. Setting Qr = R gives lb = 22 800/667.8 = 34.1 mm. The supplied 90 mm exceeds this by a factor of 2.6, so crushing of the wood perpendicular to the grain is not a concern; the practical minimum would be set by the support detail rather than by this calculation. If the beam sat on a 38 mm plate the bearing would still be adequate, which is the usual reason bearing is checked: to size the plate or post cap under it.

Answer: lb = 34.1 mm

(d)

Each check gives a limiting uniform load. Bending: w = 8 Mr/L² = 8 × 31.19/4.8² = 10.83 kN/m. Shear at d: w = Vr/(L/2 − d) = 37.8/2.10 = 18.0 kN/m. Bearing at 90 mm: Qr = 60.1 kN, so w = 2 × 60.1/4.8 = 25.0 kN/m. The smallest is 10.83 kN/m, so bending governs and the beam has about 14 percent reserve over the applied 9.5 kN/m. Deflection under service load is not requested here, but should be checked before accepting the section for a floor.

Answer: w = 10.8 kN/m, bending governs

Problem 3 [A2-103] Timber column design and slenderness

A pin-ended No. 1 spruce column in a Thunder Bay storage building is 3.60 m long between floors. It is 89 mm by 140 mm in section, with the 140 mm face against a wall that braces it in the weak direction only if a girt is fitted. Use φ = 0.80, specified compressive strength fc = 11.5 MPa, and modulus for column design E05 = 6500 MPa. All other modification factors equal 1.0. The slenderness factor is Kc = [1 + fc Cc³/(35 E05)]⁻¹ where Cc = Le/d is the effective length over the least dimension of the buckling plane. The resistance is Pr = φ fc A Kc and the slenderness ratio must not exceed 50. The factored axial load is 45 kN.

  1. (a) Find the governing slenderness ratio Cc with no intermediate bracing. [3]
  2. (b) Find Kc for the unbraced column. [5]
  3. (c) Find the unbraced resistance Pr and say whether it carries 45 kN. [6]
  4. (d) A girt at mid-height braces the weak axis only. Find the new Pr and decide whether the column now carries 45 kN. [6]
(a)

With no bracing, buckling can occur about either axis, and the weak axis, with the 89 mm dimension, gives the larger slenderness. Cc = Le/d = 3600/89 = 40.4. The strong-axis ratio would be 3600/140 = 25.7. The limit of 50 is satisfied, so the column is legal but slender. A pin-ended column has effective length equal to the actual length because both ends are free to rotate, so Le = 3.60 m about both axes. The governing ratio is the larger one, 40.4, and all later calculations in the unbraced case use it.

Answer: Cc = 40.4

(b)

Kc = [1 + fc Cc³/(35 E05)]⁻¹. First Cc³ = 40.45³ = 66 190. Then fc Cc³/(35 E05) = 11.5 × 66 190/(35 × 6500) = 761 185/227 500 = 3.346. So Kc = 1/(1 + 3.346) = 0.230. A Kc this low means slenderness reduces the compression capacity to under a quarter of the crushing strength, so buckling, not crushing, controls. The sensitivity is the cube of Cc, which is why modest bracing has a large effect on a slender timber column.

Answer: Kc = 0.230

(c)

Area A = 89 × 140 = 12 460 mm². Pr = φ fc A Kc = 0.80 × 11.5 × 12 460 × 0.2301 = 26 380 N = 26.4 kN. The factored load of 45 kN exceeds this, giving a demand-to-capacity ratio of 1.71, so the unbraced column fails. The crushing capacity without slenderness would be 0.80 × 11.5 × 12 460 = 114.6 kN, which shows how much of the strength the slenderness removes. The designer should not accept this column without bracing or a larger section.

Answer: Pr = 26.4 kN, fails

(d)

A mid-height girt holds the weak axis at mid-height, so the weak-axis Cc = 1800/89 = 20.2. The strong axis is not braced, so its Cc stays 3600/140 = 25.7, and it now governs. Cc³ = 17 000, so fc Cc³/(35 E05) = 11.5 × 17 000/227 500 = 0.859 and Kc = 1/1.859 = 0.538. Pr = 0.80 × 11.5 × 12 460 × 0.538 = 61.6 kN. This exceeds 45 kN, so the column passes with utilisation 0.73. Bracing the weak axis more than doubles the capacity, a cheap remedy compared with a larger post, provided the girt is fastened for its own bracing force.

Answer: Pr = 61.6 kN, passes

Problem 4 [A2-104] Timber tension members and net section

The lower chord of a roof truss at a curling rink near Barrie is a single piece of No. 1 spruce 89 mm thick by 235 mm deep. At a splice, two 19 mm bolts pass through the member in one line across the depth, so both holes lie in the same cross-section. Holes are drilled 1.5 mm larger than the bolt. Design values: φ = 0.90, specified tension strength parallel to grain ft = 5.5 MPa, with all modification factors equal to 1.0. The factored tensile resistance is Tr = φ ft An, where An is the net area after deducting the projected area of every hole in the cross-section. The factored chord force at this panel is 90 kN. A suggestion has been made to add more bolts.

  1. (a) Find the net area An with two bolts in the section. [4]
  2. (b) Find Tr and state whether the member carries 90 kN. [5]
  3. (c) Find the minimum net area needed for 90 kN. [4]
  4. (d) Find the largest number of bolts allowed in a single cross-section for 90 kN. [4]
  5. (e) Recommend a practical remedy and explain why more bolts in the same line are the wrong direction. [3]
(a)

The hole diameter is 19 + 1.5 = 20.5 mm. The projected hole area is the hole diameter times the member thickness, 20.5 × 89 = 1824.5 mm² per hole. The gross area is 89 × 235 = 20 915 mm². With two holes in the same section, An = 20 915 − 2 × 1824.5 = 17 266 mm². The net area is 17.5 percent smaller than gross. Holes in different cross-sections would not be deducted together unless staggered closely enough, but here both lie on the same line across the depth, so both reduce the same section, which is the worst case.

Answer: An = 17 270 mm²

(b)

Tr = φ ft An = 0.90 × 5.5 × 17 266 = 85 467 N = 85.5 kN. The factored force 90 kN exceeds this by about 5 percent, with a ratio of 1.05, so the member fails at the splice. Tension parallel to grain is governed by the net section, because wood has no yielding to redistribute stress around a hole; the stress concentration at the hole edge is carried straight to failure. The gross section would carry 0.90 × 5.5 × 20 915 = 103.5 kN, so the holes cost 18 kN of capacity.

Answer: Tr = 85.5 kN, fails

(c)

Rearranging, An,min = Tf/(φ ft) = 90 000/(0.90 × 5.5) = 18 182 mm². This is the net area the splice section must have. Compared with the 17 266 mm² available, the deficit is 916 mm², which is about half a bolt hole. The gross area is 20 915 mm², so the allowable deduction for holes is 20 915 − 18 182 = 2733 mm², and that figure is used in part (d). It is good practice to find the allowable hole deduction first, since it shows quickly how many holes can be tolerated.

Answer: An,min = 18 180 mm²

(d)

Each hole removes 1824.5 mm². The allowable deduction is 2733 mm². The number of holes n satisfies n × 1824.5 ≤ 2733, so n ≤ 1.50, and since a whole number is needed, n = 1. With one hole, An = 20 915 − 1824.5 = 19 090 mm², which exceeds 18 182 mm², giving Tr = 94.5 kN. With two holes it fails as found in (b). So only one bolt may sit in any one cross-section; extra bolts must be placed in staggered or separate sections.

Answer: 1 bolt per section

(e)

Adding bolts in the same line makes it worse, because every hole in the same section deducts more area and lowers Tr further. The correct options are to use a deeper or thicker member, to move to a higher grade of lumber with a larger ft, or to stagger the bolts so each hole falls in a different cross-section and loses its own area only once. For example, 89 × 286 mm has gross area 25 454 mm² and with two holes An = 21 800 mm², giving Tr = 107.9 kN, enough for 90 kN. Reducing the splice to one bolt per section while keeping the same member is also valid, as shown in part (d).

Answer: Use a deeper member or stagger the holes

Problem 5 [A2-105] Timber connections with bolts and nails

A hanger on a pedestrian bridge near Kingston is a 12 mm or 16 mm bolted connection through an 89 mm thick spruce main member sandwiched between two thick steel side plates, so each bolt acts in double shear. Embedment strength of the wood is fe = 30 MPa. Bolt yield moment is My = 77 000 N·mm for the 12 mm bolt and 162 000 N·mm for the 16 mm bolt. For each shear plane the resistance is the smaller of the bearing mode 0.5 fe d tm and the two-hinge bolt-yield mode 1.15 √(2 My fe d). The factored resistance of a bolt is φ times two planes, with φ = 0.80. The connection carries a factored load of 62 kN. Minimum spacing is 4d and end distance is 7d.

  1. (a) For the 12 mm bolt, find the resistance per shear plane and name the governing mode. [5]
  2. (b) Find the factored resistance of one 12 mm bolt in double shear. [4]
  3. (c) Find the number of 12 mm bolts needed for 62 kN. [3]
  4. (d) Find the number of 16 mm bolts needed for 62 kN. [4]
  5. (e) For the 16 mm option, find the shortest row length from first end to last end, with 4d spacing and 7d end distance at both ends. [4]
(a)

Bearing mode per plane: 0.5 × 30 × 12 × 89 = 16 020 N. Bolt yield mode: 1.15 √(2 × 77 000 × 30 × 12) = 1.15 √55 440 000 = 1.15 × 7446 = 8563 N. The smaller governs, so the resistance per shear plane is 8563 N = 8.56 kN, controlled by the bolt forming two plastic hinges, not by crushing of the wood. This makes sense for a slender bolt in thick timber; the 12 mm bolt is flexible compared with the 89 mm main member, so it bends before the timber crushes. Both modes are listed so the lesser can be seen.

Answer: 8.56 kN per plane, bolt yield

(b)

Double shear means two planes act, so the nominal resistance is 2 × 8563 = 17 126 N. Applying φ = 0.80 gives 0.80 × 17 126 = 13 700 N = 13.7 kN per bolt. The factor φ accounts for the variability of timber and the brittle nature of some of the connection failures. Because the side plates are steel and stiff, the load shares equally across both planes, so doubling is appropriate. If the plates were thin timber the side members would also need checking in the same way.

Answer: 13.7 kN per bolt

(c)

Number of bolts n = Pf/(resistance per bolt) = 62/13.70 = 4.53, so the next whole number is 5 bolts. Use of 5 bolts gives a capacity of 68.5 kN, a reserve of 10 percent. In a real design the row factor for several bolts in a line would reduce this further, but it is not asked for here, so the simple multiplication is accepted. It is worth noting that 4 bolts would give only 54.8 kN, 12 percent below the load, so rounding down is not acceptable.

Answer: 5 bolts

(d)

For the 16 mm bolt, bearing per plane = 0.5 × 30 × 16 × 89 = 21 360 N. Yield mode = 1.15 √(2 × 162 000 × 30 × 16) = 1.15 √155 520 000 = 1.15 × 12 471 = 14 341 N. Yield governs again at 14.34 kN. Double shear with φ gives 0.80 × 2 × 14 341 = 22 945 N = 22.9 kN per bolt. The number needed is 62/22.9 = 2.70, so 3 bolts, which carry 68.8 kN. Increasing the diameter by one third lifted the bolt resistance by 67 percent, because the yield term grows faster than linearly in d.

Answer: 3 bolts

(e)

For d = 16 mm, the end distance is 7d = 112 mm at each end and the spacing is 4d = 64 mm. With three bolts there are two gaps, so the row length is 2 × 112 + 2 × 64 = 224 + 128 = 352 mm. The 12 mm option would need 5 bolts with end distance 84 mm and spacing 48 mm, giving 2 × 84 + 4 × 48 = 360 mm, so the lengths are almost equal. The three larger bolts are preferable because fewer holes are drilled and there are fewer places to go wrong in the shop.

Answer: 352 mm

A2 Practice Paper 22

Problem 1 [A2-106] Steel tension members: gross section, net section and block shear

A 12 mm thick by 150 mm wide gusset-connected tension plate in a Windsor industrial truss has two lines of three 20 mm bolts, with holes 22 mm in diameter. The lines are 80 mm apart and 35 mm from each plate edge. Along the load direction the end distance is 40 mm and the pitch is 70 mm. The steel has Fy = 350 MPa and Fu = 450 MPa, with φ = 0.90 for yielding and φu = 0.75 for fracture. Use Tr = φ Ag Fy for gross section, Tr = 0.85 φu An Fu for net section, and for block shear Tr = φu [Ut Ant Fu + 0.6 Agv (Fy + Fu)/2] with Ut = 1.0. The factored tension is 380 kN. Agv is the gross shear area on the two shear planes and Ant is the net tension area between the lines.

  1. (a) Find the gross-section resistance. [4]
  2. (b) Find the net-section resistance and state whether it is adequate. [5]
  3. (c) Find the block shear resistance. [6]
  4. (d) Find the minimum plate thickness, using the net section criterion, to carry 380 kN. [5]
(a)

Gross area Ag = 150 × 12 = 1800 mm². Tr = φ Ag Fy = 0.90 × 1800 × 350 = 567 000 N = 567 kN. This is the yielding limit state, which is ductile because the whole length of the plate elongates before fracture, giving warning and redistribution. It is the preferred failure mode, so the code gives it the higher φ of 0.90. Note that the gross section does not see the holes, because yielding occurs along the full member length, not just at the bolted section.

Answer: Tr = 567 kN

(b)

Across the critical section there are two holes, one on each bolt line. Net width = 150 − 2 × 22 = 106 mm, so An = 106 × 12 = 1272 mm². Tr = 0.85 φu An Fu = 0.85 × 0.75 × 1272 × 450 = 364 900 N = 365 kN. The 0.85 factor accounts for shear lag and uneven stress at the hole line. The factored force of 380 kN exceeds 365 kN, a ratio of 1.04, so the plate is not adequate in net section even though it has a large gross reserve. This is the classic situation where fracture, not yielding, controls the design of a bolted tension member.

Answer: Tr = 365 kN, not adequate

(c)

The block that tears out is bounded by two shear planes along the bolt lines and one tension plane between them. Shear length = end 40 + 2 × 70 = 180 mm each, so Agv = 2 × 180 × 12 = 4320 mm². The tension plane is the 80 mm gauge less one hole, (80 − 22) × 12 = 696 mm² = Ant. Then Tr = 0.75 [1.0 × 696 × 450 + 0.6 × 4320 × (350 + 450)/2] = 0.75 [313 200 + 1 036 800] = 0.75 × 1 350 000 = 1 012 500 N = 1013 kN. This is nearly three times the load and far above the net-section value, so block shear does not control for this plate and bolt layout.

Answer: Tr = 1013 kN

(d)

The governing limit is the net section at 365 kN. Net-section resistance is proportional to thickness: Tr = 0.85 × 0.75 × 106 × t × 450 = 30 409 t newtons per mm of thickness. Setting it equal to 380 000 N gives t = 380 000/30 409 = 12.5 mm. In practice the next standard plate, 14 mm, would be chosen. With 14 mm the net resistance is 425.7 kN, which carries 380 kN. Gross section at 14 mm is 661 kN and block shear is larger still, so net section stays the controlling mode. A thicker plate is cheaper than changing the bolt layout.

Answer: t = 12.5 mm, use 14 mm

Problem 2 [A2-107] Laterally supported steel beam flexural resistance

A simply supported 8.0 m span steel floor girder in a Hamilton parking structure carries a factored uniform load of 38 kN/m (including self-weight) and one factored concentrated load of 70 kN at midspan. The beam is a Class 1 wide-flange section with plastic section modulus Zx = 1.28 × 10⁶ mm³ and is continuously supported against lateral movement by the composite deck. The resistance is Mr = φ Zx Fy with φ = 0.90. The steel is Fy = 350 MPa. The owner asks whether the same section can be reused if the project upgrades to a higher steel grade of Fy = 400 MPa to avoid changing the framing. Shear and deflection are checked separately and are not part of this question.

  1. (a) Find the factored maximum bending moment Mf. [4]
  2. (b) Find Mr with Fy = 350 MPa and the utilisation ratio Mf/Mr. [4]
  3. (c) Find the minimum Zx needed with Fy = 350 MPa. [4]
  4. (d) Find Mr for the same section in 400 MPa steel. [4]
  5. (e) Recommend whether the section can be reused and name one check that remains. [4]
(a)

The maximum moment of the combined load occurs at midspan. Uniform load contribution: wL²/8 = 38 × 8²/8 = 304 kN·m. Point load contribution: PL/4 = 70 × 8/4 = 140 kN·m. Because both peak at the same location, the moments add: Mf = 304 + 140 = 444 kN·m. Superposition is valid since the beam is elastic and statically determinate. Reactions would be 38 × 4 + 35 = 187 kN each, a useful check of the load total of 374 kN for the shear design, though not needed here.

Answer: Mf = 444 kN·m

(b)

Plastic moment Mp = Zx Fy = 1.28 × 10⁶ × 350 = 448 × 10⁶ N·mm = 448 kN·m. A Class 1 section reaches full plastic moment, so Mr = φ Mp = 0.90 × 448 = 403.2 kN·m. The beam is continuously supported laterally, so no lateral-torsional reduction applies. Utilisation Mf/Mr = 444/403.2 = 1.10, so the section is overstressed by 10 percent and fails in bending in 350 MPa steel. The gap of about 41 kN·m is too large to excuse by rounding or by reserve from the neglected composite action.

Answer: Mr = 403 kN·m, ratio 1.10

(c)

Required Zx = Mf/(φ Fy) = 444 × 10⁶/(0.90 × 350) = 444 × 10⁶/315 = 1.4095 × 10⁶ mm³. So the section must have a plastic modulus of at least 1.41 × 10⁶ mm³, which is 10 percent more than the existing 1.28 × 10⁶. A catalogue section with roughly 1.45 × 10⁶ mm³ would be chosen in practice. The calculation gives a target that can be compared directly against tabulated Zx values without repeating the moment check for each trial section.

Answer: Zx,min = 1.41 × 10⁶ mm³

(d)

With Fy = 400 MPa, Mr = 0.90 × 1.28 × 10⁶ × 400 = 460.8 × 10⁶ N·mm = 460.8 kN·m. This exceeds Mf = 444 kN·m, with utilisation 444/460.8 = 0.96. A strength gain of 14 percent (460.8/403.2) comes entirely from the higher yield strength, since Zx is unchanged, and it is the only change made to the section. The margin is narrow, only 4 percent, so any small increase in the load estimate, for example a heavier mechanical unit, would again put the girder over the limit.

Answer: Mr = 461 kN·m

(e)

The 400 MPa upgrade makes the section adequate in bending (0.96), so it can be reused. Several checks remain. Deflection does not improve with steel grade because E stays at 200 000 MPa, so a girder that was governed by strength may now be governed by serviceability. Shear, web bearing, and the cost and availability of 400 MPa girders must also be confirmed. With a margin of only 4 percent I would recommend asking for a slightly heavier section as insurance.

Answer: Reuse in 400 MPa, check deflection and shear

Problem 3 [A2-108] Lateral torsional buckling of steel beams

A simply supported 9.0 m floor beam in a Mississauga warehouse has the top flange free to move sideways between the supports, which are fork-type (twist restrained, free to warp). Section properties: Zx = 1.65 × 10⁶ mm³, Iy = 16.6 × 10⁶ mm⁴, J = 0.52 × 10⁶ mm⁴, Cw = 0.69 × 10¹² mm⁶. Take E = 200 000 MPa, G = 77 000 MPa, Fy = 350 MPa, φ = 0.90, and conservatively use ω2 = 1.0. The elastic critical moment is Mu = (ω2 π/L) √[E Iy G J + (π E/L)² Iy Cw]. For Mu > 0.67 Mp, Mr = 1.15 φ Mp (1 − 0.28 Mp/Mu), not more than φ Mp. Otherwise Mr = φ Mu. Here Mp = Zx Fy. A single lateral brace at midspan is proposed.

  1. (a) Find Mp and Mu for the unbraced 9.0 m span. [5]
  2. (b) Find Mr for the unbraced span. [4]
  3. (c) Find Mu and Mr when the brace at midspan reduces the unbraced length to 4.5 m. [7]
  4. (d) Find the ratio of braced to unbraced resistance. [4]
(a)

Mp = Zx Fy = 1.65 × 10⁶ × 350 = 577.5 × 10⁶ N·mm = 577.5 kN·m. For L = 9000 mm the two terms under the root are E Iy G J = 200 000 × 16.6 × 10⁶ × 77 000 × 0.52 × 10⁶ = 1.329 × 10²³ and (π E/L)² Iy Cw = (69.81)² × 16.6 × 10⁶ × 0.69 × 10¹² = 5.583 × 10²². Their sum is 1.887 × 10²³, whose root is 4.345 × 10¹¹. With ω2 = 1.0 and π/L = 3.491 × 10⁻⁴ mm⁻¹, Mu = 3.491 × 10⁻⁴ × 4.345 × 10¹¹ = 1.517 × 10⁸ N·mm = 151.7 kN·m. This is only 26 percent of Mp, so the beam is very prone to lateral buckling over this long unbraced length.

Answer: Mp = 577.5 kN·m, Mu = 152 kN·m

(b)

Test 0.67 Mp = 0.67 × 577.5 = 387 kN·m. Since Mu = 151.7 is less than 387, the beam buckles elastically and Mr = φ Mu = 0.90 × 151.7 = 136.5 kN·m. This is only 26 percent of the plastic design moment φ Mp = 519.8 kN·m. Elastic lateral-torsional buckling happens before the section can develop yield, so the long unbraced span wastes most of the section's strength. The beam's resistance here is governed by Iy, J and the span, not by Zx or Fy.

Answer: Mr = 136 kN·m

(c)

With L = 4500 mm, the factor π/L doubles and the warping term (π E/L)² Iy Cw quadruples. Evaluating the stated formula gives Mu = 416.7 kN·m. This exceeds 0.67 Mp = 387, so inelastic buckling applies: Mr = 1.15 × 0.90 × 577.5 × (1 − 0.28 × 577.5/416.7) = 597.8 × (1 − 0.388) = 597.8 × 0.612 = 365.8 kN·m. The upper limit φ Mp = 519.8 kN·m is not reached, so 365.8 governs. The brace changes the beam from elastic to inelastic buckling, which is why the gain is large.

Answer: Mu = 417 kN·m, Mr = 366 kN·m

(d)

The ratio is 365.8/136.5 = 2.68. A single brace at midspan therefore increases the resistance by 168 percent. The cost of a brace (a small angle or a strut to an adjacent beam) is trivial compared with the cost of selecting a deeper section. Even so, the braced Mr of 366 kN·m remains below φ Mp, so more bracing at third points would give a further increase up to 520 kN·m. The brace itself must be designed for a small force, typically a few percent of the compression flange force, and must be connected to something stiff.

Answer: Ratio 2.68

Problem 4 [A2-109] Steel beam shear resistance and web bearing

A rolled steel girder in a Guelph transfer structure has overall depth d = 457 mm, web thickness w = 9.0 mm and a distance k = 28 mm from the outer face of the flange to the web toe of the fillet. The web is stocky, so the shear stress at failure is Fs = 0.66 Fy, with Fy = 350 MPa. Shear resistance is Vr = φ Aw Fs with Aw = d w and φ = 0.90. Web bearing resistance without stiffeners is Br = φbr w (N + 4k) Fy at an end support and Br = φbr w (N + 10k) Fy at an interior load, where N is the bearing length and φbr = 0.80. The end reaction is 520 kN, and the girder also carries a 650 kN interior column load.

  1. (a) Find the shear resistance Vr. [4]
  2. (b) Find the end bearing resistance Br if the seat plate bearing length is N = 75 mm. [4]
  3. (c) Find the minimum N so that the end support carries 520 kN without stiffeners. [4]
  4. (d) Find the interior web bearing resistance under the column with N = 150 mm. [4]
  5. (e) Say whether stiffeners are needed at each location and why the interior value is so much larger. [4]
(a)

Aw = d w = 457 × 9.0 = 4113 mm². Fs = 0.66 × 350 = 231 MPa. Vr = φ Aw Fs = 0.90 × 4113 × 231 = 855 090 N = 855 kN. S16 defines Aw as overall depth times web thickness, which is the stated method; Fs = 0.66 Fy applies to stocky webs that do not buckle before yielding. Shear is far larger than the 520 kN end reaction, so shear alone is no concern.

Answer: Vr = 855 kN

(b)

At an end support, the load is only resisted by the web on one side of the bearing plate, so the allowable length is N + 4k. With k = 28 mm, 4k = 112 mm, and N + 4k = 75 + 112 = 187 mm. Br = φbr w (N + 4k) Fy = 0.80 × 9.0 × 187 × 350 = 471 240 N = 471 kN. This is below the 520 kN reaction, so the girder web would crush or buckle under a 75 mm seat if no stiffener were provided. The shortfall is 49 kN, about 9 percent.

Answer: Br = 471 kN

(c)

Set Br = 520 kN and solve for N: N + 4k = 520 000/(φbr w Fy) = 520 000/(0.80 × 9.0 × 350) = 520 000/2520 = 206.3 mm. Then N = 206.3 − 112 = 94.3 mm. A 100 mm seat is the next practical length and gives Br = 0.80 × 9.0 × 212 × 350 = 534 kN, which is adequate with a margin of 14 kN. The designer can therefore remove the need for stiffeners at the end support by adding a modestly longer seat angle, usually cheaper than welding stiffeners.

Answer: N = 94.3 mm

(d)

For a load applied away from the member end, the web can spread the load on both sides, so the dispersal length is N + 10k. With N = 150 mm, N + 10k = 150 + 280 = 430 mm. Br = 0.80 × 9.0 × 430 × 350 = 1 083 600 N = 1084 kN. The column load of 650 kN is well below this, with a utilisation of 0.60. Shear under the column must still be checked, but Vr = 855 kN exceeds the likely shear of at most about 650 kN, so the interior location is satisfactory.

Answer: Br = 1084 kN

(e)

At the end support, 75 mm gives 471 kN against 520 kN, so stiffeners are needed unless the seat is lengthened to at least 95 mm. Under the column load, the 1084 kN resistance exceeds 650 kN, so no stiffeners are needed. The interior value is larger because the load spreads through the web in both directions from the bearing, so the effective length uses 10k rather than 4k, more than doubling the effective web length. In practice I would lengthen the seat to 100 mm, saving stiffener fabrication.

Answer: Stiffeners needed at the end support unless the seat is longer

Problem 5 [A2-110] Steel beam deflection and serviceability

A simply supported 9.0 m steel beam in a Waterloo office floor has Ix = 333 × 10⁶ mm⁴ and E = 200 000 MPa. Unfactored (service) loads are a uniform dead load of 12.0 kN/m and a uniform live load of 16.0 kN/m. Use Δ = 5 w L⁴/(384 E I). The architect specifies that live-load deflection must not exceed span/480 because brittle partitions will sit on the floor. Camber may be built into a steel beam by shaping it before delivery, and the fabricator can match any camber the engineer states. A deeper section of Ix = 380 × 10⁶ mm⁴ is being considered as an alternative.

  1. (a) Find the live-load deflection and compare it with L/480. [4]
  2. (b) Find the minimum Ix needed to meet the L/480 limit. [5]
  3. (c) Find the camber to offset the dead-load deflection. [3]
  4. (d) Find the live-load deflection if the Ix = 380 × 10⁶ mm⁴ section is used. [4]
  5. (e) Discuss whether camber or the deeper section better solves the problem. [4]
(a)

Convert units: w = 16.0 kN/m = 16.0 N/mm and L = 9000 mm. Δ = 5 w L⁴/(384 E I) = 5 × 16.0 × 9000⁴/(384 × 200 000 × 333 × 10⁶). The numerator is 5 × 16.0 × 6.561 × 10¹⁵ = 5.249 × 10¹⁷ and the denominator is 2.557 × 10¹⁶, so Δ = 20.5 mm. The limit L/480 = 9000/480 = 18.75 mm. Since 20.5 mm is greater than 18.75 mm, the beam fails the live-load deflection check by about 9 percent, so the section is too flexible for brittle partitions.

Answer: Δlive = 20.5 mm, exceeds 18.75 mm

(b)

Deflection is inversely proportional to I, so the required inertia is Ix,req = Ix × (Δactual/Δlimit) = 333 × 10⁶ × 20.52/18.75 = 364.5 × 10⁶ mm⁴. This is 9.5 percent more than the present section. Equivalent reasoning on the dead load is not needed since the limit applies to live load only. The result gives a target to compare with the tables of available sections, and any section with Ix of at least 364.5 × 10⁶ mm⁴ and adequate strength would satisfy the architect.

Answer: Ix,req = 364.5 × 10⁶ mm⁴

(c)

The dead-load deflection is Δ = 5 × 12.0 × 9000⁴/(384 × 200 000 × 333 × 10⁶) = 5 × 12.0 × 6.561 × 10¹⁵/2.557 × 10¹⁶ = 15.4 mm. Building in a camber equal to this value makes the beam sit level when the dead load is applied, so the floor is flat when it is first occupied. Camber is given in the upward direction and is measured at midspan. It is normally rounded to the nearest 5 mm and would be about 15 mm here. The fabricator cambers the steel by heat or by cold bending.

Answer: Camber = 15.4 mm

(d)

With Ix = 380 × 10⁶ mm⁴, the deflection scales by the ratio of the inertias: Δ = 20.52 × 333/380 = 17.99 mm. This is below the 18.75 mm limit, with 4 percent to spare. The thin margin means the loading and span would need to be accurate. Another way to see it: Ix,req was 364.5 × 10⁶, and 380 × 10⁶ is 4.3 percent above that, which matches the 4 percent margin found. Weight per metre would also rise with the deeper section, a small cost compared with the ongoing partition cracking risk.

Answer: Δlive = 18.0 mm

(e)

Camber only offsets the dead load, which is not the loading in question, because the partitions are damaged by live-load movement after they are installed. Adding camber therefore does nothing to bring 20.5 mm down to 18.75 mm. The deeper section does satisfy the limit at 18.0 mm. I recommend the Ix = 380 × 10⁶ mm⁴ section and also camber the beam by about 15 mm, so the floor is level after dead load and the partitions are set against a flat surface. Strength should be rechecked for the heavier section in case the load changes.

Answer: Use the deeper section and also camber

A2 Practice Paper 23

Problem 1 [A2-111] Steel column compressive resistance and effective length

A rooftop mechanical platform in Sudbury is carried on a hollow structural section column whose properties are A = 4500 mm² and a governing radius of gyration r = 58 mm, equal about both axes. The steel has Fy = 350 MPa and E = 200 000 MPa. The unbraced length between the base and the platform beam is 4.2 m. Take the compressive resistance as Cr = φ A Fy / (1 + λ2n)1/n, where φ = 0.90, n = 1.34, λ = √(Fy/Fe) and Fe = π² E / (KL/r)². The base is detailed as a pin, and the beam connection is also treated as a pin, so K = 1.0. The designer asks you to judge three changes: bracing at mid-height, a more conservative K, and the longest unbraced length that still carries a factored axial load of 1050 kN.

  1. (a) Find KL/r, Fe, λ and the factored compressive resistance Cr for K = 1.0 over the full 4.2 m. [5]
  2. (b) A weak-axis brace is added at mid-height so the effective length becomes 2.1 m. Find the new Cr. [5]
  3. (c) A reviewer doubts the pinned beam joint and asks for K = 1.2 on the full 4.2 m. Find Cr and say how much resistance is lost compared with part (a). [5]
  4. (d) With K = 1.0, find the largest unbraced length L, in mm, for which Cr still equals the factored load of 1050 kN. [5]
(a)

The slenderness is KL/r = 1.0 × 4200 / 58 = 72.41. The elastic buckling stress is Fe = π² × 200 000 / 72.41² = 376.4 MPa. Then λ = √(350 / 376.4) = 0.964. The factor in the denominator is (1 + 0.9642.68)1/1.34 = (1 + 0.9066)0.7463 = 1.6188. Cr = 0.90 × 4500 × 350 / 1.6188 = 875 600 N = 875.6 kN. Because λ is close to 1, the column sits in the zone where inelastic effects and initial crookedness matter, so the curve gives a resistance well below the squash load φ A Fy of 1417.5 kN. A marker expects the sequence KL/r, Fe, λ, Cr shown in order with units.

Answer: Cr = 875.6 kN

(b)

Halving the length halves the slenderness: KL/r = 2100 / 58 = 36.21. Then Fe = π² × 200 000 / 36.21² = 1505.7 MPa and λ = √(350 / 1505.7) = 0.482. The denominator is (1 + 0.4822.68)0.7463 = (1 + 0.1415)0.7463 = 1.1038. So Cr = 0.90 × 4500 × 350 / 1.1038 = 1 284 200 N = 1284.2 kN. The brace raises the resistance by 46.7 percent, which is a large gain for a small member, and Cr is now 90.6 percent of the squash load. The brace itself must be designed for a restraint force, but that check is outside this question. State the assumption that the brace is stiff enough to act as a true node.

Answer: Cr = 1284.2 kN

(c)

With K = 1.2 the effective length is 5040 mm and KL/r = 5040 / 58 = 86.90. Fe = π² × 200 000 / 86.90² = 261.4 MPa and λ = √(350 / 261.4) = 1.157. The denominator is (1 + 1.1572.68)0.7463 = (1 + 1.4784)0.7463 = 1.9686. Cr = 0.90 × 4500 × 350 / 1.9686 = 720 000 N = 720.0 kN. The loss relative to 875.6 kN is (875.6 − 720.0) / 875.6 = 17.8 percent. This shows how sensitive a slender column is to the assumed end restraint: a 20 percent increase in K costs almost one fifth of the capacity, so the end assumption deserves care.

Answer: Cr = 720.0 kN; 17.8 percent lost

(d)

Cr falls as L grows, so the limit is found by trial or by a root solver on Cr(L) = 1050 kN. At L = 3000 mm, KL/r = 51.7 and Cr is about 1122 kN. At L = 3500 mm, KL/r = 60.3 and Cr is about 1019 kN, which is too low. Interpolating and refining gives L = 3351 mm, where KL/r = 57.8, Fe = 591.3 MPa, λ = 0.770 and Cr = 1050 kN. Any length above 3.35 m fails the 1050 kN demand. This tells the designer that the 4.2 m column needs the mid-height brace, or a larger section, to carry the load, and that the brace position should not be above 3.35 m from either end.

Answer: L = 3351 mm

Problem 2 [A2-112] Steel beam-columns under combined axial load and bending

A column in a Thunder Bay warehouse frame carries a factored axial load Cf = 700 kN together with a factored major-axis moment Mf = 120 kN·m, produced by a crane-free roof drift. The member is a W-shape whose major-axis second moment of area is I = 1.1 × 10⁸ mm⁴ with E = 200 000 MPa and an effective length KL = 3.6 m in the plane of bending. Its factored compressive resistance is Cr = 1450 kN and its factored bending resistance is Mr = 300 kN·m. Use the interaction check Cf/Cr + 0.85 U1 Mf/Mr ≤ 1.0, with U1 = ω1 / (1 − Cf/Ce) but not less than 1.0, where Ce = π² E I / (KL)² and the moment-gradient factor ω1 = 0.85. The section is Class 1, so lateral-torsional buckling is prevented by the roof framing.

  1. (a) Calculate the Euler buckling load Ce in kN. [4]
  2. (b) Calculate the amplification factor U1. [4]
  3. (c) Evaluate the interaction ratio and state whether the member passes. [6]
  4. (d) With the axial load unchanged at 700 kN, find the largest factored moment Mf, in kN·m, the member can carry, and comment on the reserve. [6]
(a)

Ce = π² E I / (KL)². Convert all quantities to newtons and millimetres: KL = 3600 mm, so (KL)² = 1.296 × 10⁷ mm². Then Ce = π² × 200 000 × 1.1 × 10⁸ / 1.296 × 10⁷ = 1.6754 × 10⁷ N = 16 754 kN. This is the elastic buckling load of the same column in the plane of bending, with no allowance for inelastic behaviour or crookedness. It is more than twenty times the applied axial load, which signals that second-order amplification of the moment will be very small. The units must be consistent: I in mm⁴ and E in MPa give force in newtons, which is then divided by 1000 for kilonewtons.

Answer: Ce = 16 754 kN

(b)

U1 captures the extra moment produced when the axial load acts through the lateral deflection of the member. Cf/Ce = 700 / 16 754 = 0.0418. Then 1 − 0.0418 = 0.9582 and the calculated value is ω1 / (1 − Cf/Ce) = 0.85 / 0.9582 = 0.887. Since this is below 1.0, the lower limit governs and U1 = 1.0. In other words, the moment of 120 kN·m is used without any amplification because the column is stiff compared with the axial load. omega1 = 0.85 is given for the moment pattern; a more uniform moment would give a larger omega1 (up to 1.0) and hence a larger U1.

Answer: U1 = 1.0

(c)

Axial term: Cf/Cr = 700 / 1450 = 0.4828. Bending term: 0.85 × U1 × Mf / Mr = 0.85 × 1.0 × 120 / 300 = 0.340. The sum is 0.4828 + 0.340 = 0.823, which is less than 1.0, so the member passes the cross-section and overall member check as stated. The utilisation is 82.3 percent, giving a margin of 17.7 percent. The axial term uses 59 percent of the total, so the member is mainly an axially loaded column with a secondary bending effect. A marker looks for each term to be shown separately, followed by a clear statement of the pass or fail conclusion.

Answer: Ratio = 0.823, passes

(d)

Set the ratio to 1.0 and solve for Mf with Cf fixed. Since U1 = 1.0 does not depend on Mf, the bending term can use up 1 − 0.4828 = 0.5172. Then 0.85 × 1.0 × Mf / 300 = 0.5172, so Mf = 0.5172 × 300 / 0.85 = 182.6 kN·m. The present Mf of 120 kN·m is 65.7 percent of this limit, giving 62.6 kN·m of moment reserve. The reserve is useful and reasonably generous, though any second-order effects from a bigger roof drift would use some of it. The designer should also check connection capacity, since the member limit is only one of several.

Answer: Mf = 182.6 kN·m

Problem 3 [A2-113] Bolted steel connections in bearing

A tension splice in a pedestrian bridge truss at Kingston joins two 12 mm thick main plates of steel with Fu = 450 MPa using 22 mm diameter high-strength bolts, nominal area Ab = 380 mm² and bolt ultimate strength Fu(bolt) = 830 MPa. The bolts are in bearing-type shear with the threads intercepted by the shear plane. Use a bolt shear resistance Vr = 0.60 φb n m Ab Fu(bolt) per bolt, and a bearing resistance Br = 3 φbr n t d Fu(plate) per bolt, with φb = φbr = 0.80, n = 1 bolt, m the number of shear planes, t the plate thickness and d the bolt diameter. Edge distances and spacing are generous, so tearing out does not govern. The factored tension to be spliced is 780 kN. The first option is a single lap with six bolts and the second uses cover plates on both faces so the bolts are in double shear.

  1. (a) Find the factored shear resistance of one bolt in single shear (m = 1). [4]
  2. (b) Find the factored bearing resistance of one bolt on a 12 mm main plate. [4]
  3. (c) For the six-bolt single-shear option, find the factored resistance of the group and say whether it carries 780 kN. [6]
  4. (d) For the cover-plate option with double shear, find the smallest number of bolts that carries 780 kN, given that bearing on the 12 mm main plate also applies and the cover plates are thick enough not to govern. [6]
(a)

In single shear m = 1, so Vr = 0.60 × 0.80 × 1 × 1 × 380 × 830 = 151 392 N = 151.4 kN per bolt. The 0.60 factor is the stated value for a shear plane that cuts the threaded portion of the bolt, which is the conservative case, and the resistance uses the ultimate bolt strength rather than yield. Each bolt therefore transfers about 151 kN across one plane. A marker expects the equation, the substitution with all four factors and the unit conversion from newtons to kilonewtons, because a missing φb or a wrong shear-plane count is the usual error in this calculation.

Answer: Vr = 151.4 kN

(b)

Bearing on the plate uses Br = 3 φbr n t d Fu = 3 × 0.80 × 1 × 12 × 22 × 450 = 285 120 N = 285.1 kN. Here t = 12 mm is the thickness of the main plate that the bolt pushes against, d = 22 mm is the bolt diameter, and Fu = 450 MPa is the plate strength, not the bolt strength. Bearing is nearly twice the single-shear value, so in the lap splice the bolt shear controls, not the plate. This ratio of 285.1 / 151.4 = 1.88 shows that the connection fails in shear first, which is a ductile enough mode for most practical detailing here.

Answer: Br = 285.1 kN

(c)

Each bolt is limited by the smaller of shear 151.4 kN and bearing 285.1 kN, so shear governs at 151.4 kN. For six bolts the group resistance is 6 × 151.4 = 908.4 kN, assuming the load is shared equally, which is reasonable for a short line of bolts with a slip-free fit. The factored load is 780 kN, so the demand to resistance ratio is 780 / 908.4 = 0.859 and the splice passes with 14 percent spare. Five bolts would give 757 kN, which is just below 780 kN, so six is the least number for single shear. The result also confirms that tearing out and net-section checks would be done separately.

Answer: Group resistance 908.4 kN; passes

(d)

With cover plates on both faces each bolt has two shear planes, so m = 2 and the shear resistance doubles to 302.8 kN. Bearing on the 12 mm main plate does not change: 285.1 kN per bolt. The smaller value, 285.1 kN, now governs. Number of bolts = 780 / 285.1 = 2.74, so 3 bolts are needed. Three bolts supply 3 × 285.1 = 855.4 kN. Compare with the single-lap option: double shear halves the bolt count from six to three, although it adds two cover plates, and the failure mode changes from bolt shear to plate bearing, which is less ductile and needs to be checked against the minimum edge distances.

Answer: 3 bolts

Problem 4 [A2-114] Eccentrically loaded bolt groups and slip-critical connections

A bracket on the flange of a steel column in an Ottawa parking structure is attached by six 22 mm high-strength bolts arranged in two vertical lines 120 mm apart, each line with three bolts at a 75 mm pitch. The group is symmetric, so its centroid is the centre bolt level between the two lines. A service vertical load of 90 kN acts at 250 mm from the centroid, measured horizontally. Use the elastic method: each bolt takes an equal share of the direct shear plus a torsional force proportional to its distance from the centroid. Bolt area is 380 mm² with Fu = 830 MPa. For slip-critical design at service load, use Vs = 0.53 c1 ks m Ab Fu with c1 = 0.82, ks = 0.33 and m = 1 shear plane.

  1. (a) Find the polar sum Σr² for the six bolts and the direct shear per bolt. [5]
  2. (b) Find the resultant force on the most heavily loaded bolt. [5]
  3. (c) Find the slip resistance Vs per bolt and state whether the connection is acceptable for slip at 90 kN. [5]
  4. (d) Find the largest service load, in kN, at the same eccentricity for which the critical bolt does not slip. [5]
(a)

Place the origin at the centroid. The four corner bolts are at x = ±60 mm and y = ±75 mm, so each has r² = 60² + 75² = 9225 mm².
