The two middle bolts are at x = ±60 mm and y = 0, so each has r² = 3600 mm². Σr² = 4 × 9225 + 2 × 3600 = 36 900 + 7200 = 44 100 mm². The direct shear is shared equally, P / 6 = 90 / 6 = 15.0 kN downward on every bolt. The torsion is M = P e = 90 × 0.250 = 22.5 kN·m. These three numbers feed the force on each bolt, and the sum of squares is the key bolt group property for torsion.

Answer: Σr² = 44 100 mm²; direct 15.0 kN

(b)

The corner bolts are farthest, r = √9225 = 96.05 mm. The torsion component has horizontal part Fx = M y / Σr² = 22.5 × 10⁶ × 75 / 44 100 = 38.27 kN and vertical part Fy = M x / Σr² = 22.5 × 10⁶ × 60 / 44 100 = 30.61 kN. The vertical component is added to the direct shear because the torsion on the correct side acts downward: 30.61 + 15.0 = 45.61 kN. The resultant is √(38.27² + 45.61²) = 59.54 kN. The corner bolt on the load side carries about four times the average direct share, which is why eccentric groups are designed for the worst bolt, not the average.

Answer: 59.5 kN

(c)

Vs = 0.53 × 0.82 × 0.33 × 1 × 380 × 830 = 45 234 N = 45.2 kN per bolt. The critical bolt demand of 59.5 kN exceeds this by 31.6 percent, so the connection would slip under service load and is not acceptable as a slip-critical joint. Slip means the plates slide until the bolts bear, which may be tolerable in a pure bearing joint, but a slip-critical designation is typically required for fatigue or vibration. The result tells the designer to add bolts, enlarge the pitch, or reduce the eccentricity of the load.

Answer: Vs = 45.2 kN; not acceptable

(d)

The bolt forces are proportional to P because the geometry is fixed, so the corner bolt force is 59.54 × P / 90 kN. Setting this equal to 45.23 kN gives P = 90 × 45.23 / 59.54 = 68.4 kN. This is 76 percent of the actual load. Another check of this value is the individual components: at P = 68.4 kN the direct share is 11.4 kN, the torsion vertical component is 23.3 kN, and the horizontal is 29.1 kN, giving a resultant of √(29.1² + 34.7²) = 45.3 kN, matching the slip resistance.

Answer: P = 68.4 kN

Problem 5 [A2-115] Fillet weld resistance and weld length

A 150 mm wide, 10 mm thick steel flat bar in a Windsor conveyor frame is lap-welded to a gusset plate and must transfer a factored tension of 480 kN. The weld metal has ultimate strength Xu = 480 MPa. Use the fillet weld resistance Vr = 0.67 φw Aw Xu (1 + 0.50 sin1.5 θ), where φw = 0.67, Aw = 0.707 D L is the throat area for leg size D and length L, and θ is the angle between the weld axis and the line of the force, so θ = 0 for a longitudinal weld and θ = 90 degrees for a transverse weld. Assume the resistances of different welds in the same joint may simply be added. Welds are placed on both long edges of the bar, and the short end weld is optional. All welds use D = 8 mm unless stated.

  1. (a) Find the resistance per millimetre of length of an 8 mm longitudinal fillet weld. [4]
  2. (b) Find the resistance per millimetre of an 8 mm transverse fillet weld. [4]
  3. (c) With only the two longitudinal edge welds, find the length of each needed for 480 kN. [6]
  4. (d) If a 150 mm transverse end weld is added across the bar, find the length of each longitudinal weld now needed. [6]
(a)

For a longitudinal weld θ = 0, so the bracket (1 + 0.50 sin1.5 θ) equals 1.0. The throat per millimetre is 0.707 × 8 = 5.656 mm. Then Vr = 0.67 × 0.67 × 5.656 × 480 × 1.0 = 1218.7 N per millimetre of weld, which is 1.219 kN/mm. Two factors of 0.67 appear: the first is the weld strength multiplier in the stated formula, and the second is the resistance factor φw. The shear acts along the throat plane, so the 0.707 conversion from leg size to throat is essential. A marker looks for the throat step to be shown clearly and for the units to be stated per millimetre.

Answer: 1218.7 N/mm

(b)

For a transverse weld θ = 90 degrees, sin 90° = 1, so the bracket is 1 + 0.50 × 1 = 1.50. The resistance is therefore 1.50 times the longitudinal value: 1218.7 × 1.50 = 1828.1 N/mm. Physically, a weld loaded across its axis acts through a stronger plane and is stiffer, but it is less ductile, which explains why the code rewards it with a higher resistance and not with greater deformation capacity. Using the transverse weld on its own is not wise in a joint that must deform, so it is combined with longitudinal welds here and the sum is allowed by the stated assumption.

Answer: 1828.1 N/mm

(c)

Two longitudinal welds share the load, so total resistance is 2 × 1.2187 kN/mm × L. Setting this to 480 kN gives L = 480 / (2 × 1.2187) = 196.9 mm for each weld. In practice the bar is lapped at least this length, and a designer would round up to 200 mm and check that the lap length is not less than the bar width of 150 mm, which it satisfies. The total length of weld is 393.9 mm, a substantial amount for a 10 mm bar, and this length reveals why a transverse end weld is attractive when the available lap on the gusset is short.

Answer: 196.9 mm each

(d)

The end weld across the 150 mm bar width has resistance 150 × 1.8281 = 274.2 kN. The remaining demand is 480 − 274.2 = 205.8 kN. This is carried by the two longitudinal welds: L = 205.8 / (2 × 1.2187) = 84.4 mm each. The longitudinal length drops from 196.9 mm to 84.4 mm, a reduction of 57 percent, because the transverse weld takes 57 percent of the load. The designer should note that the end weld is stiffer, so it attracts load first, and the simple addition used here is permitted by the problem but is unconservative; a real design would apply a reduction (S16 limits the combined resistance) because the stiffer transverse weld reaches its capacity first.

Answer: 84.4 mm each

A2 Practice Paper 24

Problem 1 [A2-116] Eccentric weld groups and simple beam connections

A bracket plate is welded to the face of a column in a Brampton precast plant using two vertical fillet welds, each 180 mm long, set 120 mm apart. A factored vertical load of 60 kN acts parallel to the welds at a horizontal distance of 200 mm from the vertical centreline of the weld group. Treat each weld as a line of unit throat, so the group properties are per millimetre of throat. The group polar moment is J = Σ(L³/12 + L d²), where d is the horizontal distance from each weld to the group centroid. Use the elastic method: the direct shear is shared by total weld length and the torsional force on a point is M r / J, resolved into components. The weld resistance per millimetre is 0.67 φw (0.707 D) Xu with φw = 0.67 and Xu = 480 MPa for leg size D, taken at θ = 0 for every point to stay conservative.

  1. (a) Find the direct shear force per millimetre of weld. [4]
  2. (b) Find the polar moment J of the weld group, in mm³. [5]
  3. (c) Find the resultant force per millimetre at the most heavily loaded end of the welds. [6]
  4. (d) Find the minimum leg size D required, in mm, and state the practical size you would specify. [5]
(a)

The total weld length is 2 × 180 = 360 mm. Direct shear per millimetre is q = P / (2L) = 60 000 N / 360 mm = 166.7 N/mm, acting downward and uniform along both welds. This is the part of the load that the group would carry if it were applied through its centroid. The remaining effect of the 200 mm offset is torsion about the centroid, which is treated in the following parts. The moment is M = 60 000 × 200 = 12.0 × 10⁶ N·mm, and a marker rewards separating the shear from the moment before combining them as vectors.

Answer: 166.7 N/mm

(b)

Each weld is a vertical line, so its own contribution is L³/12 = 180³ / 12 = 486 000 mm³. The weld is d = 60 mm from the centroid, so the transfer term is L d² = 180 × 3600 = 648 000 mm³. One weld gives 1 134 000 mm³, and two welds give J = 2 268 000 mm³. Because the welds are treated as lines of unit throat, the units are mm³ and the force per millimetre comes out directly. The L³/12 term is for bending of the line about its own centre, which matters since the welds are long compared with their spacing, and omitting it would underestimate J by about 43 percent.

Answer: J = 2 268 000 mm³

(c)

The farthest point is the end of a weld at x = 60 mm, y = 90 mm, with r = √(60² + 90²) = 108.2 mm. The torsion components are horizontal M y / J = 12.0 × 10⁶ × 90 / 2 268 000 = 476.2 N/mm and vertical M x / J = 12.0 × 10⁶ × 60 / 2 268 000 = 317.5 N/mm. The vertical torsional part acts in the same direction as the direct shear on the load side, so the vertical total is 317.5 + 166.7 = 484.1 N/mm. The resultant is √(476.2² + 484.1²) = 679.1 N/mm. This is about four times the direct shear alone, which shows how strongly the eccentricity governs.

Answer: 679.1 N/mm

(d)

The resistance per millimetre for leg size D is 0.67 × 0.67 × 0.707 × D × 480 = 152.3 D N/mm. Setting this equal to the demand of 679.1 N/mm gives D = 679.1 / 152.3 = 4.46 mm. A 4.46 mm weld cannot be built, so the practical choice is a 5 mm fillet, which gives a resistance of 761.7 N/mm and a ratio of 0.89. Many plant specifications set a larger minimum leg size for thicker plates, so the designer should confirm that 5 mm is allowed for the plate thickness. If it is not, a 6 mm weld gives 914 N/mm and a large reserve.

Answer: D = 4.46 mm; use 5 mm

Problem 2 [A2-117] Singly reinforced concrete beam flexure

A simply supported concrete beam in a Barrie community-centre gallery has a rectangular section 350 mm wide and 600 mm overall depth, with an effective depth d = 540 mm to the tension steel. Concrete strength is f'c = 30 MPa and the steel yield strength is fy = 400 MPa. Use φc = 0.65, φs = 0.85, α1 = 0.85 − 0.0015 f'c, β1 = 0.97 − 0.0025 f'c, a = φs As fy / (α1 φc f'c b), Mr = φs As fy (d − a/2), and a balanced neutral axis depth cb = 700 d / (700 + fy), with the tension steel yielding when c = a/β1 does not exceed cb. The minimum area of tension steel is As,min = 0.2 √f'c b h / fy. Four 25M bars are provided, each of area 500 mm².

  1. (a) Find the depth a of the equivalent rectangular stress block for the four 25M bars. [4]
  2. (b) Find the factored moment resistance Mr, and confirm that the steel yields. [5]
  3. (c) The gallery loading is increased so the factored moment is 420 kN·m. Find the required tension steel area. [7]
  4. (d) Find the minimum steel area As,min and state whether the original 2000 mm² satisfies it. [4]
(a)

First α1 = 0.85 − 0.0015 × 30 = 0.805. With As = 4 × 500 = 2000 mm², a = 0.85 × 2000 × 400 / (0.805 × 0.65 × 30 × 350) = 680 000 / 5494.1 = 123.8 mm. The numerator is the factored tension force in the steel, 680 kN, and the denominator is the factored concrete compressive strength per millimetre of stress block depth, 5494 N/mm. Setting them equal is horizontal equilibrium of the section. The stress block is about 23 percent of the effective depth, a moderate value, so the beam is not heavily reinforced.

Answer: a = 123.8 mm

(b)

Mr = φs As fy (d − a/2) = 680 000 × (540 − 61.9) = 680 000 × 478.1 = 325.1 × 10⁶ N·mm = 325.1 kN·m. For the yield check, β1 = 0.97 − 0.0025 × 30 = 0.895, so c = a / β1 = 123.8 / 0.895 = 138.3 mm. The balanced depth is cb = 700 × 540 / 1100 = 343.6 mm. Since c = 138.3 is well below cb, the steel yields before the concrete crushes and the failure is ductile, which means the beam would show large deflection and cracking before collapse. The formula for Mr is therefore valid as used.

Answer: Mr = 325.1 kN·m

(c)

Mf = 420 kN·m, so φs As fy (d − a/2) = 420 × 10⁶ with a = 0.85 As × 400 / 5494.1 = 0.06188 As. Writing the equation: 340 As (540 − 0.03094 As) = 420 × 10⁶, which becomes 10.52 As² − 183 600 As + 420 × 10⁶ = 0. Solving the quadratic gives As = 2708 mm² (the other root is not physical). Check: a = 0.06188 × 2708 = 167.6 mm, c = 187.3 mm, below cb = 343.6 mm, so steel yields. Six 25M bars (3000 mm²) would provide the area, possibly in two layers, which then lowers d; the designer must recheck.

Answer: As = 2708 mm²

(d)

As,min = 0.2 √f'c b h / fy = 0.2 × 5.477 × 350 × 600 / 400 = 575.1 mm². The provided 2000 mm² is 3.5 times this value, so the minimum is easily satisfied. The minimum exists so the steel can carry the moment released when the concrete cracks, so the beam does not fail suddenly at first cracking. The same check applies to the revised design of 2708 mm². Note the minimum uses the overall depth h, not the effective depth d, since cracking depends on the whole section.

Answer: As,min = 575.1 mm²; satisfied

Problem 3 [A2-118] Doubly reinforced and T-section concrete beams

A floor beam in a Mississauga office building acts monolithically with a slab, giving a T-section with effective flange width bf = 1200 mm, flange thickness hf = 100 mm, web width bw = 300 mm and effective depth d = 500 mm. Concrete strength is f'c = 25 MPa and fy = 400 MPa. Tension steel is 5500 mm². Use φc = 0.65, φs = 0.85, α1 = 0.85 − 0.0015 f'c, β1 = 0.97 − 0.0025 f'c, and cb = 700 d / (700 + fy). If the rectangular stress block depth, found using bf, exceeds hf, treat the section as a T: the flange overhangs take Asf = α1 φc f'c (bf − bw) hf / (φs fy), the web takes Asw = As − Asf with a = φs Asw fy / (α1 φc f'c bw), and Mr = φs Asf fy (d − hf/2) + φs Asw fy (d − a/2).

  1. (a) Find the depth of the stress block if the beam is treated as rectangular with width bf, and state whether T-section analysis is needed. [4]
  2. (b) Find the steel area Asf equilibrating the flange overhangs. [4]
  3. (c) Find the depth a of the web stress block and the factored moment resistance Mr. [6]
  4. (d) A later renovation cuts the effective flange width to 700 mm. Redo the T analysis and give the neutral axis depth c; state whether the section is still under-reinforced. [6]
(a)

Rectangular analysis with the full flange width: a = φs As fy / (α1 φc f'c bf). First α1 = 0.85 − 0.0015 × 25 = 0.8125. Then a = 0.85 × 5500 × 400 / (0.8125 × 0.65 × 25 × 1200) = 1 870 000 / 15 843.75 = 118.0 mm. Because 118.0 mm is greater than hf = 100 mm, the compressed concrete reaches below the flange into the web, so the rectangular assumption fails and the section must be analysed as a true T-beam. If a had been less than hf, the beam would simply behave as a rectangle 1200 mm wide, and the web would play no part.

Answer: a(rect) = 118.0 mm; T analysis needed

(b)

The compressive force in the two flange overhangs is α1 φc f'c (bf − bw) hf = 0.8125 × 0.65 × 25 × 900 × 100 = 1 188 281 N. The steel area that balances this force is Asf = 1 188 281 / (0.85 × 400) = 3494.9 mm². This is 63.5 percent of the 5500 mm² provided. The remaining steel, Asw = 5500 − 3494.9 = 2005.1 mm², works with the web rectangle of width 300 mm. Splitting the section this way makes the tricky T shape into two simple rectangles, and the marker looks for this split, with the overhang width being bf − bw, not bf.

Answer: Asf = 3494.9 mm²

(c)

The web block depth is a = 0.85 × 2005.1 × 400 / (0.8125 × 0.65 × 25 × 300) = 681 720 / 3960.9 = 172.1 mm. The flange part of the moment is 0.85 × 3494.9 × 400 × (500 − 50) = 534.7 × 10⁶ N·mm. The web part is 0.85 × 2005.1 × 400 × (500 − 86.05) = 282.2 × 10⁶ N·mm. Mr = 534.7 + 282.2 = 816.9 kN·m. For ductility, c = 172.1 / 0.9075 = 189.6 mm against cb = 700 × 500 / 1100 = 318.2 mm, so the steel yields and the use of fy is justified.

Answer: Mr = 816.9 kN·m

(d)

With bf = 700 mm the rectangular depth is 1 870 000 / (13.203 × 700) = 202.3 mm, well over hf, so T analysis applies. Asf = 13.203 × 400 × 100 / 340 = 1553.3 mm², Asw = 3946.7 mm², and a = 0.85 × 3946.7 × 400 / 3960.9 = 338.8 mm. Then c = 338.8 / 0.9075 = 373.3 mm, which exceeds cb = 318.2 mm. The steel would not yield at failure, so the section is over-reinforced and the moment formula with fy is invalid. The designer would have to reduce the steel or add compression steel. A narrower flange is thus a real hazard.

Answer: c = 373.3 mm; over-reinforced

Problem 4 [A2-119] Concrete beam shear and stirrup design

A transfer beam in a Windsor parking garage is 300 mm wide with an effective depth of 550 mm, so the shear depth is dv = 0.9 d = 495 mm. Concrete strength is f'c = 30 MPa, and closed 10M stirrups with two legs (Av = 200 mm²) have fy = 400 MPa. Use the simplified shear method: Vc = φc λ β √f'c bw dv with φc = 0.65, λ = 1.0 and β = 0.18; Vs = φs Av fy dv cot θ / s with φs = 0.85 and θ = 42 degrees; Vr = Vc + Vs. The factored shear at the critical section is Vf = 260 kN. The crushing limit of the web is Vr,max = 0.25 φc f'c bw dv. Maximum stirrup spacing is 0.7 dv, and the minimum shear steel is Av,min = 0.06 √f'c bw s / fy.

  1. (a) Find the concrete contribution Vc. [4]
  2. (b) Find the maximum stirrup spacing s that makes Vr equal to Vf = 260 kN. [6]
  3. (c) Adopt a spacing of 225 mm. Find the resulting Vr and check minimum steel and maximum spacing. [5]
  4. (d) Find the web crushing limit Vr,max and state what fraction of it the design shear represents. [5]
(a)

Vc = φc λ β √f'c bw dv = 0.65 × 1.0 × 0.18 × √30 × 300 × 495. The root is 5.477, so 0.65 × 0.18 = 0.117, times 5.477 gives 0.6408 MPa. Multiply by the area 300 × 495 = 148 500 mm² to get 95 164 N = 95.2 kN. This is the shear the cracked concrete can carry through aggregate interlock, the compression zone and dowel action. Because Vf = 260 kN is much higher, the stirrups must carry the difference of 164.8 kN. Note that the shear depth 495 mm, not d, is used in every term.

Answer: Vc = 95.2 kN

(b)

The stirrups must supply Vs = Vf − Vc = 260 − 95.2 = 164.8 kN. From Vs = φs Av fy dv cot θ / s the spacing is s = φs Av fy dv cot θ / Vs. Here cot 42° = 1.1106, so the numerator is 0.85 × 200 × 400 × 495 × 1.1106 = 37.38 × 10⁶ N·mm. Dividing by 164 836 N gives s = 226.8 mm. Any spacing at or below this value gives enough resistance, and a spacing larger than 226.8 mm would leave the beam short of the required shear capacity.

Answer: s = 226.8 mm

(c)

A practical spacing of 225 mm is a round number slightly under the limit. Then Vs = 0.85 × 200 × 400 × 495 × 1.1106 / 225 = 166.1 kN, and Vr = 95.2 + 166.1 = 261.3 kN, which is above 260 kN, so the design passes, but only by 0.5 percent. The minimum steel check gives Av,min = 0.06 × 5.477 × 300 × 225 / 400 = 55.5 mm², far less than the 200 mm² provided. The maximum spacing is 0.7 × 495 = 346.5 mm, and 225 mm is below it. All checks pass, but the narrow margin means the designer should consider 200 mm.

Answer: Vr = 261.3 kN; checks pass

(d)

Vr,max = 0.25 φc f'c bw dv = 0.25 × 0.65 × 30 × 300 × 495 = 723 938 N = 723.9 kN. This limit prevents crushing of the diagonal concrete struts regardless of the amount of stirrup steel. The design shear is 260 kN, which is 35.9 percent of the limit. Because the shear is well below the crushing limit, increasing the section size is not needed, and adding stirrups is the right remedy. If Vf had been above 723.9 kN, no amount of stirrups could have helped and the section would have had to be enlarged.

Answer: Vr,max = 723.9 kN; 36 percent used

Problem 5 [A2-120] Reinforced concrete short columns, tied and spiral, with interaction

A designer in Hamilton compares a tied column with a spiral column for a hospital parking ramp. Concrete has f'c = 35 MPa and steel fy = 400 MPa, with φc = 0.65, φs = 0.85 and α1 = 0.85 − 0.0015 f'c, β1 = 0.97 − 0.0025 f'c. Maximum axial resistance is Pr,max = 0.80 [α1 φc f'c (Ag − Ast) + φs fy Ast] for a tied column and 0.85 [same bracket] for a spiral column. The tied column is 450 mm square with 8 bars of 25M (Ast = 4000 mm²). The spiral column is circular, 450 mm in diameter, with 6 bars of 25M (Ast = 3000 mm²). For the tied column, steel is placed equally on two opposite faces, 2000 mm² each, with bar centroids 60 mm from the faces. Balanced conditions use cb = 700 d / (700 + fy), a = β1 cb, and the compression steel force is reduced by the concrete it displaces.

  1. (a) Find Pr,max for the tied column. [4]
  2. (b) Find Pr,max for the spiral column. [4]
  3. (c) Find the balanced axial resistance Prb of the tied column. [6]
  4. (d) Find the balanced moment resistance Mrb about the centroid of the tied column. [6]
(a)

α1 = 0.85 − 0.0015 × 35 = 0.7975. Ag = 450 × 450 = 202 500 mm², so Ag − Ast = 198 500 mm². The concrete term is 0.7975 × 0.65 × 35 × 198 500 = 3 601 400 N and the steel term is 0.85 × 400 × 4000 = 1 360 000 N. The bracket totals 4 961 400 N, and multiplying by 0.80 gives Pr,max = 3 969 120 N = 3969.1 kN. The factor of 0.80 allows for accidental eccentricity in a tied column. The steel ratio is 4000 / 202 500 = 1.98 percent, inside the usual 1 to 8 percent range for columns.

Answer: Pr,max = 3969.1 kN

(b)

For the circular section Ag = π × 450² / 4 = 159 043 mm². Then Ag − Ast = 156 043 mm². The concrete term is 0.518375 × 35 × 156 043, which is 18.143 × 156 043 = 2 831 100 N, and the steel term is 0.85 × 400 × 3000 = 1 020 000 N. The bracket is 3 851 100 N. Multiplied by the spiral factor 0.85, Pr,max = 3 273 400 N = 3273.4 kN. The spiral column has a higher factor, but its smaller area and fewer bars give a lower resistance than the square tied column, 17.5 percent less. A circular shape is chosen for confinement and ductility, not for plain strength.

Answer: Pr,max = 3273.4 kN

(c)

The effective depth is d = 450 − 60 = 390 mm, so cb = 700 × 390 / 1100 = 248.2 mm and a = 0.8825 × 248.2 = 219.0 mm. The strain in the compression steel is 0.0035 × (248.2 − 60) / 248.2 = 0.00265, above the yield strain 0.002, so it yields. Concrete force: 18.143 × 450 × 219.0 = 1788.1 kN. Net compression steel force: 2000 × (0.85 × 400 − 18.143) = 643.7 kN. Tension steel force: 0.85 × 2000 × 400 = 680 kN. Prb = 1788.1 + 643.7 − 680 = 1751.8 kN, about 44 percent of Pr,max, which marks the boundary between compression-controlled and tension-controlled behaviour.

Answer: Prb = 1751.9 kN

(d)

Take moments about the centroid, 225 mm from each face. Concrete: 1788.1 kN × (225 − 109.5) = 1788.1 × 115.5 mm = 206.5 kN·m. Compression steel: 643.7 kN × (225 − 60) = 643.7 × 165 mm = 106.2 kN·m. Tension steel: 680 kN × (390 − 225) = 680 × 165 mm = 112.2 kN·m. All three contributions act in the same sense, so Mrb = 206.5 + 106.2 + 112.2 = 424.9 kN·m. The corresponding eccentricity is e = Mrb / Prb = 424.9 / 1751.9 = 242.5 mm, which is more than half the 450 mm column depth, so this point is the knee of the interaction diagram.

Answer: Mrb = 424.9 kN·m

Exam A3: Municipal and Environmental Engineering

A3 Practice Paper 1

Problem 1 [A3-001] Population forecasting by arithmetic, geometric and logistic methods

The Town of Kemptville Heights, Ontario, is preparing a 25 year water and wastewater master plan. Census counts were 21,000 in 2011, 25,000 in 2016 and 27,800 in 2021, taken at equal 5 year intervals. Growth is slowing because serviced land is running out. The planner will compare three mathematical projections to the 2046 planning horizon. For the logistic curve, P = Ps/(1 + m ebt) with t measured in years from 2011, and the saturation population from three equally spaced counts is Ps = P1(2 P0 P2 − P1(P0 + P2))/(P0 P2 − P1²). Then m = (Ps − P0)/P0 and b = (1/n) ln[P0(Ps − P1)/(P1(Ps − P0))], where n is the interval between counts.

  1. (a) Project the 2046 population by the arithmetic increase method, using the average annual increase over 2011 to 2021. [4]
  2. (b) Project the 2046 population by the geometric increase method, fitted to the 2011 and 2021 counts with continuous compounding. [4]
  3. (c) Calculate the saturation population Ps of the logistic curve. [4]
  4. (d) Using the logistic curve, estimate the 2046 population (t = 35 years). Check that the curve reproduces the 2021 count. [4]
  5. (e) State which projection you would adopt for sizing 25 year infrastructure and why, and how you would treat the other two. [4]
(a)

Arithmetic method assumes a constant numerical increase per year. Average rate k = (P2021 − P2011)/10 = (27,800 − 21,000)/10 = 680 people/year. Projecting 25 years beyond 2021: P2046 = 27,800 + 680(25) = 44,800 people. The method ignores the slowing trend visible in the 2016 to 2021 census (an increase of 2,800 against 4,000 earlier), so it suits only short, stable growth periods. The arithmetic result is a straight line through the census points and therefore gives a middle figure here, above the logistic result and below the geometric result, because growth is decelerating. Planners normally use it only as an intermediate check or for very short horizons.

Answer: 44,800 people

(b)

Geometric growth assumes a constant percentage rate: P = P0 ekt. Fitting 2011 and 2021: k = ln(P2021/P2011)/10 = ln(27,800/21,000)/10 = 0.02805 per year. Then P2046 = 27,800 exp(0.02805 × 25) = 56,054 people. Compounding growth with no upper limit overshoots badly for a town running out of serviced land, so this is normally an upper bound for the planning range. Growth of this kind cannot continue indefinitely, so the figure is a ceiling rather than a forecast. The annual rate implied is about 2.8 percent, higher than the latest 5 year rate of 2.1 percent, which is a warning that extrapolating the earlier decade overstates the future.

Answer: 56,054 people

(c)

Equal-interval counts: P0 = 21,000, P1 = 25,000, P2 = 27,800. Numerator: 2 P0 P2 − P1(P0 + P2) = 2(21,000)(27,800) − 25,000(48,800) = 1.1676×10⁹ − 1.22×10⁹ = −5.24×10⁷. Denominator: P0 P2 − P1² = 5.838×10⁸ − 6.25×10⁸ = −4.12×10⁷. Ps = 25,000 × (−5.24×10⁷)/(−4.12×10⁷) = 31,796 people. Both signs are negative, as required for a valid logistic fit with decelerating growth. The saturation value is the population the serviced land can hold, so it should be checked against the official plan land supply and density targets. A result that is below the present population would signal that the logistic form does not fit the data.

Answer: 31,796 people

(d)

m = (Ps − P0)/P0 = (31,796 − 21,000)/21,000 = 0.5141. b = (1/5) ln[21,000(31,796 − 25,000)/(25,000(31,796 − 21,000))] = -0.12744 per year. Check at t = 10: P = 27,800, matching the 27,800 census count. At t = 35: P2046 = 31,796/(1 + 0.5141 e-0.12744 × 35) = 31,608 people. This is the most credible of the three for a town with a physical limit on growth. Because t is measured from 2011, the 2046 time is 35 years. The logistic value approaches the saturation population from below, so by 2046 the town is projected to be within about 1 percent of its limit, a more reasonable ceiling than either of the other two methods.

Answer: 31,608 people

(e)

Adopt the logistic projection as the planning basis, since the census increments are falling (4,000 then 2,800) and serviced land is finite, which is exactly the condition under which a saturation curve applies. Use the arithmetic result as an intermediate check and the geometric result as a high sensitivity case only. Because trunk mains and plants are staged, size the first stage for the logistic 2046 figure, reserve corridors and plant footprint for the geometric figure, and revisit with each census.

Answer: Logistic basis (lowest, 31,608); arithmetic (44,800) is an intermediate check and geometric (56,054) the high sensitivity case

Problem 2 [A3-002] Per-capita water demand, peaking factors and design flows

A municipal water supply serves a population of 38,000 in southwestern Ontario. Metered residential use averages 265 L/cap/d. Metered industrial, commercial and institutional (ICI) use is 3,900 m³/d. Non-revenue water (leakage and unmetered use) is 16 percent of total water produced. Design factors for the system are: maximum day demand = 1.75 × average day demand, and peak hour demand = 1.6 × maximum day demand. The water treatment plant uses 4 percent of its gross output for filter backwash and process water. The utility is considering a leak-reduction program that would lower non-revenue water to 8 percent of production while billed use stays unchanged.

  1. (a) Calculate the average day demand at the plant outlet, in L/s. [4]
  2. (b) Determine the maximum day demand, in L/s. [3]
  3. (c) Determine the peak hour demand, in L/s. [3]
  4. (d) Calculate the required gross treatment plant capacity, in ML/d, to deliver the maximum day demand after the 4 percent process use. [5]
  5. (e) Find the percentage reduction in required plant capacity if the leak-reduction program reaches the 8 percent target. [5]
(a)

Billed use = residential + ICI = 38,000(0.265) + 3,900 = 13,970 m³/d. Non-revenue water is 16 percent of production, so billed use is 84 percent of production: production = 13,970/0.84 = 16,631 m³/d. Converting, 1 L/s = 86.4 m³/d, so ADD = 16,631/86.4 = 192.5 L/s. This is the flow the distribution system must carry on an average day, including leakage. The 16 percent of production that is not billed is real water that must be treated and pumped, so design flows are based on production and not on billed consumption. Using billed use alone would understate every downstream design flow by almost one-fifth.

Answer: 192.5 L/s

(b)

MDD = 1.75 × ADD = 1.75 × 192.5 = 336.9 L/s. The maximum day demand governs the sizing of treatment, high-lift pumping and source works, since these operate steadily over the day and must meet the worst day of the year, usually a hot dry summer day. Converting to other units, this equals roughly 29.1 ML/d. The factor of 1.75 reflects a hot summer day when lawn watering and cooling loads push use well above the annual average, and it should be taken from local records where the utility has them.

Answer: 336.9 L/s

(c)

The peak hour factor is applied to the maximum day: PHD = 1.6 × MDD = 1.6 × 336.9 = 539.0 L/s. Peak hour flow governs the sizing of distribution mains and the balance between supply and storage, because short bursts of morning and evening use must be met from pipe capacity and elevated storage. Peak hour flow is about 1.6 times the maximum day rate. It is used for sizing distribution mains and pump capacity where no storage can buffer the flow, while storage in the system supplies the difference between peak hour and the steady maximum day treatment rate.

Answer: 539.0 L/s

(d)

The plant must produce enough gross water that 96 percent of it equals MDD. Net MDD = 336.9 L/s = 336.9 × 86.4 = 29104 m³/d. Gross capacity = net/0.96 = 30.32 ML/d after dividing by 1000 to give ML/d. Rating a plant to its net rather than gross output is a common error that leaves the plant short on the design day. The plant capacity is therefore rated higher than the maximum day delivered flow by the 4 percent used in backwashing. The value is expressed in megalitres per day, the unit used on Ontario drinking water licences and in the Municipal Drinking Water Licence.

Answer: 30.32 ML/d

(e)

New production = 13,970/0.92 = 15,185 m³/d, so new ADD = 175.7 L/s. New plant capacity = 1.75 × 175.7 × 86.4/0.96/1000 = 27.68 ML/d against 30.32 ML/d before. Reduction = (30.32 − 27.68)/30.32 × 100 = 8.7 %. Fixing leaks defers plant expansion because every demand factor multiplies the saved base flow. Halving the loss rate also reduces the peak hour demand and the pumping energy, so the saving is wider than treatment capacity alone. The program is assessed against its cost, but deferred expansion of the plant is usually the largest benefit.

Answer: 8.7 %

Problem 3 [A3-003] Fire flow requirements and design demand for a community

A three storey ordinary-construction warehouse in a Hamilton industrial park has a largest effective floor area of 3,400 m² for fire flow purposes. The needed fire flow is estimated with F = 220 C √A (F in L/min, A in m²) using construction coefficient C = 1.0. The base value is rounded to the nearest 1,000 L/min. Adjustments, applied as percentages of the base value: occupancy (limited combustibility) −15 percent, then, taken on the occupancy-adjusted flow, automatic sprinkler credit −30 percent and exposure surcharge +20 percent. The final flow is rounded to the nearest 1,000 L/min. The fire duration is 2.5 hours. The industrial area has a maximum day demand of 85 L/s and a peak hour demand of 150 L/s, and the municipality designs on the greater of peak hour or maximum day plus fire.

  1. (a) Calculate the base needed fire flow, rounded to the nearest 1,000 L/min. [4]
  2. (b) Apply the occupancy, sprinkler and exposure adjustments and give the adjusted flow before final rounding. [4]
  3. (c) State the final design fire flow (rounded to the nearest 1,000 L/min) in L/s. [3]
  4. (d) Calculate the fire storage volume required for the 2.5 hour duration, in m³. [4]
  5. (e) Determine the governing design flow for the industrial service area, in L/s, and state which condition controls. [5]
(a)

F = 220 C √A = 220(1.0)√3,400 = 220 × 58.31 = 12,828 L/min. Rounding to the nearest 1,000 L/min gives 13,000 L/min. The formula reflects that fire size grows with the square root of the effective floor area, with C = 1.0 representing ordinary construction. The base flow is the most severe condition for the building before any credit is given. The value is the reference to which the occupancy, sprinkler and exposure factors are applied, so an error here carries through every later step of the calculation.

Answer: 13,000 L/min

(b)

Occupancy adjustment: 13,000 × (1 − 0.15) = 11,050 L/min. The sprinkler credit (−30 percent) and exposure surcharge (+20 percent) are both taken on the occupancy-adjusted flow, so the net multiplier is 1 − 0.30 + 0.20 = 0.90. Adjusted flow = 11,050 × 0.90 = 9,945 L/min. Sprinklers reduce the municipal obligation because the building's own system is expected to control the fire, while exposed neighbours raise it. The net effect of the three adjustments is a reduction of about 24 percent from the base value. Sprinkler credit applies only where the system is complete, supervised and maintained, so the designer must confirm this with the building official before relying on it.

Answer: 9,945 L/min

(c)

Rounding 9,945 L/min to the nearest 1,000 gives 10,000 L/min. Converting, 10,000/60 = 166.7 L/s. This is the flow the hydrants and mains must deliver while still serving ordinary demand. The rounding to 1,000 L/min is the usual convention, because the formulas are approximate and a fire department cannot supply a more precise figure than that. This value is the fire component used in the following parts and in all later pressure checks. It is also expressed in litres per second so that it can be added directly to the maximum day demand in part e.

Answer: 166.7 L/s

(d)

Volume = flow × time = 10,000 L/min × (2.5 × 60 min) = 10,000 × 150 = 1,500,000 L, which is 1,500 m³. This is the fire component of the storage volume, to be added to equalization and emergency volumes in the reservoir sizing. The fire duration is longer than the common 2 hour value, so the volume is proportionally larger. A reservoir that holds this volume gives the system independence from the pumps for the whole fire, which is the safe assumption if power is lost.

Answer: 1,500 m³

(e)

Maximum day plus fire = 85 + 166.7 = 251.7 L/s. Peak hour = 150 L/s. The larger value governs: 251.7 L/s, controlled by maximum day plus fire. Distribution mains, pumps and the supply side must be able to deliver this flow while holding the minimum residual pressure the municipality specifies. Peak hour is lower here because a single large fire flow dominates the demand in a small industrial area. For this area the fire demand is much larger than the highest domestic demand, so fire flow, not peak hour, controls the design of the transmission and the pump selection. Always check both conditions, since in a large residential area peak hour may govern instead.

Answer: 251.7 L/s

Problem 4 [A3-004] Water source development: wells, intakes and safe yield

A village near Georgian Bay plans a new groundwater supply from a confined sandstone aquifer of uniform thickness 18 m. A 72 hour constant-rate pumping test at 0.020 m³/s reached steady state. Drawdowns were 4.20 m in an observation well 30 m from the pumping well and 2.35 m in one 90 m away. The production well has a radius of 0.15 m. Assume steady radial flow to a fully penetrating well (Thiem equation) with zero drawdown at the radius of influence R, extrapolated from the test. The maximum permitted drawdown at the face of the production well is 9.0 m. The village needs 40 L/s on the maximum day and requires one standby well of equal capacity.

  1. (a) Determine the transmissivity T of the aquifer from the two observation wells, in m²/d. [4]
  2. (b) Determine the hydraulic conductivity K, in m/d. [3]
  3. (c) Calculate the drawdown at the face of the production well at the test rate of 0.020 m³/s, in m. [4]
  4. (d) Using the extrapolated radius of influence, calculate the maximum well yield that holds the drawdown at the well face to 9.0 m, in L/s. [5]
  5. (e) How many production wells must be installed (duty plus one standby) to meet the 40 L/s maximum day demand? [4]
(a)

Thiem for a confined aquifer: s1 − s2 = [Q/(2πT)] ln(r2/r1). Solving, T = Q ln(r2/r1)/[2π(s1 − s2)] = 0.020 ln(90/30)/[2π(4.20 − 2.35)] = 0.020(1.0986)/(11.62) = 0.00189 m²/s. Multiplying by 86,400 s/d gives 163 m²/d. A transmissivity of this order is typical of a productive sandstone aquifer. The calculation assumes steady flow, a uniform confined aquifer and a fully penetrating well, so the result is an effective average over the zone tested. The 72 hour test at constant rate is long enough that drawdown at both observation wells had stabilized.

Answer: 163 m²/d

(b)

T = K b for a confined aquifer, so K = T/b = 163.3/18 = 9.07 m/d. The result lies within the range usually expected for fractured or fine sandstone, which gives a quick reasonableness check on the pumping test interpretation. Hydraulic conductivity is the property that transfers to other locations in the same formation, while transmissivity depends on the local thickness. A value of K near 9 m/d is typical of a clean medium-grained sandstone and is consistent with the geology described.

Answer: 9.07 m/d

(c)

Apply Thiem between the well face (rw = 0.15 m) and the near observation well: s_w = s1 + [Q/(2πT)] ln(r1/rw). With T = 0.00189 m²/s, Q/(2πT) = 1.684 m. Then ln(30/0.15) = 5.298, so s_w = 4.20 + 1.684(5.298) = 13.12 m. This is the drawdown that determines pump setting depth and the available head above the screens. A drawdown at the well face larger than the observed value at 30 m is expected, because the flow lines converge on the small screen radius. Part of this drawdown may in practice be well loss, which the Thiem equation ignores, so field data should be checked.

Answer: 13.12 m

(d)

Radius of influence: s1 = [Q/(2πT)] ln(R/r1) gives R = r1 exp(2πT s1/Q) = 30 exp(2.494) = 363 m. For a drawdown of 9.0 m at the well face: Q = 2πT s_w / ln(R/rw) = 2π(0.00189)(9.0)/ln(363/0.15) = 2π(0.00189)(9.0)/7.792 = 0.01372 m³/s, which is 13.7 L/s. Confined aquifer drawdown scales linearly with Q, so the test rate would exceed the allowable drawdown. The yield is limited by the allowable drawdown, so it is below the test rate. Operating below this value protects the well screens from exposure and the pump from cavitation, and the yield should be confirmed by a step test before design is finalized.

Answer: 13.7 L/s

(e)

Duty wells = 40/13.72 = 2.92, rounded up to 3 wells. Adding one standby well of equal capacity gives 4 wells. Standby capacity protects supply when one well is out for maintenance or pump failure, which is why a supply is judged on its firm capacity rather than the total installed. Ontario practice requires that firm supply capacity meets the maximum day demand with the largest source out of service. Installing three wells without a standby would give only two duty wells and would fall short of the demand if any one was out of service.

Answer: 4 wells

Problem 5 [A3-005] Transmission main sizing with the Hazen-Williams equation

A ductile iron transmission main carries treated water 6.2 km from a pump station in Barrie to a reservoir. The design flow is 185 L/s and the Hazen-Williams coefficient is C = 120. In SI units, hf = 10.67 L Q1.852 / (C1.852 D4.871), with hf and L in metres, Q in m³/s and D in metres. The designer limits the friction head loss to 3.0 m per kilometre. Available nominal diameters (equal to inside diameter) are 300, 350, 400, 450, 500 and 600 mm. The wet well low water level is 268.4 m and the reservoir high water level is 312.0 m. Minor losses in the station piping and fittings total 1.5 m at design flow. Use g = 9.81 m/s².

  1. (a) Calculate the minimum diameter that holds the friction loss to 3.0 m/km over the full length, in mm. [5]
  2. (b) Select the nominal diameter from the list that satisfies the criterion. [3]
  3. (c) Calculate the actual friction head loss in the selected pipe at design flow, in m. [4]
  4. (d) Calculate the mean velocity in the selected pipe, in m/s. [3]
  5. (e) Determine the total dynamic head the pump station must develop at design flow, in m. [5]
(a)

Allowable head loss over 6.2 km: hf = 3.0 × 6.2 = 18.6 m. Rearranging Hazen-Williams for diameter: D = [10.67 L Q1.852/(C1.852 hf)]1/4.871 with Q = 0.185 m³/s, L = 6,200 m and C = 120. The numerator is 10.67 × 6,200 × 0.1851.852 = 2906.42 and the denominator is 1201.852 × 18.6 = 131873, so D = (2.204 × 10-2)0.2053 = 0.4569 m, which is 457 mm. Because the equation raises diameter to the power 4.871, a small change in allowable head loss changes the diameter only slightly, so the size is not very sensitive to the gradient limit. The flow is the most influential input, since the diameter varies with Q to the power 0.38.

Answer: 457 mm

(b)

The next standard size not smaller than the calculated value is chosen, since a smaller pipe would exceed the allowable gradient. The calculated diameter is 457 mm, so the choice from the available list is 500 mm. Rounding up gives some reserve for pipe aging, when C falls below the new-pipe value. The calculated diameter of 457 mm falls between 450 and 500 mm. The 450 mm pipe would give a gradient slightly above 3.0 m/km, so 500 mm is the smallest size that complies. The designer should also check pressure class and transient pressures for the larger pipe.

Answer: 500 mm

(c)

hf = 10.67 L Q1.852/(C1.852 D4.871) with D = 0.500 m. D4.871 = 0.03417 and C1.852 = 7090, giving hf = 10.67(6,200)(0.04393)/(7090 × 0.03417) = 12.00 m. This is below the 18.6 m limit, as expected for a size selected conservatively. The loss is roughly two-thirds of the permitted 18.6 m, giving a margin for future flow growth and for the fall in C as the pipe ages over the design life. If the C value dropped to 100, the loss would rise by about 40 percent and still be acceptable.

Answer: 12.00 m

(d)

v = Q/A with A = πD²/4 = π(0.500)²/4 = 0.1963 m². v = 0.185/0.1963 = 0.94 m/s. This lies within the usual 0.6 to 2.0 m/s design range for transmission mains, avoiding both sediment settling and excessive surge pressure. The velocity limit also affects surge: a column of water moving at a high speed gives a larger pressure rise on sudden valve closure. Velocities below about 1.0 m/s are comfortable, so this selection meets the criterion with room to spare.

Answer: 0.94 m/s

(e)

TDH = static lift + friction loss + minor losses. Static lift = 312.0 − 268.4 = 43.6 m. Friction = 12.00 m and minor losses = 1.5 m. TDH = 43.6 + 12.00 + 1.5 = 57.1 m. The pump must be selected so that its curve crosses this head at 185 L/s with the best efficiency point close by. The result is used to select the pump and motor and to check that the pump discharge pressure rating of the forcemain is sufficient. A design margin is normally added for aging, so the pump would be checked at C values lower than 120 as well.

Answer: 57.1 m

A3 Practice Paper 2

Problem 1 [A3-006] Storage reservoir sizing for equalization, fire and emergency

A new elevated tank is to serve a growth area in Ottawa. Supply to the tank is constant at the maximum day demand of 12,000 m³/d (500 m³/h). Demand on the maximum day, as a multiple of the 500 m³/h average, is for six 4 hour blocks starting at midnight: 0.55, 1.25, 1.35, 1.05, 1.45 and 0.35. Fire storage must cover 150 L/s for 2.5 hours. Emergency storage is 25 percent of the sum of equalization and fire storage. The tank will be a cylinder with 11 m of active water depth. Equalization volume is the range of the cumulative difference between supply and demand over the day.

  1. (a) Determine the equalization storage volume from the cumulative supply minus demand curve, in m³. [6]
  2. (b) Calculate the fire storage volume, in m³. [3]
  3. (c) Calculate the emergency storage, in m³. [3]
  4. (d) Calculate the total tank volume required, in m³. [3]
  5. (e) Find the inside diameter of a cylindrical tank holding the total volume in 11 m of active depth, in m. [3]
  6. (f) Say in which block the tank is at its lowest level and what that implies for pump control. [2]
(a)

Each 4 hour block moves (supply − demand) = (1 − factor) × 500 × 4 = (1 − factor) × 2,000 m³. The surpluses are +900, −500, −700, −100, −900 and +1,300 m³. Cumulative: +900, +400, −300, −400, −1,300, 0. The maximum is +900 m³ (end of block 1) and the minimum is −1,300 m³ (end of block 5), so equalization = 900 − (−1,300) = 2,200 m³. The tank must hold this much to ride through the afternoon and evening deficit and be refilled overnight.

Answer: 2,200 m³

(b)

Fire volume = 150 L/s × 2.5 h × 3,600 s/h = 150 × 9,000 = 1,350,000 L, which is 1,350 m³ (1 m³ = 1,000 L). The fire supply is held in reserve at all times and is not available for ordinary use. The fire volume is independent of the daily demand pattern and is simply held in reserve. In many Ontario municipalities the reserve is placed at the bottom of the tank, with the intake set above it so that ordinary demand cannot draw it down.

Answer: 1,350 m³

(c)

Emergency storage = 0.25 × (equalization + fire) = 0.25 × (2,200 + 1,350) = 0.25 × 3,550 = 888 m³. It covers a pump or main failure, power loss or a short disruption in supply. The percentage rule is a planning allowance that reflects the likelihood and duration of supply interruption, and it is taken on the combined equalization and fire volumes. A more detailed approach would use a risk assessment of the specific feed arrangement. Here it adds a quarter of the combined equalization and fire volume, about 888 m³.

Answer: 888 m³

(d)

Total = equalization + fire + emergency = 2,200 + 1,350 + 888 = 4,438 m³. In practice the next larger standard tank size would be selected, with the overflow level above the top of the active volume. The total volume is made up of three components that serve different purposes, and only the equalization volume cycles daily. The other two components must be kept full, so water quality and turnover need to be managed in the tank to prevent stagnation.

Answer: 4,438 m³

(e)

V = π D² h/4, so D = √(4V/(πh)) = √(4 × 4,438/(π × 11)) = √513.6 = 22.7 m. A tank of this scale is usually a composite elevated tank or ground reservoir, depending on the head the zone needs. A tank this wide and shallow may be uneconomic, so the designer may prefer two cells, which also allows one to be cleaned while the other stays in service. The diameter also affects the turnover time and the risk of poor mixing.

Answer: 22.7 m

(f)

The cumulative curve reaches its minimum at the end of block 5 (20:00 hours), after the evening peak of 1.45. The tank is therefore emptiest at 20:00. Supply is constant, so the tank starts refilling automatically at 20:00, when demand drops to 0.35 of the average, and no special refill control is needed for that. Level controls only have to keep the fire and emergency reserve, about 2,238 m³, unused at the low point, so that the evening draw is met from the equalization volume alone. A float or level transmitter in the tank gives the operator the information needed to start pumps early enough.

Answer: Lowest at 20:00; reserve must stay untouched

Problem 2 [A3-007] Pumping station design with pump and system curves

A lift station in a Niagara region community pumps water through a forcemain to a ground-level storage tank. The system curve is H = 24 + 1,350 Q², where H is head in metres and Q in m³/s, and 24 m is the static lift. The installed centrifugal pump has the curve Hp = 58 − 1,000 Q². At its operating point the pump efficiency is 74 percent. Use ρ = 1,000 kg/m³ and g = 9.81 m/s². A second identical pump may be installed and run in parallel, discharging into the same forcemain. The operator also wants to know whether throttling a discharge valve can be used to hold the flow to 100 L/s with the single pump.

  1. (a) Find the operating flow of the single pump, in L/s. [4]
  2. (b) Find the total dynamic head at the operating point, in m. [3]
  3. (c) Calculate the shaft power drawn by the pump at the operating point, in kW. [4]
  4. (d) Find the total flow when two identical pumps run in parallel against the same system, in L/s. [5]
  5. (e) If the single pump is throttled to deliver 100 L/s, how much head must the valve absorb, in m? [4]
(a)

The operating point is where the pump head equals the system head: 58 − 1,000 Q² = 24 + 1,350 Q². So 34 = 2,350 Q², Q² = 0.01447, Q = 0.1203 m³/s, which is 120.3 L/s. The pump delivers exactly the flow at which the head it produces equals the head the forcemain demands. The system curve is the sum of static head and a friction-and-minor-loss term that varies with the square of flow. Real pumps drift from the published curve as they wear, so the operating point should be verified by a field test after commissioning.

Answer: 120.3 L/s

(b)

H = 24 + 1,350 Q² = 24 + 1,350(0.01447) = 43.5 m. Checking on the pump curve gives 58 − 1,000(0.01447) = the same value, confirming the intersection. Static lift contributes 24 m and friction and minor losses contribute the rest. The static component is 24 m, equal to the lift from the wet well to the tank water surface. The remaining 19.5 m is friction and minor losses, and this share shows that the system is moderately friction-dominated at this flow.

Answer: 43.5 m

(c)

Shaft power = ρ g Q H/η = 1,000 × 9.81 × 0.1203 × 43.5/0.74 = 69,415 W, or 69.4 kW. Motor selection must allow a margin above this figure, because the pump will see higher flow if the discharge head drops or if parallel operation is used. The hydraulic or water power is the product of flow, head and specific weight, and the shaft power is greater by the factor 1/η. The electrical input is higher still by the motor efficiency, which is typically 92 to 95 percent for this size of motor.

Answer: 69.4 kW

(d)

For identical pumps in parallel each pump delivers Q/2 at the same head, so the combined curve is H = 58 − 1,000(Q/2)² = 58 − 250 Q². Setting equal to the system curve: 58 − 250 Q² = 24 + 1,350 Q², so 34 = 1,600 Q², Q² = 0.02125, Q = 0.1458 m³/s, or 145.8 L/s. The total is well below twice the single-pump flow because the extra flow raises friction loss in the shared forcemain. With two pumps the flow rises by only about 21 percent, from 120.3 to 145.8 L/s, which shows the limit of parallel operation against a steep system curve. Each pump then runs at half of the total flow, nearer to the left of its best-efficiency point.

Answer: 145.8 L/s

(e)

At Q = 0.100 m³/s the pump develops 58 − 1,000(0.01) = 48.0 m. The system needs 24 + 1,350(0.01) = 37.5 m. The valve absorbs the difference: 10.5 m. This head is wasted as heat, so throttling costs energy; a variable speed drive or trimming the impeller is more efficient for long-term flow control. The throttled operating point lies on the pump curve, with the valve making up the difference between the pump head and the system head. This arrangement is simple but wasteful, because the valve dissipates about 10 m of head every hour that the pump runs.

Answer: 10.5 m

Problem 3 [A3-008] Water distribution network analysis by the Hardy Cross method

A single loop A-B-C-D in a subdivision distribution system in Guelph is fed at A with 150 L/s. Outflows are 40 L/s at B, 60 L/s at C and 50 L/s at D. Head loss in each pipe is h = K Q|Q| with Q in m³/s and K in s²/m⁵: AB = 2,200, BC = 3,100, CD = 2,600, DA = 1,800. Clockwise flows are positive. The first trial flows are AB = +90, BC = +50, CD = −10 and DA = −60 L/s (continuity is satisfied at every node). Use the Hardy Cross correction ΔQ = −Σ(K Q|Q|)/Σ(2K|Q|). The hydraulic grade line at A is 142.0 m. Carry out two iterations.

  1. (a) Calculate the head loss closure error Σ K Q|Q| for the first trial flows, in m. [4]
  2. (b) Compute the first correction ΔQ, in L/s. [4]
  3. (c) Give the corrected flow in pipe AB after the first iteration, in L/s. [3]
  4. (d) Carry out a second iteration and give the correction ΔQ, in L/s. [4]
  5. (e) Using the flows after the second iteration, determine the hydraulic grade line elevation at C along path A-B-C, in m. [5]
(a)

With clockwise positive, the loop head losses are AB: 2,200(0.090)² = 17.82 m; BC: 3,100(0.050)² = 7.75 m; CD: −2,600(0.010)² = −0.26 m; DA: −1,800(0.060)² = −6.48 m. Sum = 17.82 + 7.75 − 0.26 − 6.48 = 18.83 m. A non-zero sum means the trial flows violate energy conservation around the loop, so the flows need correcting. Since the sum is positive, the clockwise pipes lose more head than the anticlockwise pipes, which means too much flow is being sent clockwise. The size of the closure error gives a first measure of how far the guessed flows are from the true solution.

Answer: 18.83 m

(b)

Denominator Σ 2K|Q| = 2(2,200)(0.090) + 2(3,100)(0.050) + 2(2,600)(0.010) + 2(1,800)(0.060) = 396 + 310 + 52 + 216 = 974. ΔQ = −18.83/974 = -0.01933 m³/s, which is -19.33 L/s. The negative sign shows that flow must be shifted anticlockwise to relieve the excess clockwise head loss. The method is a Newton-type linearization of the energy equation around the loop, assuming the same correction for every pipe. For a single loop the first iteration usually removes about 90 percent of the error, and a second iteration is normally enough.

Answer: -19.33 L/s

(c)

Apply the same ΔQ to every pipe in the loop: Q_AB = 90 + (-19.33) = 70.67 L/s. Likewise BC = 30.67, CD = -29.33 and DA = -79.33 L/s. Continuity at each node remains satisfied because the same correction is added around the entire loop. Pipe AB therefore carries less than the first guess, and the flow redistributes toward the path A-D-C. The change in the flows of pipes CD and DA also reverses the direction of flow in CD, which is a legitimate result of the correction.

Answer: 70.67 L/s

(d)

Using the corrected flows, Σ K Q|Q| = 0.336 m and Σ 2K|Q| = 939.2. ΔQ = −0.336/939.2 = -0.358 L/s. The correction is far smaller than the first, which shows quadratic convergence typical of Hardy Cross, and the flows are now accurate for design purposes. A correction below 1 L/s is normally taken as converged for design of a distribution network, because the uncertainty in the demands and the pipe coefficients is much larger than the remaining error. The flows are now accepted for design.

Answer: -0.358 L/s

(e)

After iteration 2: Q_AB = 70.31 L/s and Q_BC = 30.31 L/s. HGL at B = 142.0 − 2,200(0.07031)² = 131.12 m. HGL at C = HGL_B − 3,100(0.03031)² = 128.28 m. The same result should come from the path A-D-C, which is a useful check on convergence; the pressure at C is found from HGL minus the ground elevation. The path A-B-C passes along the two clockwise pipes with their final flows. The pressure at C is the HGL minus the ground elevation at C, and it should be at least 275 kPa under normal service in the system, depending on the municipal standard.

Answer: 128.28 m

Problem 4 [A3-009] Network pressure and fire-flow checks at nodes

A hydrant at node N in a Peterborough pressure zone is fed by a single 300 mm main, 1,600 m long, from a floating elevated tank. The tank water surface is at elevation 239.0 m for this check. The ground elevation at N is 181.0 m. The main has Hazen-Williams C = 110, and hf = 10.67 L Q1.852/(C1.852 D4.871) in SI units (Q in m³/s). Take 9.81 kPa of pressure per metre of water head. Peak hour demand at N is 60 L/s. For the fire check, maximum day demand at N is 35 L/s and the required fire flow is 120 L/s. The municipality requires a residual pressure of at least 140 kPa at the hydrant during the fire. Neglect minor losses.

  1. (a) Calculate the pressure at node N under peak hour demand of 60 L/s, in kPa. [4]
  2. (b) Calculate the residual pressure at N under maximum day demand plus the 120 L/s fire flow, in kPa. [4]
  3. (c) Find the largest fire flow that can be delivered at N while keeping 140 kPa residual with the 35 L/s maximum day demand, in L/s. [6]
  4. (d) If the 300 mm main were replaced by a 350 mm main of the same length and C, find the available fire flow at 140 kPa residual, in L/s. [6]
(a)

Friction loss hf = 10.67(1,600)(0.060)1.852/(1101.852 × 0.304.871) = 5.44 m. The hydraulic grade line at N is 239.0 − 5.44 = 233.56 m, so pressure head = 233.56 − 181.0 = 52.56 m. Pressure = 9.81 × 52.56 = 516 kPa. This is an acceptable operating pressure for domestic service in the zone. Pressures above about 550 kPa may be reduced by a pressure-reducing valve at the service, and many municipalities limit the maximum pressure for this reason. The value found is high but is acceptable at the lowest-demand points of the zone.

Answer: 516 kPa

(b)

Total flow in the main = 35 + 120 = 155 L/s = 0.155 m³/s. hf = 10.67(1,600)(0.155)1.852/(1101.852 × 0.304.871) = 31.55 m. The HGL at N = 239.0 − 31.55 = 207.45 m and pressure head = 26.45 m. Pressure = 9.81 × 26.45 = 259 kPa, which is above the 140 kPa minimum, so the requirement is met. The pressure falls from 516 to 259 kPa when the flow rises from 60 to 155 L/s, because friction loss rises roughly with the square of the flow. The residual is still above the 140 kPa limit, so the main is adequate for the stated fire.

Answer: 259 kPa

(c)

A residual of 140 kPa corresponds to a head of 140/9.81 = 14.27 m, so the HGL at N must be at least 181.0 + 14.27 = 195.27 m. The allowable head loss is 239.0 − 195.27 = 43.73 m. Solve hf(Q) = 43.73 m with Hazen-Williams: Q = [43.73 C1.852 D4.871/(10.67 L)]1/1.852 = 0.1849 m³/s = 185 L/s total. Subtract the maximum day demand of 35 L/s to leave 150 L/s available for fire fighting. This exceeds the 120 L/s requirement.

Answer: 150 L/s

(d)

With D = 0.35 m the same allowable head loss of 43.73 m gives Q = [43.73 × 1101.852 × 0.354.871/(10.67 × 1,600)]1/1.852 = 0.2773 m³/s = 277 L/s total. Subtracting the 35 L/s maximum day demand leaves 242 L/s for fire. The total flow rises by about 50 percent (277 against 185 L/s) for a 17 percent increase in diameter, because the capacity of a pipe at a fixed gradient varies with D to the power 2.63, and (0.35/0.30)2.63 = 1.50. The larger main costs more, so looping the main from a second feed is the alternative to larger pipe.

Answer: 242 L/s

Problem 5 [A3-010] Coagulation and flocculation: mixing intensity and detention time

A 30 ML/d surface water treatment plant on Lake Ontario (design flow 0.350 m³/s) uses alum for coagulation. A jar test found an optimum dose of 28 mg/L as commercial alum. Design criteria: rapid mix velocity gradient G = 800 s⁻¹ with a detention time of 30 s; flocculation G = 40 s⁻¹ with a detention time of 24 min. Water temperature is 10 °C with dynamic viscosity μ = 1.30 × 10⁻³ Pa·s. Power input to a mixing basin is P = G² μ V. Each 1 mg/L of alum consumes 0.50 mg/L of alkalinity as CaCO₃. Raw water alkalinity is 95 mg/L as CaCO₃.

  1. (a) Calculate the volume of the rapid mix basin, in m³. [3]
  2. (b) Calculate the power required for the rapid mix, in W. [4]
  3. (c) Calculate the total flocculation basin volume, in m³. [3]
  4. (d) Calculate the power input to the flocculation basin at G = 40 s⁻¹, in W. [4]
  5. (e) Calculate the mass of alum required per day at the design flow, in kg/d. [3]
  6. (f) Determine the alkalinity remaining after alum addition, in mg/L as CaCO₃. [3]
(a)

Volume = flow × detention time = 0.350 m³/s × 30 s = 10.5 m³. A small, compact basin is used because coagulant must be dispersed within a second or two, before the metal hydroxide precipitate forms, and this requires intense turbulence in a small volume. The detention time is short because the chemical reaction of alum with the water is almost complete within seconds. The basin is designed for a high G to disperse the coagulant before the precipitate forms. A static mixer or a rapid mixing pump may replace the basin.

Answer: 10.5 m³

(b)

P = G² μ V = (800)²(1.30 × 10⁻³)(10.5) = 640,000 × 1.30 × 10⁻³ × 10.5 = 8,736 W. Power is delivered by a mechanical mixer or an in-line static mixer. The cold-water viscosity of 10 °C is used because higher viscosity in winter raises the power needed for the same G, and so it is the design condition. Mixer power is usually expressed in watts per cubic metre of basin, here equal to the G-squared times viscosity, or about 832 W/m³. The motor chosen is larger than this value to cover drive losses and to allow adjustment of G over a range.

Answer: 8,736 W

(c)

Volume = Q t = 0.350 m³/s × (24 × 60 s) = 0.350 × 1,440 = 504 m³. This volume is normally divided into at least two or three compartments in series, with decreasing G from first to last, to build a strong floc without breaking it up again. A long detention time allows particles to collide and join into floc large enough to settle. The volume is divided into compartments of tapered energy, and baffles keep the flow from short-circuiting, which would reduce the effective time.

Answer: 504 m³

(d)

P = G² μ V = (40)²(1.30 × 10⁻³)(504) = 1,600 × 1.30 × 10⁻³ × 504 = 1,048 W. Flocculation power per unit volume is only 1/400 of the rapid mix value because G varies with the square root of the power, and floc is easily sheared at high energy. Mixing energy is kept low to avoid floc break-up. The Gt value for this design is 40 × 1,440 = 57,600, inside the typical range of 10,000 to 100,000 for flocculation. A check on Gt confirms that the combination of G and time is sensible.

Answer: 1,048 W

(e)

Mass = dose × flow = 28 mg/L × 0.350 m³/s × 86,400 s/d. Since 1 mg/L = 1 g/m³, the mass is 28 g/m³ × 30,240 m³/d = 846,720 g/d = 847 kg/d. This sets the size of the chemical feed system and bulk storage, usually for at least 30 days of supply. The same dose applied for a year would use about 309 tonnes of alum. The dose is adjusted with the raw water quality, and jar testing is repeated whenever the temperature, turbidity or organic content changes significantly in spring and storm events.

Answer: 847 kg/d

(f)

Alkalinity consumed = 0.50 × 28 = 14.0 mg/L as CaCO₃. Remaining alkalinity = 95 − 14.0 = 81.0 mg/L. The residual is adequate to buffer pH near the optimum range for alum coagulation, so no supplementary alkali is needed at this dose. Low-alkalinity waters would require lime or soda ash addition. The effect of alum on alkalinity also reduces pH, which is checked against the optimum coagulation range of about 5.5 to 7.0. The remaining alkalinity of 81 mg/L as CaCO₃ is sufficient to keep the pH from falling below this range.

Answer: 81.0 mg/L

A3 Practice Paper 3

Problem 1 [A3-011] Sedimentation basin design by overflow rate

The Town of Orangeville is expanding its surface water treatment plant to a design flow of 18 000 m³/d. After coagulation and flocculation the water enters rectangular, horizontal-flow sedimentation basins that must be designed on an overflow rate (surface loading) of 28 m³/m²·d. The flow is split equally among three identical basins operating in parallel. Each basin has an internal width of 8.0 m and a side water depth of 3.8 m. Effluent leaves each basin over finished weirs whose total crest length is 60 m per basin. Assume ideal Type I settling, uniform flow distribution, and that the basin volume is the plan area times the side water depth (ignore sludge hopper volume and inlet and outlet zones).

  1. (a) Calculate the total plan area, in m², required for the three basins, and the area of one basin. [5]
  2. (b) Find the length of each basin, in metres, for the stated width. [5]
  3. (c) Calculate the theoretical detention time of one basin, in hours. [5]
  4. (d) Calculate the weir loading rate, in m³/m·d, and state whether it is a concern for floc carryover. [5]
(a)

The overflow rate is the flow divided by the plan area, vo = Q/A, and it equals the settling velocity of the slowest particle that is fully removed in an ideal basin. Rearranging, A = Q/vo = 18 000 m³/d ÷ 28 m³/m²·d = 642.9 m². The flow is shared by three identical basins, so each carries 6 000 m³/d and needs 6 000 ÷ 28 = 214.3 m². The total and the per-basin value are consistent: 3 × 214.3 = 642.9 m². Depth does not appear in this calculation, which is the key property of ideal settling: removal depends on surface area, not on volume or depth.

Answer: 642.9 m² total (214.3 m² per basin)

(b)

Each basin has plan area A = L × W, so the length is L = A/W. Using the per-basin area of 214.3 m² and the given width of 8.0 m, L = 214.3 ÷ 8.0 = 26.8 m. This gives a length to width ratio of 26.8/8.0 = 3.35, which is a little below the commonly preferred range of 4:1 to 5:1 for rectangular clarifiers, so a designer might narrow the basin to about 6 m to improve flow uniformity and reduce short circuiting. For this question we keep the given width. The length is rounded to 26.8 m and the overflow rate is then very slightly below 28 m³/m²·d, which is conservative for removal.

Answer: 26.8 m

(c)

Detention time is basin volume divided by the flow through that basin, t = V/Q. The volume is plan area times depth, V = 214.3 m² × 3.8 m = 814.3 m³. The flow per basin is 18 000 ÷ 3 = 6 000 m³/d. Then t = 814.3 ÷ 6 000 = 0.1357 d. Converting, 0.1357 d × 24 h/d = 3.26 h. This is within the usual 2 to 4 hour range for conventional rectangular settling basins treating coagulated surface water. Note that the same result follows from t = depth ÷ overflow rate = 3.8 ÷ 28 = 0.1357 d, because volume divided by flow equals depth divided by surface loading.

Answer: 3.26 h

(d)

Weir loading is the flow leaving per unit length of weir crest. For one basin, q = Q/Lweir = 6 000 m³/d ÷ 60 m = 100 m³/m·d. Typical design guidance for sedimentation basins keeps weir loading at or below roughly 250 m³/m·d, because a high loading creates strong upflow velocities near the effluent end that can pull light floc out of the basin. At 100 m³/m·d the loading is well under that limit, so carryover from the outlet is not a concern and the finished weirs are adequately long. If the weirs had been cut to 20 m the loading would have risen to 300 m³/m·d and extra launders would be warranted.

Answer: 100 m³/m·d

Problem 2 [A3-012] Rapid sand filtration rates and backwash

A small Ontario community on Georgian Bay is upgrading its water plant to treat 12 000 m³/d of settled water continuously (24 hours per day) through dual-media rapid gravity filters. The design filtration rate with all filters in service is 8.0 m/h. Each filter box is square, 5.0 m by 5.0 m in plan. Engineers want the minimum number of identical filters that meets the design rate, and they must confirm the rate is acceptable when one filter is out of service for backwash. Backwash is performed at 45 m/h (upward superficial velocity) for 8 minutes, and every filter is backwashed once every 48 hours. Neglect filter-to-waste and surface wash water.

  1. (a) Calculate the total filter area required, in m², at the design filtration rate. [4]
  2. (b) Determine the number of 5.0 m by 5.0 m filters needed, then find the filtration rate, in m/h, when one filter is out of service. [5]
  3. (c) Calculate the volume of backwash water used per backwash of one filter, in m³. [5]
  4. (d) Calculate the backwash water as a percentage of the daily plant production. [6]
(a)

The filtration rate (hydraulic loading) is the flow divided by the filter area, so the area follows from A = Q/vf. First convert the flow to an hourly basis: 12 000 m³/d ÷ 24 h/d = 500 m³/h. Then A = 500 m³/h ÷ 8.0 m/h = 62.5 m². This is the total of all filters operating together, so it is the minimum area the filter bank must provide when every box is on line. The result is then divided into whole filter boxes in the next part, which always rounds the number of boxes up because we cannot build part of a filter and the design rate must not be exceeded.

Answer: 62.5 m²

(b)

Each filter has an area of 5.0 × 5.0 = 25.0 m². The number of filters is 62.5 ÷ 25.0 = 2.5, so we round up to 3 filters, giving 75 m² installed. With all three on line the actual rate is 500 ÷ 75 = 6.67 m/h, well under the 8.0 m/h design value. When one filter is out of service for backwash the full 500 m³/h passes through the remaining two, which have 50 m² between them. The rate is 500 ÷ 50 = 10.0 m/h. This is still within the usual upper limit near 10 to 12 m/h for dual-media filters, but there is little margin, and a fourth filter would give better security.

Answer: 3 filters; 10.0 m/h

(c)

The backwash flow is the superficial velocity times the filter area: Qbw = 45 m/h × 25.0 m² = 1 125 m³/h, which is 0.3125 m³/s or 312.5 L/s. The wash lasts 8 minutes, which is 8/60 = 0.1333 h. The volume is V = 1 125 m³/h × 0.1333 h = 150 m³ per backwash. This should be compared with the volume of the clearwell or wash water tank, which has to hold at least this volume plus a reserve, and the pumps or elevated tank must be able to deliver 312.5 L/s for the full 8 minutes. The bed must also expand by roughly 20 to 30 percent at this velocity, which would be checked against the media size and water temperature.

Answer: 150 m³

(d)

Each filter is washed once every 48 hours, which is once per two days, so over one day the three filters together use a backwash volume of 3 filters × 150 m³ ÷ 2 days = 225 m³/d. The daily production is 12 000 m³/d, so the percentage of production used for washing is 225 ÷ 12 000 × 100 = 1.875 percent. Plants usually accept 1 to 5 percent of production for backwash, so this is a typical and acceptable figure. Note that this is gross production; the net water delivered to the distribution system is 12 000 − 225 = 11 775 m³/d if the wash water is not recovered. Recycling the spent wash water to the head of the plant is common, but needs a check on Cryptosporidium risk.

Answer: 1.875 %

Problem 3 [A3-013] Disinfection with chlorine: contact time and CT

A groundwater under the direct influence of surface water is disinfected with free chlorine in a baffled contact tank at a small treatment plant near Peterborough, Ontario. The design flow is 9 000 m³/d. The contact tank has a volume of 420 m³ and a baffling factor of 0.5, so the time for ten percent of the water to pass through, T10, equals the baffling factor times the theoretical detention time. For the cold-water design condition the regulator requires a CT of 50 mg·min/L for the required virus and protozoa inactivation at the plant's pH and temperature. The free chlorine residual at the outlet of the tank is currently 1.0 mg/L. The raw water chlorine demand is 0.8 mg/L, and the chlorine is fed as a gas.

  1. (a) Calculate T10, in minutes, for the contact tank at design flow. [4]
  2. (b) Determine the minimum free chlorine residual, in mg/L, needed at the outlet of the tank to meet the required CT. [5]
  3. (c) Calculate the chlorine dose, in mg/L, and the gas feed rate, in kg/d, needed to achieve that residual. [5]
  4. (d) If the operator prefers to keep the residual at 1.0 mg/L, find the contact tank volume, in m³, that would be required at the same baffling factor. [6]
(a)

CT credit is based on T10, the time by which ten percent of the water has reached the outlet, because short circuiting means some water leaves much sooner than the average. First convert the flow: 9 000 m³/d ÷ 1 440 min/d = 6.25 m³/min. The theoretical detention time is the volume over the flow, t = V/Q = 420 ÷ 6.25 = 67.2 min. The baffling factor of 0.5 describes a baffled tank with fair to good flow distribution. Then T10 = BF × t = 0.5 × 67.2 = 33.6 min. This is the contact time that may be used in the CT calculation, and it is only half the nominal detention time of the tank.

Answer: 33.6 min

(b)

CT is the residual concentration multiplied by the effective contact time, CT = C × T10, with C in mg/L and time in minutes. At the present residual of 1.0 mg/L the delivered CT is 1.0 × 33.6 = 33.6 mg·min/L, which is below the required 50, so the plant is not compliant. The residual needed is C = CT required ÷ T10 = 50 ÷ 33.6 = 1.49 mg/L. The residual must therefore be raised by about 49 percent. In practice an operator would add a margin, perhaps 10 to 20 percent, because the residual drops across the tank as chlorine is consumed, and the CT should be evaluated using the lowest residual, taken at the outlet.

Answer: 1.49 mg/L

(c)

The dose must satisfy the demand first and then leave the required residual, so dose = residual + demand = 1.488 + 0.8 = 2.29 mg/L. The mass feed rate is dose times flow. With 1 mg/L equal to 1 g/m³, the feed is 2.288 g/m³ × 9 000 m³/d = 20 593 g/d, which is 20.6 kg/d of chlorine gas, about 0.86 kg/h. Because the plant uses a chlorine cylinder system, this is a meaningful rate: a 68 kg cylinder would last about 3.3 days at this feed. The calculation assumes the demand is constant and that the gas is pure Cl2, so the feed should be trimmed by online residual analysis in operation.

Answer: 20.6 kg/d (dose 2.29 mg/L)

(d)

Keep CT = 50 with C = 1.0 mg/L. The required T10 is then 50 ÷ 1.0 = 50 min. Since T10 = BF × V/Q, the volume is V = T10 × Q ÷ BF = 50 min × 6.25 m³/min ÷ 0.5 = 625 m³. This is 205 m³, or 49 percent, more than the existing tank. The comparison shows the trade: enlarging the tank saves chlorine, since the residual and dose are lower, while raising the residual uses the existing tank but costs more chemical and increases disinfection by-product formation. Improving the baffling factor to 0.7 through better baffles would be a cheaper route, since V needed would then be 446 m³.

Answer: 625 m³

Problem 4 [A3-014] Wastewater flow estimation and sewer design flow

A new subdivision in Guelph will drain to a sanitary sewer that serves 3 200 residents and a 2.5 ha commercial strip. Municipal design criteria give an average residential sewage flow of 350 L/capita·d and an average commercial flow of 28 m³/ha·d. The peaking factor for the combined dry-weather flow is the Harmon formula M = 1 + 14/(4 + √P), where P is the equivalent population in thousands (use 3.2). The tributary area is 85 ha, and an infiltration and inflow allowance of 0.25 L/s per hectare is added to the peaked flow without peaking. Treat the commercial flow as part of the flow that is peaked, and assume the sewer will run partly full.

  1. (a) Calculate the average dry-weather flow, in L/s, from residents and commercial use combined. [4]
  2. (b) Calculate the Harmon peaking factor. [4]
  3. (c) Calculate the total design flow, in L/s, including infiltration. [6]
  4. (d) The municipality reduces the infiltration allowance to 0.15 L/s·ha for new PVC pipe. Find the new design flow, in L/s, and comment on the benefit. [6]
(a)

Convert each source to L/s. Residential: 3 200 persons × 350 L/capita·d = 1 120 000 L/d, and dividing by 86 400 s/d gives 12.963 L/s. Commercial: 2.5 ha × 28 m³/ha·d = 70 m³/d = 70 000 L/d, which is 0.810 L/s. The sum is 12.963 + 0.810 = 13.77 L/s. This is the average dry-weather flow that all the peaking and allowance steps build on. Remember that in practice the commercial flow is not uniform in time and may have a quite different diurnal pattern from households, but with only the average figures available a single combined peaking factor is the standard simplification.

Answer: 13.77 L/s

(b)

The Harmon formula is M = 1 + 14/(4 + √P) with P in thousands of persons. With P = 3.2, √P = 1.789. The denominator is 4 + 1.789 = 5.789, and 14 ÷ 5.789 = 2.418. Therefore M = 1 + 2.418 = 3.42. This factor is the ratio of the peak hourly dry-weather flow to the average daily flow. It decreases as the population grows, from a value near 4 for a few hundred people toward 2 for large systems, because the individual peaks average out across many users. The formula is valid for populations between about 1 000 and 1 000 000, so 3 200 is within range.

Answer: 3.42

(c)

The peak dry-weather flow is the average multiplied by the peaking factor: 13.77 L/s × 3.418 = 47.08 L/s. Infiltration and inflow is applied per unit area and not peaked: 85 ha × 0.25 L/s·ha = 21.25 L/s. The design flow is the sum, 47.08 + 21.25 = 68.33 L/s. The infiltration share of the design flow is 21.25 ÷ 68.33 = 31 percent, which is large and reflects that groundwater leaking into joints and wet-weather connections can matter as much as the sanitary flow in a small catchment. This design flow is the figure used to size the pipe with Manning's equation and to check minimum and maximum velocities.

Answer: 68.3 L/s

(d)

Only the infiltration term changes. The new allowance is 85 ha × 0.15 L/s·ha = 12.75 L/s. The peaked dry-weather flow is unchanged at 47.08 L/s. The new design flow is 47.08 + 12.75 = 59.83 L/s. This is a reduction of 68.33 − 59.83 = 8.5 L/s, or 12 percent. The benefit is a smaller required pipe or a steeper-gradient saving, and a lower capacity demand on the downstream pumping station and treatment plant. The risk is that the lower allowance is only valid if the new pipe, maintenance holes and service laterals are tested and watertight, so a leakage test requirement should be part of the contract before the allowance is relied on.

Answer: 59.8 L/s

Problem 5 [A3-015] Sanitary sewer hydraulics: Manning, velocity and partial flow

A 300 mm diameter PVC gravity sanitary sewer in a Thunder Bay residential street is laid at a uniform slope of 0.50 percent. Manning's roughness coefficient is n = 0.013. The peak dry-weather flow in the pipe is 38 L/s. For a circular pipe flowing partly full with central angle θ (radians) at the water surface, the flow area is A = (D²/8)(θ − sin θ), the hydraulic radius is R = (D/4)(1 − sin θ/θ), and the depth ratio is d/D = (1 − cos(θ/2))/2. Manning's equation in SI units is v = (1/n)R2/3S1/2. Use γ = 9 810 N/m³ for the unit weight of water. The municipality requires a velocity of at least 0.6 m/s at peak flow and a self-cleansing shear stress of at least 3.0 Pa.

  1. (a) Calculate the full-flow capacity of the pipe, in L/s. [4]
  2. (b) Find the depth ratio d/D at the peak flow of 38 L/s (solve for θ numerically). [6]
  3. (c) Calculate the flow velocity, in m/s, at 38 L/s. [4]
  4. (d) Calculate the boundary shear stress τ = γRS at the peak flow, in Pa, and state whether the sewer meets the self-cleansing criterion. [6]
(a)

For full flow, A = πD²/4 = π(0.30)²/4 = 0.07069 m² and R = D/4 = 0.075 m. Manning gives v = (1/0.013) × 0.0752/3 × 0.0051/2. Here 0.0752/3 = 0.1778 and √0.005 = 0.07071, so v = 76.92 × 0.1778 × 0.07071 = 0.9673 m/s. The capacity is Q = vA = 0.9673 × 0.07069 = 0.06838 m³/s, which is 68.4 L/s. This is the flow at which the pipe is just full without pressure. Note that a circular pipe actually reaches its peak capacity near 93 percent depth, but design practice uses the full-flow value as the reference for the partial-flow ratios.

Answer: 68.4 L/s

(b)

Set up Q = (1/n) A R2/3 S1/2 with A and R functions of θ and solve for 0.038 m³/s. The ratio Q/Qfull is 38/68.4 = 0.556, so the pipe is more than half the capacity. Trial values bracket the answer: at θ = 3.0 rad the discharge is 30.1 L/s (too low), and at θ = 3.5 rad it is 44.7 L/s (too high). Interpolating and refining by bisection, the solution is θ = 3.272 rad (187.5 degrees). Then d/D = (1 − cos(1.636))/2 = (1 + 0.0653)/2 = 0.533. The flow depth is 0.533 × 300 = 160 mm.
