A depth slightly greater than half the diameter is a reasonable loading for a lateral sewer and leaves a good reserve for surcharge.

Answer: 0.533

(c)

At θ = 3.272 rad the flow area is A = (0.30²/8)(3.272 − sin 3.272) = 0.01125 × (3.272 + 0.1296) = 0.03827 m². The hydraulic radius is R = (0.30/4)(1 − sin θ/θ) = 0.075 × (1 + 0.1296/3.272) = 0.07798 m. Check the discharge with Manning: v = 76.92 × 0.0782/3 × 0.07071, and 0.077982/3 = 0.1826, giving v = 0.993 m/s. Continuity gives Q = vA = 0.993 × 0.03827 = 0.0380 m³/s, which matches the 38 L/s given. The velocity is above the 0.6 m/s minimum, so solids will not settle out at peak flow. At lower night-time flows, the velocity will fall and should be rechecked.

Answer: 0.99 m/s

(d)

The tractive force on the pipe wall is τ = γ R S, which represents the shear the flowing water exerts on deposited solids per unit area. Using R = 0.07798 m from part c, S = 0.005 and γ = 9 810 N/m³, τ = 9 810 × 0.07798 × 0.005 = 3.83 Pa. This exceeds the 3.0 Pa criterion, so at peak flow the sewer is self-cleansing and passes the requirement. Because shear falls as the flow and hydraulic radius fall, the pipe will see lower values at average flow and should be checked there; many agencies check at the minimum daily flow or at half of full-flow velocity to be sure sediment will be flushed daily.

Answer: 3.83 Pa

A3 Practice Paper 4

Problem 1 [A3-016] Storm sewer design with the Rational method and IDF curves

A 13.4 ha residential catchment in Kitchener drains to a single storm sewer outfall. The area-weighted runoff coefficient is C = 0.55. For the 5-year design storm the municipal IDF relationship is i = 1200/(tc + 8)0.80, where i is in mm/h and tc is the time of concentration in minutes. The inlet (overland and gutter) time to the first maintenance hole is 12 minutes. The trunk sewer is 480 m long and flows at an average velocity of 1.6 m/s for the purpose of travel time. The sewer is circular concrete with Manning n = 0.013 laid at a slope of 0.40 percent. Commercially available diameters are 1 050, 1 200 and 1 350 mm. Use the Rational formula Q = C i A/360 with Q in m³/s, i in mm/h and A in hectares.

  1. (a) Determine the time of concentration, in minutes, at the downstream end of the trunk sewer. [3]
  2. (b) Calculate the design rainfall intensity, in mm/h. [3]
  3. (c) Calculate the design peak flow, in m³/s. [4]
  4. (d) Calculate the theoretical diameter, in metres, required to carry this flow just full, using D = (3.2086 Q n / S0.5)3/8. [5]
  5. (e) Select the 1 200 mm pipe and calculate its full-flow velocity, in m/s. State whether the velocity is acceptable if the allowable range is 0.9 to 4.5 m/s. [5]
(a)

The time of concentration at the end of the pipe run is the inlet time plus the travel time in the pipe, tc = ti + L/v. The travel time is 480 m ÷ 1.6 m/s = 300 s, which is 5.0 min. Adding the 12 min inlet time gives tc = 12 + 5.0 = 17.0 min. The longest route governs, so if another branch joined with a longer inlet time that value would be used instead. This tc is the duration of the design storm that produces the greatest peak at this point, because the whole catchment contributes only when the rain has lasted as long as the longest travel time to the outlet, the basic premise of the Rational method.

Answer: 17.0 min

(b)

Substitute the duration into the IDF relationship, i = 1200/(tc + 8)0.80 with tc = 17.0 min. The base is 17.0 + 8 = 25.0, and 250.80 = e0.80 × ln 25 = e0.80 × 3.2189 = e2.575 = 13.13. So i = 1200 ÷ 13.13 = 91.4 mm/h. The intensity falls as duration increases, which is why using a longer tc for the downstream sewers reduces the intensity applied to a larger area. Always check that the IDF expression is applied within the range of durations for which it was fitted, normally 10 minutes to 2 hours for this kind of relationship.

Answer: 91.4 mm/h

(c)

Apply the Rational formula in SI hectare form, Q = C i A/360. Here C = 0.55, i = 91.38 mm/h and A = 13.4 ha. The product is 0.55 × 91.38 × 13.4 = 673.5, and dividing by 360 gives Q = 1.871 m³/s. The constant 360 combines the unit conversions: 1 mm/h over 1 ha is 10 m³/h, which is 0.002778 m³/s, and 1/360 = 0.002778. The runoff coefficient of 0.55 is reasonable for medium-density housing with lawns, driveways and roofs, and it implicitly assumes a rain event with a 5-year return period and no antecedent moisture adjustment.

Answer: 1.87 m³/s

(d)

For a circular pipe flowing full, Manning's equation gives Q = (0.3117/n) D8/3 S1/2 in SI units, so D = (Q n/(0.3117 S0.5))3/8. The supplied form with 3.2086 = 1/0.3117 is identical. Substituting Q = 1.871 m³/s, n = 0.013 and S = 0.004, S0.5 = 0.06325. Then 3.2086 × 1.871 × 0.013 = 0.07804, and dividing by 0.06325 gives 1.2338. Raise it to the power 3/8: ln(1.2338) = 0.2103, multiplied by 0.375 gives 0.0789, and e0.0789 = 1.082. The theoretical diameter is 1.082 m, which is about 3 percent above 1 050 mm. A 1 050 mm pipe flowing full carries only about 1.73 m³/s, short of the 1.87 m³/s required, so it is undersized and cannot be used.

Answer: 1.082 m

(e)

Because 1 050 mm falls short, the next standard size of 1 200 mm is chosen. Its area is π(1.2)²/4 = 1.131 m², and the hydraulic radius flowing full is D/4 = 0.30 m. Manning's velocity is v = (1/0.013) × 0.302/3 × 0.0041/2 = 76.92 × 0.4481 × 0.06325 = 2.18 m/s. The capacity is 2.18 × 1.131 = 2.47 m³/s, giving the pipe about 32 percent reserve over the 1.87 m³/s design flow. The velocity lies inside the 0.9 to 4.5 m/s range, so it is high enough to be self-cleansing and low enough to avoid abrasion, and the pipe is acceptable.

Answer: 2.18 m/s

Problem 2 [A3-017] Culvert hydraulics: inlet and outlet control

A 1 200 mm diameter circular concrete culvert, 24 m long, carries a township drain beneath a county road north of Barrie. The culvert barrel slope is S0 = 0.004 and Manning's n = 0.013. The entrance is square-edged in a headwall with an entrance loss coefficient ke = 0.5. The design flow is 2.0 m³/s and the tailwater depth above the outlet invert is 1.1 m, so the barrel flows full under outlet control. Use outlet-control head loss H = (ke + 1 + 2g n² L/R4/3) V²/(2g), where R is the full-pipe hydraulic radius. The headwater above the inlet invert for outlet control is HW = H + TW − S0 L. For inlet control use the orifice equation, Q = Cd A √(2g(HW − D/2)), with Cd = 0.62, as an approximation; it is strictly valid only when the inlet is submerged (HW/D above about 1.2), so check the result against that limit and comment on it. Take g = 9.81 m/s².

  1. (a) Calculate the velocity in the culvert barrel, in m/s, at the design flow. [3]
  2. (b) Calculate the total head loss H through the culvert, in metres. [5]
  3. (c) Calculate the headwater depth under outlet control, in metres above the inlet invert. [5]
  4. (d) Calculate the headwater depth under inlet control, in metres, using the orifice approximation; comment on whether the inlet is actually submerged, and state which control governs. [4]
  5. (e) The road authority limits the headwater to 1.5 m. Find the largest flow, in m³/s, the culvert can pass under outlet control. [3]
(a)

The barrel flows full, so velocity is the flow divided by the full area. The area is A = πD²/4 = π(1.2)²/4 = 1.131 m². Then V = Q/A = 2.0 ÷ 1.131 = 1.768 m/s. The velocity head V²/(2g) = 1.768² ÷ 19.62 = 3.127 ÷ 19.62 = 0.1594 m, which will be used in the head loss equation. A velocity under 2 m/s is gentle for a concrete culvert, so scour at the outlet is unlikely to be severe, though riprap or an energy dissipation apron is usually still provided where the stream bed is erodible, such as the sandy soils of the Simcoe lowlands.

Answer: 1.77 m/s

(b)

The full-pipe hydraulic radius is R = D/4 = 0.30 m, and R4/3 = e1.3333 × ln 0.30 = e1.3333 × −1.204 = e−1.605 = 0.2008. The friction term is 2g n² L/R4/3 = 19.62 × 0.013² × 24 ÷ 0.2008 = 19.62 × 0.000169 × 24 ÷ 0.2008 = 0.3963. The sum of coefficients is ke + 1 + friction = 0.5 + 1 + 0.3963 = 1.8963. Multiplying by the velocity head, H = 1.8963 × 0.1594 = 0.3022 m. The 1 in the bracket accounts for the exit loss, and the friction term is about 21 percent of the total, so the loss is mostly local rather than from barrel friction in this short culvert.

Answer: 0.302 m

(c)

Under outlet control the headwater is the total head loss plus the tailwater elevation, less the drop in the invert along the barrel. The drop is S0 L = 0.004 × 24 = 0.096 m. So HW = H + TW − S0 L = 0.3022 + 1.1 − 0.096 = 1.306 m above the inlet invert. Physically, the downstream water level is 1.1 m above the outlet invert, which sits 0.096 m lower than the inlet invert, so the energy at the outlet is set by the tailwater; the headwater must exceed it by the friction and minor losses to push the flow through. The crown of the pipe is 1.2 m, so the inlet is submerged by about 0.1 m.

Answer: 1.31 m

(d)

Using the orifice equation as the statement directs, as an approximation, Q = Cd A √(2g(HW − D/2)). Solving for the head above the centre of the pipe gives HW − D/2 = Q²/(2g Cd² A²). Evaluating, Cd² = 0.3844, A² = 1.2793, and 2g Cd² A² = 19.62 × 0.3844 × 1.2793 = 9.649. So Q² = 4.0 gives 4.0 ÷ 9.649 = 0.4146 m. Then HW = 0.6 + 0.4146 = 1.015 m. The higher of the two headwaters controls, because the culvert will back water up to whichever limit is greater. Outlet control at 1.306 m exceeds inlet control at 1.015 m, so outlet control governs. Check of validity: HW/D = 1.015/1.2 = 0.85, below about 1.2, so the inlet is not actually submerged and the orifice result is only an approximation. An unsubmerged (weir-type) inlet-control estimate would also give a headwater near or below the barrel diameter, well under the outlet-control value, so the conclusion is unchanged and outlet control (1.306 m) governs.

Answer: 1.01 m (outlet control governs)

(e)

Set the allowable headwater to 1.5 m and solve the outlet-control equation backward. First H = HW − TW + S0 L = 1.5 − 1.1 + 0.096 = 0.496 m. Since H = K V²/(2g) with K = 1.8963, the velocity head is 0.496 ÷ 1.8963 = 0.2616 m, so V = √(2 × 9.81 × 0.2616) = √5.132 = 2.265 m/s. The flow is Q = V A = 2.265 × 1.131 = 2.562 m³/s. We should also check the inlet control headwater at this flow, which would be 0.6 + (2.562² ÷ 9.649) = 1.28 m, still below the outlet value, so outlet control continues to govern and the capacity stands at 2.56 m³/s.

Answer: 2.56 m³/s

Problem 3 [A3-018] Stormwater detention pond sizing

A 4.2 ha industrial lot in Brantford is to be developed with a post-development runoff coefficient of 0.85. The pre-development coefficient was 0.30 with a time of concentration of 25 minutes. The City requires post-development peak flow to be controlled to the pre-development 100-year peak. The 100-year IDF curve is i = 2200/(t + 12)0.85 (i in mm/h, t in minutes). Use the modified Rational method: pre-development peak Qa = C i A/360 at t = 25 min, and for each storm duration t, required storage S = (C i(t) A/360 − Qa) × 60 t, where the post-development C is 0.85. The critical duration maximizes S. The pond has a usable depth of 2.0 m with vertical idealized walls. The outlet is a single orifice with Cd = 0.62 and a design head of 1.6 m to its centreline.

  1. (a) Calculate the allowable release rate Qa, in m³/s. [4]
  2. (b) Find the critical storm duration (by calculus or trial) and the maximum required storage, in m³. [8]
  3. (c) Calculate the plan area of the pond, in m², at the usable depth of 2.0 m. [3]
  4. (d) Size the orifice: calculate its diameter, in mm, to release Qa at the design head. [5]
(a)

The allowable release equals the pre-development 100-year peak, found with the Rational method at the pre-development time of concentration. For t = 25 min, i = 2200/(25 + 12)0.85 = 2200/370.85. Now 370.85 = e0.85 × 3.6109 = e3.069 = 21.52, so i = 102.2 mm/h. Then Qa = C i A/360 = 0.30 × 102.2 × 4.2 ÷ 360 = 128.8 ÷ 360 = 0.3577 m³/s, about 358 L/s. This is equivalent to 85 L/s per hectare, a fairly typical release rate for an urban site in southern Ontario. All storage required in the pond is a consequence of limiting the larger post-development flows to this value.

Answer: 0.358 m³/s

(b)

Post-development inflow is Q(t) = 0.85 × i(t) × 4.2/360, and the storage is S(t) = (Q(t) − Qa) × 60 t. This function rises with duration at first, because the excess flow accumulates, and then falls once i(t) drops to near Qa. To find the maximum, evaluate several durations: at t = 20 min S is about 947 m³, at t = 30 min i = 91.7 mm/h, Q = 0.909 m³/s and S = (0.909 − 0.358) × 1 800 = 993 m³, and at t = 40 min S is about 963 m³. Setting dS/dt = 0 puts the peak near 30 min, with S max ≈ 994 m³. The critical duration is therefore about 30 minutes, longer than the pre-development tc of 25 minutes because the outflow is limited.

Answer: 994 m³ (critical duration about 30 min)

(c)

With vertical walls the plan area is simply the volume divided by the usable depth, A = S/d = 994 ÷ 2.0 = 497 m². That is about 1.2 percent of the 4.2 ha lot (42 000 m²), a small share for a detention facility on an industrial site. A real pond with side slopes of 4:1 for safety would need a larger footprint, since the average area over depth would be roughly the same but the top area would be larger by 4 × 2 = 8 m of added width on each side (16 m across the pond), and a sediment forebay and freeboard must also be added. The estimate here is the idealized minimum footprint for the active storage only.

Answer: 497 m²

(d)

The orifice equation is Q = Cd Ao √(2g h), so Ao = Q/(Cd √(2 g h)). With Q = 0.3577 m³/s, h = 1.6 m, Cd = 0.62, √(2 × 9.81 × 1.6) = √31.39 = 5.603 m/s. Then Ao = 0.3577 ÷ (0.62 × 5.603) = 0.3577 ÷ 3.474 = 0.1030 m². The diameter is d = √(4 Ao/π) = √(0.1311) = 0.362 m = 362 mm. This sizes the orifice at the full design head, but at lower water levels the release would be lower, so the flow is controlled for all events. A single large orifice that size is vulnerable to clogging, so a trash rack or hood is normally added, and the 1.6 m head implies the orifice centreline is 0.4 m above the pond floor, with the 362 mm opening occupying roughly 0.22 to 0.58 m above the floor.

Answer: 362 mm

Problem 4 [A3-019] Activated sludge design: SRT, F/M ratio and oxygen demand

A conventional complete-mix activated sludge plant serving a town on Lake Huron is designed for an average flow of 8 000 m³/d. Primary effluent has a BOD5 of 160 mg/L, and the secondary effluent soluble BOD5 target is 10 mg/L. Design values are: solids retention time (SRT) θc = 8 d, mixed liquor volatile suspended solids X = 2 500 mg/L, yield Y = 0.60 kg VSS/kg BOD removed, decay coefficient kd = 0.06 d⁻¹, and the ratio of BOD5 to ultimate BOD of 0.68. Use the complete-mix relation V = θc Q Y (S0 − S)/(X(1 + kd θc)). The net waste sludge production is Px = Y Q (S0 − S)/(1 + kd θc), and the oxygen requirement is O2 = Q(S0 − S)/f − 1.42 Px. Neglect nitrification.

  1. (a) Calculate the aeration tank volume, in m³. [5]
  2. (b) Calculate the hydraulic retention time, in hours. [3]
  3. (c) Calculate the food to microorganism ratio F/M based on influent BOD5, in kg BOD/kg MLVSS·d (d⁻¹). [3]
  4. (d) Calculate the net sludge production Px, in kg VSS/d. [4]
  5. (e) Calculate the oxygen requirement, in kg O2/d. [5]
(a)

The BOD removed is S0 − S = 160 − 10 = 150 mg/L, which equals 150 g/m³. Substitute into V = θc Q Y (S0 − S)/(X(1 + kd θc)) with θc = 8 d, Q = 8 000 m³/d, Y = 0.60, X = 2 500 g/m³ and 1 + kd θc = 1 + 0.06 × 8 = 1.48. The numerator is 8 × 8 000 × 0.60 × 150 = 5 760 000 g, and the denominator is 2 500 × 1.48 = 3 700 g/m³. So V = 5 760 000 ÷ 3 700 = 1 557 m³. This is the volume that holds enough biomass at the design MLVSS to remove the load while wasting at an SRT of 8 days; that SRT is long enough to avoid washout of slower-growing heterotrophs in cold winter conditions.

Answer: 1 557 m³

(b)

The hydraulic retention time is the tank volume divided by the influent flow, θ = V/Q = 1 557 ÷ 8 000 = 0.1946 d. Multiplying by 24 h/d gives 4.67 h. This is in the usual range of 4 to 8 hours for conventional activated sludge treating municipal wastewater. Note that the HRT is much shorter than the SRT of 8 days: the biological solids are retained by settling in the secondary clarifier and returned to the aeration tank, which decouples the solids age from the liquid residence time and lets the process maintain a high biomass concentration in a small volume.

Answer: 4.67 h

(c)

The food to microorganism ratio is the daily BOD applied divided by the mass of microorganisms in the tank: F/M = Q S0/(V X). The load applied is 8 000 m³/d × 160 g/m³ = 1 280 000 g/d, or 1 280 kg/d. The biomass is 1 557 m³ × 2 500 g/m³ = 3 892 500 g = 3 892 kg. Thus F/M = 1 280 ÷ 3 892 = 0.329 kg BOD/kg MLVSS·d. The conventional range is 0.2 to 0.4, so the design lies inside the normal range. A value much above 0.4 tends to give poorly flocculating sludge, while below 0.1 points to extended aeration with significant endogenous respiration and nitrification.

Answer: 0.329 d⁻¹

(d)

The net production of volatile solids, which is the mass to be wasted each day, is Px = Y Q (S0 − S)/(1 + kd θc). The product Y Q (S0 − S) = 0.60 × 8 000 × 150 = 720 000 g/d, which is 720 kg/d. Dividing by 1.48 gives Px = 486.5 kg VSS/d. The decay term reduces the observed yield from 0.60 to 0.405 kg VSS/kg BOD. At the design MLVSS of 2 500 mg/L, wasting 486.5 kg/d requires a waste activated sludge flow of about 486.5 ÷ (2.5 kg/m³) = 195 m³/d if wasted from the mixed liquor, or less if taken from the return line where solids are more concentrated.

Answer: 486.5 kg/d

(e)

The oxygen demand is the ultimate BOD removed minus the oxygen equivalent of the cells wasted. The BOD5 removed is 8 000 × 150 g/m³ = 1 200 kg/d, and dividing by f = 0.68 gives the ultimate carbonaceous demand of 1 764.7 kg/d. The cell wasting is credited at 1.42 kg O2 per kg of cells: 1.42 × 486.5 = 690.8 kg/d. So O2 = 1 764.7 − 690.8 = 1 073.9 kg/d. This corresponds to about 0.89 kg O2 per kg of BOD5 removed, a plausible figure for a non-nitrifying conventional plant. Actual field transfer must also be corrected for alpha, beta, temperature and elevation to size the blowers.

Answer: 1 074 kg/d

Problem 5 [A3-020] Primary clarifiers, BOD loading and lagoon or trickling filter sizing

A village in eastern Ontario is planning a lagoon treatment system for an average flow of 1 500 m³/d with raw BOD5 of 220 mg/L. Raw sewage first passes through a circular primary clarifier designed for a surface overflow rate of 36 m³/m²·d. The clarifier removes 30 percent of the influent BOD5. The settled sewage then flows to a facultative lagoon cell designed on a surface BOD5 loading of 28 kg/ha·d with a water depth of 1.5 m. Ignore evaporation and precipitation, and assume the lagoon volume is the surface area times the depth, with no allowance for sludge accumulation or side slopes.

  1. (a) Calculate the diameter of the circular primary clarifier, in metres. [4]
  2. (b) Calculate the BOD5 mass removed in the clarifier, in kg/d. [4]
  3. (c) Calculate the BOD5 load, in kg/d, applied to the lagoon. [4]
  4. (d) Calculate the surface area of the facultative lagoon, in hectares. [4]
  5. (e) Calculate the theoretical detention time of the lagoon, in days, and comment on whether it is reasonable. [4]
(a)

The clarifier area follows from the overflow rate, A = Q/SOR = 1 500 m³/d ÷ 36 m³/m²·d = 41.67 m². For a circular tank, A = πD²/4, so D = √(4A/π) = √(4 × 41.67 ÷ 3.1416) = √53.05 = 7.28 m. A diameter of about 7.3 m is a modest tank, and a designer would round up to a standard size such as 7.5 m, which reduces the overflow rate to 34 m³/m²·d. The overflow rate of 36 m³/m²·d is within the usual range of 30 to 50 m³/m²·d for primary clarifiers at average flow, though peak flow rates must still be checked against an upper limit near 100 m³/m²·d.

Answer: 7.28 m

(b)

The influent BOD5 load is the flow times the concentration: 1 500 m³/d × 220 g/m³ = 330 000 g/d, which is 330 kg/d. A 30 percent removal in the clarifier takes out 0.30 × 330 = 99 kg/d. Primary sedimentation removes the settleable organic solids, which are carried in the sludge to the digester or hauled away, while the dissolved BOD5 passes through unchanged. Thirty percent is within the typical 25 to 40 percent range for raw domestic sewage. The sludge that holds this removed BOD5 must be pumped on a regular schedule, since longer retention leads to septicity and floating scum in the clarifier.

Answer: 99 kg/d

(c)

What passes on to the lagoon is the remaining load: 330 − 99 = 231 kg/d. This is equivalent to a settled BOD5 concentration of 231 000 g ÷ 1 500 m³ = 154 mg/L, which equals 0.70 × 220. Note that the clarifier flow is the same as the raw flow because only a negligible volume leaves with the sludge. The reduction in load matters directly for the lagoon, because the area scales with load: without the primary clarifier the lagoon would see 330 kg/d and need 11.8 ha, so the clarifier saves about 3.5 ha of land at the cost of added mechanical equipment and sludge handling.

Answer: 231 kg/d

(d)

A facultative lagoon is sized on the surface area because oxygen comes from algae and surface reaeration, which scale with area rather than volume. The required area is the load divided by the allowable loading, A = 231 kg/d ÷ 28 kg/ha·d = 8.25 ha. In Ontario, the 28 kg/ha·d loading would be appropriate for a design that must handle winter ice cover. The area is large, about 82 500 m², or a square of roughly 287 m on each side, and the cell is typically divided into two or more cells in series to improve effluent quality and allow one cell to be isolated for maintenance. Dividing the area into two 4.1 ha cells would be a common layout.

Answer: 8.25 ha

(e)

With a depth of 1.5 m the volume is V = 82 500 m² × 1.5 m = 123 750 m³. The detention time is t = V/Q = 123 750 ÷ 1 500 = 82.5 days. This is within the 60 to 180 days that facultative lagoons commonly provide, but toward the low end of that range. It is adequate for continuous discharge only if the effluent criteria are met, and because Ontario facultative lagoons are normally given well over 100 days, the designer should check the discharge schedule. A seasonal-discharge design would need about 180 days of storage, which means a deeper or larger cell.

Answer: 82.5 d

A3 Practice Paper 5

Problem 1 [A3-021] Buried pipe loads, bedding and deflection

A 450 mm nominal PVC sanitary sewer, with a mean wall diameter of 0.46 m and a wall thickness of 14 mm, is to be installed in a trench in clay soil on a new subdivision road in Guelph. The trench is 1.20 m wide at the top of the pipe and the depth of cover to the pipe crown is 3.50 m. The backfill unit weight is 19.0 kN/m³ and the product Ku·μ' for the backfill is 0.130. Use the Marston trench load Wd = Cd·γ·Bd² with Cd = [1 - exp(-2·Ku·μ'·H/Bd)] / (2·Ku·μ'), and ignore live load. The pipe modulus is E = 3000 MPa. Estimate ring deflection with the Spangler equation Δx = DL·K·W·r³ / (E·I + 0.061·E'·r³), taking W as the Marston load per metre of pipe, DL = 1.5, K = 0.100, r as the mean radius and E' = 4.8 MPa for the compacted bedding and haunch zone. The specification limits long-term deflection to 5.0 percent of the mean diameter.

  1. (a) Calculate the load coefficient Cd for the trench. [3]
  2. (b) Calculate the Marston trench load Wd on the pipe per metre of length. [4]
  3. (c) Calculate the predicted horizontal deflection Δx of the pipe. [5]
  4. (d) Express the deflection as a percentage of the mean diameter. [3]
  5. (e) Find the minimum soil modulus E' that holds the deflection to the 5.0 percent limit, in MPa. [5]
(a)

The exponent is 2·Ku·μ'·H/Bd = 2(0.130)(3.50)/1.20 = 0.7583. Then exp(-0.7583) = 0.4685, so the numerator is 1 - 0.4685 = 0.5315. The denominator is 2·Ku·μ' = 2(0.130) = 0.260. Cd = 0.5315/0.260 = 2.044. This coefficient is less than the H/Bd ratio of 2.92 because the soil in the trench is partly carried by friction on the trench walls, which is the whole idea of the Marston trench condition. A larger Ku·μ' or a narrower trench would lower Cd further, and a wider trench would raise it, which is why trench width is controlled in the specification.

Answer: Cd = 2.04

(b)

Marston's trench load is Wd = Cd·γ·Bd². Substituting, Wd = 2.044 × 19.0 kN/m³ × (1.20 m)² = 2.044 × 19.0 × 1.44. The product 19.0 × 1.44 is 27.36 kN/m, and multiplying by 2.044 gives 55.9 kN per metre of pipe. This is the weight of the soil prism the pipe is assumed to carry after friction on the trench sides has been taken into account. It is the full width of the trench that matters, not the pipe diameter, because the trench width Bd sets the soil mass that settles on the pipe. Live load is neglected by instruction, so this value is the design vertical load per unit length.

Answer: Wd = 55.9 kN/m

(c)

Work in N, m. W = 55 940 N/m and r = 0.46/2 = 0.230 m, so r³ = 0.012167 m³. The wall inertia per metre of pipe is I = t³/12 = (0.014)³/12 = 2.287×10⁻⁷ m³, giving E·I = 3000×10⁶ × 2.287×10⁻⁷ = 686 N·m. The soil term is 0.061 × 4.8×10⁶ × 0.012167 = 3563 N·m. The denominator is 686 + 3563 = 4249 N·m. The numerator is 1.5 × 0.100 × 55 940 × 0.012167 = 102.1 N·m². Hence Δx = 102.1/4249 = 0.02403 m = 24.0 mm. Note that the soil stiffness contributes about 84 percent of the resistance, so the quality of haunch compaction controls the answer, not the pipe wall.

Answer: Δx = 24.0 mm

(d)

Deflection percentage is Δx divided by the mean diameter. Δx/D = 0.02403 m / 0.46 m = 0.05224, which is 5.22 percent. This exceeds the 5.0 percent limit in the specification by a small margin, so the installation as described would not be accepted. The exceedance is only 0.22 percent of the diameter, but because the Spangler method is an estimate and the real installation will also see construction deflection and consolidation over time, a designer would not simply accept a predicted value above the limit. The fix is either improved bedding and haunch compaction, a stiffer pipe class, or a narrower trench, and part (e) quantifies the bedding option.

Answer: 5.22 %

(e)

The allowed deflection is 0.05 × 0.46 = 0.0230 m. Rearrange the Spangler equation for the denominator: E·I + 0.061·E'·r³ = DL·K·W·r³/Δx = 102.1 / 0.0230 = 4439 N·m. Subtract the wall term: 0.061·E'·r³ = 4439 - 686 = 3753 N·m. Then E' = 3753 / (0.061 × 0.012167) = 3753 / 7.422×10⁻⁴ = 5.06×10⁶ Pa, which is 5.06 MPa. So the haunch and bedding zone must be compacted to give a modulus about 5 percent higher than the 4.8 MPa assumed. In practice that means a better granular bedding material and controlled compaction in the haunch area, with inspection of density, rather than any change in the pipe itself.

Answer: E' ≥ 5.06 MPa

Problem 2 [A3-022] Water loss, leakage and rehabilitation of mains and sewers

A town in eastern Ontario completed a water audit for last year. System input was 6.15 million m³. Billed authorized consumption was 4.62 million m³, unbilled authorized consumption (flushing and firefighting) was 0.11 million m³, and apparent losses (meter error and theft) were estimated at 0.19 million m³. The distribution system has 84 km of mains, 5600 service connections, an average length of 12 m of private pipe between the property line and each meter, and an average operating pressure of 52 m. Use the unavoidable annual real losses UARL (litres/day) = (18·Lm + 0.8·Nc + 25·Lp) × P, where Lm is main length in km, Nc is the number of connections, Lp is the total private pipe length in km, and P is the pressure in metres. The Infrastructure Leakage Index is ILI = CARL/UARL. Marginal production cost is $0.42/m³.

  1. (a) Determine the non-revenue water as a percentage of system input. [3]
  2. (b) Determine the current annual real losses CARL, in m³ per year. [4]
  3. (c) Compute the unavoidable annual real losses UARL in m³ per year. [5]
  4. (d) Compute the ILI. [3]
  5. (e) The council sets a rehabilitation target of ILI = 4.0. Find the annual volume of water saved and the value of that saving at the marginal cost. [5]
(a)

Non-revenue water is everything put into the system that is not billed, so it is system input minus billed authorized consumption. That is 6.15 - 4.62 = 1.53 million m³. As a share of input, 1.53/6.15 = 0.2488, or 24.9 percent. This figure combines unbilled authorized use, apparent losses and real losses, so on its own it hides whether the problem is leaking pipe or poor metering. That is why the audit separates the components in the remaining parts. Note that the percentage measure is also unreliable for comparing utilities, which is the reason the ILI is introduced in part (d).

Answer: 24.9 %

(b)

Total water losses are system input minus all authorized consumption: 6.15 - (4.62 + 0.11) = 1.42 million m³. Of this, the apparent losses are 0.19 million m³ and those are not physical leakage. Real losses are therefore 1.42 - 0.19 = 1.23 million m³ per year. This is the current annual real losses, CARL, the physical water that escapes from mains, joints, service connections and reservoir overflows. It is the quantity that rehabilitation and pressure management can reduce. The apparent losses would instead be addressed through meter replacement and billing system audits, so keeping the two categories separate matters for choosing the right capital program.

Answer: CARL = 1.23 million m³/yr

(c)

First find Lp. With 5600 connections at 12 m each, Lp = 5600 × 12 / 1000 = 67.2 km. Then the bracket is 18(84) + 0.8(5600) + 25(67.2) = 1512 + 4480 + 1680 = 7672 litres per day per metre of pressure. Multiply by the pressure of 52 m: 7672 × 52 = 398 944 L/day, which is 398.9 m³/day. Over a year, 398.9 × 365 = 145 600 m³. This is the technically lowest leakage that could be reached with good practice at this pressure, assuming perfect repair speed and condition. It scales directly with pressure, so a pressure reduction lowers the benchmark as well as the actual leakage.

Answer: UARL = 145 600 m³/yr

(d)

The Infrastructure Leakage Index is the ratio of what is actually lost to what is unavoidable: ILI = CARL/UARL = 1 230 000 / 145 615 = 8.45. A value of 1 would mean the system leaks no more than the technical minimum. An ILI above 8 indicates that the infrastructure is in poor condition or that leak repair is too slow, and water loss reduction is a priority. The ILI has the advantage over a percentage, because it accounts for main length, connection density and pressure, so towns of different size can be compared fairly. This result places the system in a poor performance category and justifies a rehabilitation program.

Answer: ILI = 8.45

(e)

At ILI = 4.0 the allowed real losses are 4.0 × 145 615 = 582 460 m³ per year. The reduction from current losses is 1 230 000 - 582 460 = 647 540 m³ per year. At the marginal production cost of $0.42/m³ the value of this saving is 647 540 × 0.42 = $271 970 per year, about $272 000. This figure is used to judge the economic limit of rehabilitation, because the annual saving can support the capital cost of pipe replacement, leak detection and pressure management. It uses marginal rather than average cost, since the water not produced saves only the chemicals, power and variable cost, not the fixed costs of the plant.

Answer: 647 540 m³/yr saved, about $272 000/yr

Problem 3 [A3-023] Least-cost pipe network optimization and land development servicing

A developer in Barrie must supply a new industrial park from an existing booster station through a single 2400 m watermain that carries a steady 0.18 m³/s all year. The installed cost of the main, including trenching, bedding, and restoration, is estimated as 2800·D1.4 dollars per metre of pipe, with D the inside diameter in metres. The pumping system has a wire-to-water efficiency of 70 percent and runs 8760 hours per year at an electricity price of $0.11/kWh. Use a present worth factor of 14.0 to convert the annual energy cost to a present value. Head loss follows Hazen-Williams, hf = 10.67·L·Q1.852 / (C1.852·D4.871) with C = 130. Available pipe inside diameters are 300, 350, 400 and 450 mm. Minimize the total of installed cost plus present worth of energy.

  1. (a) Find the continuous optimum diameter, in mm, that minimizes the total present cost. [6]
  2. (b) Find the head loss in the main for the 400 mm diameter. [3]
  3. (c) Find the annual energy cost for the 400 mm pipe. [4]
  4. (d) Find the total present cost for the 400 mm pipe, in millions of dollars. [3]
  5. (e) Find the total present cost for the 350 mm pipe, in millions of dollars, and state which commercial size you select. [4]
(a)

Write the head loss as hf = B'/D4.871 and the present cost per diameter as capital 2800·L·D1.4 plus energy PV = 14.0 × 8760 × 0.11 × (ρ g Q hf / η)/1000. Let K1 = 2800 × 2400 = 6.72×10⁶ and K2 = 14.0 × 8760 × 0.11 × 9.81 × 0.18 × 10.67 × 2400 × 0.181.852 / (0.70 × 1000 × 1301.852) in the form K2/D4.871. Setting the derivative to zero gives 1.4·K1·D0.4 = 4.871·K2·D-5.871, so D6.271 = 4.871·K2/(1.4·K1). Solving numerically gives D = 0.3793 m, or 379 mm. Larger pipe raises capital cost but cuts pumping energy; the optimum balances the two marginal costs, and the total cost curve is flat near the minimum.

Answer: D optimum = 379 mm

(b)

Apply Hazen-Williams with the 400 mm pipe. Q1.852 = 0.181.852 = 0.04176, C1.852 = 1301.852 = 8 223 and D4.871 = 0.44.871 = 0.011525. Then hf = 1 069.4 / (8 223 × 0.011525) = 1 069.4 / 94.77 = 11.28 m, which is about 11.3 m. The mean velocity in the pipe is 0.18/(π × 0.4²/4) = 1.43 m/s, a reasonable value for a continuously pumped main. This head must be supplied by the pump on top of the static lift, so it translates directly into power and annual energy, as the next part shows. Smaller pipes lose head very rapidly because of the D4.871 term.

Answer: hf = 11.3 m

(c)

Pumping power for friction head alone is P = ρ g Q hf / η = 1000 × 9.81 × 0.18 × 11.28 / 0.70 = 28 466 W, or 28.5 kW. Annual energy is 28.47 kW × 8760 h = 249 370 kWh. At $0.11/kWh the annual cost is 249 370 × 0.11 = $27 430 per year. Only the friction component is counted because the static lift is the same for every diameter and so does not influence the selection. This is the recurring cost that is balanced against the one-time capital cost of a bigger pipe. Although capital dominates the total (about 83 percent here), the recurring energy term falls quickly with diameter, which pushes the optimum above a pipe sized only for velocity.

Answer: $27 400 per year

(d)

Capital cost is 2800 × 0.41.4 per metre. Since 0.41.4 = 0.2773, the unit cost is $776.3/m, and for 2400 m the capital cost is $1 863 200 (2800 × 0.2773 × 2400). The present worth of energy is 14.0 × $27 430 = $384 020. The total present cost is 1 863 200 + 384 020 = $2 247 200, or $2.247 million. This single number is the figure used to compare diameters, since it puts the one-time capital outlay and the 14-year-equivalent stream of power payments on the same footing. It assumes the discount rate and period built into the present worth factor of 14.0, and would change if the utility used a different financial horizon.

Answer: $2.247 million

(e)

For the 350 mm pipe, the unit cost is 2800 × 0.351.4 = 2800 × 0.2300 = $644.0/m and the capital cost for 2400 m is $1 545 500. Head loss is 10.67 × 2400 × 0.04176 / (8 223 × 0.354.871) = 1 069.4 / (8 223 × 0.006014) = 21.6 m. Power is 1000 × 9.81 × 0.18 × 21.63 / 0.70 = 54.6 kW, annual cost 54.55 × 8760 × 0.11 = $52 570 and present worth $735 900. Total is $2.281 million, higher than the $2.247 million for 400 mm. Because the 400 mm size gives the lower total, select the 400 mm main, the commercial size nearest the 379 mm optimum on the cost curve.

Answer: $2.281 million; select 400 mm

Problem 4 [A3-024] Population forecasting by arithmetic, geometric and logistic methods

A town in the Niagara Region is planning to expand its water treatment plant for a 30-year design life ending in 2051. Census counts are: 1991, 18 000; 2001, 23 500; 2011, 27 000; 2021, 29 500. Growth has been slowing. Forecast the 2051 population by (i) the arithmetic method using the 1991 to 2021 average yearly increase, (ii) the geometric method using the 1991 to 2021 average exponential rate, and (iii) the logistic method P = Ps / (1 + m·en·t) fitted to the equally spaced 1991, 2001 and 2011 counts, where t is years after 1991, Ps = [2·P0·P1·P2 - P1²·(P0 + P2)] / (P0·P2 - P1²), m = (Ps - P0)/P0 and n = (1/Δt)·ln[P0·(Ps - P1) / (P1·(Ps - P0))]. The plant is to be sized for an average day demand of 400 L per capita per day on the forecast adopted.

  1. (a) Forecast the 2051 population by the arithmetic method. [3]
  2. (b) Forecast the 2051 population by the geometric (exponential) method. [4]
  3. (c) Determine the saturation population Ps from the logistic fit. [4]
  4. (d) Forecast the 2051 population by the logistic method. [5]
  5. (e) Adopting the logistic forecast, find the plant average day capacity required, in ML/d, and state in one sentence why the logistic forecast is the more defensible choice here. [4]
(a)

The arithmetic method assumes a constant increase per year. Over the 30 years from 1991 to 2021 the town grew from 18 000 to 29 500, an increase of 11 500, so the rate is 11 500/30 = 383.3 people per year. From 2021 to 2051 is another 30 years, so P2051 = 29 500 + 30 × 383.3 = 29 500 + 11 500 = 41 000. This method is the simplest and it normally gives the lowest forecast for a growing city, but for a town whose growth is already levelling off it is not conservative, because it continues the average pace of the past rather than the recent slowdown. Treat it as one bound on the range.

Answer: P = 41 000

(b)

The geometric method assumes a constant percentage rate. With continuous growth the rate is k = [ln(29 500) - ln(18 000)]/30 = ln(1.6389)/30 = 0.49420/30 = 0.016473 per year. The 2051 forecast is P = 29 500 × exp(0.016473 × 30) = 29 500 × exp(0.49420) = 29 500 × 1.6389 = 48 347. This method gives the highest answer because it compounds growth indefinitely, which is only reasonable for a young city with room to expand. For this town the counts show that growth per decade fell from 5 500 to 3 500 to 2 500, so the constant percentage rate is clearly contradicted by the data and the 48 350 figure should be treated as an upper limit.

Answer: P = 48 350

(c)

Take P0 = 18 000, P1 = 23 500 and P2 = 27 000. Then P0·P2 = 486 000 000 and P1² = 552 250 000, so the denominator is 486.0×10⁶ - 552.25×10⁶ = -66.25×10⁶. The numerator is 2 × 18 000 × 23 500 × 27 000 - 552.25×10⁶ × (18 000 + 27 000) = 22 842×10⁹ - 24 851×10⁹ = -2 009×10⁹. Dividing gives Ps = 30 328. The negative denominator indicates that the middle count lies above the straight line between the outer counts, which is the sign of a slowing, saturating curve. The logistic method therefore predicts a ceiling of about 30 300 people.

Answer: Ps = 30 330

(d)

Compute m = (Ps - P0)/P0 = (30 328 - 18 000)/18 000 = 0.6849. Then n = (1/10)·ln[18 000 × (30 328 - 23 500) / (23 500 × (30 328 - 18 000))] = 0.1 × ln[122.9×10⁶ / 289.7×10⁶] = 0.1 × ln(0.4242) = -0.08575. For 2051, t = 60 years, so en·t = e-5.145 = 0.005807. Then P = 30 328 / (1 + 0.6849 × 0.005807) = 30 328/1.003977 = 30 208. As a check, the same curve at t = 30 gives 28 821, about 2.3 percent below the actual 2021 count of 29 500, so the fit is reasonable. The curve is almost at its ceiling by 2051.

Answer: P = 30 210

(e)

Average day demand is population times per capita use: 30 208 × 400 L/(c·d) = 12 083 200 L/d = 12.08 ML/d, so a plant with an average day capacity of about 12.1 ML/d is needed. The logistic forecast is the more defensible choice because the census counts show growth falling steadily from 5 500 to 3 500 to 2 500 per decade, which the arithmetic and geometric methods cannot represent while the logistic curve fits it and predicts a ceiling. A designer would still check land supply and Official Plan growth targets, because a logistic ceiling is a statistical extrapolation, not a planning allocation, and annexation could change the ceiling.

Answer: 12.1 ML/d

Problem 5 [A3-025] Per-capita water demand, peaking factors and design flows

A new residential subdivision in Ajax will have a design population of 5735 people on 48 ha. Water use is taken as 360 L per capita per day on an average day, a maximum day factor of 1.9 and a peak hour factor of 3.0 (both applied to the average day). Sanitary flow is 320 L per capita per day average, with a peaking factor from the Harmon formula M = 1 + 14/(4 + P0.5), where P is the population in thousands, plus infiltration of 0.25 L/s per hectare. The trunk sewer is concrete with Manning n = 0.013, laid at a grade of 0.40 percent. Use Manning in SI form for a full circular pipe, Q = (0.3117/n)·D8/3·S1/2 with Q in m³/s and D in m. Size the facilities for the design flows below.

  1. (a) Determine the average day water demand in L/s. [3]
  2. (b) Determine the maximum day demand in L/s. [3]
  3. (c) Determine the peak hour demand in L/s. [3]
  4. (d) Determine the peak design sanitary flow including infiltration, in L/s. [5]
  5. (e) Find the minimum diameter of full-flowing sewer that carries that flow, in mm, and select the next standard size from 300, 375, 450 and 525 mm. [6]
(a)

The average day demand is the population times the per capita rate, converted to litres per second. Q_avg = 5735 × 360 L/(c·d) = 2 064 600 L/d. Dividing by 86 400 s/d gives 23.90 L/s. This is the base flow from which both the maximum day and the peak hour are derived by factors. It is used for annual volume and operating cost, and it is also the quantity against which the plant is rated, so it is the first number a designer computes. Note that 360 L/c/d is a total community figure including a small commercial and institutional allowance, which is appropriate for a mostly residential subdivision.

Answer: 23.9 L/s

(b)

The maximum day demand applies the factor of 1.9 to the average day. Q_max day = 1.9 × 23.90 L/s = 45.40 L/s. This is the flow the supply, treatment and storage are normally designed for, because it is the sustained load on the hottest day of the year when lawn watering is highest. The factor of 1.9 is a design assumption supplied in the problem. It means that on the worst day of the year the community uses 1.9 times the yearly average. The value is also the basis for fire flow design, where the maximum day plus the required fire flow is the critical combined condition for the supply main and pumps.

Answer: 45.4 L/s

(c)

The peak hour demand applies the factor of 3.0 to the average day demand. Q_peak hour = 3.0 × 23.90 L/s = 71.69 L/s, about 71.7 L/s. This short-duration rate governs the sizing of the distribution mains and the pumps that feed the system directly, as it is the highest hourly rate the network must deliver at an acceptable pressure. The factor is applied to the average day demand according to the problem statement, not to the maximum day demand, so the result is not 1.9 × 3.0. If the peak hour factor had been defined on the maximum day, the number would have been much higher, so the base of the factor must always be read carefully.

Answer: 71.7 L/s

(d)

With P = 5.735 thousand, P0.5 = 2.395, so M = 1 + 14/(4 + 2.395) = 1 + 14/6.395 = 3.189. The average sanitary flow is 5735 × 320/86 400 = 21.24 L/s. Peak dry weather flow is 3.189 × 21.24 = 67.74 L/s. Infiltration is 0.25 L/s/ha × 48 ha = 12.00 L/s, and it is added without peaking. The design flow is 67.74 + 12.00 = 79.74 L/s. Infiltration is added separately because groundwater inflow through joints is steady and does not follow the daily domestic cycle. In older areas this allowance is a major share of the sewer flow, which is why the unit allowance is often debated with the regulator.

Answer: 79.7 L/s

(e)

Convert the flow to 0.07974 m³/s and rearrange Manning for diameter: D8/3 = Q·n/(0.3117·S0.5) = 0.07974 × 0.013/(0.3117 × 0.0632456) = 0.0010366/0.019714 = 0.05258. Then D = 0.052583/8 = exp(0.375 × ln 0.05258) = exp(0.375 × -2.9459) = exp(-1.1047) = 0.3314 m, or 331 mm. This is the minimum, so choose the next standard size above, 375 mm. The 375 mm pipe has a full-flow capacity of about 111 L/s at this grade, so it flows roughly 72 percent of its capacity at design flow, leaving a reasonable margin for future growth and for flows above the estimate.

Answer: D = 331 mm; select 375 mm

A3 Practice Paper 6

Problem 1 [A3-026] Fire flow requirements and design demand for a community

A four-storey warehouse and office building in a small Ontario city is to be served from the municipal system. Use the Fire Underwriters Survey style relation F = 220·C·A0.5, with F in L/min, rounded to the nearest 1000 L/min, where C is the construction coefficient and A is the effective floor area in m². For this building C = 0.80 (non-combustible) and A = 1650 m². Adjust F in order: occupancy reduction of 15 percent (limited combustible contents), then automatic sprinkler credit of 30 percent of the occupancy-adjusted flow, then exposure surcharge of 20 percent of the occupancy-adjusted flow. Round the final value to the nearest 1000 L/min. The fire duration for needed flows up to 9000 L/min is 2 hours. The maximum day demand of the city is 41 L/s.

  1. (a) Compute the basic required fire flow F, rounded to the nearest 1000 L/min. [3]
  2. (b) Compute the net required fire flow after all adjustments, rounded to the nearest 1000 L/min. [6]
  3. (c) Determine the design demand at the point of supply, being the maximum day demand plus the net fire flow, in L/s. [3]
  4. (d) Determine the fire storage volume required, in m³. [3]
  5. (e) If the owner removed the sprinkler system, find the additional fire storage required in m³, recalculating the net flow with no sprinkler credit. [5]
(a)

Substituting into F = 220·C·A0.5 gives F = 220 × 0.80 × (1650)0.5. The square root of 1650 is 40.62, so F = 176 × 40.62 = 7149 L/min. Rounding to the nearest 1000 L/min gives 7000 L/min. This is the flow needed for the building before any credit or penalty for contents, protection or nearby buildings. The construction coefficient of 0.80 reflects the lower fire load of non-combustible construction, while the area is the floor area that could be involved in a single fire. The rounding is part of the method, because it avoids false precision in an estimate that is inherently approximate.

Answer: F = 7000 L/min

(b)

Start from the basic flow F = 7000 L/min, as the problem instructs. The occupancy reduction is 15 percent: 7000 × 0.85 = 5950 L/min. The sprinkler credit is 30 percent of the occupancy-adjusted flow, which is 0.30 × 5950 = 1785 L/min taken off. The exposure surcharge is 20 percent of the occupancy-adjusted flow, which is 0.20 × 5950 = 1190 L/min added. The net is 5950 - 1785 + 1190 = 5355 L/min. Rounded to the nearest 1000 gives 5000 L/min. Both the credit and the surcharge are taken from the same base, which is the occupancy-adjusted flow, not from each other, so they do not compound. The sprinkler credit outweighs the exposure charge.

Answer: Net fire flow = 5000 L/min

(c)

Convert the net fire flow to litres per second: 5000 L/min ÷ 60 = 83.33 L/s. The system must supply the maximum day demand and the fire flow at the same time, because a fire can start on the hottest day of the year. Design demand is therefore 41 + 83.33 = 124.33 L/s. This combined flow, not the peak hour demand, governs the sizing of the supply main and the pumping capacity in a small community, with the residual pressure at the hydrant checked at no less than 140 kPa as a standard test. The comparison with peak hour should still be made, because the larger of the two governs.

Answer: 124.3 L/s

(d)

Fire storage is the flow multiplied by the duration. The net flow is 5000 L/min and the duration is 2 hours, or 120 minutes. Volume = 5000 L/min × 120 min = 600 000 L = 600 m³. This is the volume that has to be held in reserve in the elevated tank or reservoir, over and above the equalization volume, and it must stay unavailable for ordinary use. The result is in cubic metres, with 1000 L per m³. The same method applies to the longer durations required for larger flows, but at 5000 L/min the duration is 2 hours, as the problem states, so no adjustment is needed.

Answer: V = 600 m³

(e)

With no sprinkler credit the net flow is the occupancy-adjusted flow plus the exposure surcharge: 5950 + 1190 = 7140 L/min, which rounds to 7000 L/min. This is below 9000 L/min, so the duration remains 2 hours. Storage is 7000 L/min × 120 min = 840 000 L = 840 m³. The additional storage compared with the sprinklered case of 600 m³ is 840 - 600 = 240 m³. This shows the quantitative value of the sprinkler system to the municipality, because it reduces the volume that must be built into the tank. A 240 m³ saving in a tank is a significant capital cost, and municipalities often reflect this in development agreements.

Answer: 240 m³ more

Problem 2 [A3-027] Water source development: wells, intakes and safe yield

A village in southwestern Ontario needs a groundwater supply of 15 000 m³/d on its maximum day. A test well penetrates a confined sand and gravel aquifer 24 m thick with hydraulic conductivity K = 2.5×10⁻⁴ m/s. The radius of influence is taken as 600 m and the production wells will have a radius of 0.15 m. The maximum allowable drawdown at the well face is 14 m. Use the Thiem equation for a confined aquifer, s = Q·ln(R/rw)/(2π·T), and neglect interference between wells. The wells use a continuous slot screen of 250 mm diameter and 15 percent open area. Ministry guidance limits the entrance velocity through the screen openings to 0.03 m/s. The system must meet the maximum day demand with the largest well out of service.

  1. (a) Determine the aquifer transmissivity T in m²/s. [3]
  2. (b) Determine the yield of one well at the allowable drawdown, in m³/d. [6]
  3. (c) Determine the number of wells required, including one standby, so that firm capacity meets 15 000 m³/d. [5]
  4. (d) Determine the screen length needed so the entrance velocity at the well yield does not exceed 0.03 m/s, in m. [6]
(a)

Transmissivity is the hydraulic conductivity multiplied by the saturated thickness of the confined aquifer. T = K·b = 2.5×10⁻⁴ m/s × 24 m = 6.0×10⁻³ m²/s. In daily units this is 518 m²/d, which is a moderately productive aquifer typical of a buried sand and gravel deposit. Transmissivity is the key aquifer property in the Thiem equation, since it combines how permeable the material is with how much of it the well can draw from. A thicker or more permeable aquifer gives a higher yield for the same drawdown, so a test well and pumping test are needed to confirm the real value before design.

Answer: T = 0.0060 m²/s

(b)

Rearrange the Thiem equation for the discharge: Q = 2π·T·s / ln(R/rw). The ratio R/rw is 600/0.15 = 4000, and ln(4000) = 8.294. Therefore Q = 2π × 0.0060 × 14 / 8.294 = 0.5278/8.294 = 0.06363 m³/s. Multiply by 86 400 s/d to get 5498 m³/d, about 5500 m³/d, or 63.6 L/s. This is the yield at the maximum allowable drawdown, so it is a design capacity and not a safe yield for the aquifer as a whole. The long-term safe yield also depends on recharge, which is a separate question for the whole well field, and on the interference between neighbouring wells that was neglected here.

Answer: Q = 5500 m³/d per well

(c)

The demand is 15 000 m³/d and each well yields 5498 m³/d. The number of duty wells is 15 000 / 5498 = 2.73, which must be rounded up to 3. The firm capacity requirement means the demand must still be met when the largest well is out of service, so one standby well is added, for 3 + 1 = 4 wells. Check: with one out, the remaining three provide 3 × 5498 = 16 494 m³/d, which exceeds 15 000 m³/d. With only three wells installed, an outage of one would leave 10 996 m³/d, 27 percent short of demand. The standby also allows rotation of the wells for maintenance and for pumping to rest the aquifer.

Answer: 4 wells

(d)

The entrance velocity is the well discharge divided by the open area of the screen: v = Q/(π·D·L·f), with f the fraction open. Setting v = 0.03 m/s and Q = 0.06363 m³/s, L = Q/(π·D·f·v) = 0.06363/(π × 0.25 × 0.15 × 0.03) = 0.06363/0.003534 = 18.0 m. A 12 m screen would give 0.045 m/s, which is too high, so the screen must be longer or have a bigger diameter. An 18 m screen fits within the 24 m aquifer thickness, which is practical. Low entrance velocity limits head loss through the slots, reduces the carry of fine sand into the well, and slows the build-up of incrustation on the screen.

Answer: L = 18.0 m

Problem 3 [A3-028] Transmission main sizing with the Hazen-Williams equation

A new gravity-fed transmission main runs 8.4 km from a treatment plant clearwell to a reservoir in a community near Kingston. The maximum day design flow is 0.52 m³/s. The available hydraulic head, being the difference in water level between the two ends, is 38.0 m, and all of it may be used for friction loss, with minor losses ignored. Use Hazen-Williams, hf = 10.67·L·Q1.852 / (C1.852·D4.871), with C = 120 for the design of the new ductile iron cement-lined pipe. Available inside diameters are 600, 650, 700 and 750 mm. Choose the smallest size whose head loss does not exceed the available head. Later check the effect of ageing of the pipe, taking C = 100 after 40 years of service.

  1. (a) Compute the exact diameter that would use all 38.0 m of head, in mm. [4]
  2. (b) Select the commercial inside diameter, in mm. [3]
  3. (c) Compute the head loss in the selected pipe at C = 120. [4]
  4. (d) Compute the velocity in the selected pipe. [3]
  5. (e) After 40 years of service with C = 100, find the head loss in the selected pipe and state whether the main still delivers the design flow by gravity. [6]
(a)

Rearrange Hazen-Williams for the diameter: D4.871 = 10.67·L·Q1.852/(C1.852·hf). With L = 8400 m and Q = 0.52 m³/s, Q1.852 = 0.2979, and C1.852 = 1201.852 = 7 090. The numerator is 10.67 × 8400 × 0.2979 = 26 698, the denominator is 7 090 × 38.0 = 269 420, so D4.871 = 0.09910. Taking the 1/4.871 power, D = exp(ln(0.09910)/4.871) = exp(-2.3117/4.871) = exp(-0.4746) = 0.6221 m. This is a continuous value of about 622 mm, which is not a manufactured size. A pipe of exactly this size would use every metre of head, which leaves no margin for ageing, so it is only the minimum.

Answer: D = 622 mm

(b)

The commercial sizes available are 600, 650, 700 and 750 mm. The pipe must be at least as large as the exact diameter of 622 mm so that the head loss does not exceed 38.0 m. The 600 mm pipe is smaller than 622 mm, so it would lose more than 38 m (about 45.3 m) and cannot deliver the flow by gravity. The next size up, 650 mm, is larger than 622 mm and is the smallest that works. The 650 mm size is therefore selected. A larger size such as 700 mm would carry more flow and age better, but it would cost more, and the extra capacity might never be used before the main is renewed.

Answer: 650 mm

(c)

Insert D = 0.650 m into the equation. D4.871 = exp(4.871 × ln 0.650) = exp(4.871 × -0.4308) = exp(-2.0985) = 0.12266. Then hf = 10.67 × 8400 × 0.2979 / (7 090 × 0.12266) = 26 698 / 869.7 = 30.70 m. This is well below the 38.0 m available, so the pipe delivers 0.52 m³/s with 7.3 m of head in reserve. That reserve is useful, because it is the allowance for pipe ageing, for minor losses at valves and bends that were neglected, and for a future increase in flow above the present design.

Answer: hf = 30.7 m

(d)

The velocity is the flow divided by the cross-sectional area. A = π × 0.650² / 4 = 0.3318 m². V = Q/A = 0.52/0.3318 = 1.567 m/s. A velocity of 1.57 m/s is inside the usual range of 0.6 to 2.0 m/s for water transmission mains, so it is neither so slow that sediment settles nor so fast that surge pressures become large. A velocity limit of about 2.0 m/s is common, partly to limit water hammer when a valve is closed suddenly. The result therefore passes the velocity check as well as the head loss check.

Answer: V = 1.57 m/s

(e)

With C = 100, the head loss scales by (120/100)1.852 = 1.21.852 = 1.4017. The new head loss is 30.70 × 1.4017 = 43.03 m. This is greater than the 38.0 m of head available, by about 5.0 m. The main therefore can no longer deliver 0.52 m³/s by gravity alone. With the head fixed at 38.0 m the flow would drop to about 0.52 × (38.0/43.03)0.54 = 0.486 m³/s, roughly 6.5 percent less. The practical remedies are cleaning and relining the pipe, a booster pump, or the choice of a 700 mm main at the start, which would still pass the flow with C = 100 at 29.99 m of head loss.

Answer: 43.0 m; the design flow is not delivered

Problem 4 [A3-029] Storage reservoir sizing for equalization, fire and emergency

A growing community in Simcoe County is adding an elevated storage tank to its water system. The maximum day demand for the design year is 7200 m³/d. The design fire flow is 150 L/s for a duration of 3.0 hours. Size the total storage as the sum of three parts: fire storage A, equalization storage B equal to 25 percent of the maximum day demand, and emergency storage C equal to 25 percent of the sum of A and B. The tank is a vertical cylinder with a usable water depth of 9.0 m between the lowest level that still gives acceptable system pressure and the overflow level. Ignore the dead volume below the usable depth and any freeboard above the overflow.

  1. (a) Determine the fire storage A, in m³. [4]
  2. (b) Determine the equalization storage B, in m³. [3]
  3. (c) Determine the emergency storage C, in m³. [4]
  4. (d) Determine the total storage volume required, in m³. [4]
  5. (e) Determine the inside diameter of the cylindrical tank that provides this volume within the 9.0 m usable depth, in m. [5]
(a)

Fire storage is the fire flow multiplied by its duration. The flow is 150 L/s, and 3.0 hours is 3.0 × 3600 = 10 800 s. A = 150 L/s × 10 800 s = 1 620 000 L = 1620 m³. This volume must be available for the whole fire, in addition to the normal demand during that time, which is covered by the equalization volume in the next part. The fire flow and its duration come from the fire flow estimate for the largest building to be protected. A longer duration raises this volume directly, which is why the duration assumed in the design standard matters to the capital cost of the tank, and a sprinklered building lowers both the flow and the volume.

Answer: A = 1620 m³

(b)

Equalization storage supplies the difference between the peak consumption rates and the steady rate at which the supply works can deliver water. Here it is set at 25 percent of the maximum day demand. B = 0.25 × 7200 m³/d = 1800 m³. This storage is drawn down during the morning and evening peaks and refilled overnight when demand is low, so it allows the treatment plant and the supply mains to be sized for the maximum day instead of the peak hour. A larger tank evens out demand more, and the volume is sometimes refined with a mass diagram of the hourly demand pattern when that pattern is known.

Answer: B = 1800 m³

(c)

Emergency storage covers a supply interruption, such as a main break or power loss, and is taken as 25 percent of the sum of the fire and equalization volumes. The sum A + B = 1620 + 1800 = 3420 m³. Then C = 0.25 × 3420 = 855 m³. Note that the emergency volume is based on A plus B, not on the maximum day alone, so the fire volume is included in the base. This is the portion of the tank that will normally stay full, and it is the first part of the storage that is lost when a system is drawn down during a long outage. Some utilities specify a longer emergency reserve for a system with a single source.

Answer: C = 855 m³

(d)

The total storage is the sum of the three components: Total = A + B + C = 1620 + 1800 + 855 = 4275 m³. This is about 59 percent of the maximum day demand, a typical result for a system with a significant fire requirement. The total must be provided in the usable depth of the tank, which means the volume between the minimum pressure level and the overflow, not the volume of the whole structure. The number is a design requirement and should be checked against the standard of the provincial guideline, which may allow fire volume to be reduced in some conditions, though that is not assumed here.

Answer: Total = 4275 m³

(e)

The volume of a cylinder is V = π·D²·h/4, so D = (4V/(π·h))0.5. With V = 4275 m³ and h = 9.0 m, 4V = 17 100, and π·h = 28.274. The ratio is 17 100/28.274 = 604.8 m², and the square root is 24.59 m. A tank of about 24.6 m diameter and 9 m usable depth gives the required storage. In practice the designer would round up to a convenient tank size, such as 25 m diameter, and add freeboard and a dead volume below the minimum level, making the structure taller than 9 m. The ratio of diameter to height is large, which is typical of an elevated or ground-level reservoir, not a standpipe.

Answer: D = 24.6 m

Problem 5 [A3-030] Pumping station design with pump and system curves

A booster station in a rural Ontario township must lift treated water to a reservoir. The static lift is 24.0 m. The system head loss, including pipe friction and minor losses, is 9800·Q² metres, with Q in m³/s. Each identical centrifugal pump has the characteristic H = 62.0 - 3600·Q² metres at full speed, with Q the flow through that one pump in m³/s. The pumps have an efficiency of 74 percent at the duty point. The station must deliver at least 55 L/s. Check one pump alone first, and then two pumps in parallel, with the same suction and discharge header. Then consider reducing the speed of the parallel pumps with variable frequency drives so that they deliver exactly 55 L/s, using the affinity laws H ∝ N² and Q ∝ N.

  1. (a) Find the flow delivered by a single pump operating alone, in L/s. [4]
  2. (b) Find the total head at that duty point, in m. [3]
  3. (c) Find the combined flow with two identical pumps in parallel at full speed, in L/s. [5]
  4. (d) Find the total shaft power for the two parallel pumps at the duty point of part (c), in kW. [3]
  5. (e) Find the speed ratio N/N0 at which the two parallel pumps deliver exactly 55 L/s. [5]
(a)

The duty point is where the pump head equals the system head. Set 62.0 - 3600·Q² = 24.0 + 9800·Q². This gives 38.0 = 13 400·Q², so Q² = 0.0028358 and Q = 0.05325 m³/s, or 53.25 L/s. A single pump delivers 53.3 L/s, which is below the 55 L/s requirement by about 3 percent. The pump alone therefore fails the duty, although only slightly, which is a common situation where a designer has to decide between a larger pump and a second pump. The result is found on the intersection of the pump curve and the system curve, and does not depend on efficiency, which only affects the power.

Answer: Q = 53.3 L/s

(b)

Substitute the flow into the system curve, since at the duty point the pump head equals the system head. H = 24.0 + 9800 × (0.05325)² = 24.0 + 9800 × 0.0028358 = 24.0 + 27.79 = 51.79 m. As a check, use the pump curve: 62.0 - 3600 × 0.0028358 = 62.0 - 10.21 = 51.79 m, which agrees. Of the total, 24.0 m is static lift and 27.8 m is friction, so over half the energy goes to overcoming friction at this flow. That is the reason a larger diameter force main is worth considering during design, and why the energy cost over the life of the station should be compared with the capital cost.

Answer: H = 51.8 m

(c)

For two identical pumps in parallel, each carries half of the total flow, so the combined pump curve is found by substituting Q/2 for the flow in the single-pump equation: H = 62.0 - 3600·(Q/2)² = 62.0 - 900·Q². Setting this equal to the system curve: 62.0 - 900·Q² = 24.0 + 9800·Q², so 38.0 = 10 700·Q², Q² = 0.0035514, and Q = 0.05959 m³/s, or 59.6 L/s. The head at this point is 24.0 + 9800 × 0.0035514 = 58.8 m. Two pumps do not double the flow, because the higher flow raises the friction loss, so the gain is 59.6 against 53.3 L/s, only 12 percent. This meets the requirement of 55 L/s.

Answer: Q = 59.6 L/s

(d)

The head at the parallel duty point is H = 24.0 + 9800 × 0.0035514 = 58.80 m. The hydraulic power is ρ·g·Q·H = 1000 × 9.81 × 0.05959 × 58.80 = 34 370 W. Dividing by the efficiency of 0.74 gives a shaft power of 46 450 W, or 46.5 kW for the two pumps together, so each pump takes about 23.2 kW. This is the power the motors must supply to the shafts, and the electrical input would be higher by the motor and drive efficiency, which is not given. Selecting a motor requires a margin above this duty, and a check that the motor is not overloaded at the other end of the pump curve when the system head is lower.

Answer: P = 46.5 kW

(e)

At speed ratio n = N/N0 the pump curve scales as H = 62.0·n² - 3600·Q₁², where Q₁ is the flow per pump, so for two pumps H = 62.0·n² - 900·Q². The required duty is Q = 0.055 m³/s. The system head at that flow is 24.0 + 9800 × 0.055² = 24.0 + 29.645 = 53.645 m. Then 62.0·n² = 53.645 + 900 × 0.003025 = 53.645 + 2.7225 = 56.37, so n² = 0.9092 and n = 0.9535. Running at 95.3 percent speed, the pumps deliver exactly the required flow, saving energy compared with throttling a valve to cut the flow from 59.6 L/s. The power falls since it varies roughly as the cube of speed at constant efficiency.

Answer: N/N0 = 0.953

A3 Practice Paper 7

Problem 1 [A3-031] Water distribution network analysis by the Hardy Cross method

A new industrial park in Brampton draws its water at node C from a distribution main fed at node A. Water can travel from A to C by two routes: route 1 passes through node B (pipes AB then BC) and route 2 passes through node D (pipes AD then DC). All four pipes are level. The flow entering at A and leaving at C is 120 L/s. Head loss in each pipe is h = K Q1.852, with h in metres and Q in m³/s, and K equals 700 for AB, 900 for BC, 800 for AD and 1000 for DC. A Hardy Cross analysis begins with assumed flows of 70 L/s in route 1 and 50 L/s in route 2, with route 1 taken as the positive direction. The city later wants route 1 to carry exactly 65 L/s, to be achieved by replacing pipe AB with a larger pipe while the other three pipes stay as they are.

  1. (a) For the assumed flows, find the head loss along route 1 minus the head loss along route 2 (the loop closure error). [4]
  2. (b) Find the first Hardy Cross flow correction ΔQ applied to route 1, in L/s (negative means route 1 loses flow). [5]
  3. (c) Repeat the correction until ΔQ is below 0.1 L/s and state the converged flow in route 1 for the original pipes. [5]
  4. (d) Find the K value that the replacement pipe AB must have so that route 1 carries 65 L/s. [6]
(a)

Route 1 has a combined K of 700 + 900 = 1600 and route 2 has 800 + 1000 = 1800. With Q1 = 0.070 m³/s, the route 1 loss is h1 = 1600 × 0.0701.852 = 1600 × 0.007263 = 11.62 m. With Q2 = 0.050 m³/s, the route 2 loss is h2 = 1800 × 0.0501.852 = 1800 × 0.003895 = 7.01 m. Because the two routes join the same pair of nodes, the true flows must give equal losses, so the difference h1 − h2 = 11.62 − 7.01 = 4.61 m is the closure error. It is positive, meaning route 1 is carrying too much flow for the head available, and route 2 is carrying too little. The sign tells us which way the correction must go.

Answer: 4.61 m

(b)

Hardy Cross uses ΔQ = −Σ(K Q|Q|0.852) / (1.852 Σ K|Q|0.852), with route 1 positive and route 2 counted negative when travelling around the loop. The numerator is the closure error already found, 4.61 m. For the denominator, route 1 gives 1600 × 0.0700.852 = 166.0 and route 2 gives 1800 × 0.0500.852 = 140.2, so the sum is 306.2 and 1.852 × 306.2 = 567.1. Then ΔQ = −4.61 / 567.1 = −0.00813 m³/s, which is −8.13 L/s. Route 1 therefore drops to 61.87 L/s and route 2 rises to 58.13 L/s. The magnitude looks large because the assumed split was far from the equal-loss split, but the correction moves it most of the way in one step.

Answer: -8.13 L/s

(c)

After the first pass the flows are 61.87 L/s in route 1 and 58.13 L/s in route 2. Recomputing the losses, h1 = 1600 × 0.061871.852 = 9.246 m and h2 = 1800 × 0.058131.852 = 9.267 m, so the closure error is now only −0.021 m. The denominator is about 1.852 × (1600 × 0.061870.852 + 1800 × 0.058130.852) = 565, so ΔQ = +0.021 / 565 = +0.000037 m³/s, or +0.04 L/s. That is already below the 0.1 L/s stopping limit, and one more pass changes nothing visible. The converged flows are 61.9 L/s in route 1 and 58.1 L/s in route 2, with a common head loss from A to C of about 9.26 m. Route 1 carries the larger share because its total K of 1600 is lower than the 1800 of route 2, so it offers less resistance.

Answer: 61.9 L/s

(d)

For route 1 to carry 65 L/s, route 2 carries 120 − 65 = 55 L/s, and the two route head losses must be equal. Route 2 loss is 1800 × 0.0551.852 = 1800 × 0.004647 = 8.36 m. The route 1 loss with the new pipe is (K_AB + 900) × 0.0651.852 = (K_AB + 900) × 0.006332. Setting this equal to 8.36 m gives K_AB + 900 = 8.364 / 0.006332 = 1321, so K_AB = 421. The original value of 700 therefore has to fall by about 40 percent, which means a bigger diameter, since K varies roughly as 1/D4.87. Pipe AB must have a K of about 421 or less to hold route 1 at 65 L/s. The pressure available at A is unchanged by this check, because only the split was set.

Answer: K_AB = 421

Problem 2 [A3-032] Network pressure and fire-flow checks at nodes

A subdivision near Ottawa is supplied by a single 1800 m long ductile iron main from an elevated storage tank whose water level (hydraulic grade line) is held at 148.0 m. The last hydrant, node H, sits at ground elevation 112.0 m, and no other demand is drawn along the main. The main is 300 mm in diameter with a Hazen-Williams coefficient C = 120, and minor losses are to be ignored. The maximum day demand at H is 45 L/s. The fire department requires an additional 100 L/s at H at the same time, with a residual pressure of not less than 140 kPa. Use head loss h = 10.67 L Q1.852 / (C1.852 D4.87) in SI units, and pressure in kPa as 9.81 times the pressure head in metres. Pipe sizes available from the supplier are 300 mm, 350 mm and 400 mm.

  1. (a) Find the pressure at H under maximum day demand alone with the existing 300 mm main. [4]
  2. (b) Find the pressure at H when the 100 L/s fire flow is drawn on top of the maximum day demand, and say whether the 140 kPa residual is met. [4]
  3. (c) Find the smallest pipe diameter, as a continuous value, that keeps the residual at H at 140 kPa during the fire. [6]
  4. (d) Select the smallest standard size that works and find the residual pressure at H during the fire with that size. [6]
(a)

The static head available at H is 148.0 − 112.0 = 36.0 m, which is 353 kPa. At 45 L/s (0.045 m³/s) the head loss is h = 10.67 × 1800 × 0.0451.852 / (1201.852 × 0.3004.87). The pieces are 0.0451.852 = 0.003204, 1201.852 = 7090 and 0.3004.87 = 0.002842. So h = 19206 × 0.003204 / (7090 × 0.002842) = 61.5 / 20.15 = 3.05 m. The pressure head at H is 36.0 − 3.05 = 32.95 m, and the pressure is 32.95 × 9.81 = 323 kPa. This is comfortably above any normal minimum, so the system is adequate for ordinary daily use, and the fire case is the one that controls the design.

Answer: 323 kPa

(b)

During the fire the total flow in the main is 45 + 100 = 145 L/s = 0.145 m³/s. The head loss scales as Q1.852, so h = 3.05 × (145/45)1.852 = 3.05 × 8.74 = 26.67 m, which agrees with a direct substitution using 0.1451.852 = 0.02798. The pressure head at H is 36.0 − 26.67 = 9.33 m, so the pressure is 9.33 × 9.81 = 91.5 kPa. The requirement is 140 kPa, which equals 14.27 m of head, so the residual is not met by about 48 kPa. A pressure this low also risks negative pressures elsewhere in a real network, which is a public health concern for backflow, so the existing main is not acceptable for the fire flow.

Answer: 91.5 kPa, not met

(c)

The residual limit of 140 kPa corresponds to a pressure head of 140 / 9.81 = 14.27 m. The head available for friction is therefore 36.0 − 14.27 = 21.73 m. Rearranging the Hazen-Williams equation for diameter, D = [10.67 L Q1.852 / (C1.852 h)]1/4.87. The numerator is 10.67 × 1800 × 0.02798 = 537.4 and the denominator is 7090 × 21.73 = 154,070. Their ratio is 0.003488, and raising it to the power 1/4.87 gives D = 0.313 m. Any smaller diameter produces more than 21.73 m of loss and a residual under 140 kPa, so the continuous minimum is 313 mm. Real pipe is sold only in standard sizes, so this value is a lower bound, not the purchased size.

Answer: 313 mm

(d)

The smallest standard size at or above 313 mm from the list is 350 mm, since 300 mm is too small. For 350 mm, D4.87 = 0.3504.87 = 0.006020. The head loss is h = 537.4 / (7090 × 0.006020) = 537.4 / 42.68 = 12.59 m. The pressure head at H is 36.0 − 12.59 = 23.41 m and the residual pressure is 23.41 × 9.81 = 230 kPa, well above the required 140 kPa. A 400 mm main would give 6.57 m of loss and 289 kPa, which is better still but costs more and slows the turnover of water in the main, raising the risk of low chlorine residual during ordinary demand. The 350 mm size meets the fire requirement with a reasonable margin.

Answer: 350 mm, 230 kPa

Problem 3 [A3-033] Coagulation and flocculation: mixing intensity and detention time

A surface water treatment plant on Lake Ontario is being designed for a flow of 0.30 m³/s. The coldest design water temperature is 10 °C, at which the dynamic viscosity is 1.307 × 10⁻³ Pa·s. The process designer proposes a single rapid mix tank with a detention time of 30 s and a velocity gradient G = 600 s⁻¹, followed by a tapered flocculation basin with a total detention time of 24 min. The flocculation basin has three compartments of equal volume in series, with velocity gradients of 50, 35 and 20 s⁻¹ in the first, second and third compartment. Use the relation P = μ G² V for the power transferred to the water. Assume all flow passes through one treatment train, and that the mixers are the only energy source.

  1. (a) Find the volume of the rapid mix tank. [4]
  2. (b) Find the power the rapid mixer must put into the water. [5]
  3. (c) Find the total power input needed by the three flocculator compartments. [6]
  4. (d) Find the overall dimensionless Gt for the flocculation basin, adding the G t product of each compartment. [5]
(a)

The detention time of a tank is its volume divided by the flow, so V = Q t. The flow is 0.30 m³/s and the rapid mix detention time is 30 s. Therefore V = 0.30 × 30 = 9.0 m³. This is a small volume, roughly a cube of 2.1 m on a side, which is typical of a rapid mix chamber where the aim is to disperse the coagulant throughout the water within a few seconds before any floc starts to form. A short detention time also limits short circuiting, so the tank should have a well-defined inlet and outlet and a mixer matched to the tank shape, such as a vertical turbine in a square tank with baffles.

Answer: 9.0 m³

(b)

The power input follows from P = μ G² V. Substituting μ = 1.307 × 10⁻³ Pa·s, G = 600 s⁻¹ and V = 9.0 m³ gives P = 1.307 × 10⁻³ × 600² × 9.0 = 1.307 × 10⁻³ × 360,000 × 9.0 = 4235 W, or 4.23 kW. This is the power actually delivered to the water, so the motor, gearbox and impeller efficiency must still be added when the motor is chosen. Note that viscosity is highest at the cold design temperature, so the power needed for a fixed G is highest in winter. A mixer sized for 10 °C water therefore has some spare capacity in summer, and a variable speed drive is a sensible way to hold G constant throughout the year.

Answer: 4.23 kW

(c)

Total flocculation volume is Q t = 0.30 × 24 × 60 = 432 m³, so each of the three equal compartments holds 144 m³. For each compartment P = μ G² V. Compartment 1 with G = 50 gives 1.307 × 10⁻³ × 2500 × 144 = 470.5 W. Compartment 2 with G = 35 gives 1.307 × 10⁻³ × 1225 × 144 = 230.5 W. Compartment 3 with G = 20 gives 1.307 × 10⁻³ × 400 × 144 = 75.3 W. The total is 470.5 + 230.5 + 75.3 = 776 W, or 0.776 kW. Power falls steeply with G squared, so tapering the mixing cuts the energy use sharply, and the gentler final stage protects the large floc formed earlier from shear breakup before it reaches the settling basin.

Answer: 0.776 kW

(d)

Each compartment has a detention time of 24 / 3 = 8 min = 480 s. The G t product for a compartment is the velocity gradient multiplied by its detention time. Compartment 1 gives 50 × 480 = 24,000, compartment 2 gives 35 × 480 = 16,800 and compartment 3 gives 20 × 480 = 9,600. The sum is 24,000 + 16,800 + 9,600 = 50,400. This lies within the range of roughly 10⁴ to 10⁵ commonly used as a guide for flocculation, and it shows that the design provides enough total mixing to build settleable floc. The same total could not be obtained by simply running one compartment at G = 20 for the whole 24 min, which would give only 28,800.

Answer: 50,400

Problem 4 [A3-034] Sedimentation basin design by overflow rate

A water treatment plant serving a town in southwestern Ontario must treat a design flow of 0.20 m³/s. The designer will build four identical rectangular horizontal-flow sedimentation basins operated in parallel, with equal flow to each. Pilot testing of the coagulated water showed that the required turbidity removal is achieved at an overflow rate (surface loading) of 26 m³/m²·d, and the regulator's design guideline limits weir loading to 250 m³ per metre of weir per day. Each basin is to be 5.5 m wide with a side water depth of 3.8 m. Assume ideal settling conditions, that the surface area of the basin equals its plan area at the water surface, and that the full flow leaves over weirs placed along the outlet end. Neglect the volume of sludge and inlet zones.

  1. (a) Find the total plan area of the basins needed to meet the overflow rate. [5]
  2. (b) Find the length of each basin and state the length to width ratio. [5]
  3. (c) Find the theoretical detention time in each basin. [5]
  4. (d) Find the total length of outlet weir required to meet the weir loading limit. [5]
(a)

The overflow rate is the flow divided by the surface area, v₀ = Q / A, so A = Q / v₀. Convert the flow to daily units: 0.20 m³/s × 86,400 s/d = 17,280 m³/d. Then A = 17,280 / 26 = 664.6 m², which rounds to 665 m². A particle whose settling velocity equals or exceeds the overflow rate is removed in an ideal basin regardless of depth, so area is the controlling dimension of the design. Depth and detention time are chosen separately to control scour, flow distribution and sludge storage. This total is spread over the four basins, which also lets one basin be taken out of service for cleaning while the plant keeps operating.

Answer: 665 m²

(b)

With four equal basins, each has a plan area of 664.6 / 4 = 166.15 m². The width is 5.5 m, so the length is L = 166.15 / 5.5 = 30.2 m. The length to width ratio is 30.2 / 5.5 = 5.5, which is a long, narrow shape. A ratio of at least about four is generally wanted in a horizontal-flow basin, because a long narrow tank approaches plug flow and reduces short circuiting and dead zones. The ratio here is above that minimum, so the shape is acceptable. If the width had been 8 m, the length would have been only 20.8 m and the ratio 2.6, a poorer hydraulic shape for the same area.

Answer: 30.2 m

(c)

The volume of each basin is width × length × depth = 5.5 × 30.21 × 3.8 = 631.4 m³. The flow to each basin is 0.20 / 4 = 0.050 m³/s. The theoretical detention time is t = V / Q = 631.4 / 0.050 = 12,628 s, which is 3.51 h. The same answer follows from the overflow rate, since t = depth / overflow rate = 3.8 m / (26 m/d) = 0.146 d = 3.51 h. Real basins have some short circuiting, so the actual mean time in service is shorter than this number.
