The theoretical detention time of 3.5 h sits inside the usual range of 2 to 4 h for conventional sedimentation ahead of filtration.

Answer: 3.51 h

(d)

Weir loading is the daily flow divided by the weir length, so the required total length is L_w = Q / (weir loading) = 17,280 m³/d / 250 m³/m·d = 69.1 m. Spread over four basins this is 17.3 m of weir per basin. Each basin is only 5.5 m wide, so a single straight weir across the end would be too short, and the designer must use extra weir length such as submerged launders or finger weirs extending along the tank. Using several launders also reduces the upward velocity near the outlet, which keeps fine floc from being drawn out of the basin and carried onto the filters, so it improves effluent quality as well as meeting the guideline.

Answer: 69.1 m

Problem 5 [A3-035] Rapid sand filtration rates and backwash

A municipal plant in the Region of Waterloo will install gravity rapid sand filters to treat a design flow of 0.28 m³/s. The design filtration rate under normal operation is 7.5 m/h. The designer proposes six identical filter cells, each 25 m² in plan area, and the owner requires that the filtration rate not exceed 10 m/h when one cell is out of service for backwash or repair. Each cell is backwashed at a rate of 40 m/h (as a superficial upward velocity over the plan area) for 8 min, and each cell is washed once every 48 h of operation. Assume that wash water is drawn from the clearwell, that all cells carry equal flow when in service, and that the backwash starts and ends instantly.

  1. (a) Find the total filter area required at the design filtration rate of 7.5 m/h. [4]
  2. (b) For the proposed six cells, find the filtration rate when one cell is out of service for backwash and decide if the 10 m/h limit is met. [5]
  3. (c) Find the volume of wash water used in one backwash of a single cell. [5]
  4. (d) Find the wash water used per day as a percentage of the daily volume of water produced. [6]
(a)

Convert the flow to hourly units: 0.28 m³/s × 3600 s/h = 1008 m³/h. The filtration rate is the flow divided by the filter area, so the required area is A = 1008 / 7.5 = 134.4 m². This is the minimum area that supports the design flow with every cell in service. Six cells of 25 m² give 150 m², which exceeds 134.4 m², so the proposal clears the first test with a margin of about 12 percent. At the full 150 m² the actual normal rate is 1008 / 150 = 6.72 m/h, below the design value of 7.5 m/h. The extra area acts as a reserve against future flow growth and against the cells that will always be out of service.

Answer: 134.4 m²

(b)

With one of six cells out of service, five cells remain and the area in service is 5 × 25 = 125 m². The filtration rate is the same 1008 m³/h divided by that area: 1008 / 125 = 8.06 m/h. This is below the owner's limit of 10 m/h, so the requirement is met. The rate rises 20 percent above the normal 6.72 m/h because the load of the offline cell is shared by the five others. A rate surge this size is mild and is not likely to push turbidity through the bed, but a larger rise could do so, which is why regulators check the one-out-of-service rate. Even with two cells out the rate would be 1008 / 100 = 10.1 m/h, just over the limit.

Answer: 8.06 m/h, limit met

(c)

The backwash flow equals the backwash rate times the plan area: 40 m/h × 25 m² = 1000 m³/h, which is 0.278 m³/s. The wash lasts 8 min, which is 8 / 60 = 0.1333 h. The volume used in a single wash is therefore 1000 × 0.1333 = 133.3 m³. This is about 5.3 m³ of wash water per square metre of filter. The wash pumps or elevated wash tank must be able to deliver 0.278 m³/s for the whole 8 min, and the wash trough and drain must carry that flow without backing up, or the media will not be expanded evenly and the wash will be incomplete.

Answer: 133 m³

(d)

Each of six cells is washed every 48 h, so the number of washes per day is 6 × 24 / 48 = 3. The daily wash water volume is 3 × 133.3 = 400 m³/d. The daily volume produced is the design flow, 0.28 m³/s × 86,400 s/d = 24,192 m³/d. The wash water is then 400 / 24,192 = 0.01653, or 1.65 percent of the production. This is within the 1 to 5 percent range commonly seen at conventional plants, so the loss is acceptable. Because the wash water is drawn from treated water, the plant must make about 1.65 percent more water than it delivers, which raises chemical and pumping costs in direct proportion.

Answer: 1.65 %

A3 Practice Paper 8

Problem 1 [A3-036] Disinfection with chlorine: contact time and CT

A conventional surface water plant in eastern Ontario uses a 1500 m³ baffled clearwell as its chlorine contact tank. Tracer tests show that the time for 10 percent of the water to pass through the tank, T10, equals 0.50 times the theoretical detention time V/Q. The plant must provide 3-log Giardia inactivation by free chlorine, and for the winter design condition (5 °C, pH 7.0) the regulator's CT requirement used here is 120 mg·min/L for that log removal, with log inactivation taken as proportional to the CT achieved. The peak plant flow is 0.16 m³/s. The chlorine demand of the water is 0.80 mg/L, and the free chlorine residual is measured at the outlet of the tank. Treat the residual as constant through the tank and use CT = C × T10.

  1. (a) Find T10 at the peak flow of 0.16 m³/s. [4]
  2. (b) Find the minimum free chlorine residual at the tank outlet needed at peak flow to meet the CT requirement. [5]
  3. (c) Find the chlorine dose to be applied and the chlorine feed rate in kg/d at peak flow, using the residual from part (b). [6]
  4. (d) If the operator can hold only a 1.20 mg/L residual at peak flow, find the Giardia log inactivation achieved. [5]
(a)

The theoretical detention time is the tank volume divided by the flow: 1500 m³ / 0.16 m³/s = 9375 s, which is 156.25 min. The tracer tests show that T10 is 0.50 of this value, so T10 = 0.50 × 156.25 = 78.1 min. T10 is used instead of the mean detention time because 10 percent of the water leaves the tank sooner than T10, and the disinfection rules protect the fastest-moving fraction of the water. A baffling factor of 0.5 is typical of a well baffled tank. A poorly baffled tank with a factor of 0.1 would give only 15.6 min and would need a far higher residual to achieve the same log inactivation.

Answer: 78.1 min

(b)

The CT requirement is 120 mg·min/L, and CT = C × T10, so the required residual is C = CT / T10 = 120 / 78.1 = 1.54 mg/L. This is the free chlorine concentration required at the tank outlet at peak flow. The peak flow case governs because the shorter detention time at higher flow demands a higher residual. At the average flow, for example 0.10 m³/s, T10 would be 125 min and the required residual would only be 0.96 mg/L. Operators therefore link the dosing rate to flow, or set the residual target to the peak flow value, so that the CT is never short during a flow surge in winter, when cold water slows inactivation.

Answer: 1.54 mg/L

(c)

The dose must satisfy the demand of the water plus leave the required residual, so dose = demand + residual = 0.80 + 1.54 = 2.34 mg/L, which equals 2.34 g/m³. The flow is 0.16 m³/s × 86,400 s/d = 13,824 m³/d. The mass of chlorine fed is 2.34 g/m³ × 13,824 m³/d = 32,300 g/d = 32.3 kg/d. For a gas chlorinator this is the feed capacity at peak flow, and in practice the chlorinator is sized for a margin above it, with a duty and a standby unit. If the chlorine is supplied as sodium hypochlorite of 12 percent strength, the daily volume of solution would be about 0.27 m³/d at the same available chlorine.

Answer: 32.3 kg/d

(d)

With a residual of 1.20 mg/L and the peak flow T10 of 78.1 min, the achieved CT is 1.20 × 78.1 = 93.7 mg·min/L. The requirement for 3-log is 120 mg·min/L, and inactivation is taken to be proportional to CT, so the log inactivation is 3 × 93.7 / 120 = 2.34 log. This is 0.66 log short of the 3-log target, equal to about 78 percent of the requirement. The result shows how sensitive compliance is to the residual: a 22 percent drop from 1.54 to 1.20 mg/L produces a 22 percent loss of credited log removal. The operator must either increase the dose, reduce the flow through the tank, or add more contact volume.

Answer: 2.34 log

Problem 2 [A3-037] Wastewater flow estimation and sewer design flow

A town in Simcoe County is planning a new trunk sanitary sewer for a service area with a design population of 12,500. The domestic average flow is taken as 340 L per capita per day. The service area also contains 40 ha of commercial land that generates 28 m³ per hectare per day, with a commercial peaking factor of 1.5. The whole service area covers 210 ha, and an infiltration and inflow allowance of 0.28 L/s per hectare is to be added to the peak flow as a constant. Peak domestic flow is found with the Harmon peaking factor M = 1 + 14 / (4 + √P), where P is the population in thousands. The trunk sewer will be laid at a uniform grade of 0.25 percent, circular, with Manning's n = 0.013.

  1. (a) Find the Harmon peaking factor for this population. [4]
  2. (b) Find the peak domestic flow in L/s. [4]
  3. (c) Find the total design peak flow at the end of the trunk sewer, including commercial flow and the I/I allowance. [6]
  4. (d) Find the smallest diameter of circular pipe that carries the total design flow when flowing just full at the given grade. [6]
(a)

The population is 12,500, so P = 12.5 in thousands. The square root of 12.5 is 3.536. The Harmon factor is M = 1 + 14 / (4 + 3.536) = 1 + 14 / 7.536 = 1 + 1.858 = 2.86. The factor shows that the instantaneous peak is about 2.9 times the daily average for a community of this size. The Harmon formula gives a factor falling to about 1.4 for very large cities and rising toward 4.5 for tiny ones, since a larger population smooths out the coincidence of morning and evening water use. For this town, the factor lies in the middle of that range, which is reasonable for a town of a few thousand households.

Answer: 2.86

(b)

First the average domestic flow: 12,500 persons × 340 L/cap·d = 4,250,000 L/d. Dividing by 86,400 s/d gives 49.19 L/s. The peak domestic flow is the average multiplied by the Harmon factor: 49.19 × 2.858 = 140.6 L/s. This is the flow the domestic customers produce at the daily maximum, usually a late-morning or early-evening hour. It does not include the flow from commercial customers or the extra flow that leaks into the pipes from groundwater and surface runoff. Those two parts are added separately in part (c) because they follow different peaking rules from the domestic flow and should not be multiplied by the Harmon factor.

Answer: 141 L/s

(c)

Commercial average flow is 40 ha × 28 m³/ha·d = 1120 m³/d, and dividing by 86.4 gives 12.96 L/s. Applying the commercial peaking factor of 1.5 gives 19.44 L/s. The infiltration and inflow allowance is applied to the full 210 ha area: 210 × 0.28 = 58.8 L/s. The total design flow is the sum of the three: 140.6 + 19.4 + 58.8 = 218.8 L/s. Note that the I/I allowance is more than a quarter of the total, which is why sewer design guidelines treat it carefully; a poorly built system with leaky joints can see I/I far above this figure after heavy rain. The total, about 219 L/s, is the flow the trunk must carry without surcharging.

Answer: 219 L/s

(d)

For a circular pipe flowing full, Manning's equation gives Q = (0.3117 / n) D8/3 S1/2, where D is in metres. Rearranged, D8/3 = Q n / (0.3117 √S). With Q = 0.2188 m³/s, n = 0.013 and S = 0.0025, √S = 0.05. Then D8/3 = 0.2188 × 0.013 / (0.3117 × 0.05) = 0.002844 / 0.015585 = 0.1825. Raising to the power 3/8 gives D = 0.528 m, or 528 mm. Pipe is sold in standard sizes, so the designer would select the next size up, 600 mm, which gives the pipe some reserve capacity for growth and a lower depth of flow at the design flow, helping to avoid surcharge in wet weather.

Answer: 528 mm

Problem 3 [A3-038] Sanitary sewer hydraulics: Manning, velocity and partial flow

A 450 mm diameter circular concrete sanitary sewer in a London, Ontario subdivision is laid at a grade of 0.35 percent, with Manning's n = 0.013. The peak design flow at the end of the run is 85 L/s, and the lowest daily flow, which occurs overnight in the early years of the development, is 20 L/s. The municipality's standard requires a velocity of at least 0.60 m/s at the low flow so that solids do not settle, and a velocity not above 3.0 m/s at the peak. For partial flow use the geometry of a circular segment with central angle θ in radians, area A = (D²/8)(θ − sin θ), wetted perimeter P = Dθ/2 and depth d = (D/2)(1 − cos(θ/2)).

  1. (a) Find the full-flow capacity of the pipe. [4]
  2. (b) Find the depth of flow at the peak flow of 85 L/s. [6]
  3. (c) Find the velocity at the peak flow and state whether the 3.0 m/s limit is met. [4]
  4. (d) Find the flattest grade, in percent, at which the pipe would still give 0.60 m/s while carrying the 20 L/s low flow. [6]
(a)

For a circular pipe flowing full, A = πD²/4 = π × 0.45² / 4 = 0.1590 m² and the hydraulic radius is R = D/4 = 0.1125 m. Manning's equation gives V = (1/n) R2/3 S1/2. Here R2/3 = 0.11250.6667 = 0.2330, and S1/2 = 0.00350.5 = 0.05916. So V = (1/0.013) × 0.2330 × 0.05916 = 1.0605 m/s. The capacity is Q = V A = 1.0605 × 0.1590 = 0.1687 m³/s, or 168.7 L/s. The peak design flow of 85 L/s is only about half of this, so the pipe has a large reserve capacity, as expected for a minimum size that must carry low flows without blocking.

Answer: 169 L/s

(b)

We need the central angle θ at which Manning's Q = (1/n) A R2/3 S1/2 equals 0.085 m³/s. Since Q depends on θ through both A and R = A/P, the equation must be solved by trial. At θ = 3.15 rad (about 180 degrees, a half-full pipe) the area is A = (0.45²/8)(3.15 − sin 3.15) = 0.025313 × 3.1602 = 0.0800 m², the perimeter is 0.709 m and R = 0.1128 m. Then Q = (1/0.013) × 0.0800 × 0.11282/3 × 0.05916 = 0.0850 m³/s, which matches. The depth is d = 0.225 × (1 − cos 1.575) = 0.2260 m, or 226 mm, a ratio d/D of 0.50. The peak flow is therefore carried at half depth, near the pipe centre line.

Answer: 226 mm

(c)

The flow area at peak is A = 0.0800 m² from part (b), found at θ = 3.151 rad. Velocity is V = Q / A = 0.085 / 0.0800 = 1.06 m/s, and the same result follows from Manning's equation using R = 0.1128 m, which gives V = (1/0.013) × 0.2334 × 0.05916 = 1.062 m/s. This is far below the 3.0 m/s maximum, so the upper limit is met comfortably. It is also above 0.60 m/s, so the pipe is self-cleansing at peak. At exactly half depth a circular pipe has the same velocity as when full, which is why 1.06 m/s is nearly equal to the full-flow velocity of 1.0605 m/s in part (a).

Answer: 1.06 m/s

(d)

At the low flow the required area is A = Q / V = 0.020 / 0.60 = 0.03333 m². We solve (D²/8)(θ − sin θ) = 0.03333, which means θ − sin θ = 0.03333 × 8 / 0.2025 = 1.3169. Trial gives θ = 2.152 rad, a depth of 0.225 × (1 − cos 1.076) = 0.118 m, and wetted perimeter P = 0.45 × 2.152 / 2 = 0.4843 m. The hydraulic radius is R = 0.03333 / 0.4843 = 0.06883 m. Rearranging Manning's equation, S = (V n / R2/3)² = (0.60 × 0.013 / 0.1680)² = (0.04643)² = 0.002157, or 0.216 percent. The pipe may be laid as flat as 0.216 percent and still be self-cleansing at the low flow. The chosen grade of 0.35 percent gives 0.71 m/s there, a comfortable margin.

Answer: 0.216 %

Problem 4 [A3-039] Storm sewer design with the Rational method and IDF curves

A storm sewer in a Kitchener commercial district is designed with the Rational method (Q = C i A / 360, with Q in m³/s, i in mm/h and A in hectares). The design rainfall intensity for the municipality's design storm is i = 1250 / (t + 7)0.85, with t the duration in minutes. Catchment 1 covers 6.0 ha with runoff coefficient 0.80 and an inlet time of 14 min, and drains to manhole MH1. Pipe 1 is 260 m long and runs from MH1 to MH2, with a full-flow velocity of 1.4 m/s. Catchment 2 covers 3.5 ha with runoff coefficient 0.45 and an inlet time of 10 min, and discharges directly into MH2. Pipe 2 leaves MH2 on a grade of 0.60 percent, is circular concrete with n = 0.013, and must carry the design flow just full.

  1. (a) Find the time of concentration to be used for the flow in pipe 2 at MH2. [4]
  2. (b) Find the design peak flow in pipe 2. [5]
  3. (c) Find the smallest diameter of pipe 2 that carries this flow when flowing full. [6]
  4. (d) Find by what percentage the pipe flow would be overestimated if the separate peak flows of the two catchments, each at its own inlet time, were simply added. [5]
(a)

The time of concentration at MH2 is the longest travel time of any contributing path to that point. Catchment 1 water takes its 14 min inlet time plus the travel time in pipe 1, which is 260 m / 1.4 m/s = 185.7 s = 3.10 min. This gives 14 + 3.10 = 17.10 min. Water from catchment 2 reaches MH2 after only its 10 min inlet time. The longer path governs, because at 17.10 min both catchments are contributing at once, so the time of concentration at MH2 is 17.1 min. Using 10 min would be wrong, since by then the water from catchment 1 would not yet have arrived and the full 9.5 ha would not be contributing.

Answer: 17.1 min

(b)

At t = 17.10 min the intensity is i = 1250 / (17.10 + 7)0.85 = 1250 / 24.100.85 = 1250 / 14.95 = 83.6 mm/h. The product of C and A summed over both catchments is 0.80 × 6.0 + 0.45 × 3.5 = 4.80 + 1.575 = 6.375 ha. Then Q = 6.375 × 83.6 / 360 = 1.481 m³/s. All of catchment 2 is assumed to contribute fully at this time even though its own time of concentration is shorter, which is a standard simplification and is conservative for it. The result, about 1.48 m³/s or 1480 L/s, is the design flow for pipe 2 for the selected storm frequency.

Answer: 1.48 m³/s

(c)

For a circular pipe flowing full, Manning gives Q = (0.3117 / n) D8/3 S1/2. Solve for D8/3 = Q n / (0.3117 √S). With Q = 1.481 m³/s, n = 0.013 and S = 0.006, √S = 0.07746. Then D8/3 = 1.481 × 0.013 / (0.3117 × 0.07746) = 0.019253 / 0.024144 = 0.7974. Raise to the 3/8 power: D = 0.79740.375 = 0.919 m, or 919 mm. Pipes are sold in standard sizes, so a 975 mm pipe would be used, giving a full-flow capacity of roughly 1.7 m³/s. Using the larger standard pipe leaves a modest reserve and keeps the velocity within acceptable limits for the grade.

Answer: 919 mm

(d)

Evaluate each catchment at its own time. For catchment 1 at t = 14 min, i = 1250 / 210.85 = 1250 / 13.30 = 94.0 mm/h, so Q1 = 4.80 × 94.0 / 360 = 1.253 m³/s. For catchment 2 at t = 10 min, i = 1250 / 170.85 = 1250 / 11.11 = 112.5 mm/h, so Q2 = 1.575 × 112.5 / 360 = 0.492 m³/s. The simple sum is 1.253 + 0.492 = 1.745 m³/s, against the correct 1.481 m³/s. The overestimate is 1.745 / 1.481 − 1 = 0.179, or 17.9 percent. Peaks from the two catchments do not occur at the same time because catchment 1 peaks later and under a lower intensity, so adding them oversizes the pipe and wastes money.

Answer: 17.9 %

Problem 5 [A3-040] Culvert hydraulics: inlet and outlet control

A county road crossing near Peterborough is to be drained by a single circular concrete culvert 24.0 m long, laid on a slope of 0.80 percent, for a design flow of 2.4 m³/s. Tailwater in the downstream channel is 0.90 m above the outlet invert. The culvert has a square-edged inlet in a headwall. For inlet control use HW/D = c (Ku Q / (A D0.5))² + Y − 0.5 S, with Ku = 1.811 (the SI constant), c = 0.0398 and Y = 0.67 for this inlet, where Q is in m³/s, A in m², D in m, and S is the slope as a fraction. For outlet control use HW = H + h₀ − S L, with H = (1 + Ke + 19.62 n² L / R1.33) V² / 2g, Ke = 0.5, n = 0.012, and h₀ the larger of the tailwater depth and (dc + D)/2. The headwater depth, measured from the upstream invert, must not exceed 1.30 m. A 1.20 m diameter culvert is first tried.

  1. (a) Find the headwater depth for the 1.20 m culvert under inlet control. [4]
  2. (b) Find the headwater depth for the 1.20 m culvert under outlet control, including the critical depth dc of the circular section. [6]
  3. (c) State which control governs and find by how much the governing headwater exceeds the 1.30 m limit. [4]
  4. (d) Try the next standard size, 1.35 m, and find its governing headwater depth. [6]
(a)

For D = 1.20 m the area is A = π × 1.20² / 4 = 1.131 m², and D0.5 = 1.0954. Then Q / (A D0.5) = 2.4 / (1.131 × 1.0954) = 2.4 / 1.2390 = 1.937, and with the SI constant Ku = 1.811 the bracket is 3.508. Squaring gives 12.31, and multiplying by c = 0.0398 gives 0.4899. The slope term is 0.5 × 0.008 = 0.004. So HW/D = 0.4899 + 0.67 − 0.004 = 1.156, and HW = 1.156 × 1.20 = 1.387 m. Under inlet control the culvert behaves like an orifice or weir at its mouth, and the pipe barrel, its length and the tailwater have no effect. This is one of the two checks that must be made, and here it already exceeds the 1.30 m limit.

Answer: 1.39 m

(b)

Critical depth satisfies Q²/g = A³/T for the circular segment. Trial gives a central angle of 4.016 rad, so dc = (D/2)(1 − cos(θ/2)) = 0.6 × (1 − cos 2.008) = 0.854 m. Then (dc + D)/2 = (0.854 + 1.20)/2 = 1.027 m, which exceeds the tailwater of 0.90 m, so h₀ = 1.027 m. The full-flow velocity is V = 2.4/1.131 = 2.122 m/s and R = D/4 = 0.30 m, so R1.33 = 0.2016. The friction term is 19.62 × 0.012² × 24 / 0.2016 = 0.336, so the coefficient is 1 + 0.5 + 0.336 = 1.836, and H = 1.836 × 2.122² / 19.62 = 0.421 m. Finally, HW = 0.421 + 1.027 − 0.008 × 24 = 0.421 + 1.027 − 0.192 = 1.257 m.

Answer: 1.26 m

(c)

The governing control is the one that gives the larger headwater, because the water upstream must rise to whichever level is needed. Inlet control gave 1.387 m and outlet control gave 1.257 m, so inlet control governs. The culvert is therefore limited by the shape of its mouth and not by friction in the barrel or the downstream water level. The governing headwater of 1.387 m exceeds the limit of 1.30 m by 1.387 − 1.30 = 0.087 m, so the 1.20 m culvert is not acceptable. Because the inlet controls, an improved inlet such as a bevelled edge or wingwalls would help, and so would a larger barrel. Making the barrel smoother or shorter would do nothing here.

Answer: inlet control, 0.087 m over

(d)

For D = 1.35 m, A = π × 1.35² / 4 = 1.431 m² and D0.5 = 1.162. Inlet control: Q / (A D0.5) = 2.4 / 1.663 = 1.443, times Ku = 1.811 is 2.613, squared is 6.830, times 0.0398 is 0.2718, so HW/D = 0.2718 + 0.67 − 0.004 = 0.9378 and HW = 1.266 m. Outlet control: critical depth is 0.826 m, so (dc + D)/2 = 1.088 m, which exceeds the tailwater, so h₀ = 1.088 m. Velocity is 2.4 / 1.431 = 1.677 m/s, R = 0.3375 m, R1.33 = 0.2358, and the loss coefficient is 1.5 + 19.62 × 0.000144 × 24 / 0.2358 = 1.5 + 0.288 = 1.788. Then H = 1.788 × 1.677² / 19.62 = 0.256 m, and HW = 0.256 + 1.088 − 0.192 = 1.152 m. Inlet control still governs at 1.266 m, which is below 1.30 m, so the 1.35 m culvert is acceptable.

Answer: 1.27 m (inlet control governs, acceptable)

A3 Practice Paper 9

Problem 1 [A3-041] Stormwater detention pond sizing

A 4.6 ha retail development in Barrie, Ontario must provide an on-site dry detention pond so that the post-development peak flow leaving the site for the design storm does not exceed the pre-development peak flow. The post-development runoff coefficient is C = 0.85 and the pre-development coefficient is C = 0.25. Use the Rational Method Q = C i A / 360, with Q in m³/s, i in mm/h and A in ha. The design storm intensity is i = 1150/(t + 7)0.82, where t is the duration in minutes. The pre-development time of concentration is 25 min. Storage is found by the modified Rational Method, V = 60 t (Qpost - Qallow), with Qpost evaluated at each trial duration. Test durations of 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 40 and 60 min. The pond has a uniform plan area of 520 m² over its working depth. The outlet is one circular orifice with discharge coefficient 0.62, centred 0.30 m above the pond floor; use g = 9.81 m/s² and take the head on the orifice at the maximum storage depth.

  1. (a) Calculate the allowable release rate, equal to the pre-development peak flow, in L/s. [4]
  2. (b) Which of the trial durations gives the largest required storage? Give the duration in minutes. [3]
  3. (c) Calculate the maximum required storage volume, in m³. [5]
  4. (d) Calculate the maximum water depth in the pond, in m. [3]
  5. (e) Calculate the diameter of the orifice that releases the allowable flow at that depth, in mm. [5]
(a)

The allowable flow is the pre-development flow for the same storm, so intensity is read at the pre-development time of concentration of 25 min. Then i = 1150/(25 + 7)0.82 = 1150/17.15 = 67.06 mm/h. The Rational Method gives Qallow = C i A / 360 = 0.25 × 67.06 × 4.6 / 360 = 0.2142 m³/s, which is 214.2 L/s. Using the longer pre-development concentration time, not the shorter post-development one, is what keeps the release rate honest: the site is allowed to discharge only what the natural ground would have discharged for its own critical storm. This value stays fixed for every trial duration below, because the outlet is designed to hold a constant limit.

Answer: 214.2 L/s

(b)

For each duration compute i, then Qpost = 0.85 × i × 4.6 / 360, then V = 60 t (Qpost - 0.2142). At 10 min: i = 112.6, Qpost = 1.2235, V = 606 m³. At 15 min: i = 91.2, Qpost = 0.9903, V = 699 m³. At 20 min: V = 748 m³. At 25 min: V = 771 m³. At 30 min: i = 59.5, Qpost = 0.6466, V = 778 m³. At 40 min: i = 48.9, Qpost = 0.5314, V = 761 m³. At 60 min: V = 659 m³. Storage rises while the growing duration outweighs the falling inflow, then falls once the intensity decay dominates. The largest value is at 30 min, so the critical duration is 30 min, not the 25 min time of concentration.

Answer: 30 min

(c)

At the critical duration t = 30 min the intensity is i = 1150/(30 + 7)0.82 = 1150/19.32 = 59.54 mm/h. The post-development peak is Qpost = 0.85 × 59.54 × 4.6 / 360 = 0.6466 m³/s. The excess over the allowable release is 0.6466 - 0.2142 = 0.4324 m³/s. Multiplying by the duration in seconds, V = 60 × 30 × 0.4324 = 778 m³. This is the volume that must be held in the pond. The modified Rational Method is conservative because it assumes the outflow is constant at the allowable rate through the whole duration, whereas a real orifice releases less when the pond is low, so a routing check would normally follow. For this sizing step the answer is 778 m³.

Answer: 778 m³

(d)

With a uniform plan area the depth is the storage volume divided by the area: d = V / A = 778.3 / 520 = 1.497 m, about 1.50 m. This depth is measured above the pond floor. A real pond has sloping sides, so its plan area grows with depth and the true depth for the same volume would be somewhat less, but the problem states a uniform plan area to keep the geometry simple. The depth matters twice: it sets the embankment height and freeboard, and it sets the head driving the orifice in the next part. A designer would also compare this depth with Ontario guidance on maximum ponding depth for public safety, commonly around 1.5 m on gentle slopes.

Answer: 1.50 m

(e)

The orifice centre is 0.30 m above the floor, so the head at maximum depth is h = 1.497 - 0.30 = 1.197 m. The orifice equation Q = Cd A √(2 g h) rearranges to A = Q / (Cd √(2 g h)). The velocity term is √(2 × 9.81 × 1.197) = 4.846 m/s. So A = 0.2142 / (0.62 × 4.846) = 0.07131 m². The diameter follows from A = π D² / 4, giving D = √(4 × 0.07131 / π) = 0.3013 m, or 301 mm. In practice the designer would choose the nearest standard control-structure orifice, here about 300 mm, and recheck that the release at the lower storage levels does not exceed the limit, which it cannot because the head is smaller.

Answer: 301 mm

Problem 2 [A3-042] Activated sludge design: SRT, F/M ratio and oxygen demand

A municipal plant serving a growing town in Wellington County, Ontario is adding a complete-mix activated sludge train. The average design flow is Q = 8000 m³/d. Primary effluent BOD5 is S0 = 140 mg/L and the effluent soluble BOD5 target is S = 8 mg/L. Kinetic coefficients are yield Y = 0.60 kg VSS per kg BOD5 removed and endogenous decay kd = 0.06 d⁻¹. Design sludge retention time (SRT, θc) is 8 d and the mixed liquor volatile suspended solids concentration in the aeration tank is X = 3000 mg/L. Sludge is wasted from the return line at concentration Xr = 9000 mg/L, and the solids lost in the effluent may be neglected. Assume the ratio of ultimate BOD to BOD5 is 1/0.68, so BODL = BOD5 / 0.68, and take oxygen demand as Q (S0 - S)/0.68 - 1.42 Px.

  1. (a) Calculate the required aeration tank volume, in m³. [5]
  2. (b) Calculate the food-to-microorganism ratio F/M, based on applied BOD5 and tank MLVSS, in kg BOD5 per kg MLVSS per day. [4]
  3. (c) Calculate the net mass of volatile sludge produced per day, Px, in kg VSS/d. [4]
  4. (d) Calculate the waste sludge flow from the return line, in m³/d. [3]
  5. (e) Calculate the daily oxygen requirement, in kg O2/d. [4]
(a)

For a complete-mix reactor without recycle solids in the effluent, the volume follows from the mass balance on biomass: V = Y Q θc (S0 - S) / [X (1 + kd θc)]. Substituting, the BOD removed is 140 - 8 = 132 mg/L, so V = 0.60 × 8000 × 8 × 132 / [3000 × (1 + 0.06 × 8)] with units of m³/d and mg/L cancelling consistently. The numerator is 5 068 800 and the denominator is 3000 × 1.48 = 4440, so V = 1141.6 m³. This corresponds to a hydraulic retention time of 1141.6 / 8000 × 24 = 3.4 h, a reasonable value for conventional activated sludge treating primary effluent.

Answer: 1142 m³

(b)

The food-to-microorganism ratio is the BOD5 load applied each day divided by the mass of volatile solids held in the tank. F/M = Q S0 / (V X) = 8000 × 140 / (1141.6 × 3000). The numerator is 1 120 000 and the denominator is 3 424 800, giving 0.327 kg BOD5 per kg MLVSS per day. This lies in the conventional range of about 0.2 to 0.5 d⁻¹, which tells the designer the SRT and MLVSS selected give a stable, well-flocculating sludge instead of a bulking, lightly loaded or washed-out one. Note that F/M is based on applied BOD, not removed BOD, and on the whole tank MLVSS, so it is a loading index rather than a rate constant.

Answer: 0.327 d⁻¹

(c)

The observed yield accounts for the biomass destroyed by endogenous respiration: Yobs = Y / (1 + kd θc) = 0.60 / (1 + 0.06 × 8) = 0.60 / 1.48 = 0.4054 kg VSS per kg BOD5 removed. The BOD5 removed each day is Q (S0 - S) = 8000 × 132 / 1000 = 1056 kg/d. Then Px = Yobs × 1056 = 0.4054 × 1056 = 428.1 kg VSS/d. This is the mass that must leave the process as waste each day to hold the SRT at 8 d, because at steady state the sludge wasted equals the sludge grown. A check: V X / θc = 1141.6 × 3 / 8 = 428.1 kg/d, which agrees and confirms the definition of SRT.

Answer: 428 kg/d

(d)

Wasting from the return line at concentration Xr means the mass wasted per day is Qw Xr. At the design SRT the waste mass equals V X / θc, so Qw = V X / (θc Xr). Using 3000 mg/L = 3.0 kg/m³ and 9000 mg/L = 9.0 kg/m³: Qw = 1141.6 × 3.0 / (8 × 9.0) = 3424.8 / 72 = 47.57 m³/d. This is a very small flow, about 0.6 percent of the plant flow, which is why a return-line wasting pump on a timer is practical and why thickened waste sludge goes to a small digester or holding tank. If the solids lost in the effluent were not neglected, they would carry part of the daily solids loss, so the required waste flow would be slightly smaller.

Answer: 47.6 m³/d

(e)

The oxygen demand is the ultimate carbonaceous demand of the BOD removed minus the oxygen equivalent of the cells wasted. First the ultimate demand: Q (S0 - S) / 0.68 = 1056 / 0.68 = 1552.9 kg O2/d. The cells wasted carry a chemical oxygen demand of 1.42 kg per kg VSS, and since their COD leaves the tank in the waste sludge instead of being oxidised there, 1.42 × 428.1 = 607.9 kg O2/d is subtracted. The requirement is 1552.9 - 607.9 = 945 kg O2/d. This ignores nitrification, which would add about 4.3 kg O2 per kg NH3-N oxidised and would substantially raise the blower duty at this plant.

Answer: 945 kg/d

Problem 3 [A3-043] Primary clarifiers, BOD loading and lagoon or trickling filter sizing

A small community near Kenora, Ontario will replace a failing lagoon with a primary clarifier followed by a rock-media trickling filter. The design average flow is 6500 m³/d. Raw sewage has BOD5 of 220 mg/L. The primary clarifier is a circular tank sized on a surface overflow rate of 40 m³/m²·d at the design flow, and it removes 30 percent of the influent BOD5. The trickling filter is designed for a volumetric organic loading of 0.35 kg BOD5/m³·d applied to the filter, and the filter is circular with a media depth of 2.0 m. Effluent from the clarifier leaves over a single peripheral weir whose length equals the tank circumference.

  1. (a) Calculate the required clarifier surface area, in m², and the diameter, in m. Report the diameter as your numerical answer. [4]
  2. (b) Calculate the weir overflow rate, in m³/m·d. [4]
  3. (c) Calculate the BOD5 mass load applied to the trickling filter, in kg/d. [4]
  4. (d) Calculate the required filter media volume, in m³. [4]
  5. (e) Calculate the filter diameter, in m, and state one operational reason a designer might split this into two filters. [4]
(a)

The surface overflow rate is flow divided by plan area, so the required area is A = Q / SOR = 6500 / 40 = 162.5 m². For a circular tank A = π D² / 4, therefore D = √(4 × 162.5 / π) = √206.9 = 14.38 m. The design value would be rounded up to a practical diameter, about 14.5 m. The surface overflow rate is the governing criterion for primary settling of raw sewage because it equals the settling velocity of the slowest particle that is fully removed; a value near 40 m³/m²·d at average flow is typical, with a higher limit at peak flow. The depth of the tank does not enter the area sizing, only the detention time and sludge storage.

Answer: 14.4 m

(b)

The weir loading is the flow divided by the length of weir. The peripheral weir length equals the circumference π D = π × 14.38 = 45.2 m. The overflow rate is therefore 6500 / 45.2 = 143.8 m³/m·d. Typical guidance caps weir loading near 125 to 250 m³/m·d for primary tanks, so the result is acceptable and the effluent will not draw settled solids upward near the weir. If the value had exceeded the limit, the designer could add an inboard launder, giving a second weir length, instead of enlarging the tank. Note the weir rate depends on the same flow used for the area sizing, so a peak flow check should be made as well.

Answer: 144 m³/m·d

(c)

The clarifier removes 30 percent of the influent BOD5, so the BOD5 leaving it is 220 × (1 - 0.30) = 154 mg/L. Because 1 mg/L equals 1 g/m³, the mass load is 154 g/m³ × 6500 m³/d = 1 001 000 g/d, or 1001 kg/d. This is the load the trickling filter must treat. The 30 percent removal is the stated design assumption; real clarifier BOD removal depends on the share of BOD that is particulate, which varies with the sewer length and temperature. Sizing the filter on the clarified load rather than the raw load is the main economic reason for including primary treatment ahead of a fixed-film process.

Answer: 1001 kg/d

(d)

The volumetric loading is the daily BOD5 mass divided by media volume, so V = L / loading = 1001 / 0.35 = 2860 m³. This relation holds when the loading is based on the BOD applied to the filter, excluding any recirculated flow, so recirculation need not be considered here. A loading of 0.35 kg/m³·d is at the high end for rock media, which limits nitrification and suggests an intermediate-rate design aimed at carbonaceous BOD removal only. If effluent ammonia limits applied, the designer would reduce the loading to about 0.1 to 0.2 kg/m³·d, which would more than double the media volume and change the choice of media toward plastic packing.

Answer: 2860 m³

(e)

With a media depth of 2.0 m, the plan area is A = V / depth = 2860 / 2.0 = 1430 m². The diameter is D = √(4 × 1430 / π) = √1820.7 = 42.67 m. A single rotary distributor 42.7 m across is large but not unusual in North American practice. Two filters of about 30.2 m diameter each, for a combined area of 1430 m², would let one unit be taken off line for distributor maintenance or media repair while the other carried the load at reduced efficiency, and would also allow staged construction as the community grows. This operational flexibility is the main reason to split a large single unit into parallel trains.

Answer: 42.7 m

Problem 4 [A3-044] Buried pipe loads, bedding and deflection

A 600 mm PVC gravity sewer is to be installed in a trench in clay soil in Ottawa, Ontario, with 4.5 m of cover from the pipe crown to the finished surface. The backfill has unit weight 19 kN/m³, and the vertical load on the pipe is to be taken as the soil prism pressure P = γ H above the crown (live load ignored). Long-term ring deflection is estimated with the modified Iowa equation in the form ΔY/D = DL K P / (0.149 PS + 0.061 E'), where DL = 1.5 is the deflection lag factor, K = 0.10 is the bedding constant, PS = 320 kPa is the pipe stiffness, and E' is the modulus of soil reaction of the pipe zone material, 7000 kPa for compacted granular bedding. All pressures are in kPa. The allowable long-term deflection for the design is 5.0 percent of the diameter.

  1. (a) Calculate the soil prism pressure on the pipe crown, in kPa. [4]
  2. (b) Calculate the predicted long-term deflection with granular bedding, as a percentage of the diameter. [5]
  3. (c) The contractor proposes to use the native loose clay as pipe zone backfill, for which E' = 2000 kPa. Calculate the deflection and say whether it passes. [5]
  4. (d) A later change puts the sewer under 9.0 m of cover. With the granular E' = 7000 kPa, calculate the minimum pipe stiffness, in kPa, that holds deflection to 5.0 percent. [6]
(a)

The prism load is the weight of the column of soil standing directly over the pipe, per unit plan area. P = γ H = 19 kN/m³ × 4.5 m = 85.5 kN/m², which is 85.5 kPa. This is the simplest estimate of vertical soil load and is the one used by the Iowa deflection equation. In a narrow trench, friction against the trench walls would reduce the load actually reaching a flexible pipe, which the Marston trench theory captures, but the prism load is slightly conservative for a flexible pipe because the soil beside the trench settles little relative to the pipe. The cover is measured from the crown, so the pipe diameter does not enter the calculation of P.

Answer: 85.5 kPa

(b)

Substitute into ΔY/D = DL K P / (0.149 PS + 0.061 E'). The numerator is 1.5 × 0.10 × 85.5 = 12.825 kPa. The denominator is 0.149 × 320 + 0.061 × 7000 = 47.68 + 427.0 = 474.68 kPa. The ratio is 12.825 / 474.68 = 0.02702, or 2.70 percent. This is well inside the 5.0 percent limit. Note how the soil term of 427 kPa dominates the pipe stiffness term of 47.7 kPa: for a flexible pipe like PVC the surrounding compacted soil, not the pipe wall, carries most of the load, which is why installation quality controls performance and why inspectors check compaction of the haunch zone.

Answer: 2.70 %

(c)

Change E' to 2000 kPa and keep everything else. The numerator is still 12.825 kPa. The denominator becomes 47.68 + 0.061 × 2000 = 47.68 + 122.0 = 169.68 kPa. Then ΔY/D = 12.825 / 169.68 = 0.07558, or 7.56 percent. This exceeds the allowable 5.0 percent, so the proposal fails. The deflection would almost triple compared with part b, which shows why Ontario specifications require granular bedding, haunching and compaction around flexible pipe instead of native soft clay. Excessive deflection reduces flow capacity, strains the joints and risks buckling or reversal of the pipe wall long before the material itself would fail.

Answer: 7.56 %, fails

(d)

The new prism pressure is P = 19 × 9.0 = 171 kPa. Set the deflection ratio equal to the limit of 0.05 and solve for the stiffness: 0.05 = 1.5 × 0.10 × 171 / (0.149 PS + 0.061 × 7000). The numerator is 25.65, so the denominator must equal 25.65 / 0.05 = 513 kPa. Subtract the soil term, 427 kPa, leaving 0.149 PS = 86 kPa, hence PS = 86 / 0.149 = 577 kPa. The existing 320 kPa pipe would deflect 5.40 percent, so a stiffer pipe (the next standard class is likely about 625 kPa) or a better bedding with higher E' would be required. Note that the stiffness rises sharply once the soil term alone nearly reaches the limit.

Answer: 577 kPa

Problem 5 [A3-045] Water loss, leakage and rehabilitation of mains and sewers

A district metered area in Thunder Bay, Ontario has 1100 service connections. A 3 a.m. night-flow test measured a minimum zone inflow of 11.0 L/s. Legitimate night use by customers is estimated at 1.6 L/s. The remainder is treated as leakage. Leakage occurs at a typical rate for the whole day over 21 hours, because pressure is lower during the daytime peak, so use a leakage hour-day factor of 21 h/d. The average zone pressure at night is 62 m, and the leakage flow varies with pressure as L2 = L1 (P2/P1)1.15. The utility is considering a pressure-reducing valve (PRV) that would hold the night pressure at 48 m, at a capital cost of $85 000, and it values saved water at its production cost of $0.85 per m³.

  1. (a) Calculate the night leakage rate, in L/s. [3]
  2. (b) Calculate the daily leakage volume, in m³/d. [4]
  3. (c) Express the daily leakage as litres per connection per day. [3]
  4. (d) Calculate the night leakage rate after the PRV is installed, in L/s. [4]
  5. (e) Calculate the simple payback period of the PRV, in years, based on the value of the water saved. [6]
(a)

Minimum night flow is made of two parts: what customers legitimately draw at 3 a.m. (toilet cisterns, a few shift workers, industrial process flow) and what escapes through leaks. Leakage is therefore the measured flow less the legitimate night use. L = 11.0 - 1.6 = 9.4 L/s. This works best at night because customer demand is at a minimum and pressure is at a maximum, which gives the most favourable signal-to-noise ratio for leakage. The weakness of the method is the estimate of legitimate use, so a utility will often check a sample of larger customers with temporary meters. An error of 0.5 L/s in that estimate would change the leakage result by more than 5 percent.

Answer: 9.4 L/s

(b)

Convert litres per second to cubic metres per hour by multiplying by 3.6, then multiply by the 21 hours over which the night leakage rate is taken to apply. Daily leakage = 9.4 × 3.6 × 21 = 710.6 m³/d. The hour-day factor is below 24 because leakage depends on pressure and system pressures fall in the daytime when demand is high, so applying the night rate for a full 24 h would overstate losses. In water-loss practice this factor is called the hour-day factor, and it comes from a pressure profile of the zone through the day. The result is about 8.2 L/s averaged over the 24 h day, a useful number to compare to the zone's total inflow.

Answer: 711 m³/d

(c)

Convert the zone leakage to litres per day, then divide by the number of service connections. 710.6 m³/d × 1000 L/m³ = 710 600 L/d. Divided by 1100 connections, that gives 646 L per connection per day. The metric is useful because it allows comparison between zones of different size and with benchmarks: a well-managed system in good condition may lose under 100 to 200 L/connection/d, so a value above 600 signals a zone with significant leakage that justifies active leak detection or rehabilitation. It also converts easily to an equivalent volume per connection per year, about 236 m³, which is a visible fraction of a household's own annual use.

Answer: 646 L/conn/d

(d)

Leakage flow through orifices and cracks changes with the pressure to a power, N1 = 1.15 here, as L2 = L1 (P2/P1)N1. Then L2 = 9.4 × (48/62)1.15. The ratio 48/62 = 0.7742, and its natural log is -0.2559; multiplying by 1.15 gives -0.2943, whose exponential is 0.7450. Therefore L2 = 9.4 × 0.7450 = 7.00 L/s. A reduction of 22.6 percent in pressure thus gives a 25.5 percent drop in leakage, because the exponent N1 = 1.15 exceeds 1, a good return for a valve. In older, rigid iron pipe the exponent can be near 0.5 and the gain much smaller, so the exponent should be tested rather than assumed.

Answer: 7.00 L/s

(e)

The leakage saving is 9.4 - 7.003 = 2.397 L/s at night conditions. Converting with the same hour-day factor gives 2.397 × 3.6 × 21 = 181.2 m³/d, and over a year 181.2 × 365 = 66 130 m³. At $0.85 per m³ the annual saving is 66 130 × 0.85 = $56 210. The simple payback is capital divided by the annual saving: $85 000 / $56 210 = 1.51 years. The payback ignores discounting, valve maintenance, and the possibility that lower pressure also reduces the frequency of main breaks, which would improve the benefit. Against that, it must be checked that the reduced pressure still meets the minimum 140 kPa required for fire flow at the hydrants in the zone.

Answer: 1.5 years

A3 Practice Paper 10

Problem 1 [A3-046] Least-cost pipe network optimization and land development servicing

A new subdivision in Milton, Ontario will be supplied by a 1800 m transmission main from a booster station to an elevated tank. The main must carry a continuous design flow of 0.14 m³/s. The static lift is 28 m. Candidate diameters are 300, 350, 400 and 450 mm with installed costs of $520, $610, $710 and $820 per metre respectively. Use the Hazen-Williams equation hf = 10.67 L Q1.852 / (C1.852 D4.87) in SI units with C = 120, ignoring minor losses. The pump and motor wire-to-water efficiency is 0.72, electricity costs $0.11 per kWh, and the station runs 8760 h per year. Capital cost is annualised over 50 years at 4 percent interest using the capital recovery factor CRF = i(1+i)n / ((1+i)n - 1) = 0.04655.

  1. (a) Calculate the friction head loss in the 350 mm main, in m. [3]
  2. (b) Calculate the electrical power drawn at the pump for the 350 mm main, in kW. [3]
  3. (c) Calculate the annual energy cost for the 350 mm main, in dollars. [4]
  4. (d) Calculate the annualised capital cost of the 350 mm main, in dollars. [4]
  5. (e) Repeat for all four diameters and give the total annual cost of the least-cost diameter, in dollars, and name that diameter. [6]
(a)

Use the Hazen-Williams equation with Q = 0.14 m³/s, L = 1800 m, C = 120 and D = 0.350 m. Q1.852 = 0.141.852 = 0.02622 and C1.852 = 1201.852 = 7 090; D4.87 = 0.354.87 = 0.006020. Then hf = 10.67 × 1800 × 0.02622 / (7 090 × 0.006020) = 503.6 / 42.68 = 11.8 m. The exponents are the sensitive part of this formula: head loss varies with roughly the fifth power of diameter, which is what makes the economics of diameter selection interesting. Note that Hazen-Williams with C = 120 is appropriate for ductile iron or lined pipe of moderate age and for water at ordinary temperatures, but does not apply to viscous fluids.

Answer: 11.8 m

(b)

The pump must lift the water 28 m and overcome the friction loss, so the total dynamic head is 28 + 11.8 = 39.8 m. The hydraulic power is ρ g Q H = 1000 × 9.81 × 0.14 × 39.8 = 54 660 W, or 54.7 kW. Dividing by the wire-to-water efficiency of 0.72 gives the electrical draw, 54.66 / 0.72 = 75.9 kW. Wire-to-water efficiency includes both the pump and the motor, and also the variable-frequency drive if one is fitted; a lower figure than 0.72 would raise the energy cost in direct proportion. Because friction head is only part of the total head, the energy cost does not fall as fast as the friction does when a larger pipe is chosen.

Answer: 75.9 kW

(c)

Annual energy use is the power multiplied by the operating hours: 75.9 kW × 8760 h = 665 010 kWh per year. At $0.11 per kWh the cost is 665 010 × 0.11 = $73 150 per year. The assumption of continuous operation at the design flow overstates energy for a real subdivision, which would pump only during part of the day. It is acceptable here because the problem fixes the duty, and the same bias applies to every candidate diameter, so the ranking of options is not distorted. A designer would later refine it with a demand pattern and time-of-use electricity rates.

Answer: $73 150 per year

(d)

Installed capital cost is the unit cost times the length: $610 × 1800 m = $1 098 000. Multiplying by the capital recovery factor spreads that investment over 50 years at 4 percent: 1 098 000 × 0.04655 = $51 110 per year. The CRF converts a present sum into an equivalent uniform annual amount, which allows capital and operating costs to be added on the same basis. The pipe has a long life so 50 years is a reasonable period, but the booster pump itself would need replacement sooner; since the pump is the same for every candidate diameter in capital terms except for size, it has been left out of the comparison.

Answer: $51 110 per year

(e)

Repeat the steps for each diameter. For 300 mm: hf = 25.0 m, power = 101.1 kW, energy = $97 410, capital = $43 570, total = $140 980. For 350 mm: energy $73 150, capital $51 110, total $124 260. For 400 mm: hf = 6.16 m, power = 65.2 kW, energy = $62 780, capital = 710 × 1800 × 0.04655 = $59 490, total = $122 270. For 450 mm: hf = 3.47 m, power = 60.0 kW, energy = $57 840, capital = $68 710, total = $126 550. The minimum is the 400 mm main at about $122 270 per year. The curve is quite flat between 350 and 450 mm, so a designer might choose the larger diameter for future growth in the subdivision at little extra annual cost.

Answer: $122 270 per year, 400 mm

Problem 2 [A3-047] Population forecasting by arithmetic, geometric and logistic methods

A town in Grey County, Ontario is planning a water treatment expansion with a 2046 design horizon. Census counts were 18 200 in 2001, 21 000 in 2011 and 22 800 in 2021, equally spaced at 10 years. For the geometric method, use the continuous form P = P0 ekt with k found from the 2001 and 2021 counts. For the logistic method with three equally spaced counts P0, P1 and P2, the saturation population is Ps = (2 P0 P1 P2 - P1² (P0 + P2)) / (P0 P2 - P1²), and P = Ps / (1 + ea + b t) with t in years from 2001, a = ln((Ps - P0)/P0) and b = (1/10) ln[ P0 (Ps - P1) / (P1 (Ps - P0)) ]. Later, Statistics Canada revises the 2021 count upward to 23 600 after an undercount study.

  1. (a) Using the original counts, forecast the 2046 population by the geometric method. [4]
  2. (b) Using the original counts, calculate the logistic saturation population Ps. [4]
  3. (c) Using the original counts, forecast the 2046 population by the logistic method. [4]
  4. (d) Repeat the saturation population calculation with the revised 2021 count of 23 600. [4]
  5. (e) Calculate the revised 2046 logistic forecast, and comment on what the change in Ps tells the designer about relying on the logistic method. [4]
(a)

The geometric growth rate comes from the end points: k = ln(P2/P0) / 20 = ln(22 800 / 18 200) / 20 = ln(1.2527) / 20 = 0.22534 / 20 = 0.011267 per year. The forecast horizon is 25 years after 2021, so P(2046) = 22 800 × e0.011267 × 25 = 22 800 × e0.28167 = 22 800 × 1.3254 = 30 218. The geometric method assumes a constant percentage growth rate, which means ever-increasing absolute growth. Here the town grew 2800 persons in the first decade but only 1800 in the second, so growth is slowing, and the geometric forecast is likely to be the upper bound among the methods.

Answer: 30 220

(b)

Take P0 = 18 200, P1 = 21 000, P2 = 22 800. The numerator is 2 P0 P1 P2 - P1² (P0 + P2) = 2 × 18 200 × 21 000 × 22 800 - 21 000² × 41 000 = 1.7428 × 10¹³ - 1.8081 × 10¹³ = -6.53 × 10¹¹. The denominator is P0 P2 - P1² = 414.96 × 10⁶ - 441 × 10⁶ = -26.04 × 10⁶. Their ratio is Ps = 25 065. Both numerator and denominator are negative because growth is decelerating; the middle count lies above the straight line joining the end counts. If the growth were accelerating, the formula would give a negative or meaningless Ps and the logistic curve could not be fitted at all.

Answer: 25 065

(c)

With Ps = 25 065, the constants are a = ln((25 065 - 18 200) / 18 200) = ln(0.3772) = -0.9751, and b = (1/10) ln[18 200 × (25 065 - 21 000) / (21 000 × (25 065 - 18 200))] = (1/10) ln[73 983 000 / 144 165 000] = (1/10) ln(0.5132) = -0.06672. At 2046, t = 45 years from 2001, so a + b t = -0.9751 - 3.0024 = -3.9775. Then e-3.9775 = 0.01873 and P = 25 065 / 1.01873 = 24 604. The logistic forecast is 5600 persons below the geometric one, a difference that would translate into roughly a 19 percent difference in the required plant capacity.

Answer: 24 604

(d)

Substitute P2 = 23 600. The numerator is 2 × 18 200 × 21 000 × 23 600 - 21 000² × (18 200 + 23 600) = 1.8040 × 10¹³ - 441 × 10⁶ × 41 800 = 1.8040 × 10¹³ - 1.8434 × 10¹³ = -3.94 × 10¹¹. The denominator is 18 200 × 23 600 - 441 × 10⁶ = 429.52 × 10⁶ - 441 × 10⁶ = -11.48 × 10⁶. So Ps = 34 317. A revision of only 800 persons, or 3.5 percent of the 2021 count, has moved the saturation population by 9250 persons, or 37 percent. This is the signature of an ill-conditioned formula: the denominator is a small difference of two large numbers, so tiny changes in the data are magnified.

Answer: 34 317

(e)

Recompute the constants for Ps = 34 317: a = ln((34 317 - 18 200) / 18 200) = ln(0.8856) = -0.12154, and b = (1/10) ln[18 200 × 13 317 / (21 000 × 16 117)] = (1/10) ln(0.7161) = -0.03339. At t = 45, a + b t = -0.12154 - 1.5027 = -1.6243, e-1.6243 = 0.1969, and P = 34 317 / 1.1969 = 28 668. The forecast rose by 4064 persons, about 16 percent, from a 3.5 percent data revision. The lesson is that the logistic method with three points is very sensitive to data quality when growth is only mildly decelerating, so the designer should show a range, check against land-use capacity in the official plan, and not size the plant on one curve.

Answer: 28 668

Problem 3 [A3-048] Per-capita water demand, peaking factors and design flows

A municipality in Haldimand County, Ontario serves 18 500 people. Total system demand, including residential, commercial, institutional and industrial use and an allowance for non-revenue water, averages 380 L per capita per day. Design maximum day demand (MDD) is 1.9 times the average day demand (ADD), and peak hour demand (PHD) is 3.0 times ADD. Residential use is 68 percent of total demand. The council's conservation plan is expected to cut residential use by 12 percent, with no change to other uses. Because the savings come mostly from indoor fixtures while summer lawn watering stays unchanged, the MDD factor is expected to rise from 1.9 to 1.98 once the plan takes effect, and the PHD factor is not needed for the comparison. The population is held constant.

  1. (a) Calculate the average day demand, in L/s. [4]
  2. (b) Calculate the maximum day demand, in L/s. [4]
  3. (c) Calculate the peak hour demand, in L/s. [3]
  4. (d) Calculate the maximum day demand after the conservation plan, in L/s. [5]
  5. (e) Calculate the percentage change in MDD caused by the plan (negative for a decrease) and explain what it means for treatment plant sizing. [4]
(a)

The average day demand is the population times the per-capita rate. ADD = 18 500 × 380 L/(c·d) = 7 030 000 L/d, which is 7030 m³/d. Dividing by the 86 400 seconds in a day gives 7 030 000 / 86 400 = 81.37 L/s. The 380 L/c/d figure is a system-wide number that includes industry, commercial use and losses, so it is much higher than a household use of about 200 to 250 L/c/d. Using the all-in rate matters because the treatment and transmission works carry the whole demand, not only the residential part. ADD also drives annual energy, chemical use and revenue estimates, even though the sizing flows are the peak ones.

Answer: 81.4 L/s

(b)

Maximum day demand is the largest daily total in the year and sets the capacity of the treatment plant, high-lift pumps and transmission mains. MDD = 1.9 × ADD = 1.9 × 81.37 = 154.6 L/s, equal to 13 360 m³/d. The factor of 1.9 reflects summer lawn watering and hot spells in southern Ontario. The plant is generally sized to deliver the MDD, while storage is used to meet the hourly peaks above it. A treatment plant sized only on ADD would run out of water on a hot July day, and customers on high ground would lose pressure first, which is why the MDD, not the ADD, is the basis of plant design.

Answer: 154.6 L/s

(c)

Peak hour demand is the highest hourly rate of the maximum day and governs the sizing of distribution mains and, with fire flow, the pumping or elevated storage that feeds them. PHD = 3.0 × ADD = 3.0 × 81.37 = 244.1 L/s. The peak hour is higher than MDD by a factor of 3.0 / 1.9 = 1.58, reflecting the morning and evening peaks when households wash, shower and water at the same time. The distribution system must deliver this flow at a minimum residual pressure of 275 kPa under Ontario design guidelines, but the plant need not, because storage in the system covers the difference between the MDD and the hourly peak.

Answer: 244.1 L/s

(d)

First find the new per-capita demand. Residential use is 68 percent of 380, so the cut is 0.68 × 0.12 = 8.16 percent of the total, and the new rate is 380 × (1 - 0.0816) = 349.0 L/c/d. The new ADD is 18 500 × 349.0 / 86 400 = 74.73 L/s. With the MDD factor increased to 1.98, the new MDD = 1.98 × 74.73 = 148.0 L/s. The plan reduces the average by 8.2 percent, but because the savings are indoors while the outdoor summer demand remains, the peak shrinks by only about half as much in percentage terms. The unchanged outdoor demand is a larger part of the new, smaller average, which is why the peaking factor must rise.

Answer: 148.0 L/s

(e)

The percentage change is (148.0 - 154.6) / 154.6 × 100 = -4.3 percent. So a conservation plan that cuts average demand by 8.2 percent trims the peak day by only about half as much. For plant sizing this means the capacity expansion cannot be deferred or reduced on the strength of the conservation plan alone: the plant is still designed for about 148 L/s. The plan still has value in reduced annual water use, energy and chemical costs, and lower wastewater flows, but only a programme that tackles outdoor use, such as lawn watering bylaws or rain barrels, would reduce the MDD that actually controls the capital cost of the plant.

Answer: -4.3 %

Problem 4 [A3-049] Fire flow requirements and design demand for a community

A three-storey distribution warehouse in Sarnia, Ontario is being added to a municipal water system. Use the Fire Underwriters Survey style method F = 220 C √A, with F in L/min, C = 1.0 for the ordinary construction coefficient, and A the effective area in m² equal to the largest floor area plus 50 percent of each of the two other floors. The largest floor is 5800 m² and the other two floors are 4900 m² each. Round the base flow to the nearest 1000 L/min. Then apply the occupancy adjustment of -15 percent to the base flow, and to the result apply a net factor of (1 - 0.30 + 0.20) for sprinkler credit (30 percent reduction) and exposure charge (20 percent increase), rounding to the nearest 1000 L/min. The system maximum day demand is 95 L/s. The peak hour demand is 190 L/s. The required fire flow duration is 2 hours.

  1. (a) Calculate the base required fire flow before adjustments, rounded to the nearest 1000 L/min. [4]
  2. (b) Calculate the adjusted required fire flow, rounded to the nearest 1000 L/min. [5]
  3. (c) Calculate the total system design demand for this building as maximum day demand plus fire flow, in L/s, and state which of the two design cases governs against the peak hour demand. [4]
  4. (d) Calculate the fire storage volume needed for the stated duration, in m³. [3]
  5. (e) The owner proposes to omit the sprinkler system, keeping all other factors. Calculate the new adjusted fire flow rounded to the nearest 1000 L/min. [4]
(a)

The effective area is the largest floor plus half of each other floor: A = 5800 + 0.5 × (4900 + 4900) = 5800 + 4900 = 10 700 m². Then F = 220 × 1.0 × √10 700 = 220 × 103.44 = 22 757 L/min. Rounded to the nearest 1000 L/min this is 23 000 L/min, which is 383 L/s. The square-root dependence on area is a feature of the method: doubling the floor area raises the required flow by only 41 percent. The constant C reflects how fast the structure burns and collapses, with 1.0 for ordinary construction, a lower value for fire-resistive buildings and a higher value for wood frame construction.

Answer: 23 000 L/min

(b)

Apply the occupancy adjustment first: 23 000 × (1 - 0.15) = 19 550 L/min, which recognises that a warehouse of limited combustibility burns more slowly than a typical contents load. Then apply the net factor for sprinklers and exposure: 19 550 × (1 - 0.30 + 0.20) = 19 550 × 0.90 = 17 595 L/min. Rounded to the nearest 1000 L/min this gives 18 000 L/min, or 300 L/s. Credit for sprinklers reduces the municipal water demand, because the sprinkler system takes over most of the firefighting. The exposure charge increases the demand because adjacent buildings could be ignited by radiant heat, and the two adjustments offset each other in part.

Answer: 18 000 L/min

(c)

Convert the adjusted fire flow to L/s: 18 000 / 60 = 300 L/s. The first design case is the maximum day demand plus the fire flow, because a fire is assumed to occur on the day when demand is at its highest: 95 + 300 = 395 L/s. The second design case is the peak hour demand alone, 190 L/s. The larger value, 395 L/s, governs the sizing of the supply and the pipes serving this area, since the fire case exceeds the peak hour case by more than a factor of 2. The distribution must deliver this flow while keeping a residual pressure of at least 140 kPa at the hydrant, per common Ontario practice.

Answer: 395 L/s

(d)

The storage needed for firefighting is the fire flow times the required duration. V = 300 L/s × 2 h × 3600 s/h = 300 × 7200 = 2 160 000 L, which is 2160 m³. This is only the fire component of the total storage. Under common Ontario guidance the full storage would also include an equalization component of about 25 percent of the maximum day demand and an emergency reserve of about 25 percent of the sum of the other two, so the fire volume is a large share of the requirement. A tower or reservoir holding this volume would be a major capital item for the community.

Answer: 2160 m³

(e)

Without sprinklers the sprinkler credit disappears, so the net factor becomes (1 + 0.20) = 1.20 applied to the occupancy-adjusted flow. The adjusted flow is 19 550 × 1.20 = 23 460 L/min. Rounded to the nearest 1000 L/min that is 23 000 L/min, or 383 L/s. Omitting sprinklers therefore raises the required fire flow by 5000 L/min, or about 28 percent, and adds 83 L/s to the system demand and about 600 m³ to the two-hour storage. This shows the municipality why it often requires sprinklers as a condition of approval: the building protects itself and the community avoids upsizing its mains and tower.

Answer: 23 000 L/min

Problem 5 [A3-050] Water source development: wells, intakes and safe yield

A municipal test well near Guelph, Ontario fully penetrates a confined sand and gravel aquifer 20 m thick. A steady-state pumping test at Q = 38 L/s produced a drawdown of 3.2 m in an observation well 25 m from the pumping well and 1.1 m in an observation well 120 m away. Use the Thiem equation for steady radial flow to a well in a confined aquifer, s1 - s2 = Q ln(r2/r1) / (2π T). The radius of influence R is the distance at which the drawdown extrapolates to zero on the semi-log relation s = Q ln(R/r) / (2π T). The pumping well radius is 0.15 m. A proposed second identical well would be 60 m from the first and pump simultaneously at the same rate; superposition applies and R stays unchanged.

  1. (a) Calculate the transmissivity T, in m²/d. [4]
  2. (b) Calculate the radius of influence R, in m. [3]
  3. (c) Calculate the drawdown at the face of the first well when it pumps alone at 38 L/s, in m. [4]
  4. (d) Calculate the total drawdown at the first well when both wells pump at 38 L/s. [4]
  5. (e) The drawdown at the first well must not exceed 9.0 m. Find the maximum equal pumping rate of each well, in L/s, with both wells operating. [5]
(a)

Rearrange the Thiem equation for transmissivity: T = Q ln(r2/r1) / (2π (s1 - s2)). With Q = 0.038 m³/s, r2/r1 = 120/25 = 4.8 and ln 4.8 = 1.5686, and s1 - s2 = 3.2 - 1.1 = 2.1 m, T = 0.038 × 1.5686 / (2π × 2.1) = 0.05961 / 13.195 = 4.518 × 10⁻³ m²/s. Multiplying by 86 400 s/d gives T = 390.3 m²/d. With an aquifer 20 m thick this corresponds to a hydraulic conductivity of about 19.5 m/d, or 2.3 × 10⁻⁴ m/s, typical of clean sand and gravel and a good production aquifer. The use of two observation wells avoids the need to know the drawdown in the pumping well itself, where well losses distort the reading.

Answer: 390 m²/d

(b)

Write the drawdown at the nearer observation well as s1 = Q ln(R/r1) / (2π T). The group Q / (2π T) = 0.038 / (2π × 4.518 × 10⁻³) = 1.3388 m, so ln(R/25) = 3.2 / 1.3388 = 2.390. Then R/25 = e2.390 = 10.91 and R = 272.9 m. This is the distance at which the cone of depression meets zero drawdown according to the steady-state model. In reality the cone of a confined aquifer under steady pumping keeps expanding slowly with time, so R is a fitting parameter, not a physical boundary. It is nevertheless useful for estimating the interference between neighbouring wells and for delineating a wellhead protection area.

Answer: 273 m

(c)

The drawdown at the well face is s = [Q / (2π T)] ln(R / rw), with rw = 0.15 m. Then ln(272.9 / 0.15) = ln(1819) = 7.506 and s = 1.3388 × 7.506 = 10.05 m. This is the theoretical drawdown in the aquifer just outside the well screen. The actual water level inside the pumped well would be lower because of well losses from screen entrance and casing friction. Whether 10 m of drawdown is acceptable depends on the available head above the top of the aquifer and the pump setting; a rule of thumb is to keep drawdown to no more than two-thirds of the available drawdown, to maintain the pump submergence and avoid dewatering the aquifer.

Answer: 10.05 m

(d)

By superposition, the drawdown at the first well is the sum of its own drawdown and the drawdown caused at its location by the second well, 60 m away. The interference drawdown is 1.3388 × ln(272.9 / 60) = 1.3388 × 1.5147 = 2.028 m. The total is 10.05 + 2.03 = 12.08 m. Placing wells only 60 m apart increases the drawdown at each by 20 percent, so the pair produces much less than twice the yield of a single well. The cost of the extra drawdown is more pumping energy and a higher risk of dewatering the aquifer during dry periods. Wider spacing, nearer to 150 or 200 m, would lessen interference at the price of a longer collector main.

Answer: 12.08 m

(e)

The total drawdown with both wells pumping Q each is s = [Q / (2π T)] × [ln(R/rw) + ln(R/60)], from parts c and d. The bracket is 7.506 + 1.5147 = 9.021. Setting s = 9.0 m gives Q = s × 2π T / 9.021 = 9.0 × 2π × 4.518 × 10⁻³ / 9.021 = 0.2555 / 9.021 = 0.02832 m³/s, which is 28.3 L/s per well. The combined safe yield is therefore 56.6 L/s, versus 38 L/s tested for one well alone and 9.0 / 10.05 × 38 = 34.0 L/s for a single well at the same limit. Because the aquifer is confined and the drawdown is proportional to Q, scaling is linear in this model.

Answer: 28.3 L/s

A3 Practice Paper 11

Problem 1 [A3-051] Transmission main sizing with the Hazen-Williams equation

A 600 mm cement-lined ductile iron transmission main carries treated water 4,200 m from a high-lift pumping station to an elevated tank serving a town east of Peterborough, Ontario. The design flow is 0.42 m³/s. When the main was commissioned the Hazen-Williams coefficient was C = 130, but condition assessments of similar mains in the system now suggest C = 100 after tuberculation. Use the SI form hf = 10.67 L Q1.852 / (C1.852 D4.87), with Q in m³/s and L and D in metres. Treat 600 mm as the true inside diameter, ignore minor losses and elevation changes, and consider friction loss between the two ends only.

  1. (a) Find the friction head loss at the design flow when C = 130. [3]
  2. (b) Find the friction head loss at the same flow when C = 100. [3]
  3. (c) If the pumps can only supply the friction head found in part (a), what flow can the aged main (C = 100) deliver? [4]
  4. (d) Find the inside diameter of a replacement main with C = 100 that would carry 0.42 m³/s at the head loss of part (a). [5]
  5. (e) Instead of replacing the pipe, a second 600 mm main with C = 100 is laid alongside it for the full length and the flow divides equally. Find the head loss at 0.42 m³/s. [5]
(a)

Substitute into hf = 10.67 L Q1.852 / (C1.852 D4.87). Q1.852 = 0.421.852 = 0.2006. C1.852 = 1301.852 = 8,223. D4.87 = 0.64.87 = 0.0831. The numerator is 10.67 × 4,200 × 0.2006 = 8,988. The denominator is 8,223 × 0.0831 = 683.3. So hf = 8,988 / 683.3 = 13.15 m. This is the friction head the pumps had to overcome when the main was new. It is the benchmark for the remaining parts, so keep the unrounded number. A 13 m loss over 4.2 km is a gradient of about 3.1 m per km, which is reasonable for a transmission main.

Answer: hf = 13.15 m

(b)

Only C changes, and hf varies as 1/C1.852. The ratio is (130/100)1.852 = 1.31.852 = 1.626. Therefore hf = 13.15 × 1.626 = 21.38 m. The pumps must now add about 8.2 m of extra head to move the same flow, which raises the annual energy cost in direct proportion, since power is proportional to head at constant flow and efficiency. The calculation shows why a drop in C from 130 to 100 is serious: a 23 percent fall in the coefficient produces a 63 percent rise in friction loss. This is the quantitative case for cleaning and relining the main.

Answer: hf = 21.38 m

(c)

Head loss varies as Q1.852, so at fixed hf and diameter, Q is proportional to C. With the head fixed at 13.15 m, Q = 0.42 × (100/130) = 0.3231 m³/s. The exponent cancels because the same power of C and Q appears in the equation, which gives the clean ratio. The aged main therefore delivers 323 L/s, a loss of capacity of 23 percent against the 420 L/s design flow. The utility would see this as the tank failing to recover during the maximum day, even though the pumps were never changed. This check is a quick way to translate a condition-assessment value of C into lost service capacity.

Answer: Q = 323 L/s

(d)

Set hf = 13.15 m with C = 100 and Q = 0.42 m³/s and solve the Hazen-Williams equation for D. D4.87 = 10.67 L Q1.852 / (C1.852 hf) = 10.67 × 4,200 × 0.2006 / (5,058 × 13.15) = 8,988 / 66,513 = 0.1351. Then D = 0.13511/4.87 = 0.663 m. The replacement main needs an inside diameter of about 663 mm, so a 700 mm nominal pipe would be chosen, with a margin. Note that the exponent 4.87 makes diameter very efficient: a 10.5 percent increase in diameter recovers the whole 63 percent increase in friction loss. Pipe sizes are discrete, so a commercial size above 663 mm inside diameter would be selected.

Answer: D = 663 mm

(e)

With two identical pipes in parallel and equal diameters and C, each carries half the flow, 0.21 m³/s, and the head loss of the pair equals the head loss of one pipe. Compute hf = 10.67 × 4,200 × 0.211.852 / (1001.852 × 0.64.87). The factor 0.211.852 = 0.0556. So the numerator is 10.67 × 4,200 × 0.0556 = 2,492 and the denominator is 5,058 × 0.0831 = 420.3. Then hf = 2,490 / 420.3 = 5.92 m. Halving the flow cuts the loss by 21.852 = 3.61, so 21.38 / 3.61 = 5.92 m. Twinning more than restores the original performance, but it costs a full second pipe, so the choice against relining is an economic one.

Answer: hf = 5.92 m

Problem 2 [A3-052] Storage reservoir sizing for equalization, fire and emergency

A growing community of 18,000 people in Simcoe County, Ontario, is sizing a new ground-level reservoir for its single pressure zone. The average day demand is 400 L per capita per day and the maximum day factor is 1.9. Design storage is the sum of three components: equalization, taken as 25 percent of the maximum day demand; fire storage, equal to the municipal fire flow of 150 L/s sustained for 3 hours; and emergency storage, taken as 25 percent of the sum of equalization and fire storage. The reservoir is a vertical cylindrical concrete tank with a usable water depth of 9.0 m. A planning amendment is now proposed that would allow mid-rise buildings and raise the required fire flow to 250 L/s for 4 hours, all other criteria unchanged.

  1. (a) Find the maximum day demand in m³/d. [3]
  2. (b) Find the total design storage volume under the current criteria. [5]
  3. (c) Find the inside diameter of the cylindrical tank for the volume in part (b). [3]
  4. (d) Find the total design storage volume under the proposed amendment. [5]
  5. (e) Find the tank diameter needed at the same 9.0 m depth after the amendment. [4]
(a)

The average day demand is the population times the per capita rate: 18,000 × 400 L/d = 7,200,000 L/d = 7,200 m³/d. The maximum day demand is the average day multiplied by the maximum day factor: 7,200 × 1.9 = 13,680 m³/d, which is 158 L/s. Maximum day, not average day, is the basis for equalization and for the pumping capacity feeding the reservoir, because the reservoir must be refilled during the highest-demand day of the year while still holding its fire and emergency reserves. The peak hour demand would govern the distribution mains but plays no part in storage sizing here.

Answer: 13,680 m³/d

(b)

Equalization is 0.25 × 13,680 = 3,420 m³. Fire storage is the fire flow times duration: 150 L/s = 0.150 m³/s, and 3 h = 10,800 s, so 0.150 × 10,800 = 1,620 m³. Emergency storage is 25 percent of the sum of the first two: 0.25 × (3,420 + 1,620) = 0.25 × 5,040 = 1,260 m³. The total is 3,420 + 1,620 + 1,260 = 6,300 m³. Equalization supplies the difference between pumping and instantaneous demand, fire storage is a reserve that must never be drawn on for normal use, and the emergency volume covers a pump or main failure. Check: the total equals 1.25 × (3,420 + 1,620) = 6,300 m³.

Answer: 6,300 m³

(c)

A vertical cylinder has volume V = π D² h / 4, so D = √(4V / (π h)). Here V = 6,300 m³ and h = 9.0 m, giving a plan area of 6,300 / 9.0 = 700 m². Then D = √(4 × 700 / π) = √(891.3) = 29.85 m. A tank of about 30 m diameter and 9 m depth is typical for a community this size. In practice the designer would also add freeboard above the usable depth and would check that the floor area suits the site and the turnover time, so that water does not age in the tank during the low-demand months.

Answer: D = 29.9 m

(d)

Only the fire storage and the emergency storage change. The new fire storage is 250 L/s × 4 h = 0.250 × 14,400 = 3,600 m³. Equalization is still 3,420 m³, because the maximum day demand has not changed. The emergency storage becomes 0.25 × (3,420 + 3,600) = 0.25 × 7,020 = 1,755 m³. The total is 3,420 + 3,600 + 1,755 = 8,775 m³. The rise from 6,300 m³ is 2,475 m³, or 39 percent. The result shows that fire storage dominates once the fire demand is raised, and that the emergency component, being a percentage of it, grows by the same proportion.

Answer: 8,775 m³

(e)

At the fixed depth of 9.0 m the plan area becomes 8,775 / 9.0 = 975 m². The diameter is D = √(4 × 975 / π) = √(1,241.4) = 35.23 m. The tank must therefore be about 5.4 m wider than for the current criteria, an increase in diameter of 18 percent for a 39 percent increase in volume. A designer would compare this with raising the depth, but a deeper tank costs more per cubic metre of storage and raises the pump head, while the site plan may allow the larger footprint. The calculation also shows that the amendment is not free: the planning decision carries a capital cost for the water system.

Answer: D = 35.2 m

Problem 3 [A3-053] Pumping station design with pump and system curves

A booster pumping station in Greater Sudbury, Ontario, lifts water from a clearwell through a forcemain to an elevated tank. The static lift between the clearwell low water level and the tank inlet is 38.0 m. The friction and minor losses in the forcemain follow hf = K Q², with K = 2,800 s²/m⁵ and Q in m³/s. One pump has the characteristic H = 72.0 − 9,500 Q², with H in metres and Q in m³/s. The wire-to-water efficiency at the duty point may be taken as 0.78. Take the density of water as 1,000 kg/m³ and g = 9.81 m/s². The operators report that as the tank fills during the day the effective static lift rises, and they want to know what happens to the flow and what a second pump would add.

  1. (a) Find the operating flow of one pump with a static lift of 38.0 m. [5]
  2. (b) Find the total dynamic head at that duty point. [3]
  3. (c) Find the electrical input power at the duty point. [3]
  4. (d) The tank has filled so that the static lift is 44.0 m. Find the new flow of the single pump. [4]
  5. (e) With the static lift back at 38.0 m, a second identical pump is started in parallel. Find the combined flow. [5]
(a)

The operating point is where the pump curve meets the system curve. The system head is H = Hs + K Q² = 38.0 + 2,800 Q². Setting the pump head equal to it gives 72.0 − 9,500 Q² = 38.0 + 2,800 Q². Collecting terms, 34.0 = 12,300 Q², so Q² = 0.002764 and Q = 0.05258 m³/s = 52.6 L/s. The flow is found at the intersection, not from the pump curve alone, because the pump delivers whatever head the pipe system demands at that flow. A pump operated away from its best efficiency flow wears faster, so the designer would check that 52.6 L/s lies in the preferred operating range of the selected pump.

Answer: Q = 52.6 L/s

(b)

Substitute the flow into either curve; they must agree at the duty point. The system curve gives H = 38.0 + 2,800 × 0.05258² = 38.0 + 2,800 × 0.002764 = 38.0 + 7.74 = 45.74 m. As a check, the pump curve gives 72.0 − 9,500 × 0.002764 = 72.0 − 26.26 = 45.74 m. Of this head, 38.0 m is the static lift that raises the water, and 7.74 m is friction that is dissipated as heat in the forcemain. The friction share of 17 percent is moderate; a long, small forcemain would show a far higher share and a poorer energy performance.

Answer: H = 45.7 m

(c)

The hydraulic power is ρ g Q H = 1,000 × 9.81 × 0.05258 × 45.74 = 23,592 W, or 23.6 kW. The input power divides this by the overall efficiency of 0.78: P = 23.59 / 0.78 = 30.25 kW. This is the electrical demand that sizes the motor starter and the standby generator share, and it multiplies by the hours of operation and the tariff to give the annual energy cost. A motor rated at the next standard size above about 30 kW, for example 37 kW, would be chosen so that the motor is not overloaded at the end of the pump curve.

Answer: P = 30.2 kW

(d)

With a static lift of 44.0 m, the intersection condition becomes 72.0 − 9,500 Q² = 44.0 + 2,800 Q². Then 28.0 = 12,300 Q², so Q² = 0.002276 and Q = 0.04771 m³/s = 47.7 L/s. The flow falls by 4.9 L/s, a drop of 9 percent, for a 6 m rise in static lift, and the new head is 44.0 + 2,800 × 0.002276 = 50.4 m. The pump slides back along its curve toward shut-off as the system curve rises. This is why elevated storage is usually operated within a band: a large level swing moves the duty point and the efficiency, and a variable speed drive could keep the flow constant.

Answer: Q = 47.7 L/s

(e)

Two identical pumps in parallel each deliver half of the total flow at the same head. The combined curve is therefore H = 72.0 − 9,500 (Q/2)² = 72.0 − 2,375 Q². Setting it equal to the system curve gives 72.0 − 2,375 Q² = 38.0 + 2,800 Q², so 34.0 = 5,175 Q², Q² = 0.006570 and Q = 0.08106 m³/s = 81.1 L/s. The flow rises by only 54 percent, not 100 percent, because the extra flow raises the friction loss in the common forcemain. The head also rises to 38.0 + 2,800 × 0.00657 = 56.4 m, so each pump then operates at 40.5 L/s and a higher head than alone.

Answer: Q = 81.1 L/s

Problem 4 [A3-054] Water distribution network analysis by the Hardy Cross method
