The Town rounds to the nearest 1 000 L/min, giving 13 000 L/min. The coefficient C reflects how much the construction contributes to the fire, so a non-combustible building gets a lower value than ordinary or wood-frame construction. The formula also uses the whole floor area, not the area of a single fire compartment, which is conservative for a large single-storey warehouse and is the main reason the sprinkler credit is so valuable to the owner when the flow is later reduced.

Answer: 13 000 L/min

(b)

Start from the rounded base flow of 13 000 L/min. The occupancy credit is a 15 percent reduction: 13 000 × 0.85 = 11 050 L/min. Both the sprinkler credit and the exposure charge are stated as percentages of this occupancy-adjusted flow. The sprinkler credit is 0.30 × 11 050 = 3 315 L/min, subtracted. The exposure charge is 0.20 × 11 050 = 2 210 L/min, added. The net flow is 11 050 − 3 315 + 2 210 = 9 945 L/min, which rounds to 10 000 L/min. Using the percentages of the same base, rather than compounding one on the other, is the stated method and avoids a different answer depending on the order of the steps. The sprinklers do not replace fire flow entirely because the municipal main still supplies hose streams and the sprinkler system itself.

Answer: 10 000 L/min

(c)

The stored volume is the product of the fire flow and the duration. The fire flow of 10 000 L/min is sustained for 150 minutes, so the volume is 10 000 × 150 = 1 500 000 L. Since 1 m³ = 1 000 L, this is 1 500 m³. This volume forms the fire component of the storage in the town's reservoir or elevated tank and, together with equalization and emergency components, sets the size of the tank. It is a volume that must remain in the tank at all times, so it sits below the level used for normal equalization and is never drawn down in ordinary operation. A longer duration, such as 180 minutes for a larger building, would raise the volume to 1 800 m³.

Answer: 1 500 m³

(d)

Fire flow is added to the maximum day demand because the Town designs for a fire during the day of highest consumption. Convert the fire flow: 10 000 L/min ÷ 60 = 166.67 L/s. The total design demand is 62 + 166.67 = 228.67 L/s, or 228.7 L/s. Distribution mains, the pumping station and the treatment capacity are checked against this value, with a minimum residual pressure of 140 kPa at the hydrant. Note that the town's peak hour demand is not combined with fire flow, since a fire and the peak hour of the maximum day are treated as unlikely to coincide in the design criteria. The supply source must be able to deliver the 228.7 L/s, or the storage must supply the shortfall over the duration of the fire.

Answer: 228.7 L/s

Problem 3 [A3-073] Water source development: wells, intakes and safe yield

A village in southwestern Ontario will rely on a new well field in a confined sand and gravel aquifer 24 m thick. A constant-rate pumping test was run at 2 400 m³/d until the cone of depression reached steady state. Drawdowns were 3.80 m at an observation well 15 m from the pumped well and 1.45 m at an observation well 90 m from the pumped well. Assume steady radial flow to a fully penetrating well in a confined aquifer (Thiem equation), a radius of influence R taken from the test data (the radius at which the Thiem profile through the 15 m observation well reaches zero drawdown, about 272 m), and a pumped well radius of 0.15 m. The pumps must be kept at least 4 m above the top of the aquifer, which limits the drawdown at the pumped well face to 14 m. The village needs 7 500 m³/d of firm capacity.

  1. (a) Calculate the transmissivity T of the aquifer from the test, in m²/d. [5]
  2. (b) Calculate the hydraulic conductivity K, in m/d. [3]
  3. (c) Calculate the safe yield of one well, in m³/d, when the drawdown at the well face is limited to 14 m. [6]
  4. (d) Find the number of identical wells required to meet 7 500 m³/d of firm capacity, defined as the capacity with the largest well out of service. [6]
(a)

The Thiem equation for a confined aquifer is Q = 2π T (s1 − s2) / ln(r2/r1), where s1 and s2 are drawdowns at radii r1 and r2. Solving for T gives T = Q ln(r2/r1) / [2π (s1 − s2)]. Here Q = 2 400 m³/d, r2/r1 = 90/15 = 6, ln 6 = 1.7918, and s1 − s2 = 3.80 − 1.45 = 2.35 m. Therefore T = 2 400 × 1.7918 / (2π × 2.35) = 4 300.3 / 14.765 = 291.2 m²/d. The assumptions are steady state, a fully penetrating well, a homogeneous aquifer of uniform thickness and no leakage; a confined aquifer is required, otherwise the drawdown must first be corrected for the reduced saturated thickness. Because T depends only on the difference in drawdown, errors in the absolute datum of the observation wells cancel.

Answer: 291.2 m²/d

(b)

Transmissivity is the product of hydraulic conductivity and saturated thickness, T = K b, so K = T / b. With T = 291.2 m²/d and b = 24 m, K = 291.2 / 24 = 12.13 m/d. This is equivalent to 1.4 × 10⁻⁴ m/s, which is consistent with a clean medium to coarse sand with some gravel, the material described in the borehole log. The check against typical values for sand (10 to 100 m/d range at the upper end, lower for silty sand) is a useful sanity test on a pumping test analysis. If the value had come out several orders of magnitude outside the range for the logged material, the engineer would suspect a wrong datum, a partially penetrating well or a boundary effect on the test.

Answer: 12.13 m/d

(c)

Apply the Thiem equation between the well face (rw = 0.15 m, drawdown sw = 14 m) and the radius of influence (R = 272 m, the radius of influence implied by the test data, where drawdown is zero): Q = 2π T sw / ln(R/rw). The ratio is R/rw = 272/0.15 = 1 813, and ln 1 813 = 7.503. Then Q = 2π × 291.2 × 14 / 7.503 = 25 615 / 7.503 = 3 414 m³/d. This is the largest steady rate that keeps the pumping water level at least 4 m above the top of the aquifer, so it is the drawdown-limited safe yield. In practice the designer also checks well loss and interference from neighbouring wells, which reduce the yield below this value, and the Ministry's rules limit the permitted rate to what the aquifer can sustain over the long term.

Answer: 3 414 m³/d

(d)

Firm capacity means that the demand is still met if the largest unit is out of service for maintenance or repair. With identical wells of 3 414 m³/d, the number of wells in service must satisfy (n − 1) × 3 414 ≥ 7 500. Dividing, n − 1 ≥ 2.20, so n − 1 = 3 and n = 4 wells. Check: three wells in service give 10 242 m³/d, above the 7 500 m³/d required. Three wells total would give only 6 828 m³/d with one out of service, which fails. The fourth well is therefore the redundancy. Wells must also be spaced far enough apart to limit interference, and the actual spacing would be set from a drawdown superposition check so that the combined drawdown at any well remains within the 14 m limit.

Answer: 4 wells

Problem 4 [A3-074] Transmission main sizing with the Hazen-Williams equation

A gravity transmission main will carry treated water from a reservoir to an elevated tank in the Municipality of Grey Hollow, Ontario. The main is 8 200 m long, lined ductile iron with Hazen-Williams coefficient C = 120. The hydraulic grade line is 41.0 m higher at the reservoir than at the tank, and all of this head is available for friction loss; minor losses may be neglected. The Hazen-Williams equation in SI units is Q = 0.2785 C D2.63 S0.54, with Q in m³/s, D in m and S the friction slope in m/m. The design flow is 0.140 m³/s. Available standard internal diameters are 300, 350, 400, 450 and 500 mm. The tank has a usable volume of 4 500 m³ to be filled from empty.

  1. (a) Calculate the theoretical internal diameter, in mm, needed to carry the design flow. [6]
  2. (b) Select the smallest standard diameter that works and calculate the flow it carries under the available head, in m³/s. [5]
  3. (c) Calculate the mean velocity in the selected pipe at that flow, in m/s. [4]
  4. (d) Calculate the time, in hours, to fill the empty tank at the flow from part (b), assuming no demand is drawn from the tank. [5]
(a)

The friction slope is the available head divided by the length: S = 41.0 / 8 200 = 0.00500 m/m. Rearrange Hazen-Williams for the diameter: D = [Q / (0.2785 C S0.54)]1/2.63. Evaluate S0.54 = 0.0050.54 = 0.05717. Then 0.2785 × 120 × 0.05717 = 1.911, and Q divided by that is 0.140 / 1.911 = 0.07327. Raising to the power 1/2.63 = 0.3802 gives D = 0.3701 m, or 370 mm. This is the diameter that exactly uses all of the available head at the design flow. Because it is not a standard size, the designer must round up, since a smaller diameter would need more head than is available. The equation is empirical and valid for water at ordinary temperatures in turbulent flow, so no Reynolds number check is needed.

Answer: 370 mm

(b)

The smallest listed diameter above 370 mm is 400 mm (the 350 mm pipe is too small, since it is below the theoretical 370 mm). With D = 0.400 m, D2.63 = 0.0899, and S0.54 is still 0.05717 for the same head and length. Then Q = 0.2785 × 120 × 0.0899 × 0.05717 = 0.1717 m³/s, about 172 L/s. The pipe therefore delivers 23 percent more than the design flow under the full head, which means that in service the flow would be throttled by valves or by the downstream demand. The surplus capacity is useful in a growing community and allows for the loss in carrying capacity as the C value falls with age from tuberculation or deposits.

Answer: 0.1717 m³/s

(c)

Velocity is flow divided by cross-sectional area. The area of a 400 mm pipe is A = π D² / 4 = π × 0.400² / 4 = 0.12566 m². Then v = Q / A = 0.1717 / 0.12566 = 1.367 m/s. This is within the common design range of about 0.6 to 2.0 m/s for transmission mains: fast enough to keep sediment moving, yet low enough that transient pressures from valve closure (water hammer) remain manageable. If the pipe were operated at the full 0.1717 m³/s only occasionally, a lower average velocity would result. The velocity head v²/2g is only 0.095 m, which confirms that neglecting minor losses and velocity head in the 41 m energy budget is reasonable here.

Answer: 1.367 m/s

(d)

The fill time is the volume divided by the inflow rate, assuming constant flow. Since the tank is high and fills from empty, the pressure head at the tank would change slightly during filling, but the problem says to use the part (b) flow. The inflow is 0.1717 m³/s = 618 m³/h. The time is 4 500 / (0.1717 × 3 600) = 4 500 / 618.2 = 7.28 h. This is the minimum time under maximum flow; with demand drawn from the tank, or with the flow throttled to the design 0.140 m³/s, the tank would take longer (8.93 h at 0.140 m³/s). Operators use this kind of calculation to decide whether a tank can recover its equalization and fire storage overnight, when the demand on the system is lowest.

Answer: 7.28 h

Problem 5 [A3-075] Storage reservoir sizing for equalization, fire and emergency

The Town of Millbrook Heights, Ontario, is designing a new elevated tank to serve a pressure zone with a maximum day demand of 6 800 m³/d. The Town's design criteria give the total storage as the sum of three components: equalization A, taken as 25 percent of the maximum day demand; fire storage B, equal to the design fire flow multiplied by its duration; and emergency storage C, taken as 25 percent of the sum of A and B. The design fire flow is 150 L/s for 2 hours. The tank is a vertical cylinder with a usable depth of 8.5 m between the low water level and the top water level. The most elevated customer is at ground elevation 238.0 m and must keep a minimum pressure of 275 kPa at peak hour, when the head loss from tank to that customer is 4.2 m. Use 9.81 kPa per metre of head.

  1. (a) Calculate the equalization storage A, in m³. [3]
  2. (b) Calculate the fire storage B, in m³. [3]
  3. (c) Calculate the emergency storage C and the total required storage volume, and report the total in m³. [4]
  4. (d) Calculate the inside diameter of the cylindrical tank, in m, for the total volume and the usable depth. [5]
  5. (e) Calculate the minimum elevation, in m, of the low water level of the tank needed to satisfy the pressure requirement at peak hour. [5]
(a)

Equalization storage supplies the difference between the supply rate and the demand rate during the hours when demand exceeds the constant supply from the treatment plant and wells. The Town's criterion takes it as 25 percent of the maximum day demand. A = 0.25 × 6 800 = 1 700 m³. The value is typical of the 20 to 25 percent used in Ontario design guidelines for small and medium systems that lack hourly demand records; where records exist, the designer would instead construct a mass diagram of cumulative supply against cumulative demand over the maximum day and take the largest cumulative deficit as the equalization volume. This is the part of the tank that is drawn down and refilled every day.

Answer: 1 700 m³

(b)

Fire storage is the volume that must be on hand to supply the design fire flow for the design duration without any help from the supply. The flow is 150 L/s = 0.150 m³/s, and the duration is 2 hours = 7 200 s. The volume is B = 0.150 × 7 200 = 1 080 m³. The calculation assumes that the supply cannot be counted on during a fire, which is the conservative case, for instance during a power failure at the pumps. This volume is held in reserve beneath the equalization volume so that normal daily drawdown never touches it. A longer duration of 3 hours would raise B to 1 620 m³, so the choice of duration has a large influence on tank size.

Answer: 1 080 m³

(c)

Emergency storage covers interruptions to supply such as a main break or a plant outage, and the Town takes it as 25 percent of the sum of A and B. A + B = 1 700 + 1 080 = 2 780 m³. Then C = 0.25 × 2 780 = 695 m³. The total required storage is A + B + C = 1 700 + 1 080 + 695 = 3 475 m³. Each component serves a different risk, so they are added rather than overlapped; this is the usual approach for a conservative design, and some jurisdictions allow the emergency component to double up with part of the fire storage when the supply is firm. This total will be used for the tank geometry and for checking the turnover time of the water to protect water quality.

Answer: 3 475 m³

(d)

The usable volume of a vertical cylinder is V = π D² h / 4, with h the usable depth. Solving for the diameter gives D = √(4V / (π h)). With V = 3 475 m³ and h = 8.5 m, 4V = 13 900 and π h = 26.704, so D = √(13 900 / 26.704) = √520.5 = 22.8 m. The chosen diameter would normally be rounded up to a practical value such as 23 m, which gives slightly more storage. A wide shallow tank has a lower head range between low and top water level, so the pressure in the zone varies less, which is better for customers. The tank would also be checked for mixing and water age in cold weather, since ice formation is a concern for Ontario tanks.

Answer: 22.8 m

(e)

The pressure requirement is governed by the lowest water level, because at peak hour the tank may be near its low level. The required hydraulic grade at the customer is the ground elevation plus the pressure head: 275 kPa ÷ 9.81 kPa/m = 28.03 m, so the grade is 238.0 + 28.03 = 266.03 m. The tank low water level must be higher by the head loss in the pipes from tank to customer, 4.2 m, so the elevation is 266.03 + 4.2 = 270.2 m. If the low water level were set lower, the customer would see less than 275 kPa during peak hour exactly when the tank is partly drained. The top water level is then 270.2 + 8.5 = 278.7 m, which is a 8.5 m (83 kPa) swing in pressure that the system must tolerate.

Answer: 270.2 m

A3 Practice Paper 16

Problem 1 [A3-076] Pumping station design with pump and system curves

A booster pumping station in the City of Riverton, Ontario, lifts treated water from an underground reservoir to a pressure zone. The static lift is 36.0 m. Pipe friction and minor losses follow Hf = K Q², where K = 2 500 m per (m³/s)² for the existing pipe, Q in m³/s. The pump selected has the head-flow curve H = 70 − 4 200 Q² (H in m, Q in m³/s) and an efficiency of 78 percent at its operating point. Water density is 1 000 kg/m³ and g = 9.81 m/s². The station was designed for one duty pump. The City wishes to know the benefit of adding an identical second pump in parallel, and the effect of pipe ageing, which is expected to raise K by 20 percent over the next decade.

  1. (a) Find the operating flow of the single pump, in L/s. [5]
  2. (b) Calculate the brake power required by the single pump at its operating point, in kW. [4]
  3. (c) Find the total flow when two identical pumps operate in parallel on the same system, in L/s. [5]
  4. (d) With one pump running, find the flow after K increases by 20 percent, in L/s. [3]
  5. (e) Calculate the percentage reduction in flow caused by the pipe ageing in part (d), relative to part (a). [3]
(a)

The operating point is where the pump curve meets the system curve. The system head is H = 36.0 + 2 500 Q² and the pump head is H = 70 − 4 200 Q². Equate: 36.0 + 2 500 Q² = 70 − 4 200 Q², so 6 700 Q² = 34, and Q² = 0.005075 m⁶/s². Then Q = 0.07124 m³/s = 71.24 L/s. The head at this flow is H = 36.0 + 2 500 × 0.005075 = 48.69 m. The pump delivers more than the static lift because the friction in the pipe uses the additional 12.69 m. If the pump were run at a point far from this intersection, for example by throttling a valve, it would add a further artificial loss and waste energy.

Answer: 71.24 L/s

(b)

The hydraulic power delivered to the water is P = ρ g Q H. Using Q = 0.07124 m³/s and H = 48.69 m, P = 1 000 × 9.81 × 0.07124 × 48.69 = 34 026 W = 34.03 kW. The brake power required at the shaft is the water power divided by the efficiency, 34.03 / 0.78 = 43.62 kW. The electric motor must be selected with a margin above this power, commonly 10 to 15 percent, and the motor size is then rounded up to the next standard size, for example 55 kW. Energy cost over the life of the pump is usually much larger than its purchase price, so the efficiency at the operating point is an important selection criterion in addition to getting the right flow.

Answer: 43.6 kW

(c)

For identical pumps in parallel, at a given head each pump delivers the same flow, so the combined flow is double the single-pump flow at that head. Each pump carries Q/2, so the combined curve is H = 70 − 4 200 (Q/2)² = 70 − 1 050 Q². Equate to the system curve: 36.0 + 2 500 Q² = 70 − 1 050 Q², so 3 550 Q² = 34 and Q² = 0.009577. Therefore Q = 0.09786 m³/s = 97.86 L/s, at a head of 36.0 + 2 500 × 0.009577 = 59.94 m. Adding a second pump raises the flow only 37 percent, not 100 percent, because the extra flow raises the friction loss in the shared pipe and so the head each pump works against. The efficiency of each pump should be rechecked at its new, lower flow of 48.9 L/s.

Answer: 97.86 L/s

(d)

A 20 percent increase in K gives K = 1.2 × 2 500 = 3 000 m/(m³/s)². The system curve becomes H = 36.0 + 3 000 Q². Equate with the single-pump curve: 36.0 + 3 000 Q² = 70 − 4 200 Q², so 7 200 Q² = 34, giving Q² = 0.004722. Q = 0.06872 m³/s = 68.72 L/s. The new head is 36.0 + 3 000 × 0.004722 = 50.17 m, a rise of 1.5 m. Ageing makes the system curve steeper, so the operating point slides up the pump curve, giving slightly more head at less flow. Because the static lift is dominant, the system curve is flat at the start, and a 20 percent change in K has only a small effect on the flow.

Answer: 68.72 L/s

(e)

The percentage reduction is (Q_old − Q_new) / Q_old × 100. From part (a) Q_old = 71.24 L/s and from part (d) Q_new = 68.72 L/s. The difference is 2.52 L/s, and 2.52 / 71.24 = 0.03535, or 3.53 percent. The loss of 2.5 L/s is small relative to the demand, so the station can absorb a decade of ageing without losing capability, provided the demand does not grow at the same time. In design, the engineer takes both the new and the aged pipe roughness as bounding cases and requires the pump to meet the duty flow in the aged state, since a pump that only meets the duty when new will be inadequate by the end of its life.

Answer: 3.53 percent

Problem 2 [A3-077] Water distribution network analysis by the Hardy Cross method

A single loop of mains in the Town of Cedar Falls, Ontario, joins four nodes A, B, C and D. Pipes AB and BC form the northern route from A to C; pipes AD and DC form the southern route. Water enters at node A at 120 L/s and leaves at node C at 120 L/s, with no other withdrawals. Head loss in each pipe is h = r Q1.852, with Q in L/s and h in m, using these resistance coefficients: r(AB) = 0.0030, r(BC) = 0.0042, r(AD) = 0.0026, r(DC) = 0.0048. Take clockwise flow around the loop A to B to C to D to A as positive. The first trial flows are 70 L/s through AB and BC, and 50 L/s through AD and DC. The pressure head at A is 58.0 m and all nodes are at the same elevation.

  1. (a) For the first trial, calculate the net head loss around the loop (clockwise losses minus counter-clockwise losses), in m. [4]
  2. (b) Calculate the first Hardy Cross flow correction ΔQ, in L/s. [4]
  3. (c) Carry the iterations to convergence and give the flow in pipe AB, in L/s. [4]
  4. (d) Calculate the head loss from A to C, in m, at the converged flows. [4]
  5. (e) Calculate the pressure head at node C, in m. [4]
(a)

Using h = r Q1.852, the northern route carries 70 L/s through both AB and BC, whose combined coefficient is 0.0030 + 0.0042 = 0.0072. Since 701.852 = 2 613, the clockwise loss is 0.0072 × 2 613 = 18.81 m. The southern route carries 50 L/s through AD and DC, with coefficient 0.0026 + 0.0048 = 0.0074, and 501.852 = 1 401, so the loss is 0.0074 × 1 401 = 10.37 m. These flows travel counter-clockwise around the loop, so their losses take the negative sign. The net head loss is 18.81 − 10.37 = 8.44 m. A loop that is balanced has a net loss of zero, because the head drop from A to C must be the same along either route, so 8.44 m shows the northern route is carrying too much flow.

Answer: 8.44 m

(b)

The Hardy Cross correction is ΔQ = − Σ(r Q|Q|0.852) / (1.852 Σ r |Q|0.852), where the sums run around the loop and the numerator is the signed head loss from part (a). The denominator uses absolute values: for the north route, 0.0072 × 700.852 = 0.0072 × 37.35 = 0.2689; for the south route, 0.0074 × 500.852 = 0.0074 × 28.0 = 0.2072. Their sum is 0.4761, and multiplying by 1.852 gives 0.8818. Then ΔQ = −8.44 / 0.8818 = −9.58 L/s. The negative sign means the clockwise flow must be reduced by 9.58 L/s and the counter-clockwise flow increased by the same amount, which gives 60.42 L/s north and 59.58 L/s south after the first iteration.

Answer: −9.58 L/s

(c)

After the first correction the flows are 60.42 L/s and 59.58 L/s, and the loop imbalance falls to a value of only −0.018 m. The second iteration gives a correction of ΔQ = +0.020 L/s, so the flows become 60.44 L/s north and 59.56 L/s south. A third iteration changes the flows by less than 10⁻⁷ L/s, so the solution has converged. The flow in AB (and also BC) is therefore 60.44 L/s, and the flow in AD and DC is 59.56 L/s. The total entering node A is 60.44 + 59.56 = 120.00 L/s, which satisfies continuity at the node. Practitioners stop when the correction is below about 0.1 L/s, so two iterations would be enough for a design.

Answer: 60.44 L/s

(d)

The head loss from A to C is the same along either route when the loop is balanced, so it is calculated along the northern route: h = 0.0072 × 60.441.852. Evaluate 60.441.852 = e1.852 × ln 60.44 = e1.852 × 4.1018 = e7.597 = 1 991. Then h = 0.0072 × 1 991 = 14.33 m. As a check, the southern route gives 0.0074 × 59.561.852 = 0.0074 × 1 937 = 14.33 m, equal to the northern route to the precision of the data, which confirms that the loop is balanced. This head loss is quite high for a single loop at only 120 L/s and suggests that the pipes are small or old; a larger diameter on the north route would reduce the loss and give better pressure at the demand node.

Answer: 14.33 m

(e)

With all nodes at the same elevation, the pressure head at C equals the head at A less the friction loss from A to C. The pressure head at A is 58.0 m, and the head loss from part (d) is 14.33 m. The pressure head at C is 58.0 − 14.33 = 43.67 m, equal to 428 kPa (43.67 × 9.81). This is above the minimum normal pressure of 275 kPa often required in Ontario systems, so under this flow the supply is adequate, though under a fire flow the loss would increase by roughly the ratio of flows to the power 1.852. For example, at double the flow the loss would be 3.6 times larger, which would exceed the available head, so the loop would have to be checked at the fire flow condition.

Answer: 43.67 m

Problem 3 [A3-078] Network pressure and fire-flow checks at nodes

A hydrant flow test was done at the corner of Mill Street and Concession Road in the Village of Dunmere, Ontario. With no flow the static pressure was 420 kPa. With 95 L/s discharged from the test hydrant the residual pressure was 320 kPa. The Village requires a fire flow plus maximum day demand of 180 L/s at this location with a residual pressure of not less than 140 kPa anywhere in the system. Use the usual extrapolation, in which the pressure drop from static varies as the flow to the power 1.852, so that Q_available = Q_test × [(Ps − Pmin)/(Ps − Pr)]0.54. An investigation shows 60 percent of the 100 kPa test drop occurs in a 90 m long, 200 mm cast iron main with Hazen-Williams C = 100, and the other 40 percent elsewhere. The Village considers replacing this main with a 300 mm main with C = 120, with the same length and flow path.

  1. (a) Calculate the flow available at this location at a residual pressure of 140 kPa, in L/s. [5]
  2. (b) Calculate the residual pressure in the system when 180 L/s is drawn, in kPa, and state whether the requirement is met. [5]
  3. (c) Calculate the pressure drop from static, in kPa, at the 95 L/s test flow after the main is replaced. [5]
  4. (d) Calculate the flow available at 140 kPa residual after the replacement, in L/s. [5]
(a)

The available flow at a chosen minimum residual pressure is found by extrapolating the test. Here Ps = 420 kPa, the test residual Pr = 320 kPa at Q_test = 95 L/s, and the minimum allowed Pmin = 140 kPa. The ratio of pressure drops is (420 − 140)/(420 − 320) = 280/100 = 2.80. Raising to 0.54 gives 2.800.54 = e0.54 × 1.0296 = e0.5560 = 1.744. Then Q_available = 95 × 1.744 = 165.6 L/s. This is less than the 180 L/s required, so the location is deficient. The 0.54 exponent comes from the Hazen-Williams relationship that head loss is proportional to Q1.852, since 1/1.852 = 0.54. The extrapolation is reliable only for modest extensions beyond the tested flow.

Answer: 165.6 L/s

(b)

The pressure drop from static varies with flow to the power 1.852. At the test, the drop was 420 − 320 = 100 kPa at 95 L/s. At 180 L/s the drop is 100 × (180/95)1.852. The flow ratio is 1.8947, with ln 1.8947 = 0.6393, so the power gives e1.852 × 0.6393 = e1.1840 = 3.268. The drop is therefore 326.8 kPa, and the residual is 420 − 326.8 = 93.4 kPa. This is below the required 140 kPa, so the requirement is not met. The value is also consistent with part (a): since the available flow at 140 kPa is only 165.6 L/s, any larger draw must yield a residual below 140 kPa. A residual that low risks negative pressures elsewhere in the system and potential back-siphonage.

Answer: 93.4 kPa; requirement not met

(c)

The head loss in a Hazen-Williams pipe scales as L Q1.852 / (C1.852 D4.87). With the same length and flow, the new-to-old ratio is (C_old/C_new)1.852 × (D_old/D_new)4.87 = (100/120)1.852 × (200/300)4.87. The first factor is 0.83331.852 = 0.7133 and the second is 0.66674.87 = 0.1389, so the ratio is 0.0990. The old main accounted for 60 percent of the 100 kPa drop, which is 60 kPa, and it falls to 60 × 0.0990 = 5.94 kPa. The other 40 kPa is unchanged, so the new drop is 40 + 5.94 = 45.9 kPa. The result is that the replacement removes most of the loss in the main, but the remaining system losses limit the improvement.

Answer: 45.9 kPa

(d)

Use the same extrapolation with the new drop at the test flow. The new residual at 95 L/s would be 420 − 45.9 = 374.1 kPa. The ratio of drops is (420 − 140)/45.94 = 280/45.94 = 6.095. Raising to 0.54: ln 6.095 = 1.8071, times 0.54 = 0.9758, and e0.9758 = 2.653. The available flow is 95 × 2.653 = 252 L/s. This comfortably exceeds the 180 L/s required, so the replacement fixes the deficiency, with an increase in available flow of about 52 percent over the existing 165.6 L/s. The Village should compare the cost of the replacement with other options, such as looping the main to a second feed, which could also reduce the drop and provide redundancy during a main break.

Answer: 252 L/s

Problem 4 [A3-079] Coagulation and flocculation: mixing intensity and detention time

A conventional surface water treatment plant on Lake Huron treats a design flow of 0.185 m³/s (about 16 ML/d). Raw-water temperature in summer is 10 °C, for which the dynamic viscosity is taken as 1.31 × 10⁻³ Pa·s. The rapid-mix tank is designed for a detention time of 20 s and a velocity gradient G = 800 s⁻¹. The flocculation basin has a detention time of 25 min and a mean G = 40 s⁻¹, using the relationship P = G² μ V, where P is the power dissipated in the water and V the tank volume. In winter at 2 °C the viscosity rises to 1.67 × 10⁻³ Pa·s. The designer also considers a tapered flocculation train of three equal compartments with G values of 60, 40 and 20 s⁻¹, the same total detention time of 25 min.

  1. (a) Calculate the power that must be supplied to the rapid-mix tank, in kW. [5]
  2. (b) Calculate the volume of the flocculation basin, in m³. [3]
  3. (c) Calculate the total power required by the three-compartment tapered train, in W. [6]
  4. (d) If the power of the single-compartment flocculator is held at its summer value, calculate the velocity gradient reached in winter at 2 °C, in s⁻¹. [6]
(a)

The volume of the rapid-mix tank is the flow multiplied by the detention time: V = 0.185 × 20 = 3.70 m³. The power is P = G² μ V = 800² × 1.31 × 10⁻³ × 3.70. Evaluate 800² = 640 000, and 640 000 × 1.31 × 10⁻³ = 838.4 Pa/s. Multiplying by 3.70 m³ gives P = 3 102 W = 3.10 kW. This power is dissipated in a very small volume, which is why rapid mixing needs a high power density of about 840 W/m³, and why the mixer must be a well designed unit that disperses the coagulant in seconds before hydrolysis of the metal salt is complete. The mixer motor would be sized with an allowance for the efficiency of the drive, typically 70 to 85 percent.

Answer: 3.10 kW

(b)

The detention time is 25 min = 1 500 s. The flocculation volume is V = Q t = 0.185 × 1 500 = 277.5 m³. With a typical water depth of 4 m this requires a plan area of about 69 m² for the whole train. The product G t = 40 × 1 500 = 60 000, which lies in the usual design range of 10 000 to 100 000 for flocculation, and the basin meets the common detention criterion of 20 to 30 min. A longer time would improve floc growth in cold water, but increases the basin cost. The combination of a moderate G and a long time allows the floc to grow without being sheared apart, which is the aim of flocculation after the rapid mix has destabilized the particles.

Answer: 277.5 m³

(c)

Each of the three equal compartments has a detention time of 25/3 min = 500 s, so each has a volume of 0.185 × 500 = 92.5 m³. Power in each is P = G² μ V. For G = 60: 3 600 × 1.31 × 10⁻³ × 92.5 = 436.2 W. For G = 40: 1 600 × 1.31 × 10⁻³ × 92.5 = 193.9 W. For G = 20: 400 × 1.31 × 10⁻³ × 92.5 = 48.5 W. The sum is 436.2 + 193.9 + 48.5 = 678.6 W. This is higher than the 581.6 W needed for a single compartment at G = 40, because the first stage has a higher G. The advantage of tapering is better floc growth: strong mixing early creates collisions between the many small particles, and gentle mixing later avoids breaking up the larger flocs.

Answer: 678.6 W

(d)

At constant power and volume, G² μ is constant, so G is inversely proportional to the square root of viscosity: G_winter = G_summer × √(μ_summer/μ_winter). The summer power is P = 40² × 1.31 × 10⁻³ × 277.5 = 581.6 W. In winter, G = √(P/(μ V)) = √(581.6 / (1.67 × 10⁻³ × 277.5)) = √(1 255) = 35.4 s⁻¹. Equivalently, 40 × √(1.31/1.67) = 40 × 0.8857 = 35.4 s⁻¹. The velocity gradient falls 11 percent in winter, and the colder water also slows the coagulation reactions, so the winter performance is poorer. Operators can restore G by raising the paddle speed, which needs 741 W to reach G = 40 s⁻¹ again, so variable-speed drives are justified.

Answer: 35.4 s⁻¹

Problem 5 [A3-080] Sedimentation basin design by overflow rate

Settled-water clarification for the Town of Elmwood, Ontario, is by two identical rectangular sedimentation basins in parallel following flocculation. The design flow is 21 600 m³/d (250 L/s), divided equally. Design criteria: surface overflow rate 28 m³/m²/d, a length to width ratio of 4:1, a detention time of 3.0 h, and a maximum weir loading of 250 m³/m/d. Particles of concern have a discrete settling velocity of 0.25 mm/s (21.6 m/d). Assume ideal Type I settling, so that a particle with a settling velocity at or above the overflow rate is fully removed, and a slower particle is removed in the proportion v_s divided by the overflow rate. Ignore the sludge zone and inlet and outlet zones when computing the plan area.

  1. (a) Calculate the plan area required for each basin, in m². [4]
  2. (b) Calculate the width of each basin, in m, for the 4:1 length to width ratio. [4]
  3. (c) Calculate the water depth required to give the 3.0 h detention time, in m. [4]
  4. (d) Calculate the minimum total length of effluent weir needed per basin, in m. [3]
  5. (e) Calculate the overflow rate, in m³/m²/d, when one basin is out of service and the full flow goes to the other. [3]
  6. (f) Calculate the percentage of the 0.25 mm/s particles removed with one basin out of service. [2]
(a)

The overflow rate is the flow per unit plan area, v_o = Q/A, so A = Q/v_o. Each basin takes half of the design flow, 21 600 / 2 = 10 800 m³/d. With v_o = 28 m³/m²/d, A = 10 800 / 28 = 385.7 m². The overflow rate is numerically the settling velocity of the slowest particle that is fully captured, which is why it controls clarification performance and not depth. Typical Ontario guidance for alum-coagulated water is 20 to 40 m³/m²/d, so 28 sits in the conservative half of that range. A lower rate gives better removal but a larger basin and higher cost.

Answer: 385.7 m²

(b)

The plan area is the product of width and length, A = W L, and the length is four times the width, L = 4 W. Therefore A = 4 W², and W = √(A/4) = √(385.7/4) = √96.43 = 9.82 m. The length is 4 × 9.82 = 39.3 m. The 4:1 ratio gives a long, narrow basin that favours plug flow and limits short-circuiting, which makes the actual removal closer to the ideal. Wider basins must be designed with baffles or inlet structures that spread the flow evenly across the width. The width would normally be adjusted to suit the sludge collector, for example 10 m for a standard chain-and-flight collector, with the length adjusted to keep the area.

Answer: 9.82 m

(c)

The basin volume equals the flow multiplied by the detention time. For one basin, V = 10 800 m³/d × (3.0 h / 24 h/d) = 1 350 m³. The depth is the volume divided by the plan area: d = 1 350 / 385.7 = 3.50 m. This is within the common range of 3 to 5 m for rectangular basins. Equivalently, depth = overflow rate × detention time = 28 × 0.125 d = 3.50 m, which shows that for a given overflow rate the depth and detention time are linked. A deeper basin would increase the detention time without improving the ideal removal, though it gives a larger buffer for flow surges and sludge storage, at the price of a higher flow-through velocity effect on resuspension.

Answer: 3.50 m

(d)

Weir loading is the flow per unit length of effluent weir, which must not exceed 250 m³/m/d to avoid drawing the flow upward near the outlet and carrying floc over. For a basin flow of 10 800 m³/d, the minimum weir length is L = 10 800 / 250 = 43.2 m. The basin is only 9.82 m wide, so a single weir across the end would be too short; the designer therefore uses launders or troughs extending back along the basin, with a total weir length of at least 43.2 m, for instance four troughs about 11 m long extending into the basin. Weirs on both sides of each trough double the effective length, so shorter troughs are possible.

Answer: 43.2 m

(e)

With one basin out of service, the whole flow of 21 600 m³/d goes to the remaining basin of plan area 385.7 m². The overflow rate becomes v_o = 21 600 / 385.7 = 56.0 m³/m²/d, double the design value of 28. The detention time falls to 1.5 h and the weir loading rises to 21 600 / 43.2 = 500 m³/m/d, twice the criterion. The surface loading therefore exceeds the 40 m³/m²/d upper limit in common guidance, so the treatment may be degraded and the plant would need to cut flow or accept a poorer effluent with more load on the filters. Operators must plan maintenance for periods of low demand, or provide a third basin.

Answer: 56.0 m³/m²/d

(f)

A particle whose settling velocity is below the overflow rate is removed only in proportion to the ratio of its settling velocity to the overflow rate. The particle has v_s = 0.25 mm/s = 0.25 × 10⁻³ × 86 400 = 21.6 m/d. Under normal operation the overflow rate is 28 m³/m²/d, so the fraction removed is 21.6/28 = 77.1 percent, but with one basin out of service the overflow rate is 56.0, and the fraction is 21.6/56.0 = 0.3857, or 38.6 percent. Removal of these fine particles falls by half, showing the large effect that a loss of one basin has on the load on the downstream filters. In practice, flocculated particles are more varied, so the real change would be somewhat different.

Answer: 38.6 percent

A3 Practice Paper 17

Problem 1 [A3-081] Rapid sand filtration rates and backwash

A surface-water treatment plant in southwestern Ontario must produce 18 000 m³/d of filtered water. The designer proposes identical rapid gravity sand filters, each with a plan area of 28 m², and wants the plant to meet its design filtration rate of 7.5 m/h (m³/m²·h) with one filter out of service for backwash. Each filter is washed once every 48 h at an upward wash rate of 0.90 m/min for 8 min, drawn from a clearwell. The sand bed is 0.75 m deep with an unexpanded porosity of 0.42. During backwash the bed fluidizes to an expanded porosity of 0.62. Treat the sand grains as incompressible and the plant as running 24 h/d.

  1. (a) Determine the minimum number of filters needed so that, with one filter out of service, the design filtration rate is not exceeded. [5]
  2. (b) Calculate the filtration rate when one filter is being backwashed and the other filters carry the full flow. [4]
  3. (c) Find the daily volume of backwash water as a percentage of the daily filtered production. [6]
  4. (d) Determine the expanded depth of the sand bed during backwash. [5]
(a)

Production is 18 000 m³/d, so the hourly flow is 18 000/24 = 750 m³/h. At the design rate of 7.5 m/h the total filter area in service must be at least 750/7.5 = 100 m². Each filter is 28 m², so the number of filters in service is 100/28 = 3.57, which rounds up to 4 filters, because a fraction of a filter cannot be built. One additional filter must be available to be out of service for backwash or maintenance, so the plant needs 4 + 1 = 5 filters. The rounding must always go up, since rounding down would push the filtration rate above 7.5 m/h and breach the design criterion. Total installed area is then 5 × 28 = 140 m².

Answer: 5 filters

(b)

With five filters installed and one out of service for backwash, four filters share the whole flow. Rate = Q/A = 750 m³/h ÷ (4 × 28 m²) = 750/112 = 6.70 m/h. This is below the 7.5 m/h limit, confirming the five-filter layout complies, and it shows the plant has some reserve: a second filter could be out of service for maintenance, giving 750/84 = 8.9 m/h, which would exceed the limit. When all five filters are on line the rate drops to 750/140 = 5.36 m/h. The filtration rate during backwash is the governing condition because the remaining filters pick up the load of the one washed, and a rate spike can force turbidity breakthrough.

Answer: 6.70 m/h

(c)

Backwash volume for one wash equals the wash rate times the plan area times the duration: 0.90 m/min × 28 m² × 8 min = 201.6 m³. Each of the five filters is washed once every 48 h, so the plant performs 5 washes per 48 h, which is 2.5 washes per day. Daily backwash water = 2.5 × 201.6 = 504 m³/d. Expressed against production this is 504/18 000 × 100 = 2.8 percent. Typical rapid filter plants waste about 2 to 5 percent of their product to backwash, so the figure is reasonable. The percentage matters because backwash water is not sold and must be recovered, settled or discharged to a sewer or lagoon, and the waste stream capacity must be sized for 201.6 m³ delivered over 8 min.

Answer: 2.8 percent

(d)

The mass of sand per unit plan area is unchanged when the bed expands, so the volume of solids per unit area is constant: L0(1 − ε0) = Le(1 − εe). Here L0 = 0.75 m, ε0 = 0.42 and εe = 0.62. Then Le = 0.75 × (1 − 0.42)/(1 − 0.62) = 0.75 × 0.58/0.38 = 1.145 m. The bed therefore expands by about 53 percent, an increase of 0.39 m. The wash trough lip must sit above this expanded surface, with an extra allowance of at least a few hundred millimetres, or media will be carried into the wash trough and lost. This is why filter box depth is set by the expanded depth rather than the settled bed depth.

Answer: 1.14 m

Problem 2 [A3-082] Disinfection with chlorine: contact time and CT

A small Ontario municipal system treats 1 800 m³/d of groundwater under the direct influence of surface water. Filtration is credited with 2-log removal of viruses, and the regulator requires 4-log virus inactivation overall, so free chlorine must supply the remaining 2 logs. Design assumptions: water temperature 5 °C, pH 7, and a required CT of 4.0 mg·min/L for 2-log virus inactivation under these conditions (use this value). The free chlorine residual leaving the contact tank is 1.2 mg/L and the chlorine demand of the water is 0.8 mg/L. The baffled tank has a baffling factor T10/T of 0.50. The tank must pass the peak-day flow of 3 000 m³/d. Hypochlorite is delivered as a 12 percent available chlorine solution (by mass) with density 1.16 kg/L.

  1. (a) Calculate the required T10, the time by which 10 percent of the water has passed out of the tank, at the stated residual. [4]
  2. (b) Determine the theoretical detention time and the minimum tank volume at peak-day flow. [6]
  3. (c) Compute the chlorine dose and the mass of chlorine fed per day at the average flow of 1 800 m³/d. [4]
  4. (d) Calculate the volume of 12 percent hypochlorite solution required per day at the average flow. [6]
(a)

CT is the product of the disinfectant residual concentration and the contact time, and the contact time for credit is T10, the time by which only 10 percent of the water has left the tank. The required CT is 4.0 mg·min/L and the residual at the outlet is 1.2 mg/L, so T10 = CT/C = 4.0/1.2 = 3.33 min. Using T10 rather than the mean detention time is conservative: it recognizes that short-circuiting lets part of the water pass through faster than the average. The residual used must be the lowest value occurring at the outlet of the tank during the peak flow condition, since a higher residual elsewhere in the process gives no credit for the water that leaves at the weakest concentration.

Answer: 3.33 min

(b)

The baffling factor links T10 to the theoretical detention time T: BF = T10/T. Rearranging gives T = T10/BF = 3.33/0.50 = 6.67 min. The peak flow is 3 000 m³/d = 3 000/1 440 = 2.083 m³/min. The volume equals flow times detention time: V = 2.083 m³/min × 6.67 min = 13.9 m³. A baffling factor of 0.5 is typical of a well-baffled serpentine tank, while an unbaffled tank may be only 0.1. The same performance with poorer baffling would need a much larger volume, for example 5 times the volume at BF = 0.1, which shows why baffles are cheaper than concrete.

Answer: 13.9 m³

(c)

The dose must satisfy the chlorine demand and still leave the residual: dose = demand + residual = 0.8 + 1.2 = 2.0 mg/L. Since 1 mg/L equals 1 g/m³, the daily mass is dose × flow = 2.0 g/m³ × 1 800 m³/d = 3 600 g/d = 3.6 kg/d. This is the mass of available chlorine, not of the hypochlorite solution. The chemical feed system should be designed for the peak flow of 3 000 m³/d as well, where the same dose needs 6.0 kg/d. Demand varies with season and raw water quality, so operators trim the feed from the measured residual rather than relying on a fixed calculated rate.

Answer: 3.6 kg/d

(d)

Each litre of solution has mass 1.16 kg and contains 12 percent available chlorine by mass, so the available chlorine per litre is 0.12 × 1.16 = 0.1392 kg/L. The daily requirement of 3.6 kg of chlorine then needs 3.6/0.1392 = 25.9 L/d of solution. Weekly use is about 181 L (7 × 25.9), so a 1 000 L day tank refilled weekly has ample storage, about 5.5 weeks at the average flow. Note that hypochlorite loses strength during storage and with heat and light, so the delivered strength should be tested. Pump capacity must be checked against the peak-flow requirement of 6.0 kg/d, or 43 L/d, with room to turn down.

Answer: 25.9 L/d

Problem 3 [A3-083] Wastewater flow estimation and sewer design flow

A new residential and commercial development in a southern Ontario town is to be served by a gravity sanitary trunk sewer. The tributary area is 62 ha with a design population of 4 800 persons. Use an average dry-weather domestic flow of 300 L/cap·d. The domestic peaking factor follows the Harmon equation M = 1 + 14/(4 + √P), where P is the population in thousands. A commercial strip of 3.5 ha contributes 28 m³/ha·d on average with a commercial peaking factor of 2.0. Infiltration and inflow is allowed at 0.28 L/s per hectare of tributary area, added without any peaking factor. The design flow is the sum of peak domestic flow, peak commercial flow and infiltration and inflow.

  1. (a) Calculate the average daily domestic flow in L/s. [3]
  2. (b) Determine the Harmon peaking factor and the peak domestic flow. [5]
  3. (c) Calculate the total design flow, including the commercial peak flow and infiltration and inflow. [6]
  4. (d) Express the infiltration and inflow allowance as a percentage of the total design flow and state what this suggests about the design. [6]
(a)

Average domestic flow is population times per-capita rate: 4 800 persons × 300 L/cap·d = 1 440 000 L/d. Dividing by the 86 400 seconds in a day gives 1 440 000/86 400 = 16.67 L/s. This is the flow in dry weather averaged over 24 h and is not the flow used to size the pipe, because domestic flow follows a daily pattern that peaks in the morning and early evening when many people use water at once. The per-capita figure of 300 L/cap·d is the sewage generated, which is lower than the water supplied since lawn watering and other outdoor use does not enter the sanitary sewer. The average is needed as the base value for applying the peaking factor in the next step.

Answer: 16.7 L/s

(b)

The population in thousands is P = 4.8, so √P = 2.191. The Harmon peaking factor is M = 1 + 14/(4 + 2.191) = 1 + 14/6.191 = 1 + 2.261 = 3.26. The peak domestic flow is the average multiplied by this factor: 16.67 L/s × 3.261 = 54.4 L/s. The Harmon equation gives a factor of 3.8 at P = 1 (one thousand people) and falls toward 1 for very large populations (1.39 at one million people) because individual flow variations average out as more connections feed the sewer. At this size, 4 800 people, the factor 3.26 is in the typical range of 2 to 4 used for trunk sewers.

Answer: 54.4 L/s

(c)

Commercial average flow is 3.5 ha × 28 m³/ha·d = 98 m³/d, and 98 m³/d × 1000 L/m³ ÷ 86 400 s = 1.134 L/s. With the commercial peaking factor of 2.0 the peak commercial flow is 2.27 L/s. Infiltration and inflow is 62 ha × 0.28 L/s·ha = 17.36 L/s over the whole tributary area. The total design flow adds the three parts: 54.36 + 2.27 + 17.36 = 74.0 L/s. The commercial contribution is small, only about 3 percent of the total, so the commercial peaking assumption has little influence. The pipe is sized for this total, with the capacity of the full pipe usually required to equal or exceed the design flow at the minimum permitted velocity of 0.6 m/s.

Answer: 74.0 L/s

(d)

The infiltration and inflow share is 17.36 ÷ 73.98 × 100 = 23.5 percent of the design flow. Nearly one quarter of the trunk sewer capacity is therefore reserved for clear water that enters through defective joints, manholes, and illegal roof or foundation drain connections rather than for sewage. This is a large share for a new development, so it shows that the design depends strongly on construction quality: tighter joints and testing of pipes could reduce the allowance, and the pipe diameter and slope could drop one size. It also shows the sensitivity of the pipe sizing to one allowance, a point a design report should state when an existing town with old clay sewers would instead be expected to take far higher inflows during spring melt and heavy rain.

Answer: 23.5 percent

Problem 4 [A3-084] Sanitary sewer hydraulics: Manning, velocity and partial flow

A 300 mm diameter concrete sanitary sewer (Manning n = 0.013) is laid at a constant grade of 0.45 percent between two manholes in an older neighbourhood of Hamilton. Peak wet-weather flow arriving at the upstream manhole has been measured at 38 L/s. For a partly full circular pipe, let θ be the central angle of the wetted segment in radians. Then flow area A = (D²/8)(θ − sin θ), hydraulic radius R = (D/4)(1 − sin θ/θ), and the depth ratio is d/D = (1 − cos(θ/2))/2. Use Manning's equation V = (1/n)R2/3S1/2. The specific weight of water is 9 810 N/m³ and the sewer standard calls for a minimum velocity of 0.6 m/s at peak flow.

  1. (a) Calculate the full-pipe capacity in L/s and the full-pipe velocity. [5]
  2. (b) Find the central angle θ that makes the pipe carry 38 L/s, solving Manning's equation for the partial section. [5]
  3. (c) Determine the depth ratio d/D and the velocity in the sewer at 38 L/s, and state whether the 0.6 m/s minimum is met. [5]
  4. (d) Calculate the average boundary shear stress at the design flow and comment on whether it is enough to move sewer solids. [5]
(a)

For a full circular pipe the area is A = πD²/4 = π × 0.3²/4 = 0.07069 m² and the hydraulic radius is R = D/4 = 0.075 m. Manning gives the velocity V = (1/0.013) × 0.0752/3 × 0.00451/2. The term 0.0752/3 = 0.1778 and √0.0045 = 0.06708, so V = 76.92 × 0.1778 × 0.06708 = 0.918 m/s. Capacity Q = VA = 0.918 × 0.07069 = 0.0649 m³/s = 64.9 L/s. The pipe therefore carries the 38 L/s peak at about 59 percent of its full capacity. The full-pipe velocity of 0.92 m/s exceeds the 0.6 m/s minimum, though the actual velocity at partial flow still needs checking.

Answer: 64.9 L/s

(b)

The partial flow is Q = (1/n) A R2/3 S1/2 with A and R functions of θ. The ratio Q/Q_full is 38/64.9 = 0.586, and the partial-flow equation has no direct inverse, so θ is found by trial. At θ = π (half full) A = 0.03534 m², R = 0.075 m and Q = 32.4 L/s, which is too small. Trying θ = 3.34 rad: A = (0.09/8)(3.34 − sin 3.34) = 0.01125 × (3.34 + 0.1976) = 0.03980 m², R = 0.075 × (1 + 0.1976/3.34) = 0.07944 m, giving Q = 76.92 × 0.0398 × 0.1847 × 0.06708 = 0.0379 m³/s, close to 38 L/s. Refining gives θ = 3.342 rad, which is slightly more than half full.

Answer: 3.34 rad

(c)

Using θ = 3.342 rad, the depth ratio is d/D = (1 − cos(1.671))/2 = (1 + 0.1000)/2 = 0.55, so the depth is 0.55 × 300 = 165 mm. The wetted area is A = 0.0398 m². Velocity follows from continuity: V = Q/A = 0.038/0.0398 = 0.954 m/s. This agrees with Manning's equation applied directly at the partial section, 76.92 × 0.07942/3 × 0.06708 = 0.954 m/s. The velocity is greater than 0.6 m/s, so the minimum is met at peak flow. At lower flows the velocity will fall, so self-cleansing should be checked at the typical dry-weather flow too, not only at the peak.

Answer: 0.954 m/s

(d)

The average boundary shear stress for uniform flow is τ = γRS, where R is the hydraulic radius of the actual flowing section. At θ = 3.342 rad, R = 0.075 × (1 − sin 3.342/3.342) = 0.075 × (1 + 0.1991/3.342) = 0.07947 m. Then τ = 9 810 × 0.07947 × 0.0045 = 3.51 Pa. Many design standards want a shear stress of at least 1 to 2 Pa at some stage of the daily flow cycle to move grit and organic solids, and 3.5 Pa at peak flow is comfortably above that. The value is a design check on the slope rather than the diameter, because shear depends on R and S together, and flatter pipes at low flow would need to be checked as well.

Answer: 3.51 Pa

Problem 5 [A3-085] Storm sewer design with the Rational method and IDF curves

A mixed-use catchment in Mississauga drains to a single storm sewer inlet manhole. The 12.4 ha catchment has three land uses: 6.5 ha of low-density residential lots with runoff coefficient C = 0.40, 3.2 ha of townhouses with C = 0.75, and 2.7 ha of paved retail parking with C = 0.90. Overland inlet time is 12 min, and the runoff then travels 420 m in the gutter and storm sewer at an average velocity of 1.8 m/s to the design point. The design rainfall intensity (5-year return period) is i = 1 060/(t + 7.8)0.80, with i in mm/h and t in minutes. Use the Rational method Q = CiA/360 with Q in m³/s, A in ha. The proposed pipe is concrete with n = 0.013 laid at 0.60 percent and flowing just full.

  1. (a) Calculate the area-weighted runoff coefficient. [3]
  2. (b) Determine the time of concentration at the design point. [4]
  3. (c) Calculate the design rainfall intensity. [3]
  4. (d) Calculate the peak design flow at the design point. [5]
  5. (e) Determine the smallest circular pipe diameter that carries the design flow when flowing just full. [5]
(a)

The composite coefficient weights each land use by its area: C = ΣCᵢAᵢ / ΣAᵢ. The products are 6.5 × 0.40 = 2.60, 3.2 × 0.75 = 2.40 and 2.7 × 0.90 = 2.43, summing to 7.43 ha-units over the total area of 6.5 + 3.2 + 2.7 = 12.4 ha. So C = 7.43/12.4 = 0.599, about 0.60. The retail parking is only 22 percent of the area but supplies 33 percent of the weighted product because it is almost impervious, which is why site planners limit paved coverage. The composite C is valid only if the three areas drain to the design point at similar times, and a design for much larger distinct areas would be checked at the shorter time of concentration for the paved part alone.

Answer: 0.599

(b)

The time of concentration is the longest travel time from the farthest point to the design point, equal to the inlet time plus the pipe or channel travel time. The conveyance time is length divided by velocity: 420 m ÷ 1.8 m/s = 233.3 s = 3.89 min. Adding the 12 min inlet time gives tc = 12 + 3.89 = 15.89 min, about 15.9 min. This duration is used as the rainfall duration because the peak runoff at the design point occurs when the whole catchment contributes. A shorter rain would leave the farthest area still contributing nothing, and a longer rain has lower intensity, so tc maximizes the product of intensity and contributing area.

Answer: 15.9 min

(c)

Substituting the time of concentration into the IDF equation: i = 1 060/(15.89 + 7.8)0.80 = 1 060/(23.69)0.80. The logarithm of 23.69 is 3.165, and multiplied by 0.80 gives 2.532, whose exponential is 12.58. So i = 1 060/12.58 = 84.3 mm/h. This is for a 5-year event; for a 100-year event the same duration would give considerably higher intensity, and major system flow paths must be checked for those. The IDF constants here are given for the exercise and are not taken from any named station, so the same procedure should be used with the local municipality's current IDF parameters when designing for real.

Answer: 84.3 mm/h

(d)

The Rational method gives the peak flow as Q = CiA/360 where the factor 360 converts mm/h and hectares to m³/s. Q = 0.599 × 84.27 × 12.4 / 360 = 625.9/360 = 1.739 m³/s. This is the flow at the end of the time of concentration under the assumptions of uniform rainfall, constant C, and no storage. The method is generally used only for small catchments up to about 80 ha, and our 12.4 ha is well within that. Larger catchments need hydrograph methods that account for routing and storage. The 1.74 m³/s must now be carried by the sewer without surcharge to satisfy the usual minor-system design criterion.

Answer: 1.74 m³/s

(e)

For a full circular pipe Manning's equation is Q = (1/n)(πD²/4)(D/4)2/3S1/2, which rearranges to D8/3 = 45/3 Q n/(π S1/2). With Q = 1.739 m³/s, n = 0.013 and S = 0.006: S1/2 = 0.07746. Then D8/3 = 10.079 × 1.739 × 0.013/(π × 0.07746) = 0.2279/0.2433 = 0.9366. So D = 0.93663/8 = 0.976 m. Pipes come in standard sizes, so the designer would choose the next standard diameter above 976 mm, which is 1 050 mm, and check that the velocity of the full pipe stays within about 0.8 to 6 m/s limits.

Answer: 0.976 m

A3 Practice Paper 18

Problem 1 [A3-086] Culvert hydraulics: inlet and outlet control

A 1.20 m diameter circular concrete culvert, 28 m long, carries a farm creek under a county road in eastern Ontario. The culvert invert slopes at 0.40 percent. The entrance is a square-edge headwall with entrance loss coefficient Ke = 0.5; Manning n = 0.013. For inlet control, treat the inlet as a submerged orifice: Q = Cd A √(2g(HW − D/2)) with Cd = 0.62, where HW is the headwater depth above the inlet invert. For outlet control, HW = H + h₀ − S₀L, where H = (1 + Ke + 2gn²L/R4/3) V²/2g with full flow velocity V, h₀ = the larger of the tailwater depth and (dc + D)/2. The tailwater is 0.90 m above the outlet invert and the critical depth in the barrel is dc = 1.05 m at 3.8 m³/s and dc = 1.11 m at 4.5 m³/s. The road crest is 3.00 m above the inlet invert. Use g = 9.81 m/s².

  1. (a) Calculate the headwater depth for inlet control at the design flow of 3.8 m³/s. [5]
  2. (b) Calculate the headwater depth for outlet control at 3.8 m³/s. [6]
  3. (c) State which control governs at 3.8 m³/s and the resulting freeboard below the road crest. [3]
  4. (d) Calculate the controlling headwater if the flow rises to 4.5 m³/s in a larger storm and judge whether the road is safe. [6]
(a)

The culvert area is A = πD²/4 = π × 1.2²/4 = 1.131 m². Rearranging the orifice equation, the effective head is h = (Q/(Cd A))²/(2g). Q/(Cd A) = 3.8/(0.62 × 1.131) = 5.419 m/s. Then h = 5.419²/(2 × 9.81) = 29.37/19.62 = 1.497 m. The headwater above the invert is HW = h + D/2 = 1.497 + 0.60 = 2.097 m. HW/D = 1.75, which is above the usual threshold of about 1.2 to 1.5 for a submerged inlet, so the orifice equation is appropriate. The result is the headwater needed to force 3.8 m³/s through the inlet opening if the inlet were the controlling section.

Answer: 2.10 m

(b)

Full-flow velocity is V = Q/A = 3.8/1.131 = 3.360 m/s, so V²/2g = 0.5755 m. The hydraulic radius for a full pipe is R = D/4 = 0.30 m, and R4/3 = 0.2008. The friction term is 2gn²L/R4/3 = 19.62 × 0.000169 × 28/0.2008 = 0.462. The total loss coefficient is 1 + 0.5 + 0.462 = 1.962, so H = 1.962 × 0.5755 = 1.129 m. The downstream level h₀ is the larger of tailwater 0.90 m and (1.05 + 1.20)/2 = 1.125 m, so h₀ = 1.125 m. The fall of the invert is S₀L = 0.004 × 28 = 0.112 m. HW = 1.129 + 1.125 − 0.112 = 2.142 m.

Answer: 2.14 m

(c)

The control that governs is the one giving the larger headwater, because the water must rise to at least that level for the culvert to pass the flow. Inlet control gives 2.097 m and outlet control gives 2.142 m, so outlet control governs, though only by about 45 mm, which means the culvert is near the transition between the two conditions. The freeboard is the road crest elevation minus the controlling headwater: 3.00 − 2.142 = 0.858 m. This is a comfortable margin at the design flow, and many agencies require a minimum of 0.3 m or more of freeboard under the design flood to protect the road base from saturation and overtopping.

Answer: outlet control governs; freeboard 0.86 m

(d)

At 4.5 m³/s, inlet control gives Q/(Cd A) = 4.5/(0.62 × 1.131) = 6.417 m/s, so h = 6.417²/19.62 = 2.099 m and HW = 2.099 + 0.60 = 2.699 m. For outlet control V = 4.5/1.131 = 3.979 m/s and V²/2g = 0.807 m, so H = 1.962 × 0.807 = 1.584 m and HW = 1.584 + 1.155 − 0.112 = 2.627 m, using h₀ = (1.11 + 1.20)/2 = 1.155 m. Inlet control now governs at 2.70 m, so the controlling condition has switched from outlet to inlet, a rise of 0.56 m for an 18 percent rise in flow, since inlet headwater varies with Q². The freeboard falls to 3.00 − 2.70 = 0.30 m. The road is still not overtopped, but with only 0.30 m of margin a further increase, or debris blocking the inlet, would put it at risk.

Answer: 2.70 m

Problem 2 [A3-087] Stormwater detention pond sizing

A 8.5 ha warehouse site in Brampton is being developed from farmland. The municipality requires post-development 10-year peak flow to be limited to the pre-development 10-year peak. Pre-development runoff coefficient is C = 0.25 with a time of concentration of 30 min. Post-development C = 0.70 with a time of concentration of 12 min. The 10-year IDF relation is i = 1 200/(t + 8)0.82, with i in mm/h and t in minutes. Use Q = CiA/360 (m³/s, ha). Size the pond with the modified rational method: for each storm duration t, storage = (Q_post(t) − Q_allow) × 60t, where Q_post(t) uses the post-development C and the intensity for duration t. Test whole-minute durations from 12 to 120 min. The outlet is a single circular orifice with Cd = 0.62 under an effective maximum head of 1.9 m.

  1. (a) Calculate the allowable pre-development peak outflow. [4]
  2. (b) Determine the uncontrolled post-development peak flow at its time of concentration. [3]
  3. (c) Find the required storage volume by testing durations from 12 to 120 min and identify the critical duration. [8]
  4. (d) Determine the orifice diameter that discharges the allowable flow at the maximum head. [5]
(a)

The allowable release equals the pre-development peak at its own time of concentration of 30 min. The intensity is i = 1 200/(30 + 8)0.82 = 1 200/380.82. The logarithm of 38 is 3.638; multiplied by 0.82 this gives 2.983, so 380.82 = 19.75 and i = 60.8 mm/h. Then Q_allow = 0.25 × 60.78 × 8.5/360 = 129.2/360 = 0.359 m³/s. This is the maximum flow the pond outlet may discharge. Development increases both C and, because the paved site drains faster, the peak flow, and the pond must hold back the difference so the creek downstream sees no greater peak than the farmland did.

Answer: 0.359 m³/s

(b)

At the post-development time of concentration of 12 min, i = 1 200/(12 + 8)0.82 = 1 200/200.82. The logarithm of 20 is 2.996, multiplied by 0.82 gives 2.457, so 200.82 = 11.67 and i = 102.8 mm/h. Q_post = 0.70 × 102.8 × 8.5/360 = 611.6/360 = 1.70 m³/s. The uncontrolled post-development peak is therefore 1.70 m³/s, almost five times the allowable 0.359 m³/s. This shows the scale of the control required: the pond outlet must restrict the outflow to about one fifth of the peak inflow, which demands substantial storage in the pond above the outlet.

Answer: 1.70 m³/s

(c)

For each duration the storage is S(t) = (0.70 × i(t) × 8.5/360 − 0.3588) × 60 t. The results show a peak in the middle of the range: at 12 min S = 966 m³, at 20 min 1 118 m³, at 30 min 1 162 m³, at 40 min 1 130 m³, at 60 min 953 m³ and at 90 min 557 m³. The storage rises while intensity stays high and then falls as the intensity decreases faster than the duration increases. Testing every whole minute, the maximum is S = 1 162 m³ at t = 30 min, so the critical duration is 30 min and the pond needs about 1 160 m³ of live storage. A design would add freeboard and sediment volume to this.

Answer: 1 162 m³

(d)

The orifice equation is Q = Cd A √(2gh). Solving for area: A = Q_allow/(Cd √(2gh)). With h = 1.9 m, √(2 × 9.81 × 1.9) = √37.28 = 6.106 m/s. Then A = 0.3588/(0.62 × 6.106) = 0.3588/3.786 = 0.09478 m². The diameter is D = √(4A/π) = √(0.1207) = 0.347 m, about 350 mm. In practice the outlet head varies as the pond fills and drains, and a single fixed orifice discharges less than 0.359 m³/s at lower heads, so a design usually checks that the discharge does not exceed the target at the top water level while sizing storage with an average release, which is conservative.

Answer: 0.347 m

Problem 3 [A3-088] Activated sludge design: SRT, F/M ratio and oxygen demand

A conventional activated sludge plant for an Ontario town of 60 000 receives 15 000 m³/d of settled wastewater with BOD₅ of 150 mg/L after primary treatment. The design effluent soluble BOD₅ is 10 mg/L. Assume a complete-mix reactor with no recycle of solids in the influent, a design solids retention time (SRT) of 8 d, mixed liquor suspended solids X = 3 200 mg/L, yield Y = 0.60 g VSS/g BOD removed, decay coefficient kd = 0.06 d⁻¹, and a return sludge concentration of 8 000 mg/L. Treat MLSS as equal to MLVSS. Use BOD₅ = 0.68 × ultimate BOD. Sludge is wasted from the return sludge line, so the waste flow is obtained from the SRT.

  1. (a) Calculate the required aeration tank volume. [5]
  2. (b) Determine the food-to-microorganism ratio (F/M) based on influent BOD. [3]
  3. (c) Calculate the mass of sludge solids produced per day. [4]
  4. (d) Calculate the waste sludge flow rate from the reactor. [3]
  5. (e) Calculate the daily oxygen requirement. [5]
(a)

For a complete-mix reactor the volume follows from V = θc Q Y (S₀ − S)/(X(1 + kd θc)). The BOD removed is 150 − 10 = 140 mg/L = 140 g/m³. The numerator is 8 d × 15 000 m³/d × 0.60 × 140 g/m³ = 10 080 000 g. The denominator is 3 200 g/m³ × (1 + 0.06 × 8) = 3 200 × 1.48 = 4 736 g/m³. So V = 10 080 000/4 736 = 2 128 m³. This volume carries enough biomass at 3 200 mg/L to remove 140 g/m³ of BOD from the flow while holding the solids for 8 d. A plant with higher MLSS would need a smaller tank but would load the secondary clarifiers harder.

Answer: 2 128 m³

(b)

The F/M ratio is the daily BOD mass applied per unit mass of microorganisms in the reactor: F/M = Q S₀/(V X). The BOD load is 15 000 m³/d × 150 g/m³ = 2 250 000 g/d. The biomass is 2 128.4 m³ × 3 200 g/m³ = 6 810 880 g. So F/M = 2 250 000/6 810 880 = 0.330 d⁻¹. Conventional activated sludge usually operates at 0.2 to 0.4 d⁻¹, so the design lies in the normal range. A much higher F/M would give sludge that settles poorly and a worse effluent, while a very low value, below 0.1, would indicate extended aeration with little excess sludge but high energy use.

Answer: 0.33 per day

(c)

The net observed solids production is Px = Y Q (S₀ − S)/(1 + kd θc). The numerator is 0.60 × 15 000 × 140 = 1 260 000 g/d. Dividing by (1 + 0.06 × 8) = 1.48 gives Px = 851 351 g/d = 851 kg/d of volatile solids. This is the quantity that has to be wasted to maintain the SRT of 8 d: if less were removed, the SRT would increase and the MLSS would climb until the clarifiers fail. It is lower than the gross growth Y × 140 × 15 000 = 1 260 kg/d because endogenous decay destroys about 32 percent of the cells made, and that decay also consumes oxygen.

Answer: 851 kg/d

(d)

When sludge is wasted from the return line, the SRT is the solids mass in the reactor divided by the solids mass wasted per day, ignoring solids in the effluent: θc = V X/(Qw Xr). Solving gives Qw = V X/(θc Xr) = 2 128.4 m³ × 3 200 g/m³ ÷ (8 d × 8 000 g/m³) = 6 810 880/64 000 = 106.4 m³/d. As a check, wasting at 106.4 m³/d with 8 000 g/m³ removes 851 kg of solids per day, which matches the sludge production from part c. Wasting from the return line is attractive because the stream is two and a half times as thick as the mixed liquor (8 000 versus 3 200 mg/L), so the waste flow is much smaller, which cuts the load on the thickening process that follows.

Answer: 106 m³/d

(e)

The oxygen needed equals the ultimate BOD oxidised minus the oxygen equivalent of the cells wasted: O₂ = Q(S₀ − S)/f − 1.42 Px, with f = 0.68. The first term is 15 000 × 140/0.68 = 3 088 235 g/d = 3 088 kg/d. The second is 1.42 × 851.4 = 1 209 kg/d, since each gram of cells carries 1.42 g of oxygen demand and leaves the system as sludge rather than being burned. So O₂ = 3 088 − 1 209 = 1 879 kg/d, or about 78 kg/h. The blowers must deliver this plus allowances for nitrification and peak loads, and diffused aeration transfers only a fraction of the oxygen supplied, so the real air supply is several times this figure.

Answer: 1 879 kg/d

Problem 4 [A3-089] Primary clarifiers, BOD loading and lagoon or trickling filter sizing

A lakeshore community in Ontario is planning a new secondary treatment train for an average flow of 8 000 m³/d. The raw wastewater has BOD₅ of 240 mg/L and suspended solids of 260 mg/L. A single circular primary clarifier is to be designed at a surface overflow rate of 40 m³/m²·d at average flow. It removes 30 percent of the BOD₅ and 60 percent of the suspended solids. Primary sludge is withdrawn at 5 percent solids with a density of 1 030 kg/m³. The settled effluent then goes to a trickling filter with plastic packing, designed at a volumetric organic loading of 0.40 kg BOD₅/m³·d of media, with a media depth of 6.0 m.

  1. (a) Determine the diameter of the primary clarifier. [4]
  2. (b) Calculate the weir loading on the effluent weir if it runs round the full circumference of the clarifier. [4]
  3. (c) Calculate the volume of primary sludge produced per day. [4]
  4. (d) Calculate the required volume of trickling filter media. [4]
  5. (e) Determine the diameter of a circular trickling filter tower with a 6.0 m deep bed. [4]
(a)

The surface overflow rate is flow divided by surface area, so the area is A = Q/SOR = 8 000 m³/d ÷ 40 m³/m²·d = 200 m². For a circular tank A = πD²/4, so D = √(4A/π) = √(800/π) = √254.6 = 15.96 m. The designer would round to 16 m, which gives an overflow rate of 8 000/201.1 = 39.8 m³/m²·d. An overflow rate of 30 to 50 m³/m²·d at average flow is typical for primary settling. The rate must also be checked at peak flow, where a rate of about 100 m³/m²·d is usual, so sizing only at average flow would risk solids carry-over in storm conditions.

Answer: 15.96 m

(b)

The weir loading is flow per unit length of weir. A peripheral weir has length equal to the circumference, L = πD = π × 15.96 = 50.13 m. The loading is 8 000 m³/d ÷ 50.13 m = 159.6 m³/m·d. Primary clarifiers are usually designed for weir loading below about 250 m³/m·d at average flow, so the design is satisfactory with margin, even though the peak flow will raise it. An excessive weir loading draws water upward near the weir, resuspends settled floc and lowers solids removal. If the loading were too high, the designer would add an inboard launder to double the weir length without enlarging the tank.

Answer: 159.6 m³/m·d

(c)

Solids removed are 60 percent of 260 mg/L, which is 156 mg/L = 156 g/m³. The daily mass is 156 g/m³ × 8 000 m³/d = 1 248 000 g/d = 1 248 kg/d of dry solids. The sludge contains 5 percent solids by mass, so each cubic metre of sludge holds 0.05 × 1 030 = 51.5 kg of dry solids. The volume is 1 248/51.5 = 24.2 m³/d. This is only 0.3 percent of the liquid flow, but it needs pumping, thickening and digestion, and primary sludge has an offensive odour and must not sit in the hopper longer than a few hours or it will go septic and rise.

Answer: 24.2 m³/d

(d)

The BOD leaving the primary clarifier is 70 percent of the raw value, so the settled BOD₅ is 240 × 0.70 = 168 mg/L. The load applied to the filter is 168 g/m³ × 8 000 m³/d = 1 344 000 g/d = 1 344 kg/d. The volumetric organic loading is 0.40 kg/m³·d, so the media volume is 1 344/0.40 = 3 360 m³. This assumes that the loading rate is based on BOD that reaches the filter, which excludes any recirculation. A lower loading, such as 0.2, would give a higher removal efficiency but a media volume twice as large, so the choice of loading is mainly one of capital cost against required effluent quality.

Answer: 3 360 m³

(e)

The plan area is media volume divided by depth: A = 3 360/6.0 = 560 m². For a circular bed D = √(4A/π) = √(2 240/π) = √713.0 = 26.7 m. In practice a plant this size is usually divided into two filters of 18.9 m diameter each, so one can be taken out of service for maintenance, each having half the area of 280 m². The hydraulic loading should also be checked: 8 000 m³/d over 560 m² is 14.3 m³/m²·d, or 0.6 m/h, which with recirculation can be raised to keep the plastic media wetted. A tower of this plan size is also a significant source of odour that may need covering.

Answer: 26.7 m

Problem 5 [A3-090] Buried pipe loads, bedding and deflection

A 400 mm outside diameter PVC sanitary force main is to be installed in a trench under a county road in Simcoe County, with 2.4 m of granular cover above the pipe crown. The backfill unit weight is 19 kN/m³. A single 90 kN wheel load acts at the surface over a tire patch of 0.50 m by 0.25 m, spreading through the cover at 2 to 1 (vertical to horizontal, giving a loaded area of (0.50 + H) by (0.25 + H) at the pipe crown depth H), with an impact factor of 1.15. The pipe wall is 11.4 mm thick with modulus E = 3 000 MPa. Use mean radius r = 0.20 m, deflection lag factor Dl = 1.5, bedding constant K = 0.10, and the Spangler equation Δx = Dl K W r³/(EI + 0.061 E′ r³), where W is the total vertical load per metre of pipe, I = t³/12 per metre of length, and E′ is the soil modulus. Use W = (dead plus live pressure) × outside diameter.

  1. (a) Calculate the dead load pressure at the pipe crown from the soil prism. [3]
  2. (b) Calculate the live load pressure at the pipe crown from the wheel, including the impact factor. [4]
  3. (c) Calculate the predicted horizontal deflection of the pipe using the Spangler equation with E′ = 7 000 kPa. [6]
  4. (d) Express the deflection as a percentage of the outside diameter and state whether it meets a 5 percent limit. [3]
  5. (e) Recalculate the percentage deflection if the bedding is poor, with E′ = 2 000 kPa, and comment on the result. [4]
(a)

The prism load is the weight of the soil column directly above the crown, expressed as a pressure: p = γH = 19 kN/m³ × 2.4 m = 45.6 kPa. This ignores arching, the transfer of load to the trench walls by friction, and so it is conservative for a narrow trench, which is the safe assumption for a flexible pipe in a design check. For a rigid pipe in a narrow trench the Marston trench load would be lower than the prism load, but for a flexible pipe in a wide trench or an embankment the prism load is close to what the pipe actually receives, so the prism is adopted as the design dead load here.

Answer: 45.6 kPa

(b)

With the load spreading at 2 to 1 the loaded area at depth H = 2.4 m is (0.50 + 2.4) × (0.25 + 2.4) = 2.90 × 2.65 = 7.685 m². The pressure from the 90 kN wheel is 90/7.685 = 11.71 kPa. Multiplying by the impact factor of 1.15 gives 13.47 kPa. Live load decays rapidly with depth because the area grows with the square of the depth, so at 2.4 m the live load is just 30 percent of the dead load. At shallow cover of 0.6 m the same wheel would give a pressure of 90/(1.1 × 0.85) × 1.15 = 111 kPa, which is why minimum cover for traffic is specified.

Answer: 13.5 kPa

(c)

Total vertical pressure is 45.6 + 13.47 = 59.07 kPa, and the load per metre of pipe is W = 59.07 × 0.40 m = 23.63 kN/m. The wall stiffness EI per metre of length is E t³/12 = 3 000 000 kPa × (0.0114)³/12 = 3 000 000 × 1.4815 × 10-6/12 = 0.370 kN·m. The soil term is 0.061 E′ r³ = 0.061 × 7 000 × 0.008 = 3.416. The denominator is 0.370 + 3.416 = 3.786. The numerator is 1.5 × 0.10 × 23.63 × 0.008 = 0.02835. So Δx = 0.02835/3.786 = 0.007488 m = 7.49 mm. The soil stiffness contributes about 90 percent of the resistance, which shows that a flexible pipe depends mostly on the bedding, not on its own wall.

Answer: 7.49 mm

(d)

The relative deflection is Δx/D = 7.488/400 × 100 = 1.87 percent of the outside diameter. A common design limit for the initial installed deflection of PVC sewer pipe is about 5 percent, with long-term limits of 7.5 percent often applied to account for creep and later movement, so 1.87 percent is well within the limit, using only 37 percent of the allowable. The pipe also needs checks that are not part of this calculation: buckling under external pressure and groundwater, wall crushing, and strain at the long-term deflection. This calculation only checks ring deflection under soil and traffic load.

Answer: 1.87 percent

(e)

With E′ = 2 000 kPa the soil term becomes 0.061 × 2 000 × 0.008 = 0.976, and the denominator is 0.370 + 0.976 = 1.346. The numerator is unchanged at 0.02835, so Δx = 0.02835/1.346 = 0.02106 m = 21.1 mm, which is 21.06/400 × 100 = 5.26 percent of the diameter. This exceeds the 5 percent limit, even though the loads are identical, and the deflection is nearly three times that for good bedding. The result shows how strongly performance depends on compaction of the haunching and side fill. Poor bedding cannot be fixed by a thicker wall alone, so the designer should specify well-graded granular bedding compacted to a stated density up to the springline.

Answer: 5.26 percent

A3 Practice Paper 19

Problem 1 [A3-091] Water loss, leakage and rehabilitation of mains and sewers

The Town of Elmvale has isolated a district metered area (DMA) of 1,240 service connections served by 18.6 km of cast iron and ductile iron main. At 03:00, when the area is quietest, the district meter reads 14.8 L/s. A night-time survey attributes 0.90 L/s to a food-processing plant that runs a night shift, and assigns 1.5 L per connection per hour to the remaining customers as legitimate night use. The hour-day factor for this DMA is 21.5 h/day, and the average night pressure is 62 m. Leakage varies with pressure as (P2/P1)N1 with N1 = 1.15. Private service pipes average 12 m per connection. The Town costs avoided production at $0.62 per m³. The unavoidable annual real losses are UARL = (18 Lm + 0.8 Nc + 25 Lp) × P litres per day, with Lm in km of main, Nc connections, Lp km of private pipe and P in m.

  1. (a) Find the night-time leakage flow in the DMA. [3]
  2. (b) Convert it to daily leakage in m³/day using the hour-day factor. [3]
  3. (c) A pressure-reducing valve will lower the average night pressure to 45 m. Find the annual saving in m³ and state its dollar value to the nearest dollar. [5]
  4. (d) Find the Infrastructure Leakage Index (current leakage divided by UARL). [5]
  5. (e) The PRV installation costs $85,000. Find the simple payback period and comment on what the ILI says about further rehabilitation. [4]
(a)

Night inflow is the sum of legitimate night use and leakage, so leakage is the remainder. Domestic night use is 1,240 connections × 1.5 L/h = 1,860 L/h, which is 1,860 / 3,600 = 0.517 L/s. Adding the food plant at 0.90 L/s, legitimate night use is 1.417 L/s. Leakage = 14.8 − 1.417 = 13.383 L/s. At night most customers are asleep and pressures are at their highest, so this minimum night flow is the standard basis for estimating real losses. The result assumes the 1.5 L/connection/h allowance is right for this area, and that figure is the weakest assumption, because a small error in it moves the leakage estimate noticeably.

Answer: 13.38 L/s

(b)

Leakage is driven by pressure, and pressure is highest at night, so the night rate overstates the daily average. The hour-day factor corrects for this: it is the number of hours at night-flow rate that give the same volume as the real 24-hour leakage.
