Convert first: 13.383 L/s × 3,600 s/h = 48,180 L/h = 48.18 m³/h. Multiplying by the factor, 48.18 × 21.5 h/day = 1,035.9 m³/day. This is about 1.04 ML/day, or 835 L per connection per day, which is high for a distribution system and signals a serious leakage problem worth chasing.

Answer: 1,036 m³/day

(c)

Apply the pressure-leakage relation with N1 = 1.15. The pressure ratio is 45/62 = 0.7258, and 0.72581.15 = 0.6917. New leakage = 1,035.9 × 0.6917 = 716.6 m³/day. The reduction is 1,035.9 − 716.6 = 319.3 m³/day. Over a year this is 319.3 × 365 = 116,550 m³. At $0.62 per m³ the avoided production cost is 116,550 × 0.62 = $72,261 per year. The exponent N1 above 1 is typical of old, mixed-material systems where leak openings grow with pressure, so PRVs are especially effective here. A value near 0.5 would apply to rigid metal pipe with fixed fissures and would give a much smaller saving.

Answer: $72,261/yr

(d)

First compute the unavoidable losses. Private pipe length Lp = 1,240 × 12 m = 14,880 m = 14.88 km. Then UARL = (18 × 18.6 + 0.8 × 1,240 + 25 × 14.88) × 62 = (334.8 + 992 + 372) × 62 = 1,698.8 × 62 = 105,326 L/day. Current real losses are 1,035.9 m³/day = 1,035,870 L/day. The ILI is the ratio of current to unavoidable losses: 1,035,870 / 105,326 = 9.83. An ILI near 1 means the system is leaking about as little as technically possible; 9.8 means almost ten times that, so there is a large recoverable volume.

Answer: ILI = 9.83

(e)

Simple payback = capital cost / annual saving = 85,000 / 72,261 = 1.18 years, an excellent return, so pressure management should proceed first. After the PRV the leakage is 716.6 m³/day = 716,600 L/day, giving an ILI of 716,600 / (UARL at 45 m, which is 105,326 × 45/62 = 76,444 L/day) = 9.4. The ILI barely improves because the UARL also falls with pressure, so most of the gap to technical minimum remains. That tells the Town that active leak detection and replacement of the worst mains are still justified after the PRV, and the next step should be to rank sections by break history.

Answer: 1.18 years

Problem 2 [A3-092] Least-cost pipe network optimization and land development servicing

A developer will build a 420-lot subdivision on the east edge of Barrie, and the municipality requires the single 1,800 m trunk watermain feeding it to be chosen at least cost. Design flow in the main is 62 L/s, and the main is PVC with Hazen-Williams C = 130. Three candidate pipes are available, with inside diameters and installed costs of 204 mm at $410 per metre, 255 mm at $480 per metre and 307 mm at $565 per metre. Head loss is made up by a booster pump with wire-to-water efficiency 0.70 operating the equivalent of 2,900 full-flow hours per year at $0.13 per kWh. Capital cost is annualized over 50 years at 4% interest. Use h = 10.67 L Q1.852 / (C1.852 D4.87) with Q in m³/s and D in m, and ignore minor losses.

  1. (a) Find the head loss in the 255 mm main at design flow. [3]
  2. (b) Find the annual energy cost to pump against that head loss in the 255 mm main. [4]
  3. (c) Find the annualized capital cost of the 255 mm main. [3]
  4. (d) Compare all three diameters on total annual cost and give the least total annual cost. [5]
  5. (e) Find the energy price below which the 204 mm pipe becomes the least-cost choice, and comment on how firm the choice of 255 mm is. [5]
(a)

Convert the flow to 0.062 m³/s and the diameter to 0.255 m. The Hazen-Williams form gives h = 10.67 × 1,800 × 0.0621.852 / (1301.852 × 0.2554.87). The pieces are 0.0621.852 = 5.80 × 10⁻³, 1301.852 = 8,223 and 0.2554.87 = 1.288 × 10⁻³. Then h = 10.67 × 1,800 × 5.80 × 10⁻³ / (8,223 × 1.288 × 10⁻³) = 111.4 / 10.59 = 10.52 m, a gradient of 5.84 m per km. The velocity is 0.062 / (π × 0.255² / 4) = 1.21 m/s, a normal value for a trunk main, so no velocity limit controls the choice.

Answer: 10.52 m

(b)

Pumping power must supply the head loss at the design flow. Hydraulic power is ρ g Q h = 1,000 × 9.81 × 0.062 × 10.52 = 6,399 W. Dividing by the wire-to-water efficiency of 0.70 gives an electrical demand of 9,142 W, or 9.14 kW. The annual energy is 9.14 kW × 2,900 h = 26,513 kWh. At $0.13 per kWh the energy cost is 26,513 × 0.13 = $3,446 per year. The 2,900 equivalent full-flow hours reflect that a subdivision main runs well below its design flow most of the time, so using 8,760 hours would overstate the cost of the larger losses in small pipes.

Answer: $3,446/yr

(c)

The installed cost is 1,800 m × $480 = $864,000. The capital recovery factor for i = 4% and n = 50 years is i(1+i)n / ((1+i)n − 1) = 0.04 × 7.1067 / 6.1067 = 0.04655. Annualized capital cost = 864,000 × 0.04655 = $40,219 per year. This converts the one-time construction expense into a yearly figure that can be added directly to the yearly energy cost. It treats the pipe as having a 50-year economic life, which is conservative for PVC, and ignores the cost of the booster pump and building, which would be roughly the same for all three diameters at this flow.

Answer: $40,219/yr

(d)

Repeat parts a to c for each diameter. For 204 mm, h = 31.19 m, power = 27.10 kW, energy = 27.10 × 2,900 × 0.13 = $10,217, capital = 410 × 1,800 × 0.04655 = $34,354, total $44,571. For 255 mm, energy $3,446 plus capital $40,219 gives $43,666. For 307 mm, h = 4.26 m, energy $1,396, capital 565 × 1,800 × 0.04655 = $47,342, total $48,737. The least total annual cost is the 255 mm main at $43,666 per year. The curve is flat near the optimum, since the 204 mm option is only $905 per year (2%) worse, while the 307 mm main is clearly over-built.

Answer: $43,666/yr

(e)

The 204 mm and 255 mm totals are equal when the energy price p satisfies capital204 + E204 (p/0.13) = capital255 + E255 (p/0.13), where E is the energy cost at $0.13. Rearranging, p = 0.13 × (40,219 − 34,354) / (10,217 − 3,446) = 0.13 × 5,865 / 6,771 = $0.1126 per kWh. At today's $0.13 the 255 mm main wins, but a price of only 13% lower would reverse the choice. Because the difference is under 2% of total cost and energy prices, flow growth and interest rates are uncertain, the municipality should also weigh the extra capacity the 255 mm pipe leaves for future flow, which favours it.

Answer: $0.1126/kWh

Problem 3 [A3-093] Population forecasting by arithmetic, geometric and logistic methods

The Township of North Dundas is planning a new surface-water supply to serve 2046, and the design population must be chosen. Census counts for the urban service area are 18,400 in 1996, 24,600 in 2006 and 28,900 in 2016. Growth has slowed over the 20 years because the nearby plant that drove it has stopped hiring, and the serviced land area is bounded by an agricultural greenbelt. The consulting engineer is asked to compare three standard projection methods before recommending a number: arithmetic (using the average increase per decade), geometric (using a constant annual percentage growth rate fitted to 1996 and 2016), and logistic (using the three equally spaced census points and the standard saturation-population formula). Take the horizon as the census year 2046, 30 years after the last census.

  1. (a) Project the 2046 population by the arithmetic method. [4]
  2. (b) Project the 2046 population by the geometric method using the 1996 to 2016 annual rate. [4]
  3. (c) Find the saturation population Ps from the three census points. [4]
  4. (d) Project the 2046 population by the logistic curve. [4]
  5. (e) Recommend a design population for the supply and justify the choice against the other two methods. [4]
(a)

The arithmetic method assumes a constant increase per decade. From 1996 to 2016 the population rose 28,900 − 18,400 = 10,500 over two decades, so the average increase is 5,250 persons per decade. Reaching 2046 from 2016 takes three decades, so P2046 = 28,900 + 3 × 5,250 = 44,650. The method ignores that the actual increase fell from 6,200 in the first decade to 4,300 in the second. Because the growth is clearly slowing, this method likely overshoots, though it gives a mid-range answer between the other two, so it is not the bounding case.

Answer: 44,650

(b)

The geometric method assumes a constant percentage rate. Over 20 years the ratio is 28,900 / 18,400 = 1.5707, so the annual rate is r = 1.57071/20 − 1 = 0.02283, or 2.28% per year. Projecting 30 years from 2016 gives P2046 = 28,900 × (1.02283)30 = 28,900 × 1.9684 = 56,888. This method suits a young, unconstrained city and badly overshoots here, because the township is capping its serviced area and its latest decade of growth was only 1.6% per year (24,600 to 28,900). Treat it as an upper bound that the data do not support.

Answer: 56,888

(c)

The logistic method needs equally spaced counts P0, P1, P2 with P0 P2 < P1², which holds here since 18,400 × 28,900 = 5.318 × 10⁸ and 24,600² = 6.052 × 10⁸. The saturation population is Ps = (2 P0 P1 P2 − P1² (P0 + P2)) / (P0 P2 − P1²). The numerator is 2 × 18,400 × 24,600 × 28,900 − 6.0516 × 10⁸ × 47,300 = 2.6163 × 10¹³ − 2.8624 × 10¹³ = −2.4615 × 10¹². The denominator is 5.3176 × 10⁸ − 6.0516 × 10⁸ = −7.34 × 10⁷. Ps = 33,535. This is the ceiling the data imply, close to the 2016 value because growth is already small.

Answer: Ps = 33,535

(d)

The logistic curve is P = Ps / (1 + m ea t), with t in years from 1996. Here m = (Ps − P0)/P0 = (33,535 − 18,400)/18,400 = 0.8226, and a = (1/10) ln [P0 (Ps − P1) / (P1 (Ps − P0))] = 0.1 × ln (18,400 × 8,935 / (24,600 × 15,135)) = −0.08174 per year. For 2046, t = 50, so ea t = e−4.087 = 0.01679 and P = 33,535 / (1 + 0.8226 × 0.01679) = 33,535 / 1.01381 = 33,078. A check at t = 20 returns 28,900, which agrees with the 2016 census of 28,900, so the fit is consistent.

Answer: 33,078

(e)

The three answers span 33,078 to 56,888, a factor of 1.7, so the choice matters for sizing treatment and storage. The geometric figure assumes the 2.3% rate persists for 30 more years even though the last decade ran at 1.6% and land supply is capped. The arithmetic figure assumes 5,250 per decade although the increments are falling (6,200 then 4,300). The logistic fit passes through all three counts and respects the physical land limit. I would design to a population of about 34,000, slightly above the logistic result, as a prudent margin, and phase the plant so that a review after the next census can add capacity. I would not use a number above 40,000 without evidence of rezoning.

Answer: about 34,000

Problem 4 [A3-094] Per-capita water demand, peaking factors and design flows

A new residential and light-commercial area is being added to the Town of Ingersoll's water system. The residential portion will house 3,800 people with an average day demand of 340 L per capita per day, which includes indoor use and outdoor watering averaged over the year. The commercial portion covers 12 ha at 28 m³ per hectare per day. For the Town's design, residential maximum day factor is 1.9 and peak hour factor is 3.0 (both applied to average day demand), and the commercial factors are 1.6 and 2.4. Residential use is 62% indoor and 38% outdoor on an annual average basis. The Town is considering a water conservation program that cuts indoor residential use by 15% and leaves outdoor use and commercial use unchanged. Distribution and storage are to be sized for the maximum day and peak hour demands. Work in L/s.

  1. (a) Find the residential average day demand. [3]
  2. (b) Find the total average day demand for the area, residential plus commercial. [3]
  3. (c) Find the total maximum day demand. [4]
  4. (d) Find the total peak hour demand. [4]
  5. (e) With the conservation program, keeping the residential maximum day factor at 1.9, find the percentage reduction in total maximum day demand, and say whether the factor would really stay at 1.9. [6]
(a)

Per-capita demand is converted to a flow by multiplying by population and dividing by the seconds in a day: 3,800 persons × 340 L/cap/d = 1,292,000 L/d, and 1,292,000 / 86,400 = 14.95 L/s. This is the average day demand, the total annual volume divided by 365 days and then by 86,400 s. It is the base against which all peaking factors are applied, so a poor per-capita estimate propagates directly into every pipe and tank size. The 340 L/cap/d figure is residential indoor plus outdoor use only, and the commercial area is added separately below, so nothing is counted twice.

Answer: 14.95 L/s

(b)

Commercial demand is 12 ha × 28 m³/ha/d = 336 m³/d = 336,000 L/d, which is 336,000 / 86,400 = 3.89 L/s. The total average day demand is the sum of the residential and commercial parts: 14.95 + 3.89 = 18.84 L/s. That equals 1,628 m³/d for the area, or about 428 L per resident per day when divided across the residential population alone, which is a sensible check for a mixed development. Keeping the two classes separate matters, because their peaking behaviour differs, which is the reason the next steps apply different factors to each.

Answer: 18.84 L/s

(c)

Maximum day demand is each class average multiplied by its own factor. Residential: 1.9 × 14.954 = 28.41 L/s. Commercial: 1.6 × 3.889 = 6.22 L/s. The total is 28.41 + 6.22 = 34.63 L/s. This is the flow that the source, treatment and pumping capacity must deliver on the hottest day of the year, and it is the base for storage and fire-plus-maximum-day analysis. The overall ratio is 34.63 / 18.84 = 1.84, lower than the residential factor because the commercial class peaks less, so applying 1.9 to the whole area would oversize the system by about 3%.

Answer: 34.63 L/s

(d)

Peak hour demand is again summed class by class. Residential: 3.0 × 14.954 = 44.86 L/s. Commercial: 2.4 × 3.889 = 9.33 L/s. Total = 44.86 + 9.33 = 54.19 L/s. The distribution mains, which must deliver the instantaneous peak with no help from the treatment plant, are sized for this flow or for maximum day plus fire flow, whichever is greater. The ratio of peak hour to average day is 54.19 / 18.84 = 2.88. Peak hour factors fall as the served population grows, which is why a small area such as this one needs a higher factor than a whole city.

Answer: 54.19 L/s

(e)

With conservation, residential demand becomes 14.954 × (0.62 × 0.85 + 0.38) = 14.954 × 0.907 = 13.563 L/s. Maximum day residential at 1.9 is 25.77 L/s, and adding the unchanged commercial 6.22 L/s gives 31.99 L/s. The reduction from 34.63 is 2.64 L/s, or 7.63%. The factor of 1.9 would not really stay: the saving is all in the indoor load, which is steady all year, while the hot-day peak is mostly outdoor watering, which was not reduced. Outdoor use becomes a larger share of the average, so the true maximum-day factor would rise, perhaps toward 2.0, and the 7.6% saving would be partly lost.

Answer: 7.63%

Problem 5 [A3-095] Fire flow requirements and design demand for a community

The City of Woodstock is checking fire protection for a four-storey, wood-frame apartment building with a combustible roof. The Fire Underwriters Survey (FUS) method is used with F = 220 C √A, where F is in L/min, C = 1.5 for wood frame construction and A = 3,150 m² is the effective floor area. F is rounded to the nearest 1,000 L/min. The occupancy is judged limited-combustible, which reduces F by 15%. An automatic sprinkler system supervised to the standard reduces the occupancy-adjusted value by 30%. Exposure to neighbouring buildings adds 25% of the occupancy-adjusted value. The final fire flow is rounded to the nearest 1,000 L/min. The zone's maximum day demand is 48 L/s. A hydrant sits 600 m from the source node along a 400 mm main of inside diameter 400 mm with Hazen-Williams C = 120. The hydraulic grade line at the source node is at elevation 312.0 m, and the hydrant ground elevation is 262.0 m. The city requires at least 140 kPa residual pressure at the hydrant.

  1. (a) Find the base required fire flow F, rounded to the nearest 1,000 L/min. [3]
  2. (b) Apply the occupancy, sprinkler and exposure adjustments and find the final fire flow to the nearest 1,000 L/min. [5]
  3. (c) Find the design flow in L/s, being maximum day demand plus the fire flow. [3]
  4. (d) Find the head loss in the 600 m of 400 mm main at the design flow. [4]
  5. (e) Find the residual pressure at the hydrant and state whether it meets the City's requirement. [5]
(a)

Substitute into the FUS formula: F = 220 × 1.5 × √3,150. The square root of 3,150 is 56.12, so F = 220 × 1.5 × 56.12 = 18,521 L/min. Rounding to the nearest 1,000 L/min gives 19,000 L/min. The formula reflects that the water needed to control a fire rises with the square root of the area, because firefighters attack the perimeter of a fire rather than its whole volume. The coefficient C = 1.5 applies to wood-frame construction, the most hazardous FUS class, against 1.0 for ordinary construction, 0.8 for non-combustible and 0.6 for fire-resistive, and it captures the way a wood-frame structure with combustible roof sustains rapid fire spread through its framing.

Answer: 19,000 L/min

(b)

Start from the rounded base of 19,000 L/min. The occupancy reduction of 15% gives 19,000 × 0.85 = 16,150 L/min. The sprinkler credit is 30% of that, a reduction of 4,845 L/min. The exposure charge adds 25% of the occupancy-adjusted value, or 4,037.5 L/min. Net fire flow = 16,150 − 4,845 + 4,037.5 = 15,342.5 L/min, which rounds to 15,000 L/min. The exposure charge of 4,037.5 L/min nearly cancels the sprinkler credit of 4,845 L/min, which shows why spacing between wood buildings is often as valuable as sprinklers. Both adjustments act on the same occupancy-adjusted base, not on each other, as the FUS method sets out.

Answer: 15,000 L/min

(c)

Fire flow is expected to coincide with a maximum day, so the two are added. Convert 15,000 L/min to L/s by dividing by 60: 15,000 / 60 = 250 L/s. Adding the maximum day demand of 48 L/s gives 250 + 48 = 298 L/s, or 0.298 m³/s. This is the flow that the distribution main must carry to the hydrant during the event, and it normally governs pipe size in the fire zone. Peak hour demand is not added, because a design fire is not assumed to coincide with the peak hour of daily use. The whole system must also keep a residual of at least 140 kPa at every node.

Answer: 298 L/s

(d)

Use Hazen-Williams with Q = 0.298 m³/s, L = 600 m, D = 0.400 m, C = 120: h = 10.67 × 600 × 0.2981.852 / (1201.852 × 0.4004.87). The terms are 0.2981.852 = 0.1062, 1201.852 = 7,090 and 0.4004.87 = 0.011535. Then h = 10.67 × 600 × 0.1062 / (7,090 × 0.011535) = 679.9 / 81.78 = 8.31, and unrounded values give 8.32 m. The velocity is 0.298 / 0.1257 = 2.37 m/s, which is above the usual 1.5 m/s design velocity but acceptable for a short fire-flow event.

Answer: 8.32 m

(e)

The hydraulic grade line at the hydrant is the source grade line minus the head loss: 312.0 − 8.32 = 303.68 m. The residual head at the hydrant is the grade line minus ground elevation, 303.68 − 262.0 = 41.68 m of water. Converting to pressure with 9.81 kPa per metre gives 41.68 × 9.81 = 409 kPa. This is well above the required 140 kPa, so the main supplies the fire flow with a margin of about 269 kPa. The result is only valid if the source grade line stays at 312.0 m under the 298 L/s draw, which should be checked with the pump or tank drawdown on the system.

Answer: 409 kPa

A3 Practice Paper 20

Problem 1 [A3-096] Water source development: wells, intakes and safe yield

The Township of Oro-Medonte is developing a new municipal well in a confined sand and gravel aquifer. A 72-hour constant-rate test pumped 18 L/s and reached steady drawdown. Observation wells at 15 m and 80 m from the pumped well recorded steady drawdowns of 4.20 m and 1.85 m respectively. The production well has a radius of 0.15 m, and it is assumed that no well loss occurs, so drawdown at any radius follows the Thiem equation for steady radial flow in a confined aquifer: s1 − s2 = Q ln(r2/r1) / (2π T). The top of the pump intake lies 18 m below the static water level, so the available drawdown at the pumped well is 18 m. The Township's policy is to plan on 85% of the calculated maximum sustained yield, and the pump is to run 20 hours per day.

  1. (a) Find the transmissivity T of the aquifer in m²/day. [4]
  2. (b) Predict the drawdown at the face of the pumped well at 18 L/s. [4]
  3. (c) Estimate the radius of influence, where drawdown falls to zero, using the Thiem relation. [4]
  4. (d) Find the maximum pumping rate that would use the full 18 m of available drawdown, assuming drawdown is proportional to pumping rate. [4]
  5. (e) Find the planning daily volume that can be taken at 85% of that rate for 20 hours per day. [4]
(a)

Convert the pumping rate to m³/day: 18 L/s × 86.4 = 1,555.2 m³/day. Rearrange the Thiem equation for transmissivity: T = Q ln(r2/r1) / (2π (s1 − s2)). With r1 = 15 m, r2 = 80 m, s1 = 4.20 m and s2 = 1.85 m, ln(80/15) = 1.674 and s1 − s2 = 2.35 m. T = 1,555.2 × 1.674 / (2π × 2.35) = 2,603 / 14.765 = 176.3 m²/day. This is a moderate transmissivity, typical of a clean sand and gravel unit about 6 to 10 m thick. Steady state is assumed after 72 hours, and a confined aquifer is assumed, so these drawdowns must be corrected if the aquifer is unconfined or if boundaries are nearby.

Answer: 176.3 m²/d

(b)

Apply the Thiem equation between the first observation well and the pumped well wall. The extra drawdown from r = 15 m to r = 0.15 m is Q ln(15/0.15) / (2π T) = 1,555.2 × ln(100) / (2π × 176.3) = 1,555.2 × 4.605 / 1,107.7 = 6.465 m. Adding the 4.20 m already observed at 15 m, drawdown at the well face is 4.20 + 6.465 = 10.67 m, about 10.66 m with unrounded values. Most of the drawdown occurs close to the well because flow converges, which is why the observation wells alone could not show the water level at the pump intake. Real wells also have well loss from the screen, so the true pumping level is usually deeper.

Answer: 10.66 m

(c)

The radius of influence is where s falls to zero. Use the outer observation well as the reference: 1.85 = Q ln(R/80) / (2π T). Then ln(R/80) = 2π T × 1.85 / Q = 2π × 176.3 × 1.85 / 1,555.2 = 2,049 / 1,555.2 = 1.318. R = 80 × e1.318 = 80 × 3.735 = 298.8 m. This is only an estimate because the logarithmic extrapolation assumes steady state, while in a real confined aquifer the cone keeps growing slowly with time. It is useful for checking that the nearest neighbouring wells, property lines and any surface-water body are outside roughly 300 m, to avoid interference.

Answer: 299 m

(d)

With no well loss, drawdown in a confined aquifer is proportional to pumping rate, so specific capacity is constant. At 18 L/s the drawdown is 10.665 m, so specific capacity = 18 / 10.665 = 1.688 L/s per metre. With 18 m of available drawdown, Qmax = 1.688 × 18 = 30.4 L/s. This is the largest rate that would put the water level at the top of the pump intake, which is not a safe operating rate. In practice well loss grows with the square of flow, so the actual specific capacity falls at higher rates and the real figure would be lower, which is why the next step applies a planning factor.

Answer: 30.4 L/s

(e)

The Township plans on 85% of the maximum rate: 0.85 × 30.38 = 25.82 L/s. Over 20 hours each day, the volume is 25.82 L/s × 3,600 s/h × 20 h = 1,859,000 L, or 1,859 m³/day. That is the daily volume the well can be relied on to supply, equivalent to the demand of roughly 5,000 people at 350 L per capita per day. Using a pump run time of 20 hours rather than 24 leaves 4 hours of aquifer recovery each day, which lowers long-term drawdown. This planning rate should be confirmed by a longer test covering dry-season conditions.

Answer: 1,859 m³/day

Problem 2 [A3-097] Transmission main sizing with the Hazen-Williams equation

A 7.2 km transmission main will carry treated water from the Lakeview plant to a reservoir in the neighbouring town of Goderich. The main is cement-lined ductile iron with Hazen-Williams C = 130. The design flow is 220 L/s now, and the Region expects 330 L/s after the second expansion. The design criteria are a head loss gradient no greater than 2.5 m per km at the present flow, and the use of a standard 500 mm main of inside diameter 500 mm if the computed size falls near it. The static lift from the plant clear well to the reservoir inlet is 38 m, and the pump and motor combined efficiency is 0.75. Use h = 10.67 L Q1.852 / (C1.852 D4.87) with Q in m³/s and D in m, and neglect minor losses.

  1. (a) Find the diameter that gives exactly 2.5 m/km at 220 L/s. [4]
  2. (b) For the standard 500 mm main, find the velocity at 220 L/s. [4]
  3. (c) Find the total friction head loss over 7.2 km at 220 L/s in the 500 mm main. [4]
  4. (d) Find the pump power needed at 220 L/s. [4]
  5. (e) Find the friction head loss at 330 L/s and comment on whether the 500 mm main remains acceptable. [4]
(a)

Set h/L = 2.5 m/km = 0.0025 and solve the Hazen-Williams equation for D: D = [10.67 Q1.852 / (C1.852 × 0.0025)]1/4.87. With Q = 0.220 m³/s, Q1.852 = 0.0606 and C1.852 = 8,223 (for C = 130). Then the bracket is 10.67 × 0.0606 / (8,223 × 0.0025) = 0.6466 / 20.56 = 0.03145. Taking the 1/4.87 power gives D = 0.4914 m = 491 mm. The result is not a stock size, so the next standard diameter up (500 mm) is selected, which is close and gives a gradient just under the limit. Round up rather than down, because a smaller pipe breaches the 2.5 m/km criterion.

Answer: 491 mm

(b)

Velocity is flow divided by area. For D = 0.500 m the area is π × 0.5² / 4 = 0.1963 m². With Q = 0.220 m³/s, V = 0.220 / 0.1963 = 1.12 m/s. This is within the common range of 0.6 to 1.8 m/s for treated-water transmission mains, so the velocity is low enough to limit surge risk and pumping cost but high enough to avoid sedimentation. A velocity this low also implies that the main may be tapped later for a few additional demands without the velocity limit being reached.

Answer: 1.12 m/s

(c)

Apply the Hazen-Williams formula with L = 7,200 m, D = 0.500 m, C = 130 and Q = 0.220 m³/s. The terms are Q1.852 = 0.06056, C1.852 = 8,223 and D4.87 = 0.03419. Then h = 10.67 × 7,200 × 0.06056 / (8,223 × 0.03420) = 4,652 / 281.2 = 16.5 m. This gives a gradient of 16.54 / 7.2 = 2.30 m/km, below the 2.5 m/km criterion, which confirms that the 500 mm main meets the design standard. The cement lining keeps C high, but over many decades the real value tends to fall, so reviewing the calculation at C = 110 is wise.

Answer: 16.5 m

(d)

Total dynamic head is the static lift plus friction loss: 38 + 16.54 = 54.54 m. Water power is ρ g Q H = 1,000 × 9.81 × 0.220 × 54.54 = 117,700 W = 117.7 kW. Dividing by the combined efficiency of 0.75 gives an input power of 156.96 kW, or about 157 kW. Friction is 30% of the total head, so any increase in C-factor roughness over the life of the main directly raises the energy bill. A motor of 185 kW would be a normal standard size to select, leaving about 18% margin for aging and the future flow.

Answer: 157 kW

(e)

At 330 L/s, Q1.852 = 0.06056 × (330/220)1.852 = 0.06056 × 2.119 = 0.1283. The head loss scales as Q1.852, so h = 16.54 × 2.119 = 35.06 m over 7.2 km, or 4.87 m/km. That is almost double the 2.5 m/km criterion, and the velocity is 1.68 m/s, near the upper limit of 1.8 m/s. The main will carry the future flow but only with a much larger pump and about 3.2 times the friction energy (1.5 times the flow at 2.1 times the head loss). The Region should either lay a second parallel main before the expansion, or accept the higher head if the larger pump is cheaper over its life, which a life-cycle cost comparison would show.

Answer: 35.1 m

Problem 3 [A3-098] Storage reservoir sizing for equalization, fire and emergency

The Town of Orangeville is sizing a new elevated storage reservoir for a pressure zone with a maximum day demand of 9,600 m³/day. The source and treatment plant deliver a constant rate equal to the maximum day demand, spread evenly over the day. On the maximum day, demand falls in four six-hour blocks as a fraction of the daily total: 10% from 00:00 to 06:00, 34% from 06:00 to 12:00, 26% from 12:00 to 18:00 and 30% from 18:00 to 24:00. The design fire flow is 200 L/s for a 3-hour duration. The Town's guideline for emergency storage is 25% of the sum of fire storage and equalization storage. The tank is circular with diameter set in part (e). Compute equalization from the mass curve of cumulative supply minus demand, and not from a stated percentage.

  1. (a) Find the equalization storage from the cumulative supply and demand pattern. [4]
  2. (b) Find the fire storage. [3]
  3. (c) Find the emergency storage. [3]
  4. (d) Find the total required storage and compare the equalization storage with the common rule-of-thumb of 25% of the maximum day demand. [5]
  5. (e) Find the diameter of a circular tank with a maximum effective water depth of 8.0 m that holds the total storage. [5]
(a)

The supply is 25% of the daily total in each six-hour block. The net (supply minus demand) in each block is: 00:00 to 06:00, 25 − 10 = +15%; 06:00 to 12:00, 25 − 34 = −9%; 12:00 to 18:00, 25 − 26 = −1%; 18:00 to 24:00, 25 − 30 = −5%. The cumulative net is +15%, +6%, +5%, 0%. The tank fills during the night to a high of +15% and falls to 0% at midnight, so the range between the highest and lowest points on the mass curve is 15% of the maximum day. Equalization storage = 0.15 × 9,600 = 1,440 m³. The block pattern is coarse, so a real hourly pattern would give a slightly higher peak deficit within a block.

Answer: 1,440 m³

(b)

Fire storage is the fire flow multiplied by its duration. The flow is 200 L/s, which is 0.200 m³/s × 3,600 s/h = 720 m³/h. Over 3 hours the volume is 720 × 3 = 2,160 m³. This storage must remain in the tank at all times, below the level the daily operation draws down to, since the fire may start at any time including when the tank is at its lowest equalization level. The supply system can also contribute during a fire, but the guideline conservatively ignores that, and treats fire storage as wholly stored water.

Answer: 2,160 m³

(c)

Emergency storage covers pump failures, main breaks and power outages. The Town's guideline sets it at 25% of fire plus equalization storage: 0.25 × (1,440 + 2,160) = 0.25 × 3,600 = 900 m³. This is 2.25 hours of maximum day demand for the zone. It is a policy value rather than a physical calculation, so it is open to adjustment. A zone with a single feed from the plant, and no standby power, would reasonably warrant more, while a zone with two independent connections to adjoining zones might accept less.

Answer: 900 m³

(d)

Total storage = equalization + fire + emergency = 1,440 + 2,160 + 900 = 4,500 m³. The rule of thumb says equalization is 25% of maximum day demand, 0.25 × 9,600 = 2,400 m³. The mass-curve value of 1,440 m³ is only 60% of that. The rule is deliberately conservative when no hourly pattern is known, but a measured pattern is better. The coarse six-hour blocks smear the real morning peak, so the mass-curve result probably understates the need. With the rule of thumb the total would be (2,400 + 2,160) × 1.25 = 5,700 m³, so I would use the mass-curve result only if the hourly demand pattern has been measured, and otherwise keep the larger figure.

Answer: 4,500 m³

(e)

The volume of a circular tank of diameter D and depth H is V = π D² H / 4. Solving for the diameter, D = √(4V / (π H)) = √(4 × 4,500 / (π × 8.0)) = √(716.2) = 26.76 m. The tank footprint is π × 26.76² / 4 = 562 m². With such a shallow depth-to-diameter ratio (0.30) the tank has a large footprint and a low operating pressure range: each metre of drawdown changes pressure by 9.8 kPa, so the whole equalization drawdown of 2.6 m (1,440 / 562) changes pressure by only about 25 kPa, which is a good feature for customers.

Answer: 26.8 m

Problem 4 [A3-099] Pumping station design with pump and system curves

A booster pumping station in the City of Guelph lifts water through 1,850 m of 400 mm (inside diameter 400 mm) ductile iron main, Hazen-Williams C = 120, to a reservoir with a static lift of 42 m. Minor losses are lumped as K = 6.5 on the pipe velocity head. The pump selected has a head curve H = 70 − 0.0021 Q² with H in m and Q in L/s, and a duty-point efficiency of 78%. Two identical pumps are installed, and the station can run one or both in parallel. The pumps are fitted with variable-frequency drives, and affinity laws apply with the head curve at relative speed s being H = 70 s² − 0.0021 Q². Use h = 10.67 L Q1.852 / (C1.852 D4.87) for pipe friction with Q in m³/s and D in m. The minor-loss term is K V²/(2g).

  1. (a) Find the system head required to deliver 150 L/s. [4]
  2. (b) Find the flow delivered by one pump at full speed (the duty point). [4]
  3. (c) Find the pump input shaft power at that duty point. [4]
  4. (d) Find the total flow when both pumps run in parallel at full speed. [4]
  5. (e) Find the relative speed s at which one pump delivers 90 L/s. [4]
(a)

The system curve is static lift plus friction plus minor loss. At Q = 0.150 m³/s, friction is h = 10.67 × 1,850 × 0.151.852 / (1201.852 × 0.44.87). The terms are 0.151.852 = 0.02979, 1201.852 = 7,090 and 0.44.87 = 0.011535, so h = 10.67 × 1,850 × 0.02979 / (7,090 × 0.011535) = 588.0 / 81.78 = 7.19 m. Velocity is 0.15 / 0.1257 = 1.194 m/s, so the minor loss is 6.5 × 1.194² / 19.62 = 0.47 m. Adding the 42 m static lift, the system head is 42 + 7.19 + 0.47 = 49.66 m. The static term dominates, so the system curve is quite flat.

Answer: 49.7 m

(b)

The duty point is where pump head equals system head. Solving 70 − 0.0021 Q² = 42 + hf(Q) + K V²/2g numerically, I try Q = 100 L/s: pump head = 70 − 21 = 49.0 m and system head = 42 + 3.39 + 0.21 = 45.60 m, so the pump is still above the system. At Q = 110 L/s the pump gives 44.6 m and the system needs 46.3 m, so the intersection is between them. Refinement gives Q = 106.75 L/s at H = 46.07 m. At this point the pump neither accelerates nor throttles the flow, so it is the steady operating condition at full speed.

Answer: 106.8 L/s

(c)

Shaft power at the duty point is P = ρ g Q H / η. With Q = 0.10675 m³/s, H = 46.07 m and η = 0.78, the water power is 1,000 × 9.81 × 0.10675 × 46.07 = 48,248 W. Dividing by 0.78 gives 61,852 W, or 61.9 kW. The motor must be larger than this to cover the pump's operation at other points: the shaft power may be higher at runout, so a 75 kW motor is the typical selection, which gives a service factor of about 1.2. The 78% efficiency should be confirmed against the manufacturer's curve at 106.8 L/s, since the best efficiency point may be at a different flow.

Answer: 61.9 kW

(d)

With two identical pumps in parallel, each pump delivers half of the total flow at the same head. So the combined curve is H = 70 − 0.0021 (Q/2)² = 70 − 0.000525 Q². Setting this equal to the system head and solving numerically gives Q = 180.8 L/s and H = 52.8 m. Two pumps therefore deliver only 1.69 times the flow of one, not twice, because the higher flow raises friction head in the shared pipe from 3.8 m to 10.2 m, and the pump head falls at the same time. The extra station energy per unit volume is higher in the two-pump case, which is why the second pump should only run during peaks.

Answer: 180.8 L/s

(e)

At speed ratio s, the pump head curve is H = 70 s² − 0.0021 Q². For Q = 90 L/s the system head is 42 + 2.79 + 0.17 = 44.96 m. Solving 70 s² − 0.0021 × 90² = 44.96 gives 70 s² = 44.96 + 17.01 = 61.97, so s² = 0.8853 and s = 0.941. The drive therefore runs at 94.1% speed, or 56.5 Hz on a 60 Hz supply. Slowing the pump instead of throttling a valve avoids wasting head and trims the power to roughly s³ times its value, which is a worthwhile saving where the station runs most hours below its full duty.

Answer: 0.941

Problem 5 [A3-100] Water distribution network analysis by the Hardy Cross method

The Town of Cobourg is analysing one loop of its water distribution network with the Hardy Cross method. The loop A-B-C-D-A has four pipes, all with Hazen-Williams C = 120: AB is 600 m of 300 mm, BC is 400 m of 250 mm, CD is 500 m of 200 mm and DA is 700 m of 250 mm (diameters are inside diameters). Flow enters at A at 120 L/s, and the nodal demands are 35 L/s at B, 55 L/s at C and 30 L/s at D. The first estimate of flows, with clockwise positive, is AB = 70 L/s, BC = 35 L/s, CD = −20 L/s (meaning 20 L/s flows from D to C) and DA = −50 L/s (meaning 50 L/s flows from A to D). Head loss in each pipe is h = r Q|Q|0.852 with r = 10.67 L / (C1.852 D4.87) and Q in m³/s. The hydraulic grade line at A is 330.0 m, and the ground at C is at elevation 286.0 m.

  1. (a) Find the head-loss imbalance around the loop for the first estimate, the sum of h in the clockwise sense. [3]
  2. (b) Find the Hardy Cross correction ΔQ for the first iteration. [4]
  3. (c) Find the corrected flow in pipe AB after the first iteration. [3]
  4. (d) Iterate to convergence (correction under 0.01 L/s) and give the final flow in AB. [5]
  5. (e) Find the pressure at node C with the converged flows, taking the path A to B to C. [5]
(a)

Compute r for each pipe from r = 10.67 L / (C1.852 D4.87), with C1.852 = 7,090. For AB, r = 318; for BC, r = 515; for CD, r = 1,908; for DA, r = 901 (units s1.852/m4.556). Head loss h = r Q|Q|0.852 with Q in m³/s gives AB: +2.308 m, BC: +1.036 m, CD: −1.361 m and DA: −3.509 m. The signed sum is 2.308 + 1.036 − 1.361 − 3.509 = −1.527 m. A balanced loop would sum to zero. The negative value shows the counter-clockwise route (D to C, A to D) is carrying too much head loss, so the clockwise flow must increase.

Answer: −1.53 m

(b)

The Hardy Cross correction is ΔQ = −Σh / (1.852 Σ|h/Q|). The denominator terms 1.852|h/Q| are: AB 61.06, BC 54.80, CD 126.06 and DA 129.96 (all per m³/s), summing to 371.9. Then ΔQ = −(−1.5265) / 371.9 = +0.004105 m³/s = +4.10 L/s. The sign is positive, so each pipe's clockwise-directed flow is increased by 4.10 L/s. Because the corrections act on pipes in the same direction as the loop, AB and BC get larger and CD and DA get smaller in magnitude. The method conserves continuity at each node, since the same ΔQ is added around the whole loop.

Answer: +4.10 L/s

(c)

Add the correction algebraically to the first estimate. Pipe AB carried +70 L/s clockwise, so the new flow is 70 + 4.10 = 74.10 L/s. For comparison, BC becomes 39.10 L/s, CD becomes −15.90 L/s, and DA becomes −45.90 L/s. Check continuity at A: 74.10 + 45.90 = 120.00 L/s leaves the node, matching the inflow. At B: 74.10 − 39.10 = 35.00 L/s, equal to the demand. Continuity is automatically preserved by the method, but checking is a cheap and necessary guard against sign errors when adding corrections.

Answer: 74.1 L/s

(d)

The second iteration uses the new flows. The imbalance falls to roughly 0.05 m and the correction is +0.135 L/s, giving AB = 74.24 L/s. A third pass gives a correction of about 0.002 L/s, below the 0.01 L/s stop limit. Final flows are AB = 74.24, BC = 39.24, CD = −15.76 and DA = −45.76 L/s. The convergence is fast, since each cycle reduces the error by about 30 times, as the Newton form of the method would. The small second correction shows that the first estimate was already close, and a reasonable initial guess is the best way to cut the iterations.

Answer: 74.24 L/s

(e)

Take the path from A through B to C. The head loss in AB is 600-m pipe: h = 318 × 0.07424 × 0.074240.852 = 2.573 m, and in BC, h = 515 × 0.03924 × 0.039240.852 = 1.280 m. The grade line at C is 330.0 − 2.573 − 1.280 = 326.147 m. With ground at 286.0 m, the pressure head is 40.147 m, and pressure = 40.147 × 9.81 = 393.8 kPa, about 394 kPa. Going the other way, through D, must give the same grade line at C; checking it is a useful test of the solution and shows that the loop is balanced.

Answer: 394 kPa

A3 Practice Paper 21

Problem 1 [A3-101] Network pressure and fire-flow checks at nodes

The Town of Elmvale, Ontario, is supplied to a new subdivision through a single 1400 m long PVC main running from an elevated storage tank. The tank water surface is at elevation 285.0 m and is assumed constant during the period studied; the subdivision node is at elevation 252.0 m. Treat the main as one pipe with Hazen-Williams C = 120, using hf = 10.67 L Q1.852 / (C1.852 D4.87), with hf and L in metres, Q in m³/s and D in metres. Ignore local losses and velocity head. Maximum-day demand at the node is 25 L/s, and the fire-flow requirement is 90 L/s added to that demand. The fire department requires a residual pressure of at least 140 kPa at the node during a fire. Take 1 m of head as 9.81 kPa. The existing main is 250 mm in diameter and a 300 mm replacement is being considered.

  1. (a) Find the pressure at the node under maximum-day demand alone with the 250 mm main. [4]
  2. (b) With the 250 mm main, find the head loss when the 90 L/s fire flow is added to the maximum-day demand, and from it the residual pressure at the node. Report the head loss. [5]
  3. (c) Find the residual pressure at the node for the same fire condition with the 300 mm main, and state whether the 140 kPa requirement is met. [5]
  4. (d) With the 300 mm main, find the largest fire flow, additional to the 25 L/s maximum-day demand, that can be delivered while keeping 140 kPa at the node. [6]
(a)

The only flow in the pipe is the maximum-day demand, Q = 0.025 m³/s. Hazen-Williams gives hf = 10.67 × 1400 × 0.0251.852 / (1201.852 × 0.254.87). The numerator is 14 938 × 0.001079 and the denominator is 7 090 × 0.001172, so hf = 1.94 m. The static head between tank and node is 285.0 − 252.0 = 33.0 m, so the pressure head at the node is 33.0 − 1.94 = 31.06 m. Multiplying by 9.81 kPa/m gives 304.7 kPa. This is a healthy domestic pressure, and the check shows the 250 mm main has ample capacity at ordinary demand, so any weakness must appear only when the large fire flow is added.

Answer: 304.7 kPa

(b)

With fire flow the total flow is 25 + 90 = 115 L/s = 0.115 m³/s. The head loss is hf = 14 938 × 0.1151.852 / (7 090 × 0.254.87). Since 0.1151.852 = 0.01817 and 0.254.87 = 0.001172, hf = 14 938 × 0.01817 / 8.32 = 32.8 m. Head loss rises with Q1.852, so a 4.6 times larger flow raises the loss about 17 times. The residual head is 33.0 − 32.8 = 0.2 m, which is about 2 kPa, far below the 140 kPa requirement. The 250 mm main therefore cannot support the fire flow and the node would be close to zero gauge pressure, with a real risk of negative pressure elsewhere.

Answer: hf = 32.8 m (residual about 2 kPa)

(c)

For D = 0.30 m, D4.87 = 0.002843, so the denominator becomes 7 090 × 0.002843 = 20.19. The numerator is unchanged at 14 938 × 0.01817 = 271.4. Then hf = 271.4 / 20.19 = 13.5 m. Residual head = 33.0 − 13.5 = 19.5 m, and the residual pressure is 19.5 × 9.81 = 191.3 kPa. This exceeds the 140 kPa requirement by about 51 kPa, so the 300 mm main meets the criterion. The gain is large because the loss varies as D4.87: a diameter increase of only 20 percent cuts the head loss by about 59 percent. The result is on the safe side, but it uses the assumption that the tank level does not drop.

Answer: 191.3 kPa, requirement met

(d)

The 140 kPa limit corresponds to a residual head of 140 / 9.81 = 14.27 m, so the permitted head loss is 33.0 − 14.27 = 18.73 m. Rearranging Hazen-Williams for flow, Q1.852 = hf C1.852 D4.87 / (10.67 L) = 18.73 × 7 090 × 0.002843 / 14 938 = 0.02531. Then Q = 0.025311/1.852 = 0.1372 m³/s = 137.2 L/s total. The maximum-day demand uses 25 L/s of this, leaving 137.2 − 25 = 112.2 L/s for fire fighting. That is above the 90 L/s requirement by about 25 percent, a margin that could absorb some pipe ageing. A designer would still ask what C value the pipe will have in 30 years.

Answer: 112.2 L/s

Problem 2 [A3-102] Coagulation and flocculation: mixing intensity and detention time

A water treatment plant in Peterborough, Ontario, treats 0.12 m³/s. Its flocculation train has three equal mechanically mixed stages in series, each with a detention time of 8.0 min, operated as tapered mixing with velocity gradients of 70 s⁻¹, 50 s⁻¹ and 30 s⁻¹ in stages 1, 2 and 3. Power dissipated in the water is P = G² μ V. The dynamic viscosity of water is 1.002 × 10⁻³ Pa·s at 20 °C and 1.674 × 10⁻³ Pa·s at 2 °C. The design criterion for the whole train is a G t product between 40 000 and 100 000, where t is the total detention time. Ignore the volume displaced by shafts and baffles. In January the raw water is at 2 °C, and the operators have asked whether the summer motor settings are still adequate.

  1. (a) Find the volume of one flocculation stage and the power dissipated in stage 1 at 20 °C. Report the power. [4]
  2. (b) Find the G t product for the whole train and state whether it satisfies the design criterion. [4]
  3. (c) In January the stage 1 motor still delivers the 20 °C power. Find the velocity gradient actually achieved in stage 1 at 2 °C. [5]
  4. (d) Find the power needed in stage 1 at 2 °C to restore G = 70 s⁻¹. [4]
  5. (e) Explain why the gradients are tapered from stage 1 to stage 3 rather than held constant, and what the January shortfall would do to floc formation. [3]
(a)

Each stage holds the flow for 8.0 min = 480 s, so V = Q t = 0.12 × 480 = 57.6 m³. The power needed to keep the water at G = 70 s⁻¹ comes from P = G² μ V = 70² × 1.002 × 10⁻³ × 57.6. Here 70² = 4 900, and 4 900 × 1.002 × 10⁻³ = 4.910 W·s per m³ of water, which multiplied by 57.6 m³ gives 282.8 W. This is the power actually dissipated in the water, not the motor power. The motor and gearbox must supply more, because they lose energy to friction and to the impeller drag, so the designer would divide by an efficiency near 0.7 to size the drive.

Answer: P1 = 282.8 W

(b)

The total detention time is 3 × 480 = 1 440 s, but G varies from stage to stage, so the product is summed stage by stage: Σ G t = 480 × (70 + 50 + 30) = 480 × 150 = 72 000. Equivalently the mean G is 50 s⁻¹ and 50 × 1 440 = 72 000. The criterion range is 40 000 to 100 000, so 72 000 lies in the middle and the design is acceptable. G t describes the total number of particle collisions available for floc growth, which explains why both intensity and time matter. A value above the range risks shearing flocs apart, and a value below it gives too few collisions.

Answer: G t = 72 000, satisfied

(c)

The motor power is fixed at P = 282.8 W and the volume is unchanged, so only viscosity changes. From P = G² μ V, G = √(P / (μ V)) = √(282.8 / (1.674 × 10⁻³ × 57.6)) = √(282.8 / 0.09642) = √2 933 = 54.2 s⁻¹. Equivalently G falls by the factor √(1.002/1.674) = 0.774, so 70 × 0.774 = 54.2. Cold water is about 67 percent more viscous, so the same shaft power produces a gentler velocity gradient. Stage 1 would therefore operate about 23 percent below its intended intensity, with the same fall in every later stage unless their motors are changed as well.

Answer: G = 54.2 s⁻¹

(d)

To hold G = 70 s⁻¹ at 2 °C the power must rise in proportion to viscosity: P = G² μ V = 4 900 × 1.674 × 10⁻³ × 57.6 = 472.5 W. This is 1.67 times the summer value, or an increase of 189.7 W in the water. In practice the plant would fit variable frequency drives so the operator can raise impeller speed in winter. Since power varies with the cube of rotational speed for a given impeller, a 67 percent power increase needs only about 18 percent higher speed (1.671/3 = 1.186). That is a modest change, which is why speed control is the usual remedy rather than replacing the motors.

Answer: P = 472.5 W

(e)

Tapering starts with a high gradient so that coagulant is dispersed quickly and many small microflocs collide while they are still small and strong. As flocs grow they become larger and weaker, and they are more easily sheared apart, so the gradient is reduced in later stages to let them build without breaking before the settling basin. A constant high G would break flocs near the outlet, while a constant low G would give poor early contact. In January the higher viscosity cuts the gradient in stage 1, which means that fewer collisions occur early, flocs form more slowly, and cold-water coagulation is already slower, so settled turbidity would likely rise unless power or coagulant dose is adjusted.

Answer: Non-numeric explanation

Problem 3 [A3-103] Sedimentation basin design by overflow rate

A new surface-water plant in Orillia, Ontario, has a design flow of 0.12 m³/s. Clarification is by two identical rectangular horizontal-flow sedimentation basins operated in parallel, each with a length to width ratio of 4:1 and a side water depth of 3.5 m. The design overflow rate is 25 m³/(m²·d) with both basins in service, and the effluent weir loading must not exceed 250 m³/(m·d) per basin. Because one basin may be taken out of service for several days of cleaning, the approval authority allows an overflow rate of up to 40 m³/(m²·d) for that condition only. Treat the surface area as the plan area, length times width, and ignore inlet and outlet zones, sludge storage and any short-circuiting.

  1. (a) Find the total surface area needed to meet the design overflow rate. [3]
  2. (b) Find the width and length of each basin, and report the length. [4]
  3. (c) Find the theoretical detention time in each basin at design flow. [4]
  4. (d) Find the length of effluent weir needed in each basin to meet the weir loading limit. [4]
  5. (e) Find the overflow rate when one basin is out of service, and state whether the temporary limit is met. [5]
(a)

The overflow rate is the flow divided by the plan area, v0 = Q / A, so A = Q / v0. First convert the flow to daily units: 0.12 m³/s × 86 400 s/d = 10 368 m³/d. Then A = 10 368 / 25 = 414.7 m². A particle settles out only if its settling velocity is at least v0, which is why the area, and not the depth or the volume, controls removal in an ideal basin. This total is shared by the two basins, so each must provide half of it. The depth is chosen separately, mainly for detention time and sludge handling, because in this idealized model depth does not change the removal.

Answer: A = 414.7 m²

(b)

Each basin has an area of 414.7 / 2 = 207.4 m². With L = 4W, the area is L W = 4W², so W = √(207.4 / 4) = √51.84 = 7.20 m. The length is L = 4 × 7.20 = 28.8 m, and the product 28.8 × 7.20 = 207.4 m² confirms the area. A length to width ratio of 4:1 is a common minimum for rectangular basins because a long narrow shape reduces short-circuiting and gives more uniform flow. The depth is not used in this part, but the shape is reasonable for a single sludge collector running the full width.

Answer: L = 28.8 m (W = 7.2 m)

(c)

Each basin carries half of the flow, 0.06 m³/s. Its volume is V = L W h = 28.8 × 7.20 × 3.5 = 725.8 m³. The detention time is t = V / Q = 725.8 / 0.06 = 12 096 s, which is 12 096 / 3 600 = 3.36 h. This is within the 2 to 4 h range usually seen for clarifiers following coagulation and flocculation. Detention time is the theoretical value only: real basins have dead zones and short-circuit flow, so the actual mean residence time for much of the water is shorter than the calculated 3.36 h, which is the reason designers do not rely on this number alone to judge performance.

Answer: t = 3.36 h

(d)

Each basin passes 0.06 m³/s × 86 400 = 5 184 m³/d. The weir loading limit is 250 m³/(m·d), so the minimum weir length is L_w = 5 184 / 250 = 20.74 m. The basin is only 7.2 m wide, so a single transverse weir at the outlet end would be far too short. The designer would need to add submerged launders extending back into the basin, with weirs on both sides of each launder, so that the total length reaches about 21 m. Long weirs reduce the upflow velocity near the outlet, which keeps settled floc from being drawn up and carried over into the filters.

Answer: 20.7 m

(e)

With one basin out, the whole flow of 10 368 m³/d goes to a single basin of 207.4 m². The overflow rate becomes 10 368 / 207.4 = 50.0 m³/(m²·d), exactly double the design value because the area is halved. This is above the temporary limit of 40 m³/(m²·d), so the condition is not acceptable at full plant flow. To stay within 40 m³/(m²·d) the plant flow would have to be cut to 40 × 207.4 = 8 296 m³/d, or 96 L/s, about 80 percent of design flow. The operator could also keep both basins in service in turn, or the designer could add a third basin so that two remain in service while one is cleaned.

Answer: 50.0 m³/(m²·d), limit not met

Problem 4 [A3-104] Rapid sand filtration rates and backwash

A rapid dual-media filtration plant in Sarnia, Ontario, treats 0.20 m³/s through six identical gravity filters, each 5.0 m long by 4.0 m wide. Under normal operation all six filters share the flow equally. A filter is washed in turn: it is taken out of service and backwashed at a superficial upward velocity of 0.010 m/s for 8.0 min, while the other five filters carry the full plant flow. Council's operating policy limits the filtration rate to 9.0 m/h when one filter is out of service. The planned filter run is 48 h, set by the turbidity breakthrough limit. The clean-bed head loss is 0.40 m, it builds up at 0.030 m/h, and a filter must be washed when the head loss reaches 2.2 m. Ignore the water used for surface wash and the time spent draining and refilling.

  1. (a) Find the filtration rate with all six filters in service. [3]
  2. (b) Find the filtration rate when one filter is out for backwash. [3]
  3. (c) Find the volume of water used to backwash one filter. [4]
  4. (d) Find the backwash water used in one cycle as a percentage of the water one filter produces in a 48 h run, with all six filters carrying equal shares. [5]
  5. (e) Find the time for the head loss to reach the terminal value, and state which limit sets the length of the run. [5]
(a)

The filtration rate is the plant flow divided by the total filter area. Each filter has an area of 5.0 × 4.0 = 20 m², so the six filters give 120 m². The flow is 0.20 m³/s × 3 600 = 720 m³/h. The rate is 720 / 120 = 6.0 m/h. This is the loading on the media bed expressed as a velocity, and it equals 1.67 mm/s. Conventional dual-media filters in Ontario are typically designed for a rate in the range of about 5 to 10 m/h, so the normal rate sits comfortably in the lower middle of that range and leaves room for the higher rate when a filter is out of service for backwashing.

Answer: 6.0 m/h

(b)

With one filter out, five filters carry the same 720 m³/h over 5 × 20 = 100 m² of area. The rate is 720 / 100 = 7.2 m/h. That is a 20 percent increase on normal operation, simply because the area has dropped by one sixth and the flow stays the same. The result is below the 9.0 m/h policy limit, so the plant can backwash one filter at a time without breaking the rule. Even so, a higher rate pushes more solids into the bed, so the operator should avoid backwashing during the highest turbidity events. The margin to the limit is 9.0 − 7.2 = 1.8 m/h, and with only four filters the rate with one out would be 720/60 = 12.0 m/h, exceeding the 9.0 m/h limit.

Answer: 7.2 m/h

(c)

The backwash flow is the superficial velocity times the filter area: 0.010 m/s × 20 m² = 0.20 m³/s. This equals the whole plant flow, which is why backwash pumping capacity must be checked against clearwell storage and not just the pump curve. The volume for the 8.0 min duration is 0.20 × 8.0 × 60 = 96 m³. A backwash velocity of 0.010 m/s equals 36 m/h, enough to expand a dual-media bed by roughly a quarter and lift trapped solids into the trough without washing out the media. The assumption here is that all backwash water comes at a steady flow for the full 8 minutes.

Answer: 96 m³

(d)

In a 48 h run, one filter handles one sixth of the flow: 720 / 6 = 120 m³/h, so it produces 120 × 48 = 5 760 m³ of filtered water. The backwash uses 96 m³, so the share is 96 / 5 760 = 0.01667, or 1.67 percent. The usual target for backwash water is below about 5 percent of production, so this plant is well within it. If the run were shortened to 24 h because of algae in the raw water, the production per run would halve to 2 880 m³, and the backwash share would double to 3.33 percent, with the same water use per wash. Run length is therefore the main lever on water loss.

Answer: 1.67 percent

(e)

The head loss starts at 0.40 m and may rise to 2.2 m, so the allowable build-up is 2.2 − 0.40 = 1.8 m. At 0.030 m/h this takes 1.8 / 0.030 = 60 h. The planned run of 48 h is shorter, so the head loss at the end of the run is only 0.40 + 0.030 × 48 = 1.84 m, below the terminal value. The 48 h run, set by the turbidity breakthrough limit, therefore governs, and the terminal head loss does not. Operators typically wash at whichever limit comes first, and the fact that 12 h of head loss capacity remains means that the filter could take a modest increase in solids loading without being washed sooner.

Answer: 60 h, so the 48 h turbidity-based run governs

Problem 5 [A3-105] Disinfection with chlorine: contact time and CT

A groundwater-under-the-influence plant in Barrie, Ontario, disinfects with free chlorine in a baffled clearwell of volume 450 m³. Tracer testing gave a baffling factor of 0.5, so the time T10 that 90 percent of the water exceeds is T10 = 0.5 × V / Q. The required CT for the target Giardia and virus inactivation at the winter water temperature and pH is 62 mg·min/L. The free chlorine residual leaving the clearwell is 1.2 mg/L. The average flow is 0.08 m³/s and the peak flow is 0.12 m³/s. Chlorine demand of the water is 1.5 mg/L, and the dose is demand plus residual. Assume the residual stays constant throughout the clearwell and use 86 400 s/d.

  1. (a) Find T10 at the average flow. [4]
  2. (b) Find the CT achieved at the average flow with a 1.2 mg/L residual and state whether the requirement is met. [3]
  3. (c) Find the minimum residual needed at the average flow to meet the required CT. [4]
  4. (d) Find the minimum residual needed at the peak flow of 0.12 m³/s. [4]
  5. (e) Using the residual from part (d) and the stated demand, find the chlorine feed rate at the peak flow in kg/d. [5]
(a)

T10 = 0.5 × V / Q = 0.5 × 450 / 0.08 = 2 812.5 s. Dividing by 60 gives 46.9 min. The baffling factor accounts for the fact that no real clearwell behaves as ideal plug flow: dead zones and short-circuiting mean that 10 percent of the water leaves earlier than the mean residence time. Using T10 rather than the mean time V/Q = 93.75 min is deliberately conservative, since regulators want the contact time that nine tenths of the water has at least experienced. A baffling factor of 0.5 is typical for a clearwell with a few baffles, compared with about 0.1 for an unbaffled tank.

Answer: T10 = 46.9 min

(b)

CT is the product of the residual concentration and the contact time: CT = C × T10 = 1.2 × 46.875 = 56.25 mg·min/L. The requirement is 62 mg·min/L, so the CT ratio is 56.25 / 62 = 0.907. A ratio below 1.0 means the plant provides only 91 percent of the inactivation credit it needs, so the requirement is not met under these winter conditions. Cold water is the critical case because chlorine kills organisms more slowly as temperature falls, which is why the required CT is higher in winter. The shortfall of 5.75 mg·min/L must be recovered by a higher residual, a longer contact time, or both.

Answer: CT = 56.3 mg·min/L, not met

(c)

The residual that just satisfies the requirement follows from CT = C × T10, so C = CT_required / T10 = 62 / 46.875 = 1.3227 mg/L. The plant is currently running 1.2 mg/L, so it needs an extra 0.12 mg/L, an increase of about 10 percent. Because the chlorine demand is steady, the increase would pass directly to the dose. A residual of 1.32 mg/L at the clearwell outlet is acceptable from a taste standpoint for most customers, but the operator must also confirm that the distribution system residual stays below any aesthetic or disinfection by-product limits when the higher dose is used, especially in the warm summer months.

Answer: 1.32 mg/L

(d)

At peak flow, the same clearwell has a shorter contact time: T10 = 0.5 × 450 / 0.12 = 1 875 s = 31.25 min. The minimum residual is then C = 62 / 31.25 = 1.984 mg/L. This is 50 percent higher than the 1.32 mg/L needed at average flow, because contact time varies inversely with flow. A residual set for average flow would fail disinfection credit every time the plant runs at peak. Operators handle this either by setting the residual target on peak-flow conditions all year, or by pacing the chlorine dose to flow with a feedback loop that holds the CT ratio above 1.0 as flow changes.

Answer: 1.98 mg/L

(e)

The dose is the demand plus the required residual: 1.5 + 1.984 = 3.484 mg/L. The peak flow in daily units is 0.12 × 86 400 = 10 368 m³/d. Since 1 mg/L equals 1 g/m³, the mass is 3.484 g/m³ × 10 368 m³/d = 36 125 g/d, or 36.1 kg/d. The feed system should be sized with a margin above this, for example by 25 percent, to provide for changes in demand during algal blooms or storms. The calculation assumes the 1.5 mg/L demand does not change with dose, which is reasonable for a stable groundwater source but should be confirmed by a breakpoint test.

Answer: 36.1 kg/d

A3 Practice Paper 22

Problem 1 [A3-106] Wastewater flow estimation and sewer design flow

The Town of Kincardine, Ontario, is checking a trunk sanitary sewer that serves a 190 ha area with a present population of 8 500. Average dry-weather residential flow is 350 L/(person·d). Industrial, commercial and institutional users add an average of 6.5 L/s with a peaking factor of 1.5. The residential peaking factor follows the Harmon equation, M = 1 + 14 / (4 + P0.5), where P is the population in thousands. Infiltration and inflow is allowed at 0.10 L/(s·ha) over the whole area. The design flow is the residential peak plus the commercial peak plus infiltration. The trunk sewer has a full-flow capacity of 190 L/s, and a sewer rehabilitation program is expected to cut the infiltration allowance by 40 percent.

  1. (a) Find the average dry-weather residential flow. [3]
  2. (b) Find the Harmon peaking factor for the present population. [3]
  3. (c) Find the present design flow in the trunk sewer. [4]
  4. (d) Find the population at which the design flow reaches the 190 L/s capacity, holding commercial flow and infiltration at their present values. [5]
  5. (e) Find the present design flow after infiltration is cut by 40 percent, and say how much extra population this would let the trunk serve, in rough terms. [5]
(a)

The average residential flow is the population times the per-capita rate divided by the seconds in a day: 8 500 × 350 / 86 400. The numerator is 2 975 000 L/d, and dividing by 86 400 s/d gives 34.43 L/s. This is the flow averaged over a dry day. It does not include the commercial flow of 6.5 L/s or the infiltration, which are added separately. The per-capita value of 350 L/(person·d) is typical for Ontario towns where it covers domestic use only, and the figure would be higher if the sewage from a nearby hospital or school were counted as part of the residential total instead of the institutional flow.

Answer: 34.4 L/s

(b)

The population in thousands is P = 8.5, so P0.5 = 2.915. The denominator is 4 + 2.915 = 6.915, and 14 / 6.915 = 2.025. Therefore M = 1 + 2.025 = 3.025, which rounds to 3.02. The Harmon equation recognizes that small populations have more variable flow, because many households tend to use water at the same time, while a large city has a smoother demand pattern. M is near 3.8 for very small populations and falls toward 1 for very large ones, reaching 2 at about 100 000 people. Using M = 3.02 means the morning peak is three times the daily average flow, a typical result for a town of this size.

Answer: M = 3.02

(c)

The residential peak is 34.43 × 3.024 = 104.1 L/s. The commercial peak is 6.5 × 1.5 = 9.75 L/s. Infiltration is 0.10 L/(s·ha) × 190 ha = 19.0 L/s. The design flow is the sum: 104.1 + 9.75 + 19.0 = 132.9 L/s. This is 70 percent of the 190 L/s capacity, so the sewer has about 57 L/s of spare capacity today. The infiltration portion is 14 percent of the total design flow, a significant share given that it is only part of the sewer's real wet-weather problem. Inflow from sump pumps and roof leaders during storms is not part of this allowance, so a separate wet-weather check would still be advisable.

Answer: 132.9 L/s

(d)

Let the unknown population be p persons. The design flow is p × 350 / 86 400 × M(p) + 9.75 + 19.0, where M(p) = 1 + 14 / (4 + √(p/1000)). Setting it equal to 190 L/s requires 4.051 × 10⁻³ × p × M(p) = 161.25 L/s. Because M falls as p grows, the equation must be solved by trial: at p = 14 000, M = 1 + 14 / (4 + 3.742) = 2.808, giving 159.3 L/s; at p = 14 206 M = 2.805 and the residential peak reaches about 161 L/s. The population limit is therefore about 14 200, which is 67 percent more than today. With steady growth of 2 percent per year, that capacity would last about 26 years, assuming no change in per-capita use.

Answer: About 14 200 people

(e)

After the rehabilitation program, infiltration falls to 0.60 × 19.0 = 11.4 L/s, a saving of 7.6 L/s. The design flow becomes 104.1 + 9.75 + 11.4 = 125.3 L/s. This frees capacity that equals about 7.6 L/s of the residential peak, which is the peak flow from only about 600 people at M = 3.0 and 350 L/(person·d), so the added room is modest compared with the gap to 190 L/s. The result shows that rehabilitation delays but does not remove the need for trunk upgrades, and it must be weighed against the cost of lining or replacing sewers that leak. Lower infiltration also cuts pumping and treatment costs, which adds to the benefit.

Answer: 125.3 L/s

Problem 2 [A3-107] Sanitary sewer hydraulics: Manning, velocity and partial flow

A 300 mm diameter circular PVC sanitary sewer in Mississauga, Ontario, is being designed with Manning n = 0.013 at a grade of 0.30 percent, S = 0.0030, and is assumed to have constant n at all depths. The design peak flow is 30 L/s and the minimum flow in the first years of service is 7 L/s. The municipality requires a velocity of at least 0.6 m/s at the minimum flow, so that solids do not settle, and a depth ratio d/D no greater than 0.60 at the peak flow. For a circular pipe flowing partly full, the central angle in radians is θ = 2 cos⁻¹(1 − 2y/D), the area is A = (D²/8)(θ − sin θ) and the wetted perimeter is Pw = Dθ/2, where y is the depth of flow. Use Manning in SI units, V = R2/3 S1/2 / n.

  1. (a) Find the full-flow capacity of the pipe at 0.30 percent grade. [3]
  2. (b) Find the depth ratio d/D at the peak flow of 30 L/s and say whether the 0.60 limit is met. [4]
  3. (c) Find the velocity at the minimum flow of 7 L/s and say whether the cleansing criterion is met. [4]
  4. (d) Find the smallest grade that gives 0.6 m/s at the minimum flow. [5]
  5. (e) Find the full-flow capacity at that new grade. [4]
(a)

For full flow the area is A = πD²/4 = π × 0.09 / 4 = 0.07069 m², and the hydraulic radius is R = D/4 = 0.075 m. Then R2/3 = 0.0750.6667 = 0.1778, and S1/2 = 0.00300.5 = 0.05477. Manning gives V = 0.1778 × 0.05477 / 0.013 = 0.749 m/s. The capacity is Q = V A = 0.749 × 0.07069 = 0.05297 m³/s = 53.0 L/s. The peak design flow of 30 L/s is 57 percent of this, which is a normal margin for a sanitary sewer that has to carry uncertain future flows. Full-flow values are used as a reference for the partial-flow calculations below.

Answer: Qfull = 53.0 L/s

(b)

The depth ratio is found by trial, because Manning's equation for a partially full circle cannot be inverted directly. Choose d/D, compute θ, A and R, and calculate Q = A R2/3 S1/2 / n until Q = 0.030 m³/s. At d/D = 0.539, y = 0.1616 m, θ = 2 cos⁻¹(1 − 2 × 0.539) = 3.30 rad, A = 0.0388 m², and R = 0.0785 m. This gives Q = 0.0388 × 0.07852/3 × 0.05477 / 0.013 = 0.030 m³/s as required. The depth ratio of 0.539 is below the 0.60 limit, so the criterion is met. The velocity at that depth is 0.030 / 0.0388 = 0.77 m/s, slightly more than the full flow velocity, as expected near mid-depth.

Answer: d/D = 0.539, limit met

(c)

At 7 L/s the depth is again found by trial. A depth ratio of d/D = 0.2455 (y = 0.0737 m) gives θ = 2 cos⁻¹(1 − 0.491) = 2.07 rad, A = 0.01347 m² and R = 0.0433 m. Manning's capacity there is 0.01347 × 0.04332/3 × 0.05477 / 0.013 = 0.0070 m³/s, matching the flow. The velocity is V = Q / A = 0.007 / 0.01347 = 0.52 m/s. This is below the 0.6 m/s cleansing velocity, so the criterion is not met at the minimum flow. Sediment would tend to deposit in the early years, and the maintenance crew would need to flush the line more often than would be acceptable.

Answer: 0.52 m/s, not met

(d)

Increasing the grade raises velocity at all flows. Setting up the same partial-flow calculation as in part (c) with the velocity target of 0.6 m/s at Q = 0.007 m³/s, the required flow area is A = Q / V = 0.007 / 0.6 = 0.01167 m². Solving for the depth and hydraulic radius consistent with that area and then for the slope from S = (V n / R2/3)², the result is S = 0.0045, or 0.45 percent. This is 50 percent steeper than the first trial. The sewer would need about 0.15 m more fall for every 100 m of length, which may affect the depth of excavation at the downstream end or the number of drop manholes.

Answer: S = 0.0045

(e)

At S = 0.0045, the full-flow velocity is V = 0.1778 × (0.0045)0.5 / 0.013 = 0.1778 × 0.06708 / 0.013 = 0.9175 m/s. The capacity is 0.9175 × 0.07069 = 0.06486 m³/s = 64.9 L/s, an increase of 22.5 percent over the 53.0 L/s at 0.30 percent. Because the capacity rises with the square root of the slope, the pipe now has over twice the peak design flow in reserve. The depth ratio at 30 L/s falls below 0.50, so the 0.60 limit is easily met. The designer can therefore adopt the steeper grade and meet both criteria, at the cost of extra trench depth.

Answer: 64.9 L/s

Problem 3 [A3-108] Storm sewer design with the Rational method and IDF curves

A storm sewer is being designed to drain a 6.4 ha residential block in Guelph, Ontario. The design-storm intensity-duration relation is i = 900 / (t + 6.0)0.80, with i in mm/h and t in minutes. The block has a runoff coefficient of 0.55 and an inlet time of 12.0 min. The sewer is 420 m long, and the flow travel time in it is found by assuming a mean velocity of 1.2 m/s. Use the Rational method, Q = C i A / 360, with Q in m³/s, i in mm/h and A in hectares. The pipe is circular concrete with n = 0.013 laid at 0.60 percent grade, designed to flow just full. Standard diameters are 450, 525, 600, 675, 750, 825 and 900 mm. Council expects infill housing to raise the runoff coefficient to 0.70 in future.

  1. (a) Find the time of concentration at the downstream end and the design rainfall intensity. [4]
  2. (b) Find the design flow for C = 0.55. [4]
  3. (c) Find the minimum pipe diameter required for that flow, before rounding to a standard size. [4]
  4. (d) Find the design flow after infill raises C to 0.70, with the same time of concentration. [4]
  5. (e) Find the full-flow capacity of the 750 mm standard pipe selected for part (c) and say whether it can serve the infilled catchment. [4]
(a)

The time of concentration is the inlet time plus the travel time in the pipe. Travel time is 420 m / 1.2 m/s = 350 s = 5.83 min, so tc = 12.0 + 5.83 = 17.83 min. The intensity is i = 900 / (17.83 + 6.0)0.80 = 900 / 23.830.80. Since ln 23.83 = 3.171, 0.80 × 3.171 = 2.537 and e2.537 = 12.64, so i = 900 / 12.64 = 71.2 mm/h. The design storm duration is set equal to tc because that is the duration at which the whole catchment contributes, giving the largest peak flow for this return period under the Rational method.

Answer: i = 71.2 mm/h

(b)

The Rational method gives Q = C i A / 360 = 0.55 × 71.2 × 6.4 / 360. The product 0.55 × 71.2 = 39.16, multiplied by 6.4 gives 250.6, and dividing by 360 gives 0.696 m³/s, or 696 L/s. The constant 360 converts mm/h times hectares to m³/s. This estimate assumes uniform rainfall over the whole block, a constant runoff coefficient, and that the peak occurs when the entire area contributes. Those assumptions are acceptable for a small urban block of a few hectares, and it is the reason the Rational method is normally restricted to small catchments of modest size.

Answer: Q = 0.696 m³/s

(c)

For a circular pipe flowing full, Manning gives Q = (π/4) D² (D/4)2/3 S1/2 / n. Collecting the powers of D gives D8/3 = Q n 45/3 / (π S1/2). With S = 0.006, S1/2 = 0.07746. Then D8/3 = 0.696 × 0.013 × 10.08 / (π × 0.07746) = 0.09120 / 0.24334 = 0.3748. Hence D = 0.37483/8 = 0.692 m, or 692 mm. The next larger standard size on the list is 750 mm, since 675 mm is smaller than the required 692 mm. A pipe is never rounded down in sewer design, because the calculated diameter is the minimum that can carry the flow at full depth.

Answer: D = 692 mm

(d)

With C = 0.70 and the same intensity and area, Q = 0.70 × 71.2 × 6.4 / 360. The product 0.70 × 71.2 = 49.84, times 6.4 is 318.97, and dividing by 360 gives 0.886 m³/s. The flow rises in proportion to C, so the increase is 0.70 / 0.55 = 1.273, or 27 percent. In practice infill also tends to shorten the inlet time as roofs and driveways connect directly to the sewer, which would raise the intensity as well, so this estimate is if anything a little low. A designer would note this uncertainty when deciding whether to oversize the pipe now or rely on future replacement.

Answer: Q = 0.886 m³/s

(e)

For D = 0.750 m, A = π × 0.5625 / 4 = 0.4418 m², R = D/4 = 0.1875 m, and R2/3 = 0.3275. With S1/2 = 0.07746, V = 0.3275 × 0.07746 / 0.013 = 1.951 m/s. The full-flow capacity is Q = 1.951 × 0.4418 = 0.862 m³/s. This is above the present demand of 0.696 m³/s, with a margin of 24 percent, but it is below the infill demand of 0.886 m³/s by about 3 percent. The 750 mm pipe would therefore surcharge slightly after infill. The 825 mm size would handle both cases, so the city should decide whether the extra cost of one size larger is worth avoiding future replacement.

Answer: Qfull = 0.862 m³/s, not adequate

Problem 4 [A3-109] Culvert hydraulics: inlet and outlet control

A 1200 mm diameter circular concrete culvert, 28 m long with Manning n = 0.013 and a barrel slope of 0.008, carries a creek under a county road near Cobourg, Ontario. The design flow is 3.0 m³/s. Take the inlet invert as datum, so headwater HW is measured above it. Under inlet control use the orifice form Q = Cd A √(2g(HW − D/2)) with Cd = 0.60, valid when HW > 1.2D. Under outlet control, HW = H + ho − S L, where H = (1 + Ke + 2 g n² L / R4/3) V² / (2g), Ke = 0.5, R = D/4 and V = Q/A for the full barrel, and ho is the larger of the tailwater depth and (dc + D)/2, with dc the critical depth. The road crest is 2.00 m above the inlet invert, and policy requires 0.30 m of freeboard below the crest. The tailwater is 0.90 m above the outlet invert. Use g = 9.81 m/s².

  1. (a) Find the critical depth in the barrel at the design flow. [3]
  2. (b) Find the headwater depth for inlet control and confirm that the orifice equation is valid. [4]
  3. (c) Find the headwater depth for outlet control with the 0.90 m tailwater. [5]
  4. (d) State which control governs and find the margin between the governing headwater and the allowable headwater (crest less freeboard). [3]
  5. (e) A flood in the downstream creek raises the tailwater to 1.40 m. Find the outlet-control headwater and say whether the freeboard policy is still met. [5]
(a)

Critical depth occurs where the Froude number is 1, which for any channel section means Q² T / (g A³) = 1, with T the top width. For a circular section with central angle θ at depth y, A = (D²/8)(θ − sin θ) and T = D sin(θ/2). With Q = 3.0 and D = 1.2, trial values give y = 0.952 m, where θ = 4.40 rad, A = 0.9622 m² and T = 0.9718 m, so Q² T / (g A³) = 9 × 0.9718 / (9.81 × 0.8909) = 1.0. The critical depth is therefore 0.952 m, about 79 percent of the diameter, which shows the flow is already close to filling the barrel. This value feeds into the outlet-control calculation through the term (dc + D)/2.

Answer: dc = 0.952 m

(b)

The full-barrel area is A = π × 1.2² / 4 = 1.131 m². The orifice equation rearranges to HW = D/2 + Q² / (2g (Cd A)²). Here Cd A = 0.60 × 1.131 = 0.6786 m², and its square is 0.4605. Then Q² / (2g × 0.4605) = 9.0 / (19.62 × 0.4605) = 9.0 / 9.035 = 0.996 m. The headwater is HW = 0.600 + 0.996 = 1.596 m. The validity condition requires HW > 1.2D = 1.44 m, and 1.596 m exceeds that, so the orifice equation is acceptable. The inlet is submerged, the barrel entrance acts as an orifice, and the flow is limited by the opening rather than by the barrel friction.

Answer: HW = 1.596 m

(c)

For the full barrel V = 3.0 / 1.131 = 2.653 m/s, so V²/(2g) = 7.036 / 19.62 = 0.3586 m. With R = 0.30 m, R4/3 = 0.2008 and the friction term is 2 × 9.81 × 0.013² × 28 / 0.2008 = 0.4624. Then H = (1 + 0.5 + 0.4624) × 0.3586 = 0.7037 m. The outlet depth term is ho = larger of 0.90 and (0.952 + 1.2)/2 = 1.076, which is 1.076 m. The slope drop is S L = 0.008 × 28 = 0.224 m. HW = 0.7037 + 1.076 − 0.224 = 1.556 m. The tailwater of 0.90 m is below (dc + D)/2 = 1.076 m, so (dc + D)/2 governs ho, which is the usual approach for a free outfall or low tailwater.

Answer: HW = 1.556 m

(d)

The inlet-control headwater is 1.596 m and the outlet-control headwater is 1.556 m. The larger value governs because the culvert needs the higher water level upstream to pass the flow, so inlet control governs here. The allowable headwater is the crest elevation less freeboard: 2.00 − 0.30 = 1.70 m. The margin is 1.70 − 1.596 = 0.104 m, or about 10 cm. This is a thin safety margin for a design flow, and any debris at the inlet or a flow above 3.0 m³/s would use it up. The designer should consider a bevelled or tapered inlet to improve the inlet coefficient, or a larger barrel, if a more resilient design is wanted for the road.

Answer: Inlet control governs, margin 0.104 m

(e)

With the tailwater at 1.40 m, ho is the larger of 1.40 and 1.076, so ho = 1.40 m. The velocity head loss H is unchanged at 0.7037 m. Then HW = 0.7037 + 1.40 − 0.224 = 1.880 m. This exceeds the inlet-control value of 1.596 m, so outlet control now governs. The allowable headwater is still 1.70 m, so the headwater is 0.18 m too high: the freeboard policy is not met, and the water level would be only 0.12 m below the road crest. The case shows that a culvert checked only for inlet control can fail when a downstream backwater, such as a flood in a receiving river, takes control away from the inlet.

Answer: HW = 1.880 m, policy not met

Problem 5 [A3-110] Stormwater detention pond sizing

A developer in Whitby, Ontario, plans an 8.5 ha subdivision whose runoff will be controlled by a dry detention pond that discharges through a single circular orifice. The 100-year intensity relation is i = 1800 / (t + 9.0)0.85, with i in mm/h and t in minutes. Developed runoff coefficient is C = 0.70. The pre-development site had C = 0.25 and a time of concentration of 25 min, and the pond outflow must not exceed the pre-development 100-year peak flow. Use the Rational method Q = C i A / 360 (Q in m³/s, A in ha), and size storage as the largest value of (Qin − Qout) × t over all storm durations t, with Qout held constant at the allowable release. The orifice has a discharge coefficient of 0.62, and the head on its centreline at full storage is 1.6 m. Take g = 9.81 m/s². Municipal staff are asking how much the storage grows if rainfall intensities are increased by 20 percent for climate change.

  1. (a) Find the allowable release rate, the pre-development 100-year peak flow. [4]
  2. (b) Find the required storage volume, using the largest value over all durations. [5]
  3. (c) Find the diameter of the orifice that releases the allowable flow at the full-storage head. [4]
  4. (d) Find the required storage if all rainfall intensities are increased by 20 percent. [4]
