First find the head lost across the parallel pipes using the equivalent resistance from part (b): h = Rp·Q² = 291.3 × 0.2121² = 13.11 m. Pipe 2 then carries Q2 = √(h/R2) = √(13.11/1675) = √0.007826 = 0.08845 m³/s. As a check, Pipe 3 carries √(13.11/856.9) = 0.1237 m³/s, and the two flows sum to 0.2121 m³/s, matching Pipe 1. The ratio 0.08845/0.1237 = 0.715 also agrees with part (a). Pipe 2 velocity is 0.08845/0.04909 = 1.80 m/s, while Pipe 3 velocity is 0.1237/0.07069 = 1.75 m/s, which is a sensible, nearly equal pair.

Answer: 0.0885 m³/s

(d)

The total available head is the sum of the head lost in Pipe 1 and the head lost across the parallel section, since there are no other losses and the discharge is open to the atmosphere. Head lost in Pipe 1 is h1 = R1·Q² = 242.1 × 0.04499 = 10.89 m. The head lost in the parallel section is therefore h = 24.0 − 10.89 = 13.11 m, which agrees with Rp·Q² = 291.3 × 0.04499 = 13.11 m. Slightly more than half the available head is used in the parallel section, because the two smaller, longer pipes together offer more resistance than the single larger first pipe does.

Answer: 13.1 m

(e)

With Pipe 3 closed, the whole flow passes through Pipe 1 and Pipe 2 in series, so the resistances add: Rtotal = R1 + R2 = 242.1 + 1675 = 1917 s²/m⁵. The discharge is Q = √(H/Rtotal) = √(24.0/1917) = √0.012519 = 0.1119 m³/s. Compared with 0.2121 m³/s, closing Pipe 3 reduces supply by 47 percent. This is a large loss because Pipe 3 was the lower-resistance branch. An operator would need to know that the park cannot be served at full demand while this pipe is out of service, and a bypass or storage would be needed.

Answer: 0.112 m³/s

A5 Practice Paper 16

Problem 1 [A5-076] Three-reservoir pipe problem

A regional water authority joins three reservoirs at a junction J. Reservoir A has a water surface at elevation 210.0 m, reservoir B at 195.0 m and reservoir C at 180.0 m. Pipe AJ is 1800 m long, 450 mm diameter, f = 0.019. Pipe JB is 1200 m long, 350 mm diameter, f = 0.020. Pipe JC is 2000 m long, 400 mm diameter, f = 0.018. The ground at the junction is at elevation 172.0 m. Neglect minor losses and velocity heads, and use g = 9.81 m/s² and γ = 9.81 kN/m³. Later a throttling valve is fitted in pipe JC to cut its flow to a fixed 0.120 m³/s, and the valve loss is written as K·V²/(2g) based on the pipe velocity.

  1. (a) Find the piezometric head at the junction before the valve is fitted, in m. [4]
  2. (b) Find the flow in pipe JC before the valve is fitted, in m³/s. [4]
  3. (c) Find the pressure in the water at the junction before the valve is fitted, in kPa gauge. [3]
  4. (d) With the valve fitted and the JC flow held at 0.120 m³/s, find the new piezometric head at the junction, in m. [4]
  5. (e) Find the loss coefficient K the valve must have to produce this flow. [5]
(a)

Express each head loss as h = R·Q², with R = 8fL/(π²gD⁵). This gives RA = 153.1 s²/m⁵, RB = 377.6 and RC = 290.5. The junction head HJ lies between 195 and 210, so water flows from A toward the junction, then on to B and C. The continuity condition is QA = QB + QC, that is √[(210 − HJ)/153.1] = √[(HJ − 195)/377.6] + √[(HJ − 180)/290.5]. Trial and error: at HJ = 196.0 the left side is 0.3024 and the right side is 0.0515 + 0.2347 = 0.2862, so the left is too large; at 196.5 they are 0.2969 and 0.0630 + 0.2383 = 0.3013, so the right side is too large. Interpolating, HJ = 196.39 m.

Answer: 196.4 m

(b)

The head available in pipe JC is the junction head minus the elevation of reservoir C: 196.39 − 180.0 = 16.39 m. Since h = RC·Q², the flow is QC = √(16.39/290.5) = √0.05641 = 0.2375 m³/s. The velocity in JC is 0.2375/0.12566 = 1.89 m/s, which is within the normal design range for supply mains. As a continuity check, QA = √(13.61/153.1) = 0.2981 m³/s and QB = √(1.39/377.6) = 0.0606 m³/s, and 0.0606 + 0.2375 = 0.2981 m³/s, so the flow into the junction equals the flow out. The inequality of the three flows reflects that reservoir C is 15 m below B.

Answer: 0.238 m³/s

(c)

The pressure head at the junction is the piezometric head minus the ground elevation, because velocity head is neglected: p/γ = HJ − zJ = 196.39 − 172.0 = 24.39 m. The pressure is p = γ·(p/γ) = 9.81 × 24.39 = 239.2 kPa gauge. This is a reasonable working pressure for a supply main junction, though it is below the roughly 275 kPa usually targeted in distribution design, so customers would not be connected directly here. If the junction ground were above the hydraulic grade line the pressure would be negative, which would signal that the pipe profile must be revised.

Answer: 239 kPa

(d)

With the JC flow fixed at 0.120 m³/s, the junction head must now satisfy continuity QA = QB + 0.120, with QA and QB still given by the head-loss law. Write √[(210 − H)/153.1] − √[(H − 195)/377.6] = 0.120. At H = 200.0 the left side is 0.2555 − 0.1151 = 0.1404, too large; at H = 201.0 it is 0.2424 − 0.1261 = 0.1163, a little too small. Interpolating gives H = 200.85 m, where QA = 0.2445 and QB = 0.1245 m³/s, a difference of 0.120. The junction head rises by 4.46 m because throttling JC forces more water toward B and chokes back the inflow from A.

Answer: 200.8 m

(e)

The total head available across pipe JC and its valve is H − zC = 200.85 − 180.00 = 20.85 m. The friction loss in the pipe at 0.120 m³/s is RC·Q² = 290.5 × 0.0144 = 4.18 m, so the valve must destroy 20.85 − 4.18 = 16.67 m. The pipe velocity is V = 0.120/0.12566 = 0.955 m/s and the velocity head is V²/(2g) = 0.0465 m. The loss coefficient is K = 16.67/0.0465 = 358. Rounding differences from the interpolated head give a value in the range 355 to 360. Such a high K means a heavily closed valve, which risks cavitation and noise, so the designer would look at a different valve type or at a downstream energy-dissipating arrangement.

Answer: 359

Problem 2 [A5-077] Pipe networks and equivalent pipes

A small subdivision is fed from a single loop with nodes A, B, C and D. Water enters at A at 0.250 m³/s. A take-off of 0.060 m³/s leaves at B and 0.190 m³/s leaves at C. The loop has four pipes: AB is 700 m, 300 mm, f = 0.020; BC is 500 m, 250 mm, f = 0.021; AD is 900 m, 300 mm, f = 0.019; DC is 600 m, 200 mm, f = 0.022. Head loss in each pipe is h = K·Q² with K = 8fL/(π²gD⁵) in s²/m⁵. Neglect velocity heads and elevation differences, g = 9.81 m/s². The Hardy Cross method takes clockwise (A to B to C) flow as positive, and the initial guess is AB 0.140, BC 0.080, AD 0.110 and DC 0.110 m³/s. The gauge pressure at A is 420 kPa.

  1. (a) Find the head-loss coefficient K for pipe AB, in s²/m⁵. [3]
  2. (b) Apply one Hardy Cross correction to the initial guess and give the correction ΔQ, in m³/s. [5]
  3. (c) Carry the method to convergence and give the final flow in pipe AD, in m³/s. [4]
  4. (d) Find the gauge pressure at C, in kPa. [4]
  5. (e) Find the equivalent coefficient Keq, in s²/m⁵, of a single pipe from A to C that would carry the 0.250 m³/s with the same head loss. [4]
(a)

The head-loss coefficient comes from the Darcy-Weisbach equation written in terms of discharge. Since h = f(L/D)V²/(2g) and V = 4Q/(πD²), h = 8fLQ²/(π²gD⁵), so K = 8fL/(π²gD⁵). For pipe AB: 8 × 0.020 × 700 = 112. The denominator is π² × 9.81 × 0.30⁵ = 9.8696 × 9.81 × 0.00243 = 0.23528. Then K = 112/0.23528 = 476.0 s²/m⁵. The other three coefficients, found the same way, are KBC = 888.4, KAD = 581.4 and KDC = 3408. Pipe DC has by far the largest K because its diameter is the smallest and the exponent on D is five.

Answer: 476 s²/m⁵

(b)

Check continuity at the nodes first: at B, 0.140 − 0.080 = 0.060 leaves, and at D the flow is 0.110 through. The guess is consistent. The Hardy Cross correction for the loop is ΔQ = −Σ(K·Q|Q|)/(2·Σ K|Q|), with clockwise flows positive. The head losses are AB +9.330, BC +5.686, AD −7.036 and DC −41.241 m, so the sum is −33.26 m. The denominator is 2 × (476.0 × 0.140 + 888.4 × 0.080 + 581.4 × 0.110 + 3408 × 0.110) = 2 × 576.6 = 1153.2. Then ΔQ = 33.26/1153.2 = +0.0288 m³/s, added to the clockwise pipes and subtracted from the counterclockwise pipes.

Answer: +0.0288 m³/s

(c)

Apply the correction repeatedly. After the first correction the flows are AB 0.1688, BC 0.1088, AD 0.0812 and DC 0.0812 m³/s. The second pass shows a loop head imbalance of about −2.2 m and gives a correction of about +0.0022, and a third pass gives a correction of about 0.00001. Continuing to convergence gives AB 0.1710, BC 0.1110, AD 0.0790 and DC 0.0790 m³/s. Check the closure: the clockwise path loses 476.0 × 0.1710² + 888.4 × 0.1110² = 13.92 + 10.95 = 24.87 m, and the counterclockwise path loses 581.4 × 0.0790² + 3408 × 0.0790² = 3.63 + 21.25 = 24.88 m. The two paths agree to within 0.01 m, which is acceptable.

Answer: 0.0790 m³/s

(d)

The head loss from A to C is the same along either path. Along A to B to C it is 476.0 × 0.1710² + 888.4 × 0.1110² = 24.88 m, using the converged flows. The pressure head at A is 420/9.81 = 42.81 m. With no elevation difference and velocity heads neglected, the pressure head at C is 42.81 − 24.88 = 17.93 m. The pressure at C is 17.93 × 9.81 = 175.9 kPa gauge. This is above the 140 kPa residual pressure often used as a minimum under fire flow, but the margin of 36 kPa is small, so a demand increase at C would need reinforcement of the loop.

Answer: 176 kPa

(e)

For an equivalent single pipe from A to C carrying the full network flow of 0.250 m³/s, the head loss must equal that of the network, 24.88 m. The coefficient is Keq = h/Q² = 24.88/0.250² = 24.88/0.0625 = 398.1 s²/m⁵. The result cannot be found by simply adding or combining coefficients, because the take-off at B means flow differs along the two paths, and Keq is valid only for this particular demand pattern. If the take-off at B changed, the split would change and a new Keq would be needed.

Answer: 398 s²/m⁵

Problem 3 [A5-078] Uniform open-channel flow with Manning's equation

A grass-lined trapezoidal stormwater channel in Mississauga has a bottom width of 3.00 m, side slopes of 2 horizontal to 1 vertical, a longitudinal slope of 0.0008 and a Manning roughness coefficient n = 0.030. The design discharge is 14.0 m³/s and the flow is steady and uniform. The reviewing engineer wants the normal depth, a check on whether the flow is subcritical, the critical depth that would apply at the same discharge, and the average boundary shear stress that the grass lining must resist. Use SI Manning's equation Q = (1/n)·A·R2/3·S1/2, g = 9.81 m/s² and γ = 9810 N/m³, and solve the implicit equations by trial.

  1. (a) Find the normal depth, in m. [6]
  2. (b) Find the Froude number of the uniform flow, using the hydraulic depth A/T. [4]
  3. (c) Find the critical depth at 14.0 m³/s, in m. [4]
  4. (d) Find the average boundary shear stress, in Pa. [3]
  5. (e) State whether the channel is mild or steep for this discharge, and support the answer with the critical slope. [3]
(a)

For a trapezoid the area is A = (b + zy)y, the wetted perimeter is P = b + 2y√(1 + z²) and R = A/P. With b = 3, z = 2: A = (3 + 2y)y and P = 3 + 4.472y. Try y = 1.80 m: A = 11.88 m², P = 11.05 m, R = 1.075 m, so Q = (1/0.03) × 11.88 × 1.0752/3 × 0.02828 = 11.75 m³/s, too small. Try y = 2.00: A = 14.0, P = 11.944, R = 1.172, Q = 14.66 m³/s, too large. Interpolating and rechecking at y = 1.956: A = 13.52 m², P = 11.748 m, R = 1.151 m, R2/3 = 1.0985, Q = 33.33 × 13.52 × 1.0985 × 0.028284 = 14.00 m³/s. The normal depth is 1.96 m.

Answer: 1.96 m

(b)

At the normal depth the flow area is 13.52 m², so the mean velocity is V = Q/A = 14.0/13.52 = 1.035 m/s. The top width is T = b + 2zy = 3 + 4 × 1.956 = 10.82 m, and the hydraulic depth is D = A/T = 13.52/10.82 = 1.249 m. The Froude number is Fr = V/√(gD) = 1.035/√(9.81 × 1.249) = 1.035/3.500 = 0.296. Since Fr is well below 1, the flow is subcritical, so disturbances can travel upstream and the depth is controlled from downstream. The velocity of about 1.0 m/s is also low enough to be acceptable for grass lining on this soil.

Answer: 0.296

(c)

Critical flow satisfies Q²T/(gA³) = 1, or A³/T = Q²/g = 14.0²/9.81 = 19.98 m⁵. Try y = 1.00 m: A = 5.00, T = 7.00, A³/T = 17.86, too small. Try y = 1.10 m: A = 5.72, T = 7.40, A³/T = 25.3, too large. Interpolating to y = 1.03 m: A = (3 + 2.06) × 1.03 = 5.212, T = 3 + 4.12 = 7.12, A³/T = 141.6/7.12 = 19.9. A final adjustment gives yc = 1.031 m, where A = 5.222 m² and T = 7.126 m. Critical depth is much smaller than the normal depth of 1.956 m, which already tells us the flow is subcritical.

Answer: 1.03 m

(d)

The average boundary shear stress on the wetted perimeter follows from a force balance on a length of uniform flow: τ0 = γ·R·S. The hydraulic radius at normal depth is R = 13.52/11.748 = 1.151 m. Then τ0 = 9810 × 1.151 × 0.0008 = 9.03 Pa. This is an average value; the maximum on the channel bed is somewhat larger, often taken as about 1.5 times the average for a trapezoid, and the shear on the side slopes is lower. The figure should be compared with the permissible shear stress for the grass lining and soil type, and the margin checked for the short period when the lining is bare after construction.

Answer: 9.03 Pa

(e)

A channel is mild if the normal depth exceeds the critical depth at the same discharge, and steep if the normal depth is smaller. Here yn = 1.956 m exceeds yc = 1.031 m, so the channel is mild, consistent with Fr = 0.296. The critical slope is the bed slope at which uniform flow at 14.0 m³/s would be exactly critical. At yc: A = 5.222 m², P = 3 + 2 × 1.031 × 2.236 = 7.611 m, R = 0.6861 m. Then Sc = (Q·n)²/(A²·R4/3) = (14.0 × 0.030)²/(5.222² × 0.68614/3) = 0.1764/(27.27 × 0.6055) = 0.0107. The actual slope of 0.0008 is about 13 times flatter than critical, so the channel is clearly mild.

Answer: Mild; critical slope about 0.0107

Problem 4 [A5-079] Best hydraulic sections and compound channels

Two channel problems arise on a flood-relief scheme in southern Ontario. First, a concrete-lined trapezoidal diversion channel (n = 0.014) with side slopes of 1.5 horizontal to 1 vertical and a slope of 0.0005 must carry 20.0 m³/s, and the designer wants the most efficient section. Second, the natural river channel downstream is compound: the main channel has a bottom width of 8.0 m, side slopes of 1 to 1 and a bankfull depth of 2.0 m, with n = 0.030. On each side a floodplain 25.0 m wide has n = 0.060 and, in the flood considered, the water is 1.0 m deep over it, giving a total depth of 3.0 m. Each floodplain has a wetted perimeter of 25.5 m, and the bed slope is 0.0004. Use the divided-channel method with the vertical interfaces excluded from the wetted perimeter.

  1. (a) Find the depth of flow in the best hydraulic trapezoid for the diversion channel, in m. [5]
  2. (b) Find the bottom width of that section, in m. [3]
  3. (c) Find the total discharge of the compound river channel at 3.0 m depth, in m³/s. [8]
  4. (d) Treating the whole compound section as a single channel with n = 0.030, find the percentage by which the discharge would be overestimated. [4]
(a)

For a given area the best hydraulic section has the least wetted perimeter and hence the greatest discharge; for a trapezoid with fixed side slope z this occurs when R = y/2, which requires b = 2y(√(1 + z²) − z). With z = 1.5, √(1 + z²) = 1.8028, so b = 2y(0.3028) = 0.6056y. Then A = (b + zy)y = 2.1056y² and P = b + 2y√(1 + z²) = 4.2111y, giving R = 0.5y as required. Manning: Q = (1/n)·A·R2/3·S1/2 = (1/0.014) × 2.1056y² × (0.5y)2/3 × 0.02236 = 2.1185·y8/3. Setting this to 20.0 gives y8/3 = 9.440, so y = 9.4403/8 = 2.321 m.

Answer: 2.32 m

(b)

The width follows from the best-section condition derived in part (a): b = 0.6056 × y = 0.6056 × 2.321 = 1.405 m. The section therefore has a very narrow bottom of 1.41 m and a top width of 1.405 + 2 × 1.5 × 2.321 = 8.37 m. Its area is A = 2.1056 × 2.321² = 11.34 m² and its wetted perimeter is 9.77 m, so the hydraulic radius is 1.160 m, exactly half the depth. The mean velocity is 20.0/11.34 = 1.76 m/s, comfortable for concrete lining. In practice a deep narrow section needs more excavation and a freeboard allowance, so the best hydraulic section is not always the cheapest.

Answer: 1.41 m

(c)

Divide the section by vertical lines at the bankfull edges. Main channel: area below bankfull is (8 + 12)/2 × 2.0 = 20.0 m² and the top width at bankfull is 8 + 2 × 2 = 12 m, so with 1.0 m above bankfull the area is 20 + 12 × 1.0 = 32.0 m². Its wetted perimeter is 8 + 2 × 2.0 × √2 = 13.657 m, giving R = 2.343 m and Qm = (1/0.030) × 32.0 × 2.3432/3 × 0.02 = 37.6 m³/s. Each floodplain has A = 25.0 × 1.0 = 25.0 m², P = 25.5 m, R = 0.980 m, and Qf = (1/0.060) × 25.0 × 0.9802/3 × 0.02 = 8.22 m³/s. The total is 37.6 + 2 × 8.22 = 54.1 m³/s.

Answer: 54.1 m³/s

(d)

If the section is treated as one channel with n = 0.030, the area is 32.0 + 2 × 25.0 = 82.0 m² and the wetted perimeter is the full boundary, 13.657 + 2 × 25.5 = 64.66 m, so R = 1.268 m. Then Q = (1/0.030) × 82.0 × 1.2682/3 × 0.02 = 64.05 m³/s. Compared with the divided-channel result of 54.08 m³/s, the single-channel estimate is high by (64.05 − 54.08)/54.08 = 18.4 percent. The error arises because the floodplains are rougher and shallower, so they carry much less flow per unit area than the main channel. Ignoring that difference would underpredict the flood level for the real flow.

Answer: 18.4 percent

Problem 5 [A5-080] Specific energy, critical depth and control sections

A concrete-lined rectangular approach channel, 5.00 m wide, carries 15.0 m³/s at a depth of 2.10 m on a horizontal bed upstream of a proposed flow-control structure at a water treatment plant intake. Two options are considered. Option 1 is a raised sill across the full width, with a smooth short transition so that energy losses may be neglected. Option 2 is a smooth contraction of the channel width with no sill. Assume hydrostatic pressure and uniform velocity at each section, use g = 9.81 m/s², and treat the flow upstream as subcritical in every case. The reviewing engineer wants to know how much sill the approach flow can tolerate, and what happens when the limit is exceeded.

  1. (a) Find the critical depth in the 5.00 m wide channel, in m. [4]
  2. (b) Find the maximum sill height that can be installed without raising the upstream depth, in m. [4]
  3. (c) A sill 0.90 m high is built instead. Find the new upstream depth for the same discharge, in m. [5]
  4. (d) For Option 2, find the smallest channel width at the contraction that can pass the flow without raising the upstream depth above 2.10 m, in m. [4]
  5. (e) Find the Froude number of the existing approach flow. [3]
(a)

For a rectangular channel the critical depth depends only on the discharge per unit width: q = Q/b = 15.0/5.00 = 3.00 m²/s. Then yc = (q²/g)1/3 = (9.00/9.81)1/3 = (0.9174)1/3 = 0.9717 m. At this depth the specific energy is a minimum, with Emin = 1.5yc = 1.4575 m, and the velocity equals the wave speed √(g·yc) = 3.087 m/s. Any section where the depth reaches critical acts as a control: the flow upstream cannot be influenced by conditions further downstream once critical depth forms there, so this value governs all of the sill and contraction questions that follow.

Answer: 0.972 m

(b)

The approach flow has velocity V1 = q/y1 = 3.00/2.10 = 1.4286 m/s and specific energy E1 = y1 + V1²/(2g) = 2.10 + 2.0408/19.62 = 2.10 + 0.1040 = 2.2040 m. Over a frictionless sill of height Δz the specific energy falls to E1 − Δz. This cannot go below Emin = 1.4575 m, because no flow can pass with less specific energy. The limiting sill height is therefore Δzmax = 2.2040 − 1.4575 = 0.7465 m. At that height critical flow occurs on the sill crest, which becomes a control section, and any taller sill will force the upstream water level to rise.

Answer: 0.746 m

(c)

A 0.90 m sill exceeds the 0.7465 m limit, so the sill is a control and flow over the crest is critical. Specific energy over the crest is Emin = 1.4575 m, so the upstream specific energy is E = 0.90 + 1.4575 = 2.3575 m. Solve y + q²/(2g y²) = 2.3575 on the subcritical branch, with q²/(2g) = 9/19.62 = 0.4587. Try y = 2.25: 2.25 + 0.4587/5.0625 = 2.3406, too low. Try y = 2.30: 2.30 + 0.4587/5.29 = 2.3867, too high. Interpolating and checking y = 2.268: 2.268 + 0.4587/5.1438 = 2.3572. The upstream depth rises from 2.10 to 2.27 m, an increase of 0.17 m, and the discharge is unchanged.

Answer: 2.27 m

(d)

With no sill the specific energy through the contraction equals E1 = 2.2040 m. The narrowest width that can pass 15.0 m³/s without raising the upstream level is the width at which the contraction flows at critical depth, with E1 = Emin = 1.5yc. So yc = 2.2040/1.5 = 1.4693 m. The critical discharge per unit width is q = √(g·yc³) = √(9.81 × 3.1718) = √31.116 = 5.578 m²/s. The minimum width is b = Q/q = 15.0/5.578 = 2.689 m. The width would have to fall from 5.00 m to 2.69 m, a reduction of 46 percent, before the contraction chokes the flow, whereas the sill reaches the same condition at a height of 0.746 m.

Answer: 2.69 m

(e)

The Froude number of the approach flow is Fr = V/√(g·y) = 1.4286/√(9.81 × 2.10) = 1.4286/√20.601 = 1.4286/4.539 = 0.3147. This is well below 1, so the flow is subcritical, consistent with the assumption in the statement. The same result follows from Fr² = q²/(g·y³) = 9.00/(9.81 × 9.261) = 0.0991, giving Fr = 0.3147. A low Froude number means the approach flow is deep and slow, and it is sensitive to downstream controls such as a sill or contraction, which is why the water level upstream rises when the limits found in parts (b) and (d) are exceeded.

Answer: 0.315

A5 Practice Paper 17

Problem 1 [A5-081] Flow measurement: weirs, sluice gates and flumes

A conservation authority in the Grand River watershed gauges the outflow of a stormwater retention pond with a rectangular sharp-crested weir, 2.400 m long, with full end contractions already accounted for in the coefficient. Use Q = Cd (2/3) √(2g) L H1.5 with Cd = 0.62, take g = 9.81 m/s², and neglect approach velocity. The measured head on the crest is H = 0.350 m. The weir discharge then flows to a concrete canal 1.800 m wide, where a vertical sluice gate discharges freely beneath an upstream depth of 1.500 m, with Q = Cd b a √(2g y1) and Cd = 0.60 for the gate. Farther downstream the same discharge passes through the 0.600 m wide level throat of a flume, in which critical flow forms.

  1. (a) Calculate the discharge over the weir. [5]
  2. (b) Calculate the sluice gate opening, in millimetres, that passes this same discharge. [5]
  3. (c) Calculate the critical depth in the flume throat for this discharge. [5]
  4. (d) The head gauge may be misread by 5 mm. Find the resulting percentage error in the weir discharge. [5]
(a)

Governing equation: Q = Cd (2/3) √(2g) L H1.5 for a free rectangular sharp-crested weir with the approach velocity neglected. Substitute: √(2g) = √19.62 = 4.4294 m0.5/s, and H1.5 = 0.3501.5 = 0.2071 m1.5. Then Q = 0.62 × 0.6667 × 4.4294 × 2.400 × 0.2071 = 0.910 m³/s. The coefficient 0.62 already includes the effect of contraction and the departure from hydrostatic pressure across the nappe, so no separate end-contraction correction is applied. The head is measured upstream of the drawdown, which is why the formula uses the gauge reading and not the crest-edge depth. This discharge is used for every later part, so keep the unrounded value.

Answer: 0.910 m³/s

(b)

The gate equation is Q = Cd b a √(2g y1), solved for the opening a. The same discharge must pass, 0.9098 m³/s, through the 1.800 m wide gate under y1 = 1.500 m. √(2g y1) = √(19.62 × 1.500) = √29.43 = 5.4249 m/s. Then a = Q / (Cd b √(2g y1)) = 0.9098 / (0.60 × 1.800 × 5.4249) = 0.9098 / 5.8589 = 0.1553 m, that is 155 mm. The ratio a/y1 = 0.104 is small, so the flow leaves as a thin, fast jet and the free-discharge assumption in the given coefficient is reasonable. A larger opening would pass more flow, so the gate can also be used to throttle the canal.

Answer: 155 mm

(c)

At the throat, critical flow means the Froude number is one, so the critical depth for a rectangular section is yc = (q²/g)1/3, where q is the discharge per unit width. q = Q / b = 0.9098 / 0.600 = 1.5164 m²/s. Then q² = 2.2995 m⁴/s², and q²/g = 2.2995 / 9.81 = 0.2344 m³. The cube root gives yc = 0.617 m. The corresponding specific energy at the throat is 1.5 yc = 0.925 m, so the upstream approach in the flume must supply at least that much energy above the throat bed for the control to form. Critical depth is a unique function of discharge, which is the reason a flume can serve as a flow meter.

Answer: 0.617 m

(d)

Differentiate the weir equation: Q varies as H1.5, so dQ/Q = 1.5 dH/H. With dH = 0.005 m and H = 0.350 m, dQ/Q = 1.5 × 0.005 / 0.350 = 0.0214, an error of about 2.14 percent. In absolute terms, 0.0214 × 0.910 = 0.0195 m³/s. The error is larger than the relative error in head itself because of the 3/2 power, so low heads on a weir give the worst relative error for a fixed gauge uncertainty. A candidate should recommend a stilling well and a more precise gauge, or a V-notch for small flows, since V-notch discharge varies as H2.5 but is far more sensitive at low flow.

Answer: 2.14 %

Problem 2 [A5-082] Gradually varied flow profiles and step computations

A lined diversion canal near Niagara Falls is rectangular, 6.00 m wide, with Manning's n = 0.025 and a constant bed slope of 0.0008. It carries 14.0 m³/s. A low weir across the canal holds the water at a depth of 2.80 m just upstream of the weir. Use g = 9.81 m/s² and Manning's equation in SI units. Treat the canal as prismatic and the flow as gradually varied, with the velocity coefficient equal to 1.0. For the direct step method, use the average of the friction slopes computed at the two end depths of the reach, and treat the profile from the weir upstream to a section where the depth is 2.40 m as one single step. Distances are positive upstream of the weir.

  1. (a) Calculate the critical depth. [4]
  2. (b) Calculate the normal depth and state the type of the gradually varied flow profile at the weir. [5]
  3. (c) Calculate the average friction slope for the single reach between depths of 2.80 m and 2.40 m, in units of 10⁻⁴. [5]
  4. (d) Calculate the length of the single reach from the weir to the section where the depth is 2.40 m. [6]
(a)

For a rectangular channel, critical depth is yc = (q²/g)1/3 with q = Q/b. Here q = 14.0 / 6.00 = 2.333 m²/s, so q² = 5.444 m⁴/s². Then q²/g = 5.444 / 9.81 = 0.5550 m³, and yc = 0.55501/3 = 0.822 m. This depth is independent of the bed slope and roughness, depending only on the discharge per unit width. It is the dividing line between subcritical and supercritical flow, and it will be needed in part b to decide whether the channel slope is mild or steep. Depths larger than 0.822 m at this discharge are subcritical, so the backwater curve from the weir is controlled from downstream.

Answer: 0.822 m

(b)

Normal depth satisfies Manning's equation, Q = (1/n) A R2/3 S01/2 with A = 6y and R = 6y / (6 + 2y). Solving by trial gives y = 1.875 m: A = 11.25 m², wetted perimeter 9.75 m, R = 1.154 m, R2/3 = 1.100, so Q = (1/0.025)(11.25)(1.100)(0.02828) = 14.0 m³/s as required. Since yn = 1.875 m exceeds yc = 0.822 m, the slope is mild. The weir holds the depth at 2.80 m, which is above yn, so the profile lies above both normal and critical depth: an M1 backwater curve, with depth decreasing upstream toward yn asymptotically.

Answer: 1.87 m, M1 profile

(c)

Friction slope from Manning is Sf = (n V)² / R4/3. At y = 2.80 m: A = 16.80 m², V = 14.0 / 16.80 = 0.8333 m/s, P = 11.60 m, R = 1.448 m, R4/3 = 1.636, so Sf = (0.025 × 0.8333)² / 1.636 = 4.340 × 10-4 / 1.636 = 2.65 × 10⁻⁴. At y = 2.40 m: A = 14.40 m², V = 0.9722 m/s, P = 10.80 m, R = 1.3333 m, R4/3 = 1.4678, so Sf = (0.02431)² / 1.4678 = 5.908 × 10-4 / 1.4678 = 4.03 × 10⁻⁴. The average is (2.65 + 4.03)/2 = 3.34 × 10⁻⁴. The friction slope rises as the depth falls because the velocity grows, and this average is the representative value used in the direct step formula.

Answer: 3.34 × 10⁻⁴

(d)

The direct step equation is Δx = (E2 - E1) / (S0 - Sf,avg), with specific energy E = y + V²/(2g). At the weir, y = 2.80 m and V = 0.8333 m/s, so E1 = 2.80 + 0.6944/19.62 = 2.8354 m. At y = 2.40 m, V = 0.9722 m/s, so E2 = 2.40 + 0.9452/19.62 = 2.4482 m. Then Δx = (2.4482 - 2.8354) / (0.0008 - 0.000334) = -0.3872 / 0.000466 = -830 m. The negative sign means the 2.40 m depth lies upstream of the weir, about 830 m away. One step over this large depth change is coarse, and a real design would use several smaller steps, but the single step gives a usable estimate of the backwater length.

Answer: 830 m

Problem 3 [A5-083] Hydraulic jump: sequent depths and energy loss

At the intake of a water-treatment plant on Lake Ontario, a vertical sluice gate controls flow in a rectangular concrete channel 5.00 m wide. The gate opening is 0.500 m, the upstream depth is 4.20 m, and the contraction coefficient of the jet is 0.61, so the depth at the vena contracta is 0.61 times the opening. Neglect energy loss between the upstream pool and the vena contracta, take g = 9.81 m/s², and use ρ = 1000 kg/m³. A hydraulic jump is expected downstream of the gate, and the channel is horizontal and frictionless over the length considered. The tailwater, which is the depth set by the channel downstream, is 1.70 m. The plant engineer wants to know whether the jump will stay close to the gate and how much power it dissipates.

  1. (a) Calculate the velocity of the jet at the vena contracta. [4]
  2. (b) Calculate the sequent depth required for a jump to form immediately downstream of the gate. [5]
  3. (c) Calculate the head loss in the jump. [4]
  4. (d) Calculate the power dissipated in the jump. [4]
  5. (e) Calculate the depth by which the available tailwater is short of the sequent depth. [3]
(a)

The depth at the vena contracta is y1 = Cc a = 0.61 × 0.500 = 0.305 m. Apply the energy equation between the upstream pool, where the velocity head is neglected, and the vena contracta with no loss: 4.20 = y1 + V1²/(2g). Then V1 = √(2g (4.20 - 0.305)) = √(19.62 × 3.895) = √76.42 = 8.74 m/s. The discharge per metre of width is q = y1 V1 = 0.305 × 8.742 = 2.666 m²/s, and the total flow is Q = 5.00 × 2.666 = 13.33 m³/s. The jet is thin and fast, which is the supercritical entry condition that a hydraulic jump needs.

Answer: 8.74 m/s

(b)

The Froude number at the contracted section is Fr1 = V1 / √(g y1) = 8.742 / √(9.81 × 0.305) = 8.742 / 1.730 = 5.05, so the flow is strongly supercritical. The sequent depth for a rectangular horizontal channel comes from the momentum equation: y2 = (y1/2) [√(1 + 8 Fr1²) - 1]. Here 8 Fr1² = 8 × 25.54 = 204.3, so √205.3 = 14.33 and y2 = 0.1525 × 13.33 = 2.03 m. A jump with a Froude number between 4.5 and 9 is a stable, well-formed jump, so the dissipation is predictable. This y2 is what the tailwater would have to equal to hold the jump at the gate.

Answer: 2.03 m

(c)

For a jump in a horizontal rectangular channel, the head loss is hL = (y2 - y1)³ / (4 y1 y2). With y1 = 0.305 m and y2 = 2.033 m, y2 - y1 = 1.728 m, and its cube is 5.160 m³. The denominator is 4 × 0.305 × 2.033 = 2.480 m². Then hL = 5.160 / 2.480 = 2.08 m. The check is that the specific energy before the jump is 4.20 m and after the jump it is y2 + q²/(2 g y2²) = 2.033 + 0.088 = 2.121 m, and the difference 4.20 - 2.12 = 2.08 m agrees with the formula. About half of the upstream energy is lost to turbulence in the jump.

Answer: 2.08 m

(d)

Power dissipated is P = ρ g Q hL, since each newton of water loses hL metres of head. With Q = 13.33 m³/s and hL = 2.080 m, P = 1000 × 9.81 × 13.33 × 2.080 = 272 000 W, which is 272 kW. This is the rate at which the jump turns flow energy into heat and turbulence. The channel lining downstream must resist the resulting scour and pressure fluctuations, which is why concrete lining and a stilling basin are normally used. The same energy would be available as shaft power if a turbine replaced the gate, though the head is small.

Answer: 272 kW

(e)

The jump forms at the gate only if the tailwater depth equals or exceeds y2. Here the required y2 is 2.033 m and the available tailwater is 1.70 m, so the shortfall is 2.033 - 1.70 = 0.333 m, about 0.33 m. Because the tailwater is too low, the jump is not held at the gate. In the frictionless model it simply moves downstream to where the supercritical depth has risen to the conjugate of 1.70 m; in a real channel, boundary friction downstream of the gate produces that rise. To hold the jump near the gate, the designer could raise the tailwater by about 0.33 m with an end sill or reduce the gate discharge so the sequent depth drops to 1.70 m.

Answer: 0.33 m

Problem 4 [A5-084] Energy dissipators and stilling basins

An ogee spillway on a northern Ontario river passes flood flow over a crest 24.0 m long, with the crest at elevation 212.0 m. The discharge per unit length is q = Cd H1.5, where Cd = 2.15 in SI units and H = 2.60 m is the total head above the crest, so approach velocity is already included in H. The concrete apron at the toe is at elevation 196.0 m. Between the reservoir and the toe, friction on the face dissipates energy equal to 8 percent of the velocity head at the toe, so the energy balance is: reservoir energy above the apron = y1 + 1.08 V1²/(2g). Take g = 9.81 m/s² and ρ = 1000 kg/m³. A rectangular stilling basin of the same width follows the toe, and its design tailwater depth is 5.20 m. The basin must contain the jump with a tailwater at least 10 percent above the sequent depth.

  1. (a) Calculate the design flood discharge over the spillway. [3]
  2. (b) Calculate the depth of flow at the toe, before the jump. [5]
  3. (c) Calculate the sequent depth for a jump in the basin. [4]
  4. (d) Calculate the head loss in the jump. [4]
  5. (e) Calculate the amount by which the available tailwater is short of the required tailwater of 1.10 times the sequent depth. [4]
(a)

The unit discharge is q = Cd H1.5 = 2.15 × 2.601.5. Since 2.601.5 = 2.60 × 1.6125 = 4.1923, q = 9.014 m²/s per metre of crest. Over the full crest length of 24.0 m, Q = 9.014 × 24.0 = 216.3 m³/s. Because H is the total head, including any velocity of approach, no separate velocity correction is made. The discharge is controlled at the crest, where flow passes through critical conditions, so the value does not depend on the downstream basin. This q and Q are the design values for every later part of the problem, so the unrounded unit discharge of 9.014 m²/s should be carried through.

Answer: 216 m³/s

(b)

The energy at the reservoir level above the apron is Ez = (212.0 + 2.60) - 196.0 = 18.60 m, because the total head already contains the approach velocity head. At the toe, E = y1 + 1.08 V1²/(2g) with V1 = q/y1 = 9.014/y1. So y1 + 1.08 × 81.25 / (19.62 y1²) = 18.60, that is y1 + 4.473/y1² = 18.60. Solving by trial: y1 = 0.50 gives 0.50 + 17.9 = 18.4; y1 = 0.497 gives 0.497 + 18.11 = 18.61, so y1 = 0.497 m. The velocity is V1 = 9.014 / 0.497 = 18.13 m/s. The shallow, very fast flow carries nearly all of the available head as kinetic energy.

Answer: 0.497 m

(c)

The Froude number at the toe is Fr1 = V1 / √(g y1) = 18.13 / √(9.81 × 0.497) = 18.13 / 2.208 = 8.21. The momentum equation for a rectangular horizontal basin gives y2 = (y1/2) [√(1 + 8 Fr1²) - 1]. Then 8 Fr1² = 8 × 67.4 = 539.4, √540.4 = 23.25, and y2 = 0.2485 × 22.25 = 5.53 m. A Froude number above 4.5 produces a stable jump, though above 9 the jump becomes very rough. At 8.2, this basin is at the upper part of the good performance range, and baffle blocks would help the jump hold position.

Answer: 5.53 m

(d)

The jump head loss in a horizontal rectangular channel is hL = (y2 - y1)³ / (4 y1 y2). With y2 - y1 = 5.530 - 0.497 = 5.033 m, the cube is 127.5 m³. The denominator is 4 × 0.497 × 5.530 = 10.99 m². So hL = 127.5 / 10.99 = 11.6 m. That is about 62 percent of the 18.60 m total head available at the toe, which shows how effectively a jump turns the spillway's kinetic energy into turbulence. The power converted per unit width is ρ g q hL = 9810 × 9.014 × 11.6, about 1.03 MW per metre, which explains why basin lining must be thick and anchored.

Answer: 11.6 m

(e)

Design practice here requires the tailwater to be at least 10 percent above the sequent depth, so the required depth is 1.10 × 5.530 = 6.083 m. The available tailwater is 5.20 m, so the shortfall is 6.083 - 5.20 = 0.883 m, about 0.88 m. The available tailwater is even lower than the sequent depth itself, so the jump would be swept out of the basin. To fix this, the designer could lower the basin floor, which raises the effective tailwater, or add an end sill. Lowering the floor also changes the toe energy and y1, so the basin must be recomputed after any such change.

Answer: 0.88 m

Problem 5 [A5-085] Water hammer: wave speed and valve closure

A steel penstock at a run-of-river hydro station on the Mattagami River is 1450 m long and 1.80 m in internal diameter, with a wall 22 mm thick. The modulus of elasticity of the steel is 200 GPa, the bulk modulus of the water is 2.19 GPa, and its density is 999.1 kg/m³. The pipe is anchored against axial movement. At full load, the steady velocity is 3.60 m/s and the static head at the turbine inlet is 120 m. The pipe is rated for a maximum internal head of 260 m. Take g = 9.81 m/s². For closures longer than the critical time, use the linear-closure approximation ΔH = 2 L V / (g t), where t is the closure time. The operator needs to set the minimum safe closing time of the wicket gates.

  1. (a) Calculate the pressure wave speed in the penstock. [4]
  2. (b) Calculate the critical closure time (the pipe period). [3]
  3. (c) Calculate the pressure head rise for an instantaneous gate closure within 1.8 s. [4]
  4. (d) Calculate the pressure head rise for a uniform closure over 9.0 s. [4]
  5. (e) Calculate the shortest closure time that limits the pressure head rise to 90 m. [5]
(a)

The wave speed in an elastic pipe filled with water, anchored against axial movement, is c = √[(K/ρ) / (1 + K D / (E e))]. First K/ρ = 2.19 × 109 / 999.1 = 2.192 × 106 m²/s². Next K D / (E e) = (2.19 × 109 × 1.80) / (200 × 109 × 0.022) = 3.942 × 109 / 4.40 × 109 = 0.8959. So c = √[2.192 × 106 / 1.8959] = √1.1562 × 106 = 1075 m/s. Without the flexibility of the pipe wall the speed would be √2.192 × 106 = 1480 m/s, so the steel wall slows the wave by about 27 percent. A thinner wall or a softer material such as plastic would reduce c further and lower the surge.

Answer: 1075 m/s

(b)

A pressure wave generated at the gates travels to the reservoir end and the reflection returns to the gates after the time 2L/c. So tc = 2 × 1450 / 1075.2 = 2.70 s. A closure completed in a time shorter than tc cannot be relieved by the returning negative wave, so the full Joukowsky rise develops at the gates. A closure that takes longer than tc is slow, and the reflected wave reduces the peak. This number separates rapid from slow closure for the two later parts, where 1.8 s is below it and 9.0 s is well above it.

Answer: 2.70 s

(c)

Because 1.8 s is less than the critical time of 2.70 s, the closure is rapid and the Joukowsky formula applies: ΔH = c ΔV / g. The velocity change is the full 3.60 m/s. So ΔH = 1075.2 × 3.60 / 9.81 = 394.6 m. The resulting maximum head is 120 + 394.6 = 514.6 m, which is almost twice the pipe rating of 260 m, so the pipe would be overstressed or even ruptured. This shows why wicket gates are never closed in a time near the pipe period. The result is about 3.9 MPa of added pressure on every wall of the penstock.

Answer: 395 m

(d)

For a closure time of 9.0 s, which is more than three times the critical time, the linear approximation applies: ΔH = 2 L V / (g t) = 2 × 1450 × 3.60 / (9.81 × 9.0) = 10 440 / 88.29 = 118.2 m. The peak head is 120 + 118.2 = 238.2 m, which is below the rated 260 m, so this closure is acceptable. The margin is only 21.8 m, though, so the engineer would not choose a shorter time. The rise is inversely proportional to closure time, so doubling the time to 18 s would halve it to about 59 m.

Answer: 118 m

(e)

Set ΔH = 90 m in the slow-closure formula and solve for time: t = 2 L V / (g ΔH) = 10 440 / (9.81 × 90) = 10 440 / 882.9 = 11.8 s. The allowable rise to the 260 m rating would be 260 - 120 = 140 m, which corresponds to t = 7.6 s, so the 90 m limit includes a margin of 50 m for partial-load surge and for the inexact nature of the linear approximation. The time of 11.8 s is well above 2.70 s, so the slow-closure assumption is confirmed. The governor's closing rate should be set to take no less than about 12 s from full load.

Answer: 11.8 s

A5 Practice Paper 18

Problem 1 [A5-086] Surge tanks and column separation

A headrace tunnel at a generating station on the Ottawa River is 2400 m long and 3.20 m in diameter, and it ends in a simple cylindrical surge tank just upstream of the penstock. The gross head is 85.0 m. At the full-load discharge of 18.0 m³/s, the friction head loss in the tunnel is 6.50 m, and the friction loss varies as the square of the velocity. Take g = 9.81 m/s², and neglect minor losses and the penstock. The surge tank area is chosen as 1.5 times the minimum area given by Thoma's stability criterion, which for a simple tank with friction loss hf = α V² is A = L At / (2 g α (H0 - hf0)), where hf0 is the friction loss at full load. The designer then checks the peak surge after total load rejection.

  1. (a) Calculate the steady flow velocity in the tunnel at full load. [3]
  2. (b) Calculate the Thoma minimum surge tank area. [5]
  3. (c) Using the design tank area, calculate the maximum upsurge above the reservoir level after sudden total load rejection, neglecting friction. [5]
  4. (d) Calculate the period of the undamped surge oscillation in the design tank. [3]
  5. (e) Explain how column separation could arise in the system during a downsurge and state one design measure that reduces the risk. [4]
(a)

The tunnel flow area is At = π D²/4 = π × 3.20² / 4 = 8.042 m². The velocity at full load is V0 = Q0 / At = 18.0 / 8.042 = 2.238 m/s, about 2.24 m/s. This is moderate for a pressure tunnel and gives a friction loss of 6.50 m over 2400 m. The velocity is also the starting condition for the surge calculation in part c, because after sudden load rejection the water in the tunnel still moves at V0 and must be brought to rest by the rising level in the surge tank.

Answer: 2.24 m/s

(b)

First find the friction coefficient from hf0 = α V0²: α = 6.50 / 2.238² = 6.50 / 5.009 = 1.2976 s²/m. Then the net head used in the stability criterion is H0 - hf0 = 85.0 - 6.50 = 78.5 m. Thoma's area is A = L At / (2 g α (H0 - hf0)) = 2400 × 8.042 / (2 × 9.81 × 1.2976 × 78.5) = 19 302 / 1998.5 = 9.66 m². A tank smaller than this allows surge oscillations to grow after governor action, so the oscillation would not damp. In practice the tank is made larger, which is why the problem uses a factor of 1.5, giving 14.49 m², a diameter of 4.29 m.

Answer: 9.66 m²

(c)

The design area is As = 1.5 × 9.658 = 14.49 m². After sudden total load rejection, the kinetic energy of the water in the tunnel, which is 1/2 ρ L At V0², converts to potential energy in the tank, 1/2 ρ g As z². Equating them, with friction neglected, gives z = V0 √(L At / (g As)). Here L At / (g As) = 2400 × 8.042 / (9.81 × 14.49) = 19 302 / 142.1 = 135.8 m², so the square root is 11.65 m. Then z = 2.238 × 11.65 = 26.1 m above the static reservoir level. Friction would lower this, so the frictionless value is conservative for the tank wall height.

Answer: 26.1 m

(d)

The undamped surge in a simple tank behaves as a mass-spring oscillation with period T = 2π √(L As / (g At)). Here L As / (g At) = 2400 × 14.49 / (9.81 × 8.042) = 34 776 / 78.89 = 440.8 s², whose square root is 21.0 s. So T = 2π × 21.0 = 131.9 s, about 132 s, or a little over two minutes. A governor controlling the turbines must respond far faster than this period, otherwise it will try to correct for level swings and could pump the oscillation. That is the physical meaning of the Thoma criterion in this problem.

Answer: 132 s

(e)

Column separation occurs where the pressure in the water falls to its vapour pressure and the liquid column breaks. On a downsurge, for example after a sudden increase in turbine demand, the tank level falls rapidly and the pressure head along the tunnel falls with it. At a high point on the tunnel, or at the penstock inlet if it lies close to the crown, the pressure head may drop below the vapour pressure head, creating a vapour cavity. When the column closes again, it can produce a violent pressure spike. Measures include a larger surge tank, a tank placed closer to the high point, air admission valves, or lowering the tunnel profile so no point lies near the minimum hydraulic grade line.

Answer: Pressure falls to vapour pressure at a high point; reduce by tank sizing or air valves

Problem 2 [A5-087] Surface waves and flood waves in open channels

A power canal on the Trent River is rectangular and carries water at a steady depth of 2.00 m with a mean velocity of 1.20 m/s. At the downstream end a gate at the turbine intake is closed completely and quickly, so the flow behind the advancing wave stops entirely. This sends a positive surge upstream along the canal. Use g = 9.81 m/s², and assume the canal bed is horizontal and friction can be ignored over the short time considered. For the surge, the speed of the wave relative to the water ahead of it follows from the momentum equation for a moving hydraulic jump. For the last part, treat the canal as wide, with Manning roughness.

  1. (a) Calculate the speed, relative to the bank, at which a very small disturbance travels upstream in the undisturbed canal. [4]
  2. (b) Calculate the depth behind the surge after the gate has stopped the flow completely. [5]
  3. (c) Calculate the speed of the surge relative to the bank, in the upstream direction. [4]
  4. (d) Calculate the time for the surge to reach a point 6.5 km upstream of the gate. [3]
  5. (e) Calculate the celerity of a gradually rising flood wave in the same canal treated as wide, for comparison. [4]
(a)

A small disturbance moves at the shallow-water celerity c0 = √(g y1) = √(9.81 × 2.00) = 4.43 m/s relative to the water. Moving upstream against the current of 1.20 m/s, its speed relative to the bank is 4.43 - 1.20 = 3.23 m/s. In the downstream direction the same disturbance would move at 4.43 + 1.20 = 5.63 m/s. The flow is subcritical because V = 1.20 m/s is less than 4.43 m/s, which is the condition that lets a disturbance, and so a surge, travel upstream. This small-wave speed is the lower bound for the surge speed in part c.

Answer: 3.23 m/s

(b)

Let c be the speed of the surge relative to the bank, directed upstream. In a frame moving with the surge, the water ahead approaches at c + V1 and the water behind, which has been stopped by the gate (V2 = 0), approaches at c. Continuity gives y1 (c + V1) = y2 c. Momentum for the moving jump gives (c + V1)² = g y2 (y1 + y2)/(2 y1). Solving the two equations together numerically gives y2 = 2.575 m and c + V1 = 5.375 m/s, so c = 4.175 m/s. Check: y1 (c + V1) = 2.00 × 5.375 = 10.75 and y2 c = 2.575 × 4.175 = 10.75, so both sides agree. The depth behind the surge is 2.58 m, a rise of 0.58 m.

Answer: 2.58 m

(c)

The speed of the surge relative to the water ahead is c + V1 = 5.375 m/s, from part b. That water itself moves downstream at 1.20 m/s, opposite to the surge, so the surge speed relative to the bank, in the upstream direction, is 5.375 - 1.20 = 4.175 m/s. It is larger than the small-wave speed of 3.23 m/s from part a, as it must be, since a finite wave of positive height travels faster than an infinitesimal one. The front Froude number, 5.375/4.429 = 1.21, is only slightly above one, so the front is mild enough to be an undular bore.

Answer: 4.17 m/s

(d)

The surge moves upstream at a constant 4.175 m/s, if friction and the small speed variation are neglected. The travel time over 6500 m is t = 6500 / 4.175 = 1557 s. Dividing by 60 gives 25.9 minutes. That warning time is the useful quantity for an operator, because the water level at the head of the canal begins to rise about 26 minutes after the gate shuts, and any freeboard allowance or spill gate there must be ready before then. A weaker closure, with a smaller rise in depth, would arrive later.

Answer: 25.9 min

(e)

For a wide rectangular channel with Manning's equation, V is proportional to y2/3 and the discharge per unit width is q = V y proportional to y5/3. The kinematic wave celerity is dq/dy = (5/3) V. With V = 1.20 m/s, c = (5/3)(1.20) = 2.00 m/s. This is the downstream speed of a slow flood rise in which gravity and friction balance and inertia is unimportant. It is slower than the dynamic wave speed of 5.63 m/s, and it moves downstream, while the surge in this canal moves upstream. This shows the two wave types are physically different and need different models.

Answer: 2.00 m/s

Problem 3 [A5-088] Centrifugal pump head, power and efficiency

A raw-water pumping station at a Lake Huron intake lifts water through a single 450 mm diameter steel main, 2150 m long, to a reservoir with a static lift of 38.0 m. Use a Darcy friction factor of 0.018 for the whole main, constant for this problem, and a total minor-loss coefficient of 9.0 based on the pipe velocity. Take g = 9.81 m/s² and ρ = 1000 kg/m³. One pump has the head curve H = 78.0 - 1450 Q² (H in metres, Q in m³/s) and the efficiency curve η = 10.0 Q - 31.25 Q² (Q in m³/s, η as a fraction). A second identical pump may be installed in parallel, drawing from the same suction pool. Find the operating point with one pump and then the effect of adding the second.

  1. (a) Calculate the discharge delivered by one pump operating alone. [4]
  2. (b) Calculate the head developed by the pump at that discharge. [3]
  3. (c) Calculate the shaft power required by the pump at that discharge. [5]
  4. (d) Calculate the total discharge when both pumps run in parallel. [4]
  5. (e) Calculate the total shaft power drawn by the two pumps when running in parallel. [4]
(a)

The system head is Hs = 38.0 + K Q², with K = (f L/D + Km) / (2 g A²). A = π (0.450)²/4 = 0.15904 m², so A² = 0.025294 m⁴. f L/D = 0.018 × 2150 / 0.450 = 86.0, and adding Km = 9.0 gives 95.0. Then K = 95.0 / (19.62 × 0.025294) = 95.0 / 0.49628 = 191.4 s²/m⁵. The operating point sets the pump head equal to the system head: 78.0 - 1450 Q² = 38.0 + 191.4 Q², so 40.0 = 1641.4 Q², Q² = 0.024369 and Q = 0.1561 m³/s. This is the point where the pump curve crosses the system curve, and a pump cannot operate anywhere else.

Answer: 0.156 m³/s

(b)

Substitute the discharge into the pump curve: H = 78.0 - 1450 × 0.024369 = 78.0 - 35.34 = 42.66 m, about 42.7 m. As a check, the system curve gives 38.0 + 191.4 × 0.024369 = 38.0 + 4.66 = 42.66 m, in agreement. Of this head, 38.0 m is static lift and 4.66 m is lost to friction and fittings, which is only 11 percent of the total, so energy cost is dominated by the static lift rather than by the pipe losses at this flow. A larger main would save very little energy for this duty.

Answer: 42.7 m

(c)

The efficiency at the duty point is η = 10.0 × 0.15611 - 31.25 × 0.024369 = 1.5611 - 0.7615 = 0.800. The water power is ρ g Q H = 1000 × 9.81 × 0.15611 × 42.66 = 65 330 W, that is 65.3 kW. Shaft power is water power divided by efficiency: P = 65.33 / 0.800 = 81.7 kW. The best-efficiency flow, found by setting dη/dQ = 0, is Q = 10.0 / (2 × 31.25) = 0.160 m³/s, where η peaks at 0.800. The duty point sits almost exactly at the best efficiency point, which is where a pump should run for long life, and the motor must be sized from the shaft power, with a margin above 81.7 kW.

Answer: 81.7 kW

(d)

Two identical pumps in parallel share the flow equally, so for a total flow Q each pump carries Q/2 and the head is the same for both. The combined curve is H = 78.0 - 1450 (Q/2)² = 78.0 - 362.5 Q². Setting it equal to the system curve gives 78.0 - 362.5 Q² = 38.0 + 191.4 Q², so 40.0 = 553.9 Q², Q² = 0.07221 and Q = 0.2687 m³/s. The flow rises only by 72 percent, not 100 percent, because the extra flow increases friction loss in the common main. The head is now 78.0 - 362.5 × 0.07221 = 51.8 m.

Answer: 0.269 m³/s

(e)

Each pump now delivers q = 0.2687 / 2 = 0.1344 m³/s at a head of 51.8 m. Efficiency per pump is η = 10.0 × 0.13436 - 31.25 × 0.018053 = 1.3436 - 0.5642 = 0.779. The total water power is ρ g Q H = 1000 × 9.81 × 0.26872 × 51.82 = 136.6 kW. Dividing by the efficiency gives the total shaft power, 136.6 / 0.779 = 175.3 kW. The energy per cubic metre rises from 81.7 / 0.1561 = 523 kJ/m³ to 175.3 / 0.2687 = 652 kJ/m³, so running both pumps costs about 25 percent more per unit volume, because the higher head works against it while each pump moves a little off its best efficiency point.

Answer: 175 kW

Problem 4 [A5-089] Pump similarity laws and specific speed

A manufacturer tests a model of a double-suction volute pump at 1450 rpm. The model impeller diameter is 0.250 m. At its best efficiency point the model delivers 0.0850 m³/s against a head of 21.0 m, with an efficiency of 0.840. A municipal utility in the Region of Peel wants a geometrically similar prototype with impeller diameter 0.400 m, driven by a motor at 980 rpm. Assume dynamic similarity at the corresponding point on the performance curves, with the usual affinity relations. Apply a scale effect correction to the prototype efficiency using 1 - ηp = (1 - ηm) (Dm/Dp)0.2. Take g = 9.81 m/s² and ρ = 1000 kg/m³. For specific speed, use Ns = N √Q / H0.75, with N in rpm, Q in m³/s and H in metres.

  1. (a) Calculate the prototype discharge at the corresponding point. [4]
  2. (b) Calculate the prototype head at the corresponding point. [4]
  3. (c) Calculate the prototype efficiency, as a percentage, after the scale effect correction. [4]
  4. (d) Calculate the prototype shaft power. [4]
  5. (e) Calculate the specific speed of the prototype at this point. [4]
(a)

Discharge coefficient similarity requires Q/(N D³) to be the same for model and prototype. So Qp = Qm (Np/Nm)(Dp/Dm)³. The speed ratio is 980/1450 = 0.6759, and the diameter ratio is 0.400/0.250 = 1.600, with a cube of 4.096. Then Qp = 0.0850 × 0.6759 × 4.096 = 0.2353 m³/s. The prototype passes nearly three times the model's flow even though it runs slower, because the flow capacity grows with the cube of the diameter. This is the corresponding point, the same point on the dimensionless curve, so the prototype is also at best efficiency.

Answer: 0.235 m³/s

(b)

Head coefficient similarity requires gH/(N² D²) to be constant, so Hp = Hm (Np/Nm)² (Dp/Dm)². The speed ratio squared is 0.6759² = 0.4568, and the diameter ratio squared is 1.600² = 2.560. Therefore Hp = 21.0 × 0.4568 × 2.560 = 24.56 m. The head grows only a little because the speed reduction almost cancels the larger diameter. The relationship tells the designer that a slower motor gives a lower head for the same impeller, which is why this prototype suits a low-lift municipal main rather than a high-pressure line.

Answer: 24.6 m

(c)

Apply the given scale correction: 1 - ηp = (1 - ηm)(Dm/Dp)0.2 = 0.160 × (0.625)0.2. The power of 0.2 on 0.625 is e0.2 ln 0.625 = e0.2 × -0.4700 = e-0.0940 = 0.9103. So 1 - ηp = 0.160 × 0.9103 = 0.1456, and ηp = 0.8544, about 85.4 percent. The larger machine is more efficient because relative roughness is smaller, clearances are relatively tighter and Reynolds number is higher. Exact similarity would keep 84.0 percent, so ignoring the correction understates the prototype efficiency by 1.4 points.

Answer: 85.4 %

(d)

Shaft power is water power divided by efficiency: P = ρ g Q H / η. The water power is 1000 × 9.81 × 0.2353 × 24.56 = 56 690 W, that is 56.7 kW. Dividing by 0.8544 gives 66.35 kW, about 66.4 kW. If the efficiency were kept at 0.840, the answer would be 67.5 kW; the affinity relation gives the same value, 20.85 kW × 0.6759³ × 1.600⁵ = 67.5 kW. The scale-effect correction therefore lowers the required motor power by about 1.1 kW, which is a small but real design saving.

Answer: 66.4 kW

(e)

Specific speed is Ns = N √Q / H0.75 evaluated at the best efficiency point. For the prototype, √0.2353 = 0.4851 and H0.75 = 24.560.75 = 11.03. So Ns = 980 × 0.4851 / 11.03 = 43.1. The model gives the same value, 1450 × √0.0850 / 21.00.75 = 1450 × 0.2915 / 9.80 = 43.1, because geometrically similar pumps at corresponding points have identical specific speed. A value of about 43 in these units indicates a radial-flow centrifugal impeller, which produces high head at moderate flow, suited to this duty.

Answer: 43.1

Problem 5 [A5-090] Cavitation and NPSH

A centrifugal pump at a pumping station on the Rideau River is installed 3.20 m above the surface of the water in the intake sump. The suction pipe is 300 mm in diameter and 14.0 m long, with a Darcy friction factor of 0.021, and the foot valve, strainer and bends have a combined loss coefficient of 4.2 based on the pipe velocity. The pump delivers 0.190 m³/s at a total head of 36.0 m. The manufacturer states a required net positive suction head, NPSHR, of 3.90 m at this duty. Atmospheric pressure at the site is 99.0 kPa. Water at 15 °C has a vapour pressure of 1.706 kPa and density 999.1 kg/m³; at 40 °C, in summer from a heated industrial return, 7.385 kPa and 992.2 kg/m³. Take g = 9.81 m/s². A margin of 0.60 m above NPSHR is required.

  1. (a) Calculate the available NPSH for water at 15 °C. [5]
  2. (b) Calculate the available NPSH for water at 40 °C. [4]
  3. (c) Calculate the maximum height of the pump above the sump surface that keeps the required 0.60 m margin at 15 °C. [4]
  4. (d) Calculate the available cavitation number, NPSHA divided by total head, at 15 °C. [4]
  5. (e) State whether the installation is acceptable at 40 °C and name one practical remedy. [3]
(a)

NPSH available is NPSHA = (patm - pv)/(ρ g) - zs - hL. The suction area is π (0.300)²/4 = 0.07069 m², giving V = 0.190/0.07069 = 2.688 m/s and V²/(2g) = 0.3683 m. The loss is hL = (f L/D + K) V²/(2g) = (0.021 × 14.0/0.300 + 4.2) × 0.3683 = (0.98 + 4.2) × 0.3683 = 1.908 m. The absolute pressure head is (99 000 - 1706) / (999.1 × 9.81) = 97 294 / 9802 = 9.927 m. Then NPSHA = 9.927 - 3.20 - 1.908 = 4.82 m. The suction pipe velocity head does not appear separately because NPSH is defined at the pump inlet flange with its own velocity head included.

Answer: 4.82 m

(b)

Warm water has a much higher vapour pressure, so less absolute pressure head is left to push water into the pump. At 40 °C, (99 000 - 7385) / (992.2 × 9.81) = 91 615 / 9733 = 9.413 m. The suction loss is nearly the same, 1.908 m, since the density change is tiny. So NPSHA = 9.413 - 3.20 - 1.908 = 4.31 m. That is 0.51 m lower than at 15 °C. The margin over NPSHR is 4.31 - 3.90 = 0.41 m, which is below the required 0.60 m, so warm water takes away the safety margin even though the installation itself has not changed.

Answer: 4.31 m

(c)

The requirement is NPSHA ≥ NPSHR + 0.60 = 4.50 m. Solving the NPSHA equation for the static suction lift gives zs,max = (patm - pv)/(ρ g) - hL - 4.50 = 9.927 - 1.908 - 4.50 = 3.52 m. The existing 3.20 m lift is below this, so the 15 °C installation is acceptable, with 0.32 m to spare. This limit assumes the loss does not change with height. In design, the maximum lift also falls with altitude, since the atmospheric term drops about 1.2 m of water head per 1000 m of elevation.

Answer: 3.52 m

(d)

The available cavitation number is σ = NPSHA / H = 4.82 / 36.0 = 0.134. The required number is σR = NPSHR / H = 3.90 / 36.0 = 0.108. Since σ is greater than σR, the pump is above the incipient cavitation threshold at 15 °C, by a ratio of 1.24. This dimensionless form allows comparison among pumps of different size and speed, and a pump of high specific speed needs a larger σR than a low specific speed machine. The margin ratio would be considered thin where the flow varies, because NPSHR rises sharply with flow.

Answer: 0.134

(e)

At 40 °C, NPSHA is 4.31 m, and the required value including the margin is 4.50 m, so the installation is not acceptable. The margin is 0.41 m instead of the specified 0.60 m. A practical remedy is to lower the pump to reduce the suction lift by at least 0.19 m, or even put it below the water level as a flooded suction. Other remedies include enlarging the suction pipe to cut the loss of 1.91 m, using a smoother foot valve with a lower coefficient, or choosing a pump with a lower NPSHR at the same duty.

Answer: Not acceptable; lower the pump

A5 Practice Paper 19

Problem 1 [A5-091] Pump-and-pipe system operating points, series and parallel pumps

A municipal booster station in a Southern Ontario town lifts treated water from a ground-level clearwell to an elevated storage tank. The tank water surface sits 38.0 m above the clearwell water surface, and both are open to the atmosphere. The delivery main is 1800 m of 300 mm diameter ductile iron with a constant Darcy friction factor f = 0.020. Fittings, valves and the tank inlet add minor losses totalling ΣK = 6.0 on the pipe velocity head. Each of the two identical centrifugal pumps has the head-flow curve H = 62 − 4200 Q², with H in metres and Q in m³/s. Take g = 9.81 m/s². At its duty point each pump is 78 percent efficient. The town is deciding whether to run one pump, two pumps in parallel, or two pumps in series.

  1. (a) Find the flow delivered with a single pump running. [5]
  2. (b) Find the total flow with the two pumps in parallel. [5]
  3. (c) Find the flow with the two pumps in series. [5]
  4. (d) For the parallel arrangement, find the shaft power drawn by each pump, and comment on whether the second pump is worth running for base demand. [5]
(a)

The pipe area is A = π(0.300)²/4 = 0.07069 m². Friction plus minor loss is h = (fL/D + ΣK)V²/2g with V = Q/A, so h = (0.020×1800/0.300 + 6.0) Q²/(2×9.81×0.07069²) = 126.0 Q²/0.09804 = 1285 Q². The system curve is H_s = 38.0 + 1285 Q². The operating point is where pump head equals system head: 62 − 4200Q² = 38.0 + 1285Q², so 24.0 = 5485 Q², Q² = 0.004376 and Q = 0.0661 m³/s = 66.1 L/s. The head there is 62 − 4200(0.004376) = 43.6 m, of which 38.0 m is static lift and only 5.6 m goes into friction and fittings.

Answer: 66.1 L/s

(b)

Identical pumps in parallel share the flow equally at the same head, so each carries Q/2 and the combined curve is H = 62 − 4200(Q/2)² = 62 − 1050 Q². Equating to the system curve: 62 − 1050Q² = 38.0 + 1285Q², giving 24.0 = 2335 Q², Q² = 0.010278 and Q = 0.1014 m³/s = 101.4 L/s. The operating head is 38.0 + 1285(0.010278) = 51.2 m, and each pump delivers 50.7 L/s at that head, inside its curve because its shutoff head is 62 m. Adding the second pump raises the flow by only 53 percent, not 100 percent, because the system curve climbs and each pump must work against a higher head.

Answer: 101.4 L/s

(c)

In series both pumps pass the same flow and their heads add, so the combined curve is H = 2(62 − 4200Q²) = 124 − 8400 Q². Equating to the system curve: 124 − 8400Q² = 38.0 + 1285Q², so 86.0 = 9685 Q², Q² = 0.008880 and Q = 0.0942 m³/s = 94.2 L/s. The head is 38.0 + 1285(0.008880) = 49.4 m. Parallel wins here (101.4 against 94.2 L/s) because the system curve is fairly flat, with friction small beside the slope of the pump curve. Series only wins when the system curve is steep, meaning large friction head, or when a high static lift is not reachable by one pump alone.

Answer: 94.2 L/s

(d)

In parallel each pump delivers Q/2 = 0.05069 m³/s at H = 51.2 m. Hydraulic power is ρgQH = 1000 × 9.81 × 0.05069 × 51.2 = 25.46 kW, so shaft power per pump is 25.46/0.78 = 32.6 kW, or 65.3 kW for the pair. A single pump at 66.1 L/s and 43.6 m draws 1000 × 9.81 × 0.0661 × 43.6/0.78 = 36.3 kW. Moving to two pumps therefore costs an extra 29.0 kW to gain 35.3 L/s, and the energy per cubic metre rises from 549 to 644 kJ. The second pump is justified only when peak demand exceeds about 66 L/s; for base demand the single pump uses less energy per cubic metre delivered.

Answer: 32.6 kW per pump

Problem 2 [A5-092] Hydraulic structures, spillways and water quality dilution or reaeration

A run-of-river mill dam on a small Ontario river has a free-crest ogee spillway 24.0 m long. Use the discharge equation Q = C L H1.5 with C = 2.15 (SI units) and H the head above the crest, ignoring approach velocity. The water surface falls 1.60 m from the pond to the tailwater pool over the spillway. Upstream of the dam the river is at 18 °C with dissolved oxygen (DO) of 6.2 mg/L against a saturation value of 9.1 mg/L. Gameson's weir aeration equation is r = 1 + 0.38 a b h (1 − 0.11 h)(1 + 0.046 T), where r is the ratio of upstream to downstream oxygen deficit, h is the fall in metres, T is the water temperature in °C, a = 1.25 for moderately polluted water and b = 1.0 for a free overfall. A treated effluent of 0.25 m³/s with chloride 410 mg/L joins the river below the dam at a low summer river flow of 2.40 m³/s with chloride 35 mg/L.

  1. (a) Find the discharge when the head on the crest is 1.10 m. [4]
  2. (b) Find the head on the crest needed to pass a flood of 62.0 m³/s. [4]
  3. (c) Find the deficit ratio r for the 1.60 m fall. [4]
  4. (d) Find the dissolved oxygen immediately below the spillway. [4]
  5. (e) Find the chloride concentration after complete mixing of the effluent at the low summer flow. [4]
(a)

Q = C L H1.5 = 2.15 × 24.0 × 1.101.5. Since 1.101.5 = 1.1537 and C L = 51.6, Q = 51.6 × 1.1537 = 59.5 m³/s. The equation assumes a free, unsubmerged crest, so the tailwater must stay below the crest level during the event, and a fixed C holds only near the design head because the coefficient changes at much larger heads. The unit discharge is 59.5/24.0 = 2.48 m³/s per metre of crest, a moderate value that a concrete ogee with a stilling pool can handle without special energy dissipators.

Answer: 59.5 m³/s

(b)

Rearranging the weir equation gives H = (Q/(C L))2/3. With Q = 62.0 m³/s and C L = 2.15 × 24.0 = 51.6, Q/(C L) = 1.2016. Then ln 1.2016 = 0.1836, multiplied by 2/3 gives 0.1224, and H = e0.1224 = 1.130 m. The pond must therefore rise 1.13 m above the crest, only 0.03 m above the head that passes 59.5 m³/s. Because H scales with Q2/3, a 4 percent increase in flow adds only about 2.7 percent to the head. The result should be compared with the freeboard on the dam crest and with upstream flood-prone property before the flood is accepted.

Answer: 1.130 m

(c)

Substitute into Gameson's equation r = 1 + 0.38 a b h (1 − 0.11h)(1 + 0.046T) with a = 1.25, b = 1.0, h = 1.60 m and T = 18 °C. The factors are 0.38 × 1.25 × 1.0 × 1.60 = 0.760; (1 − 0.11 × 1.60) = 0.824; and (1 + 0.046 × 18) = 1.828. Their product is 0.760 × 0.824 × 1.828 = 1.145, so r = 1 + 1.145 = 2.145. The oxygen deficit is therefore cut by more than half as water falls over the crest. A bigger fall and a warmer river raise r, while more heavily polluted water (smaller a) lowers it.

Answer: 2.145

(d)

The upstream deficit is D_u = saturation − DO = 9.1 − 6.2 = 2.9 mg/L. Since r = D_u/D_d, the deficit just below the spillway is D_d = 2.9/2.145 = 1.352 mg/L. The downstream DO is 9.1 − 1.352 = 7.75 mg/L, a gain of 1.55 mg/L at no energy cost, which helps fish in the plunge pool. The calculation takes the saturation value as unchanged and ignores oxygen demand in the pool, so it describes the condition immediately below the dam. Further downstream the BOD of the river and the effluent will draw the DO down again along the reach.

Answer: 7.75 mg/L

(e)

Treat chloride as a conservative substance that mixes completely. The mass balance is C_m = (Q_r C_r + Q_e C_e)/(Q_r + Q_e) = (2.40 × 35 + 0.25 × 410)/(2.40 + 0.25) = (84.0 + 102.5)/2.65 = 186.5/2.65 = 70.4 mg/L. The effluent is only 9.4 percent of the combined flow, yet it doubles the river chloride, which shows why the low summer flow and not the average flow controls the effluent limit. If the 59.5 m³/s flood occurred instead, mixing would give (59.5 × 35 + 102.5)/59.75 = 36.6 mg/L, nearly the background value.

Answer: 70.4 mg/L

Problem 3 [A5-093] Dimensional analysis and the Buckingham Pi theorem

A manufacturer tests a 0.250 m diameter model of a single-stage centrifugal pump in clean water at 1450 rpm. At its best efficiency point the model delivers 0.0450 m³/s at a head of 11.4 m with an efficiency of 80.0 percent. The prototype, for a Great Lakes water intake, has an impeller of diameter 0.600 m and runs at 980 rpm, pumping the same fluid at the same temperature. The relevant variables for geometrically similar machines are gH, Q, shaft power P, density ρ, viscosity μ, rotational speed N and diameter D. Assume the prototype and model operate at corresponding points. Apply the Buckingham Pi method, and use the scale-effect relation (1 − η_p)/(1 − η_m) = (Re_m/Re_p)0.2, with Re = ND²/ν, to correct the efficiency. Take g = 9.81 m/s².

  1. (a) State the number of independent dimensionless groups for these seven variables and give a suitable set. [3]
  2. (b) Find the prototype discharge at the corresponding point. [4]
  3. (c) Find the prototype head. [4]
  4. (d) Find the prototype efficiency after the scale correction, as a percentage. [4]
  5. (e) Find the prototype shaft power using the corrected efficiency, and compare with the plain affinity-law value. [5]
(a)

There are n = 7 variables (gH, Q, P, ρ, μ, N, D). They contain three fundamental dimensions, M, L and T, and the dimensional matrix has rank 3, so the number of independent dimensionless groups is 7 − 3 = 4. Choosing ρ, N and D as repeating variables gives Π1 = gH/(N²D²), the head coefficient; Π2 = Q/(ND³), the flow coefficient; Π3 = P/(ρN³D⁵), the power coefficient; and Π4 = ρND²/μ, a Reynolds number. Geometric similarity with equal Π2 gives equal Π1 and Π3 when Reynolds effects are small, which is the basis of the affinity laws used below.

Answer: 4 groups

(b)

Equal flow coefficient requires Q_p/(N_p D_p³) = Q_m/(N_m D_m³). So Q_p = Q_m (N_p/N_m)(D_p/D_m)³ = 0.0450 × (980/1450) × (0.600/0.250)³ = 0.0450 × 0.6759 × 13.824 = 0.4204 m³/s. The speed ratio is 0.6759 and the cube of the diameter ratio is 13.824. The prototype therefore passes about 420 L/s. Operation at a corresponding point means the velocity triangles in the prototype are geometrically similar to those in the model, so the best-efficiency point scales with the same flow coefficient and the specific speed is unchanged between the two machines.

Answer: 0.420 m³/s

(c)

Equal head coefficient requires gH/(N²D²) to be the same, so H_p = H_m (N_p/N_m)²(D_p/D_m)² = 11.4 × 0.6759² × 2.4² = 11.4 × 0.4569 × 5.76 = 30.0 m. The prototype tip speed is πD_pN_p/60 = π × 0.600 × 980/60 = 30.8 m/s against 19.0 m/s for the model, which is why the head rises by a factor of 2.63 even though the shaft turns more slowly. The Pi analysis fixes only the hydraulic scaling, so cavitation margin and the stress in the larger impeller at 30.8 m/s must still be checked separately.

Answer: 30.0 m

(d)

With the same fluid, the Reynolds ratio is Re_p/Re_m = (N_pD_p²)/(N_mD_m²) = (980 × 0.600²)/(1450 × 0.250²) = 352.8/90.625 = 3.893. Reynolds number cannot be matched along with the flow coefficient, so efficiency needs a scale correction. We have 1 − η_m = 0.200 and (Re_m/Re_p)0.2 = (1/3.893)0.2 = 0.762. Hence 1 − η_p = 0.200 × 0.762 = 0.1524 and η_p = 0.8476, or 84.8 percent. A larger machine has thinner relative boundary layers and smaller relative leakage clearances, so the prototype is more efficient than the model.

Answer: 84.8 percent

(e)

Hydraulic power is ρgQH = 1000 × 9.81 × 0.4204 × 30.0 = 123.7 kW. With the corrected efficiency the shaft power is P_p = 123.7/0.8476 = 146.0 kW. The plain affinity law, P_p = P_m (N_p/N_m)³(D_p/D_m)⁵ with P_m = 9810 × 0.0450 × 11.4/0.80 = 6.29 kW, gives 6.29 × 0.3088 × 79.63 = 154.6 kW because it keeps the model efficiency of 80 percent. That overstates the shaft power by about 6 percent. The efficiency correction rests on an empirical exponent, so a designer would size the motor on the conservative 154.6 kW and use 146 kW for energy estimates.

Answer: 146.0 kW

Problem 4 [A5-094] Hydraulic models and similitude (Froude and Reynolds)

A 1:30 scale Froude model of an ungated concrete spillway and stilling basin on an Ontario hydroelectric river is built in a laboratory flume, using water at the same temperature as the prototype. In a test at the design flood the model discharge is 0.0420 m³/s, the measured velocity at the toe of the spillway is 2.10 m/s, and the flow exerts a total horizontal force of 18.0 N on the model basin floor. The model basin fills to a marked level in 22.0 s. Gravity dominates the flow, so Froude similarity governs, and both model and prototype fluids are water of the same density. Separately, a pressurised bend in the plant's cooling-water line, carrying 2.40 m/s in the prototype, is to be tested in a 1:8 model with the same fluid, where Reynolds similarity governs.

  1. (a) Find the prototype design flood discharge. [4]
  2. (b) Find the prototype velocity at the toe of the spillway. [4]
  3. (c) Find the prototype force on the basin floor. [4]
  4. (d) Find the prototype time to fill to the corresponding level. [4]
  5. (e) Find the model velocity needed for the cooling-water bend, and say whether the test is practical. [4]
(a)

Under Froude similarity Fr = V/√(gL) is equal in model and prototype, and the length ratio is L_r = L_p/L_m = 30. The velocity ratio is V_r = L_r0.5 and the area ratio is L_r², so the discharge ratio is Q_r = L_r2.5 = 302.5 = 4929.5. Then Q_p = 0.0420 × 4929.5 = 207.0 m³/s. Because both fluids are water, the density ratio is 1, and gravity is the same, so no further factors enter. Discharge scales with the 2.5 power of length, which is why a modest 42 L/s flume flow represents a flood of more than 200 m³/s on the real river.

Answer: 207 m³/s

(b)

Equality of Froude number gives V_p = V_m √L_r = 2.10 × √30 = 2.10 × 5.477 = 11.50 m/s. This velocity corresponds to a free fall of V²/2g = 11.5²/19.62 = 6.7 m, a useful check on the energy that the stilling basin must dissipate at the toe. Because velocity scales with the square root of the length ratio, model readings must be multiplied by 5.48, not by 30 or 900. The check that the prototype Froude number V/√(gL) equals the model's is the defining condition of the whole model study, and any velocity result must pass it.

Answer: 11.5 m/s

(c)

Force is mass times acceleration, so F = ρ L² V² per unit of similar geometry, and with V_r² = L_r the force ratio is F_r = ρ_r L_r³. Water is used in both, so ρ_r = 1 and F_r = 30³ = 27 000. The prototype force is F_p = 18.0 × 27 000 = 486 000 N = 486 kN. The same result follows from pressure times area: pressure scales as ρgL, which is L_r, and area scales as L_r², giving L_r³ again. This force is the total on the corresponding area of the basin floor and is the load used to check sliding of the slab and the anchor design.

Answer: 486 kN

(d)

Time scales as length divided by velocity, so t_r = L_r/V_r = L_r0.5 = 5.477. Then t_p = 22.0 × 5.477 = 120.5 s, a little over two minutes. The model fills in 22 s, but the prototype basin needs 120 s to reach the corresponding level. The time ratio also governs the instruments: a 10 Hz fluctuation in the prototype appears at 10 × 5.477 = 54.8 Hz in the model, so the sampling rate of the pressure transducers must be chosen from the model timescale and not from the prototype's.

Answer: 120.5 s

(e)

Reynolds similarity requires ρVL/μ to be equal. With the same fluid, VL is constant, so V_m = V_p (L_p/L_m) = 2.40 × 8 = 19.2 m/s, and the discharge ratio becomes Q_r = L_r. A model velocity of 19.2 m/s through a small pipe is high enough to cause cavitation, severe vibration and a large pumping power requirement, so the test is not practical with water. In practice the bend is run at a lower velocity that still keeps the model Reynolds number above about 10⁵, where loss coefficients become independent of Re in fully turbulent flow, or a different fluid is used.

Answer: 19.2 m/s

Problem 5 [A5-095] Continuity and energy equation applications

A stormwater detention pond beside a Hamilton-area subdivision is drained by a 200 mm diameter steel siphon pipe, 28.0 m long, that rises over the embankment and discharges freely to a ditch. The pond surface is the datum. The pipe crest is 2.60 m above the pond surface and lies 9.0 m of pipe from the intake, and the free outlet is 3.40 m below the pond surface. Use f = 0.018 throughout. Minor loss coefficients are 0.50 at the entrance and 0.30 for each of two bends (one before the crest, one after); there is no exit loss because the jet discharges freely to the atmosphere. The pond surface area is 1850 m² and may be treated as constant. Take ρ = 1000 kg/m³, g = 9.81 m/s², atmospheric pressure 101.3 kPa and the vapour pressure of water at 20 °C as 2.3 kPa.

  1. (a) Find the discharge of the siphon. [5]
  2. (b) Estimate the time to lower the pond by 0.25 m, treating the discharge as constant. [5]
  3. (c) Find the gauge pressure at the crest. [5]
  4. (d) Find the greatest crest height above the pond surface before the water reaches vapour pressure, and comment on how this should be used. [5]
(a)

Apply the energy equation from the pond surface (V ≈ 0, gauge pressure zero) to the free outlet (gauge pressure zero, 3.40 m lower). The available head of 3.40 m equals the jet velocity head plus all losses: 3.40 = (V²/2g)(1 + ΣK + fL/D). Here ΣK = 0.50 + 0.30 + 0.30 = 1.10 and fL/D = 0.018 × 28.0/0.200 = 2.52, so the bracket is 1 + 1.10 + 2.52 = 4.62. Then V²/2g = 3.40/4.62 = 0.7359 m and V = √(2 × 9.81 × 0.7359) = 3.80 m/s. The area is π(0.200)²/4 = 0.03142 m², so Q = 3.80 × 0.03142 = 0.1194 m³/s = 119.4 L/s. Note the flow depends on the drop to the outlet, not on the crest height.

Answer: 119.4 L/s

(b)

Continuity for the pond with no inflow gives A_s dh/dt = −Q. Treating Q as constant at 0.1194 m³/s, the volume to remove for a 0.25 m drawdown is 1850 × 0.25 = 462.5 m³, so t = 462.5/0.1194 = 3874 s = 1.08 h. The constant-discharge assumption is slightly unconservative: the driving head falls from 3.40 m to 3.15 m as the pond drops, and since Q varies with the square root of head, the average flow is about 2 percent lower than the starting value. The true drawdown time is therefore close to 1.10 h, which is acceptable for a first estimate of the detention drain time.

Answer: 1.08 h

(c)

Apply the energy equation from the pond surface to the crest. The velocity is the same all along the pipe, V = 3.80 m/s with V²/2g = 0.7359 m. Losses up to the crest are the entrance 0.50, the first bend 0.30 and friction 0.018 × 9.0/0.200 = 0.81, a total of 1.61 velocity heads. The energy balance is 0 = z_c + p_c/(ρg) + V²/2g + 1.61 V²/2g with z_c = 2.60 m. Hence p_c/(ρg) = −2.60 − 0.7359 × 2.61 = −2.60 − 1.921 = −4.521 m. The gauge pressure is −4.521 × 9.81 = −44.35 kPa, a suction of 44.3 kPa. The crest is the lowest pressure point on the line.

Answer: −44.3 kPa

(d)

The absolute pressure at the crest is 101.3 − 44.35 = 56.95 kPa, well above the 2.3 kPa vapour pressure, so the siphon does not cavitate. At the limit the absolute pressure is 2.3 kPa, so p_c/(ρg) = −(101.3 − 2.3)/9.81 = −10.09 m gauge. The energy equation gives z_c = 10.09 − 1.921 = 8.17 m. Flow does not depend on crest height as long as the siphon stays full, so in theory the crest could rise to 8.2 m.
