In practice dissolved air leaves solution well before vapour pressure and breaks the siphon, so a designer would keep the crest to about 6 m to 7 m and provide a vent and priming connection.

Answer: 8.17 m

A5 Practice Paper 20

Problem 1 [A5-096] Momentum equation: forces on bends, nozzles and gates

A horizontal reducing bend in a ductile iron water main in a Kitchener industrial park turns the flow through 90° and reduces the diameter from 600 mm to 400 mm. Water enters travelling in the +x direction and leaves in the +y direction, discharging 0.550 m³/s. The gauge pressure at the inlet is 310 kPa. Neglect head loss through the bend and the weight of the water and pipe, which act vertically and do not affect the horizontal forces. Take ρ = 1000 kg/m³ and g = 9.81 m/s². The bend is restrained by a concrete thrust block cast on the trench floor, resting on compacted granular fill with a coefficient of base friction of 0.45. The design uses a factor of safety of 1.50 against sliding and ignores passive soil pressure on the sides of the block.

  1. (a) Find the gauge pressure at the outlet of the bend. [5]
  2. (b) Find the x-component of the force exerted by the water on the bend. [5]
  3. (c) Find the magnitude of the y-component of the force exerted by the water on the bend. [5]
  4. (d) Find the minimum mass of the thrust block, and comment on practical alternatives. [5]
(a)

Continuity gives the velocities. A1 = π(0.600)²/4 = 0.28274 m² and A2 = π(0.400)²/4 = 0.12566 m², so V1 = 0.550/0.28274 = 1.945 m/s and V2 = 0.550/0.12566 = 4.377 m/s. Bernoulli between the two sections at the same elevation with no loss gives p2 = p1 + ½ρ(V1² − V2²) = 310 000 + 500 × (3.784 − 19.158) = 310 000 − 7 687 = 302 313 Pa = 302.3 kPa. The velocity head rises by 0.78 m, so the pressure falls by 7.7 kPa to pay for it. This change is small beside the 310 kPa line pressure, which is why the pressure force dominates the thrust on the bend.

Answer: 302.3 kPa

(b)

Take the water in the bend as the control volume. In the x direction the forces on the water are the inlet pressure force p1A1 (acting in +x) and the wall force F_wx. The outlet leaves in +y, so the outflow x momentum is zero, while the inflow brings ρQV1. Momentum balance: p1A1 + F_wx = 0 − ρQV1, so F_wx = −(p1A1 + ρQV1). The water pushes the bend with the opposite force, F_x = p1A1 + ρQV1 = 310 000 × 0.28274 + 1000 × 0.550 × 1.945 = 87 649 + 1 070 = 88 719 N = 88.7 kN in +x. The pressure term makes up 99 percent of the answer, so the block is sized mainly for pressure, not for momentum change.

Answer: 88.7 kN

(c)

In the y direction the water enters with no y momentum and leaves with momentum flux ρQV2. The outlet pressure acts on the water at the exit face and points in −y, into the control volume. The balance is F_wy − p2A2 = ρQV2, so F_wy = ρQV2 + p2A2 = 1000 × 0.550 × 4.377 + 302 313 × 0.12566 = 2 407 + 37 991 = 40 398 N in +y on the water. The water therefore pushes the bend with 40.4 kN in the −y direction, away from the outlet opening. The resultant on the bend is R = √(88.72² + 40.40²) = 97.5 kN, directed 24.5° below the +x axis, which is the line along which the restraint must act.

Answer: 40.4 kN

(d)

The block must resist the horizontal resultant R = 97.5 kN by base friction. With the factor of safety the required friction capacity is 1.50 × 97.48 = 146.2 kN. Friction is μW, so W = 146.2/0.45 = 324.9 kN. The mass is W/g = 324 900/9.81 = 33 120 kg = 33.1 t, equal to about 13.8 m³ of concrete at 2400 kg/m³. A block this heavy is awkward in a trench, so designers often reduce it by bearing the block against undisturbed trench wall to mobilise passive soil resistance, which was ignored here, or by using restrained mechanical joints on several pipe lengths instead of a block.

Answer: 33.1 t

Problem 2 [A5-097] Single pipe flow with Darcy-Weisbach and minor losses

A 3200 m long, 450 mm diameter cement-lined ductile iron transmission main carries raw water from a lake intake reservoir to a treatment plant storage tank in the Ottawa Valley. The pipe has an absolute roughness ε = 0.26 mm, and the water is at 10 °C with kinematic viscosity ν = 1.31 × 10⁻⁶ m²/s. The fittings give minor loss coefficients of 0.50 at the entrance, 0.20 for each of two gate valves, 0.25 for each of three bends and 1.00 at the submerged exit into the tank. Use the Swamee-Jain equation for the friction factor, f = 0.25/[log₁₀(ε/(3.7D) + 5.74/Re0.9)]². The elevation difference between the reservoir surface and the tank surface is 22.0 m, and g = 9.81 m/s². The plant wants to know whether the main can meet the present demand of 0.320 m³/s and a possible higher demand.

  1. (a) Find the friction factor at Q = 0.320 m³/s. [4]
  2. (b) Find the total head loss at Q = 0.320 m³/s and say whether the 22.0 m available is enough. [5]
  3. (c) Find the greatest discharge the main can carry with the 22.0 m available. [6]
  4. (d) Find the elevation difference needed to carry 0.400 m³/s, and comment on the 25 percent increase in demand. [5]
(a)

At Q = 0.320 m³/s the area is π(0.450)²/4 = 0.15904 m², so V = 0.320/0.15904 = 2.012 m/s. Re = VD/ν = 2.012 × 0.450/1.31 × 10⁻⁶ = 6.91 × 10⁵. The relative roughness is ε/D = 0.26/450 = 5.78 × 10⁻⁴, so ε/(3.7D) = 1.562 × 10⁻⁴. Re0.9 = 1.80 × 10⁵, so 5.74/Re0.9 = 3.19 × 10⁻⁵. The sum is 1.881 × 10⁻⁴, whose log₁₀ is −3.7256; squared this is 13.88, and f = 0.25/13.88 = 0.0180. The flow is turbulent and the roughness term is the larger of the two terms, so the pipe is approaching fully rough behaviour.

Answer: 0.0180

(b)

The sum of minor loss coefficients is ΣK = 0.50 + 2(0.20) + 3(0.25) + 1.00 = 2.65. The friction term is fL/D = 0.0180 × 3200/0.450 = 128.1. The velocity head is V²/2g = 2.012²/19.62 = 0.2063 m. The total head loss is h = (128.1 + 2.65) × 0.2063 = 130.8 × 0.2063 = 26.97 m. Friction accounts for 26.4 m and the minor losses for only 0.55 m, about 2 percent, so on a long main the minor losses can be treated as a small correction. The loss of 27.0 m exceeds the 22.0 m available, so the present demand of 0.320 m³/s cannot be delivered by gravity alone and a pump or a larger main is needed.

Answer: 27.0 m

(c)

With h = 22.0 m fixed, solve h = (fL/D + ΣK)V²/2g for V, updating f with Re each time. Start with f = 0.0180: V = √(19.62 × 22.0/(0.0180 × 7111 + 2.65)) = √(431.6/130.65) = 1.818 m/s. Then Re = 1.818 × 0.450/1.31 × 10⁻⁶ = 6.2 × 10⁵ and Swamee-Jain gives f = 0.01808. Second pass: fL/D = 0.01808 × 7111 = 128.6, the bracket is 131.2, and V = √(431.6/131.2) = 1.814 m/s. Re is unchanged to three figures, so the solution has converged. Q = VA = 1.814 × 0.15904 = 0.2885 m³/s = 288.5 L/s, which is 90 percent of the 320 L/s the plant wants.

Answer: 288.5 L/s

(d)

At Q = 0.400 m³/s, V = 0.400/0.15904 = 2.515 m/s and Re = 2.515 × 0.450/1.31 × 10⁻⁶ = 8.64 × 10⁵. Swamee-Jain gives f = 0.01788. The velocity head is 2.515²/19.62 = 0.3224 m. The head loss is h = (0.01788 × 7111 + 2.65) × 0.3224 = (127.1 + 2.65) × 0.3224 = 41.8 m. A 25 percent rise in flow (0.320 to 0.400) therefore raises the required head from 27.0 m to 41.8 m, an increase of 55 percent, since loss varies very nearly as Q². Gravity cannot supply it, and the utility would have to choose between a booster pump, a parallel pipe or a larger replacement main.

Answer: 41.8 m

Problem 3 [A5-098] Pipes in series and parallel

An industrial park in Sarnia is supplied from an elevated reservoir through a 1200 m long, 400 mm diameter main that ends at a junction J. From J, two pipes run in parallel to a common downstream node K: pipe A is 900 m long and 250 mm in diameter, and pipe B is 1100 m long and 300 mm in diameter. The Darcy friction factors are fixed at 0.019 for the main, 0.022 for pipe A and 0.020 for pipe B. Neglect minor losses and velocity heads. The hydraulic grade line at the reservoir is 32.0 m higher than the hydraulic grade line at node K, which is held by a downstream tank. Take g = 9.81 m/s². The utility is considering replacing the parallel pair by a single pipe 1000 m long with f = 0.020 and wants to know what diameter would give the same hydraulic performance.

  1. (a) Find the total flow delivered. [5]
  2. (b) Find the flow carried by pipe B. [5]
  3. (c) Find the head loss across the parallel section J to K, and comment on where an upgrade would help most. [5]
  4. (d) Find the diameter of the single replacement pipe. [5]
(a)

Write each loss as h = RQ² with R = fL/(D·2g·A²). Main: A = π(0.400)²/4 = 0.12566 m², so R0 = 0.019 × 1200/0.400/(19.62 × 0.015791) = 57.0/0.30984 = 184.0 s²/m⁵. Pipe A: A = 0.049087 m², A² = 0.0024096, R_A = 0.022 × 900/0.250/(19.62 × 0.0024096) = 79.2/0.04728 = 1675 s²/m⁵. Pipe B: A = 0.070686 m², A² = 0.0049967, R_B = 0.020 × 1100/0.300/(19.62 × 0.0049967) = 73.33/0.09804 = 748.1. For parallel pipes 1/√R_p = 1/√R_A + 1/√R_B = 0.02443 + 0.03656 = 0.06099, so R_p = 268.8. The total is 184.0 + 268.8 = 452.8, and Q = √(32.0/452.8) = 0.2658 m³/s = 265.8 L/s.

Answer: 265.8 L/s

(b)

The head loss across the parallel pair is h_p = R_p Q² = 268.8 × 0.2658² = 268.8 × 0.07067 = 19.0 m. Both pipes see this same head loss, so Q_B = √(h_p/R_B) = √(19.0/748.1) = √0.02540 = 0.1594 m³/s = 159.4 L/s, and Q_A = √(19.0/1675) = 0.1065 m³/s = 106.5 L/s. Continuity check: 159.4 + 106.5 = 265.9 L/s, which matches the total of 265.8 L/s within rounding. Pipe B carries about 60 percent of the flow because its resistance (748 s²/m⁵) is less than half that of A (1675 s²/m⁵), driven by the D⁵ term, even though B is 200 m longer.

Answer: 159.4 L/s

(c)

The head loss across the parallel section was found as 19.0 m in part (b). As a check, the main takes R0Q² = 184.0 × 0.07067 = 13.0 m, and 32.0 − 13.0 = 19.0 m is left for the parallel section. The parallel pair therefore holds 19.0/32.0 = 59 percent of the total resistance. This share is where an upgrade pays most: halving R_p would give a total resistance of 184.0 + 134.4 = 318.4 and a flow of √(32.0/318.4) = 0.317 m³/s, a gain of 19 percent, whereas halving R0 gives 91.99 + 268.8 = 360.8 and 0.298 m³/s, a gain of only 12 percent.

Answer: 19.0 m

(d)

The single pipe must have the same resistance as the parallel pair, R = 268.8 s²/m⁵, with f = 0.020 and L = 1000 m. Since R = fL/(D·2g·(πD²/4)²) = 8fL/(π²gD⁵), we have R = 8 × 0.020 × 1000/(π² × 9.81 × D⁵) = 160/(96.83 D⁵) = 1.6525/D⁵. So D⁵ = 1.6525/268.8 = 0.006148 and D = 0.0061480.2 = exp(−5.0914/5) = exp(−1.0183) = 0.361 m. A 360 mm pipe, in practice the next standard size of 375 mm, would take the place of the 250 mm and 300 mm pipes. It needs only 1000 m of trench in place of 2000 m, though the single pipe has no redundancy if it fails.

Answer: 0.361 m

Problem 4 [A5-099] Three-reservoir pipe problem

Three reservoirs supply and receive water through three pipes meeting at a junction J in a rural water system in Grey County. Reservoir A has a water surface elevation of 180.0 m, reservoir B 165.0 m and reservoir C 140.0 m. Pipe AJ is 1500 m long, 400 mm in diameter, with f = 0.018. Pipe BJ is 1200 m long, 300 mm in diameter, with f = 0.020. Pipe CJ is 2000 m long, 350 mm in diameter, with f = 0.019. Neglect minor losses and velocity heads, and take g = 9.81 m/s². The junction is at ground level, so the hydraulic grade at J is the piezometric head there. The operator wants to know how reservoir B behaves, and what would be needed to stop B from acting as a source or a sink. For the last question, a new pipe AJ of the same length and friction factor, with a different diameter, would be installed.

  1. (a) Find the hydraulic grade line elevation at the junction J. [4]
  2. (b) Find the flow from reservoir A. [4]
  3. (c) Find the flow into reservoir B, stating its direction. [4]
  4. (d) Find the flow into reservoir C. [4]
  5. (e) Find the diameter of a new pipe AJ that would just stop any flow to or from B. [4]
(a)

Write each loss as h = RQ² with R = 8fL/(π²gD⁵). This gives R_A = 8 × 0.018 × 1500/(96.83 × 0.4⁵) = 217.9 s²/m⁵, R_B = 8 × 0.020 × 1200/(96.83 × 0.3⁵) = 816.1, and R_C = 8 × 0.019 × 2000/(96.83 × 0.35⁵) = 597.8. First test H_J = 165.0 m, when B carries no flow: Q_A = √(15/217.9) = 0.2624 m³/s into J, Q_C = √(25/597.8) = 0.2045 m³/s out of J. Inflow exceeds outflow, so J must rise above 165 m and B receives water. Solve continuity Q_A = Q_B + Q_C by trial: at H_J = 166.34 m, Q_A = 0.2504, Q_B = 0.0405, Q_C = 0.2099, and 0.2504 = 0.0405 + 0.2099. So H_J = 166.34 m.

Answer: 166.34 m

(b)

Flow from A is driven by the drop from reservoir A to the junction, 180.0 − 166.34 = 13.66 m. Then Q_A = √(h/R_A) = √(13.66/217.9) = √0.06269 = 0.2504 m³/s = 250.4 L/s. This flow runs from A to J. If B were disconnected from the system the junction would settle higher, and Q_A would be smaller still; with B held at 165.0 m, the test value of H_J = 165.0 m would have given 262.4 L/s from A. Reservoir B absorbs some of the supply and raises the junction level, which cuts the flow from A to 250.4 L/s. The sign of every flow follows from the junction level relative to each reservoir.

Answer: 250.4 L/s

(c)

Reservoir B is at 165.0 m and the junction at 166.34 m, so the junction is higher and flow runs from J into B. The head across BJ is 166.34 − 165.0 = 1.34 m, giving Q_B = √(1.34/816.1) = √0.001642 = 0.0405 m³/s = 40.5 L/s into B. B therefore acts as a sink, filling at 40.5 L/s, while the supply from A exceeds what C alone can draw. If reservoir B were small, it would soon overflow. The small head of 1.34 m shows that B sits close to the junction level, and a small change in the elevation of A or C would reverse its direction.

Answer: 40.5 L/s into B

(d)

Reservoir C is at 140.0 m, well below the junction at 166.34 m, so flow runs from J to C under a head of 166.34 − 140.0 = 26.34 m. Q_C = √(26.34/597.8) = √0.04406 = 0.2099 m³/s = 209.9 L/s. Check continuity at the junction: inflow from A is 250.4 L/s, outflow is 40.5 L/s to B plus 209.9 L/s to C, which totals 250.4 L/s, so continuity is satisfied. Reservoir C takes more than 80 percent of the supply, because it sits 26 m below the junction and its pipe is only moderately resistive compared with B.

Answer: 209.9 L/s

(e)

For no flow to or from B the junction must sit at the level of B, H_J = 165.0 m. Then the flow to C is Q_C = √(25.0/597.8) = 0.2045 m³/s, and this must equal the flow from A through the new pipe, which is driven by 180.0 − 165.0 = 15.0 m. So R_A,new = 15.0/0.2045² = 358.7 s²/m⁵. From R = 8fL/(π²gD⁵), D⁵ = 8 × 0.018 × 1500/(96.83 × 358.7) = 216/34 733 = 0.006219 and D = exp(ln 0.006219/5) = exp(−1.016) = 0.362 m. A 360 mm pipe in place of the 400 mm pipe is a throttling of the supply, so in practice a partly closed valve on the existing pipe would do the same job.

Answer: 0.362 m

Problem 5 [A5-100] Pipe networks and equivalent pipes

A looped distribution main serving a Peterborough neighbourhood carries water from node A to node C through two paths. Path 1 runs A to B and then B to C: pipe AB is 600 m long, 350 mm in diameter, f = 0.021, and pipe BC is 500 m long, 250 mm in diameter, f = 0.020. Path 2 runs A to D and then D to C: pipe AD is 700 m long, 400 mm in diameter, f = 0.020, and pipe DC is 400 m long, 300 mm in diameter, f = 0.022. No water is drawn at B or D. Neglect minor losses and use h = RQ² with R = 8fL/(π²gD⁵) and g = 9.81 m/s². The design inflow at A, and outflow at C, is 0.140 m³/s. The pressure head at A is 52.0 m and C is at the same elevation as A. A Hardy Cross analysis starts from an equal split of 0.070 m³/s in each path. The utility would like a single equivalent pipe 1000 m long with f = 0.020.

  1. (a) Find the first Hardy Cross flow correction, in L/s, applied to path 1. [4]
  2. (b) Find the converged flow in path 1. [4]
  3. (c) Find the head loss from A to C. [4]
  4. (d) Find the diameter of the equivalent single pipe. [4]
  5. (e) Find the residual pressure head at C if the demand rises to 0.250 m³/s, and comment on its adequacy. [4]
(a)

Resistances from R = 8fL/(π²gD⁵): R_AB = 198.2, R_BC = 846.1, R_AD = 113.0 and R_DC = 299.2 s²/m⁵. Path 1 has R1 = 198.2 + 846.1 = 1044.3 and path 2 has R2 = 113.0 + 299.2 = 412.2. Take path 1 as positive (A to B to C). Initial flows: q1 = +0.070 and q2 = 0.070 in the opposite sense around the loop. Head losses are h1 = 1044.3 × 0.070² = 5.117 m and h2 = 412.2 × 0.070² = 2.020 m, taken negative around the loop. The sum Σh = 3.097 m and Σ2R|q| = 2(1044.3 × 0.070 + 412.2 × 0.070) = 203.9. So ΔQ = −3.097/203.9 = −0.01519 m³/s, which reduces the path 1 flow by 15.2 L/s.

Answer: 15.19 L/s reduction

(b)

After one correction, path 1 carries 0.070 − 0.01519 = 0.0548 m³/s and path 2 carries 0.0852 m³/s. The converged answer requires equal head loss in the two paths, R1 Q1² = R2 Q2², so Q1/Q2 = √(R2/R1) = √(412.2/1044.3) = √0.3947 = 0.6282. With Q1 + Q2 = 0.140, Q1 = 0.140 × 0.6282/1.6282 = 0.05402 m³/s = 54.0 L/s and Q2 = 86.0 L/s. The first iteration got to 54.8 L/s, within 1.5 percent of the answer, which shows how quickly Hardy Cross converges for a simple loop when the starting split is reasonable.

Answer: 54.0 L/s

(c)

The head loss from A to C is the same along either path. Along path 1, h = R1 Q1² = 1044.3 × 0.05402² = 1044.3 × 0.002918 = 3.047 m. Check along path 2: 412.2 × 0.08598² = 412.2 × 0.007393 = 3.047 m. The agreement confirms that the loop is balanced. The loss is small, only about 6 percent of the 52.0 m pressure head at A, because the pipes are generously sized for the 0.140 m³/s design flow and the velocities are modest: in pipe BC the velocity is 0.05402/0.04909 = 1.10 m/s.

Answer: 3.05 m

(d)

The equivalent pipe must show the same head loss for the same total flow: R_eq = h/Q² = 3.047/0.140² = 155.5 s²/m⁵. For f = 0.020 and L = 1000 m, R = 8 × 0.020 × 1000/(π² × 9.81 × D⁵) = 160/(96.83 D⁵) = 1.6525/D⁵. Hence D⁵ = 1.6525/155.5 = 0.01063 and D = exp(ln(0.01063)/5) = exp(−4.5441/5) = exp(−0.9088) = 0.403 m. An equivalent pipe of 0.403 m is the same as the whole loop only for resistance purposes: it cannot represent the flows in individual pipes, and the real loop gives built-in redundancy that the single pipe does not.

Answer: 0.403 m

(e)

For the equivalent pipe, h = R_eq Q² = 155.5 × 0.250² = 9.72 m at the higher demand of 0.250 m³/s. The split between the paths stays at 39:61 because both paths have the same Q² law with constant f. Residual head at C is 52.0 − 9.72 = 42.3 m, about 415 kPa. This is well above the 14 m (about 140 kPa) commonly quoted as the minimum residual during a fire flow, so the loop is adequate. A constant f is slightly conservative, because f falls a little as flow rises, so the true residual head would be somewhat higher than 42.3 m.

Answer: 42.3 m

A5 Practice Paper 21

Problem 1 [A5-101] Uniform open-channel flow with Manning's equation

A new stormwater outfall channel is to be built through a clay-till site near Barrie, Ontario. The channel is trapezoidal, with a 4.0 m bottom width and side slopes of 2 horizontal to 1 vertical, laid on a uniform longitudinal slope of 0.0012. It must carry a design flow of 14 m³/s under steady, uniform conditions. Two lining options are being compared. A smooth cast-in-place concrete lining has a Manning roughness of n = 0.015, and a placed riprap lining has n = 0.032. The design office requires a freeboard of 0.30 m above the normal water surface, and the excavation is to be taken to that bank level for both options. Use g = 9.81 m/s² and ignore the thickness of the lining.

  1. (a) Find the normal depth for the concrete lining. [6]
  2. (b) Find the normal depth for the riprap lining. [5]
  3. (c) Find the Froude number for the concrete-lined channel and state the flow regime. [4]
  4. (d) Find the extra excavated volume per 100 m of channel needed for the riprap option compared with the concrete option, measured to the bank level including freeboard. [5]
(a)

Manning's equation for uniform flow is Q = (1/n) A R2/3 S1/2, with A = (b + zy)y and wetted perimeter P = b + 2y√(1 + z²). With b = 4, z = 2, S = 0.0012, n = 0.015, the equation is implicit in y, so I solve it by trial. At y = 1.136 m: A = (4 + 2.272)(1.136) = 7.126 m², P = 4 + 2(1.136)(2.236) = 9.081 m, R = 0.7847 m, and R2/3 = 0.851. Then Q = (1/0.015)(7.126)(0.851)(0.03464) = 14.0 m³/s, which matches the design flow. The normal depth is therefore 1.14 m, with a mean velocity V = Q/A = 1.96 m/s. This is the depth at which gravity driving force balances boundary friction exactly.

Answer: 1.14 m

(b)

Repeat the same equation with n = 0.032. Because Q = (1/n) A R2/3 √S, a rougher lining needs a larger A R2/3 to carry the same flow, so the depth must increase. At y = 1.678 m: A = (4 + 3.356)(1.678) = 12.34 m², P = 4 + 2(1.678)(2.236) = 11.50 m, R = 1.0728 m, R2/3 = 1.048. Then Q = (1/0.032)(12.34)(1.048)(0.03464) = 14.0 m³/s, as required. The riprap normal depth is 1.68 m, which is about 48 percent deeper than for concrete, and the velocity falls to 14/12.34 = 1.13 m/s. The extra roughness is paid for in extra flow area.

Answer: 1.68 m

(c)

The Froude number is Fr = V/√(gD), where the hydraulic depth D = A/T and the top width T = b + 2zy. For the concrete section T = 4 + 4(1.136) = 8.544 m, so D = 7.126/8.544 = 0.834 m. Then √(gD) = √(9.81 × 0.834) = 2.860 m/s, and V = 1.965 m/s gives Fr = 1.965/2.860 = 0.687. Because Fr is below 1, the flow is subcritical (tranquil). Downstream conditions control the depth, and a disturbance can travel upstream. Nonetheless a value near 0.7 is high enough that the surface will look lively, and a designer would check for wave action and a hydraulic jump at the outlet.

Answer: 0.687, subcritical

(d)

The excavation is cut to normal depth plus 0.30 m. Concrete: y = 1.136 + 0.30 = 1.436 m, so A = (4 + 2 × 1.436)(1.436) = 9.869 m². Riprap: y = 1.678 + 0.30 = 1.978 m, so A = (4 + 2 × 1.978)(1.978) = 15.734 m². The extra area is 15.734 - 9.869 = 5.865 m², and over 100 m the extra volume is 5.865 × 100 = 586.5 m³, about 587 m³. The riprap option therefore costs roughly 59 percent more excavation, plus the stone itself. The designer must set that against the concrete lining's cost and its lower infiltration, but also against the energy dissipated: riprap is gentler at the outlet because its velocity is only 1.13 m/s.

Answer: 587 m³

Problem 2 [A5-102] Best hydraulic sections and compound channels

A drainage authority in the Don River watershed is comparing two designs. First, a concrete-lined trapezoidal channel (n = 0.013) with side slopes 1.5 horizontal to 1 vertical on a slope of 0.0004 is to carry 20 m³/s and is to be the best hydraulic section. Second, a natural compound channel on a slope of 0.0006 has a rectangular main channel 12 m wide whose bed lies 3.5 m below the flood water surface (n = 0.030), with a floodplain on each side 30 m wide and 1.0 m deep (n = 0.060) and bounded on its outer side by a vertical bank 1.0 m high that is included in the wetted perimeter. The main-channel walls extend 2.5 m up to bankfull level. Use g = 9.81 m/s². Divide the compound section by vertical lines at the bank edges, and leave the imaginary interface lines out of the wetted perimeters.

  1. (a) Find the bottom width of the best hydraulic trapezoid for 20 m³/s. [5]
  2. (b) For the compound channel at the given flood level, find the discharge by treating main channel and floodplains separately. [7]
  3. (c) Find the discharge if the whole compound section is treated as one channel with an equivalent roughness from the weighted wetted perimeter method (n_c = [Σ P_i n_i1.5 / P]2/3). [5]
  4. (d) Find the percentage by which the single-section result is wrong relative to the divided result, and state which method a designer should trust. [3]
(a)

The best hydraulic section is the one with the smallest area for a given Q, so it has the smallest wetted perimeter: for a trapezoid, R = y/2 and b = 2y(√(1 + z²) - z). With z = 1.5, √(1 + z²) = 1.8028, so b = 2y(0.3028) = 0.6056y. The area is A = (b + zy)y = (0.6056 + 1.5)y² = 2.1056y², the perimeter is P = b + 2y(1.8028) = 4.2112y, and R = y/2. Manning gives 20 = (1/0.013)(2.1056y²)(y/2)2/3(0.02). Solving gives y = 2.354 m, so b = 0.6056 × 2.354 = 1.43 m. The section is deep and narrow, which is why it is rarely built in practice.

Answer: 1.43 m

(b)

Treat the three subareas independently with the same slope. Main channel: depth 3.5 m over a 12 m width, A = 42.0 m², P = 12 + 2(2.5) = 17.0 m (the walls are wetted only up to bankfull and the interface is excluded), R = 2.471 m, so Q = (1/0.030)(42.0)(2.471)2/3(0.0006)1/2 = (1/0.030)(42.0)(1.8275)(0.02449) = 62.67 m³/s. Each floodplain: A = 30 × 1.0 = 30 m², P = 30 + 1.0 = 31 m, R = 0.9677 m, giving Q = (1/0.060)(30)(0.9784)(0.02449) = 11.98 m³/s. Total Q = 62.67 + 2(11.98) = 86.6 m³/s. The rough floodplains carry only about 28 percent of the flow despite providing 59 percent of the area.

Answer: 86.6 m³/s

(c)

The total area is 42 + 2(30) = 102 m² and the total wetted perimeter is 17 + 2(31) = 79 m, so R = 1.291 m. The equivalent roughness is n_c = [(17 × 0.0301.5 + 62 × 0.0601.5)/79]2/3. With 0.0301.5 = 0.005196 and 0.0601.5 = 0.014697, the sum is 0.08833 + 0.91121 = 0.99954, and divided by 79 gives 0.012652, whose 2/3 power is 0.0543. Then Q = (1/0.0543)(102)(1.291)2/3(0.02449) = (1/0.0543)(102)(1.185)(0.02449) = 54.6 m³/s. The single-n method lets the long, rough floodplain perimeter dominate the average and so it drags the whole section's roughness upward.

Answer: 54.6 m³/s

(d)

The percentage difference is (54.56 - 86.64)/86.64 × 100 = -37.0 percent, so treating the section as one channel underestimates the flood discharge by more than a third. The cause is that a single average n spreads the floodplain roughness over the deep main channel, where water actually moves quickly in a smooth, deep stream. A flood-risk engineer should trust the divided-channel result, or a method that accounts for the interaction at the vertical interface, because underestimating conveyance would overstate the stage for a given flow, or equivalently understate the flow for a measured stage. The divided method is the one used in flood-plain mapping for compound sections.

Answer: -37 percent

Problem 3 [A5-103] Specific energy, critical depth and control sections

A 6.0 m wide rectangular concrete conduit carries a steady discharge of 19.2 m³/s from a municipal wet-weather storage tank in Hamilton to a treatment plant. The flow upstream is subcritical at a depth of 1.40 m. A maintenance crew wants to know how much a raised sill (a smooth, short bump in the floor, with negligible energy loss and a horizontal frictionless approach) can be built across the full width before it starts to affect the upstream flow. Assume the bump has a flat top so that the flow over it can be treated by the energy equation alone, with a uniform velocity and a hydrostatic pressure distribution. Take g = 9.81 m/s² and neglect friction over the short reach.

  1. (a) Find the critical depth over the sill and the minimum specific energy. [5]
  2. (b) Find the greatest sill height that leaves the upstream depth unchanged. [4]
  3. (c) For a sill 0.10 m high, find the subcritical depth over the sill and the Froude number there. [5]
  4. (d) For a sill 0.30 m high, find the upstream depth that results, and explain what has happened to the flow. [6]
(a)

Per unit width the discharge is q = 19.2/6.0 = 3.20 m²/s. For a rectangular channel critical flow occurs at yc = (q²/g)1/3 = (3.20²/9.81)1/3 = (1.0438)1/3 = 1.014 m. At critical flow the specific energy is a minimum and equals E_min = 1.5 yc = 1.522 m, because the velocity head is yc/2 there. At this state the Froude number equals one, the velocity is √(g yc) = 3.155 m/s, and any attempt to pass 3.20 m²/s with less energy per newton is physically impossible. This minimum energy fixes how much the floor can be raised.

Answer: yc = 1.014 m; Emin = 1.522 m

(b)

The upstream specific energy is E1 = y1 + q²/(2g y1²) = 1.40 + 10.24/(19.62 × 1.96) = 1.40 + 0.2663 = 1.666 m. Over the sill, the specific energy available is E1 - Δz. Flow can pass only if this is at least E_min, so Δz ≤ 1.666 - 1.522 = 0.145 m. Up to this height the upstream depth stays at 1.40 m, with the depth over the sill decreasing smoothly until it reaches critical depth exactly on the crest at the limit. The sill is then acting as a control section, and any greater height forces the water upstream to pile up, so 0.145 m is the greatest height before the upstream flow is affected.

Answer: 0.145 m

(c)

With Δz = 0.10 m the available energy over the sill is 1.666 - 0.10 = 1.566 m, which exceeds E_min, so the flow remains subcritical and the depth is the root of y + 10.24/(19.62 y²) = 1.566 above yc. Trying y = 1.2095 m gives 1.2095 + 0.5219/1.4629 = 1.2095 + 0.3568 = 1.566 m, which matches. The velocity is 3.20/1.2095 = 2.646 m/s and the Froude number is 2.646/√(9.81 × 1.2095) = 2.646/3.445 = 0.77. The surface dips from 1.40 m to 1.21 m over the sill, a drop of 0.19 m, while the water surface level above the datum falls by only 0.09 m because the floor has risen 0.10 m.

Answer: 1.21 m; Fr = 0.77

(d)

A 0.30 m sill exceeds the 0.145 m limit, so the sill chokes the flow. The energy on the crest must equal E_min = 1.522 m, so the upstream specific energy must rise to E1 = 1.522 + 0.30 = 1.822 m. The upstream depth solves y + 0.5219/y² = 1.822 on the subcritical branch, and y = 1.6236 m gives 1.6236 + 0.5219/2.636 = 1.6236 + 0.198 = 1.8216 m, which agrees. The upstream depth therefore rises from 1.40 m to 1.62 m, a backwater of 0.22 m. The flow passes through critical depth on the crest and then accelerates into a supercritical state downstream, so the sill acts as a control, with a depth that no longer depends on conditions further downstream.

Answer: 1.62 m

Problem 4 [A5-104] Flow measurement: weirs, sluice gates and flumes

A rectangular irrigation-style diversion canal in southwestern Ontario is controlled by a vertical sluice gate across its full 4.0 m width. The upstream depth is 2.80 m. The gate is opened to 0.60 m and the jet issues freely with a contraction coefficient Cc = 0.61, so the depth at the vena contracta is Cc times the opening. Treat the flow with the energy equation between the upstream section and the vena contracta, with uniform velocity, hydrostatic pressure, and no losses. The same flow is later to be measured by a 5.0 m long sharp-crested rectangular weir with Q = Cd (2/3)√(2g) L H3/2, Cd = 0.62, where H is the head on the crest, with negligible approach velocity. Use ρ = 1000 kg/m³ and g = 9.81 m/s².

  1. (a) Find the discharge through the gate. [5]
  2. (b) Find the horizontal force of the water on the gate per the full width, by momentum between the upstream section and the vena contracta. [6]
  3. (c) Find the head on the 5.0 m weir that would pass the same discharge. [4]
  4. (d) A reading error of 5 mm in the weir head is made. Find the resulting percentage error in the computed discharge. [5]
(a)

Between the upstream section (depth y1 = 2.80 m) and the vena contracta (y2 = Cc a = 0.61 × 0.60 = 0.366 m), the energy equation gives y1 + V1²/2g = y2 + V2²/2g. With V1 = Q/(b y1) and V2 = Q/(b y2), which rearranges to Q = Cc a b √[2g y1/(1 + Cc a/y1)]. Substituting, Q = 0.61 × 0.60 × 4.0 × √[2(9.81)(2.80)/(1 + 0.366/2.80)] = 1.464 × √(54.94/1.1307) = 1.464 × 6.970 = 10.20 m³/s. The velocity at the vena contracta is then 6.97 m/s.

Answer: 10.2 m³/s

(b)

The velocities are V1 = 10.20/(4.0 × 2.80) = 0.911 m/s and V2 = 10.20/(4.0 × 0.366) = 6.970 m/s. Take a control volume bounded by the upstream section, the vena contracta, the bed and the water surface, and write the momentum equation in the flow direction: F_upstream - F_downstream - F_gate = ρQ(V2 - V1). The hydrostatic forces are ½ρg b y², so ½(1000)(9.81)(4.0)(2.80² - 0.366²) = 19620 × (7.84 - 0.134) = 151.2 kN. The momentum flux change is 1000 × 10.20 × (6.970 - 0.911) = 61.8 kN. So F_gate = 151.2 - 61.8 = 89.4 kN, acting downstream on the gate. Bed friction is neglected, and the force is equal and opposite on the gate structure.

Answer: 89.4 kN

(c)

With negligible approach velocity, the weir equation gives H = [Q/(Cd (2/3)√(2g) L)]2/3. The coefficient is 0.62 × (2/3) × √(19.62) × 5.0 = 0.62 × 0.6667 × 4.4294 × 5.0 = 9.154. So H3/2 = 10.20/9.154 = 1.1146, and H = 1.11462/3 = 1.075 m. The weir head of 1.08 m would be measured from the crest to the water surface upstream of the drawdown, at least 3 to 4 head lengths upstream of the crest. The crest must be at least about 0.3 m above the downstream water to keep the nappe free and ventilated.

Answer: 1.08 m

(d)

Because Q is proportional to H3/2, differentiating logarithmically gives dQ/Q = 1.5 dH/H. For dH = 0.005 m and H = 1.075 m, dH/H = 0.004651, so dQ/Q = 1.5 × 0.004651 = 0.006976, or 0.70 percent. At this head, a 5 mm slip in the staff gauge reading therefore causes a discharge error of about 0.7 percent, small compared with the likely uncertainty in Cd of several percent. At a low head the same 5 mm error would matter much more, which is why weirs are poor for measuring very small flows and why the gauge must be zeroed carefully to the crest.

Answer: 0.70 percent

Problem 5 [A5-105] Gradually varied flow profiles and step computations

A low weir across a rectangular concrete-lined diversion channel near Peterborough, Ontario, backs water up the channel. The channel is 8.0 m wide, carries 20 m³/s, and has a bed slope of 0.0004 and Manning n = 0.030. Immediately upstream of the weir the depth is 4.00 m. A hydraulic engineer wants to know how far upstream the backwater reaches a depth of 3.00 m. Use the direct step method with Δy steps of 0.50 m: from 4.00 m to 3.50 m, then from 3.50 m to 3.00 m, taking the friction slope for each step as the mean of the end values from Manning's equation. Use g = 9.81 m/s² and take the specific energy as E = y + V²/2g.

  1. (a) Find the normal depth and classify the profile, using the critical depth from part (b). [6]
  2. (b) Find the critical depth. [2]
  3. (c) Find the distance between the 4.00 m and 3.50 m sections. [6]
  4. (d) Find the distance from the 4.00 m section to the 3.00 m section. [6]
(a)

Normal depth solves Q = (1/n)(by)5/3(b + 2y)-2/3 S1/2 with b = 8, n = 0.030, S = 0.0004: 20 = (1/0.030)(8y)5/3/(8 + 2y)2/3(0.02). Trying y = 2.72 m gives A = 21.76 m², P = 13.44 m, R = 1.619 m, R2/3 = 1.379, and Q = (1/0.030)(21.76)(1.379)(0.02) = 20.0 m³/s. So yn = 2.72 m. The actual depth of 4.00 m at the weir exceeds yn, which in turn exceeds the critical depth (part b), so the profile is an M1 curve: a mild slope (yn > yc) with the depth above both. The depth decreases upstream, approaching yn asymptotically.

Answer: yn = 2.72 m; M1

(b)

For a rectangular channel critical depth is yc = (q²/g)1/3, where q = 20/8 = 2.50 m²/s. Then yc = (6.25/9.81)1/3 = (0.6371)1/3 = 0.8605 m. Since yn = 2.72 m is far above yc = 0.86 m, the slope is mild, and the Froude number everywhere on the profile is below one, so the computation proceeds upstream from the control at the weir. A mild slope with a controlling structure downstream always produces a backwater curve of the M1 type when the structure holds the depth above normal.

Answer: 0.86 m

(c)

At y = 4.00 m: V = 20/(8 × 4.00) = 0.625 m/s, E = 4.00 + 0.625²/19.62 = 4.0199 m, A = 32 m², R = 32/16 = 2.0 m, Sf = (nV/R2/3)² = (0.030 × 0.625/1.5874)² = 1.395 × 10⁻⁴. At y = 3.50 m: V = 0.7143 m/s, E = 3.5260 m, R = 28/15 = 1.8667 m, Sf = (0.030 × 0.7143/1.5160)² = 2.00 × 10⁻⁴. Mean Sf = 1.697 × 10⁻⁴. The distance between the sections is Δx = ΔE/(S0 - Sf) = (4.0199 - 3.5260)/(0.0004 - 0.0001697) = 0.4939/0.0002303 = 2144 m, measured upstream from the 4.00 m station.

Answer: 2144 m

(d)

At y = 3.00 m: V = 20/24 = 0.8333 m/s, E = 3.0 + 0.8333²/19.62 = 3.0354 m, R = 24/14 = 1.7143 m, R2/3 = 1.4324, Sf = (0.030 × 0.8333/1.4324)² = 3.05 × 10⁻⁴. Mean Sf for the second step is (2.00 + 3.05)/2 × 10⁻⁴ = 2.52 × 10⁻⁴, so S0 - Sf = 0.0001478. ΔE = 3.5260 - 3.0354 = 0.4906 m, and Δx = 0.4906/0.0001478 = 3320 m. The total distance upstream is 2144 + 3320 = 5464 m. The depth is still above yn = 2.72 m there, so the backwater extends farther yet; steps this large become inaccurate as yn is approached, because Sf approaches S0.

Answer: 5464 m

A5 Practice Paper 22

Problem 1 [A5-106] Hydraulic jump: sequent depths and energy loss

Water spills down the concrete chute of a small hydroelectric station on a northern Ontario river and enters a flat, horizontal, rectangular apron at a supercritical depth of 0.55 m, with a unit discharge of 7.8 m²/s. A hydraulic jump is expected to form on the apron. The apron is smooth enough that bed friction over the jump length may be neglected, and the pressure distribution may be taken as hydrostatic before and after the jump. The tailwater depth that the downstream river channel will actually provide above the apron is 3.20 m. Use g = 9.81 m/s² and ρ = 1000 kg/m³. The station owner wants to know whether the jump will stay on the apron, and how much power the jump must dissipate to protect the downstream bank.

  1. (a) Find the Froude number of the incoming flow. [3]
  2. (b) Find the sequent depth that a jump on the apron would need. [5]
  3. (c) Find the head loss in the jump. [4]
  4. (d) Find the power dissipated per metre width of the jump. [4]
  5. (e) Find the ratio of the available tailwater to the required sequent depth, and say what will happen to the jump. [4]
(a)

The incoming velocity is V1 = q/y1 = 7.8/0.55 = 14.18 m/s. The Froude number is Fr1 = V1/√(g y1) = 14.18/√(9.81 × 0.55) = 14.18/2.323 = 6.105. A value between about 4.5 and 9 gives a well-formed, stable jump with a good energy loss, so the flow is in the range where a hydraulic jump is an effective energy dissipator. For lower values (under about 2.5) the jump would be weak and oscillating, and for much higher values it would be rough, with strong waves downstream.

Answer: 6.11

(b)

Momentum balance across a jump in a horizontal rectangular channel gives the Bélanger equation y2 = (y1/2)[√(1 + 8Fr1²) - 1]. With Fr1² = 37.27, 8Fr1² = 298.2, √(1 + 298.2) = 17.298, so y2 = 0.275 × (17.298 - 1) = 0.275 × 16.298 = 4.482 m. The jump therefore needs 4.48 m of water on the downstream side to hold it at the toe. This is more than eight times the incoming depth, and the downstream velocity falls to 7.8/4.482 = 1.74 m/s. The balance neglects bed friction, which is reasonable over the short length of a jump.

Answer: 4.48 m

(c)

The energy loss in a jump is h_L = (y2 - y1)³/(4 y1 y2). Here (4.482 - 0.55)³ = 3.932³ = 60.79 m³, and 4 y1 y2 = 4 × 0.55 × 4.482 = 9.860 m², so h_L = 60.79/9.860 = 6.165 m. As a check, the incoming specific energy is 0.55 + 14.18²/19.62 = 10.80 m, and the outgoing one is 4.482 + 1.74²/19.62 = 4.636 m, a difference of 6.165 m. So about 57 percent of the incoming energy is lost in the jump, which is why jumps are used as the energy dissipators below spillways.

Answer: 6.16 m

(d)

The power dissipated per metre width is P = ρ g q h_L = 1000 × 9.81 × 7.8 × 6.165 = 471 700 W/m, about 472 kW/m. For a 20 m wide apron this is nearly 9.4 MW of turbulence power released in a short length, mostly as heat and air entrainment, which is why the apron slab needs thickness, anchoring against uplift, and a dissipation length of a few times y2. The figure confirms that the jump is doing real work protecting the downstream river bank from high-velocity attack.

Answer: 472 kW/m

(e)

The available tailwater is 3.20 m and the required sequent depth is 4.482 m, so the ratio is 3.20/4.482 = 0.714. A ratio under one means the downstream water is too shallow to push the jump back to the toe, so the jump will be swept downstream off the apron, leaving the supercritical stream attacking the river bed and banks. The deficit is 4.482 - 3.20 = 1.28 m. The remedy is a lower apron, a sill, or baffle blocks to raise the effective tailwater, so that it equals or slightly exceeds y2 for every discharge up to the design flood.

Answer: 0.71

Problem 2 [A5-107] Energy dissipators and stilling basins

An overflow spillway on a dam in the Ottawa River basin discharges a design unit flow of 12.0 m²/s. The reservoir water surface is 38.0 m above the horizontal concrete apron at the toe. Neglect energy loss down the spillway face, so the total energy per unit weight at the toe equals 38.0 m above the apron. A stilling basin with baffle blocks and an end sill is to be built on that apron, its length taken as 2.7 times the sequent depth. The river provides a tailwater 6.8 m deep above the existing apron level, and any lowering of the apron deepens the tailwater by the same amount, because the river level at the basin outlet does not change. Use g = 9.81 m/s². The design requires the tailwater to equal the sequent depth, with no safety margin.

  1. (a) Find the depth at the toe of the spillway. [5]
  2. (b) Find the sequent depth for a jump at the toe, and the Froude number there. [5]
  3. (c) Find the length of basin required. [3]
  4. (d) Find how far the apron must be lowered so that the tailwater just equals the sequent depth. [7]
(a)

With no loss, the specific energy at the toe is the total head: y1 + q²/(2g y1²) = 38.0 m, where q²/2g = 144/19.62 = 7.339 m³. The equation y1 + 7.339/y1² = 38.0 is solved by trial for the supercritical root. At y1 = 0.442 m: 0.442 + 7.339/0.1954 = 0.442 + 37.56 = 38.00 m, which checks. The toe depth is therefore 0.442 m and the velocity is V1 = 12.0/0.442 = 27.15 m/s. In practice, friction and air entrainment on the face lower this velocity, so the loss-free assumption gives the most severe condition for the basin and is conservative for sizing.

Answer: 0.442 m

(b)

The Froude number at the toe is Fr1 = V1/√(g y1) = 27.15/√(9.81 × 0.4421) = 27.15/2.082 = 13.04. This is well above the 4.5 to 9 range of a steady jump; at such a large value (toe velocity 27 m/s) the jump is violent, and baffle blocks would be at risk of cavitation damage above about 18 m/s, so the length factor of 2.7 is a stated assumption and a different basin or a lower toe velocity should be considered. The sequent depth is y2 = (y1/2)[√(1 + 8Fr1²) - 1] = 0.2210 × [√(1 + 8 × 170.0) - 1] = 0.2210 × (36.9 - 1) = 7.93 m. The tailwater of 6.8 m is smaller than this, so the existing apron would not hold the jump at the toe.

Answer: 7.93 m

(c)

The brief gives the basin length as 2.7 times the sequent depth, which is the usual proportion for a basin with baffle blocks and a sill because the appurtenances shorten the jump. So L = 2.7 y2 = 2.7 × 7.931 = 21.4 m. This is much shorter than the roughly 6 y2 length of a free jump on a plain apron, which would be about 47 m, and the saving in concrete is substantial. Because y2 was found with no tailwater safety factor, the length is a minimum figure, and the final design would check it again once the apron level is chosen in part (d).

Answer: 21.4 m

(d)

Lowering the apron by d raises the total energy at the toe to 38.0 + d and the tailwater above the new apron to 6.8 + d. For each trial d, solve y1 + 7.339/y1² = 38 + d, then find Fr1 and y2, and compare y2 with 6.8 + d. At d = 1.199 m the toe depth is 0.4351 m, V1 = 27.58 m/s, Fr1 = 13.35, and y2 = 7.999 m, while 6.8 + 1.199 = 7.999 m. They match, so the apron must be lowered by 1.20 m. The sequent depth barely grows because it rises only slowly with energy, while the tailwater grows one for one with the excavation, so the two curves meet quickly. A designer would add a margin of 5 to 10 percent on top of this.

Answer: 1.20 m

Problem 3 [A5-108] Water hammer: wave speed and valve closure

A steel penstock supplies a small run-of-river plant in the Mattagami basin. It is 900 m long, has an internal diameter of 1.20 m and a wall thickness of 14 mm, and is anchored against axial movement throughout. The water velocity is 3.2 m/s and the static head at the turbine valve is 110 m. For the steel take E = 200 GPa and Poisson's ratio 0.30; for the water take a bulk modulus of 2.15 GPa and ρ = 1000 kg/m³. The wave speed for a thin-walled anchored pipe is a = √[(K/ρ)/(1 + (K D/(E t))(1 - ν²))]. For a gradual linear closure taking longer than the pipe period, use the Michaud estimate ΔH = 2LV₀/(gT). The allowable hoop stress is 140 MPa. Use g = 9.81 m/s².

  1. (a) Find the pressure wave speed. [4]
  2. (b) Find the head rise for a sudden valve closure. [3]
  3. (c) Find the head rise if the valve is closed linearly in 4.0 s. [4]
  4. (d) Find the shortest linear closure time that holds the surge to 40 percent of the static head. [5]
  5. (e) For the 4.0 s closure, find the hoop stress at the maximum head and compare it with the allowable stress. [4]
(a)

The ratio K D/(E t) = (2.15 × 10⁹ × 1.20)/(200 × 10⁹ × 0.014) = 2.58 × 10⁹/2.8 × 10⁹ = 0.9214. Multiplying by (1 - ν²) = 0.91 for an anchored pipe gives 0.8385. The denominator is therefore 1 + 0.8385 = 1.8385, and K/ρ = 2.15 × 10⁶ m²/s². So a = √(2.15 × 10⁶/1.8385) = √(1.1695 × 10⁶) = 1081 m/s. This is well below the 1480 m/s speed of sound in unconfined water, because the elasticity of the pipe wall adds flexibility to the system. The round-trip travel time of the wave is 2L/a = 1800/1081 = 1.66 s.

Answer: 1081 m/s

(b)

A closure faster than 2L/a = 1.66 s is sudden, because the reflected relief wave from the reservoir returns after the valve has already shut. Joukowsky's relation then gives the full surge: ΔH = aV₀/g = 1081.4 × 3.2/9.81 = 352.8 m. This is more than three times the static head of 110 m, giving a maximum head of 463 m and a pressure of about 4.5 MPa, far above what the 14 mm wall is intended to hold. The figure shows why a turbine valve must never be slammed shut and why penstocks are designed against a specific closure law.

Answer: 353 m

(c)

Since T = 4.0 s exceeds 2L/a = 1.66 s, the closure is gradual: the reflected relief wave arrives before closure ends, which limits the peak. The Michaud estimate gives ΔH = 2LV₀/(gT) = (2 × 900 × 3.2)/(9.81 × 4.0) = 5760/39.24 = 146.8 m. The peak is only about 42 percent of the sudden-closure value, even though the closure time is just 2.4 times the pipe period. The maximum head is 110 + 146.8 = 256.8 m. Michaud's formula is an approximation that ignores friction and assumes a linear change in velocity, and it is generally conservative for realistic valve characteristics.

Answer: 147 m

(d)

The limit is 0.40 × 110 = 44 m. Rearranging ΔH = 2LV₀/(gT) for the time gives T = 2LV₀/(g ΔH_allow) = (2 × 900 × 3.2)/(9.81 × 44) = 5760/431.6 = 13.34 s. So the valve must take at least about 13.3 s to close. That is eight times the pipe period, so Michaud's approximation is well within its range of validity. In practice the operator would close the valve in two stages, slowly over the final part of the stroke where the valve opening has the greatest effect on flow, and would confirm the answer with a transient simulation.

Answer: 13.3 s

(e)

The maximum head for the 4.0 s closure is 110 + 146.8 = 256.8 m, so the pressure is p = ρ g H = 1000 × 9.81 × 256.8 = 2.519 × 10⁶ Pa. The hoop stress in a thin-walled cylinder is σ = pD/(2t) = (2.519 × 10⁶ × 1.20)/(2 × 0.014) = 107.96 × 10⁶ Pa, or 108 MPa. This is below the allowable 140 MPa, with a ratio of 0.77, so the pipe wall passes under this load case, although the margin is only 23 percent. A sudden closure would raise the head to 463 m and the hoop stress to about 195 MPa, exceeding the limit, which confirms the importance of the slower closure.

Answer: 108 MPa

Problem 4 [A5-109] Surge tanks and column separation

A hydroelectric tunnel and penstock system in northern Ontario consists of a 2400 m long pressure conduit of 2.00 m diameter connecting the reservoir to a simple cylindrical surge tank located just upstream of the powerhouse. At full load the velocity in the conduit is 3.5 m/s, and the friction head loss in the conduit at that velocity is 5.2 m. The static head between the reservoir and the turbines is 160 m. The designer plans to select a tank area equal to 1.5 times the Thoma critical area, so that the system is stable against small load oscillations. Treat the tank as large in comparison with the throttle and assume the full-load rejection happens instantly. Use g = 9.81 m/s² and take the friction loss as h_f = C V². Use the Thoma critical area A_th = L A/[2 g C (H₀ - 3 h_f)].

  1. (a) Find the friction loss coefficient C. [3]
  2. (b) Find the Thoma critical area of the tank. [5]
  3. (c) Find the maximum upsurge in the tank following full-load rejection, neglecting friction. [5]
  4. (d) Find the period of the oscillation of the water level in the tank. [3]
  5. (e) Explain why the bottom pressure at a high point of the conduit is at risk of column separation during a large downsurge, and say what the designer can do about it. [4]
(a)

From h_f = C V² the coefficient is C = h_f/V₀² = 5.2/3.5² = 5.2/12.25 = 0.4245 s²/m. This lumps all of the conduit friction into a single quadratic loss, which is the usual treatment in a first surge-tank analysis. The flow is Q = AV₀ = (π × 2.00²/4) × 3.5 = 3.1416 × 3.5 = 11.0 m³/s, and the conduit area is A = 3.1416 m². The loss coefficient is needed for the Thoma stability criterion, since the friction is what damps the oscillation in the tank and makes small swings die out.

Answer: 0.4245 s²/m

(b)

The Thoma criterion states that the tank is stable against small oscillations if its area exceeds A_th = LA/(2 C g (H₀ - 3h_f)), where H₀ is the static head and h_f the full-load friction loss. Here H₀ - 3h_f = 160 - 15.6 = 144.4 m, so A_th = (2400 × 3.1416)/(2 × 0.4245 × 9.81 × 144.4) = 7539.8/1202.7 = 6.27 m². A tank of this area is about 2.8 m in diameter. A tank any smaller would see growing oscillations as the governor chases the load. The result shows that the longer the conduit and the lower the friction, the larger the tank must be.

Answer: 6.27 m²

(c)

The chosen area is A_s = 1.5 × 6.269 = 9.40 m², a tank diameter of 3.46 m. For an instantaneous full-load rejection, all of the flowing water enters the tank, and neglecting friction the kinetic energy of the conduit is converted to a rise in water level. Equating them, ½ρLA V₀² = ½ρ g A_s z², so z_max = V₀√(LA/(g A_s)) = 3.5 × √((2400 × 3.1416)/(9.81 × 9.404)) = 3.5 × √81.73 = 3.5 × 9.040 = 31.6 m. Friction would reduce this somewhat, so the frictionless value is a conservative estimate for the top-of-tank design level.

Answer: 31.6 m

(d)

The undamped oscillation of the water mass between conduit and tank has period T = 2π√(L A_s/(g A)) = 2π × √((2400 × 9.404)/(9.81 × 3.1416)) = 2π × √(732.3) = 2π × 27.06 = 170 s. A quarter of this period, about 42.5 s, is the time for the level to reach its peak after a load rejection, and the governor of the turbine must be slow enough that its action does not resonate with this 170 s swing. Friction damps the oscillation over a few cycles, with each peak noticeably lower than the one before.

Answer: 170 s

(e)

Column separation occurs when the pressure at a point falls to the vapour pressure of water, so the water column breaks and a vapour cavity forms. After a load acceptance the tank level drops below the reservoir level by a large downsurge, and at a high point of the conduit the pressure head is the static elevation difference minus that drawdown and the friction. If this falls to near -10 m of gauge head, the water vaporises. When the cavity later collapses, the column slams together with a pressure spike that can far exceed the normal surge. The designer can lower the conduit profile, raise the tank volume or area, add an air-admission valve, or slow the load acceptance.

Answer: Non-numeric

Problem 5 [A5-110] Surface waves and flood waves in open channels

During the spring melt a long, straight reach of a river in eastern Ontario is observed to carry a steady flow with a mean depth of 2.40 m. The channel is wide and rectangular, 40.0 m wide, with a bed slope of 0.0005 and a Manning roughness of 0.035. A downstream control gate is 18.0 km from a gauging station. Treat the flow at the gauge as uniform. A flood wave is modelled by kinematic wave theory, in which the wave celerity is dQ/dA, found by differentiating Manning's equation in the wide-channel form (Q proportional to A5/3). A gravity wave on the surface of the flow travels at √(gy) relative to the water. Use g = 9.81 m/s². Later the downstream gate is closed suddenly and completely, which produces a positive surge moving upstream.

  1. (a) Find the mean velocity of the uniform flow. [2]
  2. (b) Find the kinematic wave celerity and the time it takes a flood crest to travel 18.0 km. [5]
  3. (c) Find the speed of a small gravity wave travelling downstream, relative to the bank. [4]
  4. (d) Find the height of the surge produced by sudden complete closure of the downstream gate. [6]
  5. (e) Explain why the flood crest and the closure surge travel at very different speeds. [3]
(a)

The area is A = 40.0 × 2.40 = 96.0 m² and the wetted perimeter is P = 40.0 + 2(2.40) = 44.8 m, so R = 2.143 m. Manning's equation gives V = (1/n) R2/3 S1/2 = (1/0.035)(2.143)2/3(0.02236) = (1/0.035)(1.662)(0.02236) = 1.062 m/s. The discharge is Q = 96.0 × 1.062 = 101.9 m³/s. The Froude number is 1.062/√(9.81 × 2.40) = 0.219, so the flow is strongly subcritical, and disturbances can travel both upstream and downstream. The depth of 2.40 m is therefore the mean depth used in every later wave calculation.

Answer: 1.06 m/s

(b)

For a wide channel Manning's equation gives Q proportional to A5/3, so the kinematic wave celerity is c_k = dQ/dA = (5/3)(Q/A) = (5/3)V = (5/3)(1.0619) = 1.770 m/s. This is the speed at which a flood crest moves when inertia is negligible, noticeably greater than the water velocity. The travel time over 18.0 km is t = 18 000/1.770 = 10 170 s = 2.83 h. A flood forecaster uses this time to give downstream communities a warning lead time between the gauge and the gate, though real crests also attenuate as they move.

Answer: 2.83 h

(c)

A small gravity wave travels at c = √(g y) = √(9.81 × 2.40) = 4.852 m/s relative to the water. Moving with the current, its speed relative to the bank is c + V = 4.852 + 1.062 = 5.914 m/s, and against the current it is c - V = 3.790 m/s, which is still positive, confirming the subcritical state. Over the 18 km reach the downstream wave would take 18 000/5.914 = 3044 s, or 0.85 h. This is the speed at which a sudden change at the gate would be felt, and it is far faster than the flood crest.

Answer: 5.91 m/s

(d)

Let the surge move upstream at speed c relative to the bank, raising the depth from y₁ = 2.40 m to y₂, with the water behind it stopped (V₂ = 0). In a frame moving with the surge, the water ahead arrives at V₁ + c and the water behind leaves at c. Continuity requires (V₁ + c) y₁ = c y₂, so c = V₁y₁/(y₂ - y₁). Momentum requires y₁(V₁ + c)² + g y₁²/2 = y₂c² + g y₂²/2. Solving numerically gives y₂ = 2.952 m, c = 4.62 m/s. Check: left side 2.4 × 5.682² + 28.25 = 105.7, right side 2.952 × 4.62² + 42.73 = 105.7. The surge height is 2.952 - 2.40 = 0.55 m.

Answer: 0.55 m

(e)

The flood crest moves at the kinematic celerity, 1.77 m/s, because a slowly varying flood is controlled by the balance between gravity along the slope and bed friction; inertia and pressure are negligible. A closure surge is a short, abrupt disturbance, so inertia and pressure forces dominate and the disturbance moves at a speed close to the dynamic gravity-wave celerity, here 4.6 to 5.9 m/s. The surge at 4.62 m/s travels about 2.6 times as fast as the flood crest. The two models apply different physics, and picking the wrong one would mistime a warning by hours, or ignore the near-instant rise that an operator creates by closing a gate.

Answer: Non-numeric

A5 Practice Paper 23

Problem 1 [A5-111] Centrifugal pump head, power and efficiency

A municipal water utility on the north shore of Lake Huron lifts raw water from a shoreline intake well to a treatment-plant clarifier. The water surface in the intake well is at elevation 176.0 m and the clarifier water surface is at 214.0 m, both open to atmosphere. The steel pipeline is 2400 m long with a 0.450 m inside diameter, a Darcy friction factor of 0.019 and a combined minor loss coefficient of 6.5 (bends, valves and the pipe exit), based on the pipe velocity. The pump delivers 0.180 m³/s. Use ρ = 1000 kg/m³ and g = 9.81 m/s². An electrical meter shows the motor draws 118 kW, and the motor efficiency is 0.94. The utility runs the pump 7200 h per year and pays $0.105 per kWh. A supplier proposes a replacement pump of 0.82 efficiency, installed cost $38,000, driven by the same motor.

  1. (a) Calculate the total dynamic head the pump must supply at 0.180 m³/s. [4]
  2. (b) Calculate the hydraulic (water) power delivered to the flow. [3]
  3. (c) Calculate the efficiency of the existing pump, in percent. [4]
  4. (d) Calculate the present annual energy cost of running the existing pump. [4]
  5. (e) Calculate the simple payback period, in years, of the replacement pump, assuming the same flow and head, and comment on whether the saving justifies the purchase. [5]
(a)

Apply the energy equation between the two free surfaces, where pressure and velocity heads are zero: H = Δz + hf + hm. The static lift is 214.0 - 176.0 = 38.0 m. The pipe area is A = π(0.450)²/4 = 0.15904 m², so V = Q/A = 0.180/0.15904 = 1.1318 m/s and V²/2g = 0.06529 m. Friction loss by Darcy-Weisbach is hf = f(L/D)V²/2g = 0.019 × (2400/0.450) × 0.06529 = 0.019 × 5333.3 × 0.06529 = 6.616 m. Minor losses are hm = 6.5 × 0.06529 = 0.424 m. Total dynamic head H = 38.0 + 6.616 + 0.424 = 45.04 m. The pump must supply this at the stated flow; friction is about 16 percent of the head, so the static lift dominates.

Answer: 45.04 m

(b)

Hydraulic power is the rate at which energy is added to the water: Pw = ρgQH. Substituting, Pw = 1000 × 9.81 × 0.180 × 45.04 = 79,530 W, which is 79.53 kW. This is the useful output of the pump and is independent of how efficient the machine is; efficiency only decides how much shaft power must be supplied to obtain it. Note that the head used must be the total dynamic head from part (a), not the static lift alone, because the pump must also overcome pipe friction and fitting losses. Using 38 m would understate the power by about 16 percent and would also lead to an optimistic efficiency in part (c).

Answer: 79.53 kW

(c)

The motor draws 118 kW of electrical power and has an efficiency of 0.94, so the shaft power delivered to the pump is Ps = 118 × 0.94 = 110.92 kW. Pump efficiency is the ratio of hydraulic power to shaft power: ηp = Pw/Ps = 79.53/110.92 = 0.7170, or 71.7 percent. The overall wire-to-water efficiency is 79.53/118 = 67.4 percent. A pump efficiency of 72 percent is mediocre for a unit of this size, which would normally reach about 80 to 85 percent at its best efficiency point, so the result suggests either wear or operation away from the best efficiency point. That observation motivates the replacement option examined in part (e).

Answer: 71.70 percent

(d)

Annual energy is the metered input power times the operating hours: E = 118 kW × 7200 h = 849,600 kWh per year. The cost at $0.105 per kWh is 849,600 × 0.105 = $89,208 per year. This uses the measured electrical input, so it already includes pump, motor and any drive losses and needs no efficiency factor. The calculation assumes the pump runs continuously at the stated duty throughout the 7200 hours; in practice flow varies with plant demand, so the figure is an upper-bound estimate for planning. Because the cost is proportional to input power, any efficiency improvement reduces it by the same proportion, which is what part (e) quantifies.

Answer: $89,208 per year

(e)

For the same hydraulic power of 79.53 kW, the new pump needs a shaft power of 79.53/0.82 = 96.99 kW, and the motor input is 96.99/0.94 = 103.18 kW. The saving in power is 118 - 103.18 = 14.82 kW. Annual saving = 14.82 × 7200 × 0.105 = $11,204 per year. Simple payback = 38,000/11,204 = 3.39 years. A payback of about 3.4 years is attractive for a pump with a typical service life of 20 years or more, and the utility should accept it, but the estimate ignores interest, maintenance differences and the risk that the new pump's rated efficiency is not achieved over the whole demand range. A manufacturer's guaranteed efficiency at the duty point should be required in the purchase contract.

Answer: 3.39 years

Problem 2 [A5-112] Pump similarity laws and specific speed

A single-stage centrifugal pump built for an irrigation district near Leamington was tested on a laboratory rig at 1450 rpm. At its best efficiency point it delivered 0.065 m³/s against a head of 28.0 m with an efficiency of 0.84. A food processor now wants this pump line to supply 0.090 m³/s of cooling-water make-up at the best efficiency point of a similar machine, and is considering either running the same pump faster with a variable-frequency drive or buying a geometrically similar larger pump that runs at 1450 rpm. The drive motor installed on the existing pump has a shaft-power rating of 45 kW. Use ρ = 1000 kg/m³ and g = 9.81 m/s². Assume the similarity laws hold exactly and that efficiency is unchanged by speed or size.

  1. (a) Calculate the dimensionless specific speed ωs = ω√Q/(gH)0.75 of the pump at its best efficiency point, with ω in rad/s. [3]
  2. (b) Find the speed at which the existing pump must run so that its best efficiency point flow is 0.090 m³/s. [3]
  3. (c) Calculate the shaft power the pump requires at that speed. [4]
  4. (d) Because the motor limit is 45 kW, find the largest best efficiency point flow the existing pump can deliver by speed increase alone. [5]
  5. (e) For the geometrically similar larger pump running at 1450 rpm and delivering 0.090 m³/s, find the head it develops at its best efficiency point, and state which option you would recommend. [5]
(a)

Convert the speed to angular velocity: ω = 1450 × 2π/60 = 151.84 rad/s. The flow term is √Q = √0.065 = 0.2550 m1.5/s0.5. The head term is (gH)0.75 = (9.81 × 28.0)0.75 = (274.68)0.75 = 67.46. Then ωs = 151.84 × 0.2550/67.46 = 0.574. This is a low-to-moderate value, typical of a radial-flow volute pump with a Francis-type impeller. Because ωs is dimensionless and unchanged by affinity scaling at the best efficiency point, the same value describes every speed and every geometrically similar size of this machine, which is why it is used to select impeller type rather than to size a particular unit.

Answer: 0.574

(b)

The affinity laws for the same impeller give Q ∝ N, H ∝ N² and P ∝ N³. At the best efficiency point the flow scales directly with speed, so N2 = N1(Q2/Q1) = 1450 × (0.090/0.065) = 1450 × 1.3846 = 2007.7 rpm, about 2008 rpm. The head at this speed rises by the square of the ratio: H2 = 28.0 × (1.3846)² = 53.7 m. Before accepting this, the designer must check that the casing pressure rating, bearing and seal limits and the impeller stress limit allow a 38 percent speed increase. A speed ratio this large is outside what most manufacturers permit on an existing machine, and the large head rise would also change the system operating point.

Answer: 2008 rpm

(c)

First find the shaft power at the original duty: P1 = ρgQH/η = 1000 × 9.81 × 0.065 × 28.0/0.84 = 21,255 W = 21.26 kW. Power varies with the cube of speed, so P2 = P1(N2/N1)³ = 21.26 × (1.3846)³ = 21.26 × 2.654 = 56.4 kW. The same result follows directly from P = ρgQ2H2/η = 9810 × 0.090 × 53.68/0.84 = 56.4 kW, which confirms the scaling. The required power exceeds the 45 kW motor rating by about 25 percent, so the existing motor cannot be used at 2008 rpm. A larger motor and drive would be needed, and the energy cost of the added head would also have to be justified.

Answer: 56.4 kW

(d)

The limiting condition is P = 45 kW, and P ∝ N³, so the speed ratio is k = (45/21.26)1/3 = (2.117)1/3 = 1.2837. The permissible speed is 1450 × 1.2837 = 1862 rpm. Flow scales directly with speed, so Q = 0.065 × 1.2837 = 0.0835 m³/s. The head at this speed is 28.0 × (1.2837)² = 46.2 m. This is 7 percent below the requested 0.090 m³/s, so speed increase alone cannot meet the demand without replacing the motor. The designer may accept the shortfall if the process can tolerate it, but the head rise of 18 m must also be compatible with the downstream piping rating, which has to be checked.

Answer: 0.0835 m³/s

(e)

For geometrically similar pumps at the same speed, the discharge scales as Q ∝ D³ so the diameter ratio is D2/D1 = (0.090/0.065)1/3 = 1.1146. Head scales as H ∝ N²D², so at equal speed H2 = 28.0 × (1.1146)² = 28.0 × 1.2423 = 34.8 m. With efficiency unchanged, the power is P ∝ N³D⁵ and P2 = 21.26 × (1.1146)⁵ = 21.26 × 1.7242 = 36.7 kW, which is inside a 45 kW motor, so the existing motor may even be reused. I would recommend the larger pump: it needs only 35 m of head and about 37 kW, whereas the faster existing pump needs 54 m and 56 kW, and the larger machine runs at an unchanged, proven speed.

Answer: 34.8 m

Problem 3 [A5-113] Cavitation and NPSH

A low-lift pumping station on the Ottawa River draws river water through a short suction line into a centrifugal pump whose centreline is 3.2 m above the minimum water level in the wet well. The suction line is 18.0 m long, 0.300 m in inside diameter, with a Darcy friction factor of 0.020 and a total minor loss coefficient of 2.8 (strainer, entrance and one elbow). The water is at 24 °C, with ρ = 997 kg/m³, and its vapour pressure is 2.98 kPa absolute. The barometric pressure at the site is 99.3 kPa. The manufacturer states that at the design flow of 0.140 m³/s the pump requires a net positive suction head NPSHr of 4.90 m, and that NPSHr varies as the square of the flow. Use g = 9.81 m/s² and treat the wet-well surface as open to the atmosphere.

  1. (a) Calculate the available net positive suction head, NPSHa, at the design flow of 0.140 m³/s. [5]
  2. (b) State the cavitation margin NPSHa minus NPSHr at the design flow. [3]
  3. (c) Summer demand requires 0.175 m³/s. Calculate the shortfall NPSHr minus NPSHa at that flow, with the pump left where it is. [4]
  4. (d) Find the largest flow at which the pump in its present position still has NPSHa equal to NPSHr. [4]
  5. (e) To run safely at 0.175 m³/s with a margin of 0.60 m, by how much must the pump centreline be lowered from its present position, and what other measures could avoid cavitation? [4]
(a)

NPSHa = (patm - pv)/(ρg) - zs - hL, where zs is the pump height above the free surface and hL is the suction-line loss. Pressure term: (99,300 - 2,980)/(997 × 9.81) = 96,320/9780.6 = 9.848 m. Suction area A = π(0.300)²/4 = 0.07069 m², so V = 0.140/0.07069 = 1.981 m/s and V²/2g = 0.2000 m. Losses hL = (fL/D + ΣK)V²/2g = (0.020 × 18.0/0.300 + 2.8) × 0.2000 = (1.2 + 2.8) × 0.2000 = 0.800 m. NPSHa = 9.848 - 3.2 - 0.800 = 5.85 m. The pump is above the water, so static lift reduces the available head; friction in the suction line reduces it further, which is why suction lines are kept short and large.

Answer: 5.85 m

(b)

The margin is the available head less the required head: 5.85 - 4.90 = 0.95 m. In practice a margin is required because the manufacturer's NPSHr corresponds to a 3 percent head drop, which means cavitation has already begun at the incipient stage, and damage and noise can occur even when NPSHa slightly exceeds NPSHr. Many specifications ask for a margin of 0.5 to 1.0 m, or a ratio NPSHa/NPSHr of 1.1 to 1.3. Here the ratio is 5.85/4.90 = 1.19, so the design flow is acceptable but not generous. Any rise in water temperature or fall in barometric pressure would erode this margin quickly.

Answer: 0.95 m

(c)

At 0.175 m³/s the flow ratio is k = 0.175/0.140 = 1.25. Suction losses vary with the square of velocity, so hL = 0.800 × 1.25² = 1.250 m. NPSHa = 9.848 - 3.2 - 1.250 = 5.398 m. The requirement also grows with the square of flow: NPSHr = 4.90 × 1.25² = 7.656 m. Shortfall = 7.656 - 5.398 = 2.26 m. The pump would therefore be well into cavitation, with loss of head, noise, vibration and impeller pitting. The result shows the double penalty of higher flow: the available head falls while the required head rises, and both vary as Q², so the gap closes quickly.

Answer: 2.26 m

(d)

Let k = Q/0.140. Then NPSHa = 9.848 - 3.2 - 0.800k² = 6.648 - 0.800k², and NPSHr = 4.90k². Setting them equal: 6.648 = 5.700k², so k² = 1.1663 and k = 1.080. The limiting flow is 0.140 × 1.080 = 0.1512 m³/s. The present installation therefore has only 8 percent flow capacity above design before cavitation sets in, and in practice the operating flow should stay below this value by the required margin. The summer demand of 0.175 m³/s exceeds it by 16 percent, confirming that the station cannot meet the demand with the pump where it is unless the arrangement is changed.

Answer: 0.151 m³/s

(e)

For 0.175 m³/s the requirement is NPSHr = 7.656 m, and with a margin of 0.60 m the required NPSHa is 8.256 m. With hL = 1.250 m, NPSHa = 9.848 - zs - 1.250 = 8.256, so zs = 0.342 m. The centreline must therefore be only 0.34 m above the water, and the pump must be lowered by 3.2 - 0.342 = 2.86 m. Alternatives include enlarging the suction line (halving the loss), removing the strainer or elbow, using a pump with lower NPSHr, running two smaller pumps in parallel, or installing the pump below minimum water level as a submersible or flooded-suction unit, which removes the static lift altogether.

Answer: 2.86 m

Problem 4 [A5-114] Pump-and-pipe system operating points, series and parallel pumps

A pumping station serving a new subdivision in Barrie lifts water to a reservoir through a single 3200 m transmission main of 0.500 m inside diameter, with a Darcy friction factor of 0.018 and a combined minor loss coefficient of 8.0. The static lift is 28.0 m. Each of two identical centrifugal pumps has the head-flow characteristic Hp = 62.0 - 2400Q² (Hp in metres, Q in m³/s through that one pump) and an efficiency of 0.78 at the operating points considered here. Use ρ = 1000 kg/m³ and g = 9.81 m/s². The utility needs at least 0.200 m³/s at peak demand. It is considering running one pump, two pumps in parallel, or two pumps in series. After several decades of service the main is expected to tuberculate and its friction factor may rise to 0.024.

  1. (a) Find the flow delivered when one pump operates alone against the new pipe. [4]
  2. (b) Find the total flow delivered when the two pumps operate in parallel. [4]
  3. (c) Find the flow delivered when the two pumps operate in series. [3]
  4. (d) For the parallel arrangement, calculate the shaft power drawn by each pump. [4]
  5. (e) Calculate the parallel-pump flow once the friction factor has risen to 0.024, and state whether the peak demand is still met. [5]
(a)

First express the pipe losses as a coefficient times Q². The area is A = π(0.500)²/4 = 0.19635 m², and 2gA² = 19.62 × 0.038553 = 0.7564 m5/s². The loss coefficient is (fL/D + ΣK)/(2gA²) = (0.018 × 3200/0.500 + 8.0)/0.7564 = (115.2 + 8.0)/0.7564 = 162.9 s²/m5. The system curve is Hs = 28.0 + 162.9Q². At the operating point Hp = Hs: 62.0 - 2400Q² = 28.0 + 162.9Q², so 34.0 = 2562.9Q² and Q = √0.013266 = 0.1152 m³/s. The head at this point is 28.0 + 162.9 × 0.013266 = 30.16 m, which is well below the 62 m shutoff head.

Answer: 0.1152 m³/s

(b)

Pumps in parallel share the flow at a common head, so each carries Q/2 and the combined characteristic is Hp = 62.0 - 2400(Q/2)² = 62.0 - 600Q². Equating to the system curve: 62.0 - 600Q² = 28.0 + 162.9Q², so 34.0 = 762.9Q² and Q = √0.044566 = 0.2111 m³/s. The common head is 28.0 + 162.9 × 0.044566 = 35.26 m. Note that the parallel flow is 1.83 times the single-pump flow, not twice, because the higher flow increases friction loss in the common pipe; the more resistive the system, the smaller the benefit of the second pump. Each pump here carries 0.1056 m³/s.

Answer: 0.2111 m³/s

(c)

Pumps in series pass the same flow and add their heads, so the combined characteristic is Hp = 2 × (62.0 - 2400Q²) = 124.0 - 4800Q². Equating to the system curve: 124.0 - 4800Q² = 28.0 + 162.9Q², so 96.0 = 4962.9Q² and Q = √0.019344 = 0.1391 m³/s. The head is 28.0 + 162.9 × 0.019344 = 31.15 m. Series operation increases flow only by 21 percent over a single pump here, but it raises head considerably. Series helps when one pump cannot reach the static lift or the system curve is steep; here 28 m is well below the 62 m shutoff and the curve is flat, so parallel operation is better.

Answer: 0.1391 m³/s

(d)

In the parallel case each pump carries q = 0.2111/2 = 0.10556 m³/s. Its head is Hp = 62.0 - 2400 × (0.10556)² = 62.0 - 26.74 = 35.26 m, matching the system head. The hydraulic power of one pump is ρgqH = 1000 × 9.81 × 0.10556 × 35.26 = 36,510 W = 36.51 kW. Dividing by the efficiency of 0.78 gives the shaft power: 36.51/0.78 = 46.8 kW per pump. The motor for each pump must therefore be rated above 47 kW, and a standard 55 kW motor would be selected. The total installed power of about 94 kW should be compared with a single pump running alone, which draws less power but cannot meet the demand.

Answer: 46.8 kW

(e)

With f = 0.024 the loss coefficient becomes (0.024 × 6400 + 8.0)/0.7564 = (153.6 + 8.0)/0.7564 = 213.6 s²/m5. The parallel pump curve is unchanged: 62.0 - 600Q² = 28.0 + 213.6Q². So 34.0 = 813.6Q² and Q = √0.041789 = 0.2044 m³/s. The flow falls by about 3 percent from 0.2111 m³/s. This still exceeds the 0.200 m³/s requirement, but the margin has shrunk from 5.6 percent to 2.2 percent, leaving little reserve. The utility should plan on pipe cleaning or relining, or on trimming impellers upward, before the friction factor rises much further. Because the margin is thin, I would advise specifying a pump with a higher shutoff head from the outset.

Answer: 0.2044 m³/s

Problem 5 [A5-115] Hydraulic structures, spillways and water quality dilution or reaeration

A small earth-fill dam on a southern Ontario creek has an uncontrolled ogee spillway with crest elevation 214.50 m and a dam crest at 217.00 m. The spillway has a gross length of 26.0 m divided by two piers. Discharge is Q = C Le H1.5 in SI units, with C = 2.15 and effective length Le = L - 2(NKp + Ka)H, where N = 2 piers, pier coefficient Kp = 0.01 and abutment coefficient Ka = 0.10, and H is the head above the crest in metres. Upstream water at 18 °C has a dissolved oxygen (DO) concentration of 5.20 mg/L and a saturation value of 9.46 mg/L. Water falling over the structure drops 3.4 m. Aeration follows r = 1 + 0.38ab h(1 - 0.11h)(1 + 0.046T), with a = 1.25, b = 1.0, h in metres and T in °C; r = Du/Dd, the ratio of upstream to downstream oxygen deficit.

  1. (a) Find the head on the crest when the spillway passes a flood of 180 m³/s. [5]
  2. (b) Find the freeboard between the reservoir surface and the dam crest at that flood. [2]
  3. (c) Calculate the aeration ratio r for the 3.4 m drop. [4]
  4. (d) Calculate the dissolved oxygen concentration immediately downstream of the spillway. [4]
  5. (e) Calculate the discharge when the reservoir reaches the dam crest, and state whether a 250 m³/s design flood would overtop the dam. [5]
(a)

Because Le depends on H, the equation is solved iteratively. With N = 2, Kp = 0.01 and Ka = 0.10, Le = 26.0 - 2(2 × 0.01 + 0.10)H = 26.0 - 0.24H. The discharge equation is 180 = 2.15 × (26.0 - 0.24H) × H1.5. Trying H = 2.2: Le = 25.47 m, H1.5 = 3.263, and Q = 2.15 × 25.47 × 3.263 = 178.7 m³/s. Trying H = 2.22: Le = 25.467 m, H1.5 = 3.308, giving 181.1 m³/s. Interpolating (or solving with a root finder) gives H = 2.211 m, with Le = 25.47 m. The end contractions reduce the effective length by only about 2 percent, so the result is dominated by the gross crest length.

Answer: 2.21 m

(b)

The reservoir surface elevation is the crest elevation plus the head: 214.50 + 2.211 = 216.711 m. Freeboard is the dam crest elevation minus this level: 217.00 - 216.711 = 0.289 m. This is the margin available against wave run-up and wind setup during the flood. A freeboard under 0.3 m is very thin for an earth-fill dam, which is vulnerable to erosion and breaching if overtopped, so the 180 m³/s flood is already close to the dam's limit. A designer would normally want freeboard that covers wave action as well as the still-water flood level, and would not accept this margin for the design flood of a dam of this size.

Answer: 0.29 m

(c)

Substitute into the Gameson-type aeration relation with h = 3.4 m, T = 18 °C, a = 1.25 and b = 1.0. First, 1 - 0.11h = 1 - 0.374 = 0.626, and 1 + 0.046T = 1 + 0.828 = 1.828. Then 0.38ab h = 0.38 × 1.25 × 1.0 × 3.4 = 1.615. So r = 1 + 1.615 × 0.626 × 1.828 = 1 + 1.848 = 2.848. The upstream oxygen deficit is therefore reduced by a factor of nearly 2.85 as the water passes over the spillway. The factor 1 - 0.11h reflects that the benefit of a larger drop levels off, so doubling the height does not double the deficit reduction.

Answer: 2.85

(d)

The upstream deficit is Du = Cs - C = 9.46 - 5.20 = 4.26 mg/L. The downstream deficit is Dd = Du/r = 4.26/2.848 = 1.496 mg/L. The downstream concentration is Cd = Cs - Dd = 9.46 - 1.496 = 7.96 mg/L. The spillway therefore raises the oxygen level by 2.76 mg/L, restoring the creek to 84 percent of saturation. This is useful for a stream that would otherwise be depleted by upstream organic load, since fish such as brook trout need concentrations above about 6 mg/L. The calculation applies the deficit ratio at a single drop and ignores any change in temperature or further reaeration downstream.

Answer: 7.96 mg/L

(e)

When the reservoir reaches the dam crest, the head is H = 217.00 - 214.50 = 2.50 m. The effective length is Le = 26.0 - 0.24 × 2.50 = 25.40 m, and H1.5 = 3.953. The discharge is Q = 2.15 × 25.40 × 3.953 = 215.9 m³/s. A design flood of 250 m³/s exceeds this by about 16 percent, so the dam would be overtopped; for an earth-fill embankment that is a failure condition. The owner should widen the spillway, add an auxiliary spillway or raise the dam. For example, increasing the crest length to about 30 m would carry 250 m³/s at the same head, since discharge is nearly proportional to length.

Answer: 215.9 m³/s

Exam A6: Highway Design, Construction, and Maintenance

A6 Practice Paper 1

Problem 1 [A6-001] Route surveying and horizontal curve layout by deflection angles

A new alignment for a rural arterial near Peterborough, Ontario, is being set out on the ground. Two tangents meet at a point of intersection (PI) at chainage 12+480.00 (that is, 12 480.00 m from the project origin). The measured deflection angle between the tangents is 34°20' to the right, and the Region has specified a simple circular curve of radius 600 m. Pegs are to be set at every full 20 m chainage, and the curve is to be laid out by the deflection angle method with the theodolite set up at the point of curvature (PC), sighting back along the tangent.

  1. (a) Calculate the tangent length T of the curve. [4]
  2. (b) Calculate the length L of the curve along its arc. [3]
  3. (c) Determine the chainage of the PC, in metres. [3]
  4. (d) Determine the deflection angle, measured at the PC from the tangent, to the first full 20 m peg on the curve. Treat the short first arc as its own sub-chord of equal arc and chord length and give the answer in degrees. [5]
  5. (e) Calculate the length of the long chord from the PC to the point of tangency (PT), and state how a check on the closing deflection angle at the PT would be made. [5]
(a)

The tangent length of a simple circular curve is T = R tan(Δ/2). With Δ = 34°20' = 0.59923 rad and R = 600 m, Δ/2 = 17.1667° and tan(17.1667°) = 185.3/600. Hence T = 600 × tan(17.1667°) = 185.35 m.
