This is the distance from the PC back to the PI and from the PI forward to the PT along the tangents. Both tangents must be chained and pegged to this distance from the PI before the curve is set out. The geometry assumes a circular arc with no spirals, as specified by the Region, so the same T applies at both ends.

Answer: 185.3 m

(b)

The arc length of a circular curve in radians is L = R Δ, where Δ is the deflection angle expressed in radians. Here Δ = 0.59923 rad, so L = 600 × 0.59923 = 359.54 m. This is the length along the centreline between the PC and the PT, and it sets how many 20 m pegs will be needed. An approximate check uses the degree-of-curve definition, L = πRΔ(degrees)/180 = π × 600 × 34.3333/180 = 359.5 m, which agrees with the radian calculation. Arc length rather than the chord governs chainage, because chainage is measured along the road centreline.

Answer: 359.5 m

(c)

Chainage is measured along the alignment, so the PC lies one tangent length back from the PI: PC = PI − T. With the PI at 12 480.00 m and T = 185.35 m, PC = 12 480.00 − 185.35 = 12294.65 m, that is 12+294.65. The PT follows by adding the arc length to the PC: PT = 12294.65 + 359.54 = 12654.19 m. Note that the chainage does not jump at the PI, because chainage continues along the curve; the PT chainage is not simply the PI chainage plus T. This is the standard point of confusion in route surveying.

Answer: 12294.7 m

(d)

The first full peg beyond the PC is at the next multiple of 20 m, chainage 12300 m. The sub-chord from the PC is c1 = 12300 − 12294.65 = 5.35 m. For a circular curve the deflection angle from the tangent to any chord equals half the central angle subtended by that arc, so δ1 = (c1/R)/2 in radians = 5.35/(2 × 600) = 0.004457 rad = 0.255°. This is the angle set on the theodolite after backsighting along the tangent from the PC. Subsequent pegs add the standard deflection for a 20 m arc, 20/(2 × 600) rad = 0.955°, to this value.

Answer: 0.255 deg

(e)

The long chord joining the PC and PT subtends the full central angle Δ, so C = 2R sin(Δ/2) = 2 × 600 × sin(17.1667°) = 354.18 m. For the closing check, the theodolite remains at the PC and the cumulative deflection to the PT must equal Δ/2 = 17.1667° = 17°10'. If the last peg misses the PT by more than the allowable misclosure, the tape and angle readings are rechecked. The chord to the PT should also read 354.18 m when taped directly. This independent check catches blunders in either chainage or angle.

Answer: 354.2 m

Problem 2 [A6-002] Horizontal curve design: radius, superelevation and side friction

A two-lane Ontario provincial highway is being realigned through rolling terrain with a design speed of 100 km/h. The agency's criteria cap the maximum superelevation at e_max = 0.060 m/m and the maximum design side friction factor at f_max = 0.120 for this design speed. Use the point-mass relation e + f = V²/(127 R), with V in km/h and R in metres. A particular curve in the alignment has already been fixed by the right-of-way at a radius of 520 m. For that curve the designer proposes to use a design side friction factor of 0.100 for comfort. After construction, a posted speed review notes that some vehicles travel at 120 km/h, and wet-pavement tests show the available tyre-pavement friction in the curve is only 0.090.

  1. (a) Calculate the minimum radius for the design speed using the maximum superelevation and the maximum side friction factor. [5]
  2. (b) For the 520 m curve with the design side friction factor of 0.100, calculate the superelevation rate required (as a decimal) and state whether it is within the agency maximum. [4]
  3. (c) With the pavement built at the maximum superelevation of 0.060 on the 520 m curve, calculate the side friction demand for a vehicle travelling at 120 km/h. [5]
  4. (d) Using the wet-pavement friction of 0.090 and e = 0.060, calculate the maximum speed at which a vehicle can negotiate the 520 m curve without skidding sideways, and comment briefly on the result compared with 120 km/h. [6]
(a)

Rearranging e + f = V²/(127R) gives R_min = V²/[127 (e_max + f_max)]. Substituting V = 100 km/h, e_max = 0.060 and f_max = 0.120, R_min = 10 000/[127 × (0.060 + 0.120)] = 10 000/22.86 = 437.4 m. Any curve flatter than this radius can be built with e at or below the maximum and f below its limit. A smaller radius would require either more superelevation, which risks sliding of slow or stopped vehicles in ice and snow, or more friction than comfort criteria allow. Ontario winter conditions are the reason e_max is capped at 0.06 on rural roads.

Answer: 437.4 m

(b)

At the fixed radius of 520 m the total demand is e + f = V²/(127R) = 10 000/(127 × 520) = 0.1514. With f = 0.100 assigned to friction, the required superelevation is e = 0.1514 − 0.100 = 0.0514 m/m, which is 0.0514 or about 5.1 percent. Since this is less than e_max = 0.060, the curve is acceptable under the agency criteria. The result leaves a margin of about 0.9 percentage points before the superelevation cap is reached. In practice the designer would round to 5.2 or 5.5 percent and check runoff lengths for transitioning the cross-slope.

Answer: 0.0514 m/m

(c)

With e fixed at 0.060 by construction, the friction needed to hold a vehicle on the curve at 120 km/h is f = V²/(127R) − e. Substituting, f = 14 400/(127 × 520) − 0.060 = 0.2180 − 0.060 = 0.158. This exceeds the design side friction factor of 0.120 for 100 km/h, but the margin must be compared with the friction actually available. At 120 km/h the demand is higher than the 0.100 the designer allowed. The excess is the reason posted speeds above the design speed are discouraged on this curve, since the safety margin against skidding shrinks quickly because demand rises with the square of speed.

Answer: 0.158

(d)

The skidding limit occurs when the demand equals the available friction. Setting f = 0.090 and e = 0.060 gives V = √[127 R (e + f)] = √[127 × 520 × (0.060 + 0.090)] = √[9 906] = 99.5 km/h. A vehicle at 120 km/h is therefore well above this wet-pavement limit, and since the demand of 0.158 exceeds the available 0.090 it would skid outward. The result shows a design that is adequate at 100 km/h under dry conditions becomes marginal when the pavement is wet and speeds exceed the posted limit. Recommended actions are advisory speed signs, pavement friction treatment such as grooving, and enforcement.

Answer: 99.5 km/h

Problem 3 [A6-003] Spiral transition curves

A ramp connecting Highway 401 to a municipal arterial in the Region of Durham is to be designed with symmetrical clothoid spirals at each end of a central circular curve. The design speed is 80 km/h, the central curve radius is R = 250 m, and the total deflection angle between the tangents is Δ = 48°. The agency's rate of change of lateral acceleration (Shortt) is C = 0.60 m/s³, and the minimum spiral length is Ls = V³/(C R) with V in m/s. After computing the minimum, the designer adopts Ls = 75 m. For the adopted spiral use the standard approximations: shift p = Ls²/(24 R) and tangent offset k = Ls/2 − Ls³/(240 R²). The overall tangent distance from the PI to the TS is Ts = (R + p) tan(Δ/2) + k.

  1. (a) Calculate the minimum spiral length required by the Shortt criterion. [5]
  2. (b) For the adopted Ls = 75 m, calculate the spiral angle θs, in degrees. [4]
  3. (c) Calculate the shift p, the lateral distance by which the circular curve is moved inward. [5]
  4. (d) Calculate the total tangent distance Ts from the PI to the TS (tangent to spiral point). [6]
(a)

Convert the speed to metres per second: V = 80/3.6 = 22.222 m/s. The Shortt criterion limits the rate at which lateral acceleration builds up on entering the curve, giving Ls = V³/(C R) = 22.222³/(0.60 × 250) = 10973.9/150 = 73.2 m. A shorter spiral would make the lateral jerk exceed the agency comfort limit of 0.60 m/s³. In practice the designer rounds up, here to 75 m, which also suits a 25 m stationing interval. Check that the spiral is at least as long as the superelevation runoff needed for the roadway, which can govern on wide ramps.

Answer: 73.2 m

(b)

For a clothoid spiral the spiral angle is θs = Ls/(2R) in radians. With Ls = 75 m and R = 250 m, θs = 75/(2 × 250) = 0.1500 rad. Converting to degrees, θs = 0.1500 × 180/π = 8.59°. This is the angle between the tangent at the TS and the tangent to the spiral at the SC, where it joins the circular curve. The central circular arc then subtends Δ − 2θs = 48 − 17.19 = 30.81°. This must be positive, otherwise the spirals alone would use up all the deflection, which is not the case here.

Answer: 8.59 deg

(c)

The shift p is the distance by which the circular arc must be moved inward from the original tangent so that the spiral can be inserted. Using the stated approximation p = Ls²/(24R) = 75²/(24 × 250) = 5 625/6 000 = 0.9375 m. The tangent offset of the spiral end, k = Ls/2 − Ls³/(240R²) = 37.5 − 421 875/15 000 000 = 37.472 m, is the distance along the original tangent from the TS to the point opposite the beginning of the shifted circular curve. The shift is small compared with the radius, which confirms that the series approximation is accurate to well under the 1 percent level.

Answer: 0.938 m

(d)

Combine the shifted-circle tangent with the offset: Ts = (R + p) tan(Δ/2) + k. Here R + p = 250 + 0.9375 = 250.9375 m and tan(24°) = 0.44523, so (R + p) tan(Δ/2) = 250.9375 × 0.44523 = 111.72 m. Adding k = 37.472 m, Ts = 149.2 m. The TS is therefore located 149.2 m back from the PI along the entry tangent, and the ST the same distance forward on the exit tangent. This is the control dimension for staking the ramp, since the total length of curve, 2Ls plus the circular arc, is then checked against it.

Answer: 149.2 m

Problem 4 [A6-004] Stopping and decision sight distance

A municipal engineer is reviewing sight distance on an urban arterial in London, Ontario, that descends a 6 percent grade toward a signalized intersection. For all stopping calculations use a perception-reaction time of 2.5 s and a constant braking deceleration of a = 3.4 m/s² on a level road; on a grade G (decimal, negative for downgrade) the effective deceleration is a + gG with g = 9.81 m/s². The posted speed is 70 km/h. At one location a crest in the downgrade limits the available stopping sight distance to 95 m. Separately, for a rural section of an Ontario highway with a design speed of 90 km/h the designer wants the decision sight distance for an avoidance manoeuvre, to be computed as DSD = 0.278 V t + 0.039 V²/a, with V in km/h, a = 3.0 m/s² and t = 11.0 s of pre-manoeuvre time.

  1. (a) Calculate the stopping sight distance at 70 km/h on a level road. [4]
  2. (b) Calculate the stopping sight distance at 70 km/h on the 6 percent downgrade. [5]
  3. (c) Determine the maximum speed, in km/h, at which a driver can stop within the available 95 m on the 6 percent downgrade. [6]
  4. (d) Calculate the decision sight distance at 90 km/h and state why it is greater than stopping sight distance. [5]
(a)

Convert 70 km/h to 19.444 m/s. Stopping distance is the sum of the distance travelled during perception-reaction and the braking distance: SSD = v t + v²/(2a). Reaction distance = 19.444 × 2.5 = 48.61 m. Braking distance = 19.444²/(2 × 3.4) = 55.60 m. SSD = 48.61 + 55.60 = 104.2 m. This is the minimum length of road ahead a driver must be able to see to stop for a stationary object. The method assumes wet pavement and a constant deceleration, and the value is used to set minimum crest curve lengths and the placement of signs and signals.

Answer: 104.2 m

(b)

On a downgrade of G = −0.06 gravity assists the vehicle, so the effective deceleration is a + gG = 3.4 + 9.81 × (−0.06) = 2.811 m/s². Reaction distance is unchanged at 48.61 m. Braking distance = v²/(2 × 2.811) = 378.09/5.623 = 67.24 m. SSD = 48.61 + 67.24 = 115.9 m. The downgrade adds about 11.6 m to the level-road requirement. Since the available sight distance at the crest is only 95 m, the location is deficient at the posted speed, and either the speed or the geometry must change.

Answer: 115.9 m

(c)

Set the total stopping distance equal to the available 95 m with the downgrade deceleration of 2.811 m/s²: v t + v²/(2 × 2.811) = 95, which is v²/5.623 + 2.5 v − 95 = 0. Solving the quadratic, v = [−2.5 + √(2.5² + 4 × 95/5.623)]/(2/5.623) = 17.13 m/s. In km/h this is 17.13 × 3.6 = 61.7 km/h. A posted or advisory speed near 60 km/h would therefore be required at this crest unless the vertical curve is lengthened. The nearest standard sign speed below this value, 60 km/h, would be adopted.

Answer: 61.7 km/h

(d)

Using DSD = 0.278 V t + 0.039 V²/a with V = 90 km/h, t = 11.0 s and a = 3.0 m/s²: the pre-manoeuvre term is 0.278 × 90 × 11.0 = 275.2 m, and the braking term is 0.039 × 8 100/3.0 = 105.3 m. DSD = 275.2 + 105.3 = 380.5 m. The distance is much greater than stopping sight distance because the driver needs additional time to detect an unexpected or difficult-to-perceive hazard, decide on a response, and carry out a speed, path or direction change rather than a simple stop. It is provided at complex locations such as interchanges and lane drops.

Answer: 381 m

Problem 5 [A6-005] Crest and sag vertical curves and K values

A new county road near Sudbury, Ontario, has a crest vertical curve joining an entering grade of +3.0 percent to an exiting grade of −2.5 percent. The point of vertical intersection (PVI) is at station 4+200 (4 200 m) and elevation 215.00 m. Design the crest for a stopping sight distance of S = 130 m with a driver eye height of h1 = 1.05 m and an object height of h2 = 0.15 m, using L = A S²/[100 (√(2h1) + √(2h2))²] when S < L, where A is the algebraic difference in grades in percent. The designer then adopts a curve length of L = 240 m. Further along the road, a separate sag curve with A = 6.0 percent must be checked for headlight sight distance, with S = 100 m, using L = A S²/(120 + 3.5 S) for S < L. Elevations on the parabolic curve follow y = y_PVC + g1 x + (g2 − g1) x²/(2L), with grades as decimals.

  1. (a) Calculate the minimum length of the crest curve for S = 130 m, and verify that S < L. [5]
  2. (b) For the adopted L = 240 m, calculate the distance from the PVC to the high point of the curve. [4]
  3. (c) Calculate the elevation of the high point of the curve. [5]
  4. (d) Calculate the minimum length of the sag curve with A = 6.0 percent for headlight sight distance of 100 m, and state the K value of this curve. [6]
(a)

A = 3.0 − (−2.5) = 5.5 percent. The denominator uses √(2 × 1.05) = 1.4491 and √(2 × 0.15) = 0.5477, so the sum squared is (1.4491 + 0.5477)² = 3.987. Then L = 5.5 × 130²/(100 × 3.987) = 92950/398.7 = 233.1 m. Since S = 130 m is less than L = 233.1 m, the assumption of the sight line lying within the curve is valid. The curve is adopted at 240 m for a rounded length. If S had exceeded L, the formula L = 2S − 200(√h1 + √h2)²/A would have applied instead.

Answer: 233.1 m

(b)

The high point is where the slope of the parabola is zero. The slope at distance x from the PVC is g1 + (g2 − g1) x/L = 0, so x = g1 L/(g1 − g2). With g1 = 0.030, g2 = −0.025 and L = 240 m, x = 0.030 × 240/0.055 = 130.9 m from the PVC. The equivalent expression x = K × g1 uses K = L/A = 43.64 m per percent, giving the same result. The high point is not at the PVI, which is at 120 m from the PVC, because the entering grade is steeper than the exiting grade, so the summit sits beyond the midpoint of the curve.

Answer: 130.9 m

(c)

First find the PVC elevation: the PVC is L/2 = 120 m before the PVI on the entering grade, so E_PVC = 215.00 − 0.030 × 120 = 211.40 m. Then at x = 130.9 m: E = E_PVC + g1 x + (g2 − g1) x²/(2L) = 211.40 + 0.030 × 130.9 + (−0.055) × 17137/480 = 211.40 + 3.927 − 1.964 = 213.36 m. The summit lies below the PVI by 1.64 m, consistent with the property that the curve lies below the tangent intersection on a crest by A L/800 at the PVI. This elevation is used to check drainage, because the summit is where surface water must be shed laterally.

Answer: 213.36 m

(d)

For headlight sight distance on a sag curve with S < L, L = A S²/(120 + 3.5 S). With A = 6.0 and S = 100 m, L = 6.0 × 10 000/(120 + 350) = 60 000/470 = 127.7 m. The corresponding K value is L/A = 127.7/6.0 = 21.3 m per percent. The 120 and 3.5 factors represent a headlamp height of 0.6 m and an upward beam divergence of 1 degree. Because S = 100 m is less than L, the formula is valid. Sag curves are also checked for comfort and drainage, but headlight control normally governs at moderate speeds.

Answer: 127.7 m

A6 Practice Paper 2

Problem 1 [A6-006] Vertical alignment, grades and passing sight distance

A two-lane rural highway near Thunder Bay, Ontario, is being checked for passing opportunities. Compute the passing sight distance as the sum of four components. d1 = 0.278 t1 (v − m + a t1/2) is the initial manoeuvre distance, d2 = 0.278 v t2 is the distance the passing vehicle occupies the opposing lane, d3 = 75 m is the clearance length, and d4 = (2/3) d2 is the distance travelled by the opposing vehicle. Speeds are in km/h and times in seconds. Use passing vehicle speed v = 95 km/h, speed difference m = 15 km/h, average acceleration a = 2.30 km/h/s, t1 = 4.4 s and t2 = 10.0 s. A crest curve on the highway joins grades of +1.5 and −1.5 percent, and its length for passing is L = A S²/[200 (√h1 + √h2)²] with eye and object heights both 1.08 m and A in percent. Further on, the highway climbs a continuous 3.5 percent grade for 1.8 km starting at elevation 240.00 m, where loaded trucks slow to 45 km/h while cars hold 90 km/h.

  1. (a) Calculate the passing sight distance. [6]
  2. (b) Calculate the minimum crest curve length that provides this passing sight distance, assuming S < L. [5]
  3. (c) Calculate the elevation at the top of the 1.8 km climb. [4]
  4. (d) Calculate how much longer, in seconds, a truck takes than a car to travel the 1.8 km grade, and comment on whether a climbing lane is worth considering. [5]
(a)

Compute each component. d1 = 0.278 × 4.4 × (95 − 15 + 2.30 × 4.4/2) = 1.2232 × (80 + 5.06) = 104.0 m. d2 = 0.278 × 95 × 10.0 = 264.1 m. The clearance d3 is given as 75 m. The opposing vehicle travels d4 = (2/3) × 264.1 = 176.1 m. The passing sight distance is the sum: 104.0 + 264.1 + 75 + 176.1 = 619.2 m. This is a long distance; rounded to about 620 m, it governs the vertical alignment wherever passing is to be permitted. If the sight distance is not available, a no-passing zone is marked with pavement markings.

Answer: 619 m

(b)

The algebraic difference in grade is A = 1.5 − (−1.5) = 3.0 percent. With eye and object heights both 1.08 m, (√1.08 + √1.08)² = (2 × 1.0392)² = 4.320. The curve length for S < L is L = A S²/(200 × 4.320) = 3.0 × 619.2²/(200 × 4.320) = 1150271/864.0 = 1331 m. Check: S = 619 m is less than L = 1331 m, so the assumption holds. A crest this long is expensive, which is why passing sight distance is usually provided only on flat or long crest curves and why designers mark many crests as no-passing zones.

Answer: 1331 m

(c)

The elevation gain on a constant grade is the grade times the horizontal length. A 3.5 percent grade is 0.035 m per metre, so the gain over 1 800 m is 0.035 × 1 800 = 63.0 m. The top of the climb is at elevation 240.00 + 63.0 = 303.00 m. Vertical curves at the ends of the grade are ignored since their length is small compared with the 1.8 km grade. This neglect is acceptable at the planning level, though final design elevations would include the curve corrections. The result is also needed to estimate the truck energy loss in the next part.

Answer: 303.00 m

(d)

A truck at 45 km/h covers 1.8 km in 1.8/45 × 3 600 = 144 s. A car at 90 km/h takes 1.8/90 × 3 600 = 72 s. The truck takes 72 s longer, so a following car held behind it loses 72 s on this grade unless it can pass. Because passing on a 3.5 percent grade with a speed differential of 45 km/h often needs more than the available sight distance, delays and unsafe passes are likely. A climbing lane would be worth evaluating where upgrade traffic volumes and truck percentage are high, using the agency warrants for volume and speed reduction.

Answer: 72 s

Problem 2 [A6-007] Intersection design: turning radii, sight triangles and channelization

A city in the Region of Waterloo is rebuilding two intersections. At Intersection X, a minor street meets a major arterial with a posted speed of 80 km/h and is controlled by stop signs on the minor approach. The departure sight distance for a left turn from the stop, looking both ways along the arterial, is computed as d = 0.278 V tg, with V the arterial design speed in km/h and tg the gap time in seconds: tg = 7.5 s for a two-lane arterial, plus 0.5 s for each additional lane crossed beyond the first two. A later phase will widen the arterial to four lanes. At Intersection Y, which is signalized with a 90 s cycle, the design left-turn volume is 180 vehicles per hour. Design the left-turn storage as twice the average number of vehicles arriving per cycle, with 7.5 m of storage per vehicle. A raised island forces right-turning vehicles at 20 km/h onto a turning roadway with no superelevation (e = 0) and a design side friction factor of 0.30.

  1. (a) Calculate the minimum radius of the right-turn roadway at 20 km/h, using R = V²/[127 (e + f)]. [4]
  2. (b) Calculate the departure sight distance at Intersection X for the existing two-lane arterial. [5]
  3. (c) Calculate the departure sight distance required after the arterial is widened to four lanes (two additional lanes). [5]
  4. (d) Calculate the required left-turn storage length at Intersection Y. [6]
(a)

For a turning roadway the same point-mass relation used for horizontal curves applies, e + f = V²/(127 R). With V = 20 km/h, e = 0 and f = 0.30, R = 20²/[127 × (0 + 0.30)] = 400/38.1 = 10.50 m. A practical design rounds up to at least 11 m for the inner edge of pavement, and the designer must check that the design vehicle (WB-20 or a bus) can still turn using a compound or three-centred curve. The island and lane widths are then built around this radius. A tighter radius would require speeds below 20 km/h for the same side friction.

Answer: 10.5 m

(b)

The departure sight distance from a stopped position uses d = 0.278 V tg, with V = 80 km/h and tg = 7.5 s for the two-lane case: d = 0.278 × 80 × 7.5 = 166.8 m. This is the length of the legs of the sight triangle along the arterial in each direction that must be kept clear of obstructions such as signs, hedges and parked vehicles. A driver at the stop line must be able to see a vehicle approaching at the design speed at this distance so as to complete the manoeuvre without forcing the through vehicle to brake severely.

Answer: 166.8 m

(c)

With two additional lanes the gap time increases by 0.5 s per lane: tg = 7.5 + 2 × 0.5 = 8.5 s. Then d = 0.278 × 80 × 8.5 = 189.0 m. This is 22.2 m more than the existing requirement. The extra crossing width gives the left-turner more time exposed to traffic, so the sight triangle must grow. If the existing hedge and utility poles are closer than this distance they will have to be removed or relocated as part of the widening. The design should be checked for both directions along the arterial.

Answer: 189.0 m

(d)

The average left-turn arrivals per cycle are 180 veh/h × 90 s/3 600 s/h = 4.5 vehicles. The design storage uses twice the average to cover random cycle-to-cycle variation, so the design queue is 2 × 4.5 = 9.0 vehicles. With 7.5 m per vehicle, the storage length is 9.0 × 7.5 = 67.5 m, exclusive of the taper. A bay of about 70 m plus a taper is therefore needed. Where the calculated queue exceeds the available block length, the cycle splits or signal phasing, for example a protected left-turn phase, should be reviewed.

Answer: 67.5 m

Problem 3 [A6-008] Earthwork volumes and the mass haul diagram

A 120 m reconstruction of a municipal road in Ottawa is being graded. Cross-sections were taken every 20 m, with the following end areas in square metres. Cut areas at stations 0+000, 0+020, 0+040, 0+060, 0+080, 0+100 and 0+120 are 10, 22, 30, 18, 6, 0 and 0. Fill areas at the same stations are 0, 0, 0, 3, 14, 21 and 24. Use the average end area method between consecutive stations for both cut and fill, ignoring transitions between cut and fill within a 20 m interval. Cut volumes are measured in the bank (in situ) condition. Cut material compacts into the embankment at a factor of 0.88, so that 1 m³ of bank cut yields 0.88 m³ of compacted fill. Fill volumes are measured as compacted volume. Any surplus is hauled off site, and bank material swells by 25 percent to loose volume when excavated.

  1. (a) Calculate the total cut volume in the bank condition. [5]
  2. (b) Calculate the total fill volume in the compacted condition. [4]
  3. (c) Determine the net surplus (or deficit) of material in bank cubic metres after the cut is used to build the fill. A positive value is a surplus. [5]
  4. (d) Calculate the loose volume of surplus to be hauled away and the number of truck loads if each truck carries 10 m³ of loose material. [6]
(a)

By the average end area method, V = (A1 + A2)/2 × distance for each 20 m interval. Cut: (10 + 22)/2 × 20 = 320, (22 + 30)/2 × 20 = 520, (30 + 18)/2 × 20 = 480, (18 + 6)/2 × 20 = 240, (6 + 0)/2 × 20 = 60, and (0 + 0)/2 × 20 = 0. The total is 1620 m³ of bank cut. The method slightly overestimates volume where the sections change from a large to a small area, because the true shape is a prismoid, but the error is small for a 20 m spacing and is accepted for payment quantities in this size of project.

Answer: 1620 m³

(b)

Apply the same method to the fill areas: (0 + 0)/2 × 20 = 0, (0 + 0)/2 × 20 = 0, (0 + 3)/2 × 20 = 30, (3 + 14)/2 × 20 = 170, (14 + 21)/2 × 20 = 350, and (21 + 24)/2 × 20 = 450. The total compacted fill is 1000 m³. This volume is measured in place after compaction, so it cannot be compared directly with the bank cut volume. The conversion factor is applied in the next part. Note that the fill increases toward the end of the section, which means the project may need more material than is excavated at the far end if the road is extended.

Answer: 1000 m³

(c)

The bank volume of cut needed to build the compacted fill is 1000/0.88 = 1136 m³. The cut available is 1620 m³, so the net balance is 1620 − 1136 = 484 m³ of surplus in the bank condition. The positive sign means the job has excess excavated material and no borrow is required. This balance is the final ordinate of the mass haul diagram, taken in bank volumes. The shrinkage factor of 0.88 corresponds to the compaction of the soil to a higher density than its in situ state.

Answer: 484 m³

(d)

Surplus material swells when it is excavated and loaded. Loose volume = bank volume × 1.25 = 484 × 1.25 = 605 m³. With 10 m³ per truck the number of loads is 605/10 = 60.5, so 61 loads are needed, rounded up. The truck count controls the haul cost and the traffic impact on the street. Truck capacity is always rated in loose cubic metres because that is what the box holds, which is why swell must be applied before counting loads. The haul distance to the disposal site then determines the total cost.

Answer: 605 m³

Problem 4 [A6-009] Embankment, borrow, shrinkage, swell and compaction

A 1.2 km section of a new access road in northern Ontario is built on an embankment 3.5 m high with a top width of 12 m and side slopes of 2 horizontal to 1 vertical. The embankment is to be compacted to 95 percent of a laboratory maximum dry density of 1.95 t/m³ at an optimum moisture content of 11.5 percent. Granular borrow material is available from a pit where its in situ (bank) bulk density is 1.92 t/m³ at a natural moisture content of 14 percent. Treat the embankment as a prism of constant trapezoidal cross-section, neglect foundation settlement and waste, and assume no loss of material in transport.

  1. (a) Calculate the total volume of the compacted embankment. [4]
  2. (b) Calculate the dry mass of soil required, in tonnes. [4]
  3. (c) Calculate the bank volume of borrow required. [6]
  4. (d) The borrow arrives at 14 percent moisture and must be brought to the optimum of 11.5 percent. Calculate the mass of water, in tonnes, that has to be removed by drying (windrow aeration) across the whole fill. [6]
(a)

The base width of the cross-section is top width + 2 × (side slope × height) = 12 + 2 × 2 × 3.5 = 26 m. The trapezoidal area is (12 + 26)/2 × 3.5 = 66.5 m². Multiplying by the length of 1 200 m gives V = 66.5 × 1 200 = 79800 m³ of compacted embankment. This assumes constant section along the 1.2 km. Real projects vary the height with the profile, in which case the average end area method is applied between stations. The quantity is measured in the compacted condition and is the basis of payment for embankment construction.

Answer: 79800 m³

(b)

The required compacted dry density is 95 percent of the laboratory maximum: 0.95 × 1.95 = 1.8525 t/m³. The dry mass of soil solids in the embankment is the volume times this density: Md = 79800 × 1.8525 = 147829 t. Dry mass is used because it is unaffected by changes in water content during hauling, drying or wetting. It is also the quantity that relates the borrow and embankment states, since the mass of solids stays constant while the volume changes through excavation and compaction.

Answer: 147829 t

(c)

The in situ dry density of the borrow is the bulk density divided by (1 + w): 1.92/1.14 = 1.6842 t/m³. The bank volume that holds 147829 t of dry soil is Md/ρ_d,bank = 147829/1.6842 = 87774 m³. The borrow volume is therefore 1.100 times the embankment volume, so each cubic metre of bank material compacts to a smaller volume (a shrinkage of about 9.1 percent of the bank volume). The pit must supply at least this quantity, plus an allowance for waste, which is neglected here.

Answer: 87774 m³

(d)

The mass of water in the soil at the borrow moisture content is 14 percent of the dry mass, and at the optimum it is 11.5 percent. The difference is 0.140 − 0.115 = 0.025 of the dry mass. The water to be removed is 147829 × 0.025 = 3696 t, which is 3696 m³ of water. In practice the contractor spreads and windrows the soil to dry it in the sun and wind, which depends on the weather. Where drying is slow, lime or cement stabilization or a switch to a drier borrow source may be economic compared with delays.

Answer: 3696 t

Problem 5 [A6-010] Roadway drainage: ditches, culverts and subdrains

A concrete circular culvert is to carry runoff under a township road in eastern Ontario. The contributing catchment is 18 ha of mixed rural land with a runoff coefficient C = 0.45. For the 10-year storm the design rainfall intensity at the time of concentration is i = 95 mm/h, and the rational formula Q = C i A/360 applies, with Q in m³/s, i in mm/h and A in ha. The existing culvert is a 900 mm diameter concrete pipe with Manning n = 0.013 laid at a slope of 1.2 percent and flowing full. Downstream of the culvert, a trapezoidal grassed roadside ditch with a bottom width of 0.60 m, side slopes of 3 horizontal to 1 vertical, a longitudinal slope of 0.80 percent and n = 0.035 carries a separate flow of 0.55 m³/s from a smaller catchment. Use Manning's equation Q = (1/n) A R2/3 S1/2.

  1. (a) Calculate the design peak flow from the 18 ha catchment. [4]
  2. (b) Calculate the full-flow capacity of the existing 900 mm culvert and state whether it is adequate. [4]
  3. (c) Calculate the minimum pipe diameter, in millimetres (exact computed value, not rounded to a standard size), that carries the design flow flowing full at 1.2 percent. [5]
  4. (d) Calculate the normal depth of flow in the grassed ditch for 0.55 m³/s, and the flow velocity at that depth. [7]
(a)

The rational method gives the peak flow as Q = C i A/360 = 0.45 × 95 × 18/360. The product is 0.45 × 95 × 18 = 769.5, and dividing by 360 gives Q = 2.138 m³/s. The method assumes a rainfall of duration equal to the time of concentration, uniform intensity over the catchment, and a constant runoff coefficient, which suits small rural catchments of this size. The 10-year return period is typical for township road culverts, where the consequence of overtopping is moderate, and larger structures would be checked for a longer return period.

Answer: 2.138 m³/s

(b)

For a circular pipe flowing full, A = πD²/4 = π × 0.9²/4 = 0.6362 m² and R = D/4 = 0.225 m. Manning gives Q_full = (1/0.013) × 0.6362 × 0.2252/3 × 0.0121/2 = 76.92 × 0.6362 × 0.3700 × 0.10954 = 1.983 m³/s. The design flow is 2.138 m³/s, which is greater than the pipe capacity, so the existing 900 mm culvert is not adequate: it would surcharge and the headwater would rise above the pipe crown. The upstream embankment would need to be checked for overtopping, and the culvert replaced or supplemented.

Answer: 1.983 m³/s

(c)

Set the full-flow capacity equal to the design flow and solve for the diameter: Q = (0.3117/n) D8/3 S1/2. With n = 0.013 and S = 0.012, 0.3117/0.013 × 0.10954 = 2.626, so D8/3 = 2.138/2.626 = 0.8138, and D = 0.81383/8 = 0.926 m, or 926 mm. The next standard size above this value, 1 050 mm, would be chosen to leave a margin, since the 900 mm pipe is too small. The 926 mm pipe flowing full at 2.138 m³/s has V = 3.17 m/s; in the 1 050 mm pipe the design flow gives V = 2.47 m/s, which is reasonable for concrete pipe without scour.

Answer: 926 mm

(d)

For the trapezoid, A = (b + z y) y and P = b + 2y√(1 + z²) with b = 0.60 m and z = 3. Set Q = (1/0.035) A R2/3 (0.008)1/2 = 0.55 and solve by trial. At y = 0.361 m, A = (0.60 + 3 × 0.361) × 0.361 = 0.608 m², P = 0.60 + 2 × 0.361 × 3.162 = 2.884 m, and R = 0.211 m, which reproduces Q = 0.55 m³/s. The velocity is V = Q/A = 0.55/0.608 = 0.91 m/s. Grass lining generally tolerates about 1.5 m/s, so the velocity is acceptable and no riprap is needed on this reach.

Answer: 0.361 m

A6 Practice Paper 3

Problem 1 [A6-011] Aggregate properties: gradation and specific gravity

A quarry near Kingston supplies crushed limestone for a surface course on a municipal arterial. A 2500 g dry sample washed over the 0.075 mm sieve was shaken through a nest of sieves, and the masses retained were: 19 mm sieve 0 g; 12.5 mm 210 g; 9.5 mm 310 g; 4.75 mm 640 g; 2.36 mm 480 g; 1.18 mm 330 g; 0.6 mm 220 g; 0.3 mm 130 g; 0.15 mm 90 g; 0.075 mm 60 g; pan 30 g. The agency specification for the surface mix requires 2 to 7 percent passing the 0.075 mm sieve. The 2 to 7 percent limit applies to this aggregate sample before filler is added, and no material is assumed lost in washing beyond the pan mass. A separate coarse fraction was tested for density: oven-dry mass A = 1985.2 g, saturated surface-dry mass in air B = 2012.6 g, mass submerged in water C = 1259.3 g. The fine aggregate has bulk specific gravity 2.702 and the mineral filler 2.750. The blend is 55 percent coarse, 40 percent fine and 5 percent filler by mass.

  1. (a) Compute the percent passing the 2.36 mm sieve. [4]
  2. (b) Compute the percent passing the 0.075 mm sieve and state whether the specification is met. [3]
  3. (c) Compute the bulk specific gravity Gsb of the coarse fraction. [5]
  4. (d) Compute the water absorption of the coarse fraction. [3]
  5. (e) Using the Gsb from part (c) rounded to three decimals, compute the bulk specific gravity of the blended aggregate. [5]
(a)

Percent passing is the mass finer than the sieve divided by the total sample mass, so first accumulate the mass retained down to and including the 2.36 mm sieve. Cumulative retained = 0 + 210 + 310 + 640 + 480 = 1640 g. The total of all retained masses plus pan is 2500 g, which agrees with the original dry mass, so no sieving loss needs to be corrected. Mass passing the 2.36 mm sieve = 2500 - 1640 = 860 g. Percent passing = 860 / 2500 × 100 = 34.4 percent. As a check, adding the masses retained on the finer sieves and in the pan gives 330 + 220 + 130 + 90 + 60 + 30 = 860 g, which matches the subtraction and confirms the cumulative retained figure.

Answer: 34.4 percent

(b)

Material passing the 0.075 mm sieve is the pan only, because the 60 g on the 0.075 mm sieve was retained on it. Percent passing = 30 / 2500 × 100 = 1.2 percent. The specification asks for 2 to 7 percent, so the gradation is deficient in fines by 0.8 percentage points. No material is assumed lost in washing, so the 30 g in the pan is taken as the true fines content of the sample. Because the result is below the lower limit, the crushed stone alone does not meet the requirement, and the mix designer would either add mineral filler, as the 5 percent filler in this blend does, or change the gradation of the fine fraction. In the blend the filler supplies the shortfall, which must be confirmed by recomputing the combined gradation, not assumed.

Answer: 1.2 percent, below the 2 percent minimum, so the specification is not met

(c)

Bulk specific gravity on the oven-dry basis is Gsb = A / (B - C), where B - C is the mass of water displaced by the aggregate volume including surface-permeable voids. Substituting, B - C = 2012.6 - 1259.3 = 753.3 g. Then Gsb = 1985.2 / 753.3 = 2.635. The denominator is the bulk volume expressed as grams of water, because water has unit density, so the result is the ratio of the dry particle mass to that of an equal volume of water. The apparent specific gravity would be A / (A - C) = 1985.2 / 725.9 = 2.735, which is larger because the volume of water-permeable pores is excluded. Gsb is the value used in VMA calculations because it counts those pores as part of the particle volume, which is why the mix designers use it rather than the apparent value.

Answer: 2.635

(d)

Absorption is the water held in the permeable pores expressed as a percentage of the oven-dry mass. Absorption = (B - A) / A × 100 = (2012.6 - 1985.2) / 1985.2 × 100. The mass of absorbed water is 27.4 g, and dividing by 1985.2 g gives 0.01380, so absorption = 1.38 percent. This is a moderate value for limestone and tells the designer that some binder will be absorbed into the pores, so the effective specific gravity Gse of the aggregate will lie between the bulk and apparent values. A value this low is within the range commonly accepted for hot mix, and aggregates above about 2 percent usually draw more scrutiny for binder demand. The absorption also drives how much of the binder is lost to the stone rather than coating it.

Answer: 1.38 percent

(e)

For a blend, the combined bulk specific gravity is not a mass-weighted average of the Gsb values; it is the harmonic form Gsb,blend = 100 / (P1/G1 + P2/G2 + P3/G3), where Pi is the percent by mass and Gi the Gsb of each component. This follows because mass fractions divide by density to give volume fractions, and the volumes add. Substituting P1 = 55, G1 = 2.635, P2 = 40, G2 = 2.702, P3 = 5, G3 = 2.750: 55/2.635 = 20.872, 40/2.702 = 14.804, 5/2.750 = 1.818. The sum is 37.494, so Gsb,blend = 100 / 37.494 = 2.667. A simple weighted average would give 2.668, a slight overestimate that would bias VMA and air voids in the mix design, which is why the harmonic form is used.

Answer: 2.667

Problem 2 [A6-012] Asphalt cement properties and performance grading

A Performance Graded binder is to be selected for a new two-lane highway outside Barrie at latitude 44.0 degrees N. Weather records give a mean seven-day maximum air temperature of 33.0 °C with a standard deviation of 2.5 °C, and a mean annual minimum air temperature of -31.0 °C with a standard deviation of 4.0 °C. Use the Superpave relation for the high temperature at 20 mm depth, T20 = (Tair - 0.00618 lat² + 0.2289 lat + 42.2)(0.9545) - 17.78, where lat is in degrees. The surface low temperature is Tmin = 0.859 Tair + 1.7. For 98 percent reliability use z = 2.055: the high design temperature is T20 + z s with s = 2.5 °C, while the low-temperature reliability is applied to the air temperature before it is converted. Grades step in 6 °C increments. A recovered RTFO-aged sample was tested in the dynamic shear rheometer at 64 °C and gave G* = 4.6 kPa with phase angle 79 degrees.

  1. (a) Find the 50 percent reliability high pavement design temperature at 20 mm depth. [4]
  2. (b) Find the high pavement design temperature at 98 percent reliability. [4]
  3. (c) Find the low pavement design temperature at 98 percent reliability. [4]
  4. (d) Using the stepped high-temperature grade at or above part (b), and adding one grade for slow heavy traffic, give the PG high-temperature number of the binder. [3]
  5. (e) Compute the rutting parameter G*/sin δ for the RTFO-aged sample and compare it with a minimum of 2.20 kPa. [5]
(a)

The Superpave model converts the air temperature to a pavement temperature at 20 mm below the surface using the stated regression. Start with lat² = 44.0² = 1936. Then 0.00618 × 1936 = 11.964 and 0.2289 × 44.0 = 10.072. The bracket is Tair - 0.00618 lat² + 0.2289 lat + 42.2 = 33.0 - 11.964 + 10.072 + 42.2 = 73.308. Multiply by 0.9545: 73.308 × 0.9545 = 69.973. Subtract 17.78 to obtain T20 = 52.19 °C. This is the temperature that is exceeded half the time in the hottest seven-day period of a typical year, so it carries no safety margin. The binder must still be chosen with reliability applied, which is done in the next part, otherwise half of all pavements built on this basis would experience a hotter week than the binder was selected for.

Answer: 52.2 °C

(b)

Reliability is added by increasing the design temperature by z times the standard deviation of the seven-day maximum. The pavement value at 98 percent is therefore T20 + z s = 52.19 + 2.055 × 2.5 = 52.19 + 5.14 = 57.33 °C. The stepped bound is therefore just above 57 °C. Because binder grades step in 6 °C increments from 46, 52, 58, 64, the next grade at or above 57.3 °C is 58 °C. This is a design condition, so the grade cannot be rounded down even when the margin of the shortfall would be tiny; rounding up gives about 0.7 °C of extra margin here.

Answer: 57.3 °C

(c)

The low-temperature model is linear in the air temperature, so the reliability adjustment is applied to the air temperature before the conversion. The air temperature at 98 percent reliability is Tair,98 = -31.0 - 2.055 × 4.0 = -31.0 - 8.22 = -39.22 °C, because a colder year than the mean must be allowed for. Substituting into Tmin = 0.859 Tair + 1.7 gives 0.859 × (-39.22) + 1.7 = -33.69 + 1.7 = -31.99 °C. The minus sign is retained throughout, so the surface is colder than -32 °C only about once in fifty years. The low-temperature grade steps in 6 °C increments of -22, -28, -34, -40, so the required low grade is the next colder step below -31.99, which is -34. A binder graded -28 would be warmer than needed and could thermally crack during the coldest winters in this area.

Answer: -32.0 °C

(d)

From part (b) the 98 percent high temperature is 57.33 °C, and the standard grades are 46, 52, 58, 64, 70, 76, 82, so the first grade that is at or above 57.33 is 58. Standing or very slow heavy truck traffic reduces the effective loading rate, and the usual practice is to raise the high-temperature grade by one 6 °C step to compensate for the longer loading time, which brings the binder to 58 + 6 = 64. The binder is then PG 64-34, using the low grade of -34 from part (c). Raising the high grade is an engineering decision rather than a calculated quantity, and for expressways or climbing lanes designers often raise it again for very high traffic. A grade of 64 is reasonable here since the same PG 64-28 or PG 64-34 range is commonly used for Ontario highways.

Answer: 64

(e)

The rutting parameter for aged binder is G*/sin δ, since a stiff elastic binder has a large G* and a small phase angle δ, and the elastic share of the response is what resists permanent deformation. Convert the phase angle: sin 79° = 0.9816. G*/sin δ = 4.6 / 0.9816 = 4.686 kPa. The criterion for RTFO-aged binder is a minimum of 2.20 kPa at the grade temperature, and the measured value is 4.686 kPa, which is 2.13 times the minimum. The binder therefore passes the rutting criterion at 64 °C, and the high-temperature grade of 64 is confirmed for the aged condition. Because the margin is large, the same binder might meet the next higher grade of 70 when tested at 70 °C, but this would require another test at that temperature rather than an extrapolation from a single point.

Answer: 4.69 kPa, which exceeds 2.20 kPa so the binder passes at 64 °C

Problem 3 [A6-013] Marshall mix design and volumetrics

A trial Marshall specimen for a base course on a regional road was prepared using 5.2 percent asphalt cement by mass of total mix, the binder having specific gravity 1.030. The bulk specific gravity of the combined aggregate is Gsb = 2.652. The specimen has dry mass in air 1203.4 g, saturated surface-dry mass in air 1206.1 g and mass in water 700.8 g. A loose mix sample from the same batch has a maximum theoretical specific gravity Gmm = 2.489. The agency requires 3 to 5 percent air voids, minimum 14 percent VMA and 65 to 78 percent VFA for this mix. Treat the density of water as one gram per cubic centimetre, and compute the effective specific gravity of the aggregate from the maximum theoretical value.

  1. (a) Compute the bulk specific gravity Gmb of the compacted specimen. [4]
  2. (b) Compute the percent air voids Va. [4]
  3. (c) Compute the voids in the mineral aggregate VMA. [4]
  4. (d) Compute the voids filled with asphalt VFA. [3]
  5. (e) Compute the effective binder content Pbe, as a percent of total mix, allowing for binder absorbed into the aggregate. [5]
(a)

For a compacted mix, Gmb is the dry mass divided by the bulk volume expressed as the mass of displaced water. The bulk volume equals the saturated surface-dry mass minus the mass in water, because the buoyant loss equals the weight of the water displaced by the whole specimen including its surface voids. Substituting: B - C = 1206.1 - 700.8 = 505.3 g. Gmb = 1203.4 / 505.3 = 2.3816. The small difference between the SSD and dry masses, 2.7 g or 0.22 percent, indicates a dense, nearly impermeable specimen, which is what a base course mix should be. If the absorption exceeded about 2 percent, the paraffin or vacuum sealing method would be needed in place of the SSD method used here. The result is used for every volumetric property that follows, so a weighing error here would carry through to air voids, VMA and VFA.

Answer: 2.382

(b)

Air voids are the part of the compacted volume not occupied by aggregate or binder. They follow from comparing the specimen density with the theoretical maximum density that the same mix would have with no air voids: Va = (1 - Gmb/Gmm) × 100. Substituting, Gmb/Gmm = 2.3816 / 2.489 = 0.95685, so Va = (1 - 0.95685) × 100 = 4.32 percent. This lies within the 3 to 5 percent requirement, so the specimen is acceptable in terms of voids. The value is closer to the upper limit than the lower, which means that further compaction under traffic is unlikely to push the voids below 3 percent and cause bleeding or loss of stability, but a small binder increase would still be possible within the allowed range.

Answer: 4.32 percent

(c)

VMA is the volume of voids between the aggregate particles, including both air and the effective binder, expressed as a percent of the bulk volume of the compacted mix. Using the aggregate share by mass Ps = 100 - 5.2 = 94.8 percent and the bulk specific gravity Gsb to compute the aggregate volume, VMA = 100 - Gmb Ps / Gsb. Substituting: 2.3816 × 94.8 / 2.652 = 225.77 / 2.652 = 85.13, so VMA = 100 - 85.13 = 14.87 percent. This exceeds the 14 percent minimum, though by only 0.87 percentage points. VMA is computed with Gsb and not Gse because the aggregate volume must include the pores that absorb binder; the volume of absorbed binder is then part of the aggregate volume, not part of the void volume available for effective binder and air.

Answer: 14.87 percent

(d)

VFA is the part of the VMA that is filled with effective binder, expressed as a percent. Since VMA is made up of air voids plus effective binder volume, VFA = (VMA - Va) / VMA × 100. Substituting VMA = 14.87 percent and Va = 4.32 percent gives (14.87 - 4.32) / 14.87 = 10.55 / 14.87 = 0.7096, so VFA = 70.96 percent, essentially 71 percent. This lies inside the 65 to 78 percent requirement. The three volumetric properties therefore satisfy every criterion with the VMA being the tightest check, so a binder content slightly higher or an aggregate gradation adjusted to give a little more VMA would give more margin without breaking the VFA criterion.

Answer: 71.0 percent

(e)

First find the effective specific gravity of the aggregate from the maximum theoretical value: Gse = Ps / (100/Gmm - Pb/Gb) = 94.8 / (100/2.489 - 5.2/1.030). Here 100/2.489 = 40.177 and 5.2/1.030 = 5.049, so the denominator is 35.128 and Gse = 2.6987. Absorbed binder as percent of aggregate mass is Pba = 100 (Gse - Gsb) / (Gsb Gse) × Gb = 100 × 0.0467 / (2.652 × 2.6987) × 1.030 = 0.672 percent. Effective binder is then Pbe = Pb - Pba Ps / 100 = 5.2 - 0.672 × 0.948 = 4.563 percent. About 12 percent of the added binder is absorbed and does not coat the particles. Pbe, rather than the total Pb, governs film thickness and durability, so it is the value a mix designer compares between trial mixtures.

Answer: 4.56 percent

Problem 4 [A6-014] Superpave mix design and binder content

A Superpave volumetric mix design for a 19 mm surface mix on a Highway 400 series ramp reconstruction uses a trial binder content of 5.0 percent by mass of total mix. Gyratory specimens of 4800 g are compacted in a 150 mm diameter mould to the design number of gyrations, Ndes. At Ndes the specimen height is 115.6 mm, and the height after 8 gyrations (Nini) was 127.4 mm. After extraction and weighing in water, the measured bulk specific gravity at Ndes is Gmb = 2.398, and the maximum theoretical specific gravity is Gmm = 2.512. Use a water density of 1 g/cm³, and the height-based estimate of density, which treats the specimen as a plain cylinder, corrected to the measured value by a single factor. The mix must have 4.0 percent air voids at Ndes and not more than 89 percent of Gmm at Nini. For the binder adjustment use Pb,est = Pb,tr - 0.4 (4.0 - Va).

  1. (a) Compute the estimated bulk specific gravity of the specimen at Ndes from its mass and height. [5]
  2. (b) Compute the correction factor C that converts the height-based estimate at Ndes to the measured Gmb. [3]
  3. (c) Compute the corrected percent of Gmm at Nini. [4]
  4. (d) Compute the air voids at Ndes. [3]
  5. (e) Estimate the binder content needed to reach 4.0 percent air voids. [5]
(a)

The height-based estimate assumes the specimen is a perfect cylinder, so its volume is the cross-sectional area times the height. The area of the 150 mm mould is π/4 × 15² = 176.71 cm². The height is 115.6 mm = 11.56 cm, so the volume is 176.71 × 11.56 = 2042.8 cm³. With water density 1 g/cm³ the estimated specific gravity equals the mass divided by that volume expressed in grams of water: Gmb,est = 4800 / 2042.8 = 2.350. This is lower than the measured value of 2.398 because a real specimen has rough, slightly pitted sides, so the cylinder volume overstates the bulk volume. The estimate is still very useful because it can be computed at every gyration from the machine height record and corrected afterwards.

Answer: 2.350

(b)

The correction factor is the ratio of the measured bulk specific gravity to the estimated one at the same gyration level, C = Gmb,measured / Gmb,est = 2.398 / 2.3497 = 1.0206. The factor is greater than 1 because the cylinder-volume estimate is always too large when the sides are rough. It is applied to every density that was estimated from the height record, including that at Nini, because the surface texture error is assumed to be roughly proportional at all gyration levels. If the factor were much larger, say above 1.02 to 1.03, the technician would check the mould calibration or the dryness of the sample, and a factor close to 1.00 would suggest that a measurement of mass in water was in error.

Answer: 1.0206

(c)

The estimated density at Nini is found with the same cylinder method: height 127.4 mm = 12.74 cm, volume 176.71 × 12.74 = 2251.4 cm³, so Gmb,est = 4800 / 2251.4 = 2.1320. Multiply by the correction factor: 2.1320 × 1.0206 = 2.1759. The percent of maximum theoretical density is 2.1759 / 2.512 × 100 = 86.62 percent. The limit at Nini is 89 percent, so the mix passes with a margin of 2.4 points. The initial compactibility check is intended to screen for tender mixes, which are easy to compact at the start but then slide under rollers; a value well under 89 percent suggests the aggregate skeleton is not locking up too quickly, and the mix will compact in the field without excessive rolling effort.

Answer: 86.6 percent, below the 89 percent limit

(d)

Air voids at the design number of gyrations come from the measured density: Va = (1 - Gmb/Gmm) × 100 = (1 - 2.398 / 2.512) × 100. The ratio is 0.95462, so Va = 4.538 percent. This is equivalent to 95.46 percent of Gmm at Ndes. The target is 4.0 percent, so the mix has 0.54 points too many voids. Voids that are too high mean the mix is too dry or too open, which accelerates oxidation and moisture damage, so the binder content should be raised or the gradation adjusted. A small increase in Pb is the simplest fix, and the standard rule of thumb for how much to add follows in part (e).

Answer: 4.54 percent

(e)

The rule of thumb says that each 1 percent change in air voids is offset by a 0.4 percent change in binder content, in the opposite direction. With Va = 4.538 percent the voids are 0.538 above the 4.0 target, so the required change in binder content is 0.4 × 0.538 = 0.215 percent more binder. Pb,est = Pb,tr - 0.4 (4.0 - Va) = 5.0 - 0.4 × (4.0 - 4.538) = 5.0 + 0.215 = 5.215 percent, say 5.2 percent. The result is an estimate only: the designer must prepare new specimens at the revised binder content and recheck VMA, VFA and the dust proportion because changing Pb also changes effective film thickness. This is why the standard procedure compacts several trial binder contents rather than relying on a single adjustment.

Answer: 5.22 percent

Problem 5 [A6-015] Flexible pavement design with ESALs and structural number

A new two-lane county road in Wellington County is to be designed for 6.5 million 80 kN equivalent single axle loads (W18) over a 20 year period. Use the 1993 AASHTO equation, with W18 as the design traffic: log10 W18 = ZR S0 + 9.36 log10(SN + 1) - 0.20 + log10[ΔPSI / 2.7] / [0.40 + 1094/(SN + 1)5.19] + 2.32 log10 MR - 8.07, where MR is in psi and SN is the structural number in inch units. The reliability is 95 percent (ZR = -1.645), overall standard deviation S0 = 0.45, initial serviceability 4.4, terminal serviceability 2.5, and subgrade MR = 55 MPa (1 MPa = 145.04 psi). Layer coefficients are 0.44 per inch for asphalt concrete, 0.14 per inch for granular base and 0.11 per inch for granular subbase, with drainage coefficients m = 1.0 for both unbound layers. The layers proposed are 120 mm asphalt and 250 mm granular base.

  1. (a) Find the required structural number SN for the design traffic. [6]
  2. (b) Compute the structural number contributed by the 120 mm asphalt layer. [3]
  3. (c) Compute the structural number contributed by the 250 mm granular base. [3]
  4. (d) Find the minimum thickness of granular subbase, in mm, needed to reach the required SN. [5]
  5. (e) The subbase is built 300 mm thick. Find the traffic W18 that the as-built section can carry. [3]
(a)

Convert the subgrade modulus: MR = 55 × 145.04 = 7977 psi. The serviceability loss is ΔPSI = 4.4 - 2.5 = 1.9. The required log10 W18 = log10(6.5 × 10⁶) = 6.8129. The equation is implicit in SN, so it is solved by trial. For SN = 4.675: log10(5.675) = 0.7540, so 9.36 × 0.7540 = 7.057. The serviceability term is log10(1.9/2.7) = -0.1526 divided by [0.40 + 1094/5.6755.19]; 5.6755.19 = 8,160 so 1094/8,160 = 0.134 and the divisor is 0.534, giving -0.286. The reliability term is -1.645 × 0.45 = -0.740, and 2.32 log10(7977) = 9.0525. Sum: -0.740 + 7.057 - 0.20 - 0.286 + 9.0525 - 8.07 = 6.813, which matches 6.8129. Hence SN = 4.67, or about 4.7 in inch units.

Answer: 4.67

(b)

The structural number is the sum of each layer's coefficient times its thickness in inches (and a drainage coefficient for unbound layers). Convert the asphalt layer to inches: 120 / 25.4 = 4.724 in. The layer coefficient is a1 = 0.44 per inch, so SN1 = a1 D1 = 0.44 × 4.724 = 2.079. Asphalt concrete has the highest coefficient because it is the stiffest layer and carries the largest part of the load, so even a thin layer contributes a large share, here 2.08 of the required 4.67, which is 44.5 percent. The asphalt thickness is often fixed first by minimum values and by frost and constructability considerations, with the lower layers sized to make up the remaining structural number.

Answer: 2.08

(c)

The base thickness in inches is 250 / 25.4 = 9.843 in. The structural number of an unbound layer includes its drainage coefficient, SN2 = a2 D2 m2. With a2 = 0.14 per inch and m2 = 1.0, SN2 = 0.14 × 9.843 × 1.0 = 1.378. A drainage coefficient of 1.0 corresponds to a well-drained base that is not exposed to saturation for a large share of the time. If drainage were poor and m2 dropped to 0.8, the contribution would fall to 1.10, a loss of 0.28, which would then require an additional 2.5 in or 64 mm of subbase to compensate. The base therefore supplies 29.5 percent of the required SN of 4.67.

Answer: 1.38

(d)

The remaining structural number is SN required - SN1 - SN2 = 4.6746 - 2.0787 - 1.3780 = 1.2179. The subbase contributes a3 D3 m3, so D3 = 1.2179 / (0.11 × 1.0) = 11.07 in. Converting to millimetres, 11.07 × 25.4 = 281.2 mm. In practice the thickness is rounded up to a constructable increment, 300 mm, since a lift thinner than about 150 mm is hard to compact and rounding down would leave the section structurally short. The subbase is the weakest layer in the system but is also the cheapest per millimetre, so designers use it to make up the structural number that thin layers of expensive asphalt would otherwise provide.

Answer: 281 mm

(e)

The 300 mm subbase is 11.811 in, so SN3 = 0.11 × 11.811 × 1.0 = 1.299. The as-built structural number is SN = 2.079 + 1.378 + 1.299 = 4.756. Substituting SN = 4.756 into the design equation with the same reliability, ΔPSI and MR gives log10 W18 = 6.8656, so W18 = 7.34 × 10⁶ ESALs. This is 13 percent more than the 6.5 million required. Because log W18 is nearly linear in SN over this range, a 0.08 increase in SN increases the allowable traffic by about 13 percent. The margin is the cost of rounding up, but it also gives some protection against traffic being underestimated or construction thickness falling short of the specified values.

Answer: 7.34 million ESALs

A6 Practice Paper 4

Problem 1 [A6-016] Traffic loading, growth factors and ESAL computation

A four-lane divided provincial highway north of Sudbury carries a two-way annual average daily traffic of 14,000 vehicles in the opening year, of which 14 percent are trucks. The truck population is made up of 50 percent two-axle single-unit trucks with a load equivalency factor (LEF) of 0.28, 18 percent three-axle single-unit trucks with LEF 1.10, and 32 percent five-axle tractor-trailers with LEF 1.85. Half of the trucks travel in each direction, and the design lane, the outside lane in each direction, carries 80 percent of the directional trucks. Traffic grows at 3.5 percent per year, compounded, and the pavement is designed for 20 years. Use 365 days per year, and count only trucks as damaging.

  1. (a) Compute the average load equivalency factor per truck. [4]
  2. (b) Compute the number of ESALs in the design lane in the first year. [5]
  3. (c) Compute the growth factor for 20 years at 3.5 percent. [3]
  4. (d) Compute the design ESALs over 20 years. [4]
  5. (e) After how many years will the cumulative ESALs in the design lane first reach 5.0 million? [4]
(a)

The average LEF is the weighted mean of the LEFs of the truck classes, each weighted by its share of the truck population. Multiply each class by its proportion: 0.50 × 0.28 = 0.140; 0.18 × 1.10 = 0.198; 0.32 × 1.85 = 0.592. The sum is 0.140 + 0.198 + 0.592 = 0.930. The average truck therefore causes 0.93 times the damage of one standard 80 kN single axle pass. Note that the five-axle tractor-trailers make up only 32 percent of trucks but account for 0.592 / 0.930 = 63.7 percent of the damage, which is why accurate counts of heavy trucks matter much more than the total truck count when predicting pavement life, and why weight enforcement on the heaviest class has the greatest effect.

Answer: 0.930 ESAL per truck

(b)

Start with the truck count: 14,000 × 0.14 = 1960 trucks per day in both directions. The directional share is 0.5, so 980 trucks per day travel in one direction, and the design lane carries 80 percent of them: 980 × 0.8 = 784 trucks per day in the design lane. Each truck causes 0.930 ESAL, so the daily ESAL is 784 × 0.930 = 729.1. Over a year of 365 days, the first-year ESAL is 729.1 × 365 = 266,129, say 266,000. This is the base year load. It is computed for the opening year with no growth applied, so the growth factor in the next part brings it to the cumulative design total. The accuracy is limited by the estimated truck percentage and the LEFs, which are themselves averages over many axle weights.

Answer: 266,000 ESALs

(c)

With compound growth the traffic in year t is the first-year traffic times (1 + r)t - 1, and the cumulative total over n years relative to the first year is the sum of a geometric series. The growth factor is GF = [(1 + r)n - 1] / r. Substituting r = 0.035 and n = 20: (1.035)20 = 1.9898, so GF = (1.9898 - 1) / 0.035 = 0.9898 / 0.035 = 28.28. Without growth the factor would be 20, so growth raises the cumulative traffic by 41 percent. At lower growth rates the factor falls: at 1.5 percent it would be 23.12, which shows how sensitive the design load is to the growth assumption. A growth assumption that proves wrong therefore shifts the design life considerably.

Answer: 28.28

(d)

The design ESAL is the first-year design lane ESAL times the growth factor. Using the values already found, 266,129 × 28.28 = 7.526 × 10⁶. This is about 7.5 million ESALs, a figure that would be taken to the structural design equation along with reliability, serviceability loss and subgrade support. The product assumes the truck percentage, directional split, lane share and LEFs stay constant for the full 20 years; if the share of five-axle trucks increases, the actual damage will exceed the estimate even when the truck count does not. For this reason many agencies choose a design reliability above 50 percent to cover uncertainty in this number instead of simply inflating it.

Answer: 7.53 million ESALs

(e)

The cumulative ESAL after n years is ESAL1 × [(1 + r)n - 1]/r. Setting this equal to 5.0 × 10⁶ with ESAL1 = 266,129: [(1.035)n - 1]/0.035 = 5.0 × 10⁶ / 266,129 = 18.788. Then (1.035)n = 1 + 0.035 × 18.788 = 1.6576. Take logarithms: n = ln 1.6576 / ln 1.035 = 0.5054 / 0.034401 = 14.69 years. The pavement reaches two-thirds of its 7.5 million design total in about 15 years, because growth makes later years heavier. It means that if an overlay is scheduled when cumulative traffic reaches 5 million ESALs, it falls in year 15, which can be used for programming rehabilitation funds.

Answer: 14.7 years

Problem 2 [A6-017] Subgrade support, CBR and resilient modulus

A silty clay subgrade along a new arterial in Peterborough was sampled for soaked California Bearing Ratio testing on a compacted specimen. The standard piston load is 13.35 kN at 2.5 mm penetration and 20.0 kN at 5.0 mm penetration. The specimen carried 1.07 kN at 2.5 mm and 1.88 kN at 5.0 mm. The test was repeated with the same load pattern and the readings were confirmed. Agency practice is to adopt the larger of the 2.5 mm and 5.0 mm ratios once a repeat test confirms the readings. Eight soaked CBR results from different stations are 6.2, 7.5, 9.4, 8.8, 5.6, 7.9, 10.1 and 6.9 percent. The design CBR is taken as the mean minus 1.04 standard deviations, to represent the 85th percentile of a normal population. Use the sample standard deviation (divisor n - 1). Use the correlation MR (MPa) = 10.3 × CBR (percent), and 1 MPa = 145.04 psi.

  1. (a) Compute the CBR from the 2.5 mm penetration. [3]
  2. (b) Compute the CBR from the 5.0 mm penetration. [3]
  3. (c) State the governing CBR of this specimen. [4]
  4. (d) Compute the design CBR from the eight results using the mean minus 1.04 standard deviations. [6]
  5. (e) Convert the design CBR to a resilient modulus in psi for use in the AASHTO design equation. [4]
(a)

The CBR is the ratio of the load required to push the standard piston into the specimen by a given depth to the load required to push it into a standard crushed stone by the same depth, multiplied by 100. At 2.5 mm penetration the standard load is 13.35 kN. CBR2.5 = 1.07 / 13.35 × 100 = 8.015 percent. This is the usual governing value for most soils, because the 2.5 mm penetration represents the stiffness of the top of the layer, which is where the wheel load is most concentrated. The result is a dimensionless ratio, which is why the percentage sign is a ratio and not a unit. For this soil the 2.5 mm result is not the governing value because the 5.0 mm result is higher, as shown next.

Answer: 8.01 percent

(b)

At 5.0 mm penetration the standard load is 20.0 kN. CBR5.0 = 1.88 / 20.0 × 100 = 9.40 percent. This is higher than the 8.015 percent found at 2.5 mm. In ordinary soils the load-penetration curve is concave and the 2.5 mm CBR is higher; when the 5.0 mm ratio is larger, it generally signals a surface effect at the start of the test, such as a soft top layer or a seating error, followed by stiffer soil beneath. The test is therefore repeated to confirm that this is a real property of the soil. In this problem the repeat test confirmed the readings, so the agency rule can be applied in the next part.

Answer: 9.40 percent

(c)

The rule given is that, once a repeat test confirms the readings, the larger of the two ratios is adopted. The two values are 8.015 percent at 2.5 mm and 9.40 percent at 5.0 mm, and the larger of them is adopted because of the confirmation, so the governing CBR is 9.40 percent. Note that this specimen result is not the design value. It is one test, and the design must account for variability along the route, which is why part (d) combines eight tests into a percentile value. A single favourable result such as this one, being 20 percent above the 7.8 percent mean of all the stations, should never be used alone to size the pavement.

Answer: 9.40 percent

(d)

Mean = (6.2 + 7.5 + 9.4 + 8.8 + 5.6 + 7.9 + 10.1 + 6.9) / 8 = 62.4 / 8 = 7.80 percent. The squared deviations from the mean are 2.56, 0.09, 2.56, 1.00, 4.84, 0.01, 5.29 and 0.81, summing to 17.16. The sample standard deviation uses n - 1 = 7 in the divisor: s = √(17.16 / 7) = √2.451 = 1.566 percent. The design CBR is 7.80 - 1.04 × 1.566 = 7.80 - 1.63 = 6.17 percent. Using the 85th percentile means that 85 percent of the subgrade is expected to be stronger than the design value, a common choice for a lightly trafficked arterial. Using the mean would leave half the road weaker than the design assumption, which is why a percentile is used.

Answer: 6.17 percent

(e)

First apply the correlation in MPa: MR = 10.3 × 6.17 = 63.57 MPa. Then convert to psi: 63.57 × 145.04 = 9,220 psi. The correlation is empirical and was developed for fine-grained soils with a CBR below about 10, which suits this silty clay, but it carries scatter of roughly a factor of two, so the result is only an estimate. Where possible, a laboratory repeated-load resilient modulus test or a falling weight deflectometer back-calculation should be used to confirm it. In the design equation this value, 9,220 psi, would be used directly as the effective roadbed soil modulus after any seasonal adjustment for spring thaw, which is significant in Ontario.

Answer: 9,220 psi

Problem 3 [A6-018] Rigid pavement slab thickness, joints and dowels

A jointed plain concrete pavement is proposed for a truck-route intersection approach in Hamilton. Design traffic is W18 = 9.0 million ESALs. Use the 1993 AASHTO rigid equation in inch units: log10 W18 = ZR S0 + 7.35 log10(D + 1) - 0.06 + log10[ΔPSI / 3.0] / [1 + 1.624×10⁷ / (D + 1)8.46] + (4.22 - 0.32 pt) log10{ S'c Cd (D0.75 - 1.132) / [215.63 J (D0.75 - 18.42 / (Ec/k)0.25)] }. The inputs are ZR = -1.645, S0 = 0.35, ΔPSI = 2.0, terminal serviceability pt = 2.5, mean modulus of rupture S'c = 650 psi, drainage coefficient Cd = 1.00, load transfer coefficient J = 3.2, concrete modulus Ec = 4.0×10⁶ psi and effective modulus of subgrade reaction k = 220 pci. D is the slab thickness in inches. Transverse joints are spaced at 4.5 m. For joint movement use ΔL = C L (α ΔT + ε), with C = 0.8, α = 10×10⁻⁶ per °C, ΔT = 35 °C and shrinkage ε = 200×10⁻⁶.

  1. (a) Find the required slab thickness in mm. [9]
  2. (b) Round the thickness up to the nearest 10 mm for construction and state the adopted thickness in mm. [3]
  3. (c) Compute the maximum joint opening, in mm, at a 4.5 m transverse joint spacing. [4]
  4. (d) Estimate the dowel diameter using the rule of thumb of one-eighth of the adopted slab thickness. [4]
(a)

The equation cannot be solved for D directly, so use trial and error. Compute the constant terms: ZR S0 = -1.645 × 0.35 = -0.576; (4.22 - 0.32 × 2.5) = 3.42; log10(ΔPSI/3.0) = log10(0.6667) = -0.1761; the target is log10(9.0 × 10⁶) = 6.9542; and (Ec/k)0.25 = (18,182)0.25 = 11.61, so 18.42/11.61 = 1.587. For D = 10.14 in: D + 1 = 11.14, log10 = 1.0469 and 7.35 × 1.0469 = 7.695. The serviceability term denominator is 1 + 1.624×10⁷ / 11.148.46; 11.148.46 = 7.2×10⁸, so it is 1.0226 and the term is -0.1722. D0.75 = 5.682, so numerator 650 × (5.682 - 1.132) = 2958 and denominator 215.63 × 3.2 × (5.682 - 1.586) = 2826; the log of 1.0465 is 0.0198, times 3.42 gives 0.0675. Sum: -0.576 + 7.695 - 0.06 - 0.172 + 0.0675 = 6.9545, within 0.0003 of the target. The solution is D = 10.14 in = 257.6 mm.

Answer: 258 mm

(b)

Pavement slabs are specified in whole centimetres, or in 10 mm steps, because the paving equipment is set to the nearest few millimetres and the quantity estimates use rounded numbers. The computed thickness is 257.6 mm, so the next multiple of 10 mm above it is 260 mm. The thickness cannot be rounded down to 250 mm because that would be below the required value, which would make the design traffic exceed the capacity of the section. The 2.4 mm increase is small, about 0.9 percent of the thickness, but because the traffic capacity is highly sensitive to thickness (roughly 28 percent more traffic for each 10 mm), the rounding raises the capacity to about 9.5 million ESALs, a useful small margin. The adopted value, 260 mm, is used in the dowel sizing in part (d).

Answer: 260 mm

(c)

Joint movement comes from slab shortening, which is the sum of thermal contraction and drying shrinkage, reduced by friction between slab and base. The strain is α ΔT + ε = 10×10⁻⁶ × 35 + 200×10⁻⁶ = 350×10⁻⁶ + 200×10⁻⁶ = 550×10⁻⁶. The slab length is 4500 mm and the friction coefficient C = 0.8 allows for the restraint of the base, so ΔL = 0.8 × 4500 × 550×10⁻⁶ = 1.98 mm. The joint opening is half this at each side of a slab, but the full opening occurs at the joint that is between the two slabs. A joint movement near 2 mm is small enough for a conventional saw cut sealed with a hot-poured sealant, which is rated for roughly 25 percent extension of the reservoir width.

Answer: 1.98 mm

(d)

Dowel bars carry shear across the transverse joint, and a common design rule is to make the diameter about one-eighth of the slab thickness, because bar stiffness and bearing area must increase with thickness to keep concrete bearing stress within safe limits. Applying the rule to the adopted thickness gives 260 / 8 = 32.5 mm. Standard sizes are normally 32 mm or 38 mm in Ontario, so the designer would choose 32 mm for this slab, or 38 mm for heavy truck traffic, and place them at 300 mm centres across the width. A bar smaller than the rule, such as 25 mm, concentrates bearing stress on the concrete and will cause the joint to loosen, spall and fault over time, whereas a larger bar costs more but provides little additional benefit.

Answer: 32.5 mm

Problem 4 [A6-019] Concrete pavement stresses and load transfer

A 250 mm jointed concrete slab on a granular base carries a 40 kN single wheel load at the interior of the slab, away from joints and edges. The concrete has modulus E = 30,000 MPa and Poisson's ratio 0.15, and the subgrade reaction modulus is k = 50 MPa/m (0.05 MPa/mm). The load is applied over a circular area of radius a = 150 mm. Use Westergaard's radius of relative stiffness l = [E h³ / (12 (1 - μ²) k)]0.25, the equivalent radius b = √(1.6 a² + h²) - 0.675 h when a is less than 1.724 h, and the interior stress σi = [3 (1 + μ) P / (2 π h²)] [ln(l/b) + 0.6159]. A temperature differential of 18 °C between top and bottom of the slab produces a curling stress σ = C E α ΔT / 2 with C = 0.70 and α = 10×10⁻⁶ per °C. At a transverse joint a falling weight test gives 0.42 mm deflection under the loaded side and 0.21 mm on the unloaded side.

  1. (a) Compute the radius of relative stiffness l, in mm. [4]
  2. (b) Compute the interior tensile stress σi in MPa under the wheel load. [5]
  3. (c) Compute the curling stress, in MPa, produced by the temperature differential. [4]
  4. (d) Compute the load transfer efficiency of the joint, as a percentage, using the deflection ratio of unloaded to loaded slab. [3]
  5. (e) Assuming each slab carries a share of the wheel load proportional to its deflection, find the load carried by the loaded slab, in kN, when the 40 kN wheel is at the joint. [4]
(a)

The radius of relative stiffness measures how stiff the slab is compared with the supporting spring foundation; a larger l means the load is spread over a wider area. Work in newtons and millimetres: E = 30,000 N/mm², h = 250 mm and k = 0.05 N/mm³. h³ = 15.625×10⁶ mm³. Then E h³ = 4.6875×10¹¹. The denominator is 12 (1 - 0.0225) × 0.05 = 12 × 0.9775 × 0.05 = 0.5865. The ratio is 4.6875×10¹¹ / 0.5865 = 7.992×10¹¹, and the fourth root is 945.5 mm. A radius near one metre is typical for a 250 mm slab on a medium subgrade. Doubling k to 100 MPa/m would reduce l by a factor of 20.25 = 1.19, to about 795 mm, so l is not very sensitive to subgrade stiffness.

Answer: 945 mm

(b)

Check the condition first: 1.724 h = 431 mm and a = 150 mm is smaller, so the equivalent radius formula applies. b = √(1.6 × 150² + 250²) - 0.675 × 250 = √(36,000 + 62,500) - 168.75 = 313.85 - 168.75 = 145.1 mm. The ratio l/b = 945.5 / 145.1 = 6.516, with ln(6.516) = 1.874. The stress factor is ln(l/b) + 0.6159 = 2.490. The load factor is 3 (1.15) × 40,000 / (2π × 250²) = 138,000 / 392,699 = 0.3514 MPa. So σi = 0.3514 × 2.490 = 0.875 MPa. This is small compared with a typical flexural strength of 4.5 MPa because the wheel is at the interior, the least severe position. Edge loading would produce roughly twice this stress, which is why joint and edge design governs.

Answer: 0.875 MPa

(c)

A slab with a temperature differential tries to curl, with the top expanding relative to the bottom or the reverse, but its own weight and the subgrade restrain the curling and produce stress. The stated expression is σ = C E α ΔT / 2. Substituting: E α ΔT = 30,000 × 10×10⁻⁶ × 18 = 5.40 MPa. Multiply by C = 0.70 and divide by 2: 5.40 × 0.70 / 2 = 1.89 MPa. This is more than twice the interior wheel stress of part (b), which shows how important temperature is in rigid pavement design. Adding the two stresses, 0.875 + 1.89 = 2.77 MPa, which is 62 percent of a 4.5 MPa flexural strength, so fatigue under repeated loading is already a significant consideration.

Answer: 1.89 MPa

(d)

Load transfer efficiency is defined as the deflection of the unloaded slab divided by the deflection of the loaded slab, times 100: LTE = δu / δl × 100. Substituting the measured values: 0.21 / 0.42 × 100 = 50 percent. A value of 100 percent would mean that both slabs deflect equally and the joint transfers load perfectly, while 0 percent would be a free edge. Values below about 70 percent are generally considered poor and are the sign of a loose dowel or aggregate interlock that has worn out. At 50 percent, the joint needs attention, such as dowel bar retrofit, since faulting and corner breaks develop faster.

Answer: 50 percent

(e)

If the load is shared in proportion to the deflection each slab experiences, then the loaded slab carries a fraction δl / (δl + δu) of the total, and the unloaded slab carries the rest. With δl = 0.42 mm and δu = 0.21 mm, the fraction on the loaded slab is 0.42 / 0.63 = 0.6667. The load carried by the loaded slab is 0.6667 × 40 = 26.67 kN, and 13.33 kN is passed across the joint into the unloaded slab. The same result follows from dividing by (1 + LTE/100) = 1.5, giving 40/1.5 = 26.67 kN. Thus the joint reduces the edge load by one-third, so edge stresses will be about a third lower than for a free edge; a joint with 100 percent LTE would reduce them by half.

Answer: 26.7 kN

Problem 5 [A6-020] Pavement condition evaluation: PCI, IRI and deflection testing

A 500 m section of a regional road near Guelph was surveyed. Three distress types were found, with deduct values read from the agency curves: alligator cracking 18, rutting 9 and longitudinal cracking 7. Because three distresses exceed the threshold, the agency applies a correction factor of 0.82 to the sum of deducts to obtain the corrected deduct value, and PCI = 100 - corrected deduct. A response-type profiler travelling the section recorded an accumulated suspension travel of 3.15 m over the 500 m, and IRI is the accumulated travel divided by the length. A falling weight deflectometer test with a 40 kN load on a 150 mm radius plate gave deflections of 0.412 mm at the load centre, 0.339 mm at 300 mm and 0.062 mm at 1.5 m from the load centre. The subgrade modulus is back-calculated with MR = 0.24 P / (dr r), valid at distances beyond the influence of the pavement layers. The agency intervenes when PCI falls to 60 and assumes PCI declines by 3 points per year.

  1. (a) Compute the PCI of the section. [6]
  2. (b) Compute the IRI of the section in m/km. [4]
  3. (c) Back-calculate the subgrade resilient modulus in MPa from the deflection at 1.5 m. [5]
  4. (d) Compute the surface curvature index SCI = d0 - d300 in mm. [2]
  5. (e) How many years until the PCI falls to the intervention threshold of 60, at 3 points per year? [3]
(a)

Add the individual deducts: 18 + 9 + 7 = 34. Apply the stated correction for three distresses: corrected deduct value = 0.82 × 34 = 27.88. The deduct values are not simply additive in a real pavement because the distress effects overlap, which is why the correction factor below 1 is applied; without it the PCI would be 66.0, understating the condition. PCI = 100 - 27.88 = 72.12. A PCI of 72 falls in the good to satisfactory band, where preventive maintenance such as crack sealing is typically recommended rather than rehabilitation. The alligator cracking contributes more than half the total deduct, 18 of 34 or 53 percent, so repairing that single distress would raise the PCI most per dollar spent.

Answer: 72.1

(b)
