IRI is the accumulated suspension travel of a standard quarter-car travelling at 80 km/h, divided by the distance, so it is a slope measured in metres of vertical movement per kilometre. The section length is 500 m = 0.5 km. IRI = 3.15 m / 0.5 km = 6.3 m/km. This is a rough road for its class; typical new pavements have IRI below 1.5 m/km, and a value above about 4 m/km is generally considered poor for a paved road with a 80 km/h speed limit. At 6.3 m/km the ride is rough enough to affect vehicle operating costs and passenger comfort. Roughness complements the PCI, because a pavement can have a moderate PCI but high IRI when distresses such as heaves or settlements affect only ride quality.

Answer: 6.3 m/km

(c)

At distances of about 1.5 m or more from the load the surface deflection is controlled by the subgrade alone, so the Boussinesq-based relation MR = 0.24 P / (dr r) applies. Use consistent units: P = 40 kN, dr = 0.062 mm = 0.000062 m, and r = 1.5 m. MR = 0.24 × 40 / (0.000062 × 1.5) = 9.6 / 0.000093 = 103,226 kPa = 103 MPa. The factor 0.24 includes the effects of Poisson's ratio and a plate loaded over a finite area, and the answer is a back-calculated modulus that is typically a factor of 1.3 to 2 below the laboratory value because of the in-situ confinement. The deflection also falls off with distance roughly as 1/r (0.339 mm at 0.3 m scales to about 0.07 mm at 1.5 m), which supports using the 1.5 m reading. The result is comparable to a CBR of about 10 percent, a reasonably firm subgrade, so foundation strengthening does not look necessary before the surface is renewed.

Answer: 103 MPa

(d)

The surface curvature index is the difference between the deflection at the load centre and that 300 mm away. It reflects the stiffness of the upper pavement layers because the deflection near the load is dominated by them. SCI = d0 - d300 = 0.412 - 0.339 = 0.073 mm. A low SCI like this one indicates a reasonably stiff upper structure, and the subgrade modulus of part (c) is moderate to good, so the centre deflection of 0.412 mm is modest and neither the asphalt nor the foundation shows a structural weakness. The conclusion matters for the repair: the distress found in part (a) is mainly surface related, so a thin overlay or surface treatment is a reasonable response, and the relation of SCI to d0 guides whether the surface or the foundation needs treatment.

Answer: 0.073 mm

(e)

The remaining service life is the PCI above the threshold divided by the rate of decline. PCI is 72.12 now and the trigger is 60, a margin of 12.12 points. At 3 points per year, the time is 12.12 / 3 = 4.04 years. In practice the decline is not linear, as deterioration speeds up when cracks admit water, so the agency would inspect again after about two years and update the forecast. With a four year window the agency can schedule design and tendering for a rehabilitation contract in time, and has the option of applying crack sealing now to slow the rate and extend the window by perhaps one to two years at a modest cost.

Answer: 4.0 years

A6 Practice Paper 5

Problem 1 [A6-021] Pavement management and life-cycle cost comparison

The County of Wellington is choosing between two ways to deal with a deteriorated 8 km collector road. Costs are quoted per kilometre of two-lane road in present dollars. Alternative A is a mill-and-overlay rehabilitation now at $185,000, followed by a resurfacing costing $95,000 at the end of years 12, 24 and 36, with routine maintenance of $3,200 per year. Alternative B is full reconstruction now at $410,000, followed by a single resurfacing costing $95,000 at the end of year 20, with routine maintenance of $1,800 per year. The analysis period is 40 years, the real discount rate is 4 percent, maintenance is paid at the end of each year, and salvage value and user costs are ignored. Use end-of-year discounting throughout.

  1. (a) Calculate the present worth of all costs of Alternative A per kilometre. [5]
  2. (b) Calculate the present worth of all costs of Alternative B per kilometre. [5]
  3. (c) Express Alternative A as an equivalent uniform annual cost over the 40 years. [4]
  4. (d) Find the annual maintenance cost for Alternative A, in place of $3,200, at which the two alternatives have equal present worth, and comment on what it tells the road authority. [6]
(a)

Use PW = P/(1+i)n for each single payment and the uniform series factor for maintenance. The factors at 4 percent are 1.04-12 = 0.6246, 1.04-24 = 0.3901 and 1.04-36 = 0.2437, which sum to 1.2584. The three resurfacings are worth 95,000 x 1.2584 = $119,547. The 40-year uniform series factor is (1 - 1.04-40)/0.04 = 19.793, so maintenance is worth 3,200 x 19.793 = $63,337. Adding the initial $185,000 gives PW_A = 185,000 + 119,547 + 63,337 = $367,884 per kilometre. The resurfacing at year 36 is the last one, so nothing is owed at year 40 other than maintenance.

Answer: $367,900

(b)

The single resurfacing at year 20 has a factor of 1.04-20 = 0.4564, so its worth is 95,000 x 0.4564 = $43,357. Maintenance at $1,800 per year over 40 years uses the same series factor, 19.793, giving 1,800 x 19.793 = $35,627. Reconstruction is paid now, so it needs no discounting. The total is PW_B = 410,000 + 43,357 + 35,627 = $488,984 per kilometre. Alternative B costs about $121,000 more in present worth than A, because its large initial outlay is only partly offset by the long gap before the first resurfacing and by the lower maintenance bill.

Answer: $489,000

(c)

An equivalent uniform annual cost converts a present worth to level yearly payments using the capital recovery factor, A = PW x i/(1 - (1+i)-n). For 4 percent and 40 years the factor is 0.04/(1 - 0.2083) = 0.050523, which is simply 1/19.793. Then EUAC_A = 367,884 x 0.050523 = $18,587 per year per kilometre. For comparison the same factor applied to B gives about $24,704 per year. Expressing costs per year helps a road authority fit the result into an annual budget and compare against alternatives that have different service lives, although with equal 40-year periods the ranking is identical to the present worth ranking.

Answer: $18,590 per year

(d)

Set PW_A equal to PW_B and solve for the maintenance cost m. The non-maintenance part of A is 185,000 + 119,547 = $304,547. Equality requires 304,547 + 19.793 m = 488,984, so m = 184,437/19.793 = $9,318 per year per kilometre. The result says Alternative A stays the cheaper choice until its upkeep is almost three times the assumed $3,200, so the decision is robust to moderate errors in maintenance cost. It would be more sensitive to the discount rate and to the 12-year resurfacing cycle, which a pavement management system should confirm from condition surveys before the choice is final.

Answer: $9,320 per year

Problem 2 [A6-022] Maintenance and rehabilitation: overlay design and treatment selection

A rural arterial in Grey County has 125 mm of hot mix asphalt (HMA), 200 mm of granular base and 350 mm of granular subbase. A condition survey shows alligator cracking and rutting, so the existing HMA is assigned a condition factor of 0.80 against its layer coefficient. Use structural number SN = sum of a x D x m with thickness D in inches and a drainage coefficient m of 1.0. Layer coefficients are 0.44 per inch for HMA, 0.14 per inch for base and 0.11 per inch for subbase. Traffic projections and a soil modulus test give a required future structural number of 5.2. The new overlay mix has the same coefficient as the existing HMA, 0.44 per inch, and 1 inch is 25.4 mm.

  1. (a) Calculate the effective structural number of the existing pavement. [5]
  2. (b) Calculate the structural number the overlay must supply. [3]
  3. (c) Determine the required overlay thickness in millimetres. [5]
  4. (d) The agency proposes milling 40 mm of the existing HMA before overlaying. Find the new overlay thickness required (laid after milling) and state what the milling does to the net thickness added above the original surface. [7]
(a)

Convert each thickness to inches and apply SN = a D m. HMA: 125/25.4 = 4.921 in, so 0.44 x 4.921 x 0.80 = 1.732. Base: 200/25.4 = 7.874 in, so 0.14 x 7.874 x 1.0 = 1.102. Subbase: 350/25.4 = 13.780 in, so 0.11 x 13.780 x 1.0 = 1.516. The effective structural number is SN_eff = 1.732 + 1.102 + 1.516 = 4.350. The condition factor lowers only the cracked, rutted HMA layer, because the granular layers are assumed sound. This is the value the existing structure can still be relied on to carry.

Answer: 4.35

(b)

The overlay must make up the deficiency between the required future structural number and what the existing structure provides: SN_ol = SN_f - SN_eff = 5.20 - 4.35 = 0.85. A deficiency method like this treats the overlay as new HMA with its own coefficient and a drainage factor of 1.0, placed on a structure whose strength has been reduced by distress. If the survey had shown a stronger existing section, say a condition factor of 0.9, the deficiency would shrink, so the quality of the condition survey directly affects how much asphalt is bought.

Answer: 0.85

(c)

The overlay thickness follows from SN_ol = a_ol x D_ol, so D_ol = 0.85/0.44 = 1.931 inches. In millimetres this is 1.931 x 25.4 = 49.0 mm. Asphalt is placed in practical lift thicknesses, so the designer would round up to 50 mm, which gives SN_ol = 0.44 x 50/25.4 = 0.866 and a total of 5.216, slightly above the 5.2 requirement. A rounded-down 45 mm lift would give a total of 5.13, which would fall short of the requirement and should not be adopted.

Answer: 49 mm, say 50 mm

(d)

After milling 40 mm, 85 mm of HMA remains, or 85/25.4 = 3.346 in. The remaining HMA contributes 0.44 x 3.346 x 0.80 = 1.178. Adding base 1.102 and subbase 1.516 gives SN_eff = 3.796. The deficiency is 5.20 - 3.796 = 1.404, so the overlay is 1.404/0.44 = 3.191 in = 81.0 mm. The net added thickness is 81 - 40 = 41 mm, about 8 mm less than the 49 mm direct overlay, because the milled 40 mm carried only 80 percent of the new-mix coefficient and is replaced by full-strength new asphalt.

Answer: 81 mm

Problem 3 [A6-023] Frost, drainage and economic comparison of pavement alternatives

A 10 m wide new roadbed near Ottawa passes through a silty subgrade with dry density 1,750 kg/m3, moisture content 14 percent by mass and thermal conductivity 1.9 W/(m K). Use the Stefan equation for frost penetration, D = sqrt(2 k F / L), with F the freezing index of 1,100 degree-days Celsius (1 degree-day = 86,400 K s) and L the volumetric latent heat of the soil water, using 334 kJ/kg for water. The designer will replace frost-susceptible soil with non-frost-susceptible granular fill to 60 percent of the frost depth. Option X is full 60 percent replacement at $48 per cubic metre. Option Y replaces only 0.80 m, adds two longitudinal subdrains at $85 per metre each, and incurs $4,500 per kilometre per year of extra patching for 25 years at a 5 percent discount rate. Compare costs per kilometre.

  1. (a) Calculate the frost penetration depth. [5]
  2. (b) Calculate the thickness of granular replacement for Option X. [3]
  3. (c) Calculate the construction cost of Option X per kilometre. [4]
  4. (d) Calculate the present worth of Option Y per kilometre, including drains and patching. [5]
  5. (e) State which option is cheaper and by how much in present worth. [3]
(a)

First find the latent heat per cubic metre of soil. The water mass is 1,750 x 0.14 = 245 kg per cubic metre of soil, so L = 334,000 x 245 = 8.18 x 107 J/m3. The freezing index in SI units is F = 1,100 x 86,400 = 9.50 x 107 K s. Then D = sqrt(2 x 1.9 x 9.504 x 107 / 8.183 x 107) = sqrt(4.414) = 2.10 m. The Stefan equation neglects the heat stored in unfrozen soil, so it overestimates the true depth; that conservatism is acceptable for design but should be known when comparing against a field frost tube.

Answer: 2.10 m

(b)

Partial frost protection is the usual approach in southern Ontario: enough non-frost-susceptible material is placed so that the remaining heave in the susceptible silt is tolerable. At 60 percent of the frost depth, t = 0.60 x 2.10 = 1.26 m. This depth includes the pavement structure in practice, but here the full amount is treated as granular replacement. A thicker replacement reduces differential heave but costs more, which is why the designer weighs it against drainage, which removes the water the ice lenses need to grow.

Answer: 1.26 m

(c)

The volume per kilometre is thickness x width x length = 1.26 x 10 x 1,000 = 12,600 m3. At $48 per cubic metre, the cost is 12,600 x 48 = $604,800, or about $605,000 when the unrounded thickness 1.2605 m is used. This is a first-cost figure only. Option X has no recurring drainage maintenance in the problem, so its present worth equals its construction cost. The earthwork unit price would normally include excavation, hauling, compaction and disposal of the removed silt.

Answer: $605,000

(d)

Replacement of 0.80 m costs 0.80 x 10 x 1,000 x 48 = $384,000. Two subdrains over 1,000 m cost 2 x 1,000 x 85 = $170,000, so the initial cost is $554,000. The extra patching is a uniform series for 25 years at 5 percent, with factor (1 - 1.05-25)/0.05 = 14.094, giving 4,500 x 14.094 = $63,423. The present worth of Option Y is 554,000 + 63,423 = $617,423 per kilometre. The shallower replacement leaves more silt exposed to frost, which is why the patching allowance appears, and the drains reduce but do not remove it.

Answer: $617,400

(e)

Compare the present worths: Option X costs $605,036 and Option Y costs $617,423. Option X is cheaper by 617,423 - 605,036 = $12,387 per kilometre, about 2 percent. The gap is small compared with the uncertainty in unit prices and in the patching estimate, so the economic ranking alone is weak. The designer would also weigh performance: X gives better frost protection and less risk of a heave-related failure, while Y relies on the drains staying clear for 25 years. A modest increase in patching cost would widen the gap in favour of Option X.

Answer: Option X by $12,400

Problem 4 [A6-024] Route surveying and horizontal curve layout by deflection angles

A new county road in Simcoe County turns through a deflection angle of 42.5 degrees between two long tangents that meet at a point of intersection (PI) at chainage 3+864.50. A landowner on the inside of the bend limits the tangent length to at most 120 m from the PI, so the designer must select the radius to fit. The designer will adopt a round radius of 300 m, which is less than the largest radius the constraint allows. The curve will be set out with a total station at the point of curvature (PC), using deflection angles to full 20 m stations, and with a first sub-chord from the PC to the next full 20 m station. Chainages are in the form kilometres plus metres.

  1. (a) Find the largest radius for which the tangent length does not exceed 120 m. [4]
  2. (b) For R = 300 m, calculate the tangent length. [4]
  3. (c) Calculate the chainage of the point of tangency (PT) in metres from zero, for example 3+970.37 is 3970.37. [5]
  4. (d) Calculate the deflection angle in degrees at the PC to the first full 20 m station. [4]
  5. (e) Calculate the long chord from PC to PT. [3]
(a)

For a simple curve the tangent length is T = R tan(Delta/2). Requiring T <= 120 m gives R <= T/tan(Delta/2). With Delta/2 = 21.25 degrees, tan(21.25 degrees) = 0.38891, so R_max = 120/0.38891 = 308.6 m. Any radius at or below this keeps the PC and PT inside the landowner's limit, and the designer picks a smaller round value. A larger radius would give a gentler curve and better sight distance, so it is better to choose the largest practical radius, here 300 m, rather than something much smaller.

Answer: 308.6 m

(b)

With R = 300 m and Delta/2 = 21.25 degrees, T = 300 x 0.38891 = 116.66 m. This is 3.3 m less than the 120 m limit, so the constraint is met with a small margin. The same tangent length is used on both sides of the PI, so the PC is 116.66 m back along the incoming tangent and the PT is 116.66 m forward along the outgoing tangent. The margin leaves room for survey error in the PI position, which is important when a boundary constrains the alignment.

Answer: 116.7 m

(c)

The arc length is L = R x Delta in radians = 300 x (42.5 x pi/180) = 300 x 0.74176 = 222.53 m. The PC is at PI chainage minus T: 3864.50 - 116.66 = 3747.84 m, that is 3+747.84. The PT is the PC plus the arc length: 3747.84 + 222.53 = 3970.37 m, that is 3+970.37. Chainage is measured along the centreline, so the PT chainage is not 3864.50 + 116.66 = 3981.16. That tangent-based sum would overstate it, because the curve is shorter than twice the tangent length.

Answer: 3+970.37, i.e. 3970.37 m

(d)

The first full 20 m station after the PC at 3+747.84 is 3+760, so the first sub-chord has arc length c1 = 3760 - 3747.84 = 12.16 m. The deflection angle at the PC to a point on the curve is half the central angle subtended by the arc, delta = c1/(2R) in radians = 12.16/600 = 0.020269 rad = 1.1615 degrees. The instrument is set up at the PC, with zero on the PI, and this is the angle to turn for the first stake. Each further full station adds 20/600 rad = 1.910 degrees. The last deflection angle, at the PT, must equal Delta/2 = 21.25 degrees as a check.

Answer: 1.162 degrees

(e)

The long chord joining PC and PT subtends the whole central angle, so C = 2R sin(Delta/2) = 2 x 300 x sin(21.25 degrees) = 600 x 0.36243 = 217.46 m. It is slightly shorter than the arc length of 222.53 m, as expected for a curve of this deflection. The long chord is used as a field check: after staking the curve with deflection angles, the distance from PC to the PT stake should agree with 217.46 m to within the closure tolerance of the survey, which for a road of this class might be 1 in 5,000.

Answer: 217.5 m

Problem 5 [A6-025] Horizontal curve design: radius, superelevation and side friction

A rural arterial in Northumberland County has a design speed of 90 km/h. For this class of road, the road authority sets a maximum superelevation of 0.06 m/m and a maximum side friction factor of 0.13 at 90 km/h. Use the point-mass relationship e + f = V2/(127 R), with V in km/h and R in metres. The existing alignment includes a curve of radius 280 m, and a proposed realignment includes a curve of radius 450 m where the assumed side friction at design speed is 0.11. Lanes are 3.75 m wide on a two-lane road, and the pavement is rotated about the centreline. Edge-of-pavement rise relative to the centreline is limited to a relative gradient of 0.50 percent (1 in 200).

  1. (a) Find the minimum radius for 90 km/h at the maximum superelevation and friction. [5]
  2. (b) Find the highest speed that the existing 280 m curve supports at maximum e and f. [4]
  3. (c) Find the superelevation required on the 450 m curve at 90 km/h with f = 0.11, as a fraction. [5]
  4. (d) Find the length of superelevation runoff needed to raise the outer edge to full 0.06 superelevation above the centreline level. [6]
(a)

Rearranging e + f = V2/(127 R) gives R_min = V2/(127 (e_max + f_max)). With V = 90, e_max = 0.06 and f_max = 0.13, R_min = 8,100/(127 x 0.19) = 8,100/24.13 = 335.7 m. A curve tighter than this cannot be driven at 90 km/h without exceeding either the superelevation the authority will build or the friction a driver finds comfortable. This is the radius below which the design speed cannot be met, so it is a limit rather than a target; larger radii give margin.

Answer: 336 m

(b)

For a fixed radius the same relationship gives V = sqrt(127 R (e + f)). With R = 280 m, e = 0.06 and f = 0.13, V = sqrt(127 x 280 x 0.19) = sqrt(6,756) = 82.2 km/h. The existing curve therefore supports about 82 km/h, roughly 8 km/h below the 90 km/h design speed. Practice would sign it with an advisory speed plate of 80 km/h, round down to the nearest 10 km/h, or recommend realignment if crash records show over-speed run-offs.

Answer: 82 km/h

(c)

Substitute into e = V2/(127 R) - f. The speed term is 8,100/(127 x 450) = 8,100/57,150 = 0.1417. Subtracting the assumed friction demand of 0.11 gives e = 0.1417 - 0.11 = 0.0317, close to 3.2 percent. This is well below the 6 percent maximum because the radius is large; the minimum radius would need the full maximum. The designer would still provide at least the normal crown slope, usually 2 percent, so a value of 3.2 percent would be built, and the pavement is then superelevated only slightly beyond the normal cross-section.

Answer: 0.032

(d)

The outer edge must rise above the centreline by w x e = 3.75 x 0.06 = 0.225 m when the whole pavement is rotated about the centreline. The relative gradient between edge and centreline is limited to 0.005, so the runoff length is L = 0.225/0.005 = 45 m. A steeper gradient would give a shorter transition, but it produces a visible kink in the edge line and uncomfortable roll for drivers. If the authority also needed to remove the adverse crown first, a tangent runout would be added before this length, so 45 m is a minimum for the runoff alone.

Answer: 45 m

A6 Practice Paper 6

Problem 1 [A6-026] Spiral transition curves

A two-lane highway in Haldimand County is being redesigned for 80 km/h on a curve with a circular radius of 250 m and a total deflection angle between tangents of 52 degrees. The designer will insert a clothoid (Euler) spiral at each end of the circular arc. The minimum spiral length is set by a limit on the rate of change of lateral acceleration, C = 0.6 m/s3, using Ls = 0.0214 V3/(R C) with V in km/h, R in metres and Ls in metres. The designer adopts a rounded spiral length of 75 m. For checking, use the approximations p = Ls2/(24 R) for the shift, k = Ls/2 - Ls3/(240 R2) for the tangent offset, and the spiral angle in radians as theta_s = Ls/(2 R).

  1. (a) Compute the minimum spiral length from the lateral acceleration criterion. [4]
  2. (b) Compute the spiral angle theta_s in degrees for Ls = 75 m. [3]
  3. (c) Compute the shift p of the circular curve from the original tangent. [4]
  4. (d) Compute the total tangent length from the PI to the tangent-to-spiral point (TS). [5]
  5. (e) Compute the length of the central circular arc. [4]
(a)

Lateral acceleration is introduced gradually along the spiral. The criterion in the problem gives Ls = 0.0214 x V3/(R C). With V = 80, V3 = 512,000; R C = 250 x 0.6 = 150. Then Ls = 0.0214 x 512,000/150 = 10,956.8/150 = 73.05 m. The designer can then round up to 75 m, which meets the limit and is a convenient multiple of the 25 m staking interval. A smaller C, which would make the curve more comfortable, would lengthen the spiral, and a higher speed would lengthen it rapidly because Ls varies with the cube of speed.

Answer: 73.0 m

(b)

The spiral angle is the change in tangent direction from the TS to the spiral-to-curve point (SC). Using theta_s = Ls/(2R) in radians gives 75/(2 x 250) = 0.15 rad. Converted to degrees, 0.15 x 180/pi = 8.594 degrees. The two spirals together use 2 x 8.594 = 17.19 degrees of the 52 degree deflection, leaving 34.81 degrees to be turned by the circular arc. The spiral angle is also needed for the field layout, where the deflection from the TS to points on the spiral is a fraction of this angle.

Answer: 8.59 degrees

(c)

Inserting a spiral moves the circular curve inward from the original tangent by the shift p. Using the stated approximation, p = Ls2/(24 R) = 752/(24 x 250) = 5,625/6,000 = 0.9375 m. This shift is small, but it matters for the right-of-way and for the position of the PC of the previous circular curve, because the same radius now sits about 0.94 m inside the tangent. The tangent offset k is needed with it: k = 37.5 - 753/(240 x 2502) = 37.5 - 0.028 = 37.47 m, which locates the start of the shift along the tangent.

Answer: 0.94 m

(d)

The total tangent from the PI to the TS combines the circular curve's tangent, measured from the shifted centre, with the offset k. Ts = (R + p) tan(Delta/2) + k. Here R + p = 250.9375 m and tan(26 degrees) = 0.48773, so (R + p) tan(Delta/2) = 122.39 m. Adding k = 37.47 m gives Ts = 159.86 m. This is longer than the 121.9 m tangent of the same circular curve without spirals, because the spirals begin further back; the PI must therefore be farther from the TS, and chainages should be computed from this value.

Answer: 159.9 m

(e)

The circular arc is whatever deflection remains after the two spirals: central angle = Delta - 2 theta_s = 0.90757 - 0.30000 = 0.60757 rad, where 52 degrees = 0.90757 rad and 2 x 0.15 = 0.30. The arc length is Lc = R x 0.60757 = 250 x 0.60757 = 151.89 m. The total length of the transition-curve-transition combination is 151.89 + 2 x 75 = 301.89 m. The arc must be positive and preferably longer than about 2 seconds of travel at design speed, which is 44 m at 80 km/h, so 151.9 m is satisfactory.

Answer: 151.9 m

Problem 2 [A6-027] Stopping and decision sight distance

A rural freeway in Ontario is being checked for a design speed of 100 km/h. Use the stopping sight distance relationship SSD = 0.278 V t + V2 / (254 (a/9.81 + G)), with V in km/h, perception-reaction time t = 2.5 s, deceleration a = 3.4 m/s2, and grade G in decimal form (positive uphill, negative downhill). A safety review of a long descent asks whether the available sight distance of 200 m, set by a forested roadside, remains adequate. The designer also checks decision sight distance at a lane-drop exit where drivers need a lane-change manoeuvre, using DSD = 0.278 V t with a combined detection, decision and manoeuvre time of t = 12.5 s.

  1. (a) Calculate the stopping sight distance on level grade. [4]
  2. (b) Calculate the stopping sight distance on a 5 percent downgrade. [4]
  3. (c) Find the steepest downgrade, in percent, for which 200 m of available sight distance is still adequate. [6]
  4. (d) Calculate the decision sight distance at the lane drop. [3]
  5. (e) Express the decision sight distance as a multiple of the level-grade stopping sight distance. [3]
(a)

On level grade G = 0, so the braking term uses a/9.81 = 3.4/9.81 = 0.3466. The reaction distance is 0.278 x 100 x 2.5 = 69.5 m. The braking distance is 1002/(254 x 0.3466) = 10,000/88.04 = 113.6 m. The sum is SSD = 69.5 + 113.6 = 183.1 m. The reaction portion is travelled at constant speed before the brake is touched, and the braking portion is the distance to bring the vehicle to rest at the comfortable deceleration. Drivers must see a 150 mm object at least this far ahead to stop safely.

Answer: 183 m

(b)

A 5 percent downgrade has G = -0.05, which reduces the effective deceleration: a/9.81 + G = 0.3466 - 0.05 = 0.2966. The braking distance becomes 10,000/(254 x 0.2966) = 10,000/75.33 = 132.7 m. The reaction distance is unchanged at 69.5 m, so SSD = 69.5 + 132.7 = 202.2 m. The downgrade adds 19 m, about 10 percent, to the level-grade value. This is why designers check long descents separately, especially where trucks with poorer braking use the road, and why 183 m is not enough there.

Answer: 202 m

(c)

With available distance 200 m, the braking distance allowed is 200 - 69.5 = 130.5 m. Setting 10,000/(254 x (0.3466 + G)) = 130.5 gives 254 x (0.3466 + G) = 10,000/130.5 = 76.63, so 0.3466 + G = 0.3017 and G = -0.0449. The steepest acceptable downgrade is therefore 4.49 percent. On the 5 percent descent in part (b), the stopping distance of 202 m exceeds the 200 m available, so that grade would fail marginally. Options include clearing the vegetation, flattening the grade or posting a lower speed.

Answer: 4.49 percent

(d)

Decision sight distance is longer than stopping sight distance because the driver has to detect an unexpected or hard-to-see hazard, decide what to do and carry out a lane change or speed change, not just stop. With the combined time of 12.5 s, DSD = 0.278 x 100 x 12.5 = 347.5 m. The formula treats the vehicle as moving at a constant speed throughout, which is appropriate for a manoeuvre where the driver maintains speed or changes lanes rather than braking. At this location the exit sign and gore must therefore be visible from at least this distance.

Answer: 347.5 m

(e)

The ratio is DSD/SSD = 347.5/183.1 = 1.898, or about 1.9. Decision sight distance is therefore roughly double the stopping sight distance at this speed. The ratio shows why decision sight distance is provided only at complex locations such as lane drops, interchange exits and urban-rural transitions, not along the whole road: providing 347.5 m everywhere would be uneconomical in rolling or wooded terrain. Where it cannot be fully met, advance warning signs and extra delineation give drivers the time they need.

Answer: 1.90

Problem 3 [A6-028] Crest and sag vertical curves and K values

A provincial highway climbs a hill in Muskoka and then descends. A crest vertical curve joins a +3.0 percent grade to a -2.5 percent grade. The design requires stopping sight distance S = 160 m, with eye height 1.08 m and object height 0.60 m. For S less than L on a crest, use L = A S2 / 658, with A the algebraic difference in grades in percent. A sag curve elsewhere on the route joins a -3.5 percent grade to a +2.5 percent grade, and for S less than L uses headlight control with L = A S2/(120 + 3.5 S) and S = 160 m. The crest PVI is at elevation 215.40 m. Use K = L/A.

  1. (a) Calculate the minimum length of the crest vertical curve. [5]
  2. (b) Calculate the K value of the crest curve. [3]
  3. (c) Calculate the minimum length of the sag curve. [5]
  4. (d) Adopt L = 214 m for the crest curve. Calculate the elevation of the high point on the curve. [7]
(a)

The algebraic difference in grades is A = 3.0 - (-2.5) = 5.5 percent. Assuming S < L, the stated expression gives L = 5.5 x 1602/658 = 5.5 x 25,600/658 = 140,800/658 = 213.98 m. The constant 658 comes from the eye height and object height of 1.08 m and 0.60 m. Because 160 m is less than 214 m, the assumption S < L holds and the result is valid. If S had exceeded L, the other branch of the equation, L = 2S - 658/A, would be needed.

Answer: 214 m

(b)

The rate of vertical curvature is K = L/A = 213.98/5.5 = 38.9 metres of curve per percent change in grade. K is useful because it depends only on the design speed and criterion and not on the particular grades, so agencies tabulate K values by design speed and check any crest curve by comparing the actual K against the tabulated minimum. A K of 38.9 is typical of a design speed near 90 km/h for stopping sight distance control, and any larger value would be acceptable on safety grounds.

Answer: 38.9 m per percent

(c)

For the sag curve A = 2.5 - (-3.5) = 6.0 percent. With headlight control and S < L, L = A S2/(120 + 3.5 S) = 6.0 x 25,600/(120 + 560) = 153,600/680 = 225.9 m. The numbers 120 and 3.5 come from a headlight height of 0.60 m and an upward beam angle of 1 degree, so the beam must reach S ahead at the road surface. S = 160 m is less than L = 225.9 m, so the assumption is valid. The corresponding K is 225.9/6.0 = 37.6, close to the crest value even though the controls are different.

Answer: 226 m

(d)

Locate the PVC first: it lies L/2 = 107 m before the PVI, so its elevation is 215.40 - 0.03 x 107 = 212.19 m. The high point occurs where the tangent grade is zero, at distance x = g1 L/A = 3.0 x 214/5.5 = 116.7 m from the PVC. The curve elevation is y = y_PVC + g1 x/100 - (A/100) x2/(2L). Substituting gives 212.19 + 0.03 x 116.7 - (0.055/(2 x 214)) x 116.72 = 212.19 + 3.50 - 1.75 = 213.94 m. This is 1.46 m below the PVI, which agrees with the mid-curve offset formula A L/800 = 1.47 m, the nearby value at the point of maximum height.

Answer: 213.94 m

Problem 4 [A6-029] Vertical alignment, grades and passing sight distance

A two-lane rural highway in Bruce County is designed for 100 km/h and passing zones must be checked against minimum passing sight distance. Use a four-component model: d1 = 0.278 t1 (v - m + a t1/2), d2 = 0.278 v t2, d3 = 60 m clearance, and d4 = 2/3 d2, with speeds in km/h and times in seconds. The passing vehicle travels at v = 100 km/h, the vehicle being passed is m = 15 km/h slower, the passing vehicle accelerates at a = 2.4 km/h per second, the initial manoeuvre time is t1 = 4.3 s, and the time in the opposing lane is t2 = 10.5 s. For a crest with equal eye and object height of 1.08 m, use L = A S2/864 when S is less than L, and the K value for stopping sight distance at 100 km/h is 52.

  1. (a) Calculate the initial manoeuvre distance d1. [5]
  2. (b) Calculate the total passing sight distance. [5]
  3. (c) Find the minimum length of a crest curve, with grade change A = 3 percent, that gives full passing sight distance. [5]
  4. (d) Express the K value of that curve as a multiple of the stopping sight distance K of 52, and say what the result implies for providing passing zones. [5]
(a)

The initial manoeuvre includes the time the driver spends deciding and accelerating to move into the opposing lane. Using d1 = 0.278 t1 (v - m + a t1/2), the average speed during acceleration is v - m + a t1/2 = 100 - 15 + 2.4 x 4.3/2 = 85 + 5.16 = 90.16 km/h. Then d1 = 0.278 x 4.3 x 90.16 = 107.8 m. The passing driver begins at the speed of the slower vehicle, 85 km/h, and ends at 95.3 km/h by the time the vehicle moves into the left lane. The distance is travelled while the opposing lane is still being observed.

Answer: 107.8 m

(b)

The distance travelled in the opposing lane is d2 = 0.278 x 100 x 10.5 = 291.9 m. The clearance at the end of the manoeuvre is d3 = 60 m, and the opposing vehicle travels d4 = 2/3 x 291.9 = 194.6 m during the passing, assuming it moves at the same speed. The total is d1 + d2 + d3 + d4 = 107.8 + 291.9 + 60 + 194.6 = 654.3 m. This is more than three times the stopping sight distance of 183 m at 100 km/h, because a passing driver needs to see an oncoming car early enough to complete or abort the pass.

Answer: 654 m

(c)

Passing sight distance is much larger than any normal crest curve provides. Using the equal-height crest formula for S < L, L = A S2/864 = 3 x 654.32/864 = 3 x 428,085/864 = 1,284,255/864 = 1,486 m. Since S = 654 m is less than L = 1,486 m, the S < L expression applies. A curve this long, for a grade change of only 3 percent, is rarely economical. Passing zones are therefore usually provided on tangents or flat crests, and on crests the length is checked with the permitted cut in the vertical profile.

Answer: 1,486 m

(d)

The rate of vertical curvature of the passing curve is K = L/A = 1,486/3 = 495.5. The stopping-sight-distance K at the same speed is 52, so the ratio is 495.5/52 = 9.53. A crest with K = 52 provides only about 212 m of equal-height sight distance, roughly one third of the 654 m needed, and needs 9.5 times the length per percent of grade change. The implication is that continuous passing opportunity would demand a nearly flat profile or very large curves, so most hilly alignments cannot offer it and the designer marks no-passing zones by pavement markings wherever sight distance falls below the minimum.

Answer: 9.5 times

Problem 5 [A6-030] Intersection design: turning radii, sight triangles and channelization

A stop-controlled minor road meets a two-lane municipal arterial in Peterborough, where the posted speed is 70 km/h. A passenger car turning left from the stop needs a time gap of t_g = 8.0 s in the major-road traffic, and the intersection sight distance along the major road is ISD = 0.278 V t_g. The minimum turning radius for a slow turn at 15 km/h is checked with R = V2/(127 (e + f)), taking e = 0 and f = 0.30. A separate left-turn bay on the arterial serves 420 veh/h arriving randomly and is modelled as a single-server queue with a service capacity of 600 veh/h, for which the probability that n or more vehicles are present is rhon. Each queued vehicle occupies 7.5 m. Storage is sized for n vehicles, where n is the smallest whole number for which the probability of n or more vehicles being present does not exceed 5 percent, and storage = n x 7.5 m.

  1. (a) Calculate the intersection sight distance required along the major road. [4]
  2. (b) Calculate the minimum radius for a 15 km/h turn. [4]
  3. (c) Calculate the utilization rho of the left-turn bay. [3]
  4. (d) Find the smallest whole number of vehicles n for which rhon does not exceed 0.05. [4]
  5. (e) Calculate the storage length of the left-turn bay. [5]
(a)

The sight triangle must let a driver stopped on the minor road see far enough along the major road to complete the turn before an approaching car, travelling at 70 km/h, closes the gap. With ISD = 0.278 V t_g = 0.278 x 70 x 8.0 = 155.7 m. The 8.0 s gap is taken as an acceptance time for a car; longer gaps are needed for trucks and for wider or multilane roads. Trees, hedges, signs and parked vehicles must be kept out of the triangle that this distance forms with the setback point on the minor road.

Answer: 155.7 m

(b)

For a slow turn the superelevation is negligible, so e = 0 and the lateral demand is carried by side friction alone. With V = 15 km/h and f = 0.30, R = V2/(127 f) = 225/(127 x 0.30) = 225/38.1 = 5.91 m. This is the path radius a car can follow at 15 km/h without skidding. The edge-of-pavement radius at a real corner is made much larger, often 9 to 15 m, because trucks and buses offtrack, and the vehicle path sits within the lane, not on the kerb.

Answer: 5.9 m

(c)

The utilization is the arrival rate divided by the service rate: rho = lambda/mu = 420/600 = 0.70. A value of 0.70 means the bay is busy 70 percent of the time. The queue is therefore often non-empty, and the probability of a long queue falls off geometrically at 0.7 per additional vehicle. If the left-turn volume rose to 540 veh/h, rho would be 0.90 and the required storage would be much longer, so the design depends strongly on a reliable volume forecast.

Answer: 0.70

(d)

The probability of n or more vehicles is rhon, so we need 0.7n <= 0.05, which means n >= ln(0.05)/ln(0.7). Evaluating, ln(0.05) = -2.9957 and ln(0.7) = -0.3567, so n >= 8.40. The count of vehicles must be a whole number, and rounding up gives 9 vehicles. Check: 0.78 = 0.0576, which is above 5 percent, and 0.79 = 0.0404, which is below it. A smaller design percentile would allow fewer vehicles but risk blocking the through lane more often.

Answer: 9 vehicles

(e)

Storage length equals the design queue times the length each vehicle occupies, including the gap between stopped cars: 9 x 7.5 = 67.5 m. This length excludes the approach taper, which is added upstream and is where the bay is first entered. Storage is the length of the full-width bay, and the taper brings the lane out of the through lane. The design criterion is applied to the probability that n or more vehicles are present in the bay, which is about 4 percent for nine, so 67.5 m is the storage that satisfies the stated 5 percent test.

Answer: 67.5 m

A6 Practice Paper 7

Problem 1 [A6-031] Earthwork volumes and the mass haul diagram

A county road in Oxford County, Ontario, is being regraded over a 160 m length, and the Ministry-style earthwork quantities are to be settled before tender. Cross-sections were cut at 20 m spacing, and the end areas in square metres are: chainage 0+000 cut 12, fill 0; 0+020 cut 26, fill 0; 0+040 cut 18, fill 0; 0+060 cut 4, fill 3; 0+080 cut 0, fill 15; 0+100 cut 0, fill 24; 0+120 cut 0, fill 20; 0+140 cut 5, fill 6; 0+160 cut 16, fill 0. The excavated glacial till swells and then compacts so that every 1.00 m³ measured in the bank gives 0.90 m³ of compacted fill. Use the average end area method between stations, treat the shared sections as given, measure cut in bank m³ and fill in compacted m³, and build the mass diagram from zero at 0+000 using ordinates of (0.90 × cut) minus fill, in compacted m³.

  1. (a) Find the total excavation between 0+000 and 0+160, in bank m³. [4]
  2. (b) Find the largest positive mass diagram ordinate, in compacted m³, which occurs at 0+060. [5]
  3. (c) Find the chainage, in metres from 0+000, at which the mass diagram crosses zero between 0+100 and 0+120 (the balance point), assuming the ordinate varies linearly over the interval. [5]
  4. (d) Find the volume of borrow, in bank m³, needed to complete the fill over the whole 160 m. [6]
(a)

Average end area volume between stations i and i+1 is V = L (A1 + A2)/2 with L = 20 m. Cut areas are 12, 26, 18, 4, 0, 0, 0, 5, 16. Interval volumes: 0+000 to 0+020: 20 × (12 + 26)/2 = 380; 0+020 to 0+040: 20 × (26 + 18)/2 = 440; 0+040 to 0+060: 20 × (18 + 4)/2 = 220; 0+060 to 0+080: 20 × (4 + 0)/2 = 40; the next two intervals have zero cut; 0+120 to 0+140: 20 × (0 + 5)/2 = 50; 0+140 to 0+160: 20 × (5 + 16)/2 = 210. Summing 380 + 440 + 220 + 40 + 50 + 210 gives 1340 m³. Because cut areas are measured in the undisturbed ground, this is a bank volume, which is the basis on which excavation is normally paid.

Answer: 1340 m³

(b)

Fill volumes (compacted) by the same rule: 0+040 to 0+060: 20 × (0 + 3)/2 = 30; 0+060 to 0+080: 20 × (3 + 15)/2 = 180; 0+080 to 0+100: 20 × (15 + 24)/2 = 390; 0+100 to 0+120: 20 × (24 + 20)/2 = 440; 0+120 to 0+140: 20 × (20 + 6)/2 = 260; 0+140 to 0+160: 20 × (6 + 0)/2 = 60; the first two intervals have no fill. Net change per interval is 0.90 × cut minus fill: interval 1 gives 0.90 × 380 = +342; interval 2 gives 0.90 × 440 = +396; interval 3 gives 0.90 × 220 − 30 = +168; interval 4 gives 0.90 × 40 − 180 = −144. Running totals are 342, 738, 906 and then 762 at 0+080. The ordinate rises while the net is positive and peaks at 906 m³ at 0+060, where the diagram changes from excess cut to deficit.

Answer: 906 m³

(c)

Continuing the running total: interval 0+080 to 0+100 has net 0 − 390 = −390, giving 372 at 0+100; interval 0+100 to 0+120 has net 0 − 440 = −440, giving −68 at 0+120. The curve therefore crosses zero between 0+100 and 0+120. With linear variation the fraction of the interval used is 372/440 = 0.8455, so the distance beyond 0+100 is 0.8455 × 20 = 16.9 m. Balance point chainage = 100 + 16.9 = 116.9 m. The point matters in practice because cut to the left of it can be hauled to fill to its right, while beyond it the diagram shows a deficit that no haul along the road can remove, so material must come from elsewhere.

Answer: 116.9 m

(d)

The last two intervals give net ordinates of 0.90 × 50 − 260 = −215 and 0.90 × 210 − 60 = +129, so the running total goes from −68 at 0+120 to −283 at 0+140 and then back to −154 at 0+160. The final ordinate is the net balance for the whole job: total cut converted to compacted terms is 0.90 × 1340 = 1206 compacted m³, total fill is 30 + 180 + 390 + 440 + 260 + 60 = 1360 compacted m³, and 1206 − 1360 = −154 compacted m³, a deficit. Borrow is paid in bank m³, so divide by the 0.90 factor: 154/0.90 = 171.1 bank m³. Borrow would be sourced from a nearby pit, with haul to be priced separately.

Answer: 171.1 m³

Problem 2 [A6-032] Embankment, borrow, shrinkage, swell and compaction

A 1200 m long approach embankment for a rural interchange near Woodstock, Ontario, has a constant trapezoidal section: crest width 12.0 m, height 3.5 m and side slopes of 3 horizontal to 1 vertical. The specification requires compaction to 95 percent of a Standard Proctor maximum dry density of 1920 kg/m³ at an optimum moisture content of 12 percent. Borrow comes from a glacial till pit where the bank (in-place) bulk density is 1790 kg/m³ at a natural moisture content of 9 percent. Once excavated, the till has a loose bulk density of 1250 kg/m³. Hauling is by 14 m³ (struck, loose measure) tandem dump trucks, each completing a 36 minute round trip. The contractor works 9 productive hours a day for 25 working days. Water for the till is added at the pit to reach the optimum moisture content, and there is no loss of fines or spillage.

  1. (a) Find the bank volume of borrow, in m³, required to build the embankment to the specified density. [5]
  2. (b) Find the number of 14 m³ truck loads needed, using the loose volume of the excavated material. [4]
  3. (c) Find the volume of water, in megalitres, that must be added to bring all the borrow from its natural moisture content to the optimum moisture content. [5]
  4. (d) Find the minimum whole number of trucks needed to haul all of the borrow within the 25 working days. [6]
(a)

Embankment cross-section area = (b + zh)h = (12.0 + 3 × 3.5) × 3.5 = 22.5 × 3.5 = 78.75 m², so the compacted volume is 78.75 × 1200 = 94 500 m³. Required compacted dry density = 0.95 × 1920 = 1824 kg/m³. The solid (dry) mass of soil that must be delivered is the compacted volume times this density, 94 500 × 1824 = 172.37 million kg, or 172 368 t. The borrow pit holds dry soil at ρd = ρ/(1 + w) = 1790/1.09 = 1642.2 kg/m³ in the bank. Bank volume = dry mass ÷ bank dry density = 94 500 × 1824/1642.2 = 104 962 m³. The ratio 1642.2/1824 = 0.900 is the shrinkage factor, meaning each bank m³ yields 0.900 compacted m³.

Answer: 104 962 m³

(b)

Swell is the increase in volume on excavation. The bulk mass in the bank is the same material that ends up loose in the truck, so the loose volume equals the bank volume times the ratio of bank bulk density to loose bulk density: 104 962 × 1790/1250 = 150 305 m³. This gives a swell of 1790/1250 − 1 = 0.432, or 43.2 percent. Trucks are paid and loaded in loose measure, so the number of loads is 150 305/14 = 10 736.1, which rounds up to 10 737 loads because a fraction of a load still requires a trip. Using the bank volume instead would badly understate the haul, since each truck carries only 14/1.432 = 9.8 bank m³ per trip.

Answer: 10 737 loads

(c)

The mass of dry soil to be moistened is the same 172 368 t found in part (a), since the dry solids are what compaction and water content are defined against. The pit moisture is 9 percent and the target is 12 percent, so the water to add is 0.12 − 0.09 = 0.03 of the dry mass: 172 368 t × 0.03 = 5171 t. At a density of 1000 kg/m³ one tonne of water is 1000 L, so the volume is 5171 × 1000 L = 5.171 × 10⁶ L = 5.17 ML. This is the net requirement; in the field extra water is needed for evaporation during hauling and spreading, which is usually allowed for by a contractor's water truck program.

Answer: 5.17 ML

(d)

Trips per truck per day = productive minutes ÷ cycle time = (9 × 60)/36 = 15 trips. Over 25 days one truck makes 15 × 25 = 375 trips, and so can move 375 × 14 = 5250 m³ loose. The total loose volume to move is 150 305 m³, so the number of trucks is 150 305/5250 = 28.63, which must be rounded up to 29. Equivalently, 10 737 loads divided by 375 trips per truck gives 28.63. Twenty-nine trucks give a capacity of 29 × 5250 = 152 250 m³, a margin of about 1.3 percent. This margin is thin, so a realistic plan would carry a spare truck for breakdowns and weather days.

Answer: 29 trucks

Problem 3 [A6-033] Roadway drainage: ditches, culverts and subdrains

A two-lane highway on the Oak Ridges Moraine crosses a small tributary at a skewed alignment, and a concrete pipe culvert is to carry the 10-year flow from a 42.0 ha rural catchment. The runoff coefficient is 0.35 and the design rainfall intensity at the time of concentration is 95 mm/h. The culvert is to be sized as a pipe flowing just full under open-channel conditions, with Manning's n = 0.013 and a barrel slope of 1.2 percent. Available circular concrete pipe diameters are 0.90 m, 1.05 m, 1.20 m, 1.35 m and 1.50 m. A separate roadside ditch on the downstream side carries 0.45 m³/s. It is a trapezoid with a 0.60 m bottom width, 3H:1V side slopes, a longitudinal grade of 1.5 percent and a grassed lining with n = 0.035. Neglect inlet control and tailwater effects.

  1. (a) Use the rational method to find the design peak flow Q, in m³/s, for the catchment. [4]
  2. (b) Find the minimum diameter, in metres, of a pipe that will carry Q when just full. [4]
  3. (c) Select the smallest standard pipe from the list and find its full-flow capacity, in m³/s. [4]
  4. (d) Find the full-flow velocity, in m/s, in the selected pipe. [3]
  5. (e) Find the normal depth of flow, in metres, in the roadside ditch at 0.45 m³/s. [5]
(a)

The rational method in metric units is Q = C i A/360, where Q is in m³/s, i is in mm/h and A is in hectares. Substituting C = 0.35, i = 95 mm/h and A = 42.0 ha gives Q = 0.35 × 95 × 42.0/360 = 1396.5/360 = 3.879 m³/s. The factor 360 comes from converting hectares to square metres (10 000), millimetres per hour to metres per second (1/3.6 × 10⁻⁶) and combining them. The method assumes that rainfall is uniform over the catchment for a duration equal to its time of concentration, so that the whole area contributes at the peak. For a 42 ha rural area this is acceptable, although the result is a peak flow estimate rather than a hydrograph.

Answer: 3.88 m³/s

(b)

For a circular pipe flowing full, the hydraulic radius is R = D/4 and the area is πD²/4, so Manning's equation becomes Q = (1/n)(πD²/4)(D/4)2/3 S1/2, which simplifies to Q = 0.3117 D8/3 S1/2/n. Solving for D: D8/3 = Q n/(0.3117 S1/2) = 3.879 × 0.013/(0.3117 × 0.1095) = 0.05043/0.03414 = 1.4773. Then D = 1.47733/8 = 1.157 m. A pipe smaller than this cannot carry the design flow even when just full, so this value is a lower bound. A culvert is usually sized with additional allowance for headwater limits, debris and fill depth, which the question has told us to neglect.

Answer: 1.157 m

(c)

The smallest standard diameter that is at least 1.157 m is 1.20 m. Its full-flow capacity is Q = 0.3117 D8/3 S1/2/n. With D = 1.20 m, D8/3 = 1.202.6667 = 1.6264, and S1/2 = 0.1095. Then Q = 0.3117 × 1.6264 × 0.1095/0.013 = 4.27 m³/s. The pipe therefore runs at 3.879/4.271 = 91 percent of its full capacity, leaving about 9 percent in reserve. The smaller 1.05 m pipe would carry only 2.99 m³/s and surcharge, so it is rejected. A reserve this small means the culvert would be close to full for the design event, which is accepted only where headwater depth is acceptable.

Answer: 4.27 m³/s

(d)

Velocity in a full pipe is the capacity divided by the cross-sectional area. For D = 1.20 m, A = πD²/4 = π × 1.44/4 = 1.131 m². Then V = Q/A = 4.271/1.131 = 3.78 m/s. Because the full-flow equation is the same as Manning's with R = D/4, the velocity can also be checked as V = (1/n) R2/3 S1/2 = (1/0.013) × 0.3002/3 × 0.1095 = 76.92 × 0.4481 × 0.1095 = 3.77 m/s, in agreement. This velocity is high enough to keep the barrel self-cleaning, but it also exceeds the limits normally placed on unprotected outlets, so an energy dissipator or riprap apron at the outlet would be called for.

Answer: 3.78 m/s

(e)

The ditch discharge is given by Manning's equation, Q = (1/n) A R2/3 S1/2, with A = (b + zy)y and wetted perimeter P = b + 2y√(1 + z²). With b = 0.60 m, z = 3, S = 0.015 and n = 0.035, the target is Q n/S1/2 = 0.45 × 0.035/0.1225 = 0.1286. Try y = 0.285 m: A = (0.60 + 0.855) × 0.285 = 0.4147 m²; P = 0.60 + 2 × 0.285 × 3.1623 = 2.402 m; R = 0.1726 m; A R2/3 = 0.4147 × 0.3099 = 0.1285, matching the target. So the normal depth is 0.285 m, with mean velocity 0.45/0.4147 = 1.09 m/s. This is under a typical limit of about 1.2 m/s for grassed channels, so the lining is acceptable.

Answer: 0.285 m

Problem 4 [A6-034] Aggregate properties: gradation and specific gravity

A quarry near Milton, Ontario, supplies stockpiles for a dense-graded asphalt surface course. Stockpile A is 12.5 mm crushed limestone chip, of which 9 percent passes the 4.75 mm sieve. Stockpile B is manufactured sand, of which 93 percent passes the 4.75 mm sieve and whose bulk specific gravity is 2.658. Mineral filler (baghouse fines, all passing 4.75 mm) has a specific gravity of 2.740 and must make up exactly 5 percent of the blend by mass. To find the bulk specific gravity of stockpile A, a 2.5 kg washed sample was tested: oven-dry mass in air 2013 g, saturated surface-dry mass in air 2045 g, and mass submerged in water 1278 g. The job formula requires 55 percent of the total blend by mass to pass the 4.75 mm sieve, and the other two stockpiles are blended to make up the remaining 95 percent.

  1. (a) Find the bulk specific gravity Gsb of stockpile A. [4]
  2. (b) Find the water absorption of stockpile A, as a percentage of oven-dry mass. [3]
  3. (c) Find the percentage of the total blend (by mass) that must be stockpile A to meet the 55 percent passing requirement at 4.75 mm. [7]
  4. (d) Using the proportions from part (c), find the bulk specific gravity of the combined aggregate, filler included. [6]
(a)

For coarse aggregate the bulk specific gravity (oven-dry basis) is Gsb = A/(B − C), where A is the oven-dry mass in air, B is the saturated surface-dry mass in air and C is the mass in water. The difference B − C = 2045 − 1278 = 767 g is the mass of water displaced by the particles including their permeable pores, so it represents the bulk volume in cm³ at a water density of 1.00 g/cm³. Then Gsb = 2013/767 = 2.6245. Dividing by the apparent specific gravity would instead exclude pores, which is why Gsb is lower than apparent gravity (2013/735 = 2.739). Gsb is the value used in volumetric calculations of asphalt mixes because the pore volume counts as part of the aggregate volume.

Answer: 2.6245

(b)

Absorption is the water held in the permeable pores at the saturated surface-dry condition, expressed as a percentage of the oven-dry mass. Absorption = (B − A)/A × 100 = (2045 − 2013)/2013 × 100 = 32/2013 × 100 = 1.59 percent. This is a moderate value for limestone. It matters in mix design because an aggregate that absorbs 1.59 percent water will also absorb some asphalt binder, though usually less than water, and the absorbed binder is not available to coat the particle surfaces. The mix designer therefore separates total binder from effective binder using the effective specific gravity Gse, which sits between the bulk and apparent values.

Answer: 1.59 %

(c)

Let f be the fraction of the 95 percent aggregate portion that is stockpile A. The filler passes 4.75 mm entirely, so the passing balance is 0.95 [9 f + 93 (1 − f)] + 5 = 55. Then 0.95 [93 − 84 f] = 50, which gives 93 − 84 f = 52.632 and f = 40.368/84 = 0.4806. Stockpile A is 0.4806 × 95 = 45.65 percent of the total blend, stockpile B is 95 − 45.65 = 49.35 percent and filler is 5.00 percent. Check: 45.65 × 0.09 + 49.35 × 0.93 + 5.00 = 4.109 + 45.896 + 5.00 = 55.0. The blend therefore meets the 4.75 mm target, but the other sieve sizes would still have to be checked against the control points of the specification.

Answer: 45.65 %

(d)

For a blend of components with masses P₁, P₂, P₃ (percent) and specific gravities G₁, G₂, G₃, the combined gravity is G = 100/(P₁/G₁ + P₂/G₂ + P₃/G₃), because volume is mass divided by gravity and the total mass is 100. Using the proportions from part (c): 45.65/2.6245 = 17.395; 49.35/2.658 = 18.566; 5.00/2.740 = 1.825. The sum is 37.786. Then Gsb(blend) = 100/37.786 = 2.6465. This value lies between the lowest and highest component gravities, as it must. Because the blend contains 5 percent filler and about half sand, the combined gravity is greater than that of chip alone. It will be used as the bulk specific gravity in the Marshall or Superpave volumetric calculations.

Answer: 2.6465

Problem 5 [A6-035] Asphalt cement properties and performance grading

A performance-graded binder is to be selected for a new surface course on a four-lane arterial in Barrie, Ontario (latitude 44.2° N), where traffic is slow and heavy because of a nearby quarry. Climate records give a 7-day mean maximum air temperature of 34.0 °C and a 1-day minimum air temperature of −29.0 °C. Use these relations, stated here so no chart is needed: the maximum pavement temperature 20 mm below the surface is (Tair − 0.00618 φ² + 0.2289 φ + 42.2) × 0.9545 − 17.78, where φ is latitude in degrees; the minimum pavement surface temperature is 0.859 Tair + 1.7. Binders are graded in 6 °C steps (high-temperature grades 52, 58, 64, 70; low-temperature grades −22, −28, −34), and slow heavy traffic requires raising the high-temperature grade by one step. The selected binder has measured Brookfield viscosities of 480 mPa·s at 135 °C and 175 mPa·s at 165 °C.

  1. (a) Find the maximum design pavement temperature, in °C, at 20 mm depth. [4]
  2. (b) Find the minimum design pavement temperature, in °C, at the surface. [4]
  3. (c) State the high-temperature number of the grade to be specified after the traffic adjustment (the full grade is written as that number followed by the low-temperature number). [4]
  4. (d) Using a straight-line relation between log log viscosity (mPa·s) and log absolute temperature (K), find the mixing temperature, in °C, at which the viscosity is 170 mPa·s. [4]
  5. (e) With the same relation, find the compaction temperature, in °C, at which the viscosity is 280 mPa·s. [4]
(a)

First find the surface-related quantity inside the bracket: Tair − 0.00618 φ² + 0.2289 φ + 42.2 with Tair = 34.0 and φ = 44.2. The latitude term is 0.00618 × 44.2² = 0.00618 × 1953.64 = 12.07, and 0.2289 × 44.2 = 10.12. So the bracket is 34.0 − 12.07 + 10.12 + 42.2 = 74.24 °C. Multiplying by 0.9545 gives 70.87 and subtracting 17.78 gives 53.09 °C, which is rounded to 53.1 °C. This is the temperature at 20 mm depth, where rutting due to shear in the binder is most critical. The surface itself would be hotter, but the grade is selected for the depth at which the dynamic shear test is representative, so 53.1 °C is the controlling value for the high-temperature grade.

Answer: 53.1 °C

(b)

The minimum pavement temperature is taken at the surface, where cold-weather thermal cracking begins. The relation gives Tmin = 0.859 × (−29.0) + 1.7 = −24.91 + 1.7 = −23.21 °C. The pavement is therefore a little warmer than the coldest air temperature because the ground below stores heat and the surface does not drop quite to the air minimum. The low-temperature grade is the next available step that is at or below this value: the available grades are −22, −28 and −34, and −22 would be too warm because the pavement can be colder than −22 °C, so the grade selected is −28. Note that this grading is conservative by design, using a single worst day.

Answer: -23.2 °C

(c)

The high-temperature grade must be at least equal to the design pavement temperature of 53.1 °C. Grade 52 would be too low, so the base grade is 58. The statement requires that slow heavy traffic raise the grade by one 6 °C step, so 58 + 6 = 64. This extra step compensates for the longer loading time of slow vehicles, which lets the binder behave more like a viscous fluid at a given temperature, increasing the rutting risk. Combined with the low-temperature grade of −28 from part (b), the specified binder is PG 64-28. The additional grade increases stiffness at high temperature and may slightly hurt low-temperature flexibility, so the low grade is verified after the change rather than assumed.

Answer: 64 (PG 64-28)

(d)

The viscosity-temperature relation is log log η = A + VTS log T with T in kelvin. For the two measurements: T₁ = 408.15 K, η₁ = 480 gives log log 480 = log 2.6812 = 0.4283; T₂ = 438.15 K, η₂ = 175 gives log log 175 = log 2.2430 = 0.3508. With log T₁ = 2.6108 and log T₂ = 2.6416 the slope is VTS = (0.3508 − 0.4283)/(2.6416 − 2.6108) = −2.516, and A = 0.4283 + 2.516 × 2.6108 = 6.997. For η = 170: log log 170 = log 2.2304 = 0.3484; log T = (0.3484 − 6.997)/(−2.516) = 2.6423, so T = 439.1 K = 166.0 °C. This is slightly above the 165 °C point because 170 mPa·s is lower than 175.

Answer: 166.0 °C

(e)

Apply the same line, log log η = 6.997 − 2.516 log T. For η = 280 mPa·s: log 280 = 2.4472 and log of that is 0.3887. Solving for log T gives (6.997 − 0.3887)/2.516 = 2.6265, so T = 102.6265 = 423.3 K, which is 150.1 °C. The compaction temperature is lower than the mixing temperature because the higher viscosity of 280 mPa·s makes the binder stiff enough that the mix can hold its shape under the roller. If compaction were carried out much hotter, the mix would shove under the roller; if it were colder, the mat would not reach target density. This temperature is only a guide, and field control adjusts for the mix, thickness and ambient conditions.

Answer: 150.1 °C

A6 Practice Paper 8

Problem 1 [A6-036] Marshall mix design and volumetrics

A municipal laboratory in London, Ontario, is developing a Marshall mix for a 12.5 mm surface course on a collector road. The aggregate blend has a bulk specific gravity Gsb = 2.640 and the asphalt cement has a specific gravity Gb = 1.025. Two trial binder contents, expressed as a percentage of total mix mass, were tested. At 5.0 percent binder the compacted specimens had a bulk specific gravity Gmb = 2.358 and the loose mix had a theoretical maximum specific gravity Gmm = 2.470. At 5.5 percent binder the corresponding values were Gmb = 2.389 and Gmm = 2.452. The agency's design criterion is 4.0 percent air voids in the compacted mix. Treat the air void content as varying linearly with binder content between the two trials, and assume the absorbed binder fraction is the same at both contents.

  1. (a) Find the air void content Va, in percent, of the compacted mix at 5.0 percent binder. [4]
  2. (b) Find the voids in the mineral aggregate, VMA, in percent, at 5.0 percent binder. [4]
  3. (c) Find the effective binder content Pbe, in percent of total mix mass, at 5.0 percent binder (use the effective specific gravity of the aggregate found from Gmm). [6]
  4. (d) Find the binder content, in percent, that gives 4.0 percent air voids. [6]
(a)

Air voids are the fraction of the compacted volume that is not occupied by aggregate or binder, so Va = (1 − Gmb/Gmm) × 100. With Gmb = 2.358 and Gmm = 2.470 the ratio is 0.95465, so Va = (1 − 0.95465) × 100 = 4.534 percent. This is slightly above the 4.0 percent design value, which says the mix at 5.0 percent binder is a little under-asphalted for that void target. Adding binder fills voids, so the second trial at 5.5 percent should show lower air voids, and part (d) uses this trend. Note that Gmm is measured on loose mix, so it automatically accounts for binder absorbed into the aggregate pores.

Answer: 4.53 %

(b)

VMA is the volume of voids between aggregate particles, including air voids and effective binder, as a percent of total volume. It is computed from the aggregate content: VMA = 100 − (Gmb × Ps)/Gsb, where Ps = 100 − Pb is the aggregate percentage by mass of the mix, here 95.0. Then VMA = 100 − (2.358 × 95.0)/2.640 = 100 − 224.01/2.640 = 100 − 84.85 = 15.15 percent. The bulk gravity Gsb is used for the aggregate because VMA treats absorbed binder as part of the aggregate volume, since the absorbed portion fills pores that are not void space between particles. VFA then follows as (VMA − Va)/VMA = (15.15 − 4.53)/15.15 = 70.1 percent.

Answer: 15.15 %

(c)

First find the effective specific gravity of the aggregate from the loose mix: Gse = Ps/(100/Gmm − Pb/Gb) = 95.0/(100/2.470 − 5.0/1.025) = 95.0/(40.486 − 4.878) = 95.0/35.608 = 2.668. Because Gse (2.668) is greater than Gsb (2.640), some binder has been absorbed. The absorbed binder as a percent of aggregate mass is Pba = 100 × (Gse − Gsb)/(Gse × Gsb) × Gb = 100 × 0.028/(2.668 × 2.640) × 1.025 = 0.407 percent. Effective binder is the total less the absorbed share of the mix: Pbe = Pb − Pba × Ps/100 = 5.0 − 0.407 × 0.95 = 5.0 − 0.387 = 4.614 percent. This is the binder that actually coats particles and governs film thickness and durability.

Answer: 4.61 %

(d)

At 5.5 percent binder, Va = (1 − 2.389/2.452) × 100 = (1 − 0.97431) × 100 = 2.569 percent. At 5.0 percent, Va = 4.534 percent from part (a). With linear variation, the slope is (2.569 − 4.534)/0.5 = −3.930 percentage points of air voids per one percent binder. To reach Va = 4.0 percent from 4.534 requires a decrease of 0.534, so the binder must increase by 0.534/3.930 = 0.136 percent above 5.0. The design binder content is therefore 5.0 + 0.136 = 5.136 percent, say 5.1 percent. The design must then be checked for VMA, VFA, stability and flow at that binder content, since meeting air voids alone does not make a mix acceptable.

Answer: 5.14 %

Problem 2 [A6-037] Superpave mix design and binder content

A Superpave 12.5 mm trial blend is being evaluated for a Highway 11 rehabilitation north of Orillia. The trial binder content is Pbi = 5.1 percent by total mix mass, the aggregate bulk gravity is Gsb = 2.690, the binder gravity is Gb = 1.030, and the loose mix has Gmm = 2.534. A 150 mm diameter gyratory specimen with dry mass 4875 g was compacted. The gyratory recorded heights of 124.0 mm at the initial number of gyrations (Ninitial = 8) and 114.0 mm at the design number (Ndesign = 100). After extrusion the specimen's measured bulk gravity, found by weighing in water, was Gmb = 2.405. The gyratory density estimates are made from the recorded heights using a water density of 1.000 g/cm³ and are then multiplied by the single correction factor C = (measured Gmb)/(estimated Gmb at Ndesign). The mix is designed for 4.0 percent air voids at Ndesign. The dust proportion (percent passing the 0.075 mm sieve, here 5.0 percent, divided by effective binder) must lie between 0.6 and 1.2.

  1. (a) Find the corrected percent of Gmm at Ninitial. [5]
  2. (b) Find the air void content, in percent, at Ndesign from the measured Gmb. [4]
  3. (c) Using the estimate Pb,est = Pbi − 0.40 (4.0 − Va), where Va is the air void content from part (b), find the estimated binder content, in percent, that should give 4.0 percent air voids. [5]
  4. (d) At the estimated binder content from part (c), and keeping the same effective gravity of the aggregate Gse found from the trial mix, find the dust proportion. [6]
(a)

The gyratory estimate of bulk gravity at any recorded height h is Gest = M/(π d² h/4), with M in grams, d and h in cm and a water density of 1.000 g/cm³. At Ndesign, volume = π × 15.0² × 11.40/4 = 2014.5 cm³, so Gest = 4875/2014.5 = 2.4199. The correction factor is C = 2.405/2.4199 = 0.99384. At Ninitial, volume = π × 15.0² × 12.40/4 = 2191.3 cm³, giving Gest = 2.2248, and the corrected value is 2.2248 × 0.99384 = 2.2110. Then %Gmm at Ninitial = 2.2110/2.534 × 100 = 87.26 percent. Compare this with the limit for the traffic category, commonly 89 percent or lower; here the mix is within the limit, indicating that it will not be too tender during early compaction.

Answer: 87.26 %

(b)

At Ndesign the corrected bulk gravity equals the measured value by definition of the correction factor, so Gmb = 2.405. Percent of Gmm = 2.405/2.534 × 100 = 94.91 percent, and air voids Va = 100 − 94.91 = 5.09 percent. The target is 96.0 percent of Gmm, or 4.0 percent air voids, so the trial mix has about 1.1 percentage points too many air voids (95 percent of Gmm instead of 96), so it is too open and needs more binder, not less. The measured gravity is used rather than the height-based estimate because weighing in water is more accurate than computing volume from a specimen height, which cannot account for surface texture. The correction factor transfers that accuracy to the other gyration levels.

Answer: 5.09 %

(c)

Substituting Pbi = 5.1 and Va = 5.09 into the estimate gives Pb,est = 5.1 − 0.40 × (4.0 − 5.09) = 5.1 + 0.40 × 1.09 = 5.1 + 0.436 = 5.536 percent. The sign is important: the specimen has too many voids (5.09 > 4.0), so the term (4.0 − Va) is negative and the binder must increase. The rule of thumb, that each one percent change in air voids needs about 0.4 percent change in binder, is a starting estimate for the next trial only. Superpave procedure requires that the mix be remade at the new binder content, and at several contents around it, and the volumetric properties are then checked directly rather than trusted from the estimate.

Answer: 5.54 %

(d)

First find Gse from the trial mix: Gse = (100 − Pb)/(100/Gmm − Pb/Gb) = 94.9/(100/2.534 − 5.1/1.030) = 94.9/(39.463 − 4.951) = 94.9/34.512 = 2.7498. Absorbed binder Pba = 100 × (Gse − Gsb)/(Gse × Gsb) × Gb = 100 × 0.0598/(2.7498 × 2.690) × 1.030 = 0.832 percent of aggregate mass. At Pb = 5.536, aggregate percentage Ps = 94.464, so Pbe = 5.536 − 0.832 × 0.94464 = 5.536 − 0.786 = 4.750 percent. Dust proportion = 5.0/4.750 = 1.053, inside the 0.6 to 1.2 range, so the extra binder does not push the mix out of the dust control. Had the ratio exceeded 1.2, the mix would likely be stiff and brittle.

Answer: 1.05

Problem 3 [A6-038] Flexible pavement design with ESALs and structural number

A new rural arterial near Peterborough, Ontario, is to be designed as a flexible pavement for 4.5 million 80 kN equivalent single axle loads (W18) over its design life. Use the 1993 AASHTO empirical equation in this form: log10 W18 = ZR S0 + 9.36 log10(SN + 1) − 0.20 + log10[ΔPSI/(4.2 − 1.5)]/[0.40 + 1094/(SN + 1)5.19] + 2.32 log10 MR − 8.07, where MR is the roadbed resilient modulus in psi. Design inputs: reliability 90 percent with ZR = −1.282, overall standard deviation S0 = 0.45, initial serviceability 4.2 and terminal serviceability 2.5, so ΔPSI = 1.7, and roadbed MR = 45 MPa (1 MPa = 145.038 psi). Layer coefficients per millimetre of thickness are 0.0165 for hot-mix asphalt, 0.0054 for granular base and 0.0039 for granular subbase, all with drainage coefficients of 1.0. SN = a1 D1 + a2 m2 D2 + a3 m3 D3. The asphalt is 150 mm thick and the granular base is 250 mm thick. Subbase is placed in 25 mm increments.

  1. (a) Find the required design structural number SN for the roadbed. [6]
  2. (b) Find the minimum thickness of granular subbase, in mm, needed to provide that SN. [5]
  3. (c) Round the subbase up to the next 25 mm and find the structural number actually provided. [4]
  4. (d) Find the number of ESALs that the as-built pavement could carry under the same design inputs. [5]
(a)

Convert the modulus: MR = 45 × 145.038 = 6527 psi, so 2.32 log10 MR = 2.32 × 3.8147 = 8.850. The fixed terms are ZR S0 = −1.282 × 0.45 = −0.577 and the constants −0.20 and −8.07, so the left side must equal log10(4.5 × 10⁶) = 6.6532. The unknown SN appears in two terms and cannot be isolated, so solve by trial and error. Try SN = 4.63: 9.36 log10(5.63) = 9.36 × 0.7505 = 7.025; the ΔPSI term is log10(1.7/2.7) = −0.2008, divided by 0.40 + 1094/5.635.19 = 0.40 + 1094/7 855 = 0.5393, giving −0.3723. Total = −0.577 + 7.025 − 0.20 − 0.372 + 8.850 − 8.07 = 6.656, matching 6.653 within rounding. So SN = 4.63.

Answer: 4.63

(b)

The SN contributions of the asphalt and base are: asphalt a1 D1 = 0.0165 × 150 = 2.475; granular base a2 m2 D2 = 0.0054 × 1.0 × 250 = 1.350. Their sum is 3.825. The shortfall to be made up by subbase is 4.627 − 3.825 = 0.802. With a3 m3 = 0.0039 × 1.0 = 0.0039 per mm, D3 = 0.802/0.0039 = 205.5 mm. Because this is the exact minimum, the real thickness will be rounded up, which also gives a small margin. The designer should also check that the base thickness and asphalt thickness are not less than minimum practical values, and that the subbase stays above the frost-susceptible depth where heave is a concern, though this question only asks for the structural thickness.

Answer: 205.5 mm

(c)

Subbase is placed in 25 mm increments, so the next multiple of 25 mm above 205.5 mm is 225 mm, since 200 mm would be too thin to meet the required SN. Subbase contribution is 0.0039 × 225 = 0.8775. Adding the asphalt (2.475) and base (1.350) gives SN provided = 2.475 + 1.350 + 0.8775 = 4.7025, say 4.70. This exceeds the required 4.627 by 0.076, so the pavement is slightly stronger than needed. Rounding up always favours safety here and costs only 19.5 mm of extra subbase. The alternative of using 200 mm subbase would give SN = 4.605, which is just short of the requirement, so the 225 mm thickness is the correct practical choice.

Answer: 4.70

(d)

Now the equation is used forward: with SN = 4.7025, 9.36 log10(5.7025) = 9.36 × 0.75610 = 7.0775. The denominator is 0.40 + 1094/5.70255.19 = 0.40 + 1094/8 394 = 0.5303 (5.70255.19 = exp(5.19 × 1.7410) = 8 394), so the serviceability term is −0.2008/0.5303 = −0.3787. Then log10 W18 = −0.577 + 7.0775 − 0.20 − 0.3787 + 8.850 − 8.07 = 6.7011 using 2.32 log10 MR = 8.850. Therefore W18 = 106.7011 = 5.02 × 10⁶, about 5.0 million ESALs. The extra 0.076 of SN therefore increases the life from 4.5 to about 5.0 million ESALs, about 12 percent more traffic, which shows how sensitive life is to structure.

Answer: 5.02 million

Problem 4 [A6-039] Traffic loading, growth factors and ESAL computation

Traffic data are needed for a pavement rehabilitation on a four-lane section of Highway 7 east of Lindsay, Ontario. The first-year two-way annual average daily traffic is 8200 vehicles. The directional split is 50 percent, and the design lane (the outside lane in each direction) carries 90 percent of the trucks in its direction. Passenger vehicles are taken to cause negligible damage. Trucks make up the following shares of the two-way AADT, with average load equivalency factors (80 kN ESALs per vehicle pass) in brackets: single-unit trucks 6.0 percent (0.31), five-axle tractor-trailers 4.5 percent (1.58) and B-trains 1.2 percent (2.35). Traffic volumes grow at a compound rate of 3.5 percent per year, and a year has 365 days. Assume the truck mix and the load equivalency factors do not change with time.

  1. (a) Find the first-year design-lane ESALs. [5]
  2. (b) Find the growth factor for a 20 year design period. [4]
  3. (c) Find the 20 year cumulative design-lane ESALs, in millions. [5]
  4. (d) Find the number of years, to one decimal place, after which the cumulative design-lane ESALs first reach 2.0 million. [6]
(a)

First find the average ESALs per vehicle in the two-way AADT by weighting the equivalency factors by their shares: 0.060 × 0.31 + 0.045 × 1.58 + 0.012 × 2.35 = 0.01860 + 0.07110 + 0.02820 = 0.11790 ESAL per vehicle. Each day, the design direction carries AADT × 0.50 = 4100 vehicles and the design lane carries 90 percent of the damage, so daily design-lane ESALs = 8200 × 0.50 × 0.90 × 0.1179 = 435.1. Multiplying by 365 days gives 158 794 ESALs in the first year. The directional and lane factors apply because pavement damage is accumulated only by the vehicles in the lane being designed, not by all lanes together. Passenger cars are ignored because their load equivalency is of the order of 0.0004, which is negligible.

Answer: 158 794 ESALs

(b)

The growth factor for compound growth at rate r over n years is GF = [(1 + r)ⁿ − 1]/r. With r = 0.035 and n = 20, (1.035)²⁰ = exp(20 × ln 1.035) = exp(20 × 0.034401) = exp(0.68802) = 1.98979. Then GF = (1.98979 − 1)/0.035 = 0.98979/0.035 = 28.28. This factor converts the first-year ESALs into a total over 20 years when traffic increases each year by 3.5 percent. A zero growth rate would give GF = 20 exactly, so the 3.5 percent growth raises the total by about 41 percent. The formula assumes growth occurs at the same percentage rate every year, and it sums the geometric series of yearly ESAL values from year 1 to year 20, with the first year undiscounted.

Answer: 28.28

(c)

Cumulative design ESALs equal the first-year design-lane ESALs multiplied by the growth factor: W18 = 158 794 × 28.28 = 4.49 × 10⁶, or 4.49 million ESALs. This is the traffic that the pavement structure must carry, and it is the quantity entered into the AASHTO structural design equation. Note the sensitivity of the result to the truck factor: the five-axle tractor-trailers contribute 0.0711 of the 0.1179 ESAL per vehicle, about 60 percent of the damage although they are only 4.5 percent of the traffic. If their share were measured wrongly by a count error of 1 percentage point, the design ESALs would shift by more than half a million, which is why a classification count is worth commissioning.

Answer: 4.49 million

(d)

Cumulative ESALs after n years are W(n) = E₁ × [(1 + r)ⁿ − 1]/r, with E₁ = 158 794 and r = 0.035. Setting W = 2.0 × 10⁶ gives [(1.035)ⁿ − 1]/0.035 = 2 000 000/158 794 = 12.594. Then (1.035)ⁿ = 1 + 0.035 × 12.594 = 1.4408. Taking logarithms, n = ln 1.4408/ln 1.035 = 0.36520/0.034401 = 10.62 years. So the pavement reaches 2.0 million ESALs after about 10.6 years, a little more than half of the 20 year period, because the early years carry less traffic than the later ones. This is useful where a staged design is considered, with a thin overlay placed at the 10 year point to carry the remaining traffic.

Answer: 10.6 years

Problem 5 [A6-040] Subgrade support, CBR and resilient modulus

A new collector road near Kitchener, Ontario, will be built on a silty clay subgrade. A soaked laboratory CBR test on the compacted subgrade soil gave a penetration load of 0.62 kN at 2.5 mm and 0.86 kN at 5.0 mm. The standard crushed-stone loads are 13.2 kN at 2.5 mm and 19.8 kN at 5.0 mm. The designer estimates the summer resilient modulus from CBR by MR (MPa) = 10.3 × CBR. The other seasonal moduli are 150 MPa for winter (frozen), 28 MPa for spring thaw and 40 MPa for fall. The year is divided into four equal seasons. For the effective roadbed modulus, use the relative damage relation uf = 1.18 × 10⁸ MR−2.32, where MR is in psi (1 MPa = 145.038 psi); the effective modulus is the one whose damage equals the average of the four seasonal damages. The owner wants to improve the thaw-season support by lime treatment so that the effective roadbed modulus reaches 45 MPa.

  1. (a) Find the design CBR value, in percent, taking the larger of the values at the two penetrations. [4]
  2. (b) Find the summer resilient modulus, in MPa. [4]
  3. (c) Find the present effective roadbed resilient modulus, in MPa, from the four seasonal values. [6]
  4. (d) With winter, summer and fall values unchanged, find the spring thaw modulus, in MPa, that lime treatment must provide to reach an effective modulus of 45 MPa. [6]
(a)

CBR is the ratio of the test load at a given penetration to the standard load at the same penetration, times 100. At 2.5 mm: CBR = 0.62/13.2 × 100 = 4.70 percent. At 5.0 mm: CBR = 0.86/19.8 × 100 = 4.34 percent. Because the 2.5 mm value is the larger one, it governs the design value, so CBR = 4.70 percent. If the 5.0 mm value had been the larger, the test would normally be repeated to confirm it, since a higher value at 5.0 mm suggests surface disturbance of the sample. Here the result is consistent with a soft silty clay, which is typical for the area and is poor support, so the improvement the owner is asking about is realistic.

Answer: 4.70 %

(b)

The relation given in the question is MR (MPa) = 10.3 × CBR. With CBR = 4.70, MR = 10.3 × 4.697 = 48.4 MPa, using the unrounded CBR of 4.697 percent. This is the summer value, taken as the representative modulus for the soaked, unfrozen soil. Such correlations are approximate and are usually considered valid only for fine-grained soils with CBR up to about 10 percent, which is true here. In practice the designer would confirm with a resilient modulus test or a falling weight deflectometer survey on the existing ground, because a CBR correlation can be wrong by a factor of two either way for an individual soil.

Answer: 48.4 MPa

(c)

Convert each seasonal modulus to psi and compute uf = 1.18 × 10⁸ MR−2.32. Winter: 150 MPa = 21 756 psi, uf = 0.0102. Spring: 28 MPa = 4061 psi, uf = 0.5010. Summer: 48.4 MPa = 7017 psi, uf = 0.1409. Fall: 40 MPa = 5802 psi, uf = 0.2190. The average damage is (0.0102 + 0.5010 + 0.1409 + 0.2190)/4 = 0.8711/4 = 0.2178. The effective modulus is the MR whose damage equals this average: MR = (0.2178/1.18 × 10⁸)−1/2.32 = 5815 psi = 40.1 MPa. The result is far below the simple average of the four moduli, about 66.6 MPa, because the weak spring season does the most damage and dominates the average. That is exactly what the damage weighting is meant to reveal.

Answer: 40.1 MPa

(d)
