Borrow dug from the pit swells 25 percent as it is loosened, so the loose volume to be carried is 162.3 × 1.25 = 202.8 m³. Dividing by the truck capacity of 12 m³ gives 202.8/12 = 16.9 loads, and a whole number of loads is required, so 17 truck loads are needed. Rounding up is needed because 16 loads would carry only 192 m³, leaving the section short. In a real contract the trucking is paid by the compacted or bank volume, not by loads, and the contractor allows the swell factor in the haul cost.

Answer: 17 loads

Problem 3 [A6-078] Embankment, borrow, shrinkage, swell and compaction

A 800 m long approach embankment for a new interchange near Barrie has a crest width of 12 m, a height of 6.5 m and side slopes of 2 horizontal to 1 vertical on both sides. The contract specifies compaction to 95 percent of the standard Proctor maximum dry density of 1.95 t/m³, at a moisture content of 12 percent. Borrow sand and silt in the pit has an in-place dry density of 1.68 t/m³ and a natural moisture content of 9 percent. The material swells 22 percent when excavated and loaded. Scrapers carry 14 m³ loose per load. Water is added at the fill site, and one cubic metre of water has a mass of 1 t. Assume the fill is compacted dry density exactly equal to the specified minimum.

  1. (a) Compute the compacted volume of the embankment. [3]
  2. (b) Compute the minimum dry density the fill must reach. [3]
  3. (c) Compute the bank volume of borrow needed. [5]
  4. (d) Compute the volume of water to be added to bring borrow from 9 to 12 percent moisture. [5]
  5. (e) Compute the number of scraper loads needed. [4]
(a)

The embankment cross-section is a trapezoid with top width 12 m, height 6.5 m and slope 2:1 each side, so the base width is 12 + 2 × (2 × 6.5) = 38 m. The area is (12 + 38)/2 × 6.5 = 25 × 6.5 = 162.5 m². Multiplying by the length of 800 m gives V = 162.5 × 800 = 130 000 m³ of compacted fill. The same result follows from the formula A = h (b + z h) = 6.5 × (12 + 13) = 162.5 m². This is the compacted volume, the quantity the contractor must place and the figure against which the owner measures compaction, not the quantity excavated from the borrow pit.

Answer: 130 000 m³

(b)

Compaction is specified as a percent of the standard Proctor maximum dry density, so the minimum dry density the fill must reach is 0.95 × 1.95 = 1.8525 t/m³. The specification is on dry density because water content changes with weather and handling, while the dry mass of soil solids in a given volume is the property that determines strength and settlement. The fill dry density is also the figure needed to convert between volumes, since a given dry mass of soil occupies a different volume in the borrow pit than in the compacted embankment.

Answer: 1.85 t/m³

(c)

The dry mass of soil needed in the embankment is 130 000 × 1.8525 = 240 825 t. The same dry mass must come from the pit, where each bank cubic metre holds 1.68 t of dry soil. The bank volume is therefore 240 825/1.68 = 143 348 m³. Equivalently V_bank = V_fill × (γd,fill/γd,bank) = 130 000 × 1.8525/1.68. The ratio exceeds 1, so the pit volume is larger than the fill volume: the borrow compacts into a smaller volume, which is shrinkage of about 9.3 percent when measured on the bank volume.

Answer: 143 350 m³

(d)

Water is added to dry soil mass to raise moisture from 9 to 12 percent, a change of 3 percentage points of the dry mass. The water mass is 0.03 × 240 825 = 7 224.8 t. At 1 t per cubic metre this is 7 225 m³ of water. This can be delivered by water trucks of say 10 m³ each, which is about 722 loads. Moisture control matters because compaction at a moisture content well off optimum gives low density or leaves a pumping, unstable layer. The contractor adds water in the pit or on the fill using a spray bar and mixes by blading.

Answer: 7 225 m³

(e)

Loose volume is the bank volume increased by the 22 percent swell: 143 348 × 1.22 = 174 885 m³. Dividing by the scraper capacity of 14 m³ loose gives 174 885/14 = 12 492 loads. This number is of use for estimating hours, cycle time and cost. Swell is applied once to the bank volume, not to the compacted volume, because the loosened material is carried from the pit and the bank volume is what is excavated. A mistake would be to start from the compacted 130 000 m³ and apply swell, which would understate the loads by about 9 percent.

Answer: 12 492 loads

Problem 4 [A6-079] Roadway drainage: ditches, culverts and subdrains

A rural road in Grey County crosses a small stream. The tributary area upstream of the crossing is 18 ha of pasture and woodlot with a rational runoff coefficient of 0.35 and a time of concentration of 22 min. The design storm intensity is given by i = 1 000/(t + 7)0.82 in mm/h, with t in minutes. The road's cross-culvert is a corrugated steel pipe with Manning n = 0.024 on a slope of 1.2 percent, and it is designed to flow just full at the design flow, treating inlet control as not governing. The road ditch carrying the water to the inlet is trapezoidal with a bottom width of 0.60 m, side slopes of 3 horizontal to 1 vertical, a longitudinal slope of 2.0 percent, n = 0.030 and flow depth of 0.50 m. Standard culvert diameters available are 600, 750, 900 and 1 050 mm.

  1. (a) Compute the design rainfall intensity. [3]
  2. (b) Compute the design peak flow using the rational method. [3]
  3. (c) Compute the exact circular diameter that flows exactly full at this discharge. [5]
  4. (d) Compute the flow capacity of the ditch at the 0.50 m depth. [5]
  5. (e) Compute the full-flow capacity of the 900 mm standard culvert and state whether it is adequate. [4]
(a)

Substitute t = tc = 22 min into the given intensity relation: i = 1 000/(22 + 7)0.82 = 1 000/290.82. Since ln 29 = 3.3673, 0.82 × 3.3673 = 2.7612 and e2.7612 = 15.82, so i = 1 000/15.82 = 63.2 mm/h. The design duration is set equal to the time of concentration because that duration maximises the intensity that the whole catchment contributes at once. A shorter storm would be more intense but would not cover the whole area at the outlet. A longer storm would give lower intensity and a lower peak flow.

Answer: 63.2 mm/h

(b)

The rational method with metric units is Q = C i A/360, where Q is in m³/s, i in mm/h and A in hectares. Q = 0.35 × 63.22 × 18/360 = 398.3/360 = 1.106 m³/s. The method assumes uniform rainfall over the watershed, a constant runoff coefficient and that peak flow occurs when the entire area contributes. It is acceptable for small rural catchments of this size, say up to a few hundred hectares, and the coefficient of 0.35 reflects the permeable soil and vegetation. For an urban catchment the same equation would give a far larger flow for the same intensity.

Answer: 1.11 m³/s

(c)

For a circular pipe flowing full, A = πD²/4 and R = D/4, so Manning gives Q = (1/n)(πD²/4)(D/4)2/3 S0.5. Solving for D gives D8/3 = Q n 45/3/(π S0.5). With Q = 1.106, n = 0.024, 45/3 = 10.079 and S0.5 = 0.10954: numerator 1.106 × 0.024 × 10.079 = 0.2675, denominator π × 0.10954 = 0.3441, ratio 0.7775. Then D = 0.77753/8 = e0.375 × ln 0.7775 = e0.375 × −0.2515 = e−0.0943 = 0.910 m. Hence a minimum diameter of 910 mm is required.

Answer: 0.910 m

(d)

For the trapezoid, flow area A = y (b + z y) = 0.50 × (0.60 + 3 × 0.50) = 0.50 × 2.10 = 1.05 m². The wetted perimeter is P = b + 2 y √(1 + z²) = 0.60 + 2 × 0.50 × √10 = 0.60 + 3.162 = 3.762 m, so R = 1.05/3.762 = 0.2791 m. Manning: Q = (1/0.030) × 1.05 × 0.27912/3 × 0.020.5 = 33.33 × 1.05 × 0.4271 × 0.14142 = 2.114 m³/s. The ditch can therefore deliver more flow than the culvert is designed for, so the ditch is not the limiting element and the culvert inlet will control the water level upstream.

Answer: 2.11 m³/s

(e)

For the 900 mm pipe flowing full: A = π × 0.9²/4 = 0.6362 m² and R = 0.9/4 = 0.225 m, so V = (1/0.024) × 0.2252/3 × 0.0120.5 = 41.67 × 0.3698 × 0.10954 = 1.688 m/s. Then Q = V A = 1.688 × 0.6362 = 1.075 m³/s. That is less than the design flow of 1.106 m³/s by about 3 percent, so the 900 mm pipe is slightly inadequate for the full-flow condition, and the next standard size of 1 050 mm should be selected. A 900 mm pipe could be accepted only with a hydraulic analysis showing the headwater is acceptable.

Answer: 1.07 m³/s

Problem 5 [A6-080] Aggregate properties: gradation and specific gravity

A contractor in Ontario is preparing an asphalt concrete surface mix from two stockpiles. The coarse stockpile has 12 percent passing the 4.75 mm sieve and the fine stockpile has 96 percent passing it. The target blend has 55 percent passing 4.75 mm. Coarse aggregate has a bulk specific gravity of 2.690 and absorption of 0.8 percent, and the fine aggregate 2.640 and 1.4 percent. Laboratory testing of the loose mix at 5.2 percent asphalt by total mass of mix gave a maximum theoretical specific gravity Gmm of 2.485, and asphalt binder has specific gravity 1.030. Express stockpile proportions as percentages of the total dry aggregate mass, and use the standard volumetric relations for the effective specific gravity of the aggregate and the absorbed binder.

  1. (a) Compute the proportion of coarse stockpile in the blend, as a percentage of dry aggregate mass. [4]
  2. (b) Compute the bulk specific gravity of the combined aggregate. [4]
  3. (c) Compute the water absorption of the blend, in percent. [3]
  4. (d) Compute the effective specific gravity of the aggregate from Gmm. [4]
  5. (e) Compute the asphalt absorbed into the aggregate, as a percentage of dry aggregate mass. [5]
(a)

Let x be the fraction of coarse aggregate. The percent passing the 4.75 mm sieve is the weighted average: 12 x + 96 (1 − x) = 55. Rearranging gives 96 − 84 x = 55, so x = 41/84 = 0.4881. The blend is therefore 48.8 percent coarse and 51.2 percent fine by dry mass. This is a mixing rule for any single sieve: the sieve passing of a blend is the mass-weighted mean of the stockpile passings. The same proportions would be checked on every other sieve of the gradation band, and the full blend must lie inside the specification limits at all sieves, not just at 4.75 mm.

Answer: 48.8 percent

(b)

The bulk specific gravity of a blend is found from volumes, not masses: Gsb = 100/(P1/G1 + P2/G2), where P are percentages by mass. With P1 = 48.81 and G1 = 2.690, P1/G1 = 18.145. With P2 = 51.19 and G2 = 2.640, P2/G2 = 19.390. The sum is 37.535, so Gsb = 100/37.535 = 2.664. A weighted average of specific gravities would give 2.664 only by chance, and is wrong in principle, since the volume occupied per unit mass is what adds. The dry bulk specific gravity includes the volume of the pores permeable to water.

Answer: 2.664

(c)

Absorption is a mass ratio, so the blend absorption is the mass-weighted average of the stockpile absorptions: Ab = (48.81 × 0.8 + 51.19 × 1.4)/100 = (39.05 + 71.67)/100 = 1.107 percent. The value is the water that the dry aggregate soaks up through its permeable pores, as a percentage of dry mass. It is useful when comparing with binder absorption, which is usually lower than water absorption because the viscous binder cannot enter the finest pores. A high absorption blend needs more binder to coat the surface.

Answer: 1.11 percent

(d)

The effective specific gravity is found from the loose mix: Gse = (100 − Pb)/(100/Gmm − Pb/Gb), with Pb = 5.2 percent. Evaluating: 100/2.485 = 40.241 and 5.2/1.030 = 5.049, so the denominator is 35.192. The numerator is 94.8. Therefore Gse = 94.8/35.192 = 2.694. It lies between bulk Gsb (2.664) and the apparent specific gravity, as expected, since the effective volume includes the surface voids but excludes the pores filled with absorbed binder. The mix test itself fixes Gse, so the same mix design can use any binder content once Gse is known.

Answer: 2.694

(e)

The absorbed binder is Pba = 100 × (Gse − Gsb)/(Gse × Gsb) × Gb. Gse − Gsb = 2.6937 − 2.6642 = 0.0295. The product Gse × Gsb = 7.1769. So the ratio is 0.0295/7.1769 = 0.004110, multiplied by 100 and by Gb = 1.030 gives Pba = 0.424 percent of dry aggregate mass. This is the binder lost into pores and is not available to bond the particles. Only the remaining effective binder content counts toward the film thickness and durability, so a mix with high absorption must be given extra binder.

Answer: 0.424 percent

A6 Practice Paper 17

Problem 1 [A6-081] Asphalt cement properties and performance grading

A new two-lane collector near Barrie, Ontario (latitude 44.0 degrees north) will be paved with hot-mix asphalt. Climate records give a 7-day average maximum air temperature of 34.0 °C and a 1-day minimum air temperature of -31.0 °C. Use these design relations. Maximum pavement temperature at 20 mm depth: T20 = 0.9545 (Tair - 0.00618 φ² + 0.2289 φ + 42.2) - 17.78, with φ the latitude in degrees. Minimum pavement surface temperature: Tmin = 0.859 Tair + 1.7. Binder grades come in 6 °C steps for both the high and low number. A candidate binder has penetration 62 (0.1 mm units at 25 °C) and a ring-and-ball softening point of 49.5 °C. Its rotational viscosity is 480 mPa·s at 135 °C and 95 mPa·s at 165 °C. The mixing plant targets a binder viscosity of 170 mPa·s.

  1. (a) Find the design high pavement temperature and state the high-temperature grade number. [4]
  2. (b) Find the design low pavement temperature and state the low-temperature grade number. [4]
  3. (c) Compute the penetration index using A = (log 800 - log pen)/(SP - 25) and PI = 20(1 - 25A)/(1 + 50A). [5]
  4. (d) The viscosity-temperature relation is log log (η + 0.8) = A' - B log T with η in mPa·s and T in kelvin. Fit A' and B to the two measurements and find the mixing temperature for 170 mPa·s. [7]
(a)

Substitute φ = 44.0 and Tair = 34.0 into the relation. The bracket is 34.0 - 0.00618 × 44.0² + 0.2289 × 44.0 + 42.2 = 34.0 - 11.96 + 10.07 + 42.2 = 74.31 °C. Multiplying by 0.9545 gives 70.93 °C, and subtracting 17.78 gives T20 = 53.15 °C. The binder must resist rutting at this temperature, so we round up to the next 6 °C step available. Grades run 46, 52, 58, 64, so 53.15 °C needs a high-temperature grade of 58. Rounding down to 52 would leave the binder softer than the design pavement temperature and invite rutting in slow truck lanes.

Answer: 53.1 °C, so PG 58

(b)

Apply Tmin = 0.859 × (-31.0) + 1.7. The product is -26.63, and adding 1.7 gives -24.93 °C. The pavement surface stays a little warmer than the air in a cold snap, which is why the pavement value is less severe than -31. Low-temperature grades come in steps of 6 °C: -16, -22, -28, -34. The binder must stay flexible at or below -24.93 °C, so we round to the colder grade, -28. The grade is therefore PG 58-28. Choosing -22 would leave thermal cracking risk because the binder would stiffen before the pavement reaches its coldest design temperature.

Answer: -24.9 °C, so PG xx-28

(c)

Compute A = (log 800 - log 62)/(49.5 - 25). Here log 800 = 2.9031 and log 62 = 1.7924, so the numerator is 1.1107. Dividing by 24.5 gives A = 0.04534. Then 25A = 1.1334 and 50A = 2.2667. PI = 20(1 - 1.1334)/(1 + 2.2667) = 20(-0.1334)/3.2667 = -0.82. Values near zero describe a typical road bitumen. A PI between -2 and +2 is normal, so this binder is a conventional straight-run asphalt, moderately temperature susceptible, not a highly blown or polymer-modified grade. A value below -2 would signal brittleness at low temperature.

Answer: PI = -0.82

(d)

Convert each viscosity: η + 0.8 is 480.8 and 95.8. log of these is 2.6820 and 1.9814, and log of those is 0.42843 and 0.29697. Temperatures are 408.15 K and 438.15 K, with logs 2.61083 and 2.64160. B = (0.42843 - 0.29697)/(2.64160 - 2.61083) = 4.27 and A' = 0.42843 + 4.27 × 2.61083 = 11.57. For 170 mPa·s: log(170.8) = 2.2325 and its log is 0.34876. Then log T = (11.57 - 0.34876)/4.27 = 2.6295, so T = 426 K = 152.9 °C. Mixing at about 153 °C keeps the binder fluid enough to coat aggregate without oxidising it.

Answer: about 153 °C

Problem 2 [A6-082] Marshall mix design and volumetrics

A Marshall mix design for a surface course on a regional road uses dense-graded limestone aggregate and a binder of specific gravity 1.030. A trial mix has 5.2 percent binder by total mass of mix. Laboratory results are: bulk specific gravity of compacted specimens Gmb = 2.352, theoretical maximum specific gravity of the loose mix Gmm = 2.455, and bulk specific gravity of the aggregate blend Gsb = 2.640. The agency requires air voids from 3.0 to 5.0 percent, VMA of at least 14.0 percent, and VFA from 65 to 75 percent. Use the usual relations: Va = 100 (1 - Gmb/Gmm); VMA = 100 - Gmb Ps / Gsb with Ps the aggregate percentage by mix mass; VFA = 100 (VMA - Va)/VMA; Gse = Ps / (100/Gmm - Pb/Gb); Pba = 100 (Gse - Gsb) Gb /(Gsb Gse); Pbe = Pb - Pba Ps/100.

  1. (a) Compute the air voids Va of the compacted mix. [4]
  2. (b) Compute the voids in mineral aggregate, VMA. [4]
  3. (c) Compute the voids filled with asphalt, VFA, and check all three volumetric limits. [3]
  4. (d) Compute the effective specific gravity of the aggregate, Gse. [3]
  5. (e) Compute the absorbed binder Pba and the effective binder content Pbe, and report Pbe. [6]
(a)

The relation is Va = 100 (1 - Gmb/Gmm). Gmb/Gmm = 2.352/2.455 = 0.95805. Then Va = 100 × (1 - 0.95805) = 4.20 percent. The limit is 3.0 to 5.0 percent, so the mix is inside the target. The air voids figure matters because it sets the room the binder has to expand into at summer pavement temperatures. Too few voids leads to bleeding and rutting, too many lets air and water reach the binder and speeds oxidation. A reading of 4.2 percent is close to the common 4 percent design target, so no immediate binder change is needed.

Answer: Va = 4.20 %

(b)

First Ps = 100 - 5.2 = 94.8 percent. Then the volume of aggregate per 100 volumes of mix is Gmb Ps / Gsb = 2.352 × 94.8 / 2.640 = 84.46. So VMA = 100 - 84.46 = 15.54 percent. VMA is the space between aggregate particles, including both air and effective binder, and it is computed from the bulk gravity of the aggregate because absorbed binder is not part of the space between particles. The agency minimum is 14.0 percent, so the mix passes with a margin of 1.5 points. A thin film of binder around the particles depends on enough VMA being available.

Answer: VMA = 15.5 %

(c)

VFA = 100 (VMA - Va)/VMA = 100 × (15.54 - 4.20)/15.54 = 100 × 11.34/15.54 = 73.0 percent. Checking the limits: Va 4.20 percent lies in 3.0 to 5.0, VMA 15.54 is above 14.0, and VFA 73.0 lies in the 65 to 75 band. All three requirements are met. The VFA is near the upper end of its band, so any extra binder would push it over 75 and raise rutting risk in hot weather. This is why designers watch VFA together with Va when adjusting binder content rather than adjusting either one in isolation.

Answer: VFA = 73.0 %, all limits met

(d)

Gse = Ps / (100/Gmm - Pb/Gb). Compute 100/2.455 = 40.733 and Pb/Gb = 5.2/1.030 = 5.049. The difference is 35.685. Then Gse = 94.8 / 35.685 = 2.657. This is the specific gravity of the aggregate when only the water-permeable voids filled by binder are excluded. It lies between the bulk value 2.640 and the apparent value, as it should, which is a useful check: if Gse were smaller than Gsb, the data would contain an error, since an aggregate cannot absorb negative binder. Here 2.657 is larger than 2.640, so the data are consistent.

Answer: Gse = 2.657

(e)

Pba = 100 (Gse - Gsb) Gb / (Gsb Gse) = 100 × (2.6566 - 2.640) × 1.030 / (2.640 × 2.6566) = 100 × 0.01660 × 1.030 / 7.013 = 0.244 percent of aggregate mass. Then Pbe = Pb - Pba Ps/100 = 5.2 - 0.244 × 0.948 = 5.2 - 0.231 = 4.97 percent. The effective binder is the part that coats particles and acts as the working film, so a slightly smaller value than the 5.2 percent total is expected. Because the aggregate absorbs little, the loss is small. The effective binder content, not the total, is what controls durability and the dust proportion check.

Answer: Pbe = 4.97 %

Problem 3 [A6-083] Superpave mix design and binder content

A Superpave design for a 12.5 mm surface mix on a county road is being refined. The trial blend has 4.8 percent binder by total mix mass. For the design gyration level Ndes the compacted specimens have bulk specific gravity Gmb = 2.381 and the loose mix has maximum specific gravity Gmm = 2.489. At Ndes the specimen height is 115.0 mm and at the initial gyration level Nini it is 127.2 mm; assume the mass and mould diameter do not change, so Gmb varies inversely with height. The agency limit is no more than 89.0 percent of Gmm at Nini. The aggregate blend has Gsb = 2.650, effective specific gravity Gse = 2.682, binder specific gravity 1.025, and 5.1 percent of the aggregate mass passing the 0.075 mm sieve. The estimated binder for 4.0 percent air voids is Pb,est = Pb,trial - 0.4 (4.0 - Va). Use Pba and Pbe relations from Marshall practice and dust proportion DP = P0.075/Pbe.

  1. (a) Compute the air voids of the trial blend at Ndes. [4]
  2. (b) Estimate the binder content that should give 4.0 percent air voids. [4]
  3. (c) Compute the percent of Gmm at Nini and compare with the limit. [4]
  4. (d) Compute the effective binder content at the estimated binder content. [4]
  5. (e) Compute the dust proportion. [4]
(a)

Va = 100 (1 - Gmb/Gmm) = 100 × (1 - 2.381/2.489). The ratio is 0.95661, so Va = 4.34 percent. The target is 4.0 percent, so the trial mix is slightly under-asphalted, because fewer binder-filled voids leave more air in the compacted mix. A mix with more air than the target will usually have low film thickness and poor durability. The result tells us the next trial should contain a little more binder, which part (b) quantifies. The difference of 0.34 percent is small but meaningful in a mix that is supposed to hold 4.0 percent exactly under design compaction.

Answer: Va = 4.34 %

(b)

Pb,est = Pb,trial - 0.4 (4.0 - Va) = 4.8 - 0.4 × (4.0 - 4.339) = 4.8 - 0.4 × (-0.339) = 4.8 + 0.136 = 4.94 percent. The negative term in brackets reflects air voids above target, which require more binder to fill. The coefficient 0.4 is an empirical rule that each 1 percent change in air voids needs roughly 0.4 percent change in binder. The estimate is a starting point, not a final answer: new specimens would be made at this binder content and tested, because aggregate absorption and compaction response shift slightly with binder.

Answer: Pb,est = 4.94 %

(c)

Gmb at Nini = Gmb at Ndes × hdes / hini = 2.381 × 115.0 / 127.2 = 2.153. Then %Gmm = 100 × 2.153 / 2.489 = 86.5 percent. The limit is 89.0 percent, so the mix passes the Nini check. This check guards against tender mixes: a mix that densifies too quickly in the first gyrations may shove under rollers or rut under early traffic. A value of 86.5 percent shows the aggregate skeleton is still carrying the load at low compaction effort, which is the behaviour wanted. Because 86.5 is a full 2.5 points below the limit, a modest adjustment of binder will not change the verdict.

Answer: 86.5 %, below 89.0 %

(d)

Use Pb = 4.936 percent so Ps = 95.064 percent. Pba = 100 (Gse - Gsb) Gb / (Gsb Gse) = 100 × 0.032 × 1.025 / (2.650 × 2.682) = 3.28 / 7.107 = 0.461 percent of aggregate mass. Then Pbe = Pb - Pba Ps / 100 = 4.936 - 0.461 × 0.95064 = 4.936 - 0.439 = 4.50 percent. The aggregate absorbs about 0.46 percent of its own mass in binder, a modest amount, so the effective binder is only 0.44 percent less than the total. Effective binder, not total, governs the dust proportion that follows.

Answer: Pbe = 4.50 %

(e)

DP = P0.075 / Pbe = 5.1 / 4.497 = 1.13. Superpave practice allows dust proportion in a band of roughly 0.6 to 1.2, so the mix is acceptable, though near the upper edge. A high DP means too much filler for the binder, which stiffens the mortar, makes the mix harsh and hard to compact, and can lead to cracking. A low DP leaves the mix tender and prone to rutting. If the plant produced extra baghouse fines, DP would rise above 1.2, and the designer would need to cut fines or raise binder. At 1.13 the gradation is acceptable and the binder is adequate.

Answer: DP = 1.13

Problem 4 [A6-084] Flexible pavement design with ESALs and structural number

A new arterial in Waterloo Region carries 6000 vehicles per day (AADT, both directions) in the opening year, of which 8 percent are trucks averaging 1.15 ESALs per truck. Half of the traffic is in each direction and the design lane carries 90 percent of the directional trucks. Traffic grows at 3 percent per year, compounded, over a 20-year design life. Use the AASHTO 1993 flexible pavement equation: log W18 = ZR S0 + 9.36 log(SN + 1) - 0.20 + log[ΔPSI/(4.2 - 1.5)]/[0.40 + 1094/(SN + 1)5.19] + 2.32 log MR - 8.07, with MR in psi (1 MPa = 145.04 psi). Take reliability 90 percent (ZR = -1.282), S0 = 0.45, ΔPSI = 2.0, and subgrade MR = 50 MPa. Layer coefficients per inch: asphalt 0.42, granular base 0.14 (drainage coefficient 1.0), granular subbase 0.11 (drainage coefficient 0.9). SN = a1 D1 + a2 m2 D2 + a3 m3 D3 with D in inches (25.4 mm per inch). The asphalt is 125 mm and the base is 200 mm.

  1. (a) Compute the 20-year design ESALs in the design lane (W18). [4]
  2. (b) Find the required structural number SN. [5]
  3. (c) Find the subbase thickness required, in millimetres. [5]
  4. (d) The subbase is built 200 mm thick (rounded up to 25 mm). Compute the number of ESALs the as-built structure can carry. [6]
(a)

Growth factor GF = ((1 + r)n - 1)/r = (1.0320 - 1)/0.03 = (1.8061 - 1)/0.03 = 26.87. First-year design-lane ESALs = AADT × 0.08 trucks × 0.5 direction × 0.90 lane × 1.15 ESAL per truck × 365 days. Compute 6000 × 0.08 = 480 trucks per day, × 0.5 = 240, × 0.9 = 216, × 1.15 = 248.4 ESALs per day, × 365 = 90 666 per year. Multiplying by 26.87 gives W18 = 2.436 million. The growth factor accounts for yearly traffic increases, so the later years carry more than the first year. The calculation assumes the truck factor is constant over the design life.

Answer: 2.44 million ESALs

(b)

Take MR = 50 × 145.04 = 7252 psi, so 2.32 log MR = 2.32 × 3.8604 = 8.956. log W18 = log 2 436 229 = 6.3867. ZR S0 = -1.282 × 0.45 = -0.577. Solve the equation for SN by trial: at SN = 3.909 the terms are 9.36 log 4.909 = 6.468; -0.20; log(2.0/2.7) = -0.1303 divided by (0.40 + 1094/4.9095.19 = 0.40 + 0.284 = 0.684) = -0.191; so the sum is -0.577 + 6.468 - 0.20 - 0.191 + 8.956 - 8.07 = 6.386, matching the required 6.387. Hence SN = 3.91. A smaller SN gives a lower log W18, so this is the minimum that carries 2.44 million ESALs.

Answer: SN = 3.91

(c)

Convert thicknesses: D1 = 125/25.4 = 4.921 in and D2 = 200/25.4 = 7.874 in. The asphalt contributes 0.42 × 4.921 = 2.067. The base contributes 0.14 × 1.0 × 7.874 = 1.102. Together 3.169. The subbase must supply 3.909 - 3.169 = 0.740. With a3 m3 = 0.11 × 0.9 = 0.099 per inch, D3 = 0.740/0.099 = 7.48 in = 189.9 mm. This is the thickness that meets the requirement exactly; practical construction rounds up to a convenient layer thickness, which part (d) uses. The drainage coefficient below 1.0 on the subbase makes it work harder, so more thickness is needed than with perfect drainage.

Answer: about 190 mm

(d)

As built, D3 = 200 mm = 7.874 in, so the subbase supplies 0.099 × 7.874 = 0.779. SN = 2.067 + 1.102 + 0.779 = 3.949. Put this into the equation: 9.36 log 4.949 = 6.501; ΔPSI term = -0.1303/(0.40 + 1094/4.9495.19 = 0.40 + 0.272 = 0.672) = -0.194. The sum is -0.577 + 6.501 - 0.20 - 0.194 + 8.956 - 8.07 = 6.416, so W18 = 106.416 = 2.61 million ESALs. The extra 10 mm of subbase raises capacity by about 7 percent, a modest safety margin above the design traffic of 2.44 million.

Answer: 2.61 million ESALs

Problem 5 [A6-085] Traffic loading, growth factors and ESAL computation

A rural highway truck survey on Highway 11 north of Huntsville found two truck classes in the design lane direction totals. In the opening year there are 420 two-axle single-unit trucks per day and 310 five-axle tractor-trailers per day, counted in both directions. Axle loads: the single-unit truck has a 25 kN front axle and a 70 kN rear single axle; the tractor-trailer has a 50 kN steering axle, a 150 kN drive tandem and a 140 kN trailer tandem. Use a fourth-power law: a single axle has load equivalency (P/80)4 and a tandem axle group has (P/150)4, with P the axle or group load in kN. Take 365 operating days, a directional split of 0.50, a design-lane factor of 0.85 and traffic growth of 4 percent per year, compounded, over 25 years. Treat the load equivalency factors as fixed for the whole period.

  1. (a) Compute the truck factor (ESALs per truck) of the single-unit truck. [3]
  2. (b) Compute the truck factor of the five-axle tractor-trailer. [4]
  3. (c) Compute the growth factor for 25 years at 4 percent. [3]
  4. (d) Compute the design-lane ESALs over 25 years. [5]
  5. (e) Overloading raises the drive tandem of every tractor-trailer to 180 kN. Find the percentage increase in design-lane ESALs. [5]
(a)

Front axle: (25/80)4 = 0.31254 = 0.00954. Rear single axle: (70/80)4 = 0.8754 = 0.5862. The truck factor is the sum, 0.5957 ESAL per truck. Almost all of the damage comes from the rear axle because the fourth-power law makes equivalency grow very fast with load: a 70 kN axle is 2.8 times heavier than the 25 kN axle but is about 61 times as damaging. A single-unit truck is therefore a light contributor compared with a loaded tractor-trailer, which part (b) quantifies.

Answer: 0.596 ESAL per truck

(b)

Steering axle: (50/80)4 = 0.6254 = 0.1526. Drive tandem: (150/150)4 = 1.000. Trailer tandem: (140/150)4 = 0.93334 = 0.7588. Sum = 0.1526 + 1.000 + 0.7588 = 1.911 ESAL per truck. This is about 3.2 times the damage of a single-unit truck, even though it has only two and a half times as many axles. Tandems share load between two axles, which is why the tandem divisor is larger. Loads near the legal limit on the tandem groups give factors close to one, so the 310 tractor-trailers per day dominate the traffic stream even though they are fewer than the single-unit trucks.

Answer: 1.911 ESAL per truck

(c)

Growth factor GF = ((1 + r)n - 1)/r with r = 0.04 and n = 25. Compute 1.0425 = 2.6658. Then GF = (2.6658 - 1)/0.04 = 1.6658/0.04 = 41.65. This factor converts the first-year ESALs into the cumulative total over 25 years, assuming traffic grows each year at the same rate. It exceeds 25 because later years carry more traffic than year one. A zero-growth stream would give a factor of 25, so the compounding adds about two thirds more to the total over the period.

Answer: 41.6

(d)

Daily ESALs in the opening year, both directions: 420 × 0.5957 = 250.2 and 310 × 1.9114 = 592.5, total 842.7. Annual: 842.7 × 365 = 307 590. Apply directional split and lane factor: 307 590 × 0.5 × 0.85 = 130 726 in the design lane in year one. Multiply by the growth factor: 130 726 × 41.646 = 5.444 million ESALs. The design lane carries the heaviest loading, so the pavement structural design should be based on this number, not the total two-way ESALs, which would be about 2.35 times larger.

Answer: 5.44 million ESALs

(e)

With a 180 kN drive tandem the group factor is (180/150)4 = 1.24 = 2.0736. The new tractor-trailer truck factor is 0.1526 + 2.0736 + 0.7588 = 2.985. Daily ESALs become 420 × 0.5957 + 310 × 2.985 = 250.2 + 925.4 = 1175.6, against 842.7 before. The ratio is 1.395, so design ESALs rise by 39.5 percent, to about 7.59 million. A 20 percent overload on one axle group lifts total damage by almost 40 percent, which is why enforcement of axle limits protects the pavement far more than the load increase alone suggests.

Answer: +39.5 %

A6 Practice Paper 18

Problem 1 [A6-086] Subgrade support, CBR and resilient modulus

A laboratory soaked CBR test on a silty clay subgrade for a municipal road in Peterborough gives a load of 1.05 kN at 2.5 mm penetration and 1.58 kN at 5.0 mm penetration. The standard loads are 13.2 kN at 2.5 mm and 20.0 kN at 5.0 mm, and the reported CBR is the larger of the two ratios. Seven soaked CBR results along the route are 6.2, 8.5, 7.1, 9.4, 5.8, 7.7 and 6.6 percent. The agency takes the design CBR as the mean minus one sample standard deviation (n - 1 divisor). The resilient modulus is estimated by MR (MPa) = 10.34 CBR. For seasonal effects, the subgrade has the design MR for 8 months a year and only 40 percent of that value for 4 months of spring thaw. Use the relative damage relation uf = 1.18 × 108 MR-2.32 with MR in psi (1 MPa = 145.04 psi) and the average damage over the year to find the effective MR.

  1. (a) Compute the CBR from the load-penetration data. [3]
  2. (b) Compute the design CBR from the seven results. [5]
  3. (c) Compute the design resilient modulus. [4]
  4. (d) Compute the seasonally effective resilient modulus. [8]
(a)

CBR at 2.5 mm = 100 × 1.05/13.2 = 7.95 percent. CBR at 5.0 mm = 100 × 1.58/20.0 = 7.90 percent. The reported CBR is the larger of the two, so CBR = 7.95 percent. The values agree closely, which is the normal pattern. If the 5.0 mm ratio were noticeably larger, the test would be repeated, because that behaviour suggests surface disturbance of the specimen. The agreement here gives confidence that the specimen was compacted evenly and the penetration piston seated properly. A value near 8 percent is typical of a firm silty clay.

Answer: CBR = 7.95 %

(b)

Mean = (6.2 + 8.5 + 7.1 + 9.4 + 5.8 + 7.7 + 6.6)/7 = 51.3/7 = 7.329. Deviations squared: 1.273, 1.372, 0.052, 4.280, 2.332, 0.138, 0.532, summing to 9.979. Variance = 9.979/6 = 1.663, so s = 1.291. Design CBR = 7.329 - 1.291 = 6.04 percent. Subtracting one standard deviation gives a design value that about 84 percent of the sampled subgrade exceeds if the data are normal, so the design is not governed by the weakest single spot. A single weak pocket like 5.8 percent should be handled separately by local subgrade improvement.

Answer: 6.04 %

(c)

MR = 10.34 × CBR = 10.34 × 6.038 = 62.4 MPa. In psi this is 62.43 × 145.04 = 9055 psi. The relation is an empirical rule of thumb, and it is only used for fine-grained soils with CBR below about 10 percent, as here. Scatter around the line is large, easily plus or minus 50 percent, so the value is a design estimate, not a measured modulus. Using the design CBR rather than the mean ensures the resilient modulus corresponds to the more conservative subgrade strength found along the route.

Answer: 62.4 MPa

(d)

Relative damage at full strength: uf1 = 1.18 × 108 × 9055-2.32 = 0.0780. In thaw, MR = 0.4 × 9055 = 3622 psi and uf2 = 1.18 × 108 × 3622-2.32 = 0.6533, which is 8.4 times larger. Average damage = (8 × 0.0780 + 4 × 0.6533)/12 = (0.624 + 2.613)/12 = 0.2697. Invert: MR,eff = (1.18 × 108 / 0.2697)1/2.32 = 5291 psi = 36.5 MPa. The four thaw months produce 81 percent of the annual damage, so the effective modulus is far below a simple time-weighted average of the two moduli, which would be about 50 MPa. Design on the effective value.

Answer: about 36.6 MPa

Problem 2 [A6-087] Rigid pavement slab thickness, joints and dowels

A concrete pavement for a 2-lane municipal truck route in Hamilton is designed with the AASHTO 1993 rigid equation, in inch-pound units: log W18 = ZR S0 + 7.35 log(D + 1) - 0.06 + log[ΔPSI/3.0]/[1 + 1.624×107/(D + 1)8.46] + (4.22 - 0.32 pt) log{ Sc' Cd (D0.75 - 1.132) / [215.63 J (D0.75 - 18.42/(Ec/k)0.25)] }, with D the slab thickness in inches, Sc' the modulus of rupture in psi, Ec in psi and k in pci. Data: W18 = 9.5×106, reliability 90 percent (ZR = -1.282), S0 = 0.35, ΔPSI = 1.7, terminal serviceability pt = 2.8, Sc' = 700 psi, Cd = 1.0, J = 3.2, Ec = 4.2×106 psi, k = 100 pci. One inch is 25.4 mm. The slab is rounded up to the next 10 mm. Joints are spaced 4.5 m apart; use joint opening ΔL = C L (α ΔT + ε) with C = 0.65, α = 10×10-6 per °C, ΔT = 35 °C and shrinkage ε = 0.00020. Dowel diameter is taken as slab thickness divided by 8. Tie bars at the longitudinal joint use steel stress fs = 200 MPa, concrete unit weight 24 kN/m³, friction factor F = 1.5 and a lane width of 3.75 m.

  1. (a) Solve for the slab thickness D in millimetres. [7]
  2. (b) Round the slab to the next 10 mm and find the dowel diameter. [4]
  3. (c) Compute the joint opening. [4]
  4. (d) Tie bars follow As = (unit weight × h × F × lane width)/fs per metre of joint. Find As. [5]
(a)

Required log W18 = log(9.5×106) = 6.978. Solve by trial for D. At D = 10.005 in: ZR S0 = -0.449; 7.35 log 11.005 = 7.656; the ΔPSI term is log(1.7/3.0) = -0.2467 divided by (1 + 1.624×107/11.0058.46 = 1.0253), giving -0.2406; the exponent (4.22 - 0.896) = 3.324. Inside the log, D0.75 = 5.626, Ec/k = 42 000, so 18.42/42 0000.25 = 1.287. The ratio is 700 × (5.626 - 1.132)/(215.63 × 3.2 × (5.626 - 1.287)) = 3146/2994 = 1.0508, log = 0.0215, times 3.324 = 0.0713. The sum -0.449 + 7.656 - 0.06 - 0.2406 + 0.0713 = 6.978, matching. D = 10.005 in = 254 mm.

Answer: about 254 mm

(b)

Round 254.1 mm up to the next 10 mm, giving h = 260 mm. Rounding up is the safe direction: a thicker slab lowers stress and raises fatigue life. The dowel diameter is h/8 = 260/8 = 32.5 mm. In practice a standard bar size, 32 mm or 35 mm, would be chosen, but the computed value is the design target. Dowels are placed at mid-depth across transverse joints at about 300 mm spacing so a wheel load is shared with the next slab. A diameter near one eighth of the thickness keeps bearing stress on the concrete around the bar within limits under repeated truck loading.

Answer: 260 mm slab, dowel 32.5 mm

(c)

ΔL = C L (α ΔT + ε) with L = 4500 mm. Thermal strain: 10×10-6 × 35 = 0.000350. Add shrinkage 0.000200 to get 0.000550. Multiply by C = 0.65: 0.0003575. Then ΔL = 4500 × 0.0003575 = 1.609 mm. The joint sealant must be able to follow about 1.6 mm of movement without failing. The factor C below one accounts for slab-base friction, which prevents the slab contracting freely. A longer spacing would give a proportionally larger opening, and sealants usually allow about 25 percent strain, so the reservoir width should be at least about 6 mm.

Answer: 1.61 mm

(d)

The weight of slab above a one-metre strip of longitudinal joint, per metre of joint, is 24 kN/m³ × 0.260 m × 3.75 m = 23.4 kN/m of lane width acting as friction-resisted load. Multiplying by F = 1.5 gives 35.1 kN per metre of joint. Convert to newtons: 35 100 N/m. Divide by fs = 200 N/mm²: As = 35 100/200 = 175.5 mm² per metre of joint. For example, 12 mm bars (113 mm²) at about 600 mm spacing would provide this. Tie bars hold adjacent lanes together; they do not carry load transfer, so they are deformed bars, not smooth dowels.

Answer: 175 mm² per metre

Problem 3 [A6-088] Concrete pavement stresses and load transfer

A jointed plain concrete pavement on a regional highway has slabs 250 mm thick on a granular base. Concrete modulus Ec = 30 000 MPa, Poisson's ratio 0.15 and modulus of rupture 4.6 MPa. The modulus of subgrade reaction is k = 0.040 N/mm³. A dual-tyre wheel load of 40 kN acts at the free edge of a slab, with a circular contact radius a = 150 mm. Use Westergaard relations in SI form: radius of relative stiffness l = [E h³ / (12 (1 - μ²) k)]0.25; equivalent radius b = √(1.6 a² + h²) - 0.675 h when a < 1.724 h; edge stress σe = 0.572 P/h² [4 log10(l/b) + 0.359]. Daily temperature curling gives a top-to-bottom difference of 18 °C, and the warping stress is σt = C E α ΔT / 2 with restraint coefficient C = 0.8 and α = 10×10-6 per °C. A falling-weight deflectometer test across a transverse joint gives 0.31 mm on the unloaded slab and 0.42 mm on the loaded slab.

  1. (a) Compute the radius of relative stiffness l. [3]
  2. (b) Compute the edge stress under the wheel load. [5]
  3. (c) Compute the curling (warping) stress. [4]
  4. (d) Compute the joint load transfer efficiency, defined as 100 times unloaded deflection over loaded deflection. [4]
  5. (e) Compute the stress ratio (σe + σt)/modulus of rupture. [4]
(a)

l = [E h³/(12 (1 - μ²) k)]0.25. Compute h³ = 250³ = 1.5625×107 mm³, so E h³ = 30 000 × 1.5625×107 = 4.6875×1011. The denominator is 12 × (1 - 0.0225) × 0.040 = 12 × 0.9775 × 0.040 = 0.4692. The ratio is 9.990×1011, and its fourth root is 999.8 mm, nearly exactly 1 m. The radius of relative stiffness measures how widely the slab spreads a load over the subgrade. A larger l means a stiffer slab or a softer support, and it spreads the load further. This value is typical for a 250 mm slab on a medium-strength base.

Answer: l = 1000 mm

(b)

Since a = 150 mm is less than 1.724 h = 431 mm, use b = √(1.6 a² + h²) - 0.675 h = √(1.6 × 22 500 + 62 500) - 168.75 = √98 500 - 168.75 = 313.85 - 168.75 = 145.1 mm. Then l/b = 999.8/145.1 = 6.890 and log10 = 0.8382. The bracket is 4 × 0.8382 + 0.359 = 3.712. The coefficient is 0.572 × 40 000/250² = 0.572 × 0.64 = 0.3661 MPa. The product gives σe = 0.3661 × 3.712 = 1.36 MPa. The edge is the critical loading position for a free joint because there is no slab on the far side to share the load.

Answer: 1.36 MPa

(c)

σt = C E α ΔT/2 = 0.8 × 30 000 × 10×10-6 × 18 / 2. The strain term is 10×10-6 × 18 = 1.8×10-4. Multiply by E: 30 000 × 1.8×10-4 = 5.4 MPa. Then × 0.8 = 4.32, and divided by 2 = 2.16 MPa. Night-time curling (cooler top) lifts the slab edges off the base, which increases tension at the bottom under an edge load; daytime curling presses the edges down and puts the bottom of the slab interior in tension. This stress adds to the load stress when the wheel is placed where the slab is already curled. The warping stress is larger than the load stress here, so temperature control through joint spacing is as important as thickness.

Answer: 2.16 MPa

(d)

LTE = 100 × unloaded deflection/loaded deflection = 100 × 0.31/0.42 = 73.8 percent. A value of 100 percent would mean the two slabs deflect equally, so the load is shared perfectly. Values above about 70 percent are generally regarded as fair to good, and more than 80 percent good. Here the joint is functioning, but dowels or tie action are not perfect. A falling LTE over time points to loss of aggregate interlock or support under the joint, which leads to faulting. Retesting every few years tracks that trend and indicates when dowel retrofit might be worthwhile.

Answer: 73.8 %

(e)

Combined tensile stress = σe + σt = 1.359 + 2.16 = 3.519 MPa. Stress ratio = 3.519/4.6 = 0.765. Fatigue life of plain concrete rises rapidly as the ratio falls: below about 0.45 the slab can carry an essentially unlimited number of repetitions, while 0.765 means the slab will consume part of its fatigue life with every repetition and eventually crack. It is a hybrid result because it adds the two stresses at the same instant, which is conservative since the maximum load stress and maximum curling stress do not always coincide.

Answer: 0.765

Problem 4 [A6-089] Pavement condition evaluation: PCI, IRI and deflection testing

A 100 m sample unit of an asphalt-surfaced arterial in London, Ontario was surveyed. Deduct values for the four distress types found are 26, 19, 12 and 7 points. The corrected deduct value (CDV) method is used: the number of deducts to consider is m = 1 + (9/98)(100 - HDV), where HDV is the highest deduct; deducts are then reduced one at a time to 2.0, starting with the smallest value above 2.0, and the CDV is read for each total. Chart readings for this unit are: q = 4 gives CDV 41; q = 3 gives CDV 42; q = 2 gives CDV 39; q = 1 gives CDV 33. PCI = 100 - maximum CDV. A roughness profile gave IRI = 3.2 m/km; use present serviceability PSI = 5 exp(-0.26 IRI). A falling-weight deflectometer with a 150 mm radius plate applies 40 kN. The centre deflection is 0.45 mm and the deflection at 900 mm radial offset is 0.10 mm. Poisson's ratio is 0.40. Surface modulus E0 = 2(1 - μ²) σ a / d0 and subgrade modulus Er = (1 - μ²) σ a² / (r dr).

  1. (a) Find the allowable number of deducts and the Pavement Condition Index. [6]
  2. (b) Compute the present serviceability index from the IRI. [4]
  3. (c) Compute the plate contact stress and the surface modulus E0. [5]
  4. (d) Compute the subgrade modulus Er from the outer sensor. [5]
(a)

HDV = 26, so m = 1 + (9/98) × (100 - 26) = 1 + 0.0918 × 74 = 7.80. The unit has only four deducts, so all four are used. The sequence of reductions is q = 4: 26, 19, 12, 7 (total 64); q = 3: 26, 19, 12, 2 (total 59); q = 2: 26, 19, 2, 2 (total 49); q = 1: 26, 2, 2, 2 (total 32). The chart CDVs given are 41, 42, 39 and 33. The maximum is 42, at q = 3, not at q = 4, which shows why every step must be checked. PCI = 100 - 42 = 58. A PCI in the 55 to 70 range usually indicates fair condition needing preventive maintenance or thin overlay.

Answer: m = 7.8 so all four used; PCI = 58

(b)

PSI = 5 exp(-0.26 × IRI) = 5 exp(-0.26 × 3.2) = 5 exp(-0.832). The exponential is 0.4352, so PSI = 2.176. On the 0 to 5 scale a value near 2.2 means the road rides poorly and sits close to the terminal serviceability of 2.0 to 2.5 that many agencies adopt for arterials. Roughness explains how a driver feels the road, while PCI explains the type and extent of distress. The two measures often disagree, so agencies track both. Here both tell a consistent story, a fairly worn surface that needs treatment soon.

Answer: PSI = 2.18

(c)

Contact stress σ = F/(π a²) = 40 000 N/(π × 150²) = 40 000/70 686 = 0.5659 MPa. Then E0 = 2 (1 - 0.40²) σ a/d0 = 2 × 0.84 × 0.5659 × 150 / 0.45. Compute 2 × 0.84 = 1.68; 1.68 × 0.5659 = 0.9507; × 150 = 142.6; divided by 0.45 gives 316.9 MPa. This composite modulus reflects the entire structure seen beneath the plate, not just the asphalt. A surface modulus of this size suggests a moderately stiff structure. Comparing it over successive tests along the road shows where the structure is weaker than the average.

Answer: E0 = 317 MPa

(d)

At 900 mm the deflection is controlled by the subgrade, so use Er = (1 - μ²) σ a²/(r dr) = 0.84 × 0.5659 × 150² / (900 × 0.10). Compute 0.84 × 0.5659 = 0.4753; × 22 500 = 10 695; divided by 90 gives 118.8 MPa. So the subgrade modulus is about 119 MPa, nearly double the 62 MPa that a 6 percent CBR would give by the 10.34 CBR rule. Back-calculated values are usually larger than laboratory values, so a correction factor of about 0.33 to 0.5 is commonly applied before using them in design.

Answer: Er = 119 MPa

Problem 5 [A6-090] Pavement management and life-cycle cost comparison

A regional road authority compares two alternatives for 1 lane-kilometre of a rural arterial over a 40-year analysis period using a real discount rate of 4 percent. Alternative A is asphalt: initial construction $520 000, resurfacing at $230 000 in years 12, 24 and 36, and routine maintenance of $6 000 per year. At year 40 the last resurfacing has 8 of its 12 years of life remaining, and salvage value is taken as that fraction of its cost. Alternative B is concrete: initial construction $890 000, diamond grinding at $150 000 in year 25, and maintenance of $2 500 per year. At year 40 salvage value is 25 percent of the initial cost. All costs are in constant dollars at year zero. Ignore user delay costs. For part (d) hold the salvage value of B at the figure found in part (b). Use present worth of a single sum P = F/(1 + i)n and of a uniform series P = A [1 - (1 + i)-n]/i. Work in thousands of dollars.

  1. (a) Compute the present worth of costs for Alternative A, in thousands of dollars. [5]
  2. (b) Compute the present worth of costs for Alternative B, in thousands of dollars. [5]
  3. (c) Convert both present worths to equivalent uniform annual cost and find how much more B costs per year than A. [4]
  4. (d) Find the initial cost of B at which the two alternatives have equal present worth. [6]
(a)

Use i = 0.04. Present-worth factors: year 12, 0.6246; year 24, 0.3901; year 36, 0.2437. Resurfacing: 230 × (0.6246 + 0.3901 + 0.2437) = 230 × 1.2584 = 289.4. Uniform series factor for 40 years: (1 - 1.04-40)/0.04 = 19.793, so maintenance is 6 × 19.793 = 118.8. Salvage: 230 × 8/12 = 153.3 at year 40, and 1.04-40 = 0.2083, so the credit is 31.9. Total = 520 + 289.4 + 118.8 - 31.9 = 896.2 thousand dollars. Salvage is subtracted because it is residual value the authority keeps at the end of the analysis period.

Answer: $896.2 thousand

(b)

Grinding at year 25: factor 1.04-25 = 0.3751, so 150 × 0.3751 = 56.3. Maintenance: 2.5 × 19.793 = 49.5. Salvage: 25 percent of 890 = 222.5 at year 40, discounted by 0.2083 gives 46.3. Present worth = 890 + 56.3 + 49.5 - 46.3 = 949.4 thousand dollars. Alternative B has the higher initial cost by $370 000 but needs far fewer later interventions, and these later costs are heavily discounted, so the early money dominates. That is why the present-worth gap remains in favour of A despite B's lower maintenance and long life.

Answer: $949.4 thousand

(c)

The capital recovery factor for 40 years at 4 percent is 0.04/(1 - 1.04-40) = 0.05052. EUAC for A = 896.25 × 0.05052 = 45.28 thousand per year. EUAC for B = 949.4 × 0.05052 = 47.97 thousand per year. The difference is 47.97 - 45.28 = 2.69 thousand dollars per year, so B costs about $2 690 more each year per lane-kilometre. The annual form is helpful when the authority budgets yearly. It also shows that the gap is small, about 6 percent of the annual cost, so a modest change in assumptions could reverse the ranking.

Answer: B costs $2.69 thousand per year more

(d)

Let C be the initial cost of B. Everything else in B is fixed: grinding 56.3 + maintenance 49.5 - salvage. The salvage depends on C, because it is 25 percent of C, but in part (b) it was based on 890. As stated in the problem, the salvage credit is held at 46.3, so the non-initial part of B is 56.3 + 49.5 - 46.3 = 59.5. Setting present worth equal to A: C + 59.5 = 896.2, giving C = 836.8 thousand dollars. Concrete would need to be about 6 percent cheaper to break even. A cost reduction of $53 000 per lane-km is plausible if competitive tendering lowers unit prices.

Answer: $836.8 thousand

A6 Practice Paper 19

Problem 1 [A6-091] Maintenance and rehabilitation: overlay design and treatment selection

Wilson Road is a two-lane Ontario regional road that carries heavy aggregate trucks. Pavement cores show 130 mm of cracked asphalt over 250 mm of granular base and 300 mm of granular subbase. Use these structural layer coefficients per millimetre of thickness: cracked asphalt 0.0080, granular base 0.0045, granular subbase 0.0035, all with drainage coefficient 1.0. New asphalt has a coefficient of 0.0110 per millimetre. For the next 20 years the pavement needs a future structural number SNf = 4.10, which already includes the reliability, serviceability loss and subgrade modulus. The overlay thickness is D = (SNf minus SNeff) divided by the overlay coefficient, where SNeff is the sum of coefficient times thickness for the existing layers. Option A is a direct overlay. Option B mills off 40 mm of the cracked asphalt and then overlays. Overlay asphalt costs $0.19 per m² per millimetre and milling costs $3.50 per m². Existing curb reveals limit the net rise of the finished surface to 70 mm.

  1. (a) Calculate the effective structural number SNeff of the existing pavement. [4]
  2. (b) Find the overlay thickness required for Option A. [4]
  3. (c) Find the overlay thickness required for Option B, after milling. [4]
  4. (d) Find the net rise of the surface for Option B, and state which option satisfies the 70 mm curb limit. [4]
  5. (e) Find the cost difference per m² (Option B minus Option A) and recommend an option. [4]
(a)

The effective structural number is the sum of layer coefficient times thickness, with drainage coefficients of 1.0 so they do not change the result. Cracked asphalt: 0.0080 × 130 = 1.040. Granular base: 0.0045 × 250 = 1.125. Granular subbase: 0.0035 × 300 = 1.050. Adding the three contributions gives SNeff = 1.040 + 1.125 + 1.050 = 3.215. The cracked asphalt carries a reduced coefficient (0.0080 against 0.0110 for new mix) because cracking has already cost it part of its strength, so the existing structure supplies only about 78 percent of the 4.10 needed for the next 20 years. The shortfall is what the overlay must make up.

Answer: SNeff = 3.215

(b)

The overlay must supply the structural shortfall: SNf minus SNeff = 4.10 minus 3.215 = 0.885. Dividing by the new asphalt coefficient of 0.0110 per millimetre gives D = 0.885 / 0.0110 = 80.45 mm. In practice the designer rounds up to a placeable lift, so 85 mm or two 40 mm lifts would be specified, but the computed minimum is 80.5 mm. Because the overlay sits directly on the existing cracked surface, the design assumes the existing layers keep contributing 3.215 and that reflective cracking is controlled by the mix design or a stress-absorbing layer. The 80.5 mm is also the net rise of the road surface for this option, which matters in part (d).

Answer: 80.5 mm

(c)

Milling removes 40 mm of cracked asphalt, so the remaining asphalt is 90 mm. The reduced effective number is SNeff = 0.0080 × 90 + 1.125 + 1.050 = 0.720 + 2.175 = 2.895. The shortfall is now 4.10 minus 2.895 = 1.205. The required overlay is D = 1.205 / 0.0110 = 109.5 mm. This is thicker than Option A by 29 mm because the milled material was worth 40 × 0.0080 = 0.320 of structural number, whereas the thicker new asphalt replaces it at 0.0110 per millimetre. Milling therefore does not save structural thickness; it only changes the finished grade, which is the reason for choosing it.

Answer: 109.5 mm

(d)

The finished surface for Option B ends higher than the original surface by the new overlay thickness less the milled depth: 109.5 minus 40 = 69.5 mm. This is just inside the 70 mm curb reveal limit, so Option B is acceptable. Option A raises the surface by the full 80.5 mm, which exceeds 70 mm by 10.5 mm and would reduce the curb reveal below the allowed value, creating drainage and snowplough problems at the gutter. Only Option B therefore satisfies the geometric constraint. The margin is thin (0.5 mm), so the contract should control milling depth and overlay tolerance tightly, and a thickness measurement should be taken after milling before paving begins.

Answer: 69.5 mm; Option B passes, Option A fails

(e)

Option A costs 80.45 mm × $0.19 = $15.29 per m². Option B costs the milling at $3.50 plus the overlay at 109.55 mm × $0.19 = $20.81, for a total of $24.31 per m². The difference is 24.31 minus 15.29 = $9.03 per m² in favour of Option A on cost alone. However Option A breaks the curb reveal limit, so it is not a feasible choice unless the curbs are rebuilt. Recommend Option B if the curbs stay, and Option A only if curb replacement costs less than about $9 per m² of road surface. A fair answer states the cost premium and ties the decision to the geometric constraint rather than to price alone.

Answer: $9.03 per m² more for Option B; choose B to meet the curb limit

Problem 2 [A6-092] Frost, drainage and economic comparison of pavement alternatives

A new 6 km arterial near Sudbury is being designed over a silty subgrade. Local records give a surface freezing index of 1250 degree-days (°C·days). Use Stefan's equation X = √(2 k n F / L), where k = 1.8 W/(m·K) is the frozen soil conductivity, n = 0.85 converts air to surface freezing index, F is in °C·s, and L is the volumetric latent heat. The soil has dry density 1850 kg/m³, moisture content 11 percent by mass and latent heat of fusion of water 334 kJ/kg. Partial frost protection is chosen: the pavement structure plus non-frost-susceptible granular material must total 65 percent of the frost depth. The proposed pavement structure is 0.55 m thick. Two alternatives are compared per lane-kilometre over 30 years at a 4 percent discount rate. Alternative A: $1.20 M initial, $0.35 M overlays at years 14 and 28, $9000 per year maintenance, $0.15 M salvage at year 30. Alternative B: $1.55 M initial, $0.30 M rehabilitation at year 25, $6000 per year maintenance, $0.40 M salvage.

  1. (a) Calculate the frost penetration depth by Stefan's equation. [5]
  2. (b) Find the additional thickness of non-frost-susceptible granular material needed beyond the 0.55 m structure. [4]
  3. (c) Calculate the present worth of cost of Alternative A per lane-kilometre. [4]
  4. (d) Calculate the present worth of cost of Alternative B per lane-kilometre. [4]
  5. (e) State the present worth difference (A minus B) and which alternative is economical. [3]
(a)

First find the latent heat per unit volume of soil: L = w × γd × 334 000 J/kg = 0.11 × 1850 × 334 000 = 6.797 × 10⁷ J/m³. The freezing index in SI is F = 1250 °C·days × 86 400 s/day = 1.08 × 10⁸ °C·s. Stefan's equation then gives X = √(2 × 1.8 × 0.85 × 1.08 × 10⁸ / 6.797 × 10⁷) = √(4.863) = 2.205 m. The n-factor of 0.85 reduces the air freezing index to the pavement surface value because asphalt surfaces are cleared of snow and absorb heat. The result is a theoretical maximum, since Stefan's equation neglects the sensible heat in the soil, which slightly lowers real depths, and it assumes a uniform soil.

Answer: X = 2.21 m

(b)

Partial protection requires the total protected thickness to be 0.65 × 2.205 = 1.433 m. The pavement structure already contributes 0.55 m, so the extra non-frost-susceptible material is 1.433 minus 0.55 = 0.883 m. This material is placed under the subbase as a free-draining sand or crushed layer with a low fines content so that ice lenses cannot grow in it. The remaining 35 percent of the frost depth (0.77 m) penetrates the subgrade, and the design accepts some heave and thaw weakening there; spring load restrictions on the road remain necessary. Full protection would need 2.205 minus 0.55 = 1.655 m, nearly double the extra thickness.

Answer: 0.88 m

(c)

Convert each future amount to present worth with P = F / (1 + i)ⁿ at i = 0.04. The overlays are 0.35 / 1.04¹⁴ = 0.2021 M and 0.35 / 1.04²⁸ = 0.1166 M. The annual maintenance is a uniform series: 9000 × [(1.04³⁰ minus 1) / (0.04 × 1.04³⁰)] = 9000 × 17.292 = 0.1556 M. The salvage value is a credit: 0.15 / 1.04³⁰ = 0.0462 M. Summing, PW(A) = 1.20 + 0.2021 + 0.1166 + 0.1556 minus 0.0462 = 1.628 M. The overlays at years 14 and 28 carry the same dollar amount but their present worths differ because later money is discounted more heavily.

Answer: PW(A) = $1.628 M

(d)

Alternative B has a single rehabilitation at year 25: 0.30 / 1.04²⁵ = 0.30 / 2.6658 = 0.1125 M. Maintenance is 6000 × 17.292 = 0.1038 M. The salvage credit is 0.40 / 1.04³⁰ = 0.40 / 3.2434 = 0.1233 M. Adding the initial cost of 1.55 M: PW(B) = 1.55 + 0.1125 + 0.1038 minus 0.1233 = 1.643 M. The large salvage value at year 30 reflects the thicker, more durable structure still in service, and it offsets part of the higher initial cost. The uniform series factor 17.292 is the same as in part (c) because the discount rate and the 30-year period are the same.

Answer: PW(B) = $1.643 M

(e)

The difference is PW(A) minus PW(B) = 1.628 minus 1.643 = minus 0.0147 M, so Alternative A is cheaper by roughly $14,700 per lane-kilometre, or less than 1 percent of the total. A difference that small lies well within the uncertainty of the cost estimates, so economy alone should not decide. Test sensitivity: at a 3 percent discount rate the later salvage and rehabilitation in B are worth more and B likely becomes cheaper. A sound recommendation selects B if the agency values lower maintenance and fewer work-zone disruptions, and A if capital is constrained. State the PW result with this caveat.

Answer: A is cheaper by about $14,700; effectively a tie

Problem 3 [A6-093] Route surveying and horizontal curve layout by deflection angles

A rural highway realignment near Kenora uses chainage in metres. The two tangents intersect at the PI at chainage 4+215.60 with a deflection angle Δ = 38°20′. Option 1 is a simple circular curve of radius 450 m. Option 2 is a flatter curve of radius 600 m through the same PI. A bridge abutment begins at chainage 4+400, and the owner will not accept any part of the curve on the structure, so the PT must fall at or before 4+400. Layout is by deflection angles from the transit at the PC, with the line of sight along the back tangent. Use arc length equal to chord length for the layout and the relation deflection angle = (arc length / R) × (90°/π).

  1. (a) For Option 1, compute the tangent length T and the curve length L. [4]
  2. (b) For Option 1, find the PC chainage in metres (give the chainage as a single number of metres). [4]
  3. (c) For Option 1, find the deflection angle from the PC to chainage 4+200. [4]
  4. (d) For Option 2, find the PT chainage in metres. [4]
  5. (e) State by how many metres Option 2 breaks the 4+400 limit and whether Option 1 complies. [4]
(a)

Convert the deflection angle to decimal degrees: 38°20′ = 38.3333°, and in radians Δ = 0.66905. The tangent length is T = R tan(Δ/2) = 450 × tan(19.1667°) = 450 × 0.34758 = 156.41 m. The curve length is the arc subtended by the full deflection: L = R Δ = 450 × 0.66905 = 301.07 m. These two quantities govern layout: T locates the PC and PT back and ahead of the PI along the tangents, and L locates the PT along the curve. A quick check on the geometry is that L must be less than 2T = 312.8 m, which holds for any simple curve, and here L is 301.07 m.

Answer: T = 156.41 m; L = 301.07 m

(b)

The PC lies one tangent length before the PI along the back tangent, so the PC chainage is 4215.60 minus 156.41 = 4059.19 m, written 4+059.19. The PT chainage is the PC chainage plus the curve length: 4059.19 + 301.07 = 4360.26 m, written 4+360.26. Note that the PT chainage is not PI plus T, because chainage is measured along the route and the curve is shorter than the sum of the two tangents. For Option 1 the PT is 39.74 m before the abutment at 4+400. These chainages are the starting information for the field crew who set up the instrument over the PC.

Answer: PC = 4+059.19; PT = 4+360.26

(c)

The arc length from the PC to chainage 4+200 is 4200.00 minus 4059.19 = 140.81 m. The deflection angle at the PC is half the central angle subtended by that arc: δ = (140.81 / 450) × (90°/π) = 0.31291 × 28.6479 = 8.964°, which is 8°57.9′. The same value comes from δ = (central angle)/2 where the central angle is 140.81/450 rad = 17.93°. As a check, the deflection to the PT must equal Δ/2 = 19.17°, and (301.07/450) × 28.6479 = 19.17°, so the formula is consistent. The instrument is set to 8°58′ and the tape or total station distance is measured from the PC.

Answer: 8.96° (8°57.9′)

(d)

For R = 600 m the tangent length is T = 600 × tan(19.1667°) = 208.55 m, and the curve length is L = 600 × 0.66905 = 401.43 m. The PC chainage is 4215.60 minus 208.55 = 4007.05 m. The PT is then 4007.05 + 401.43 = 4408.47 m, written 4+408.47. The larger radius pushes the PC back by 52 m but lengthens the curve by 100 m, so the PT moves forward by about 48 m relative to Option 1. This is the reason a flatter curve is not always compatible with a fixed structure location downstream of the PI.

Answer: PT = 4+408.47

(e)

The owner requires the PT at or before 4+400. Option 2 gives 4408.47 minus 4400 = 8.47 m on the structure, so it violates the condition. Option 1 ends at 4+360.26, which is 39.74 m clear, so it complies. A judgement-based recommendation is to adopt Option 1 at R = 450 m. If the design speed demands a flatter curve, a radius of about 574 m would put the PT at the limit, since PT = PI + R(Δ minus tan(Δ/2)) changes by 0.3215 m for each metre of radius: 8.47 / 0.3215 = 26 m less radius gives about R = 574 m. State that the choice should be checked against the superelevation and stopping sight distance criteria of the design speed.

Answer: Option 2 exceeds by 8.47 m; Option 1 complies

Problem 4 [A6-094] Horizontal curve design: radius, superelevation and side friction

A rural two-lane highway in northern Ontario has a design speed of 100 km/h. The agency's maximum superelevation is e = 0.06 and the maximum allowable side friction factor at this speed is f = 0.12. Use the point-mass relation e + f = V² / (127 R), with V in km/h and R in metres. An existing curve of radius 380 m on this road has been superelevated at the maximum 0.06 and has had several run-off-road crashes in wet weather. The district proposes either to post an advisory speed on the existing curve or to rebuild it at a radius of 600 m, in which case the designer wants to keep the side friction demand at no more than 0.08 for driver comfort. The pavement is two lanes, 3.6 m each, and is rotated about the centreline of the road.

  1. (a) Find the minimum radius permitted for the 100 km/h design speed. [4]
  2. (b) Find the side friction demanded on the existing 380 m curve at 100 km/h with e = 0.06. [4]
  3. (c) Find the highest speed the existing curve supports when e = 0.06 and f = 0.12. [4]
  4. (d) Find the superelevation needed for the 600 m curve at 100 km/h with f = 0.08. [4]
  5. (e) Find how much the outside edge of pavement is raised above the centreline in the 600 m curve. [4]
(a)

Rearranging the point-mass relation gives R = V² / [127 (e + f)]. With V = 100 km/h, e = 0.06 and f = 0.12, R = 10 000 / (127 × 0.18) = 10 000 / 22.86 = 437.4 m. This is the smallest radius at which the vehicle can negotiate the curve at 100 km/h without exceeding either limit; both e and f are used at their maxima. Designers normally choose a radius larger than the minimum, because a curve at Rmin uses all the margin the agency provides and leaves nothing for wet or icy surfaces. The existing curve of 380 m is therefore below the minimum for this design speed, which is the first hint of the crash history.

Answer: Rmin = 437 m

(b)

Solve the same relation for the friction demand: f = V² / (127 R) minus e. For R = 380 m, V² / (127 R) = 10 000 / (127 × 380) = 10 000 / 48 260 = 0.2072. Subtracting the superelevation of 0.06 leaves f = 0.1472. The demand of 0.147 exceeds the allowable 0.12 by about 23 percent, and on a wet or snow-covered road the available friction can fall below 0.15, so a vehicle at design speed would be at or beyond the limit of tyre grip. This explains the run-off-road crashes in wet weather and confirms that the curve is sub-standard for 100 km/h.

Answer: f = 0.147 (exceeds 0.12)

(c)

With the superelevation and friction capped at 0.06 and 0.12, the highest speed on a 380 m curve follows from V = √[127 R (e + f)] = √(127 × 380 × 0.18) = √8686.8 = 93.2 km/h. An advisory speed sign would normally be rounded down to a posted multiple of 5 km/h, so 90 km/h. The 7 km/h reduction from the design speed is modest, but drivers often ignore advisory signs, so the sign alone is not a full remedy. It does however provide a lower-cost interim measure while the curve is rebuilt, and it gives a defensible basis for a warning sign and chevrons.

Answer: V = 93.2 km/h (post 90 km/h)

(d)

For a 600 m curve at 100 km/h, V² / (127 R) = 10 000 / (127 × 600) = 10 000 / 76 200 = 0.1312. With the designer limiting side friction to 0.08, the superelevation must supply the rest: e = 0.1312 minus 0.08 = 0.0512, about 5.1 percent. That is below the agency maximum of 0.06, so it is allowed. If the friction limit were relaxed to 0.12, e would fall to 0.011, and the curve would be nearly flat; this shows why designers tend to put more of the lateral demand into superelevation and keep friction small, which leaves a reserve for wet pavement.

Answer: e = 0.0512

(e)

Rotating about the centreline, the outside edge is raised by the superelevation times the distance from the centreline to the edge. The half width is 3.6 m (one lane each side), so the rise is 0.0512 × 3.6 = 0.184 m, or 184 mm. The inside edge drops by the same amount, so the total cross fall across the 7.2 m pavement is 0.0512 × 7.2 = 0.369 m. This rotation is built in over the superelevation runoff length, and the designer must check that the 0.18 m of rise does not create a problem with shoulder breakpoints or roadside drainage on the inside of the curve.

Answer: 0.184 m

Problem 5 [A6-095] Spiral transition curves

A freeway interchange ramp in Ottawa is being realigned with a design speed of 90 km/h, a central circular curve of radius 350 m and a total deflection angle between tangents Δ = 52°. A symmetrical spiral is to be inserted at each end of the circular curve. Use the minimum spiral length Ls = V³ / (46.66 R C), with V in km/h, R in metres and C = 0.8 m/s³ as the allowable rate of change of lateral acceleration. The designer adopts a spiral length of 60 m, a convenient multiple of the layout station interval. For the adopted spiral use the standard approximations: spiral angle θs = Ls / (2R) in radians, shift p = Ls² / (24 R), tangent offset k = Ls/2 minus Ls³ / (240 R²), spiral tangent Ts = (R + p) tan(Δ/2) + k, and total length = R (Δ minus 2θs) + 2 Ls with Δ in radians.

  1. (a) Compute the minimum spiral length from the comfort criterion. [4]
  2. (b) For the adopted 60 m spiral, find the spiral angle in degrees. [4]
  3. (c) Find the shift p of the circular curve. [4]
  4. (d) Find the spiral tangent length Ts from the PI to the TS. [4]
  5. (e) Find the total length of the transition-curve-transition alignment. [4]
(a)

Apply the comfort formula directly. V³ = 90³ = 729 000. The denominator is 46.66 × R × C = 46.66 × 350 × 0.8 = 13 064.8. Therefore Ls = 729 000 / 13 064.8 = 55.8 m. The formula comes from requiring the lateral acceleration V²/R to build up at the constant rate C while the vehicle travels the spiral at speed V; converting V to m/s gives the coefficient 46.66. A spiral shorter than 55.8 m would give an abrupt build-up of lateral acceleration, above 0.8 m/s³, and the driver would feel a jerk when entering the curve. The adopted 60 m exceeds this minimum, so it meets the criterion.

Answer: Ls,min = 55.8 m

(b)

The spiral angle is the angle between the tangent at the TS and the tangent at the SC. θs = Ls / (2R) = 60 / (2 × 350) = 0.085714 rad. Converting to degrees: 0.085714 × 180/π = 4.911°, about 4°54.7′. This angle is used to set out the spiral by deflection angles and to find the central angle left for the circular portion, which is Δ minus 2θs = 52° minus 9.82° = 42.18°. A small θs like this one means the spiral is gentle; the angle grows in direct proportion to the spiral length and falls with the inverse of the radius, so a long spiral on a large radius still gives a small angle.

Answer: θs = 4.91°

(c)

The shift p is the distance the circular curve is moved inward from the original tangent so that the spiral can be inserted. p = Ls² / (24 R) = 60² / (24 × 350) = 3600 / 8400 = 0.4286 m. This is small, only 43 cm, which is typical of spirals designed from the comfort criterion on a large radius. The shift matters in layout because the PC of the original simple curve is no longer on the ground; the circular arc now begins at the SC and is displaced inward by p from its original position. On a narrow right of way this displacement should be checked against the clear zone and the shoulder.

Answer: p = 0.429 m

(d)

First find the tangent offset k = Ls/2 minus Ls³ / (240 R²) = 30 minus 216 000 / (240 × 122 500) = 30 minus 216 000 / 29 400 000 = 30 minus 0.00735 = 29.9927 m. Then Ts = (R + p) tan(Δ/2) + k = (350 + 0.4286) × tan 26° + 29.9927. tan 26° = 0.48773, so (350.4286)(0.48773) = 170.914 m. Adding k gives Ts = 170.914 + 29.993 = 200.91 m. This is the distance from the PI back along the tangent to the TS, where the transition begins. It is longer than the tangent of the simple 350 m curve alone (170.7 m) by 30 m, which is almost half of Ls.

Answer: Ts = 200.9 m

(e)

The circular arc covers the central angle left after the two spirals: Δ minus 2θs = 52° minus 9.822° = 42.178° = 0.73616 rad. Its length is 350 × 0.73616 = 257.66 m. Adding the two 60 m spirals gives a total of 257.66 + 120 = 377.66 m, in agreement with the formula result. The simple curve alone would have been 350 × 0.9076 = 317.7 m, so the spirals add about 60 m of alignment. Because the TS to ST length is known, the chainage of the ST is the TS chainage plus 377.6 m. A sound check is that the spiral-curve-spiral length must be greater than the simple curve length.

Answer: L = 377.6 m

A6 Practice Paper 20

Problem 1 [A6-096] Stopping and decision sight distance

A rural highway through the Muskoka rock cut has a design speed of 90 km/h. Stopping sight distance is SSD = 0.278 V t + V² / [254 (a/9.81 + G)], where V is in km/h, t = 2.5 s is the perception-reaction time, a = 3.4 m/s² is the deceleration rate used for design, and G is the grade as a decimal (positive uphill, negative downhill). At one location the roadway descends at 5 percent for a long distance. For decision sight distance at a complex decision point, use d = 0.278 V t with a total pre-manoeuvre and manoeuvre time t = 11.2 s, appropriate for a speed, path or direction change on a rural road. A sight-distance survey shows that only 150 m of roadway is visible ahead at the downgrade location because of the rock face on the inside of a curve.

  1. (a) Calculate the stopping sight distance on level grade at 90 km/h. [4]
  2. (b) Calculate the stopping sight distance on the 5 percent downgrade at 90 km/h. [4]
  3. (c) Calculate the decision sight distance for the complex manoeuvre. [4]
  4. (d) Find the highest speed for which the 150 m of visible roadway is adequate on the downgrade. [4]
  5. (e) State the shortfall in sight distance at 90 km/h on the downgrade. [4]
(a)

The reaction distance is 0.278 × 90 × 2.5 = 62.55 m, the distance travelled before the driver applies the brakes. The braking distance on level grade is V² / [254 (a/9.81)] = 8100 / [254 × 0.3466] = 8100 / 88.04 = 92.0 m. The sum is SSD = 62.55 + 92.0 = 154.6 m. The reaction portion is 40 percent of the total at this speed. It is a function of speed alone, whereas the braking part depends on the deceleration, which is why the deceleration of 3.4 m/s² (about 0.35 g) is chosen as a value comfortable for most drivers and achievable on wet pavement.

Answer: SSD = 154.6 m

(b)

On a downgrade of 5 percent, G = minus 0.05, so the denominator becomes 254 × (0.3466 minus 0.05) = 254 × 0.2966 = 75.34. The braking distance is 8100 / 75.34 = 107.5 m. Adding the unchanged reaction distance of 62.55 m gives SSD = 170.1 m. The downgrade increases the stopping distance by 15.5 m, or 10 percent, over the level case because gravity helps the vehicle keep moving. A designer who tabulates SSD for level grade only will undersize the sight line at this location; the grade correction should be applied wherever grades exceed about 3 percent.

Answer: SSD = 170.1 m

(c)

Decision sight distance is based on a longer time, because the driver must detect an unexpected or hard-to-perceive condition, decide, and then manoeuvre. With t = 11.2 s, d = 0.278 × 90 × 11.2 = 280.2 m. This is 1.8 times the level SSD of 154.6 m. Decision sight distance is recommended at lane drops, interchange gores and toll plazas, where a stop is not the expected response. The formula has no braking term because the driver is steering or changing speed rather than braking to a halt. The value of 280 m is a long distance in a rock cut, so the designer must check which features need it.

Answer: DSD = 280.2 m

(d)

Set the SSD on the downgrade equal to the available 150 m and solve for V. Write 0.278 × 2.5 × V + V² / (254 × 0.2966) = 150, which is 0.695 V + V² / 75.34 = 150. Multiply by 75.34: V² + 52.36 V minus 11 301 = 0. The quadratic formula gives V = [minus 52.36 + √(52.36² + 4 × 11 301)] / 2 = [minus 52.36 + √(2741.6 + 45 204)] / 2 = [minus 52.36 + 218.97] / 2 = 83.3 km/h. A sign of 80 km/h would be a normal posted value, and it gives a small margin. The result shows that the visible sight line supports a speed 6.7 km/h below the design speed.

Answer: V = 83.3 km/h (post 80 km/h)

(e)

At the design speed of 90 km/h the required stopping sight distance on the downgrade is 170.07 m, but only 150 m is visible. The shortfall is 170.07 minus 150 = 20.07 m, about 12 percent of the requirement. A shortfall of this size can be corrected by widening the inside shoulder or cutting back the rock face to increase the lateral clearance to the sight line. The required offset can be estimated from the curve geometry, but it is simpler to compare the cost of the cut to the cost of the safety reduction through an advisory speed. Where the cost of rock removal is high, the agency may prefer to post 80 km/h and warn drivers.

Answer: Shortfall = 20.1 m

Problem 2 [A6-097] Crest and sag vertical curves and K values

A two-lane highway near Peterborough has a design speed of 100 km/h, for which the required stopping sight distance is S = 185 m. A crest curve joins a +3.2 percent grade to a minus 2.4 percent grade. The driver eye height is 1.05 m and the object height for stopping is 0.15 m. For a crest curve longer than S, use L = A S² / [200 (√h1 + √h2)²], where A is the algebraic grade difference in percent. The curve's PVC is at station 3+250 (metres) at elevation 212.40 m. The agency also controls a sag curve nearby, where A = 4.5 percent, with headlights 0.60 m above the road and a beam upward divergence of 1 degree; for a sag curve longer than S use L = A S² / [200 (0.60 + S tan 1°)]. Take stations in metres along the road.

  1. (a) Find the rate of vertical curvature K = L/A for the crest curve. [4]
  2. (b) Find the length of the crest curve and confirm that L exceeds S. [4]
  3. (c) Find the station of the high point on the crest curve, in metres. [4]
  4. (d) Find the elevation of the high point. [4]
  5. (e) Find the minimum length of the sag curve for headlight sight distance. [4]
(a)

The grade difference is A = 3.2 minus (minus 2.4) = 5.6 percent. Rearranging the length formula for K = L/A gives K = S² / [200 (√h1 + √h2)²]. The square roots are √1.05 = 1.0247 and √0.15 = 0.3873, which sum to 1.4120; squared, that is 1.9937. The denominator is 200 × 1.9937 = 398.7. Then K = 185² / 398.7 = 34 225 / 398.7 = 85.8 m per percent of grade change. K is a design control that depends only on the speed and the eye and object heights, so a table of K values can be reused for any grade difference. A larger K means a flatter crest.

Answer: K = 85.8 m/%

(b)

The length is L = K A = 85.83 × 5.6 = 480.7 m. The formula assumed that the curve is longer than the sight distance (S less than L), so verify: 185 m is less than 480.7 m, which confirms the assumption and the use of this form of the equation. If L had come out smaller than S, the other form L = 2S minus 398.7 / A would have applied. A curve of 481 m is long, roughly 2.6 times S, because the grade change is large and the stopping sight distance is large for 100 km/h. Rounding up to 500 m would be common practice and would give K = 89.3, above the minimum.

Answer: L = 480.7 m; L is greater than S = 185 m

(c)

For a parabolic curve with the PVC at the origin, the grade at distance x is g1 plus (g2 minus g1) x / L. The high point occurs where the grade is zero: x = g1 L / (g1 minus g2) = 3.2 × 480.66 / 5.6 = 274.66 m from the PVC. The high point station is therefore 3250 + 274.66 = 3524.66 m, written 3+524.7. This lies 205.99 m before the PVT at 3+730.66, so it falls in the first part of the curve, as expected since the leading grade is steeper than the trailing grade. The high point is the location of the minimum drainage grade, which must be checked for ponding or drainage inlet placement.

Answer: Station 3+524.7

(d)

The elevation along a parabolic vertical curve is y = y0 + g1 x + (g2 minus g1) x² / (2L), with grades in decimals. At x = 274.66 m, g1 x = 0.032 × 274.66 = 8.789 m. The quadratic term is (minus 0.056) × 274.66² / (2 × 480.66) = minus 0.056 × 75 438 / 961.3 = minus 4.395 m. Therefore y = 212.40 + 8.789 minus 4.395 = 216.79 m.
